topic: Cardiology — ACS, heart failure, arrhythmias, valvular disease

cards.q: Most common cause of ACS?
cards.a: Rupture of an unstable atherosclerotic plaque with subsequent thrombus formation.

cards.q: Definition of Unstable Angina (UA)?
cards.a: Ischemic symptoms at rest, new-onset severe angina, or increasing intensity/frequency without cardiac biomarker elevation.

cards.q: Difference between NSTEMI and STEMI on EKG?
cards.a: NSTEMI shows ST-depression or T-wave inversion; STEMI shows ST-segment elevation or new LBBB.

cards.q: Gold standard biomarker for myocardial necrosis?
cards.a: Cardiac Troponin I or T.

cards.q: Timeframe for Troponin elevation after MI?
cards.a: Elevates in 3–12 hours, peaks at 24 hours, stays elevated for 5–14 days.

cards.q: Primary goal for "Door-to-Balloon" time in STEMI?
cards.a: Less than 90 minutes.

cards.q: Indication for Fibrinolytics in STEMI?
cards.a: PCI unavailable within 120 minutes of medical contact.

cards.q: Absolute contraindication for Fibrinolytics?
cards.a: Prior intracranial hemorrhage, active internal bleeding, or ischemic stroke within 3 months.

cards.q: Standard "MONA" therapy for ACS?
cards.a: Morphine, Oxygen (if <90%), Nitroglycerin, Aspirin.

cards.q: Role of Beta-blockers in ACS?
cards.a: Reduce myocardial oxygen demand by decreasing heart rate and contractility.

cards.q: Contraindications for Nitroglycerin in ACS?
cards.a: Right ventricular infarction, hypotension, or recent PDE-5 inhibitor use (e.g., Sildenafil).

cards.q: Post-MI complication occurring 2–7 days later with a new holosystolic murmur?
cards.a: Ventricular septal rupture or Papillary muscle rupture.

cards.q: Clinical sign of Right Ventricular (RV) Infarction?
cards.a: Hypotension, clear lungs, and JVD (Kussmaul’s sign).

cards.q: Treatment for RV Infarction?
cards.a: Aggressive IV fluid resuscitation; avoid nitrates.

cards.q: Definition of Dressler Syndrome?
cards.a: Post-MI autoimmune pericarditis occurring 2–10 weeks after the event.

cards.q: First-line long-term antiplatelet therapy post-ACS?
cards.a: Dual Antiplatelet Therapy (DAPT) with Aspirin and a P2Y12 inhibitor (e.g., Clopidogrel, Ticagrelor).

cards.q: Primary distinction between HFrEF and HFpEF?
cards.a: HFrEF (Systolic) has LVEF ≤40%; HFpEF (Diastolic) has LVEF ≥50%.

cards.q: Most common cause of Left-sided Heart Failure?
cards.a: Ischemic heart disease and Hypertension.

cards.q: Most common cause of Right-sided Heart Failure?
cards.a: Left-sided heart failure.

cards.q: Key physical exam finding for Left HF?
cards.a: Pulmonary rales, S3 gallop, and displaced apical impulse.

cards.q: Key physical exam finding for Right HF?
cards.a: Jugular Venous Distention (JVD), hepatomegaly, and peripheral edema.

cards.q: Meaning of a Positive Hepatojugular Reflux?
cards.a: Suggests elevated pulmonary artery wedge pressure (Left heart congestion).

cards.q: Diagnostic utility of B-type Natriuretic Peptide (BNP)?
cards.a: High sensitivity to rule out HF in patients with acute dyspnea.

cards.q: Four pillars of Guideline-Directed Medical Therapy (GDMT) for HFrEF?
cards.a: ARNI (or ACEi/ARB), Beta-blocker, MRA (Spironolactone), and SGLT2 inhibitor.

cards.q: Which Beta-blockers are proven to reduce mortality in HFrEF?
cards.a: Carvedilol, Metoprolol succinate, and Bisoprolol.

cards.q: Indication for Spironolactone in HF?
cards.a: NYHA Class II-IV with LVEF ≤35%.

cards.q: Common side effect of ACE inhibitors?
cards.a: Cough and angioedema due to increased bradykinin.

cards.q: Mechanism of Sacubitril (in ARNI)?
cards.a: Neprilysin inhibitor that prevents breakdown of natriuretic peptides.

cards.q: Digoxin’s role in HF management?
cards.a: Symptom control and reduction of hospitalizations; does not improve mortality.

cards.q: Sign of Digoxin toxicity on EKG?
cards.a: Downsloping ST-segment depression ("Salvador Dali mustache") and arrhythmias.

cards.q: Criteria for Cardiac Resynchronization Therapy (CRT)?
cards.a: LVEF ≤35%, NYHA II-IV, and QRS duration ≥150ms with LBBB morphology.

cards.q: CXR findings in Acute Decompensated HF?
cards.a: Cephalization of vessels, Kerley B lines, pleural effusions, and cardiomegaly.

cards.q: Most common chronic arrhythmia?
cards.a: Atrial Fibrillation (AFib).

cards.q: EKG characteristics of AFib?
cards.a: Irregularly irregular rhythm with absent P-waves.

cards.q: Scoring system used to assess stroke risk in AFib?
cards.a: CHA2DS2-VASc score.

cards.q: Treatment for hemodynamically unstable AFib?
cards.a: Immediate synchronized electrical cardioversion.

cards.q: First-line pharmacological rate control for AFib?
cards.a: Beta-blockers or Non-dihydropyridine Calcium Channel Blockers (Diltiazem/Verapamil).

cards.q: Target INR for AFib patients on Warfarin?
Classic EKG finding in Atrial Flutter?
cards.a: "Sawtooth" flutter waves, typically seen in leads II, III, and aVF.

cards.q: First-line treatment for Paroxysmal Supraventricular Tachycardia (PSVT)?
cards.a: Vagal maneuvers followed by IV Adenosine.

cards.q: Characteristic EKG triad of Wolff-Parkinson-White (WPW)?
cards.a: Short PR interval, widened QRS, and a Delta wave.

cards.q: Avoided drugs in WPW with AFib?
cards.a: AV nodal blockers (ABCD: Adenosine, Beta-blockers, CCBs, Digoxin).

cards.q: Definition of Torsades de Pointes?
cards.a: Polymorphic Ventricular Tachycardia associated with a prolonged QT interval.

cards.q: Immediate treatment for Torsades de Pointes?
cards.a: IV Magnesium Sulfate.

cards.q: EKG finding in First-degree AV block?
cards.a: Fixed PR interval prolongation >200ms without dropped beats.

cards.q: Distinguishing feature of Mobitz Type I (Wenckebach)?
cards.a: Progressive PR interval lengthening until a QRS is dropped.

cards.q: Management of Mobitz Type II block?
cards.a: Permanent pacemaker (due to high risk of progression to 3rd-degree block).

cards.q: Definition of Third-degree (Complete) Heart Block?
cards.a: Complete dissociation between P-waves and QRS complexes.

cards.q: Classic triad of Aortic Stenosis (AS)?
cards.a: Angina, Syncope, and Dyspnea (SAD).

cards.q: Murmur description for Aortic Stenosis?
cards.a: Harsh crescendo-decrescendo systolic murmur at the right upper sternal border radiating to carotids.

cards.q: Physical exam sign "Pulsus parvus et tardus" indicates?
cards.a: Severe Aortic Stenosis.

cards.q: Most common cause of Aortic Stenosis in patients <70 years old?
cards.a: Bicuspid aortic valve.

cards.q: Murmur description for Aortic Regurgitation (AR)?
cards.a: Early diastolic blowing decrescendo murmur at the left sternal border.

cards.q: What is "Water-hammer pulse" (Corrigan pulse)?
cards.a: Rapidly rising and falling arterial pulse seen in chronic Aortic Regurgitation.

cards.q: Most common cause of Mitral Stenosis (MS) worldwide?
cards.a: Rheumatic Heart Disease.

cards.q: Murmur description for Mitral Stenosis?
cards.a: Mid-diastolic rumbling murmur with an opening snap at the apex.

cards.q: Relationship between Opening Snap and MS severity?
cards.a: A shorter A2-to-opening snap interval indicates more severe stenosis.

cards.q: Murmur description for Mitral Regurgitation (MR)?
cards.a: Holosystolic, blowing murmur at the apex radiating to the axilla.

cards.q: Acute Mitral Regurgitation is a common complication of?
cards.a: Papillary muscle rupture post-MI or Infective Endocarditis.

cards.q: Murmur of Mitral Valve Prolapse (MVP)?
cards.a: Midsystolic click followed by a late systolic murmur.

cards.q: Maneuver that makes MVP and HOCM murmurs louder?
cards.a: Valsalva or standing (decreases preload).

cards.q: Murmur of Tricuspid Regurgitation?
cards.a: Holosystolic murmur at the left lower sternal border that increases with inspiration.

cards.q: Definitive diagnostic test for all valvular lesions?
cards.a: Echocardiography.

cards.q: Most common type of cardiomyopathy?
cards.a: Dilated Cardiomyopathy.

cards.q: Characteristic finding on Echo for Hypertrophic Obstructive Cardiomyopathy (HOCM)?
cards.a: Asymmetric septal hypertrophy and Systolic Anterior Motion (SAM) of the mitral valve.

cards.q: First-line medication for symptomatic HOCM?
cards.a: Beta-blockers (to increase diastolic filling time).

cards.q: Classic EKG finding in Acute Pericarditis?
cards.a: Diffuse ST-segment elevation and PR-segment depression.

cards.q: Beck’s Triad for Cardiac Tamponade?
cards.a: Hypotension, JVD, and muffled heart sounds.

cards.q: Definition of Pulsus Paradoxus?
cards.a: A drop in systolic blood pressure >10 mmHg during inspiration.

cards.q: EKG finding in Cardiac Tamponade?
cards.a: Electrical alternans (alternating QRS amplitude).

cards.q: Kussmaul’s sign is most associated with which pericardial pathology?
cards.a: Constrictive Pericarditis.

cards.q: Treatment of choice for Cardiac Tamponade?
cards.a: Urgent pericardiocentesis.

cards.q: Common etiology of Restrictive Cardiomyopathy?
cards.a: Amyloidosis, Sarcoidosis, or Hemochromatosis.

cards.q: Preferred treatment for Hypertensive Emergency?
cards.a: IV Labetalol, Nicardipine, or Nitroprusside (with controlled BP reduction).

cards.q: Calculation for Mean Arterial Pressure (MAP)?
cards.a: $MAP = \frac{SBP + 2(DBP)}{3}$

cards.q: Medication that improves survival in African Americans with HFrEF?
cards.a: Hydralazine plus Isosorbide Dinitrate.

cards.q: Mechanism of Statins?
cards.a: Inhibition of HMG-CoA reductase, the rate-limiting step in cholesterol synthesis.

cards.q: Most common side effect of Statin therapy?
cards.a: Myalgia or transaminitis (liver enzyme elevation).

cards.q: Treatment for cocaine-induced chest pain?
cards.a: Benzodiazepines and Nitrates; avoid Beta-blockers (risk of unopposed alpha-agonism).

cards.q: Duke Criteria is used for the diagnosis of?
cards.a: Infective Endocarditis.

cards.q: Major Duke Criteria?
cards.a: Positive blood cultures (typical organism) and Evidence of endocardial involvement (Echo showing vegetation).

cards.q: Physical signs of Endocarditis?
cards.a: Roth spots (retina), Janeway lesions (painless palms/soles), Osler nodes (painful fingertips), and Splinter hemorrhages.

cards.q: First-line treatment for most patients with Pericarditis?
cards.a: NSAIDs and Colchicine.

cards.q: Aortic Dissection: Type A vs Type B management?
cards.a: Type A (ascending) requires surgery; Type B (descending) is typically managed with medical BP control.

cards.q: Classic CXR finding in Aortic Dissection?
cards.a: Widened mediastinum.

cards.q: What is the "Bainbridge Reflex"?
cards.a: Increase in heart rate due to an increase in central venous pressure (atrial stretch).

cards.q: Most common cause of sudden cardiac death in young athletes?
cards.a: Hypertrophic Cardiomyopathy (HOCM).

cards.q: Screening recommendation for Abdominal Aortic Aneurysm (AAA)?
cards.a: One-time ultrasound for men aged 65–75 who have ever smoked.

cards.q: Definitive treatment for sick sinus syndrome?
cards.a: Permanent Pacemaker.

cards.q: Primary mechanism of action of Lidocaine as an antiarrhythmic?
cards.a: Class IB Sodium channel blocker; shortens action potential duration.

cards.q: Drug of choice for symptomatic Bradycardia?
cards.a: Atropine.

cards.q: Most common cause of Myocarditis in the US?
cards.a: Viral infections (e.g., Coxsackievirus B, Parvovirus B19).

cards.q: Gold standard for diagnosing Coronary Artery Disease?
cards.a: Coronary Angiography.

cards.q: Treatment for Hyperkalemia-induced EKG changes?
cards.a: IV Calcium gluconate (to stabilize the cardiac membrane).

cards.q: Which valvular lesion is associated with Head Bobbing (De Musset sign)?
cards.a: Chronic Aortic Regurgitation.

cards.q: EKG finding of a "Brugada Pattern"?
cards.a: Pseudo-RBBB and persistent ST elevation in leads V1–V2.

cards.q: Management of a patient with WPW and Atrial Fibrillation?
cards.a: Procainamide or Cardioversion (Avoid AV nodal blockers).

cards.q: Major side effect of Amiodarone?
cards.a: Pulmonary fibrosis, thyroid dysfunction (hypo/hyper), and hepatotoxicity.

cards.q: Goal BP for most patients according to ACC/AHA guidelines?
cards.a: Less than 130/80 mmHg.

cards.q: Most sensitive EKG finding for Posterior Wall MI?
cards.a: ST-segment depression in leads V1–V3 with prominent R waves.

cards.q: What is the "de Winter" T-wave pattern?
cards.a: Upsloping ST-depression with tall, symmetric T-waves in precordial leads; indicates proximal LAD occlusion.

cards.q: Clinical utility of the HEART score?
cards.a: Risk stratifies patients with undifferentiated chest pain in the ED to identify those safe for discharge.

cards.q: Which score predicts 6-month mortality in patients admitted with ACS?
cards.a: The GRACE score (Global Registry of Acute Cardiac Events).

cards.q: Goal time for Fibrinolytics if PCI is unavailable?
cards.a: Door-to-needle time <30 minutes.

cards.q: Indication for urgent CABG in ACS?
cards.a: Failed PCI, cardiogenic shock, or mechanical complications (e.g., VSD, papillary muscle rupture).

cards.q: Significance of elevated Troponin in End-Stage Renal Disease (ESRD) without ACS?
cards.a: Chronic microinjury to the myocardium; however, a rising/falling trend still suggests acute ischemia.

cards.q: Recommended duration of P2Y12 inhibitor therapy after DES placement in ACS?
cards.a: At least 12 months.

cards.q: Standard management for HFrEF patient with persistent symptoms on Triple Therapy?
cards.a: Add an SGLT2 inhibitor (e.g., Dapagliflozin) or consider ARNI if on ACEi/ARB.

cards.q: Contraindication for starting ARNI immediately after ACE inhibitor?
cards.a: Requires a 36-hour washout period to prevent angioedema.

cards.q: Electrolyte abnormality associated with Spironolactone?
cards.a: Hyperkalemia and metabolic acidosis.

cards.q: When to initiate Hydralazine-Isosorbide Dinitrate in HFrEF?
cards.a: Symptomatic African American patients despite optimal GDMT or patients unable to tolerate ACEi/ARBs due to renal failure.

cards.q: Mechanism of Ivabradine?
cards.a: Selective $I_f$ current inhibitor in the SA node; reduces heart rate without affecting contractility.

cards.q: Indication for Ivabradine?
cards.a: HFrEF (LVEF ≤35%) in sinus rhythm with resting heart rate ≥70 bpm despite maximally tolerated Beta-blockers.

cards.q: Key hemodynamic difference between Systolic and Diastolic HF?
cards.a: Systolic HF involves reduced contractility; Diastolic HF involves impaired ventricular relaxation/compliance.

cards.q: First-line treatment for a patient with AFib and Wolff-Parkinson-White?
cards.a: Procainamide (avoid Adenosine, Beta-blockers, CCBs, and Digoxin).

cards.q: Pathophysiology of Ashman’s Phenomenon?
cards.a: Aberrantly conducted QRS (usually RBBB) following a short R-R interval preceded by a long R-R interval, common in AFib.

cards.q: Definition of "Holiday Heart Syndrome"?
cards.a: Acute AFib triggered by excessive alcohol consumption in a healthy individual.

cards.q: Classic EKG finding in MAT (Multifocal Atrial Tachycardia)?
cards.a: HR >100 bpm with ≥3 different P-wave morphologies; often seen in COPD patients.

cards.q: Initial treatment for MAT?
cards.a: Oxygenation and treatment of underlying pulmonary disease; CCBs for rate control if needed.

cards.q: Most specific EKG sign of Digoxin toxicity?
cards.a: Atrial tachycardia with variable AV block.

cards.q: Characteristic EKG of Wellens’ Syndrome?
cards.a: Deeply inverted or biphasic T-waves in V2–V3; indicates critical proximal LAD stenosis.

cards.q: Most common cause of chronic Aortic Regurgitation in developed countries?
cards.a: Aortic root dilation (e.g., hypertension, Marfan syndrome, aortic dissection).

cards.q: Meaning of "Austin Flint" murmur?
cards.a: Mid-to-late diastolic rumble at the apex heard in severe Aortic Regurgitation (due to regurgitant jet impinging on the mitral valve).

cards.q: Management of symptomatic severe Mitral Stenosis with favorable morphology?
cards.a: Percutaneous Mitral Balloon Valvotomy.

cards.q: Preferred diagnostic tool to assess for Mitral Valve vegetations or thrombus?
cards.a: Transesophageal Echocardiography (TEE).

cards.q: Characteristic murmur of Tricuspid Stenosis?
cards.a: Diastolic rumble at the left lower sternal border that increases with inspiration (Carvallo’s sign).

cards.q: Key indication for valve replacement in asymptomatic Aortic Stenosis?
cards.a: LVEF <50% or patient undergoing other cardiac surgery.

cards.q: Murmur change during Handgrip in Mitral Regurgitation?
cards.a: Murmur intensity increases due to increased afterload.

cards.q: First-line treatment for Symptomatic Bradycardia?
cards.a: Atropine 1mg IV; if ineffective, provide transcutaneous pacing or Dopamine/Epinephrine infusion.

cards.q: Classic CXR sign of Coarctation of the Aorta?
cards.a: Rib notching (due to collateral intercostal arteries) and the "3" sign.

cards.q: Most common primary cardiac tumor in adults?
cards.a: Atrial Myxoma (usually in the left atrium).

cards.q: Most common primary cardiac tumor in children?
cards.a: Rhabdomyoma (highly associated with Tuberous Sclerosis).

cards.q: Treatment for Type B Aortic Dissection?
cards.a: IV Beta-blockers (e.g., Esmolol) to reduce heart rate and shear stress, followed by vasodilators if needed.

cards.q: ECG sign for Hypercalcemia?
cards.a: Shortened QT interval.

cards.q: ECG sign for Hypocalcemia?
cards.a: Prolonged QT interval.

cards.q: Definitive management for Pulseless Electrical Activity (PEA)?
cards.a: CPR and Epinephrine; look for reversible causes (Hs and Ts).

cards.q: Effect of Valsalva maneuver on the murmur of Aortic Stenosis?
cards.a: Decreases (due to decreased preload).

cards.q: Effect of Squatting on the murmur of HOCM?
cards.a: Decreases (increased preload and afterload increase LV volume, reducing outflow obstruction).

cards.q: Murmur that increases with Sustained Handgrip?
cards.a: Mitral Regurgitation, Aortic Regurgitation, and VSD (due to increased afterload).

cards.q: Murmur that decreases with Sustained Handgrip?
cards.a: HOCM and Aortic Stenosis.

cards.q: Definition of the "Gallavardin Phenomenon"?
cards.a: Dissociation between the noisy and musical components of the Aortic Stenosis murmur, often heard at the apex.

cards.q: Clinical significance of a prominent 'a' wave in JVP?
cards.a: Right atrial contraction against a closed or stiff valve (Tricuspid Stenosis, Pulmonary HTN, or Right Ventricular Hypertrophy).

cards.q: Clinical significance of "Cannon a-waves"?
cards.a: Atrial contraction against a closed tricuspid valve (AV dissociation: V-Tach or 3rd-degree Heart Block).

cards.q: Clinical significance of a prominent 'v' wave in JVP?
cards.a: Tricuspid Regurgitation (blood flows back into the atrium during ventricular systole).

cards.q: Next best step for a patient with chest pain and new Left Bundle Branch Block (LBBB)?
cards.a: Treat as an emergent STEMI (Immediate reperfusion therapy).

cards.q: First-line treatment for Prinzmetal (Vasospastic) Angina?
cards.a: Calcium Channel Blockers and Nitrates.

cards.q: Avoided medication in Prinzmetal Angina?
cards.a: Non-selective Beta-blockers (may worsen vasospasm due to unopposed alpha-1 activity).

cards.q: TIMI Risk Score parameters?
cards.a: Age ≥65, ≥3 CAD risk factors, Known CAD (>50% stenosis), Aspirin use in last 7 days, Severe angina (2+ in 24h), ST deviation, Elevated biomarkers.

cards.q: Management of a NSTEMI patient with refractory ischemia or hemodynamic instability?
cards.a: Immediate Cardiac Catheterization (within 2 hours).

cards.q: Common EKG finding in Acute Pulmonary Embolism (PE)?
cards.a: Sinus tachycardia (most common) or S1Q3T3 pattern (specific but rare).

cards.q: Most common cause of death within the first few hours of a myocardial infarction?
cards.a: Ventricular Fibrillation.

cards.q: Most common cause of Cor Pulmonale?
cards.a: Chronic Obstructive Pulmonary Disease (COPD).

cards.q: First-line treatment for Acute Pulmonary Edema?
cards.a: "LMNOP" (Loop diuretics, Morphine, Nitrates, Oxygen, Position/BiPAP).

cards.q: Lab test used to differentiate heart failure from primary lung disease?
cards.a: BNP or NT-proBNP.

cards.q: Classic EKG finding in Dilated Cardiomyopathy?
cards.a: Non-specific ST-T wave changes and Left Bundle Branch Block.

cards.q: Most common cause of Restrictive Cardiomyopathy in the US?
cards.a: Amyloidosis.

cards.q: Definitive diagnosis of Myocarditis?
cards.a: Endomyocardial Biopsy (though Cardiac MRI is often used first).

cards.q: Classic EKG in Arrhythmogenic Right Ventricular Cardiomyopathy (ARVC)?
cards.a: Epsilon wave (small notch at the end of the QRS in V1–V3).

cards.q: Preferred treatment for hemodynamically stable Ventricular Tachycardia?
cards.a: IV Amiodarone or Procainamide.

cards.q: Next step for Pulseless Ventricular Tachycardia or Ventricular Fibrillation?
cards.a: Immediate unsynchronized defibrillation.

cards.q: Treatment for symptomatic Sinus Bradycardia if Atropine fails?
cards.a: Transcutaneous pacing.

cards.q: EKG finding of Trifascicular Block?
cards.a: RBBB, Left axis deviation (LAFB), and 1st-degree AV block.

cards.q: Medication used for chemical stress testing in patients who cannot exercise?
cards.a: Adenosine, Regadenoson, or Dobutamine.

cards.q: What does "Capture Beats" and "Fusion Beats" on EKG signify?
cards.a: Diagnostic of Ventricular Tachycardia (helps distinguish from SVT with aberrancy).

cards.q: Management of a pregnant patient with symptomatic Mitral Stenosis?
cards.a: Percutaneous Mitral Balloon Valvotomy.

cards.q: Most common complication of Mitral Stenosis?
cards.a: Atrial Fibrillation (due to left atrial enlargement).

cards.q: Best indicator of the severity of Mitral Regurgitation?
cards.a: Presence of an S3 gallop.

cards.q: Classic presentation of Atrial Myxoma?
cards.a: Fever, weight loss, and a "tumor plop" sound on auscultation (often mimics Mitral Stenosis).

cards.q: Indication for surgery in chronic Aortic Regurgitation?
cards.a: Symptomatic, or asymptomatic with LV dysfunction (EF <50%) or severe LV dilation.

cards.q: Classic finding on fundoscopy in a patient with Hypertension?
cards.a: AV nicking, silver/copper wiring, and cotton wool spots.

cards.q: Definition of Hypertensive Urgency?
cards.a: BP >180/120 mmHg without evidence of acute end-organ damage.

cards.q: Definition of Hypertensive Emergency?
cards.a: BP >180/120 mmHg with acute end-organ damage (e.g., encephalopathy, MI, stroke, renal failure).

cards.q: First-line treatment for Hypertriglyceridemia (>500 mg/dL)?
cards.a: Fibrates (to prevent pancreatitis).

cards.q: Most common site of origin for an embolus causing a stroke in a patient with AFib?
cards.a: Left Atrial Appendage.

cards.q: Management of Cardiac Tamponade while waiting for pericardiocentesis?
cards.a: Aggressive IV fluid bolus to increase preload.

cards.q: Significance of an S4 gallop?
cards.a: Atrial contraction into a stiff, non-compliant ventricle (e.g., LVH, restrictive cardiomyopathy).

cards.q: Next step for a patient with a "tearing" chest pain radiating to the back?
cards.a: CT Angiography of the chest/abdomen or TEE (if unstable).

cards.q: Mechanism of action of Ezetimibe?
cards.a: Inhibits cholesterol absorption at the brush border of the small intestine.

cards.q: Most common side effect of Niacin and how to prevent it?
cards.a: Prostaglandin-mediated flushing; prevented by pre-treatment with Aspirin.

cards.q: Class of antiarrhythmics that exhibit "Use-Dependence"?
cards.a: Class IC (e.g., Flecainide); their effect is stronger at higher heart rates.

cards.q: Major electrolyte side effect of Thiazide diuretics?
cards.a: Hypokalemia, Hyponatremia, and Hypercalcemia.

cards.q: Major electrolyte side effect of Loop diuretics?
cards.a: Hypokalemia, Hyponatremia, and Hypocalcemia.

cards.q: Antihypertensive class known to cause peripheral edema?
cards.a: Dihydropyridine Calcium Channel Blockers (e.g., Amlodipine).

cards.q: Drug-induced Lupus is most commonly associated with which cardiac medication?
cards.a: Hydralazine or Procainamide.

cards.q: Which anti-lipid medication can lead to gallstones?
cards.a: Fibrates (by increasing cholesterol excretion into bile).

cards.q: Timing of Ventricular Free Wall Rupture post-MI?
cards.a: 5 days to 2 weeks.

cards.q: Clinical presentation of Ventricular Free Wall Rupture?
cards.a: Sudden onset of Cardiac Tamponade and PEA.

cards.q: Post-MI complication presenting with "Step-up" in oxygen saturation from RA to RV?
cards.a: Ventricular Septal Rupture.

cards.q: EKG finding of a Ventricular Aneurysm?
cards.a: Persistent ST-segment elevation several weeks after the MI.

cards.q: Most common cause of death in the "Late" phase (weeks) post-MI?
cards.a: Heart Failure or Ventricular Arrhythmias.

cards.q: Definition of "Sick Sinus Syndrome"?
cards.a: Tachycardia-Bradycardia Syndrome due to SA node dysfunction.

cards.q: Standard of care for a patient with Brugada Syndrome and prior syncope?
cards.a: Implantable Cardioverter Defibrillator (ICD).

cards.q: First-line treatment for Vasovagal Syncope?
cards.a: Reassurance, avoidance of triggers, and physical counter-pressure maneuvers.

cards.q: Distinguishing feature of Orthostatic Hypotension on vitals?
cards.a: Drop in SBP >20 mmHg or DBP >10 mmHg upon standing.

cards.q: Management of symptomatic Carotid Sinus Hypersensitivity?
cards.a: Permanent pacemaker.

cards.q: What is "Quincke’s Pulse"?
cards.a: Capillary pulsations in the fingertips/nailbeds seen in Aortic Regurgitation.

cards.q: What is "Duroziez’s Sign"?
cards.a: A systolic and diastolic bruit heard over the femoral artery when compressed by a stethoscope.

cards.q: Graham-Steell murmur description?
cards.a: Early diastolic murmur at the left sternal border due to Pulmonary Regurgitation in the setting of Pulmonary HTN.

cards.q: Primary valvular lesion associated with IV drug use?
cards.a: Tricuspid Regurgitation (Infective Endocarditis).

cards.q: Which valvular lesion presents with a "large V-wave" in the PCWP trace?
cards.a: Mitral Regurgitation.

cards.q: Goal LDL for a patient with known CAD or high-risk diabetes?
cards.a: <70 mg/dL (or <55 mg/dL in very high-risk patients per newest guidelines).

cards.q: Components of the ASCVD Risk Calculator?
cards.a: Age, Sex, Race, BP, Cholesterol levels, Diabetes, and Smoking status.

cards.q: Indication for high-intensity statin regardless of LDL level?
cards.a: Clinical ASCVD or Diabetes with a 10-year risk >20%.

cards.q: First-line antihypertensive in a patient with Diabetes and Proteinuria?
cards.a: ACE inhibitor or ARB (for renal protection).

cards.q: Significance of a "Pulsus Bisferiens"?
cards.a: Two systolic peaks; seen in Aortic Regurgitation or HOCM.

cards.q: Classic cause of "Water-Bottle" Heart on CXR?
cards.a: Large Pericardial Effusion.

cards.q: Management of a patient with suspected Aortic Dissection and Hypotension?
cards.a: Immediate TEE and surgical consult (suggests rupture into pericardium/tamponade).

cards.q: Classic EKG finding in Hypothermia?
cards.a: J-waves (Osborn waves) — an upward deflection at the R-ST junction.

cards.q: Key finding on Echo for Cardiac Amyloidosis?
cards.a: Increased wall thickness with "speckled" or "granular" myocardium.

cards.q: Treatment for a patient with persistent stable Angina despite Beta-blocker and Nitrate therapy?
cards.a: Add Ranolazine.

cards.q: Most common location of a Coarctation of the Aorta?
cards.a: Just distal to the origin of the left subclavian artery.

cards.q: Significance of a "Fixed Splitting of S2"?
cards.a: Atrial Septal Defect (ASD).

cards.q: First-line treatment for a hemodynamically stable patient with WPW and AFib?
cards.a: IV Procainamide.

cards.q: Most common cause of death in patients with Marfan Syndrome?
cards.a: Aortic Root Dissection.

cards.q: Mechanism of nitrates in relieving angina?
cards.a: Systemic venodilation resulting in decreased preload and reduced myocardial wall tension.

cards.q: Most common congenital heart defect found in adults?
cards.a: Bicuspid Aortic Valve.

cards.q: Physical exam finding for a small Ventricular Septal Defect (VSD)?
cards.a: Loud, harsh holosystolic murmur at the left lower sternal border; often palpated as a thrill.

cards.q: Murmur of a Patent Ductus Arteriosus (PDA)?
cards.a: Continuous "machine-like" murmur heard best at the left infraclavicular area.

cards.q: Management of a large PDA in an adult?
cards.a: Percutaneous or surgical closure to prevent pulmonary hypertension and endocarditis.

cards.q: Definition of Eisenmenger Syndrome?
cards.a: Reversal of a left-to-right shunt to right-to-left due to severe, irreversible pulmonary hypertension.

cards.q: Clinical signs of Eisenmenger Syndrome?
cards.a: Cyanosis, clubbing, and polycythemia.

cards.q: Why is the murmur of VSD or PDA "missing" in Eisenmenger Syndrome?
cards.a: The pressures in the systemic and pulmonary circulations have equalized, eliminating the pressure gradient.

cards.q: Normal Pulmonary Artery Wedge Pressure (PAWP)?
cards.a: 6–12 mmHg.

cards.q: Hemodynamic profile of Cardiogenic Shock?
cards.a: Low Cardiac Output, High PAWP (Preload), and High SVR (Afterload).

cards.q: Hemodynamic profile of Hypovolemic Shock?
cards.a: Low Cardiac Output, Low PAWP, and High SVR.

cards.q: Hemodynamic profile of Septic (Distributive) Shock?
cards.a: High Cardiac Output, Low PAWP, and Low SVR.

cards.q: Pulmonary capillary wedge pressure in non-cardiogenic pulmonary edema (ARDS)?
cards.a: Normal (typically <18 mmHg).

cards.q: Most common cardiac complication during pregnancy in women with Mitral Stenosis?
cards.a: Acute pulmonary edema or Atrial Fibrillation due to increased plasma volume.

cards.q: Definition of Peripartum Cardiomyopathy?
cards.a: Dilated cardiomyopathy/HF occurring in the last month of pregnancy or within 5 months postpartum.

cards.q: Management of Peripartum Cardiomyopathy with LVEF <25%?
cards.a: Anticoagulation (high risk of thrombus) and standard HF therapy (avoiding ACEi/ARBs if still pregnant).

cards.q: Preferred anticoagulation for a pregnant patient with a mechanical heart valve?
cards.a: Low Molecular Weight Heparin (LMWH) in the first trimester; Warfarin may be used in the 2nd/3rd trimester.

cards.q: First-line antihypertensive for a pregnant patient?
cards.a: Labetalol, Nifedipine, or Methyldopa.

cards.q: Next step for an asymptomatic 45-year-old with a Grade 1/6 mid-systolic murmur?
cards.a: Reassurance; no further workup needed for soft, short systolic murmurs in asymptomatic patients.

cards.q: Next step for any diastolic or continuous murmur found on exam?
cards.a: Echocardiogram (these are always pathologic until proven otherwise).

cards.q: When is S4 considered "normal"?
cards.a: In healthy older adults due to age-related decrease in ventricular compliance.

cards.q: Best initial test for suspected stable CAD in a patient with a baseline LBBB on EKG?
cards.a: Stress Echocardiogram or Nuclear Stress Test (exercise EKG is non-diagnostic with LBBB).

cards.q: Major advantage of a bioprosthetic (bovine/porcine) valve over a mechanical valve?
cards.a: No requirement for long-term anticoagulation.

cards.q: Major disadvantage of a bioprosthetic valve?
cards.a: Limited durability (typically lasts 10–15 years); prone to calcification.

cards.q: Preferred valve type for a 30-year-old patient?
cards.a: Mechanical valve (due to longevity), provided they can tolerate lifelong  Warfarin.

topic: Pulmonology — Pneumonia, COPD, asthma, PE, TB

cards.q: Most common cause of Community-Acquired Pneumonia (CAP)?
cards.a: Streptococcus pneumoniae.

cards.q: CURB-65 criteria for pneumonia admission?
cards.a: Confusion, Urea >7 mmol/L, RR ≥30, BP (S <90 or D ≤60), Age ≥65.

cards.q: Standard outpatient treatment for CAP in a healthy patient (no comorbidities)?
cards.a: Amoxicillin, Doxycycline, or a Macrolide (if local resistance <25%).

cards.q: Empiric inpatient treatment for non-ICU CAP?
cards.a: Respiratory Fluoroquinolone (e.g., Levofloxacin) OR Beta-lactam + Macrolide.

cards.q: Common causative agent of pneumonia in alcoholics with "currant jelly" sputum?
cards.a: Klebsiella pneumoniae.

cards.q: Pneumonia associated with air conditioning or contaminated water sources?
cards.a: Legionella pneumophila.

cards.q: Diagnostic test for Legionella?
cards.a: Urine antigen test.

cards.q: Physical exam finding: Increased tactile fremitus and dullness to percussion?
cards.a: Consolidation (Pneumonia).

cards.q: Definition of Hospital-Acquired Pneumonia (HAP)?
cards.a: Pneumonia occurring ≥48 hours after admission.

cards.q: Treatment for suspected MRSA pneumonia?
cards.a: Vancomycin or Linezolid.

cards.q: Management of a parapneumonic effusion with pH <7.2 or glucose <60?
cards.a: Chest tube drainage (indicates empyema or complicated effusion).

cards.q: Primary TB chest X-ray finding?
cards.a: Ghon complex (calcified parenchymal lesion and hilar node).

cards.q: Reactivation TB typically affects which part of the lung?
cards.a: Apical/Posterior segments of upper lobes.

cards.q: Gold standard for diagnosing active TB?
cards.a: Sputum culture (though AFB stain is the rapid initial step).

cards.q: Standard 4-drug regimen for active TB (RIPE)?
cards.a: Rifampin, Isoniazid, Pyrazinamide, Ethambutol.

cards.q: Side effect of Ethambutol requiring monitoring?
cards.a: Optic neuritis (decreased visual acuity/red-green color blindness).

cards.q: Side effect of Pyrazinamide?
cards.a: Hyperuricemia (can trigger gout).

cards.q: Medication given with Isoniazid to prevent peripheral neuropathy?
cards.a: Vitamin B6 (Pyridoxine).

cards.q: Screening test for latent TB in a patient with prior BCG vaccine?
cards.a: IGRA (Interferon-Gamma Release Assay).

cards.q: Definition of a positive PPD in a healthcare worker?
cards.a: ≥10 mm induration. Pulmonology Part 2: Asthma & COPD

cards.q: The "Classic Triad" of asthma pathophysiology?
cards.a: Airway inflammation, reversible airway obstruction, and bronchial hyperresponsiveness.

cards.q: Diagnostic criteria for asthma on spirometry?
cards.a: Increase in FEV1 >12% and >200 mL after bronchodilator.

cards.q: Gold standard for diagnosing asthma when spirometry is normal?
cards.a: Methacholine challenge (PC20 <8 mg/mL).

cards.q: Step 1 treatment for intermittent asthma (GINA/NAEPP update)?
cards.a: PRN low-dose ICS-formoterol.

cards.q: Characteristic finding in sputum of asthmatics?
cards.a: Curschmann spirals or Charcot-Leyden crystals.

cards.q: Definition of "Moderate Persistent" asthma?
cards.a: Daily symptoms or nighttime awakenings >1x/week.

cards.q: Side effect of inhaled corticosteroids (ICS)?
cards.a: Oral candidiasis (thrush).

cards.q: Definition of Chronic Bronchitis?
cards.a: Productive cough for ≥3 months in 2 consecutive years.

cards.q: Major genetic risk factor for COPD in a young non-smoker?
cards.a: Alpha-1 Antitrypsin deficiency.

cards.q: Typical FEV1/FVC ratio in COPD?
cards.a: <0.70 (post-bronchodilator).

cards.q: Only two interventions proven to reduce mortality in COPD?
cards.a: Smoking cessation and Long-term Oxygen Therapy (LTOT).

cards.q: Criteria for initiating LTOT in COPD?
cards.a: PaO2 ≤55 mmHg or SaO2 ≤88% at rest.

cards.q: Best initial treatment for symptomatic COPD (Group A)?
cards.a: SABA or SAMA (Short-acting bronchodilator).

cards.q: Common CXR findings in emphysema?
cards.a: Flattened diaphragm, hyperlucency, and increased retrosternal airspace.

cards.q: Most common cause of COPD exacerbation?
cards.a: Viral or bacterial infection (e.g., H. influenzae).

cards.q: Three cardinal symptoms requiring antibiotics in COPD exacerbation?
cards.a: Increased dyspnea, increased sputum volume, and increased sputum purulence.

cards.q: Target oxygen saturation in a COPD exacerbation?
First-line ventilation for COPD exacerbation with respiratory acidosis?
cards.a: Non-invasive positive pressure ventilation (NPPV/BiPAP).

cards.q: Characteristic EKG finding in severe COPD/Cor Pulmonale?
cards.a: Multifocal Atrial Tachycardia (MAT) or Right Axis Deviation.

cards.q: Lung volume change pathognomonic for air trapping in COPD?
cards.a: Increased Residual Volume (RV) and Total Lung Capacity (TLC). Pulmonology Part 3: Pulmonary Embolism (PE)

cards.q: Most common symptom of Pulmonary Embolism?
cards.a: Dyspnea.

cards.q: Most common EKG finding in PE?
cards.a: Sinus tachycardia.

cards.q: The "Classic" but rare EKG sign of PE?
cards.a: S1Q3T3 (Deep S in I, Q wave in III, inverted T in III).

cards.q: Initial step for a patient with low clinical suspicion of PE?
cards.a: D-dimer (to rule out).

cards.q: Gold standard imaging for diagnosing PE?
cards.a: CT Angiography (CTPA).

cards.q: Alternative imaging for PE if the patient has renal failure or contrast allergy?
cards.a: V/Q Scan.

cards.q: Arterial Blood Gas (ABG) finding typically seen in PE?
cards.a: Respiratory alkalosis (due to hyperventilation) with hypoxemia.

cards.q: Hampton’s Hump on CXR represents?
cards.a: Pulmonary infarction (wedge-shaped opacity).

cards.q: Westermark sign on CXR represents?
cards.a: Avascularity distal to the PE (oligemia).

cards.q: Treatment for a hemodynamically unstable PE (Massive PE)?
cards.a: Systemic Thrombolysis (e.g., tPA).

cards.q: First-line anticoagulation for a stable PE?
cards.a: DOACs (e.g., Rivaroxaban, Apixaban) or LMWH bridge to Warfarin.

cards.q: Indication for an IVC filter?
cards.a: Documented DVT/PE with absolute contraindication to anticoagulation.

cards.q: Minimum duration of anticoagulation for a first-time provoked PE?
cards.a: 3 months.

cards.q: Definition of "Submassive" PE?
cards.a: Hemodynamically stable but with evidence of Right Ventricular (RV) strain.

cards.q: Echocardiographic sign of RV strain in PE?
cards.a: McConnell’s sign (RV free wall akinesia with sparing of the apex). Pulmonology Part 4: Advanced Physiology & Mixed Topics

cards.q: Flow-volume loop: Scooped-out appearance?
cards.a: Obstructive lung disease (Asthma/COPD).

cards.q: Flow-volume loop: Tall, narrow, "witch's hat" appearance?
cards.a: Restrictive lung disease (IPF/Sarcoidosis).

cards.q: West Zone of the lung where PA > Pa > Pv?
cards.a: Zone 1 (Apex).

cards.q: Effect of PE on V/Q ratio?
cards.a: V/Q = infinity (Dead space ventilation).

cards.q: Effect of airway obstruction/mucus plug on V/Q ratio?
cards.a: V/Q = 0 (Shunt).

cards.q: Definition of Type 1 Respiratory Failure?
cards.a: Hypoxemic (PaO2 <60) with normal or low PaCO2.

cards.q: Definition of Type 2 Respiratory Failure?
cards.a: Hypercapnic (PaCO2 >50).

cards.q: Light's Criteria for Exudative Effusion?
cards.a: LDH >2/3 upper limit, Fluid/Serum LDH >0.6, or Fluid/Serum Protein >0.5.

cards.q: Most common cause of transudative pleural effusion?
cards.a: Congestive Heart Failure.

cards.q: Fluid analysis of a Chylothorax?
cards.a: High triglycerides (>110 mg/dL) and milky appearance.

cards.q: Management of a primary spontaneous pneumothorax <2 cm in a stable patient?
cards.a: Observation and supplemental oxygen.

cards.q: Management of a Tension Pneumothorax?
cards.a: Immediate needle decompression followed by chest tube.

cards.q: Location for needle decompression in tension pneumothorax?
cards.a: 2nd intercostal space, mid-clavicular line (or 4th/5th anterior axillary).

cards.q: Classic CXR finding in Asbestosis?
cards.a: Pleural plaques (calcified) involving the diaphragm.

cards.q: Silicosis increases the risk of which infection?
cards.a: Tuberculosis (impaired macrophage function).

cards.q: "Eggshell" calcifications of hilar lymph nodes?
cards.a: Silicosis.

cards.q: Bilateral hilar lymphadenopathy and non-caseating granulomas?
cards.a: Sarcoidosis.

cards.q: Electrolyte abnormality common in Sarcoidosis?
cards.a: Hypercalcemia (due to 1-alpha hydroxylase activity in macrophages).

cards.q: First-line treatment for symptomatic Sarcoidosis?
cards.a: Glucocorticoids (Prednisone).

cards.q: Meaning of a "normal" PaCO2 in a severe asthma attack?
cards.a: Impending respiratory failure (patient is tiring).

cards.q: DLCO in Emphysema vs. Asthma?
cards.a: Decreased in Emphysema; Normal or Increased in Asthma.

cards.q: DLCO in Restrictive Lung Disease (Interstial)?
cards.a: Decreased.

cards.q: Primary drug for smoking cessation that is a nicotinic receptor partial agonist?
cards.a: Varenicline (Chantix).

cards.q: Contraindication for Bupropion in smoking cessation?
cards.a: Seizure disorder or eating disorders.

cards.q: Most common lung cancer in non-smokers?
cards.a: Adenocarcinoma.

cards.q: Lung cancer associated with PTHrP and hypercalcemia?
cards.a: Squamous Cell Carcinoma.

cards.q: Lung cancer associated with SIADH or Lambert-Eaton?
cards.a: Small Cell Lung Cancer.

cards.q: Standard of care for diagnosing a peripheral lung nodule?
cards.a: Transthoracic needle aspiration or VATS.

cards.q: Standard of care for diagnosing a central lung lesion?
cards.a: Bronchoscopy.

cards.q: Definition of Acute Respiratory Distress Syndrome (ARDS) P/F ratio?
cards.a: PaO2/FiO2 ≤300 mmHg.

cards.q: Primary ventilator strategy for ARDS?
cards.a: Low tidal volume ventilation (6 mL/kg ideal body weight).

cards.q: Common CXR finding in ARDS?
cards.a: Diffuse bilateral "fluffy" infiltrates (sparing costophrenic angles).

cards.q: PCWP in ARDS?
cards.a: <18 mmHg (suggests non-cardiogenic origin).

cards.q: Characteristic finding on sleep study for Obstructive Sleep Apnea (OSA)?
cards.a: Apnea-Hypopnea Index (AHI) ≥5 with symptoms or ≥15 without.

cards.q: First-line treatment for OSA?
cards.a: CPAP and weight loss.

cards.q: Most common cause of Cor Pulmonale?
cards.a: COPD.

cards.q: Medication of choice for Pulmonary Arterial Hypertension (Group 1)?
cards.a: PDE-5 inhibitors (Sildenafil), Endothelin antagonists (Bosentan), or Prostanoids.

cards.q: Initial test for suspected Pulmonary Hypertension?
cards.a: Echocardiogram (to estimate PASP).

cards.q: Gold standard for definitive diagnosis of Pulmonary Hypertension?
cards.a: Right heart catheterization (mPAP >20 mmHg).

cards.q: Physical exam sign of right-sided heart failure?
cards.a: Jugular Venous Distension (JVD) and peripheral edema.

cards.q: "Sudden onset chest pain, tachycardia, and clear lungs" suggests?
cards.a: Pulmonary Embolism.

cards.q: Difference between Hypoxemia and Hypoxia?
cards.a: Hypoxemia is low arterial O2 tension; Hypoxia is low O2 delivery to tissues.

cards.q: Effect of high altitude on the oxygen-dissociation curve?
cards.a: Right shift (increased 2,3-BPG).

cards.q: Characteristic of Malignant Pleural Effusion?
cards.a: Exudative, often bloody, positive cytology.

cards.q: Treatment for Latent TB (standard)?
cards.a: 4 months of Rifampin OR 9 months of Isoniazid.

cards.q: Recommended vaccine for adults >65 to prevent pneumonia?
cards.a: PCV20 (or PCV15 followed by PPSV23).

cards.q: Mainstay of treatment for allergic bronchopulmonary aspergillosis (ABPA)?
cards.a: Oral corticosteroids and Itraconazole.

cards.q: Diagnostic finding for ABPA?
cards.a: High IgE, eosinophilia, and "finger-in-glove" opacities on CT.

cards.q: Common cause of lung abscess?
cards.a: Aspiration of anaerobic oral flora.

cards.q: Preferred antibiotic for lung abscess?
cards.a: Ampicillin-sulbactam or Clindamycin.

cards.q: "Honeycombing" on High-Resolution CT?
cards.a: Idiopathic Pulmonary Fibrosis (IPF).

cards.q: Distinguishing feature of Hypersensitivity Pneumonitis?
cards.a: Exposure history (e.g., birds, hay) and reversal upon removal of agent.

cards.q: Carbon Monoxide poisoning effect on SaO2 (pulse ox)?
cards.a: Often shows 100% (pulse ox cannot distinguish HbO2 from Carboxy-Hb).

cards.q: Treatment for Carbon Monoxide poisoning?
cards.a: 100% Oxygen (Hyperbaric if severe).

cards.q: Formula for A-a gradient?
cards.a: $PAO2 - PaO2$ where $PAO2 = (FiO2 \times (Patm - PH2O)) - (PaCO2 / 0.8)$.

cards.q: Causes of Hypoxemia with a NORMAL A-a gradient?
cards.a: Hypoventilation or High Altitude.

cards.q: Causes of Hypoxemia with an INCREASED A-a gradient?
cards.a: V/Q mismatch, Shunt, or Diffusion limitation.

cards.q: Typical CXR finding in Mycoplasma pneumonia?
cards.a: Interstitial "patchy" infiltrates (looks worse than patient feels).

cards.q: Most likely diagnosis: Smoker, weight loss, hyponatremia?
cards.a: Small Cell Lung Cancer (SIADH).

cards.q: Superior Vena Cava (SVC) Syndrome is most commonly caused by?
cards.a: Bronchogenic carcinoma (Small Cell).

cards.q: Samter’s Triad?
cards.a: Asthma, Aspirin sensitivity, Nasal polyps.

cards.q: Why is Aspirin avoided in Samter's Triad?
cards.a: Leads to overproduction of leukotrienes.

cards.q: Mechanism of Albuterol?
cards.a: Beta-2 agonist (increases cAMP → bronchodilation).

cards.q: Mechanism of Tiotropium?
cards.a: Muscarinic antagonist (blocks M3 → prevents bronchoconstriction).

cards.q: Management of massive hemoptysis (>600mL)?
cards.a: Secure airway, place "bleeding side down," and perform bronchoscopy/embolization.

cards.q: Pneumonia associated with exposure to birds (parrots, turkeys)?
cards.a: Chlamydia psittaci (Psittacosis).

cards.q: Pneumonia associated with exposure to livestock or parturient cats?
cards.a: Coxiella burnetii (Q fever).

cards.q: Most common cause of pneumonia in patients with Cystic Fibrosis (adults)?
cards.a: Pseudomonas aeruginosa.

cards.q: Treatment for Pneumocystis jirovecii pneumonia (PCP)?
cards.a: Trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole (TMP-SMX).

cards.q: When to add steroids to PCP treatment in HIV patients?
cards.a: PaO2 <70 mmHg or A-a gradient ≥35 mmHg.

cards.q: Fungal pneumonia associated with bat or bird droppings in the Ohio/Mississippi River valleys?
cards.a: Histoplasmosis.

cards.q: Fungal infection associated with "Broad-based budding yeast" on microscopy?
cards.a: Blastomycosis.

cards.q: Fungal pneumonia common in the Southwest US (desert) presenting with erythema nodosum?
cards.a: Coccidioidomycosis.

cards.q: Characteristic finding of Aspergillus on silver stain?
cards.a: Septate hyphae with 45-degree (dichotomous) branching.

cards.q: Characteristic finding of Mucor species?
cards.a: Non-septate hyphae with wide-angle (90-degree) branching. Pulmonology Part 6: Pleural & Mediastinal Disease

cards.q: Definition of a "complicated" parapneumonic effusion?
cards.a: Presence of bacteria on Gram stain/culture or pH <7.2.

cards.q: Treatment for an uncomplicated parapneumonic effusion?
cards.a: Antibiotics alone (no drainage needed).

cards.q: Most common cause of a pleural effusion that is "milky" and has high lymphocytes?
cards.a: Chylothorax (often due to thoracic duct trauma or lymphoma).

cards.q: Light's Criteria: Pleural fluid LDH to Serum LDH ratio threshold for exudate?
Light's Criteria: Pleural fluid Protein to Serum Protein ratio threshold for exudate?
Common cause of a very low pleural fluid glucose (<30 mg/dL)?
cards.a: Rheumatoid Arthritis or Empyema.

cards.q: Definition of an Empyema?
cards.a: Frank pus in the pleural space.

cards.q: Most common cause of an anterior mediastinal mass (The 4 T's)?
cards.a: Thymoma, Teratoma, Thyroid (ectopic), "Terrible" Lymphoma. Pulmonology Part 7: Advanced COPD & Asthma Management

cards.q: Next step for a COPD patient with frequent exacerbations despite LAMA + LABA?
cards.a: Add Inhaled Corticosteroid (Triple Therapy: ICS + LABA + LAMA).

cards.q: Role of Roflumilast in COPD?
cards.a: PDE-4 inhibitor used to reduce exacerbations in patients with chronic bronchitis and severe obstruction.

cards.q: Common EKG finding in a patient with a massive PE and Right Heart Strain?
cards.a: New Right Bundle Branch Block (RBBB).

cards.q: Definition of "Pulsus Paradoxus"?
cards.a: Drop in systolic BP >10 mmHg during inspiration (seen in severe asthma/COPD or tamponade).

cards.q: Indication for Omalizumab in asthma?
cards.a: Severe persistent asthma with high IgE levels and poor control on ICS/LABA.

cards.q: Mechanism of Montelukast?
cards.a: Leukotriene receptor antagonist (CysLT1).

cards.q: Management of "Silent Chest" in an acute asthma exacerbation?
cards.a: Immediate intubation (indicates no air movement/impending arrest).

cards.q: First-line medication for Exercise-Induced Bronchospasm?
cards.a: SABA 10-20 minutes before exercise. Pulmonology Part 8: Critical Care & Miscellaneous

cards.q: Best initial test for suspected Sleep Apnea?
cards.a: Polysomnography (Sleep Study).

cards.q: Characteristic PFT finding in Vocal Cord Dysfunction?
cards.a: Flattened inspiratory loop (Extrathoracic obstruction).

cards.q: Diagnosis for: Young woman, recurrent pneumothorax, chylous effusion, CT shows thin-walled cysts?
cards.a: Lymphangioleiomyomatosis (LAM).

cards.q: "Flesh-colored" nodules on the shins in a patient with respiratory symptoms?
cards.a: Erythema Nodosum (highly suggestive of Sarcoidosis or Coccidioidomycosis).

cards.q: Löfgren Syndrome triad (variant of Sarcoidosis)?
cards.a: Erythema nodosum, bilateral hilar lymphadenopathy, and migratory polyarthritis.

cards.q: Preferred diagnostic step for a centrally located lung mass?
cards.a: Flexible Bronchoscopy.

cards.q: Preferred diagnostic step for a peripherally located lung mass?
cards.a: Percutaneous (Transthoracic) needle biopsy.

cards.q: Formula for calculating the PaO2 from SaO2 (The 40-50-60/70-80-90 rule)?
cards.a: SaO2 70% ≈ PaO2 40; SaO2 80% ≈ PaO2 50; SaO2 90% ≈ PaO2 60.

cards.q: Most common cause of death in patients with Sarcoidosis?
cards.a: Pulmonary Fibrosis (Respiratory Failure).

cards.q: Primary treatment for Alpha-1 Antitrypsin deficiency?
cards.a: Smoking cessation and IV Alpha-1 Antitrypsin augmentation therapy.

cards.q: Characteristic finding on CT in Bronchiectasis?
cards.a: "Signet ring" sign (dilated bronchus larger than its adjacent artery).

cards.q: Most common cause of Bronchiectasis in the US?
cards.a: Cystic Fibrosis.

cards.q: Best drug to prevent high-altitude pulmonary edema (HAPE)?
cards.a: Nifedipine (if prophylactic) or gradual ascent.

cards.q: Standard treatment for Carbon Monoxide (CO) poisoning?
cards.a: 100% Hyperbaric oxygen (if CO levels >25% or neurologic symptoms).

cards.q: Cyanide poisoning antidote often paired with CO treatment?
cards.a: Hydroxocobalamin or Sodium Thiosulfate.

cards.q: Most common EKG finding in Pulmonary Hypertension?
cards.a: Right ventricular hypertrophy (Tall R wave in V1, Right Axis Deviation). Pulmonology Part 9: Tuberculosis (Deep Dive)

cards.q: Appearance of Tuberculosis on Histology?
cards.a: Caseating granulomas with central necrosis and Langhans giant cells.

cards.q: Definition of "Miliary" TB?
cards.a: Hematogenous spread of TB resulting in small "millet seed" lesions throughout the lungs and organs.

cards.q: Site of "Pott's Disease"?
cards.a: Tuberculosis of the spine (vertebrae).

cards.q: Most common extrapulmonary site of TB?
cards.a: Lymph nodes (Scrofula).

cards.q: Screening frequency for TB in healthcare workers with a baseline negative test?
cards.a: Only after an exposure (per latest CDC guidelines; no longer annually for all).

cards.q: Minimum time for "Standard" TB treatment duration?
cards.a: 6 months (2 months RIPE, 4 months RI).

cards.q: Major side effect of Rifampin?
cards.a: Orange discoloration of body fluids (urine, tears) and CYP450 induction.

cards.q: Which TB drug is contraindicated in pregnancy?
