cards.q: Definition of a "solitary pulmonary nodule"?
cards.a: A single, well-circumscribed lesion <3 cm in diameter.

cards.q: Management of a lung nodule with "popcorn" calcification on CT?
cards.a: Observation (indicates a benign Hamartoma).

cards.q: Most important risk factor for lung cancer (besides smoking)?
cards.a: Radon gas exposure.

cards.q: Paraneoplastic syndrome associated with Squamous Cell Lung Cancer?
cards.a: Hypercalcemia due to PTHrP production.

cards.q: Paraneoplastic syndrome associated with Small Cell Lung Cancer (renal)?
cards.a: SIADH (causing euvolemic hyponatremia).

cards.q: Paraneoplastic syndrome associated with Small Cell Lung Cancer (adrenal)?
cards.a: Ectopic ACTH production (Cushing Syndrome).

cards.q: Classic presentation of Lambert-Eaton Myasthenic Syndrome?
cards.a: Proximal muscle weakness that improves with use.

cards.q: Pancoast Tumor (Superior Sulcus Tumor) typically presents with?
cards.a: Horner Syndrome (Ptosis, Miosis, Anhidrosis) and shoulder pain.

cards.q: Standard screening protocol for lung cancer (USPSTF)?
cards.a: Annual Low-Dose CT for adults 50–80 with a 20 pack-year history who currently smoke or quit in the last 15 years.

cards.q: Which lung cancer is "central" and characterized by intercellular bridges on histology?
cards.a: Squamous Cell Carcinoma. Pulmonology Part 11: Occupational & Environmental Lung Disease

cards.q: Pneumoconiosis associated with coal mining?
cards.a: Coal Worker’s Pneumoconiosis (Black Lung).

cards.q: Caplan Syndrome?
cards.a: Combination of Rheumatoid Arthritis and pneumoconiosis (usually coal or silica) with intrapulmonary nodules.

cards.q: Occupational exposure associated with Berylliosis?
cards.a: Aerospace, electronics, or nuclear power industries.

cards.q: Pathological similarity between Berylliosis and Sarcoidosis?
cards.a: Both present with non-caseating granulomas.

cards.q: Primary treatment for Berylliosis?
cards.a: Systemic Corticosteroids.

cards.q: Distinction between "Farmer’s Lung" and "Silicosis"?
cards.a: Farmer’s Lung is Hypersensitivity Pneumonitis (moldy hay); Silicosis is a fibrotic pneumoconiosis (sandblasting/rock mining).

cards.q: Byssinosis is caused by inhalation of?
cards.a: Cotton dust ("Monday morning chest tightness").

cards.q: Asbestos exposure significantly increases the risk of which two cancers?
cards.a: Bronchogenic Carcinoma (more common) and Mesothelioma (more specific). Pulmonology Part 12: Rare but High-Yield Entities

cards.q: Pulmonary Alveolar Proteinosis (PAP) is caused by?
cards.a: Accumulation of surfactant in the alveoli due to anti-GM-CSF antibodies.

cards.q: Characteristic "Periodic Acid-Schiff (PAS) positive" material in alveoli?
cards.a: Pulmonary Alveolar Proteinosis.

cards.q: Treatment for Pulmonary Alveolar Proteinosis?
cards.a: Whole-lung lavage.

cards.q: Characteristic finding of Goodpasture Syndrome?
cards.a: Anti-GBM antibodies attacking the lungs (hemoptysis) and kidneys (hematuria).

cards.q: Primary treatment for Wegener's (Granulomatosis with Polyangiitis)?
cards.a: Corticosteroids and Cyclophosphamide (or Rituximab).

cards.q: Serological marker for Granulomatosis with Polyangiitis?
cards.a: c-ANCA (PR3-ANCA).

cards.q: Serological marker for Churg-Strauss (Eosinophilic Granulomatosis with Polyangiitis)?
cards.a: p-ANCA (MPO-ANCA) and high peripheral eosinophil count. Pulmonology Part 13: Pulmonary Critical Care (Mechanical Ventilation)

cards.q: Initial Tidal Volume setting for a patient with ARDS?
cards.a: 6 mL/kg of Ideal Body Weight.

cards.q: Goal for Plateau Pressure in ARDS management?
cards.a: <30 cm H2O.

cards.q: Primary purpose of PEEP (Positive End-Expiratory Pressure) in ARDS?
cards.a: To recruit collapsed alveoli and improve oxygenation.

cards.q: Potential complication of high PEEP or high Tidal Volumes?
cards.a: Barotrauma (Pneumothorax) or Volutrauma.

cards.q: First-line management for a patient with Acute Cardiogenic Pulmonary Edema?
cards.a: Supplemental O2, Loop Diuretics (Lasix), and Nitroglycerin (if BP allows).

cards.q: How does PEEP affect cardiac output?
cards.a: Decreases cardiac output by increasing intrathoracic pressure and reducing venous return (preload).

cards.q: Clinical sign of Carbon Dioxide Narcosis?
cards.a: Somnolence, confusion, and asterixis in a patient with high PaCO2.

cards.q: Management of "Auto-PEEP" (breath stacking) in an intubated COPD patient?
cards.a: Disconnect the circuit briefly to allow full exhalation and decrease the respiratory rate.

cards.q: Mechanism of Roflumilast in COPD management?
cards.a: Phosphodiesterase-4 (PDE-4) inhibitor that increases cAMP to reduce inflammation.

cards.q: Side effect of Theophylline toxicity?
cards.a: Seizures and cardiac arrhythmias (narrow therapeutic index).

cards.q: Primary drug class for the treatment of Pulmonary Arterial Hypertension (Group 1)?
cards.a: Endothelin receptor antagonists (e.g., Bosentan) or PDE-5 inhibitors (e.g., Sildenafil).

cards.q: Common side effect of inhaled Tiotropium?
cards.a: Dry mouth (Anticholinergic effect).

cards.q: Best initial antibiotic for a "Rusty" sputum pneumonia?
cards.a: Ceftriaxone plus Azithromycin (covering S. pneumoniae).

cards.q: Preferred antibiotic for a "foul-smelling" sputum pneumonia?
cards.a: Ampicillin-sulbactam (covers anaerobes and aerobes in aspiration).

cards.q: Mechanism of Omalizumab in severe asthma?
cards.a: Monoclonal antibody that binds to IgE, preventing it from binding to mast cells.

cards.q: First-line medication to treat a stable patient with Pneumocystis jirovecii and a sulfa allergy?
cards.a: Pentamidine or Atovaquone. Pulmonology Part 15: Clinical "Buzzwords" & Physical Exam

cards.q: Physical exam finding: "Velcro-like" inspiratory crackles?
cards.a: Idiopathic Pulmonary Fibrosis.

cards.q: Egophony (E to A change) indicates?
cards.a: Lung consolidation (Pneumonia).

cards.q: Definition of "Whispered Pectoriloquy"?
cards.a: Whispered sounds are heard clearly through the stethoscope, indicating consolidation.

cards.q: Physical exam finding in a large Pleural Effusion?
cards.a: Decreased tactile fremitus, dullness to percussion, and decreased breath sounds.

cards.q: Tracheal deviation AWAY from the affected side?
cards.a: Tension Pneumothorax or Large Pleural Effusion.

cards.q: Tracheal deviation TOWARD the affected side?
cards.a: Atelectasis or Pneumonectomy.

cards.q: Meaning of "Tactile Fremitus" in Pneumothorax?
cards.a: Decreased (air in the pleural space blocks vibration).

cards.q: Meaning of "Tactile Fremitus" in Pneumonia?
cards.a: Increased (solid/liquid medium conducts vibration better). Pulmonology Part 16: Sleep Medicine & Ventilation Nuances

cards.q: Distinction between OSA and Central Sleep Apnea (CSA)?
cards.a: CSA lacks respiratory effort (no chest wall movement); OSA has respiratory effort against an obstruction.

cards.q: "Cheyne-Stokes" respiration is commonly seen in?
cards.a: Heart Failure or Stroke (form of Central Sleep Apnea).

cards.q: Primary risk factor for Obesity Hypoventilation Syndrome (Pickwickian)?
cards.a: BMI ≥30.

cards.q: Definition of Obesity Hypoventilation Syndrome?
cards.a: Daytime hypercapnia (PaCO2 >45 mmHg) in an obese patient not explained by other causes.

cards.q: What is "Veno-venous (VV) ECMO" used for?
cards.a: Severe ARDS refractory to conventional mechanical ventilation.

cards.q: Target PaO2 for a patient with ARDS?
cards.a: 55–80 mmHg (avoiding oxygen toxicity).

cards.q: Definition of "Permissive Hypercapnia" in ARDS?
cards.a: Allowing high PaCO2 to maintain low tidal volumes and protect the lungs from barotrauma. Pulmonology Part 17: Differential Diagnosis "Red Flags"

cards.q: Unilateral wheezing in a child/toddler?
cards.a: Foreign body aspiration.

cards.q: Unilateral wheezing in an adult smoker?
cards.a: Endobronchial tumor (Lung cancer).

cards.q: "Sudden onset of dyspnea and pleuritic chest pain in a tall, thin male smoker"?
cards.a: Primary Spontaneous Pneumothorax.

cards.q: "Chest pain, dyspnea, and friction rub" 2-3 days after a viral illness?
cards.a: Pleurisy (Pleuritis).

cards.q: Recurrent pneumonia in the SAME lung lobe?
cards.a: Suggests localized obstruction (e.g., Bronchogenic carcinoma or foreign body).

cards.q: "Bat-wing" or "Butterfly" opacities on CXR?
cards.a: Pulmonary Edema (CHF).

cards.q: "Kerley B lines" on CXR indicate?
cards.a: Increased pulmonary venous pressure (CHF/Pulmonary Edema).

cards.q: Common cause of "Eggshell calcification" of hilar nodes besides Silicosis?
cards.a: Sarcoidosis (rarely) or Treated Lymphoma. Pulmonology Part 18: Critical Lab Values

cards.q: A pH <7.2 in pleural fluid always necessitates?
cards.a: Drainage (Chest tube).

cards.q: What is a "Normal" A-a gradient for a 20-year-old?
cards.a: ~9 mmHg (Formula: Age/4 + 4).

cards.q: Meaning of a "high" DLCO?
cards.a: Alveolar hemorrhage (e.g., Goodpasture) or Asthma.

cards.q: A PaO2/FiO2 ratio of <100 defines?
cards.a: Severe ARDS.

cards.q: Gold standard test for Cystic Fibrosis?

topic: Gastroenterology — IBD, GI bleed, liver disease, pancreatitis

cards.q: Primary site of involvement in Crohn’s Disease?
cards.a: Terminal ileum (though it can affect any part of the GI tract).

cards.q: Defining endoscopic appearance of Crohn’s Disease?
cards.a: Cobblestoning and skip lesions.

cards.q: Characteristic biopsy finding in Crohn’s Disease?
cards.a: Non-caseating granulomas.

cards.q: Most common site for Ulcerative Colitis (UC)?
cards.a: Rectum (always involved) with continuous proximal spread.

cards.q: Depth of inflammation in Ulcerative Colitis?
cards.a: Mucosa and submucosa only.

cards.q: Depth of inflammation in Crohn’s Disease?
cards.a: Transmural inflammation.

cards.q: Radiographic sign associated with chronic Ulcerative Colitis?
cards.a: "Lead pipe" appearance due to loss of haustra.

cards.q: Serologic marker often positive in UC?
cards.a: p-ANCA.

cards.q: Serologic marker often positive in Crohn’s Disease?
cards.a: ASCA (Anti-Saccharomyces cerevisiae antibodies).

cards.q: Most common fistula type in Crohn's Disease?
cards.a: Perianal fistula.

cards.q: IBD subtype associated with Primary Sclerosing Cholangitis (PSC)?
cards.a: Ulcerative Colitis.

cards.q: Extra-intestinal manifestation common to both UC and Crohn's?
cards.a: Erythema nodosum or Pyoderma gangrenosum.

cards.q: Maintenance therapy for mild-to-moderate UC?
cards.a: 5-ASA compounds (Mesalamine, Sulfasalazine).

cards.q: Standard treatment for an acute IBD flare?
cards.a: Corticosteroids (Prednisone or IV Methylprednisolone).

cards.q: Curative surgical procedure for Ulcerative Colitis?
cards.a: Total proctocolectomy. Part 2: Gastrointestinal Bleeding (GIB)

cards.q: Anatomical landmark separating Upper from Lower GI bleed?
cards.a: Ligament of Treitz.

cards.q: Most common cause of Upper GI Bleed (UGIB)?
cards.a: Peptic Ulcer Disease (PUD).

cards.q: Primary diagnostic test for suspected UGIB?
cards.a: Upper Endoscopy (EGD).

cards.q: Laboratory ratio suggestive of UGIB?
cards.a: Elevated BUN/Creatinine ratio (>20:1).

cards.q: Medication to initiate immediately in suspected Variceal Bleed?
cards.a: Octreotide (somatostatin analog).

cards.q: Prophylactic antibiotic class for cirrhotic patients with UGIB?
cards.a: Fluoroquinolones or Ceftriaxone.

cards.q: Most common cause of Lower GI Bleed (LGIB) in adults >60?
cards.a: Diverticulosis.

cards.q: Presentation of bleeding from Angiodysplasia?
cards.a: Painless hematochezia in elderly patients (often associated with aortic stenosis).

cards.q: First step in managing a hemodynamically unstable GI bleed?
cards.a: Two large-bore IVs and fluid resuscitation.

cards.q: Definitive management for refractory esophageal variceal bleeding?
cards.a: TIPS (Transjugular Intrahepatic Portosystemic Shunt).

cards.q: Common cause of UGIB following forceful vomiting?
cards.a: Mallory-Weiss Tear.

cards.q: Definition of "Hematochezia"?
cards.a: Bright red blood per rectum, usually indicating a lower GI source.

cards.q: Definition of "Melena"?
cards.a: Black, tarry stools indicating digested blood, usually from an upper GI source.

cards.q: Finding on EGD that suggests a high risk of ulcer re-bleeding?
cards.a: Visible vessel or adherent clot (Forrest classification). Part 3: Liver Disease & Cirrhosis

cards.q: Physical exam finding specific to hepatic encephalopathy?
cards.a: Asterixis (flapping tremor).

cards.q: Standard medical treatment for Hepatic Encephalopathy?
cards.a: Lactulose (to trap ammonia) and Rifaximin.

cards.q: Common cause of Budd-Chiari Syndrome?
cards.a: Hepatic vein thrombosis.

cards.q: SAAG score indicating portal hypertension-related ascites?
cards.a: SAAG ≥ 1.1 g/dL.

cards.q: Primary screening test for Hepatocellular Carcinoma (HCC)?
cards.a: Ultrasound and Alpha-fetoprotein (AFP) every 6 months.

cards.q: Gold standard for diagnosing Wilson’s Disease?
cards.a: Increased 24-hour urinary copper or Liver biopsy.

cards.q: Triad of Hemochromatosis?
cards.a: Cirrhosis, Diabetes ("Bronze Diabetes"), and Skin hyperpigmentation.

cards.q: Genetic mutation associated with Hemochromatosis?
cards.a: HFE gene (C282Y).

cards.q: First-line treatment for Hereditary Hemochromatosis?
cards.a: Therapeutic phlebotomy.

cards.q: Classic laboratory finding in Alcoholic Liver Disease?
cards.a: AST:ALT ratio > 2:1.

cards.q: Diagnostic criteria for Spontaneous Bacterial Peritonitis (SBP)?
cards.a: Ascitic fluid Absolute Neutrophil Count (ANC) > 250 cells/mm³.

cards.q: Empiric antibiotic for SBP?
cards.a: Third-generation cephalosporin (Cefotaxime).

cards.q: Primary Biliary Cholangitis (PBC) target population?
cards.a: Middle-aged women.

cards.q: Hallmark antibody for Primary Biliary Cholangitis?
cards.a: Anti-mitochondrial antibody (AMA).

cards.q: Key laboratory abnormality in Nonalcoholic Fatty Liver Disease (NAFLD)?
cards.a: ALT > AST (usually in the setting of metabolic syndrome). Part 4: Pancreatitis

cards.q: Two most common causes of Acute Pancreatitis?
cards.a: Gallstones and Alcohol.

cards.q: Most specific serum enzyme for Acute Pancreatitis?
cards.a: Lipase.

cards.q: Diagnostic imaging of choice for Acute Pancreatitis?
cards.a: Abdominal CT with contrast (though often clinical diagnosis).

cards.q: Criteria used to predict severity/mortality in Pancreatitis?
cards.a: Ranson’s Criteria or APACHE II score.

cards.q: Classic physical sign of hemorrhagic pancreatitis (periumbilical)?
cards.a: Cullen’s sign.

cards.q: Classic physical sign of hemorrhagic pancreatitis (flank)?
cards.a: Grey Turner’s sign.

cards.q: Most common complication of Acute Pancreatitis (weeks later)?
cards.a: Pancreatic pseudocyst.

cards.q: Classic triad of Chronic Pancreatitis?
cards.a: Steatorrhea, Diabetes Mellitus, and Pancreatic calcifications.

cards.q: Best initial test for Chronic Pancreatitis?
cards.a: Abdominal X-ray or CT showing calcifications.

cards.q: Treatment for malabsorption in Chronic Pancreatitis?
cards.a: Pancreatic enzyme supplementation (Lipase/Amylase/Protease).

cards.q: Major risk factor for Pancreatic Adenocarcinoma?
cards.a: Smoking.

cards.q: Tumor marker for Pancreatic Cancer?
Painless jaundice and a palpable gallbladder (Courvoisier sign) suggests?
cards.a: Pancreatic Head Carcinoma. Part 5: Advanced GI & Hepatobiliary Integration

cards.q: Most common cause of jaundice in pregnancy?
cards.a: Viral hepatitis.

cards.q: Management of asymptomatic gallstones?
cards.a: Observation (no surgery).

cards.q: Treatment of choice for Choledocholithiasis?
cards.a: ERCP (Endoscopic Retrograde Cholangiopancreatography).

cards.q: Charcot’s Triad for Ascending Cholangitis?
cards.a: Fever, RUQ pain, and Jaundice.

cards.q: Reynolds’ Pentad (for Cholangitis)?
cards.a: Charcot’s Triad + Hypotension + Altered Mental Status.

cards.q: Primary risk factor for Esophageal Adenocarcinoma?
cards.a: Barrett’s Esophagus (from chronic GERD).

cards.q: Type of esophageal cancer associated with smoking and alcohol?
cards.a: Squamous Cell Carcinoma.

cards.q: First-line medication for symptomatic GERD?
cards.a: Proton Pump Inhibitors (PPIs).

cards.q: Gold standard for diagnosing GERD (if diagnosis unclear)?
cards.a: 24-hour pH monitoring.

cards.q: Best test to confirm H. pylori eradication?
cards.a: Urea Breath Test or Stool Antigen Test.

cards.q: Classic laboratory finding in Autoimmune Hepatitis?
cards.a: Anti-smooth muscle antibodies (ASMA).

cards.q: Treatment for Wilson's Disease?
cards.a: Penicillamine or Trientine (Copper chelators).

cards.q: Definitive treatment for Alpha-1 Antitrypsin deficiency liver disease?
cards.a: Liver transplantation.

cards.q: Medication used to decrease portal pressure in Cirrhosis?
cards.a: Non-selective beta-blockers (Propranolol, Nadolol).

cards.q: Most common cause of Small Bowel Obstruction (SBO)?
cards.a: Post-surgical adhesions.

cards.q: Most common cause of Large Bowel Obstruction?
cards.a: Colorectal cancer.

cards.q: Presentation of Achalasia on Barium Swallow?
cards.a: "Bird’s beak" tapering of the distal esophagus.

cards.q: Pathophysiology of Achalasia?
cards.a: Loss of myenteric (Auerbach) plexus in the distal esophagus.

cards.q: Initial treatment for C. difficile infection?
cards.a: Oral Vancomycin or Fidaxomicin.

cards.q: Complication of C. difficile characterized by colonic dilation?
cards.a: Toxic Megacolon.

cards.q: Classic biopsy finding in Celiac Disease?
cards.a: Villous atrophy and crypt hyperplasia.

cards.q: Highly sensitive antibody for Celiac Disease?
cards.a: Anti-tissue transglutaminase (tTG) IgA.

cards.q: Condition associated with Dermatitis Herpetiformis?
cards.a: Celiac Disease.

cards.q: Screening recommendation for Colon Cancer (average risk)?
cards.a: Colonoscopy every 10 years starting at age 45.

cards.q: First-line management for Zenker’s Diverticulum?
cards.a: Surgical cricopharyngeal myotomy.

cards.q: Diagnostic finding in Boerhaave Syndrome?
cards.a: Pneumomediastinum (air in the mediastinum) on X-ray.

cards.q: Difference between Mallory-Weiss and Boerhaave?
cards.a: Mallory-Weiss is a mucosal tear; Boerhaave is a full-thickness rupture.

cards.q: Primary electrolyte abnormality in refeeding syndrome?
cards.a: Hypophosphatemia.

cards.q: Presentation of Vitamin B12 deficiency in GI disease?
cards.a: Megaloblastic anemia and subacute combined degeneration of the spinal cord.

cards.q: GI disorder associated with "string sign" on contrast imaging?
cards.a: Crohn's Disease (terminal ileum narrowing).

cards.q: Risk factor for Porcelain Gallbladder?
cards.a: Chronic cholecystitis (high risk for gallbladder carcinoma).

cards.q: Most common cause of drug-induced liver injury in the US?
cards.a: Acetaminophen.

cards.q: Antidote for Acetaminophen toxicity?
cards.a: N-acetylcysteine (NAC).

cards.q: Serum marker for primary hepatocellular carcinoma?
cards.a: Alpha-fetoprotein (AFP).

cards.q: Key ultrasound finding for Acute Cholecystitis?
cards.a: Gallbladder wall thickening and pericholecystic fluid.

cards.q: Most sensitive test for Acute Cholecystitis?
cards.a: HIDA scan (Cholescintigraphy).

cards.q: Treatment for primary biliary cholangitis?
cards.a: Ursodeoxycholic acid.

cards.q: Defining feature of Dubin-Johnson syndrome?
cards.a: Conjugated hyperbilirubinemia and a "black liver."

cards.q: Cause of Gilbert Syndrome?
cards.a: Reduced UGT1A1 activity leading to unconjugated hyperbilirubinemia during stress.

cards.q: Major risk of Crigler-Najjar Syndrome Type I?
cards.a: Kernicterus (due to absent UGT enzyme).

cards.q: Management of a Pancreatic Pseudocyst <6cm and asymptomatic?
cards.a: Observation/Expectant management.

cards.q: Complication of TPN (Total Parenteral Nutrition)?
cards.a: Gallstones/Biliary sludge.

cards.q: Primary cause of Mesenteric Ischemia?
cards.a: Embolism (often from Atrial Fibrillation).

cards.q: Clinical presentation of Chronic Mesenteric Ischemia?
cards.a: "Abdominal angina" (post-prandial pain) and weight loss.

cards.q: Most common benign liver tumor?
cards.a: Hemangioma.

cards.q: Liver tumor associated with Oral Contraceptive Use?
cards.a: Hepatic Adenoma.

cards.q: Treatment for Hepatic Adenoma >5cm?
cards.a: Surgical resection (due to rupture/malignancy risk).

cards.q: Hallmark of Zollinger-Ellison Syndrome?
cards.a: Gastrinoma leading to multiple, refractory peptic ulcers.

cards.q: Screening test for Zollinger-Ellison Syndrome?
cards.a: Serum gastrin levels (>1000 pg/mL).

cards.q: Confirmatory test for Zollinger-Ellison Syndrome?
cards.a: Secretin stimulation test (gastrin levels remain high).

cards.q: Major site for Gastrinomas?
cards.a: Pancreas or Duodenum (Gastrinoma Triangle).

cards.q: Primary management of Boerhaave Syndrome?
cards.a: Emergent surgical repair.

cards.q: Classic presentation of Ischemic Colitis?
cards.a: Pain followed by bloody diarrhea in the "watershed" areas (splenic flexure).

cards.q: Finding on CT for Ischemic Colitis?
cards.a: "Thumbprinting" (mucosal edema).

cards.q: Screening for patients with FAP (Familial Adenomatous Polyposis)?
cards.a: Annual sigmoidoscopy starting at age 10-12.

cards.q: Diagnostic finding for Whipple's Disease?
cards.a: PAS-positive macrophages in the lamina propria.

cards.q: Treatment for Whipple's Disease?
cards.a: Ceftriaxone followed by TMP-SMX for one year.

cards.q: Definition of Barrett's Esophagus?
cards.a: Intestinal metaplasia (Squamous to Columnar epithelium).

cards.q: Most common cause of viral hepatitis worldwide?
cards.a: Hepatitis B (HBV).

cards.q: Serologic marker indicating active Hepatitis B replication?
cards.a: HBeAg.

cards.q: Serologic marker indicating immunity to Hepatitis B (vaccination)?
cards.a: Anti-HBs only.

cards.q: Serologic marker indicating immunity to Hepatitis B (prior infection)?
cards.a: Anti-HBs and Anti-HBc (IgG).

cards.q: First-line treatment for Hepatitis C (HCV)?
cards.a: Direct-acting antivirals (e.g., Sofosbuvir).

cards.q: Standard of care for achalasia if myotomy is refused?
cards.a: Botulinum toxin injection or pneumatic dilation.

cards.q: Most common cause of secretory diarrhea?
cards.a: Vibrio cholerae or Enterotoxigenic E. coli (ETEC).

cards.q: Osmotic gap in Osmotic Diarrhea?
cards.a: High (>125 mOsm/kg).

cards.q: Common cause of esophageal webs and iron deficiency anemia?
cards.a: Plummer-Vinson Syndrome.

cards.q: Highest risk factor for Gastric Adenocarcinoma?
cards.a: H. pylori infection.

cards.q: Physical exam sign for Gastric Cancer metastasis to the supraclavicular node?
cards.a: Virchow's Node.

cards.q: Physical exam sign for Gastric Cancer metastasis to the periumbilical area?
cards.a: Sister Mary Joseph nodule.

cards.q: Presentation of Menetrier's Disease?
cards.a: Hyperplastic gastropathy, protein loss, and "brain-like" rugae.

cards.q: Most common site for a Diverticulum?
cards.a: Sigmoid colon.

cards.q: Management of uncomplicated Diverticulitis?
cards.a: Bowel rest and antibiotics (Ciprofloxacin + Metronidazole).

cards.q: Complication of Diverticulitis requiring surgery?
cards.a: Abscess, perforation, or fistula.

cards.q: Best imaging for Diverticulitis?
cards.a: CT scan with oral and IV contrast.

cards.q: Why avoid Colonoscopy during acute Diverticulitis?
cards.a: High risk of perforation.

cards.q: Characteristic of Meckel’s Diverticulum?
cards.a: Rule of 2s (2 inches long, 2 feet from ileocecal valve, 2% of population).

cards.q: Diagnostic test for Meckel’s Diverticulum?
cards.a: Technetium-99m pertechnetate scan ("Meckel scan").

cards.q: Common cause of Small Intestinal Bacterial Overgrowth (SIBO)?
cards.a: Dysmotility (e.g., Scleroderma, Diabetes) or Roux-en-Y surgery.

cards.q: Gold standard diagnosis for SIBO?
cards.a: Jejunal aspirate culture (though breath tests are common).

cards.q: Treatment for SIBO?
cards.a: Rifaximin.

cards.q: Mechanism of Lactulose in Cirrhosis?
cards.a: Converted to lactic acid, acidifying the gut and converting NH3 to NH4+.

cards.q: Most common cause of Budd-Chiari in young women?
cards.a: Oral contraceptive use or underlying hypercoagulability.

cards.q: Major risk of Primary Sclerosing Cholangitis?
cards.a: Cholangiocarcinoma.

cards.q: "Onion skin" fibrosis of bile ducts is seen in?
cards.a: Primary Sclerosing Cholangitis.

cards.q: Finding on ERCP for PSC?
cards.a: "Beading" of the intrahepatic and extrahepatic bile ducts.

cards.q: Management of Gastric Varices in the absence of esophageal varices?
cards.a: Splenic vein thrombosis (often due to pancreatitis).

cards.q: Treatment for Splenic Vein Thrombosis?
cards.a: Splenectomy.

cards.q: Leading cause of death in patients with Cirrhosis?
cards.a: Variceal hemorrhage or Hepatocellular carcinoma.

cards.q: First marker to appear in acute Hepatitis B infection?
cards.a: HBsAg (Hepatitis B surface antigen).

cards.q: Only marker present during the "Window Period" of Hep B?
cards.a: Anti-HBc IgM.

cards.q: Marker indicating high infectivity and active viral replication in HBV?
cards.a: HBeAg (Envelope antigen).

cards.q: Presence of Anti-HBs and Anti-HBc IgG indicates?
cards.a: Recovery from natural Hepatitis B infection and lifelong immunity.

cards.q: Presence of Anti-HBs alone (without Anti-HBc) indicates?
cards.a: Immunity via Hepatitis B vaccination.

cards.q: Requirement for Hepatitis D (Delta agent) infection?
cards.a: Co-infection or superinfection with Hepatitis B (requires HBsAg).

cards.q: Mode of transmission for Hepatitis A and E?
cards.a: Fecal-oral route ("The vowels hit the bowels").

cards.q: Hepatitis virus with high mortality rate in pregnant women?
cards.a: Hepatitis E.

cards.q: Definition of Chronic Hepatitis B?
cards.a: HBsAg persistence for >6 months. Part 7: Gastric Pathologies & PUD

cards.q: Most common cause of chronic gastritis?
cards.a: H. pylori infection.

cards.q: Location of H. pylori colonization in the stomach?
cards.a: Antrum.

cards.q: Type of Gastritis involving the fundus and associated with Pernicious Anemia?
cards.a: Autoimmune Metaplastic Atrophic Gastritis (Type A).

cards.q: Mechanism of Pernicious Anemia in Type A Gastritis?
cards.a: Antibodies against Parietal cells and Intrinsic Factor.

cards.q: Complication of H. pylori besides PUD?
cards.a: MALT Lymphoma and Gastric Adenocarcinoma.

cards.q: First-line "Triple Therapy" for H. pylori?
cards.a: PPI + Amoxicillin + Clarithromycin.

cards.q: Preferred H. pylori treatment in areas with high Clarithromycin resistance?
cards.a: Bismuth Quadruple Therapy (PPI + Bismuth + Metronidazole + Tetracycline).

cards.q: Classic symptom of a Duodenal Ulcer?
cards.a: Pain that improves with food.

cards.q: Classic symptom of a Gastric Ulcer?
cards.a: Pain that worsens with food (leads to weight loss).

cards.q: Most common location for a Gastric Cancer?
cards.a: Lesser curvature of the antrum. Part 8: Malabsorption & Small Bowel

cards.q: Pathophysiology of Celiac Disease?
cards.a: Immune-mediated damage to small bowel villi due to gluten exposure (gliadin).

cards.q: Skin manifestation of Celiac Disease?
cards.a: Dermatitis Herpetiformis (IgA deposits at dermal papillae).

cards.q: Definitive diagnosis for Celiac Disease?
cards.a: Small bowel biopsy showing villous atrophy.

cards.q: Findings in Tropical Sprue compared to Celiac?
cards.a: Similar villous atrophy but affects the entire small bowel (Celiac is distal duo/proximal jejunum).

cards.q: Diagnostic test for Lactose Intolerance?
cards.a: Hydrogen Breath Test.

cards.q: Stool findings in Malabsorption/Steatorrhea?
cards.a: Increased fecal fat (>7g/day) and decreased Sudam III stain.

cards.q: Vitamin deficiency common after ileal resection?
cards.a: Vitamin B12 and Bile Acid deficiency.

cards.q: Classic presentation of Whipple’s Disease?
cards.a: Diarrhea, Weight loss, Arthralgia, and Neurological symptoms.

cards.q: Characteristic of Small Intestinal Bacterial Overgrowth (SIBO)?
cards.a: Premature deconjugation of bile acids leading to fat malabsorption. Part 9: Vascular & Structural Disorders

cards.q: Definition of "Angiodysplasia"?
cards.a: Tortuous, dilated submucosal veins; common cause of painless hematochezia in elderly.

cards.q: Risk factors for Ischemic Colitis?
cards.a: Hypotension (shock), vasculitis, or extreme exercise (marathons).

cards.q: Most common site for Ischemic Colitis?
cards.a: Splenic flexure (Griffith’s point) and Rectosigmoid junction (Sudek’s point).

cards.q: Presentation of Acute Mesenteric Ischemia?
cards.a: "Pain out of proportion to exam" in a patient with Atrial Fibrillation.

cards.q: Management of a Sigmoid Volvulus?
cards.a: Sigmoidoscopic decompression (detorsion).

cards.q: Radiographic appearance of Sigmoid Volvulus?
cards.a: "Coffee bean" sign on X-ray.

cards.q: Definitive treatment for recurrent Sigmoid Volvulus?
cards.a: Elective sigmoid resection.

cards.q: Most common site for an indirect inguinal hernia?
cards.a: Through the deep inguinal ring (lateral to inferior epigastric vessels). Part 10: Advanced Liver & Biliary (Sleisenger/Harrison level)

cards.q: Pathophysiology of Hepatorenal Syndrome?
cards.a: Splanchnic vasodilation leading to renal vasoconstriction and failure.

cards.q: Treatment for Hepatorenal Syndrome?
cards.a: Midodrine, Octreotide, and Albumin.

cards.q: Best initial step for a patient with jaundice and dilated ducts on US?
cards.a: ERCP or MRCP.

cards.q: Primary risk factor for Gallbladder Adenocarcinoma?
cards.a: Chronic cholelithiasis and Porcelain Gallbladder.

cards.q: Management of symptomatic cholelithiasis in a pregnant patient?
cards.a: Conservative management first, then cholecystectomy in 2nd trimester if needed.

cards.q: Expected lab findings in Extrahepatic Biliary Obstruction?
cards.a: Elevated Conjugated Bilirubin, High Alk Phos, and High GGT.

cards.q: What does an isolated elevation of Alk Phos (normal GGT) suggest?
cards.a: Bone disease or pregnancy, not liver/biliary disease.

cards.q: Cause of "Pre-hepatic" jaundice?
cards.a: Hemolysis (excess Unconjugated Bilirubin).

cards.q: Definition of Gilbert Syndrome?
cards.a: Mildly decreased UGT activity; asymptomatic jaundice during stress/fasting. Part 11: Miscellaneous High-Yield GI

cards.q: Most common cause of lower GI bleed in children?
cards.a: Meckel’s Diverticulum.

cards.q: Cause of a "Corkscrew Esophagus" on barium swallow?
cards.a: Diffuse Esophageal Spasm (DES).

cards.q: First-line treatment for Diffuse Esophageal Spasm?
cards.a: Calcium channel blockers or Nitrates.

cards.q: Criteria for diagnosing Irritable Bowel Syndrome (IBS)?
cards.a: Rome IV Criteria (recurrent abdominal pain 1 day/week for 3 months).

cards.q: Alarm symptoms in IBS that warrant further workup?
cards.a: Weight loss, nocturnal diarrhea, blood in stool, or age >50.

cards.q: Management of Ogilvie Syndrome (Colonic Pseudo-obstruction)?
cards.a: Neostigmine or colonic decompression.

cards.q: Most common cause of Boerhaave Syndrome?
cards.a: latrogenic (endoscopy) or forceful retching.

cards.q: Characteristic finding in Intussusception?
cards.a: "Currant jelly" stools and "Target sign" on ultrasound.

cards.q: Primary management of Intussusception in children?
cards.a: Air or Contrast enema (both diagnostic and therapeutic). Part 12: Pancreatic & Biliary Complications

cards.q: Lab marker to differentiate Pancreatitis from other causes of RUQ pain?
cards.a: Serum Lipase >3x upper limit of normal.

cards.q: Management of infected pancreatic necrosis?
cards.a: Antibiotics (Meropenem) and delayed necrosectomy.

cards.q: Most common location of a Gastrinoma?
cards.a: Duodenum (60-90%).

cards.q: Association of Gastrinomas with which genetic syndrome?
cards.a: MEN1 (Multiple Endocrine Neoplasia type 1).

cards.q: Best test to visualize the "Onion Skinning" of PSC?
cards.a: Liver biopsy (though MRCP/ERCP are often used for diagnosis).

cards.q: Drug that can cause drug-induced pancreatitis?
cards.a: Valproic acid, Diuretics (Furosemide, Thiazides), Azathioprine.

cards.q: Classic electrolyte complication of Acute Pancreatitis?
cards.a: Hypocalcemia (due to saponification in fat necrosis). Part 13: Colorectal & Anorectal

cards.q: Definition of Internal Hemorrhoids?
cards.a: Above the dentate line; painless bleeding.

cards.q: Definition of External Hemorrhoids?
cards.a: Below the dentate line; painful (especially if thrombosed).

cards.q: First-line treatment for Anal Fissures?
cards.a: Fiber, stool softeners, and topical nitroglycerin or diltiazem.

cards.q: Most common location for an Anal Fissure?
cards.a: Posterior midline.

cards.q: Lynch Syndrome (HNPCC) genetic defect?
cards.a: DNA Mismatch Repair (MMR) genes (MLH1, MSH2).

cards.q: Extracolonic cancers associated with Lynch Syndrome?
cards.a: Endometrial, Ovarian, and Gastric cancer.

cards.q: Gardner Syndrome presentation?
cards.a: FAP + Osteomas + Soft tissue tumors + Impacted teeth.

cards.q: Peutz-Jeghers Syndrome features?
cards.a: Hamartomatous polyps + Hyperpigmented macules on lips/buccal mucosa. Section: Quick-Fire Integration

cards.q: Jaundice + Weight Loss + Palpable Gallbladder?
cards.a: Pancreatic Cancer (Courvoisier sign).

cards.q: RUQ Pain + Jaundice + Fever?
cards.a: Acute Cholangitis.

cards.q: Cirrhosis + New onset Fever + Abdominal Pain?
cards.a: Spontaneous Bacterial Peritonitis (SBP).

cards.q: Heartburn + Dysphagia to solids + History of asthma/atopy?
cards.a: Eosinophilic Esophagitis.

cards.q: Endoscopic finding in Eosinophilic Esophagitis?
cards.a: Stacked rings or linear furrows ("feline esophagus").

cards.q: Treatment for Eosinophilic Esophagitis?
cards.a: Dietary modification or swallowed aerosolized steroids (Fluticasone).

cards.q: Primary mechanism of Ascites in Cirrhosis?
cards.a: Portal hypertension leading to splanchnic vasodilation and decreased effective arterial volume.

cards.q: Most common cause of death in patients with Hemochromatosis?
cards.a: Hepatocellular Carcinoma (HCC).

cards.q: Defining characteristic of Type 1 Hepatorenal Syndrome (HRS)?
cards.a: Rapidly progressive renal failure (doubling of Cr >2.5 in <2 weeks).

cards.q: SAAG < 1.1 g/dL with high protein (>2.5) in ascitic fluid suggests?
cards.a: Malignancy, Nephrotic syndrome, or TB peritonitis.

cards.q: Treatment for symptomatic Grade II/III Hepatic Encephalopathy?
cards.a: Lactulose titrated to 2-3 soft bowel movements per day.

cards.q: Indication for adding Rifaximin in Hepatic Encephalopathy?
cards.a: Prevention of recurrence after a second episode.

cards.q: Most common organism causing Spontaneous Bacterial Peritonitis (SBP)?
cards.a: E. coli.

cards.q: Long-term prophylaxis for SBP after the first episode?
cards.a: Daily Ciprofloxacin or Trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole.

cards.q: MELD score components?
cards.a: Bilirubin, Creatinine, INR, and Sodium.

cards.q: Use of the MELD score?
cards.a: Predicting 3-month mortality and prioritizing liver transplant candidates. Part 15: IBD — Nuanced Management & Complications

cards.q: IBD type associated with "Creeping Fat" on gross specimen?
cards.a: Crohn’s Disease.

cards.q: Highest risk factor for Toxic Megacolon?
cards.a: Ulcerative Colitis (though it can occur in Crohn's or C. diff).

cards.q: Initial imaging for suspected Toxic Megacolon?
cards.a: Abdominal X-ray (showing colonic diameter >6 cm).

cards.q: Contraindicated procedures in acute Toxic Megacolon?
cards.a: Colonoscopy and Barium enema (due to perforation risk).

cards.q: Maintenance therapy for Crohn’s Disease if 5-ASA fails?
cards.a: Azathioprine, 6-Mercaptopurine, or Anti-TNF (Infliximab).

cards.q: IBD medication requiring TPMT enzyme activity testing before start?
cards.a: Azathioprine / 6-Mercaptopurine.

cards.q: Most common site of stricture formation in Crohn’s?
cards.a: Terminal Ileum.

cards.q: Surveillance colonoscopy timing for UC patients?
cards.a: Starting 8 years after diagnosis, then every 1-2 years.

cards.q: Extraintestinal manifestation of IBD that does NOT correlate with bowel activity?
cards.a: Ankylosing spondylitis and Primary Sclerosing Cholangitis. Part 16: Pancreatitis — Advanced Management

cards.q: Most common cause of death in the first week of Acute Pancreatitis?
cards.a: Systemic Inflammatory Response Syndrome (SIRS) and multiorgan failure.

cards.q: Most common cause of death AFTER the first week of Acute Pancreatitis?
cards.a: Pancreatic infection (Infected Necrosis).

cards.q: Preferred fluid for resuscitation in Acute Pancreatitis?
cards.a: Lactated Ringer’s (associated with lower SIRS risk than Normal Saline).

cards.q: "Sentinel Loop" on abdominal X-ray indicates?
cards.a: Localized ileus of the jejunum associated with nearby Pancreatitis.

cards.q: Definition of "Chronic" Pancreatitis?
cards.a: Irreversible structural damage leading to exocrine and endocrine insufficiency.

cards.q: Gold standard test for Pancreatic Exocrine Insufficiency?
cards.a: 72-hour fecal fat collection (though Fecal Elastase-1 is the common initial test).

cards.q: Classic pain description for Pancreatic Cancer?
cards.a: Dull epigastric pain radiating to the back, worse at night.

cards.q: Trousseau’s Syndrome in Pancreatic Cancer?
cards.a: Migratory superficial thrombophlebitis. Part 17: GI Bleeding — Special Scenarios

cards.q: Management of a "Dieulafoy Lesion"?
cards.a: Endoscopic clipping or thermal coagulation (it is a large submucosal artery).

cards.q: Presentation of "Aortoenteric Fistula"?
cards.a: Brisk "herald bleed" followed by massive hematochezia in a patient with a prior aortic graft.

cards.q: Primary location of an Aortoenteric Fistula?
cards.a: Third part of the duodenum.

cards.q: Scintigraphy (Tagged RBC Scan) is used for what GIB scenario?
cards.a: Detecting slow or intermittent LGIB when colonoscopy is inconclusive.

cards.q: Most common cause of UGIB in a patient with chronic NSAID use?
cards.a: Gastric ulcer (NSAIDs inhibit prostaglandin synthesis).

cards.q: Cameron Lesions are found in what structural abnormality?
cards.a: Hiatal hernia (linear erosions in the gastric folds).

cards.q: Key management for bleeding secondary to Mallory-Weiss tear?
cards.a: Most stop spontaneously; if not, epinephrine injection or clipping. Part 18: Liver Disease — Immunology & Metabolism

cards.q: High Serum Ceruloplasmin levels are found in?
cards.a: Actually, Ceruloplasmin is low in Wilson's Disease.

cards.q: Kayser-Fleischer rings are found in which layer of the cornea?
cards.a: Descemet’s membrane.

cards.q: Most common liver disease in the Western world?
cards.a: Nonalcoholic Fatty Liver Disease (NAFLD).

cards.q: Histological hallmark of Alcoholic Hepatitis?
cards.a: Mallory-Denk bodies (intracytoplasmic eosinophilic inclusions).

cards.q: Medical treatment for severe Alcoholic Hepatitis (Maddrey Score >32)?
cards.a: Prednisolone (Corticosteroids).

cards.q: Drug used in Alcoholic Hepatitis if steroids are contraindicated?
cards.a: Pentoxifylline.

cards.q: Difference between PBC and PSC location?
cards.a: PBC is intrahepatic ducts only; PSC is both intra- and extrahepatic. Part 19: Structural & Functional Integration

cards.q: Diagnosis for "Doughnut sign" or "Target sign" on CT?
cards.a: Intussusception.

cards.q: Most common site for Volvulus in the elderly?
cards.a: Sigmoid colon.

cards.q: Most common site for Volvulus in children?
cards.a: Midgut (associated with malrotation).

cards.q: "Whirl sign" on CT abdomen indicates?
cards.a: Volvulus (torsion of the mesentery).

cards.q: Pathophysiology of Zenker’s Diverticulum?
cards.a: Herniation through Killian’s triangle (weakness in the pharyngeal constrictor). Final Section: Step 2 CK "Best Next Step" Rapid Fire

cards.q: Best next step: Patient with cirrhosis, ascites, and altered mental status?
cards.a: Diagnostic paracentesis (rule out SBP).

cards.q: Best next step: Hematochezia in a patient over 50 with stable vitals?
cards.a: Colonoscopy.

cards.q: Best next step: Suspected Peptic Ulcer perforation?
cards.a: Upright Chest X-ray (look for free air under the diaphragm).

cards.q: Best next step: Post-ERCP patient with severe epigastric pain?
cards.a: Check serum Amylase/Lipase (Post-ERCP pancreatitis).

cards.q: Best next step: Jaundice, pruritus, and elevated Alk Phos?
cards.a: Right upper quadrant ultrasound.

cards.q: IBD-associated skin lesion that shows pathergy (worsens with trauma)?
cards.a: Pyoderma gangrenosum.

cards.q: Most common vitamin deficiency in Crohn's disease patients with ileal involvement?
cards.a: Vitamin B12 (leading to macrocytic anemia).

cards.q: Type of kidney stone most common in Crohn’s disease?
cards.a: Calcium Oxalate stones (due to increased oxalate absorption).

cards.q: Gallstone type associated with Crohn’s disease?
cards.a: Cholesterol stones (due to decreased bile acid resorption in the ileum).

cards.q: Primary site of inflammation in microscopic colitis?
cards.a: Colon (appears endoscopically normal but shows inflammation on biopsy).

cards.q: Common trigger for Microscopic Colitis?
cards.a: NSAIDs, PPIs, or Sertraline.

cards.q: Drug of choice for treating Microscopic Colitis?
cards.a: Oral Budesonide.

cards.q: Most common complication of an ileal pouch-anal anastomosis (IPAA)?
cards.a: Pouchitis.

cards.q: Initial treatment for Pouchitis?
cards.a: Ciprofloxacin or Metronidazole. Part 21: GI Bleeding — Nuance & Management

cards.q: Standard of care for preventing re-bleeding in non-variceal peptic ulcers?
cards.a: High-dose IV Proton Pump Inhibitors (PPI) for 72 hours.

cards.q: Most common cause of a "brisk" Upper GI Bleed in a patient with Cirrhosis?
cards.a: Esophageal varices.

cards.q: Mechanism of Octreotide in variceal bleeding?
cards.a: Causes splanchnic vasoconstriction, reducing portal venous pressure.

cards.q: Next step if endoscopic therapy fails twice to control a variceal bleed?
cards.a: TIPS (Transjugular Intrahepatic Portosystemic Shunt).

cards.q: Contraindication for TIPS procedure?
cards.a: Severe Congestive Heart Failure or Hepatic Encephalopathy.

cards.q: Appearance of Gastric Antral Vascular Ectasia (GAVE) on endoscopy?
cards.a: "Watermelon stomach" (streaky redness in the antrum).

cards.q: Presentation of Blue Rubber Bleb Nevus Syndrome?
cards.a: Multiple cavernous hemangiomas of the skin and GI tract leading to chronic GIB. Part 22: Liver Disease — Advanced Diagnostics

cards.q: Mnemonic for the causes of Acute Liver Failure?
cards.a: A-B-C-D-E-F (Acetaminophen/Amanita, Hep B, Hep C, Delta/Drugs, Eschemia, Fatty liver).

cards.q: Definition of "Fulminant Hepatic Failure"?
cards.a: Acute liver injury with encephalopathy and coagulopathy (INR >1.5) within 8 weeks of jaundice.

cards.q: Most common cause of jaundice in the first 24 hours of life?
cards.a: Hemolytic disease (Pathological).

cards.q: Histological finding in Alpha-1 Antitrypsin deficiency?
cards.a: PAS-positive, diastase-resistant globules in hepatocytes.

cards.q: Lab finding that differentiates Alcoholic Hepatitis from Viral Hepatitis?
cards.a: AST and ALT are rarely >500 U/L in alcoholic disease.

cards.q: Medication used to reduce pruritus in Primary Biliary Cholangitis?
cards.a: Cholestyramine (bile acid sequestrant).

cards.q: Association between HLA-B8/DR3 and which liver disease?
cards.a: Autoimmune Hepatitis.

cards.q: Presentation of Hepatic Hydrothorax?
cards.a: Right-sided pleural effusion in a cirrhotic patient without primary lung disease. Part 23: Pancreatitis & Biliary "Gray Areas"

cards.q: Most common cause of Chronic Pancreatitis in children?
cards.a: Cystic Fibrosis (CFTR mutations).

cards.q: Serum marker often elevated in Autoimmune Pancreatitis?
cards.a: IgG4.

cards.q: First-line treatment for Autoimmune Pancreatitis?
cards.a: Corticosteroids.

cards.q: Diagnosis for a "Double Duct Sign" (dilation of both CBD and pancreatic duct)?
cards.a: Pancreatic Head Cancer or Ampullary Cancer.

cards.q: Preferred diagnostic test for suspected Choledocholithiasis when US is equivocal?
cards.a: MRCP (Magnetic Resonance Cholangiopancreatography).

cards.q: Most common cause of Pyogenic Liver Abscess?
cards.a: Biliary tract disease (e.g., ascending cholangitis).

cards.q: Characteristic CT finding of an Amoebic Liver Abscess?
cards.a: Single lesion in the right lobe with "anchovy paste" aspirate.

cards.q: Treatment for Amoebic Liver Abscess?
cards.a: Metronidazole (Paromomycin follows to clear intraluminal cysts). Part 24: High-Yield Potpourri

cards.q: Definition of Ogilvie's Syndrome?
cards.a: Acute pseudo-obstruction of the colon in hospitalized/elderly patients.

cards.q: Most common complication of a Meckel's Diverticulum in an adult?
cards.a: Small bowel obstruction.

cards.q: Cause of "Pneumatosis Intestinalis" (air in the bowel wall) on X-ray?
cards.a: Mesenteric ischemia or Necrotizing Enterocolitis (NEC).

cards.q: Diagnostic finding for Sclerosing Mesenteritis?
cards.a: "Misty mesentery" on CT scan.

cards.q: Drug of choice for prophylaxis of NSAID-induced ulcers?
cards.a: Misoprostol (Prostaglandin E1 analog).

cards.q: Primary risk of long-term PPI use?
cards.a: C. difficile infection, hip fractures (decreased Ca absorption), and B12 deficiency.

cards.q: Hallmark of Dubin-Johnson Syndrome on laparoscopy?
cards.a: Grossly black/dark liver.

cards.q: Diagnosis for a patient with RUQ pain, jaundice, and palpable gallbladder?
cards.a: Courvoisier sign (likely distal malignant biliary obstruction).

cards.q: Most common site for Gastric Carcinoid tumors?
cards.a: Gastric body (associated with hypergastrinemia).

cards.q: Diagnosis for a patient with ascites, hepatomegaly, and RUQ pain after starting OCPs?
cards.a: Budd-Chiari Syndrome (Hepatic vein thrombosis).

cards.q: "Nutmeg liver" on gross pathology indicates?
cards.a: Chronic passive congestion due to Right-Sided Heart Failure.

cards.q: Primary treatment for a Pyogenic Liver Abscess?
cards.a: Percutaneous drainage and systemic antibiotics.

cards.q: Causative organism for "Hydatid Cysts" in the liver?
cards.a: Echinococcus granulosus.

cards.q: Pathognomonic CT finding for Echinococcus liver cyst?
cards.a: Eggshell calcification of the cyst wall.

cards.q: Why is aspiration contraindicated in suspected Echinococcus cysts?
cards.a: Risk of anaphylactic shock from leakage of cyst contents.

cards.q: Most common cause of portal hypertension in the absence of cirrhosis?
cards.a: Schistosomiasis (worldwide) or Portal Vein Thrombosis.

cards.q: Diagnosis for a patient with jaundice and "Hamman’s Crunch" (mediastinal emphysema)?
cards.a: Boerhaave Syndrome (esophageal rupture). Part 26: Biliary Nuances & Gallbladder Disease

cards.q: Definition of "Acalculous Cholecystitis"?
cards.a: Gallbladder inflammation without stones, typically in critically ill/ICU patients.

cards.q: Best initial treatment for Acalculous Cholecystitis in an unstable patient?
cards.a: Percutaneous cholecystostomy tube.

cards.q: "Gallstone Ileus" usually results from a fistula between which two organs?
cards.a: Gallbladder and Duodenum.

cards.q: Classic X-ray triad (Rigler’s Triad) for Gallstone Ileus?
cards.a: Small bowel obstruction, gallstone in ectopic location, and pneumobilia (air in biliary tree).

cards.q: Most common site of impaction in Gallstone Ileus?
cards.a: Ileocecal valve.

cards.q: Finding of "Strawberry Gallbladder" (Cholesterolosis) indicates?
cards.a: Yellow specks of cholesterol esters within the gallbladder wall (usually asymptomatic).

cards.q: Primary risk factor for Cholangiocarcinoma in the Western world?
cards.a: Primary Sclerosing Cholangitis (PSC). Part 27: Chronic Pancreatitis & Functional Disorders

cards.q: Most common cause of Chronic Pancreatitis in adults (Western world)?
cards.a: Alcohol abuse.

cards.q: Diagnosis for a patient with oily, foul-smelling stools and weight loss?
cards.a: Steatorrhea (Pancreatic Exocrine Insufficiency).

cards.q: Best initial step for suspected Pancreatic Exocrine Insufficiency?
cards.a: Fecal Elastase-1 test.

cards.q: Treatment for abdominal pain in Chronic Pancreatitis?
cards.a: Alcohol/smoking cessation, small low-fat meals, and pancreatic enzyme supplementation.

cards.q: Pathophysiology of Gastroparesis?
cards.a: Delayed gastric emptying in the absence of mechanical obstruction (common in Diabetes).

cards.q: Prokinetic agent of choice for Gastroparesis?
cards.a: Metoclopramide (D2 receptor antagonist) or Erythromycin.

cards.q: Primary side effect of long-term Metoclopramide?
cards.a: Tardive dyskinesia. Part 28: Complex GI Bleeding & Small Bowel Pearls

cards.q: Diagnosis for "watermelon stomach" appearance in a patient with Systemic Sclerosis?
cards.a: GAVE (Gastric Antral Vascular Ectasia).

cards.q: First-line management for GAVE?
cards.a: Endoscopic Argon Plasma Coagulation (APC).

cards.q: Most common cause of Small Bowel Bleeding in patients <40 years old?
cards.a: Meckel’s Diverticulum or IBD.

cards.q: Most common cause of Small Bowel Bleeding in patients >40 years old?
cards.a: Angiodysplasia or NSAID-induced ulcers.

cards.q: Initial step for a patient with Hematochezia and hemodynamic instability?
cards.a: Rule out an Upper GI source with EGD (Upper GI bleed can present with red blood if brisk).

cards.q: Interpretation of a "High SAAG" (>1.1) with "Low Protein" (<2.5) in ascites?
cards.a: Cirrhosis.

cards.q: Interpretation of a "High SAAG" (>1.1) with "High Protein" (>2.5) in ascites?
cards.a: Heart Failure or Budd-Chiari Syndrome. Part 29: Pharmacological Pearls in GI

cards.q: Mechanism of Ursodeoxycholic acid in PBC?
cards.a: Decreases cholesterol content of bile and reduces immune-mediated duct damage.

cards.q: Prophylactic medication for esophageal varices in stable cirrhotics?
cards.a: Non-selective Beta-blockers (Nadolol or Propranolol).

cards.q: Mechanism of Terlipressin in Variceal Bleeding?
cards.a: Vasopressin analogue that causes splanchnic vasoconstriction.

cards.q: Treatment for Pruritus in cholestatic liver disease?
cards.a: Cholestyramine, Rifampin, or Naltrexone.

cards.q: Most common electrolyte side effect of PPIs?
cards.a: Hypomagnesemia.

cards.q: Medication that causes "black tongue" and "black stools"?
cards.a: Bismuth subsalicylate. Part 30: Step 2 CK "Management Next Steps" Final Fire

cards.q: Next step for a patient with suspected Achalasia and a "Bird’s Beak" on Barium Swallow?
cards.a: Esophageal Manometry (to confirm absence of peristalsis and failed LES relaxation).

cards.q: Next step for a 55-year-old with new-onset GERD?
cards.a: Upper Endoscopy (to rule out Barrett's or malignancy due to age).

cards.q: Next step for a patient with a positive H. pylori stool antigen?
cards.a: Initiate Triple or Quadruple therapy.

cards.q: Next step after a diagnosis of Colon Cancer is made via biopsy?
cards.a: CT scan of Chest/Abdomen/Pelvis for staging.

cards.q: Next step for a cirrhotic patient with a new solid liver mass <1cm on US?
cards.a: Repeat Ultrasound in 3-4 months.

cards.q: Next step for a cirrhotic patient with a new solid liver mass >1cm on US?
cards.a: Triple-phase CT or MRI with contrast (looking for arterial enhancement/venous washout).

cards.q: Diagnosis for a patient with ascites, hepatomegaly, and RUQ pain after starting OCPs?
cards.a: Budd-Chiari Syndrome (Hepatic vein thrombosis).

cards.a: Metoclopramide (D2 receptor antagonist) or Erythromycin.

cards.q: Primary side effect of long-term Metoclopramide?
cards.a: Tardive dyskinesia. Part 28: Complex GI Bleeding & Small Bowel Pearls

cards.q: Diagnosis for "watermelon stomach" appearance in a patient with Systemic Sclerosis?
cards.a: GAVE (Gastric Antral Vascular Ectasia).

cards.q: First-line management for GAVE?
cards.a: Endoscopic Argon Plasma Coagulation (APC).

cards.q: Most common cause of Small Bowel Bleeding in patients <40 years old?
cards.a: Meckel’s Diverticulum or IBD.

cards.q: Most common cause of Small Bowel Bleeding in patients >40 years old?
cards.a: Angiodysplasia or NSAID-induced ulcers.

cards.q: Initial step for a patient with Hematochezia and hemodynamic instability?
cards.a: Rule out an Upper GI source with EGD (Upper GI bleed can present with red blood if brisk).

cards.q: Interpretation of a "High SAAG" (>1.1) with "Low Protein" (<2.5) in ascites?
cards.a: Cirrhosis.

cards.q: Interpretation of a "High SAAG" (>1.1) with "High Protein" (>2.5) in ascites?
cards.a: Heart Failure or Budd-Chiari Syndrome. Part 29: Pharmacological Pearls in GI

cards.q: Mechanism of Ursodeoxycholic acid in PBC?
cards.a: Decreases cholesterol content of bile and reduces immune-mediated duct damage.

cards.q: Prophylactic medication for esophageal varices in stable cirrhotics?
cards.a: Non-selective Beta-blockers (Nadolol or Propranolol).

cards.q: Mechanism of Terlipressin in Variceal Bleeding?
cards.a: Vasopressin analogue that causes splanchnic vasoconstriction.

cards.q: Treatment for Pruritus in cholestatic liver disease?
cards.a: Cholestyramine, Rifampin, or Naltrexone.

cards.q: Most common electrolyte side effect of PPIs?
cards.a: Hypomagnesemia.

cards.q: Medication that causes "black tongue" and "black stools"?
cards.a: Bismuth subsalicylate. Part 30: Step 2 CK "Management Next Steps" Final Fire

cards.q: Next step for a patient with suspected Achalasia and a "Bird’s Beak" on Barium Swallow?
cards.a: Esophageal Manometry (to confirm absence of peristalsis and failed LES relaxation).

cards.q: Next step for a 55-year-old with new-onset GERD?
cards.a: Upper Endoscopy (to rule out Barrett's or malignancy due to age).

cards.q: Next step for a patient with a positive H. pylori stool antigen?
cards.a: Initiate Triple or Quadruple therapy.

cards.q: Next step after a diagnosis of Colon Cancer is made via biopsy?
cards.a: CT scan of Chest/Abdomen/Pelvis for staging.

cards.q: Next step for a cirrhotic patient with a new solid liver mass <1cm on US?
cards.a: Repeat Ultrasound in 3-4 months.

cards.q: Next step for a cirrhotic patient with a new solid liver mass >1cm on US?

topic: Nephrology — AKI, CKD, electrolyte & acid-base disorders

cards.q: Definition of AKI by KDIGO criteria?
cards.a: Increase in SCr $\ge 0.3$ mg/dL within 48h or $\ge 1.5\times$ baseline within 7 days.

cards.q: Most common cause of intrinsic AKI in hospitalized patients?
cards.a: Acute Tubular Necrosis (ATN).

cards.q: Calculation for Fractional Excretion of Sodium (FeNa)?
cards.a: $FeNa = \frac{U_{Na} \times P_{Cr}}{P_{Na} \times U_{Cr}} \times 100$.

cards.q: FeNa value suggestive of Pre-renal azotemia?
cards.a: Less than 1%.

cards.q: FeNa value suggestive of Acute Tubular Necrosis (ATN)?
cards.a: Greater than 2%.

cards.q: Urine sediment finding in ATN?
cards.a: Muddy brown (granular) casts.

cards.q: Urine sediment finding in Prerenal azotemia?
cards.a: Hyaline casts.

cards.q: BUN:Creatinine ratio in Prerenal AKI?
cards.a: Greater than 20:1.

cards.q: Two major phases of ATN?
cards.a: Maintenance phase (oliguric) and Recovery phase (polyuric).

cards.q: Classic triad of Acute Interstitial Nephritis (AIN)?
cards.a: Fever, rash, and peripheral eosinophilia.

cards.q: Common drug triggers for AIN?
cards.a: NSAIDs, Penicillins, Sulfonamides, and Proton Pump Inhibitors.

cards.q: Urinary finding diagnostic of AIN?
cards.a: White blood cell casts and eosinophiluria.

cards.q: Pathogenesis of Contrast-Induced Nephropathy?
cards.a: Direct tubular toxicity and renal vasoconstriction.

cards.q: Preferred prevention for Contrast-Induced Nephropathy?
cards.a: Isotonic saline hydration before and after the procedure.

cards.q: Cause of AKI after starting an ACE inhibitor in a patient with hypertension?
cards.a: Bilateral Renal Artery Stenosis.

cards.q: Pathognomonic biopsy finding in Ethylene Glycol poisoning?
cards.a: Envelope-shaped calcium oxalate crystals.

cards.q: Treatment for Rhabdomyolysis-induced AKI?
cards.a: Aggressive IV fluid resuscitation and correction of electrolytes.

cards.q: Formula for Urine Anion Gap (UAG)?
cards.a: $UAG = Na + K - Cl$.

cards.q: Absolute indications for urgent dialysis (mnemonic AEIOU)?
cards.a: Acidosis, Electrolytes (K+), Ingestion (toxins), Overload (volume), Uremia. Part 2: Chronic Kidney Disease (CKD)

cards.q: Definition of CKD?
cards.a: GFR $< 60$ mL/min/1.73m² or markers of kidney damage for $\ge 3$ months.

cards.q: Most common cause of CKD in the US?
cards.a: Diabetes Mellitus.

cards.q: Target Blood Pressure for CKD patients (KDIGO)?
cards.a: $< 120$ mmHg systolic.

cards.q: Preferred antihypertensive for CKD with albuminuria?
cards.a: ACE inhibitors or ARBs.

cards.q: GFR range for Stage 3 CKD?
Definition of Nephrotic-range proteinuria?
First-line treatment for CKD-associated anemia?
cards.a: Iron supplementation, then Erythropoiesis-Stimulating Agents (ESAs).

cards.q: Target Hemoglobin in CKD patients on ESAs?
cards.a: $10$ to $11.5$ g/dL (avoiding $> 13$ due to stroke risk).

cards.q: Mechanism of Secondary Hyperparathyroidism in CKD?
cards.a: Phosphate retention and decreased $1,25(OH)_2D$ (Calcitriol) leading to hypocalcemia.

cards.q: Classic X-ray finding in Renal Osteodystrophy?
cards.a: "Rugger-jersey" spine (subperiosteal bone resorption).

cards.q: First-line management for Hyperphosphatemia in CKD?
cards.a: Dietary phosphate restriction and phosphate binders (e.g., Sevelamer).

cards.q: Why is Metformin contraindicated in advanced CKD?
cards.a: Increased risk of Lactic Acidosis.

cards.q: Screening test for Diabetic Nephropathy?
cards.a: Annual urine albumin-to-creatinine ratio (UACR). Part 3: Electrolyte Disorders - Sodium & Water

cards.q: Primary determinant of Plasma Osmolality?
cards.a: Sodium concentration.

cards.q: Formula for Serum Osmolality?
cards.a: $2[Na] + \frac{Glucose}{18} + \frac{BUN}{2.8}$.

cards.q: Definition of Hyponatremia?
cards.a: Serum Sodium $< 135$ mEq/L.

cards.q: Cause of Hypertonic Hyponatremia?
cards.a: Hyperglycemia (glucose pulls water into the extracellular space).

cards.q: Correction factor for Sodium in Hyperglycemia?
cards.a: Add $1.6$ mEq/L to Na for every $100$ mg/dL glucose above normal.

cards.q: Lab findings in SIADH?
cards.a: Hyponatremia, low serum osm, high urine osm ($> 100$), and high urine sodium ($> 40$).

cards.q: Treatment for severe symptomatic hyponatremia?
cards.a: Hypertonic ($3\%$) saline.

cards.q: Maximum rate of Sodium correction to avoid Central Pontine Myelinolysis?
cards.a: $8$ mEq/L per 24 hours.

cards.q: Treatment for Hypovolemic Hyponatremia?
cards.a: Isotonic ($0.9\%$) saline.

cards.q: Primary symptom of Central Diabetes Insipidus?
cards.a: Polyuria and polydipsia with low urine osmolality.

cards.q: Diagnostic test to differentiate Central vs. Nephrogenic DI?
cards.a: Desmopressin (DDAVP) challenge.

cards.q: Response to DDAVP in Central Diabetes Insipidus?
cards.a: Significant increase in urine osmolality ($> 50\%$).

cards.q: Common medication causing Nephrogenic DI?
cards.a: Lithium. Part 4: Electrolyte Disorders - Potassium

cards.q: Most common ECG change in Hyperkalemia?
cards.a: Peaked T-waves.

cards.q: Order of ECG changes in worsening Hyperkalemia?
cards.a: Peaked T $\rightarrow$ PR prolongation $\rightarrow$ QRS widening $\rightarrow$ Sine wave.

cards.q: First step in treating Hyperkalemia with ECG changes?
cards.a: Calcium Gluconate (membrane stabilization).

cards.q: Medications that shift Potassium intracellularly?
cards.a: Insulin (+ glucose), $\beta_2$-agonists, and Sodium Bicarbonate.

cards.q: Definitive methods for Potassium removal from the body?
cards.a: Loop diuretics, Cation exchange resins (Patiromer), or Hemodialysis.

cards.q: ECG findings in Hypokalemia?
cards.a: U-waves, T-wave flattening, and ST depression.

cards.q: Electrolyte deficiency that makes Hypokalemia refractory to treatment?
cards.a: Hypomagnesemia.

cards.q: Common cause of Hypokalemia with Hypertension and Metabolic Alkalosis?
cards.a: Primary Hyperaldosteronism (Conn Syndrome). Part 5: Acid-Base Disorders

cards.q: Formula for Anion Gap (AG)?
cards.a: $Na - (Cl + HCO_3)$.

cards.q: Normal range for Serum Anion Gap?
cards.a: $8$ to $12$ mEq/L.

cards.q: Mnemonic for High Anion Gap Metabolic Acidosis (HAGMA)?
cards.a: MUDPILES (Methanol, Uremia, DKA, Propylene glycol, Iron/INH, Lactic acid, Ethylene glycol, Salicylates).

cards.q: Winter’s Formula for expected $PCO_2$ in Metabolic Acidosis?
Significance of a measured $PCO_2$ higher than Winter’s Formula calculation?
cards.a: Concomitant Respiratory Acidosis.

cards.q: Two major causes of Normal Anion Gap Metabolic Acidosis (NAGMA)?
cards.a: Diarrhea and Renal Tubular Acidosis (RTA).

cards.q: Defect in Type 1 (Distal) RTA?
cards.a: Inability to secrete $H^+$ in the distal tubule.

cards.q: Urine pH in Type 1 (Distal) RTA?
cards.a: Abnormally high ($> 5.5$).

cards.q: Defect in Type 2 (Proximal) RTA?
cards.a: Inability to reabsorb $HCO_3$ in the proximal tubule.

cards.q: Association of Type 2 RTA with other proximal transport defects?
cards.a: Fanconi Syndrome.

cards.q: Defect in Type 4 RTA?
cards.a: Hypoaldosteronism or aldosterone resistance.

cards.q: Distinguishing lab feature of Type 4 RTA?
cards.a: Hyperkalemia.

cards.q: Acid-base disturbance in early Salicylate toxicity?
cards.a: Respiratory Alkalosis (direct stimulation of respiratory center).

cards.q: Acid-base disturbance in late Salicylate toxicity?
cards.a: Mixed Respiratory Alkalosis and High Anion Gap Metabolic Acidosis.

cards.q: Next step if Metabolic Alkalosis is "Chloride Responsive"?
cards.a: Give Isotonic Saline (usually due to vomiting or diuretics).

cards.q: Examples of "Chloride Resistant" Metabolic Alkalosis?
cards.a: Hyperaldosteronism and Cushing Syndrome. Part 6: Glomerular Diseases

cards.q: Characteristics of Nephrotic Syndrome?
cards.a: Proteinuria $> 3.5$ g/day, hypoalbuminemia, edema, and hyperlipidemia.

cards.q: Most common Nephrotic Syndrome in children?
cards.a: Minimal Change Disease.

cards.q: Treatment of choice for Minimal Change Disease?
cards.a: Corticosteroids.

cards.q: Most common Nephrotic Syndrome in African Americans and HIV patients?
cards.a: Focal Segmental Glomerulosclerosis (FSGS).

cards.q: Nephrotic Syndrome associated with Hepatitis B, NSAIDs, and solid tumors?
cards.a: Membranous Nephropathy.

cards.q: Appearance of Membranous Nephropathy on Electron Microscopy?
cards.a: "Spike and dome" subepithelial deposits.

cards.q: Definition of Nephritic Syndrome?
cards.a: Hypertension, hematuria (RBC casts), and mild-to-moderate proteinuria.

cards.q: Most common cause of Glomerulonephritis worldwide?
cards.a: IgA Nephropathy (Berger Disease).

cards.q: Timing of IgA Nephropathy hematuria vs. Post-streptococcal GN?
cards.a: IgA is "synpharyngitic" (days); PSGN is 1-3 weeks post-infection.

cards.q: Lab finding specific to Post-streptococcal Glomerulonephritis?
cards.a: Low C3 complement and high Antistreptolysin O (ASO) titers.

cards.q: Light microscopy finding in Post-streptococcal GN?
cards.a: "Starry sky" granular appearance (lumpy-bumpy).

cards.q: Hallmark of Rapidly Progressive Glomerulonephritis (RPGN)?
cards.a: Crescents in Bowman’s space on light microscopy.

cards.q: Mechanism of Goodpasture Syndrome?
cards.a: Anti-GBM antibodies against Type IV collagen.

cards.q: Organ systems involved in Goodpasture Syndrome?
cards.a: Lungs (hemoptysis) and Kidneys (hematuria).

cards.q: Immunofluorescence pattern in Goodpasture Syndrome?
cards.a: Linear IgG deposits along the GBM.

cards.q: Diagnosis for Nephritic syndrome + Hemoptysis + c-ANCA positive?
cards.a: Granulomatosis with Polyangiitis (Wegener’s).

cards.q: Diagnosis for Nephritic syndrome + Asthma + p-ANCA positive?
cards.a: Eosinophilic Granulomatosis with Polyangiitis (Churg-Strauss).

cards.q: Alport Syndrome inheritance and classic triad?
cards.a: X-linked dominant; Sensorineural deafness, eye abnormalities, and glomerulonephritis. Part 7: Cystic & Vascular Diseases

cards.q: Genetics of Adult Polycystic Kidney Disease (ADPKD)?
cards.a: Autosomal Dominant (PKD1 or PKD2 mutations).

cards.q: Extra-renal manifestations of ADPKD?
cards.a: Berry aneurysms (Circle of Willis), hepatic cysts, and Mitral Valve Prolapse.

cards.q: Common cause of death in ADPKD patients?
cards.a: Subarachnoid hemorrhage (ruptured Berry aneurysm) or Cardiovascular disease.

cards.q: Gold standard for diagnosing Renal Artery Stenosis?
cards.a: Renal Arteriography.

cards.q: Typical patient demographic for Fibromuscular Dysplasia?
cards.a: Young females with new-onset hypertension.

cards.q: Radiologic sign of Fibromuscular Dysplasia?
cards.a: "String of pearls" appearance of the renal artery.

cards.q: Cause of AKI after a vascular procedure (e.g., cardiac cath)?
cards.a: Cholesterol Atheroembolism.

cards.q: Physical exam finding in Cholesterol Embolization?
cards.a: Livedo reticularis or "blue toe" syndrome. Part 8: Calcium, Magnesium, & Phosphate

cards.q: Most common cause of Hypercalcemia in outpatients?
cards.a: Primary Hyperparathyroidism.

cards.q: Most common cause of Hypercalcemia in hospitalized patients?
cards.a: Malignancy.

cards.q: ECG change in Hypercalcemia?
cards.a: Shortened QT interval.

cards.q: Initial treatment for severe Hypercalcemia?
cards.a: Aggressive Isotonic Saline hydration.

cards.q: Signs of Hypocalcemia (Neuromuscular irritability)?
cards.a: Chvostek sign (facial twitch) and Trousseau sign (carpal spasm).

cards.q: ECG change in Hypocalcemia?
cards.a: Prolonged QT interval.

cards.q: Common cause of Hypomagnesemia?
cards.a: Chronic alcoholism, diarrhea, and diuretics.

cards.q: Life-threatening arrhythmia associated with Hypomagnesemia?
cards.a: Torsades de Pointes. Part 9: Diuretics

cards.q: Site of action for Acetazolamide?
cards.a: Proximal Convoluted Tubule (Carbonic Anhydrase inhibitor).

cards.q: Mechanism of Loop Diuretics (e.g., Furosemide)?
cards.a: Inhibition of Na-K-2Cl cotransporter in the thick ascending limb.

cards.q: Major side effects of Loop Diuretics?
cards.a: Ototoxicity, Hypokalemia, Hypocalcemia, and Hyperuricemia.

cards.q: Mechanism of Thiazide Diuretics?
cards.a: Inhibition of Na-Cl cotransporter in the distal convoluted tubule.

cards.q: Distinctive electrolyte effect of Thiazides compared to Loops?
cards.a: Thiazides cause Hypercalcemia (Loops cause Hypocalcemia).

cards.q: Site of action for Spironolactone?
cards.a: Cortical collecting duct (Aldosterone receptor antagonist).

cards.q: Major side effect of Spironolactone in males?
cards.a: Gynecomastia. Part 10: Miscellaneous High-Yield

cards.q: Most common type of kidney stone?
cards.a: Calcium Oxalate.

cards.q: Radiologic appearance of Magnesium Ammonium Phosphate (Struvite) stones?
cards.a: "Staghorn" calculus.

cards.q: Organism associated with Struvite stones?
cards.a: Urease-positive bacteria (e.g., Proteus, Klebsiella).

cards.q: Stones that are radiolucent on X-ray?
cards.a: Uric Acid stones.

cards.q: Treatment for Uric Acid stones?
cards.a: Alkalinization of urine (Potassium Citrate).

cards.q: Pathogenesis of Nephrogenic Systemic Fibrosis?
cards.a: Exposure to Gadolinium-based contrast in patients with low GFR.

cards.q: Definition of the "Delta-Delta" ($\Delta \Delta$)?
cards.a: The ratio of the change in Anion Gap to the change in Bicarbonate ($\Delta AG / \Delta HCO_3$).

cards.q: Interpretation of a $\Delta \Delta$ ratio $> 2$?
cards.a: Concomitant Metabolic Alkalosis underlying the High Anion Gap Metabolic Acidosis.

cards.q: Interpretation of a $\Delta \Delta$ ratio $< 0.4$?
cards.a: Concomitant Normal Anion Gap Metabolic Acidosis (NAGMA).

cards.q: Formula for the Osmolar Gap?
cards.a: $Measured\ Osmolality - Calculated\ Osmolality$.

cards.q: Significance of an Osmolar Gap $> 10$ mOsm/kg?
cards.a: Presence of unmeasured osmotically active substances (e.g., Ethanol, Methanol, Ethylene Glycol).

cards.q: Gold standard for diagnosing the specific cause of NAGMA?
cards.a: Urine Anion Gap (UAG).

cards.q: Meaning of a Positive Urine Anion Gap in the setting of Metabolic Acidosis?
cards.a: Low urinary $NH_4^+$ excretion, suggesting a Renal Tubular Acidosis (RTA).

cards.q: Meaning of a Negative Urine Anion Gap in the setting of Metabolic Acidosis?
cards.a: High urinary $NH_4^+$ excretion, suggesting gastrointestinal bicarbonate loss (Diarrhea). Part 12: Nephrotic & Nephritic Deep Dive

cards.q: Pathogenesis of Membranoproliferative Glomerulonephritis (MPGN) Type II?
cards.a: C3 Nephritic Factor (antibody that stabilizes C3 convertase).

cards.q: Classic EM finding in MPGN Type II (Dense Deposit Disease)?
cards.a: Ribbon-like deposits within the Glomerular Basement Membrane.

cards.q: Most common cause of secondary FSGS?
cards.a: Obesity, Heroin use, or HIV infection.

cards.q: Primary pathology in Diabetic Nephropathy?
cards.a: Non-enzymatic glycosylation of the GBM and efferent arteriole hyalinization.

cards.q: Pathognomonic light microscopy finding in Diabetic Nephropathy?
cards.a: Kimmelstiel-Wilson nodules (nodular glomerulosclerosis).

cards.q: Effect of ACE inhibitors on glomerular hemodynamics?
cards.a: Vasodilation of the efferent arteriole, decreasing intraglomerular pressure.

cards.q: Renal pathology associated with Hepatitis C virus?
cards.a: Cryoglobulinemia leading to MPGN.

cards.q: Characteristic renal biopsy finding in Systemic Lupus Erythematosus (Class IV)?
cards.a: "Wire-loop" lesions (subendothelial immune complex deposits).

cards.q: Most common cause of Nephrotic Syndrome in adults in the US?
cards.a: Focal Segmental Glomerulosclerosis (FSGS).

cards.q: Only Nephrotic Syndrome that may present with low complement levels?
cards.a: Membranoproliferative Glomerulonephritis (MPGN). Part 13: Complex Electrolyte Management

cards.q: Definition of "Pseudohyponatremia"?
cards.a: Factitiously low sodium due to extreme Hyperlipidemia or Hyperproteinemia.

cards.q: Treatment of choice for Euvolemic Hyponatremia (SIADH) resistant to fluid restriction?
cards.a: Salt tablets, Urea, or Vaptans (Vasopressin antagonists).

cards.q: Electrolyte abnormality that increases the risk of Digoxin toxicity?
cards.a: Hypokalemia.

cards.q: Common cause of Hypermagnesemia?
cards.a: Excessive intake of Magnesium-containing antacids/laxatives in CKD patients.

cards.q: Management of severe Hypermagnesemia with respiratory depression?
cards.a: IV Calcium Gluconate (antagonizes Magnesium effects).

cards.q: Definition of "Hungry Bone Syndrome"?
cards.a: Severe hypocalcemia and hypophosphatemia following parathyroidectomy.

cards.q: Characteristic lab profile of Vitamin D deficiency?
cards.a: Low Calcium, Low Phosphate, High PTH.

cards.q: Characteristic lab profile of Hypoparathyroidism?
cards.a: Low Calcium, High Phosphate, Low PTH. Part 14: Genetic & Rare Tubular Disorders

cards.q: Inheritance and defect in Bartter Syndrome?
cards.a: Autosomal recessive; defect in the Na-K-2Cl cotransporter (Loop of Henle).

cards.q: Clinical presentation of Bartter Syndrome?
cards.a: Mimics chronic Loop Diuretic use (Hypokalemia, Metabolic Alkalosis, Hypercalciuria).

cards.q: Inheritance and defect in Gitelman Syndrome?
cards.a: Autosomal recessive; defect in the Na-Cl cotransporter (Distal Tubule).

cards.q: Clinical presentation of Gitelman Syndrome?
cards.a: Mimics Thiazide Diuretic use (Hypokalemia, Metabolic Alkalosis, Hypocalciuria, Hypomagnesemia).

cards.q: Difference in Urinary Calcium between Bartter and Gitelman?
cards.a: Bartter has High Urine Calcium; Gitelman has Low Urine Calcium.

cards.q: Inheritance and defect in Liddle Syndrome?
cards.a: Autosomal dominant; gain-of-function mutation in ENaC (Collecting Duct).

cards.q: Clinical presentation of Liddle Syndrome?
cards.a: Hypertension, Hypokalemia, and Metabolic Alkalosis with low Aldosterone/Renin levels.

cards.q: Treatment for Liddle Syndrome?
cards.a: Amiloride or Triamterene (blocks ENaC); Spironolactone is ineffective. Part 15: Acute Kidney Injury Nuances

cards.q: Indication for starting a "Renal Dose" of Dopamine in AKI?
cards.a: None; "Renal Dose" Dopamine is no longer recommended and provides no benefit.

cards.q: Most sensitive indicator of early recovery from ATN?
cards.a: Increase in urine output (Polyuric phase).

cards.q: Common cause of AKI in a patient with a "fountain-like" rash and eosinophilia?
cards.a: Acute Interstitial Nephritis (AIN).

cards.q: Likely diagnosis for AKI + palpable purpura + abdominal pain?
cards.a: IgA Vasculitis (Henoch-Schönlein Purpura).

cards.q: Diagnosis for AKI + Schistocytes on peripheral smear + Thrombocytopenia?
cards.a: Hemolytic Uremic Syndrome (HUS) or Thrombotic Thrombocytopenic Purpura (TTP).

cards.q: Pathogenesis of HUS in children?
cards.a: Shiga toxin (E. coli O157:H7) causing endothelial damage.

cards.q: Why are NSAIDs contraindicated in AKI?
cards.a: They inhibit prostaglandins, leading to afferent arteriole vasoconstriction and reduced GFR.

cards.q: Preferred fluid for resuscitation in a patient with severe Metabolic Acidosis and AKI?
cards.a: Isotonic Sodium Bicarbonate or Lactated Ringer’s (avoiding normal saline to prevent hyperchloremic acidosis). Part 16: Stones and Obstruction

cards.q: Management of a kidney stone $< 5$ mm?
cards.a: Spontaneous passage with hydration and Alpha-blockers (Tamsulosin).

cards.q: Absolute indication for surgical intervention in Urolithiasis?
cards.a: Urosepsis, intractable pain, or stone in a solitary kidney.

cards.q: Diagnostic test of choice for suspected Nephrolithiasis?
cards.a: Non-contrast CT Abdomen and Pelvis.

cards.q: Dietary recommendation to prevent Calcium Oxalate stones?
cards.a: Low sodium, normal calcium intake, and increased fluid intake.

cards.q: Why is low-calcium diet NOT recommended for Calcium Oxalate stones?
cards.a: Low calcium increases intestinal oxalate absorption, leading to hyperoxaluria.

cards.q: Diagnosis for sudden onset flank pain + hematuria + enlarged kidney in a Nephrotic patient?
cards.a: Renal Vein Thrombosis.

cards.q: Nephrotic Syndrome most commonly associated with Renal Vein Thrombosis?
cards.a: Membranous Nephropathy. Part 17: Dialysis and Transplant

cards.q: Most common cause of death in Dialysis patients?
cards.a: Cardiovascular disease (Arrhythmias and Heart Failure).

cards.q: Most common complication of Peritoneal Dialysis?
cards.a: Peritonitis (usually Staphylococcus species).

cards.q: First-line treatment for Hyperacute Transplant Rejection (within minutes)?
cards.a: Immediate surgical removal of the graft.

cards.q: Mechanism of Hyperacute Rejection?
cards.a: Pre-formed recipient antibodies against donor HLA (Type II Hypersensitivity).

cards.q: Mechanism of Acute Transplant Rejection (weeks to months)?
cards.a: T-cell mediated response against donor HLA (Type IV Hypersensitivity).

cards.q: Biopsy finding in Acute Cellular Rejection?
cards.a: Lymphocytic infiltration of the renal tubules (Tubulitis).

cards.q: Major side effect of Cyclosporine?
cards.a: Nephrotoxicity and gingival hyperplasia.

cards.q: Characteristic toxicity of Tacrolimus?
cards.a: Nephrotoxicity and new-onset Diabetes Mellitus.

cards.q: Drug of choice for CMV prophylaxis in renal transplant?
cards.a: Valganciclovir. Part 18: Pregnancy and the Kidney

cards.q: Normal change in GFR during pregnancy?
cards.a: Increases by approximately $50\%$.

cards.q: Normal Serum Creatinine range in a healthy pregnant woman?
cards.a: $0.4$ to $0.8$ mg/dL (values $> 0.8$ are abnormal).

cards.q: Definition of Preeclampsia?
cards.a: New-onset Hypertension ($> 140/90$) and Proteinuria ($> 300$ mg/24h) after 20 weeks gestation.

cards.q: Preferred treatment for Preeclamptic Hypertensive crisis?
cards.a: IV Hydralazine, Labetalol, or Nifedipine.

cards.q: Goal of Magnesium Sulfate in Preeclampsia/Eclampsia?
cards.a: Seizure prophylaxis.

cards.q: Treatment for Magnesium toxicity in a pregnant patient?
cards.a: IV Calcium Gluconate.

cards.q: Explanation for "Normal Anion Gap" in some cases of Multiple Myeloma?
cards.a: Cationic IgG paraproteins decrease the measured anion gap toward zero or negative values.

cards.q: Effect of severe Hypoalbuminemia on the Anion Gap?
cards.a: Every 1 g/dL drop in Albumin decreases the "normal" AG by 2.5 mEq/L.

cards.q: Acid-base status in a patient with both persistent vomiting and DKA?
cards.a: Mixed High Anion Gap Metabolic Acidosis and Metabolic Alkalosis (pH may appear normal).

cards.q: Typical electrolyte profile in Adrenal Insufficiency (Addison's)?
cards.a: Hyponatremia, Hyperkalemia, and Normal Anion Gap Metabolic Acidosis (Type 4 RTA).

cards.q: Mechanism of "Milk-Alkali Syndrome"?
cards.a: Excessive intake of Calcium and absorbable alkali leading to Hypercalcemia, Metabolic Alkalosis, and AKI.

cards.q: Why does Hypokalemia worsen Hepatic Encephalopathy?
cards.a: It stimulates renal $NH_3$ production (ammoniagenesis), which crosses the blood-brain barrier. Part 20: Advanced Tubular & Glomerular Physiology

cards.q: Primary function of the "Principal Cell" in the Collecting Duct?
cards.a: Sodium reabsorption (via ENaC) and Potassium secretion.

cards.q: Primary function of the "Alpha-Intercalated Cell"?
cards.a: Hydrogen ion ($H^+$) secretion and Bicarbonate ($HCO_3^-$) regeneration.

cards.q: Definition of the "Myogenic Response" in renal autoregulation?
cards.a: Afferent arterioles constrict in response to high stretch (pressure) to protect the glomerulus.

cards.q: Mechanism of "Tubuloglomerular Feedback"?
cards.a: Macula densa senses high $NaCl$ delivery and triggers afferent arteriole constriction via Adenosine.

cards.q: Impact of Prostaglandins on the Afferent Arteriole?
cards.a: Vasodilation (keeps the "pipe" open to maintain GFR).

cards.q: Definition of "Nephron Loss Compensation"?
cards.a: Remaining nephrons undergo hypertrophy and hyperfiltration to maintain total GFR. Part 21: Clinical Nephrology & Systemic Disease

cards.q: Pathogenesis of Hepatorenal Syndrome (HRS)?
cards.a: Splanchnic vasodilation leading to severe renal vasoconstriction and "functional" AKI.

cards.q: First-line medical therapy for Hepatorenal Syndrome?
cards.a: Vasoconstrictors (Terlipressin or Midodrine/Octreotide) plus Albumin.

cards.q: Classic renal finding in Scleroderma Renal Crisis?
cards.a: "Onion-skin" thickening of the arterial walls and malignant hypertension.

cards.q: Treatment of choice for Scleroderma Renal Crisis?
cards.a: ACE Inhibitors (even if Serum Creatinine is rising).

cards.q: Significance of "Dismorphic RBCs" in urine microscopy?
cards.a: Suggests the source of bleeding is glomerular (passed through the basement membrane).

cards.q: Definition of "Orthostatic Albuminuria"?
cards.a: Increased protein excretion while upright, but normal while supine (common in adolescents). Part 22: Toxicology & The Kidney

cards.q: Treatment for Ethylene Glycol or Methanol poisoning?
cards.a: Fomepizole (inhibits Alcohol Dehydrogenase) and Hemodialysis.

cards.q: Major renal side effect of Amphotericin B?
cards.a: Distal (Type 1) RTA and significant Magnesium/Potassium wasting.

cards.q: Renal toxicity associated with Acyclovir?
cards.a: Crystalline nephropathy (obstructive AKI); prevented by aggressive hydration.

cards.q: Likely toxin in a patient with AKI and "Fanconi-like" symptoms (glycosuria, phosphaturia)?
cards.a: If old: Expired Tetracyclines; If modern: Ifosfamide or Tenofovir.

cards.q: Mechanism of Aristolochic Acid nephropathy (Chinese Herb Nephropathy)?
cards.a: Severe tubulointerstitial fibrosis and high risk of urothelial malignancy. Part 23: CKD-MBD (Mineral and Bone Disorder)

cards.q: Why is Calcitriol ($1,25(OH)_2D$) low in CKD?
cards.a: Loss of 1-alpha-hydroxylase enzyme in the proximal tubule and high FGF-23 levels.

cards.q: Role of FGF-23 in early CKD?
cards.a: Increases urinary phosphate excretion to prevent hyperphosphatemia (at the cost of lowering Vitamin D).

cards.q: Definition of "Calciphylaxis" (Calcific Uremic Arteriolopathy)?
cards.a: Systemic calcification of arterioles leading to skin ischemia and necrotic ulcers.

cards.q: Primary risk factor for Calciphylaxis?
