cards.a: Inhibits bacterial DNA-dependent RNA polymerase.

cards.q: Benign, classic side effect of Rifampin that patients must be counseled on?
cards.a: Red-orange discoloration of bodily fluids (urine, tears, sweat).

cards.q: Unique toxic side effect of Ethambutol requiring baseline and periodic visual testing?
cards.a: Optic neuritis (reversible red-green color blindness and decreased visual acuity).

cards.q: Major metabolic side effect associated with Pyrazinamide?
cards.a: Hyperuricemia (which can precipitate acute gouty arthritis).

cards.q: Screening test cut-off for a positive Tuberculin Skin Test (TST) in a healthcare worker with no other risk factors?
cards.a: $\ge 10\text{ mm}$ of induration.

cards.q: Screening test cut-off for a positive Tuberculin Skin Test (TST) in an HIV-infected or severely immunosuppressed patient?
cards.a: $\ge 5\text{ mm}$ of induration.

cards.q: Screening test cut-off for a positive Tuberculin Skin Test (TST) in a person with no known risk factors for TB?
cards.a: $\ge 15\text{ mm}$ of induration.

cards.q: Preferred preferred regimen for treating Latent Tuberculosis Infection (LTBI) to optimize compliance?
cards.a: 3 months of weekly Isoniazid plus Rifapentine OR 4 months of daily Rifampin. Sexually Transmitted Infections (STIs)

cards.q: Causative organism of Syphilis?
cards.a: Treponema pallidum.

cards.q: Classic presentation of primary Syphilis?
cards.a: A single, painless ulcer (chancre) with clean bases and indurated margins.

cards.q: Clinical features characteristic of secondary Syphilis?
cards.a: Maculopapular rash on palms and soles, lymphadenopathy, and condylomata lata.

cards.q: Screening (nontreponemal) serologic tests for Syphilis?
cards.a: VDRL (Venercal Disease Research Laboratory) and RPR (Rapid Plasma Reagin).

cards.q: Confirmatory (treponemal) serologic tests for Syphilis?
cards.a: FTA-ABS (Fluorescent Treponemal Antibody Absorption) and TP-PA (Treponema pallidum particle agglutination).

cards.q: Treatment of choice for primary, secondary, or early latent Syphilis?
cards.a: A single intramuscular dose of Benzathine Penicillin G ($2.4\text{ million units}$).

cards.q: Acute febrile reaction accompanied by headache and myalgias that can occur within 24 hours of starting penicillin for syphilis?
cards.a: Jarisch-Herxheimer reaction.

cards.q: Preferred treatment for Neurosyphilis?
cards.a: Intravenous Aqueous Crystalline Penicillin G for 10 to 14 days.

cards.q: Painful, friable genital ulcer accompanied by painful, suppurative inguinal lymphadenopathy (buboes)?
cards.a: Chancroid (caused by Haemophilus ducreyi).

cards.q: First-line empirical treatment for uncomplicated urogenital Chlamydia trachomatis infection?
cards.a: Doxycycline ($100\text{ mg}$ orally twice daily for 7 days).

cards.q: First-line empirical treatment for uncomplicated Gonococcal urethritis?
cards.a: A single intramuscular dose of Ceftriaxone ($500\text{ mg}$).

cards.q: Diagnostic finding on a wet mount for Trichomonas vaginalis?
cards.a: Motile, flagellated trichomonads.

cards.q: First-line treatment for both the patient and sexual partner in a Trichomonas vaginalis infection?
cards.a: Oral Metronidazole. Systemic Mycoses and Fungal Infections

cards.q: Fungal infection endemic to the Ohio and Mississippi River valleys, associated with bird or bat droppings?
cards.a: Histoplasmosis (Histoplasma capsulatum).

cards.q: Diagnostic tissue finding for Histoplasma capsulatum?
cards.a: Small intracellular yeasts within macrophages.

cards.q: Fungal infection endemic to the Southwestern United States, presenting with valley fever (fever, arthralgias, erythema nodosum)?
cards.a: Coccidioidomycosis (Coccidioides immitis).

cards.q: Diagnostic tissue finding for Coccidioides immitis?
cards.a: Large spherules filled with endospores.

cards.q: Fungal infection endemic to the Great Lakes and Ohio River valley, causing inflammatory cutaneous and osteolytic lesions?
cards.a: Blastomycosis (Blastomyces dermatitidis).

cards.q: Diagnostic tissue finding for Blastomyces dermatitidis?
cards.a: Large, round yeasts with broad-based budding.

cards.q: First-line treatment for mild-to-moderate localized systemic fungal infections (e.g., Histoplasmosis, Blastomycosis)?
cards.a: Itraconazole.

cards.q: First-line treatment for severe, disseminated systemic fungal infections?
cards.a: Amphotericin B.

cards.q: Invasive fungal infection causing rapidly progressive paranasal sinus necrosis in a patient with diabetic ketoacidosis (DKA)?
cards.a: Mucormycosis (caused by Mucor or Rhizopus species).

cards.q: Microscopic appearance of Mucor or Rhizopus hyphae in tissue biopsy?
cards.a: Broad, nonseptate hyphae branching at right ($90^\circ$) angles.

cards.q: Microscopic appearance of Aspergillus fumigatus hyphae?
cards.a: Septate hyphae branching at acute ($45^\circ$) angles. Gastrointestinal and Intra-abdominal Infections

cards.q: Most common bacterial cause of bloody diarrhea (dysentery) in the United States, associated with poultry?
cards.a: Campylobacter jejuni.

cards.q: Complication of Campylobacter jejuni infection presenting as ascending paralysis?
cards.a: Guillain-Barré syndrome.

cards.q: Gram stain morphology of Campylobacter jejuni?
cards.a: Comma- or S-shaped Gram-negative rod with polar flagella.

cards.q: Bacterial diarrheal pathogen associated with undercooked ground beef and Hemolytic Uremic Syndrome (HUS)?
cards.a: Enterohemorrhagic Escherichia coli (EHEC), specifically O157:H7.

cards.q: Why are antibiotics contraindicated in children suspected of having EHEC O157:H7 infection?
cards.a: They increase the release of Shiga toxin, raising the risk of Hemolytic Uremic Syndrome (HUS).

cards.q: Triad of signs defining Hemolytic Uremic Syndrome (HUS)?
cards.a: Microangiopathic hemolytic anemia, thrombocytopenia, and acute kidney injury.

cards.q: Protozoan parasite causing foul-smelling, fatty diarrhea (steatorrhea) after drinking water from mountain streams?
cards.a: Giardia lamblia.

cards.q: Treatment of choice for Giardiasis?
cards.a: Tinidazole or Metronidazole.

cards.q: Empiric antibiotic regimen for acute diverticulitis?
cards.a: Ciprofloxacin plus Metronidazole OR Amoxicillin-Clavulanate monotherapy.

cards.q: Most common cause of spontaneous bacterial peritonitis (SBP) in cirrhotic patients?
cards.a: Escherichia coli.

cards.q: Diagnostic threshold of polymorphonuclear leukocytes (PMNs) in ascitic fluid to confirm spontaneous bacterial peritonitis?
cards.a: $\ge 250\text{ cells/mm}^3$.

cards.q: First-line antibiotic choice for Spontaneous Bacterial Peritonitis?
cards.a: A third-generation cephalosporin (e.g., Cefotaxime or Ceftriaxone). Urinary Tract and Soft Tissue Infections

cards.q: Most common causative organism of uncomplicated Urinary Tract Infections (UTIs)?
cards.a: Escherichia coli.

cards.q: First-line antibiotic options for acute uncomplicated cystitis in women?
cards.a: Nitrofurantoin, Trimethoprim-Sulfamethoxazole (TMP-SMX), or Fosfomycin.

cards.q: First-line empiric treatment for outpatient acute uncomplicated pyelonephritis?
cards.a: Oral Fluoroquinolones (e.g., Ciprofloxacin or Levofloxacin).

cards.q: Soft tissue infection characterized by painful, well-demarcated, bright red erythema of the superficial dermis, often on the face?
cards.a: Erysipelas (most commonly caused by Streptococcus pyogenes).

cards.q: Soft tissue infection presenting as ill-defined, flat, warm erythema of the deeper dermis and subcutaneous tissue?
cards.a: Cellulitis (commonly caused by Streptococcus pyogenes or Staphylococcus aureus).

cards.q: Surgical emergency presenting with soft tissue swelling, severe pain out of proportion to exam findings, and gas (crepitus) on X-ray?
cards.a: Necrotizing fasciitis. Zoonotic and Miscellaneous Bacterial Infections

cards.q: Causative organism of Cat Scratch Disease?
cards.a: Bartonella henselae.

cards.q: First-line antibiotic therapy to shorten the duration of painful lymphadenopathy in Cat Scratch Disease?
cards.a: Azithromycin.

cards.q: Causative agent of Q fever, typically transmitted via inhalation of aerosols from farm animal amniotic fluid?
cards.a: Coxiella burnetii.

cards.q: Classic clinical presentation of acute Q fever?
cards.a: Culture-negative endocarditis, severe flu-like symptoms, and hepatitis or atypical pneumonia.

cards.q: Causative agent of Brucellosis, acquired via unpasteurized dairy products?
cards.a: Brucella species.

cards.q: Standard antibiotic regimen for treating Brucellosis?
cards.a: Doxycycline plus Rifampin.

cards.q: Causative organism of Tularemia, associated with handling infected rabbits or tick bites?
cards.a: Francisella tularensis.

cards.q: First-line antibiotic treatment for severe Francisella tularensis (Tularemia) infection?
cards.a: Streptomycin or Gentamicin.

cards.q: Causative organism of Pasteurellosis, following a domestic dog or cat bite?
cards.a: Pasteurella multocida.

cards.q: Prophylactic and definitive first-line oral antibiotic for mammalian bite wounds?
cards.a: Amoxicillin-Clavulanate. Viral Pathogens and Vaccines

cards.q: Causative virus of Infectious Mononucleosis?
cards.a: Epstein-Barr Virus (EBV).

cards.q: Diagnostic test that detects heterophile antibodies in patients with suspected EBV?
cards.a: Monospot test.

cards.q: Classic adverse drug reaction seen when treating a patient who has EBV mononucleosis with Amoxicillin?
cards.a: A diffuse maculopapular rash.

cards.q: Serious splenic complication of Infectious Mononucleosis requiring avoidance of contact sports for at least 3-4 weeks?
cards.a: Splenic rupture.

cards.q: Preferred antiviral drug used to treat severe Influenza infections within 48 hours of symptom onset?
cards.a: Oseltamivir.

cards.q: Antiviral mechanism of action of Oseltamivir?
cards.a: Inhibits neuraminidase, preventing the release of new viral particles from host cells.

cards.q: First-line treatment for chronic Hepatitis C infection across major genotypes?
cards.a: Direct-acting antivirals (DAAs) such as Sofosbuvir/Velpatasvir.

cards.q: Post-exposure prophylaxis regimen for an unvaccinated individual exposed to Hepatitis B?
cards.a: Hepatitis B vaccine series plus Hepatitis B Immune Globulin (HBIG).

cards.q: Post-exposure prophylaxis protocol for a person bitten by a wild, potentially rabid animal?
cards.a: Rabies vaccine series (days 0, 3, 7, 14) plus Rabies Immune Globulin (RIG) infiltrated around the wound. Sepsis and Healthcare-Associated Infections

cards.q: Definition of Sepsis according to Sepsis-3 guidelines?
cards.a: Life-threatening organ dysfunction caused by a dysregulated host response to infection.

cards.q: Clinical scoring system used to identify worsening organ dysfunction in the intensive care unit?
cards.a: Sequential Organ Failure Assessment (SOFA) score.

cards.q: Definition of Septic Shock according to Sepsis-3 guidelines?
cards.a: Sepsis requiring vasopressors to maintain a mean arterial pressure (MAP) $\ge 65\text{ mmHg}$ and serum lactate $>2\text{ mmol/L}$ despite adequate fluid resuscitation.

cards.q: First-line vasopressor of choice for fluid-refractory septic shock?
cards.a: Norepinephrine.

cards.q: Initial fluid resuscitation volume recommended for patients with sepsis-induced tissue hypoperfusion?
cards.a: $30\text{ mL/kg}$ of intravenous crystalloids within the first 3 hours.

cards.q: Most common source of bacteremia leading to healthcare-associated infections?
cards.a: Central venous catheters.

cards.q: Diagnostic action required when a central venous catheter-associated bloodstream infection is suspected?
cards.a: Draw simultaneous blood cultures from both the catheter lumen and a peripheral vein. Parasitic and Helminthic Infections

cards.q: Vector responsible for transmitting Malaria (Plasmodium species)?
cards.a: Female Anopheles mosquito.

cards.q: Gold standard diagnostic test for confirming Malaria and determining parasitemia levels?
cards.a: Thick and thin microscopic blood smears.

cards.q: First-line agent for treating uncomplicated chloroquine-resistant Plasmodium falciparum malaria?
cards.a: Artemether-Lumefantrine OR Atovaquone-Proguanil.

cards.q: Medication added to eradicate hypnozoites in latent hepatic phases of Plasmodium vivax and Plasmodium ovale?
cards.a: Primaquine.

cards.q: Vital pre-screening requirement before initiating Primaquine therapy?
cards.a: Glucose-6-Phosphate Dehydrogenase (G6PD) activity assay to avoid severe hemolysis.

cards.q: Parasitic infection causing perianal pruritus, diagnosed via the cellophane tape test?
cards.a: Enterobiasis (Pinworm infection, caused by Enterobius vermicularis).

cards.q: Drug of choice for treating Enterobius vermicularis (Pinworm) infections?
cards.a: Pyrantel pamoate or Albendazole.

cards.q: Parasitic tissue infection caused by ingesting undercooked pork containing cysts, presenting with periorbital edema, myalgias, and eosinophilia?
cards.a: Trichinellosis (Trichinella spiralis).

cards.q: Treatment of choice for tissue microfilariae in Onchocerciasis (River Blindness)?
cards.a: Ivermectin.

cards.q: Treatment of choice for Neurocysticercosis?
cards.a: Albendazole plus corticosteroids (e.g., Dexamethasone). Bioterrorism & Rare Pathogens

cards.q: Initial diagnostic test of choice for a patient presenting with a painless cutaneous black eschar surrounded by extensive edema?
cards.a: Gram stain and culture of the skin lesion to evaluate for Bacillus anthracis.

cards.q: First-line antimicrobial treatment for naturally acquired or inhalational Anthrax?
cards.a: Ciprofloxacin or Doxycycline (combined with an antitoxin for systemic disease).

cards.q: Flaccid, descending paralysis beginning with cranial nerve palsies after consuming home-canned foods?
cards.a: Botulism (caused by Clostridium botulinum toxin).

cards.q: Mechanism of action of the Botulinum neurotoxin?
cards.a: Cleaves SNARE proteins, preventing the presynaptic release of Acetylcholine at the neuromuscular junction.

cards.q: Treatment for foodborne Botulism in adults?
cards.a: Equine-derived heptavalent botulinum antitoxin.

cards.q: Treatment for infant Botulism caused by ingestion of Clostridium botulinum spores (e.g., from honey)?
cards.a: Human-derived botulinum immune globulin (BabyBIG). Specific Exposure & Environmental Associations

cards.q: Prophylactic antibiotic regimen for a patient who sustained a puncture wound through the sole of a sneaker?
cards.a: Ciprofloxacin (to cover Pseudomonas aeruginosa).

cards.q: Organism responsible for a rapidly progressive, necrotizing soft-tissue infection after exposure to warm seawater or raw oysters in a patient with chronic liver disease?
cards.a: Vibrio vulnificus.

cards.q: First-line treatment for a systemic or necrotizing Vibrio vulnificus infection?
cards.a: Doxycycline plus a third-generation cephalosporin (e.g., Ceftriaxone).

cards.q: Causative organism of a localized cutaneous ulcer with painful regional lymphadenopathy following a scratch from a wild rabbit?
cards.a: Francisella tularensis.

cards.q: Flu-like illness with severe calf muscle tenderness, conjunctival suffusion, and jaundice after swimming in water contaminated with animal urine?
cards.a: Leptospirosis (caused by Leptospira interrogans).

cards.q: Classic clinical triad of severe Leptospirosis (Weil disease)?
cards.a: Jaundice, acute kidney injury, and hemorrhage. Infection Control & Isolation Precautions

cards.q: Type of isolation precaution required for a patient with active Pulmonary Tuberculosis?
cards.a: Airborne precautions (requires an airborne infection isolation room [AIIR] and N95 respirator).

cards.q: Type of isolation precaution required for a patient with Clostridioides difficile infection?
cards.a: Contact precautions (requires gowns, gloves, and mandatory handwashing with soap and water instead of alcohol gel).

cards.q: Type of isolation precaution required for a patient with Neisseria meningitidis meningitis?
cards.a: Droplet precautions (requires a surgical mask for healthcare providers; can be discontinued after 24 hours of effective antibiotic therapy).

cards.q: Type of isolation precaution required for a patient with disseminated Herpes Zoster (shingles)?
cards.a: Airborne and Contact precautions. Surgical Prophylaxis & Medical Conditions

cards.q: Standard timing for the administration of pre-operative prophylactic antibiotics to maximize tissue concentration?
cards.a: Within 60 minutes prior to the surgical incision.

cards.q: Preferred first-line antibiotic for routine surgical prophylaxis in clean procedures (e.g., orthopedic joint replacement)?
cards.a: Cefazolin.

cards.q: Empiric prophylactic antibiotic added to surgical regimens involving the colorectal tract to cover anaerobes?
cards.a: Cefoxitin, Cefotetan, or Cefazolin plus Metronidazole.

cards.q: Empiric antimicrobial management for a patient presenting with febrile neutropenia (Absolute Neutrophil Count $<500/\mu\text{L}$)?
cards.a: Monotherapy with an antipseudomonal beta-lactam (e.g., Piperacillin-Tazobactam, Cefepime, or Meropenem).

cards.q: Target window to administer post-exposure prophylaxis (PEP) after an occupational needle-stick exposure to HIV?
cards.a: Ideally within 2 hours, and no later than 72 hours after exposure.

cards.q: Standard duration of antiretroviral therapy for HIV post-exposure prophylaxis (PEP)?
cards.a: 28 days.

cards.q: Standard three-drug regimen used for HIV post-exposure prophylaxis (PEP)?
cards.a: Tenofovir, Emtricitabine, and an integrase strand transfer inhibitor (e.g., Dolutegravir or Raltegravir). Central Nervous System & Head/Neck Extensions

cards.q: Organism causing a rapidly fatal meningoencephalitis in a healthy individual with a recent history of swimming in warm, fresh water?
cards.a: Naegleria fowleri.

cards.q: Diagnostic finding on a wet mount of cerebrospinal fluid in a patient with Naegleria fowleri infection?
cards.a: Motile, trophozoite amebae.

cards.q: Severe, painful otitis externa with granulation tissue at the floor of the ear canal in an elderly diabetic patient?
cards.a: Malignant Otitis Externa.

cards.q: Most common causative pathogen of Malignant Otitis Externa?
cards.a: Pseudomonas aeruginosa.

cards.q: Preferred first-line intravenous antibiotic therapy for Malignant Otitis Externa?
cards.a: Ciprofloxacin or Cefepime.

cards.q: Rapidly progressive, bilateral cellulitis of the submandibular and sublingual spaces, typically originating from an infected mandibular molar?
cards.a: Ludwig angina.

cards.q: Primary immediate clinical priority in managing a patient with Ludwig angina?
cards.a: Secure and maintain a patent airway. Endocarditis & Vascular Additions

cards.q: Culture-negative infective endocarditis organism associated with poor dental hygiene or periodontal disease?
cards.a: Eikenella corrodens (part of the HACEK group).

cards.q: Culture-negative infective endocarditis organism associated with exposure to farm animals and presenting as a chronic, indolent infection?
cards.a: Coxiella burnetii.

cards.q: Most common causative organism of prosthetic valve endocarditis within the first year after valve replacement surgery?
cards.a: Staphylococcus epidermidis.

cards.q: Classic immunologically mediated physical exam finding in infective endocarditis presenting as painful nodules on the pads of fingers or toes?
cards.a: Osler nodes.

cards.q: Classic physical exam finding in infective endocarditis presenting as painless, erythematous macules on the palms or soles?
cards.a: Janeway lesions.

cards.q: Diagnostic criteria schema used to establish a clinical diagnosis of Infective Endocarditis?
cards.a: Modified Duke Criteria. Travel Medicine & Prophylaxis

cards.q: Preferred malaria chemoprophylaxis regimen for a pregnant traveler visiting a chloroquine-resistant region?
cards.a: Mefloquine.

cards.q: Malaria chemoprophylaxis agent that must be started 1 to 2 weeks before travel and continued for 4 weeks after returning?
cards.a: Mefloquine or Doxycycline.

cards.q: Malaria chemoprophylaxis agent that can be started 1 to 2 days before travel and stopped 7 days after returning?
cards.a: Atovaquone-Proguanil.

cards.q: Live-attenuated vaccine required for entry into certain sub-Saharan African and South American countries, documented via an International Certificate of Vaccination?
cards.a: Yellow Fever vaccine.

cards.q: Most common bacterial cause of traveler's diarrhea?
cards.a: Enterotoxigenic Escherichia coli (ETEC).

cards.q: First-line antibiotic choice for empirical self-treatment of severe traveler's diarrhea accompanied by high fever or systemic symptoms?
cards.a: Azithromycin or a fluoroquinolone (e.g., Ciprofloxacin). High-Yield Antibiotic Toxicities & Crossover Interactions

cards.q: Antibiotic class classic for causing tendonitis and Achilles tendon rupture, particularly in elderly patients or those taking glucocorticoids?
cards.a: Fluoroquinolones.

cards.q: Antibiotic known to cause serotonin syndrome when co-administered with selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors (SSRIs) due to its weak monoamine oxidase inhibitor (MAOI) activity?
cards.a: Linezolid.

cards.q: Reversible hematologic adverse effect associated with prolonged ($>2$ weeks) Linezolid therapy?
cards.a: Bone marrow suppression, most commonly presenting as thrombocytopenia.

cards.q: Classic electrolyte abnormality associated with high-dose Trimethoprim-Sulfamethoxazole (TMP-SMX) administration?
cards.a: Hyperkalemia (due to trimethoprim blocking sodium channels in the distal nephron).

cards.q: Antimicrobial agent associated with a disulfiram-like reaction (flushing, tachycardia, nausea) when consumed with alcohol?
cards.a: Metronidazole.

cards.q: Class of antibiotics that carries a small risk of cross-reactivity in patients with a confirmed, IgE-mediated anaphylactic allergy to penicillins?
cards.a: Cephalosporins (specifically first-generation agents). Adult Immunizations & Special Populations

cards.q: Pneumococcal vaccination strategy recommended for all immunocompetent adults aged 65 years or older who have never received a pneumococcal vaccine?
cards.a: A single dose of PCV20 OR a single dose of PCV15 followed by PPSV23 one year later.

cards.q: Vaccine recommended for all pregnant individuals during weeks 27 through 36 of each pregnancy to provide passive immunity to the neonate?
cards.a: Tdap (Tetanus, Diphtheria, Acellular Pertussis).

cards.q: Age at which the recombinant Zoster vaccine (Shingrix) is routinely recommended for immunocompetent adults to prevent shingles?
cards.a: 50 years and older (administered as a 2-dose series).

cards.q: Two core vaccinations that must be administered to patients prior to undergoing an elective splenectomy?
cards.a: Meningococcal conjugate and Pneumococcal vaccines (along with Haemophilus influenzae type b). Fever of Unknown Origin & Culture-Negative Entities

cards.q: Classic definition of Fever of Unknown Origin (FUO) in an outpatient setting?
cards.a: Fever $\ge 38.3^\circ\text{C}$ ($101^\circ\text{F}$) on several occasions lasting for at least 3 weeks with no diagnosis after 3 days of in-hospital investigation or 3 outpatient visits.

cards.q: Most common overall category of diseases responsible for Fever of Unknown Origin in adults?
cards.a: Infections (followed closely by malignancies and non-infectious inflammatory diseases).

cards.q: Zoonotic bacterial cause of culture-negative endocarditis or FUO associated with consuming unpasteurized goat cheese?
cards.a: Brucella melitensis.

cards.q: Systemic infectious disease caused by Tropheryma whipplei, presenting with arthralgias, weight loss, chronic diarrhea, and hyperpigmentation?
cards.a: Whipple disease.

cards.q: Classic diagnostic finding on a small bowel biopsy for a patient with Whipple disease?

topic: Rheumatology — SLE, RA, vasculitis, crystal arthropathies

cards.q: Initial diagnostic imaging of choice for a patient suspected of having Rheumatoid Arthritis?
cards.a: Bilateral hand and wrist radiographs.

cards.q: Earliest radiographic finding seen in early Rheumatoid Arthritis?
cards.a: Periarticular osteopenia and soft tissue swelling.

cards.q: Definitive late-stage radiographic features pathognomonic for Rheumatoid Arthritis?
cards.a: Marginal joint erosions and joint space narrowing.

cards.q: Most specific autoantibody for diagnosing Rheumatoid Arthritis?
cards.a: Anti-Cyclic Citrullinated Peptide (anti-CCP) antibody.

cards.q: Joint classification that is characteristically spared in Rheumatoid Arthritis?
cards.a: Distal Interphalangeal (DIP) joints.

cards.q: Most common deformity of the thumb seen in advanced Rheumatoid Arthritis?
cards.a: Boutonniere deformity.

cards.q: Name of the deformity characterized by PIP hyperextension and DIP flexion?
cards.a: Swan-neck deformity.

cards.q: Life-threatening cervical spine complication of Rheumatoid Arthritis that requires screening before elective surgery?
cards.a: Atlantoaxial subluxation.

cards.q: First-line disease-modifying antirheumatic drug (DMARD) used for moderate-to-severe Rheumatoid Arthritis?
cards.a: Methotrexate.

cards.q: Supplement that must be co-prescribed with Methotrexate to reduce side effects?
cards.a: Folic acid.

cards.q: Serious pulmonary complication associated with chronic Methotrexate therapy?
cards.a: Interstitial lung disease (methotrexate pneumonitis).

cards.q: Best initial screening test required before initiating any TNF-alpha inhibitor therapy?
cards.a: Interferon-gamma release assay (IGRA) or PPD test for latent Tuberculosis.

cards.q: Triad defining Felty Syndrome?
cards.a: Rheumatoid Arthritis, splenomegaly, and neutropenia.

cards.q: Most accurate diagnostic test for Felty Syndrome when presenting with severe neutropenia?
cards.a: Bone marrow biopsy showing myeloid maturation arrest.

cards.q: Constellation of symptoms defining Caplan Syndrome?
cards.a: Rheumatoid Arthritis combined with coal worker's pneumoconiosis. Systemic Lupus Erythematosus (SLE)

cards.q: Most sensitive screening autoantibody for Systemic Lupus Erythematosus?
cards.a: Antinuclear Antibody (ANA).

cards.q: Most specific autoantibodies for diagnosing Systemic Lupus Erythematosus?
cards.a: Anti-double-stranded DNA (anti-dsDNA) and Anti-Smith (anti-Sm) antibodies.

cards.q: Autoantibody closely correlated with disease activity and lupus nephritis development in SLE?
cards.a: Anti-double-stranded DNA (anti-dsDNA).

cards.q: Autoantibody associated with Drug-Induced Lupus Erythematosus?
cards.a: Anti-histone antibody.

cards.q: Top three medications most frequently implicated in Drug-Induced Lupus?
cards.a: Procainamide, Hydralazine, and Isoniazid.

cards.q: Classic skin manifestation of SLE triggered or exacerbated by sunlight exposure?
cards.a: Malar (butterfly) rash sparing the nasolabial folds.

cards.q: Type of endocarditis characterized by sterile verrucous vegetations on both sides of cardiac valves in SLE patients?
cards.a: Libman-Sacks endocarditis.

cards.q: Best initial management for mild systemic manifestations of SLE like arthritis or cutaneous lesions?
cards.a: Hydroxychloroquine.

cards.q: Mandatory routine screening test for patients on long-term Hydroxychloroquine therapy?
cards.a: Annual ophthalmologic exam to screen for retinal toxicity.

cards.q: Most accurate diagnostic method to confirm and classify Lupus Nephritis?
cards.a: Renal biopsy.

cards.q: Standard induction therapy for severe, proliferative Lupus Nephritis (Class III or IV)?
cards.a: Mycophenolate mofetil or Cyclophosphamide combined with high-dose glucocorticoids.

cards.q: Serum complement levels characteristically seen during an active SLE flare?
cards.a: Decreased C3 and C4 levels.

cards.q: Primary mechanism of anemia commonly seen in active, severe SLE?
cards.a: Warm Autoimmune Hemolytic Anemia (Coombs-positive).

cards.q: Severe, life-threatening complication of systemic juvenile idiopathic arthritis or adult SLE involving massive macrophage activation?
cards.a: Macrophage Activation Syndrome (MAS).

cards.q: Key laboratory hallmarks of Macrophage Activation Syndrome?
cards.a: Precipitous drop in ESR, skyrocketing Ferritin, cytopenias, and elevated triglycerides. Antiphospholipid Syndrome (APS)

cards.q: Paradoxical laboratory finding seen in Antiphospholipid Syndrome despite an increased risk of thrombosis?
cards.a: Prolonged Activated Partial Thromboplastin Time (aPTT).

cards.q: The three diagnostic autoantibodies for Antiphospholipid Syndrome?
cards.a: Lupus anticoagulant, anti-beta-2-glycoprotein I, and anti-cardiolipin antibodies.

cards.q: Common false-positive screening result seen in patients with high titers of anti-cardiolipin antibodies?
cards.a: False-positive VDRL or RPR test for Syphilis.

cards.q: Preferred long-term anticoagulation therapy for a non-pregnant patient with confirmed Antiphospholipid Syndrome and a history of DVT?
cards.a: Warfarin.

cards.q: Target INR range for a patient with Antiphospholipid Syndrome experiencing a first venous thromboembolic event?
cards.a: INR of 2.0 to 3.0.

cards.q: Preferred anticoagulation regimen for a pregnant patient with Antiphospholipid Syndrome?
cards.a: Low-molecular-weight heparin (LMWH) combined with low-dose aspirin.

cards.q: Rare, life-threatening form of APS causing simultaneous multi-organ microvascular failure?
cards.a: Catastrophic Antiphospholipid Syndrome (CAPS).

cards.q: First-line management triad for Catastrophic Antiphospholipid Syndrome?
cards.a: High-dose IV glucocorticoids, therapeutic anticoagulation, and plasma exchange or IVIG. Scleroderma (Systemic Sclerosis)

cards.q: Autoantibody most specific for Diffuse Cutaneous Systemic Sclerosis?
cards.a: Anti-Scl-70 (anti-topoisomerase I) antibody.

cards.q: Autoantibody most specific for Limited Cutaneous Systemic Sclerosis (CREST syndrome)?
cards.a: Anti-centromere antibody.

cards.q: The components that comprise the acronym CREST syndrome?
cards.a: Calcinosis, Raynaud phenomenon, Esophageal dysmotility, Sclerodactyly, and Telangiectasia.

cards.q: Most common cause of death in patients with Diffuse Cutaneous Systemic Sclerosis?
cards.a: Interstitial Lung Disease (pulmonary fibrosis).

cards.q: Leading vascular cause of death in patients with Limited Cutaneous Systemic Sclerosis?
cards.a: Pulmonary Arterial Hypertension.

cards.q: Sudden, life-threatening renal complication of Diffuse Scleroderma presenting with malignant hypertension and microangiopathic hemolytic anemia?
cards.a: Scleroderma Renal Crisis.

cards.q: Drug class of choice that is lifesaving in the management of Scleroderma Renal Crisis?
cards.a: Angiotensin-Converting Enzyme (ACE) inhibitors.

cards.q: Class of medications strictly contraindicated in high doses in systemic sclerosis due to the risk of precipitating Scleroderma Renal Crisis?
cards.a: Glucocorticoids.

cards.q: First-line medical therapy for managing severe Raynaud phenomenon in scleroderma patients?
cards.a: Calcium channel blockers (e.g., Nifedipine). Sjögren Syndrome

cards.q: Classic diagnostic triad of primary Sjögren Syndrome?
cards.a: Keratoconjunctivitis sicca (dry eyes), xerostomia (dry mouth), and parotid gland enlargement.

cards.q: The two autoantibodies most highly associated with Sjögren Syndrome?
cards.a: Anti-Ro (SS-A) and Anti-La (SS-B) antibodies.

cards.q: Fetal risk associated with pregnant patients carrying positive anti-Ro (SS-A) antibodies?
cards.a: Neonatal lupus and congenital complete heart block.

cards.q: Best objective initial test to evaluate for decreased tear production in suspected Sjögren Syndrome?
cards.a: Schirmer test.

cards.q: Most definitive diagnostic test to confirm Sjögren Syndrome if serology is ambiguous?
cards.a: Lip biopsy showing focal lymphocytic sialadenitis.

cards.q: Patients with Sjögren Syndrome have a markedly elevated risk for developing which specific malignancy?
cards.a: Non-Hodgkin Lymphoma (specifically B-cell MALT lymphoma). Inflammatory Myopathies (Dermatomyositis & Polymyositis)

cards.q: Pattern of muscle weakness characteristically seen in Polymyositis and Dermatomyositis?
cards.a: Symmetrical, proximal muscle weakness affecting the shoulders and hips.

cards.q: Most specific autoantibody for Polymyositis and Dermatomyositis associated with interstitial lung disease?
cards.a: Anti-Jo-1 (anti-tRNA synthetase) antibody.

cards.q: Autoantibody highly specific for Dermatomyositis presenting with classic cutaneous signs?
cards.a: Anti-Mi-2 antibody.

cards.q: Pathognomonic violaceous rash over the eyelids seen in Dermatomyositis?
cards.a: Heliotrope rash.

cards.q: Pathognomonic erythematous, scaly papules found over the bony prominences of the MCP and PIP joints?
cards.a: Gottron papules.

cards.q: Cutaneous finding in Dermatomyositis characterized by hyperkeratosis and scaling on the lateral aspects of the fingers?
cards.a: Mechanic's hands.

cards.q: Key histological difference on muscle biopsy between Polymyositis and Dermatomyositis?
cards.a: Polymyositis shows endomysial inflammation, while Dermatomyositis shows perimysial/perivascular inflammation.

cards.q: Crucial age-appropriate screening required upon diagnosing a patient with Dermatomyositis?
cards.a: Internal malignancy screening.

cards.q: First-line systemic pharmacotherapy for both Polymyositis and Dermatomyositis?
cards.a: High-dose oral glucocorticoids. Seronegative Spondyloarthropathies

cards.q: Genotypic human leukocyte antigen highly associated with all seronegative spondyloarthropathies?
cards.a: HLA-B27.

cards.q: Classic radiographic spine finding in advanced, long-standing Ankylosing Spondylitis?
cards.a: Bamboo spine due to marginal syndesmophytes and fusion.

cards.q: Clinical pattern of low back pain classic for Ankylosing Spondylitis?
cards.a: Chronic back pain that improves with exercise and worsens with rest.

cards.q: Most common extra-articular manifestation of Ankylosing Spondylitis?
cards.a: Acute anterior uveitis.

cards.q: Screening test of choice for early Ankylosing Spondylitis when plain radiographs are normal?
cards.a: MRI of the sacroiliac joints.

cards.q: Classic clinical triad defining Reactive Arthritis?
cards.a: Uveitis/conjunctivitis, urethritis, and arthritis ("Can't see, can't pee, can't climb a tree").

cards.q: Common infectious triggers preceding Reactive Arthritis?
cards.a: Chlamydia trachomatis, Campylobacter, Salmonella, Shigella, and Yersinia.

cards.q: Characteristic cutaneous lesion of Reactive Arthritis found on the palms or soles resembling pustular psoriasis?
cards.a: Keratoderma blennorrhagica.

cards.q: Unique radiographic and clinical finding of the digits seen in Psoriatic Arthritis?
cards.a: Dactylitis ("sausage digits").

cards.q: Classic radiographic feature of the phalanges seen in severe Psoriatic Arthritis?
cards.a: "Pencil-in-cup" deformity.

cards.q: Class of medications used as first-line therapy for the symptomatic management of Ankylosing Spondylitis?
cards.a: NSAIDs. Crystal-Induced Arthropathies (Gout & Pseudogout)

cards.q: Polarized light microscopy appearance of monosodium urate crystals in Gout?
cards.a: Needle-shaped and negatively birefringent (yellow when parallel to the slow wave of the compensator).

cards.q: Polarized light microscopy appearance of calcium pyrophosphate dihydrate (CPPD) crystals in Pseudogout?
cards.a: Rhomboid-shaped and weakly positively birefringent (blue when parallel to the slow wave of the compensator).

cards.q: Name given to the classic involvement of the first metatarsophalangeal (MTP) joint in acute Gout?
cards.a: Podagra.

cards.q: Radiographic hallmark of chronic, tophaceous Gout?
cards.a: Punched-out lytic bone erosions with overhanging cortical edges.

cards.q: Radiographic hallmark of Pseudogout (CPPD) found within joint cartilage?
cards.a: Chondrocalcinosis.

cards.q: First-line abortive therapies for an acute flare of Gout in a patient with normal renal function?
cards.a: NSAIDs (e.g., Indomethacin) or systemic/intra-articular glucocorticoids.

cards.q: Mechanism of action of Colchicine in acute gout management?
cards.a: Inhibits microtubule polymerization, disrupting neutrophil chemotaxis and degranulation.

cards.q: Major toxicities of Colchicine that restrict its use in patients with severe renal failure?
cards.a: Diarrhea, neuromyopathy, and bone marrow suppression.

cards.q: Best long-term, first-line urate-lowering therapy for chronic gout prevention?
cards.a: Allopurinol.

cards.q: Severe, life-threatening hypersensitivity syndrome associated with Allopurinol therapy?
cards.a: DRESS syndrome (Drug Reaction with Eosinophilia and Systemic Symptoms) or Stevens-Johnson Syndrome.

cards.q: Genetic screening test recommended for Asian patients before initiating Allopurinol to prevent severe cutaneous adverse reactions?
cards.a: HLA-B*5801 allele testing.

cards.q: Primary mechanism of action of Allopurinol and Febuxostat?
cards.a: Xanthine oxidase inhibition.

cards.q: Dangerous phenomenon that can occur if urate-lowering therapy is started during an acute gout flare without anti-inflammatory prophylaxis?
cards.a: Precipitation or worsening of the acute gout flare.

cards.q: Three systemic metabolic conditions strongly associated with secondary Pseudogout (CPPD)?
cards.a: Hyperparathyroidism, Hemochromatosis, and Hypomagnesemia. Vasculitis (Large, Medium, Small Vessel)

cards.q: Most dreaded complication of untreated Giant Cell (Temporal) Arteritis?
cards.a: Permanent blindness due to anterior ischemic optic neuropathy.

cards.q: Immediate management step when Giant Cell Arteritis is strongly suspected, prior to obtaining a biopsy?
cards.a: High-dose intravenous or oral systemic glucocorticoids.

cards.q: Most definitive diagnostic test for confirming Giant Cell Arteritis?
cards.a: Temporal artery biopsy.

cards.q: Condition characterized by proximal limb girdle stiffness and high ESR, occurring in 50% of patients with Giant Cell Arteritis?
cards.a: Polymyalgia Rheumatica (PMR).

cards.q: Large-vessel vasculitis predominantly affecting young Asian females, causing upper extremity pulse deficits?
cards.a: Takayasu Arteritis.

cards.q: Medium-vessel necrotizing vasculitis strongly associated with chronic Hepatitis B infection?
cards.a: Polyarteritis Nodosa (PAN).

cards.q: Classic angiographic finding seen in the mesenteric or renal vessels of a patient with Polyarteritis Nodosa?
cards.a: Microaneurysms with a "string-of-beads" appearance.

cards.q: Organ system characteristically spared in Polyarteritis Nodosa?
cards.a: The lungs.

cards.q: Pediatric medium-vessel vasculitis presenting with high fever, strawberry tongue, and desquamating rash?
cards.a: Kawasaki Disease.

cards.q: Most critical cardiac complication of untreated Kawasaki Disease?
cards.a: Coronary artery aneurysms.

cards.q: Standard first-line medical regimen for acute Kawasaki Disease to reduce coronary artery risks?
cards.a: Intravenous Immunoglobulin (IVIG) and high-dose Aspirin.

cards.q: Small-vessel vasculitis characterized by granulomatous inflammation of the respiratory tract and necrotizing glomerulonephritis?
cards.a: Granulomatosis with Polyangiitis (GPA / Wegener's).

cards.q: Highly specific serum autoantibody marker for Granulomatosis with Polyangiitis?
cards.a: c-ANCA (PR3-ANCA).

cards.q: Small-vessel vasculitis presenting with asthma, prominent blood eosinophilia, and transient pulmonary infiltrates?
cards.a: Eosinophilic Granulomatosis with Polyangiitis (EGPA / Churg-Strauss).

cards.q: Highly specific serum autoantibody marker for Eosinophilic Granulomatosis with Polyangiitis and Microscopic Polyangiitis?
cards.a: p-ANCA (MPO-ANCA).

cards.q: Most common systemic vasculitis in children, presenting with palpable purpura, arthralgias, abdominal pain, and hematuria?
cards.a: IgA Vasculitis (Henoch-Schönlein Purpura).

cards.q: Deposition finding on renal biopsy pathognomonic for IgA Vasculitis?
cards.a: Mesangial IgA immune complex deposition.

cards.q: Small-vessel vasculitis precipitated by cold temperatures, causing palpable purpura, arthralgias, and strongly associated with Hepatitis C?
cards.a: Mixed Cryoglobulinemia.

cards.q: Key serum complement profile finding in patients presenting with a Mixed Cryoglobulinemia flare?
cards.a: Markedly depressed C4 levels with normal or mildly low C3. Other Rheumatologic Conditions

cards.q: Diagnostic criteria combination used to confirm Behcet Syndrome?
cards.a: Recurrent painful oral aphthous ulcers plus two of: recurrent genital ulcers, ocular lesions (uveitis), or pachyderma skin lesions.

cards.q: Simple, non-invasive physical exam test demonstrating skin hyperreactivity used to support Behcet Syndrome diagnosis?
cards.a: Pathergy test (pustule formation 24-48 hours after a sterile needle prick).

cards.q: Serious neurological manifestation of Behcet Syndrome that can mimic multiple sclerosis?
cards.a: Neuro-Behcet disease (meningoencephalitis or dural sinus thrombosis).

cards.q: Best initial screening tool for assessing bone mineral density to diagnose Osteoporosis?
cards.a: Dual-energy X-ray absorptiometry (DEXA) scan.

cards.q: T-score threshold on a DEXA scan defining the diagnostic cutoff for Osteoporosis?
cards.a: T-score of -2.5 or lower.

cards.q: First-line pharmacotherapy class for the prevention and treatment of postmenopausal Osteoporosis?
cards.a: Oral Bisphosphonates (e.g., Alendronate).

cards.q: Rare, severe jaw complication associated with long-term, high-dose Bisphosphonate therapy?
cards.a: Osteonecrosis of the jaw.

cards.q: Atypical skeletal fracture complication associated with prolonged Bisphosphonate therapy exceeding 5 years?
cards.a: Atypical subtrochanteric femoral fractures.

cards.q: Core chronic widespread pain syndrome characterized by specific tender points, normal inflammatory markers, and sleep disturbance?
cards.a: Fibromyalgia.

cards.q: First-line FDA-approved non-opioid medications for the management of Fibromyalgia?
cards.a: Amitriptyline, Duloxetine, or Pregabalin. Rheumatology-Hematology Overlap & Drug Toxicities

cards.q: Most common drug-induced cytopenia associated with high-dose Azathioprine therapy?
cards.a: Leukopenia (bone marrow suppression).

cards.q: Genetic enzyme deficiency that exponentially increases the risk of severe bone marrow toxicity when taking Azathioprine?
cards.a: Thiopurine Methyltransferase (TPMT) deficiency.

cards.q: Mechanism by which Allopurinol co-administration causes life-threatening cytopenias in a patient taking Azathioprine?
cards.a: Allopurinol inhibits xanthine oxidase, preventing the metabolism of active azathioprine metabolites.

cards.q: Signature hematologic abnormality seen in the peripheral blood smear of a patient with active Macrophage Activation Syndrome?
cards.a: Hemophagocytosis (macrophages engulfing erythrocytes, leukocytes, and platelets).

cards.q: The classic presentation of Adult-Onset Still’s Disease?
cards.a: Quotidien (daily) high fevers, salmon-pink evanescent rash, arthritis, and extreme leukocytosis.

cards.q: Serum biomarker that is characteristically elevated to extreme levels in Adult-Onset Still's Disease?
cards.a: Ferritin.

cards.q: Serious hematologic adverse effect of Cyclophosphamide therapy that requires monitoring with regular urinalyses?
cards.a: Hemorrhagic cystitis.

cards.q: Co-administered agent utilized to neutralize the metabolite acrolein and prevent Cyclophosphamide-induced hemorrhagic cystitis?
cards.a: Mesna (2-mercaptoethane sulfonate).

cards.q: Malignancy that patients treated with Cyclophosphamide have a significantly increased long-term risk of developing?
cards.a: Transitional cell carcinoma of the bladder. Osteoarthritis (OA)

cards.q: Most important non-pharmacologic intervention for slowing the progression of knee and hip Osteoarthritis?
cards.a: Weight loss and low-impact exercise.

cards.q: First-line pharmacotherapy for symptomatic management of mild-to-moderate Osteoarthritis?
cards.a: Topical or oral NSAIDs (e.g., Diclofenac, Naproxen).

cards.q: Radiographic hallmarks of advanced Osteoarthritis?
cards.a: Asymmetric joint space narrowing, subchondral sclerosis, osteophytes, and subchondral cysts.

cards.q: Name given to the palpable osteophyte nodules located at the Distal Interphalangeal (DIP) joints in Osteoarthritis?
cards.a: Heberden nodes.

cards.q: Name given to the palpable osteophyte nodules located at the Proximal Interphalangeal (PIP) joints in Osteoarthritis?
cards.a: Bouchard nodes.

cards.q: Character of joint stiffness in Osteoarthritis compared to Rheumatoid Arthritis?
cards.a: Morning stiffness lasting less than 30 minutes that worsens with use and improves with rest. Infectious & Reactive Arthritides

cards.q: Most common causative organism of acute bacterial septic arthritis in the general adult population?
cards.a: Staphylococcus aureus.

cards.q: Most common causative organism of septic arthritis in sexually active young adults?
cards.a: Neisseria gonorrhoeae.

cards.q: Classic disseminated triad of Disseminated Gonococcal Infection (DGI)?
cards.a: Polyarthralgias, tenosynovitis, and painless pustular skin lesions.

cards.q: Synovial fluid analysis findings pathognomonic for acute Septic Arthritis?
cards.a: Purulent fluid, WBC count greater than 50,000/µL, and greater than 75% polymorphonuclear leukocytes.

cards.q: Empiric antibiotic regimen of choice for a patient with suspected acute Septic Arthritis while cultures are pending?
cards.a: Intravenous Vancomycin combined with a third-generation cephalosporin (e.g., Ceftriaxone).

cards.q: Standard diagnostic protocol for a patient presenting with an acute, hot, swollen monoarticular joint?
cards.a: Immediate joint aspiration (arthrocentesis) and synovial fluid analysis.

cards.q: Classic rheumatologic manifestation of late-stage, untreated Lyme Disease?
cards.a: Intermittent or chronic monoarticular or oligoarticular arthritis, most commonly affecting the knee.

cards.q: Preferred first-line oral antibiotic for early localized Lyme disease and early Lyme arthritis?
cards.a: Doxycycline. Sarcoidosis

cards.q: Classic chest radiographic finding pathognomonic for Stage I Sarcoidosis?
cards.a: Bilateral hilar adenopathy.

cards.q: Distinct triad defining Löfgren Syndrome (an acute presentation of Sarcoidosis)?
cards.a: Bilateral hilar adenopathy, erythema nodosum, and migratory polyarthritis.

cards.q: Histopathological hallmark finding on biopsy of an affected organ in Sarcoidosis?
cards.a: Non-caseating granulomas.

cards.q: Serum electrolyte and enzyme abnormalities classic for active systemic Sarcoidosis?
cards.a: Hypercalcemia, hypercalciuria, and elevated Angiotensin-Converting Enzyme (ACE) levels.

cards.q: Primary mechanism causing hypercalcemia in patients with Sarcoidosis?
cards.a: Unregulated 1-alpha-hydroxylase activity in granulomatous macrophages converting vitamin D to its active form.

cards.q: First-line systemic treatment for symptomatic or progressive organ-threatening Sarcoidosis?
cards.a: Systemic glucocorticoids. Adult-Onset Still's Disease (AOSD)

cards.q: Classic triad of symptoms defining Adult-Onset Still's Disease?
cards.a: Quotidian (daily) high spiking fevers, an evanescent salmon-pink maculopapular rash, and arthritis.

cards.q: The unique timing characteristic of the salmon-pink rash in Adult-Onset Still's Disease?
cards.a: The rash appears or worsens concurrently with the daily fever spikes.

cards.q: Extreme laboratory abnormality characteristic of Adult-Onset Still's Disease that helps differentiate it from other rheumatologic conditions?
cards.a: Markedly elevated serum Ferritin levels (often exceeding 5,000 ng/mL) and profound leukocytosis.

cards.q: First-line pharmacotherapy for mild manifestations of Adult-Onset Still's Disease?
cards.a: High-dose NSAIDs.

cards.q: Preferred biologic drug targets for refractory or severe cases of Adult-Onset Still's Disease?
cards.a: Interleukin-1 (IL-1) inhibitors (e.g., Anakinra) or Interleukin-6 (IL-6) inhibitors (e.g., Tocilizumab). Systemic Autoinflammatory & IgG4 Diseases

cards.q: Most common hereditary autoinflammatory periodic fever syndrome, caused by mutations in the MEFV gene?
cards.a: Familial Mediterranean Fever (FMF).

cards.q: Classic clinical presentation of a Familial Mediterranean Fever flare?
cards.a: Recurrent, self-limiting episodes of fever accompanied by peritonitis, pleuritis, or synovitis lasting 1 to 3 days.

cards.q: First-line maintenance medication used to decrease the frequency of flares and prevent systemic amyloidosis in Familial Mediterranean Fever?
cards.a: Colchicine.

cards.q: Type of systemic amyloidosis that develops as a long-term complication of untreated Familial Mediterranean Fever?
cards.a: AA (Secondary) Amyloidosis.

cards.q: Fibroinflammatory condition characterized by tumefactive lesions, elevated serum titers, and lymphoplasmacytic infiltrates?
cards.a: IgG4-Related Disease.

cards.q: Pathognomonic histopathological features of IgG4-Related Disease on tissue biopsy?
cards.a: Dense lymphoplasmacytic infiltrate rich in IgG4+ plasma cells, storiform fibrosis, and obliterative phlebitis.

cards.q: Common clinical manifestations or organ involvements seen in IgG4-Related Disease?
cards.a: Autoimmune pancreatitis (Type 1), Riedel thyroiditis, Mikulicz syndrome (enlarged lacrimal and salivary glands), and retroperitoneal fibrosis. Advanced Biologics & Mechanisms of Action

cards.q: Specific molecular target of Rituximab used in severe granulomatosis with polyangiitis and refractory SLE?
cards.a: CD20 antigen on B lymphocytes.

cards.q: Mechanism of action of Belimumab used as an adjunctive therapy in systemic lupus erythematosus?
cards.a: Inhibits B-lymphocyte stimulator (BLyS), preventing B-cell survival and differentiation.

cards.q: Mechanism of action of Abatacept used in refractory Rheumatoid Arthritis?
cards.a: Binds to CD80 and CD86 on antigen-presenting cells, blocking the costimulatory signal required for T-cell activation.

cards.q: Mechanism of action of Tocilizumab used in Giant Cell Arteritis and Rheumatoid Arthritis?
cards.a: Interleukin-6 (IL-6) receptor antagonist.

cards.q: Mechanism of action of Secukinumab used in the treatment of severe Psoriatic Arthritis and Ankylosing Spondylitis?
cards.a: Interleukin-17A (IL-17A) inhibitor.

cards.q: Mechanism of action of Ustekinumab utilized in Psoriatic Arthritis?
cards.a: Inhibits the p40 subunit of both Interleukin-12 (IL-12) and Interleukin-23 (IL-23).

cards.q: Mechanism of action of Tofacitinib and Upadacitinib used in severe Rheumatoid Arthritis?
cards.a: Janus Kinase (JAK) inhibitors, blocking intracellular cytokine signaling.

cards.q: Black box warning or screening required before starting a patient on Janus Kinase (JAK) inhibitors?
cards.a: Screening for latent tuberculosis and monitoring for an increased risk of deep vein thrombosis (DVT) and malignancy. ===================================================================== ===================================================================== Section: Internal Medicine

topic: Neurology — Stroke, seizures, headache, dementia, MS

cards.q: Most common overall site for a hypertensive intraparenchymal hemorrhage?
cards.a: Putamen.

cards.q: Classical presentation of a putaminal hemorrhage?
cards.a: Contralateral hemiparesis and gaze deviation toward the side of the lesion.

cards.q: Clinical presentation distinguishing cerebellar hemorrhage from other intracranial bleeds?
cards.a: Sudden ataxia and vomiting without hemiparesis.

cards.q: Definitive emergency intervention for an expanding cerebellar hemorrhage with neurological decline?
cards.a: Surgical decompression.

cards.q: Initial neuroimaging diagnostic step when evaluating an acute stroke-like presentation?
cards.a: Non-contrast CT scan of the head to rule out hemorrhage.

cards.q: Time window for administering intravenous alteplase in acute ischemic stroke?
cards.a: Within 4.5 hours of when the patient was last seen normal.

cards.q: Primary absolute contraindication to thrombolytic therapy in acute ischemic stroke?
cards.a: History of any intracranial hemorrhage.

cards.q: Eligibility window for mechanical thrombectomy in large vessel occlusion of the anterior circulation?
cards.a: Within 24 hours of symptom onset.

cards.q: Preferred initial antiplatelet management for acute ischemic stroke outside the thrombolytic window?
cards.a: Aspirin.

cards.q: Pathophysiological structure occluded in Lateral Medullary (Wallenberg) Syndrome?
cards.a: Posterior Inferior Cerebellar Artery or vertebral artery.

cards.q: Classic clinical triad of Lateral Medullary Syndrome?
cards.a: Ipsilateral Horner syndrome, ipsilateral facial loss of pain/temperature, and contralateral body loss of pain/temperature.

cards.q: Cranial nerve deficits explaining hoarseness and dysphagia in Wallenberg Syndrome?
cards.a: Nucleus ambiguus involvement affecting cranial nerves IX and X.

cards.q: Clinical presentation of a total basilar artery occlusion?
cards.a: Locked-in syndrome with preserved consciousness and vertical eye movements.

cards.q: Classic visual field deficit associated with a posterior cerebral artery occlusion?
cards.a: Homonymous hemianopsia with macular sparing.

cards.q: Characteristic shape of a subdural hematoma on a non-contrast head CT?
cards.a: Crescent-shaped collection crossing suture lines.

cards.q: Vessel ruptured causing a subdural hematoma?
cards.a: Bridging cortical veins.

cards.q: Predisposed patient populations for chronic subdural hematomas?
cards.a: Elderly individuals and chronic alcoholics.

cards.q: Characteristic shape of an epidural hematoma on a non-contrast head CT?
cards.a: Biconvex or lens-shaped collection restricted by suture lines.

cards.q: Vessel ruptured causing an epidural hematoma?
cards.a: Middle meningeal artery.

cards.q: Classical clinical progression of an epidural hematoma?
cards.a: Head trauma followed by a lucid interval and then rapid neurological demise.

cards.q: Most common etiology of a non-traumatic subarachnoid hemorrhage?
cards.a: Rupture of a saccular or berry aneurysm.

cards.q: First-line medication used to prevent vasospasm following a subarachnoid hemorrhage?
cards.a: Nimodipine. Section 2: Neurodegenerative Disorders & Dementias

cards.q: Definitive histopathological features of Alzheimer disease?
cards.a: Extracellular amyloid-beta plaques and intracellular neurofibrillary tangles of hyperphosphorylated tau protein.

cards.q: Core cognitive presentation that differentiates Alzheimer disease from frontotemporal dementia?
cards.a: Early loss of short-term memory with preserved personality in early stages.

cards.q: Characterizing presentation of frontotemporal dementia?
cards.a: Early changes in personality, social disinhibition, and executive dysfunction.

cards.q: Clinical triad defining Dementia with Lewy Bodies?
cards.a: Fluctuating cognition, visual hallucinations, and spontaneous Parkinsonism.

cards.q: Classical clinical triad of Normal Pressure Hydrocephalus?
cards.a: Gait apraxia, urinary incontinence, and cognitive decline.

cards.q: Diagnostic and temporary therapeutic intervention for Normal Pressure Hydrocephalus?
cards.a: Large-volume lumbar puncture.

cards.q: Definitive definitive long-term treatment for Normal Pressure Hydrocephalus?
cards.a: Ventriculoperitoneal shunting.

cards.q: Distinguishing clinical feature of vascular dementia?
cards.a: Stepwise decline in cognitive function matching focal ischemic events.

cards.q: Characterizing clinical feature of Creutzfeldt-Jakob disease?
cards.a: Rapidly progressive dementia accompanied by myoclonus and ataxia.

cards.q: Diagnostic EEG finding associated with Creutzfeldt-Jakob disease?
cards.a: Periodic sharp wave complexes.

cards.q: Core diagnostic criteria required for a diagnosis of Parkinson disease?
cards.a: Bradykinesia combined with either a resting tremor or rigidity.

cards.q: Mechanism of action of carbidopa when co-administered with levodopa?
cards.a: Inhibits peripheral DOPA decarboxylase to maximize central nervous system bioavailability.

cards.q: Genetic inheritance pattern and mutation associated with Huntington disease?
cards.a: Autosomal dominant CAG trinucleotide repeat expansion on chromosome 4.

cards.q: Specific neuroanatomical structure that atrophies in Huntington disease?
cards.a: Caudate nucleus. Section 3: Neuromuscular & Peripheral Nerve Disorders

cards.q: Classical cerebrospinal fluid analysis finding in Guillain-Barré Syndrome?
cards.a: Albuminocytologic dissociation featuring elevated protein with normal white blood cell count.

cards.q: Most common infectious trigger associated with Guillain-Barré Syndrome?
cards.a: Campylobacter jejuni enteritis.

cards.q: Most critical monitoring parameters for a patient admitted with acute Guillain-Barré Syndrome?
cards.a: Forced vital capacity and negative inspiratory force to monitor respiratory failure.

cards.q: Proven effective treatments for Guillain-Barré Syndrome?
cards.a: Intravenous immunoglobulin or plasmapheresis.

cards.q: Contraindicated medication class in the management of acute Guillain-Barré Syndrome?
cards.a: Systemic corticosteroids.

cards.q: Underlying pathophysiology of Myasthenia Gravis?
cards.a: Autoantibodies directed against postsynaptic nicotinic acetylcholine receptors.

cards.q: Classic presentation of muscle weakness in Myasthenia Gravis?
cards.a: Fluctuating skeletal muscle weakness that worsens with repetitive use and improves with rest.

cards.q: Screening test that must be performed on all patients newly diagnosed with Myasthenia Gravis?
cards.a: CT scan of the chest to rule out a thymoma.

cards.q: First-line long-term medical management for symptomatic Myasthenia Gravis?
cards.a: Pyridostigmine.

cards.q: Immediate medical management for a patient in myasthenic crisis?
cards.a: Endotracheal intubation followed by plasmapheresis or intravenous immunoglobulin.

cards.q: Underlying pathophysiology of Lambert-Eaton Myasthenic Syndrome?
cards.a: Autoantibodies directed against presynaptic voltage-gated calcium channels.

cards.q: Classical physical exam finding that differentiates Lambert-Eaton from Myasthenia Gravis?
cards.a: Proximal muscle weakness that improves with repetitive contraction.

cards.q: Most common neoplastic condition associated with Lambert-Eaton Myasthenic Syndrome?
cards.a: Small cell lung carcinoma.

cards.q: Sensory distribution altered in a classic stocking-glove pattern?
cards.a: Length-dependent peripheral polyneuropathy.

cards.q: First-line pharmacological management for painful diabetic neuropathy?
cards.a: Gabapentin, pregabalin, or duloxetine.

cards.q: Sensory and motor deficits found in a patient with a common peroneal nerve injury?
cards.a: Foot drop with loss of sensation on the dorsum of the foot.

cards.q: Physical exam finding pointing to a lesion of the long thoracic nerve?
cards.a: Winging of the scapula.

cards.q: Nerve compressed in carpal tunnel syndrome?
cards.a: Median nerve. Section 4: Demyelinating & Neuroinflammatory Diseases

cards.q: Core diagnostic requirement for Multiple Sclerosis according to McDonald criteria?
cards.a: Neurological lesions disseminated in time and space.

cards.q: Gold standard neuroimaging modality for diagnosing Multiple Sclerosis?
cards.a: MRI of the brain and spine with gadolinium.

cards.q: Classic cerebrospinal fluid finding in patients with Multiple Sclerosis?
cards.a: Oligoclonal IgG bands on electrophoresis.

cards.q: Preferred initial treatment for an acute exacerbation of Multiple Sclerosis?
cards.a: Intravenous high-dose methylprednisolone.

cards.q: Mechanism of action of interferon-beta used in relapsing-remitting Multiple Sclerosis?
cards.a: Immunomodulation to reduce the frequency of clinical relapses.

cards.q: Defining clinical feature of Internuclear Ophthalmoplegia?
cards.a: Impaired adduction of the ipsilateral eye with nystagmus of the contralateral abducting eye during lateral gaze.

cards.q: Specific neuroanatomical structure damaged in Internuclear Ophthalmoplegia?
cards.a: Medial longitudinal fasciculus.

cards.q: Target antigen in Neuromyelitis Optica (Devic disease)?
cards.a: Aquaporin-4 water channels.

cards.q: Typical presentation of acute disseminated encephalomyelitis?
cards.a: Multifocal neurological deficits and encephalopathy following a viral infection or vaccination. Section 5: Epilepsy & Seizures

cards.q: First-line pharmacological agent used to abort status epilepticus?
cards.a: Intravenous lorazepam or diazepam.

cards.q: Clinical definition of status epilepticus?
cards.a: Continuous seizure activity lasting greater than 5 minutes or recurrent seizures without recovery between episodes.

cards.q: Preferred long-term antiepileptic drug for generalized tonic-clonic seizures?
cards.a: Levetiracetam, valproic acid, or lamotrigine.

cards.q: Characteristic EEG abnormality seen in absence seizures?
cards.a: Generalized 3-Hz spike-and-wave discharges.

cards.q: First-line pharmacological treatment for absence seizures?
cards.a: Ethosuximide.

cards.q: Antiepileptic medication known to cause gingival hyperplasia and hirsutism?
cards.a: Phenytoin.

cards.q: Teratogenic risk uniquely associated with valproic acid exposure in utero?
cards.a: Neural tube defects.

cards.q: Severe dermatological adverse reaction associated with rapid titration of lamotrigine?
cards.a: Stevens-Johnson syndrome.

cards.q: Electrolyte abnormality classically induced by carbamazepine therapy?
cards.a: Hyponatremia due to syndrome of inappropriate antidiuretic hormone secretion.

cards.q: Defining feature that separates a complex focal seizure from a simple focal seizure?
cards.a: Impairment of consciousness or awareness. Section 6: Headache Syndromes & Cranial Neuralgias

cards.q: Classical clinical presentation of a cluster headache?
cards.a: Unilateral, excruciating periorbital pain accompanied by ipsilateral lacrimation and rhinorrhea.

cards.q: First-line abortive therapy for an acute attack of cluster headache?
cards.a: 100% high-flow oxygen via non-rebreather mask or subcutaneous sumatriptan.

cards.q: First-line prophylactic medication used to prevent cluster headaches?
cards.a: Verapamil.

cards.q: Abortive medication class for severe migraines contraindicated in patients with coronary artery disease?
cards.a: Triptans.

cards.q: Prophylactic medication options for frequent migraine headaches?
cards.a: Topiramate, valproic acid, propranolol, or amitriptyline.

cards.q: Clinical presentation of a tension headache?
cards.a: Bilateral, band-like, non-pulsatile headache without photophobia or phonophobia.

cards.q: First-line abortive treatment for a tension-type headache?
cards.a: Acetaminophen or nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs.

cards.q: Clinical presentation of trigeminal neuralgia?
cards.a: Unilateral, lancinating, shock-like facial pain triggered by light touch or chewing.

cards.q: First-line pharmacological management for trigeminal neuralgia?
cards.a: Carbamazepine.

cards.q: Diagnostic criteria that must be checked immediately in a patient over 50 presenting with a new headache and jaw claudication?
cards.a: Erythrocyte sedimentation rate and C-reactive protein to screen for Giant Cell Arteritis. Section 7: CNS Infections & Altered Mental Status

cards.q: Classic triad of bacterial meningitis?
cards.a: Fever, altered mental status, and nuchal rigidity.

cards.q: Cerebrospinal fluid profile typical of acute bacterial meningitis?
cards.a: Elevated polymorphonuclear leukocytes, markedly decreased glucose, and elevated protein.

cards.q: Empirical antibiotic regimen for suspected bacterial meningitis in an adult aged 18 to 50?
cards.a: Ceftriaxone plus vancomycin.

cards.q: Additional empirical antibiotic required for meningitis in patients over age 50 or immunocompromised?
cards.a: Ampicillin to cover Listeria monocytogenes.

cards.q: Adjunctive medication that should be administered prior to or concurrently with antibiotics in suspected pneumococcal meningitis?
cards.a: Dexamethasone.

cards.q: Cerebrospinal fluid profile typical of viral meningitis?
cards.a: Elevated lymphocytes, normal glucose, and normal to mildly elevated protein.

cards.q: Most common focal lobe involved in Herpes Simplex Virus encephalitis?
cards.a: Temporal lobe.

cards.q: Preferred antiviral therapy for confirmed or highly suspected HSV encephalitis?
cards.a: Intravenous acyclovir.

cards.q: Classic diagnostic finding on cerebrospinal fluid analysis for Cryptococcal meningitis?
cards.a: Positive India ink preparation or cryptococcal antigen assay.

cards.q: Defining clinical difference between delirium and dementia?
cards.a: Delirium features an acute onset with fluctuating attention and awareness, whereas dementia is progressive and chronic. Section 8: Spinal Cord & Neuro-oncology/Vascular Compression

cards.q: Clinical syndrome presenting with ipsilateral loss of motor function and contralateral loss of pain/temperature sensation?
cards.a: Brown-Séquard syndrome (spinal cord hemisection).

cards.q: Specific spinal cord pathways affected in Vitamin B12 deficiency?
cards.a: Dorsal columns and lateral corticospinal tracts.

cards.q: Clinical triad of spinal epidural abscess?
cards.a: Severe localized spinal pain, fever, and progressive neurological deficits.

cards.q: Best next step in management for a patient with suspected neoplastic spinal cord compression?
cards.a: Intravenous dexamethasone followed by an emergency MRI of the spine.

cards.q: Clinical features differentiating Cauda Equina Syndrome from Conus Medullaris Syndrome?
cards.a: Cauda Equina presents with asymmetric, hyporeflexic lower motor neuron signs and saddle anesthesia, whereas Conus Medullaris presents with symmetric, hyperreflexic signs and early bowel/bladder dysfunction.

cards.q: Pathophysiological cause of Idiopathic Intracranial Hypertension?
cards.a: Decreased resorption of cerebrospinal fluid in the presence of normal ventricular size.

cards.q: Medication used as first-line therapy to decrease cerebrospinal fluid production in Idiopathic Intracranial Hypertension?
cards.a: Acetain-induced or acetazolamide.

cards.q: Primary ophthalmologic risk associated with untreated Idiopathic Intracranial Hypertension?
cards.a: Permanent vision loss due to optic atrophy from chronic papilledema. Section 9: Neuro-Ophthalmology, Otology, & Autonomic Disorders

cards.q: Clinical test used to differentiate benign paroxysmal positional vertigo from central causes of vertigo?
cards.a: Dix-Hallpike maneuver.

cards.q: Definitive bedside repositioning maneuver used to treat benign paroxysmal positional vertigo?
cards.a: Epley maneuver.

cards.q: Distinguishing clinical feature that separates vestibular neuritis from labyrinthitis?
cards.a: Labyrinthitis presents with unilateral sensorineural hearing loss, while vestibular neuritis preserves hearing.

cards.q: Classic presentation of Meniere disease?
cards.a: Episodic vertigo, sensorineural hearing loss, and tinnitus accompanied by a sensation of fullness in the ear.

cards.q: Clinical triad defining Horner syndrome?
cards.a: Ptosis, miosis, and anhidrosis.

cards.q: Underlying pupillary defect seen in an Argyll Robertson pupil?
cards.a: Pupil constricts to accommodation but fails to constrict to direct light.

cards.q: Most common infectious disease associated with an Argyll Robertson pupil?
cards.a: Neurosyphilis ( tertiary syphilis).

cards.q: Diagnostic pupillary finding seen in an afferent pupillary defect (Marcus Gunn pupil)?
cards.a: Paradoxical dilation of the affected eye when light is swung from the unaffected eye to the affected eye. Section 10: Toxic, Metabolic, & Nutritional Encephalopathies

cards.q: Classical clinical triad of Wernicke encephalopathy?
cards.a: Encephalopathy, oculomotor dysfunction, and gait ataxia.

cards.q: Irreversible cognitive syndrome that develops if Wernicke encephalopathy is left untreated?
cards.a: Korsakowski syndrome, characterized by anterograde amnesia and confabulation.

cards.q: Crucial administration sequence rule for thiamine and glucose in an unresponsively malnourished patient?
cards.a: Administer thiamine before or concurrently with glucose to prevent worsening of encephalopathy.

cards.q: Specific neuroanatomical structures damaged in Wernicke encephalopathy?
cards.a: Mammillary bodies and medial thalamic nuclei.

cards.q: Pathophysiological complication of correcting chronic hyponatremia too rapidly?
cards.a: Central pontine myelinolysis or osmotic demyelination syndrome.

cards.q: Clinical presentation of central pontine myelinolysis?
cards.a: Acute paralysis, dysphagia, dysarthria, and locked-in syndrome occurring days after electrolyte correction.

cards.q: Pathophysiological complication of correcting acute hypernatremia too rapidly?
cards.a: Cerebral edema and seizures.

cards.q: Characteristic physical exam finding pathognomonic for hepatic encephalopathy?
cards.a: Asterixis, or flapping tremor of the extended wrists.

cards.q: First-line pharmacological agent used to decrease serum ammonia in hepatic encephalopathy?
cards.a: Lactulose.

cards.q: Secondary mechanism of action of rifaximin in the management of hepatic encephalopathy?
cards.a: Decreases ammonia-producing gut bacteria.

cards.q: Classic neuroimaging finding in carbon monoxide poisoning?
cards.a: Bilateral necrosis of the globus pallidus. Section 11: Atypical Movement Disorders & Cerebellar Pathology

cards.q: Core clinical features of Progressive Supranuclear Palsy?
cards.a: Parkinsonism, early falls, and impairment of vertical downgaze.

cards.q: Distinguishing clinical feature of Multiple System Atrophy?
cards.a: Parkinsonism accompanied by severe, early autonomic failure and orthostatic hypotension.

cards.q: First-line medical treatment for an isolated essential tremor?
cards.a: Propranolol or primidone.

cards.q: Classic physical characteristic of an essential tremor?
cards.a: Action or postural tremor that improves with alcohol consumption.

cards.q: Pathophysiological cause of Wilson disease?
cards.a: Autosomal recessive mutation leading to impaired copper transport and toxic accumulation.

cards.q: Ocular physical exam finding diagnostic for Wilson disease?
cards.a: Kayser-Fleischer rings in the cornea.

cards.q: Preferred initial medical treatment for symptomatic Wilson disease?
cards.a: Penicillamine or trientine copper chelators.

cards.q: Classic gait abnormality seen in a patient with a cerebellar midline hemispheric lesion?
cards.a: Wide-based, unsteady gait known as truncal ataxia. Section 12: Neuro-Oncology & Paraneoplastic Syndromes

cards.q: Most common primary malignant brain tumor in adults?
cards.a: Glioblastoma multiforme.

cards.q: Classic neuroimaging appearance of a glioblastoma multiforme on MRI?
cards.a: Ring-enhancing lesion crossing the corpus callosum with a necrotic center.

cards.q: Most common benign primary brain tumor in adults?
cards.a: Meningioma.

cards.q: Histopathological hallmark of a meningioma?
cards.a: Whorled pattern of cells and psammoma bodies.

cards.q: Most common sources of metastatic tumors found in the central nervous system?
cards.a: Lung cancer, breast cancer, and melanoma.

cards.q: Paraneoplastic syndrome presenting with opsoclonus-myoclonus ataxia in children?
cards.a: Neuroblastoma.

cards.q: Target antigen in paraneoplastic limbic encephalitis associated with ovarian teratomas?
cards.a: Anti-NMDA receptors. Section 13: Neuro-Trauma, Intracranial Pressure, & Brain Death

cards.q: Clinical triad pointing to increased intracranial pressure and impending herniation?
cards.a: Cushing triad, featuring bradycardia, respiratory irregularity, and hypertension.

cards.q: Immediate medical intervention used to acutely hyperventilate a patient with elevated intracranial pressure?
cards.a: Lowering arterial carbon dioxide tension to induce cerebral vasoconstriction.

cards.q: Osmotic diuretic agent used to acutely reduce brain volume in cerebral edema?
cards.a: Intravenous mannitol.

cards.q: Specific cranial nerve compromised when uncal herniation causes a fixed and dilated pupil?
cards.a: Oculomotor nerve.

cards.q: Clinical definition of brain death?
cards.a: Irreversible loss of all brain function, including the brainstem, confirmed by an apnea test. Section 14: Neuro-Rheumatology & Autoimmune Neuro-Pathology

cards.q: Classical presentation of Central Nervous System Vasculitis?
cards.a: Multifocal ischemic strokes of varying ages combined with chronic headache and encephalopathy.

cards.q: Preferred initial management for confirmed Giant Cell Arteritis to prevent ischemic blindness?
cards.a: High-dose intravenous or oral systemic corticosteroids.

cards.q: Neurological presentation of neuro-Behçet disease?
cards.a: Recurrent meningoencephalitis and brainstem lesions in a patient with oral and genital ulcers.

cards.q: Classic neurological manifestation of Neuro-Sarcoidosis?
cards.a: Unilateral or bilateral cranial nerve VII palsies with granulomatous basilar meningitis. Section 15: Autonomic, Sleep, & Cranial Nerve Disorders

cards.q: Clinical triad diagnostic for Narcolepsy?
cards.a: Excessive daytime sleepiness, cataplexy, and hypnagogic hallucinations.

cards.q: First-line pharmacological treatment for the maintenance of wakefulness in Narcolepsy?
cards.a: Modafinil.

cards.q: Preferred medical intervention used to treat acute cataplexy in narcoleptic patients?
cards.a: Sodium oxybate or selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors.

cards.q: Clinical presentation of Bell Palsy?
cards.a: Sudden onset unilateral facial paralysis involving both the upper and lower face.

cards.q: Preferred early medical intervention for optimal recovery from Bell Palsy?
cards.a: Oral corticosteroids administered within 72 hours of symptom onset.

cards.q: Primary physical sign distinguishing a peripheral Bell Palsy from a central stroke lesion?
cards.a: Bell palsy involves the forehead muscles, whereas a stroke spares the forehead due to bilateral cortical innervation. Section 16: Systemic Disease Manifestations & Spinal Pathology

cards.q: Most common spinal cord tract involved in tabes dorsalis?
cards.a: Posterior or dorsal columns.

cards.q: Clinical signs of tabes dorsalis?
cards.a: Sensory ataxia, lightning pains, and loss of proprioception.

cards.q: Classic presentation of syringomyelia?
cards.a: Capelike, bilateral loss of pain and temperature sensation across the shoulders and upper extremities with preserved touch.

cards.q: Neuroanatomical structure compressed first by an expanding syrinx in syringomyelia?
cards.a: Anterior white commissure.

cards.q: Spinal cord tracts degenerated in Amyotrophic Lateral Sclerosis?
cards.a: Corticospinal tracts and anterior horn cells.

cards.q: Clinical physical exam findings characterizing Amyotrophic Lateral Sclerosis?
cards.a: Combined upper motor neuron and lower motor neuron signs without sensory loss.

cards.q: Only approved medication demonstrated to modestly prolong survival in Amyotrophic Lateral Sclerosis?
cards.a: Riluzole.

cards.q: Mechanism of action of riluzole in Amyotrophic Lateral Sclerosis?
cards.a: Decreases presynaptic glutamate release.

cards.q: Spinal cord structures damaged in anterior spinal artery occlusion?
cards.a: Anterior two-thirds of the spinal cord, sparing the dorsal columns.

cards.q: Clinical presentation of an anterior spinal artery infarction?
cards.a: Sudden bilateral loss of motor function and pain/temperature sensation below the lesion with preserved proprioception.

cards.q: Diagnostic imaging step for a patient presenting with new onset spinal cord compression symptoms?
cards.a: Urgent emergent MRI of the entire spine.

cards.q: Most common cause of neurogenic claudication?
cards.a: Lumbar spinal stenosis.

cards.q: Classic physical positioning that relieves the pain of lumbar spinal stenosis?
cards.a: Flexion of the spine or leaning forward.

cards.q: Clinical feature distinguishing neurogenic claudication from vascular claudication?
cards.a: Neurogenic claudication is strictly positional, while vascular claudication is volume-of-exertion dependent.

cards.q: Classic neurological complication of untreated idiopathic intracranial hypertension?
cards.a: Progressive optic atrophy and permanent blindness. Section 17: Neuro-Toxicology & Drug-Induced Emergencies

cards.q: Classic neuroimaging finding in acute methanol poisoning?
cards.a: Bilateral necrosis of the putamen.

cards.q: Clinical presentation of methanol poisoning distinguishing it from ethylene glycol toxicity?
cards.a: Severe visual impairment or blindness described as "being in a snowstorm."

cards.q: Classic neuroimaging and clinical finding in ethylene glycol poisoning?
cards.a: Acute kidney injury with calcium oxalate crystals in the urine and cranial neuropathy.

cards.q: Antidote used to competitively inhibit alcohol dehydrogenase in toxic alcohol ingestions?
cards.a: Fomepizole.

cards.q: Life-threatening condition characterized by severe rigidity, hyperthermia, and autonomic instability following dopamine antagonist administration?
cards.a: Neuroleptic Malignant Syndrome.

cards.q: First-line medical treatment for severe Neuroleptic Malignant Syndrome?
cards.a: Dantrolene or bromocriptine.

cards.q: Pathophysiological cause of Serotonin Syndrome that distinguishes its physical exam from Neuroleptic Malignant Syndrome?
cards.a: Presence of neuromuscular hyperreactivity featuring hyperreflexia and clonus.

cards.q: First-line pharmacological management for severe Serotonin Syndrome?
cards.a: Cyproheptadine.

cards.q: Acute movement emergency presenting with involuntary sustained muscle contractions of the neck or tongue within hours of taking an antipsychotic?
cards.a: Acute dystonia.

cards.q: First-line medication used to reverse an acute dystonic reaction?
cards.a: Intravenous or intramuscular benztropine or diphenhydramine. Section 18: Neurocutaneous Syndromes & Transitional Pathology

cards.q: Autosomal dominant neurocutaneous disorder presenting with café-au-lait spots, axillary freckling, and Lisch nodules?
cards.a: Neurofibromatosis Type 1.

cards.q: Most common central nervous system tumors associated with Neurofibromatosis Type 2?
cards.a: Bilateral vestibular schwannomas.

cards.q: Clinical presentation of Tuberous Sclerosis?
cards.a: Infantile spasms, ash-leaf spots, shagreen patches, and facial angiofibromas.

cards.q: Classic neuroimaging findings associated with Tuberous Sclerosis?
cards.a: Cortical tubers and subependymal nodules.

cards.q: Neurocutaneous syndrome characterized by a facial port-wine stain in the V1/V2 distribution and leptomeningeal angiomas?
cards.a: Sturge-Weber syndrome.

cards.q: Primary neurological complication associated with Sturge-Weber syndrome?
cards.a: Refractory seizures and contralateral hemiparesis.

cards.q: Central nervous system vascular tumors characteristically found in Von Hippel-Lindau disease?
cards.a: Hemangioblastomas of the retina and cerebellum. Section 19: Autonomic Bladder Disorders & Advanced Stroke Mimics

cards.q: Bladder dysfunction characterized by an overactive detrusor muscle due to a spinal cord lesion above T12?
cards.a: Neurogenic detrusor overactivity or spastic bladder.

cards.q: Bladder dysfunction characterized by an underactive detrusor muscle due to a conus medullaris or cauda equina lesion?
cards.a: Flaccid bladder or detrusor arreflexia resulting in overflow incontinence.

cards.q: Clinical condition presenting with acute stroke-like deficits following severe hypoglycemia?
cards.a: Neuroglycopenic focal deficit or hypoglycemia stroke mimic.

cards.q: Immediate diagnostic step for any patient presenting with acute focal neurological deficits prior to ordering a head CT?
cards.a: Point-of-care fingerstick blood glucose measurement.
