cards.q: Clinical syndrome presenting with severe headache, visual changes, seizures, and posterior white matter edema on MRI?
cards.a: Posterior Reversible Encephalopathy Syndrome.

cards.q: Most common systemic trigger for Posterior Reversible Encephalopathy Syndrome?
cards.a: Acute, severe hypertension or hypertensive emergency.

cards.q: Clinical presentation of Transient Global Amnesia?
cards.a: Sudden onset of anterograde amnesia with repetitive questioning that completely resolves within 24 hours.

cards.q: Diagnostic criteria distinguishing transient ischemic attacks from ischemic strokes?
cards.a: Transient ischemic attacks feature focal deficits lasting under 24 hours with absolutely no evidence of infarction on diffusion-weighted MRI. ===================================================================== =====================================================================

topic: Surgical principles — wound healing, fluid & electrolytes, shock

cards.q: Most reliable clinical indicator of general nutritional status in a preoperative patient?
cards.a: A recent history of unintentional weight loss greater than 10% of baseline body weight.

cards.q: Best objective serum lab marker for long-term nutritional status due to its half-life of 20 days?
cards.a: Serum albumin level.

cards.q: Best objective serum lab marker for acute nutritional status changes due to its short 2-day half-life?
cards.a: Prealbumin level.

cards.q: Minimum duration of smoking cessation required to significantly reduce postoperative pulmonary complications?
cards.a: At least 4 weeks.

cards.q: Absolute minimum timeline for cessation of smoking to improve ciliary clearing function before surgery?
cards.a: 8 weeks.

cards.q: Single most important predictor of postoperative cardiac risk based on the Goldman Index?
cards.a: Presence of an uncompensated third heart sound or jugular venous distention.

cards.q: Length of time surgery must be delayed following an acute myocardial infarction to minimize re-infarction risk?
cards.a: 6 months.

cards.q: Ejection fraction threshold below which non-cardiac elective surgery carries a prohibitive risk of mortality?
cards.a: Less than 35%.

cards.q: Standard classification system used by anesthesiologists to stratify a patient’s baseline physical status?
cards.a: American Society of Anesthesiologists Physical Status Classification System.

cards.q: Clinical presentation of an ASA Class 3 patient?
cards.a: A patient with severe systemic disease that limits activity but is not constantly life-threatening.

cards.q: Clinical presentation of an ASA Class 4 patient?
cards.a: A patient with severe systemic disease that is a constant threat to life.

cards.q: Primary perioperative management tool for a patient with Child-Pugh Class C hepatic cirrhosis?
cards.a: Postpone all elective surgical procedures due to an expected mortality rate exceeding 80%.

cards.q: First-line screening test for patients with suspected underlying bleeding disorders prior to major surgery?
cards.a: Thorough clinical history of bleeding tendencies and family history.

cards.q: Management of a patient taking chronic therapeutic warfarin who needs to undergo a major elective operation?
cards.a: Stop warfarin 5 days prior and bridge with low-molecular-weight heparin once INR drops below 2.0.

cards.q: Target international normalized ratio before a patient can safely undergo general elective major surgery?
cards.a: An INR less than or equal to 1.5.

cards.q: Preoperative management strategy for a patient on chronic therapeutic aspirin undergoing high-bleeding-risk surgery?
cards.a: Hold aspirin for 7 to 10 days prior to the operation.

cards.q: Preoperative management strategy for a patient taking clopidogrel prior to elective major surgery?
cards.a: Discontinue the medication 5 to 7 days before the planned procedure.

cards.q: Perioperative target range for blood glucose levels in a diabetic patient undergoing major surgery?
cards.a: Between 140 and 180 milligrams per deciliter.

cards.q: Preoperative adjustment required for a patient taking long-acting insulin the night before major surgery?
cards.a: Administer 60% to 80% of the normal evening dose.

cards.q: Preoperative adjustment required for a patient taking oral hypoglycemic medications the morning of surgery?
cards.a: Hold the medication the morning of the procedure.

cards.q: Primary rationale for giving stress-dose corticosteroids perioperatively to patients on chronic steroid therapy?
cards.a: Prevention of acute adrenal crisis due to secondary adrenal insufficiency.

cards.q: Standard perioperative stress-dose hydrocortisone regimen for a patient undergoing a high-stress major operation?
cards.a:
Administer 100 milligrams intravenously before induction, followed by 50 milligrams every 8 hours for 24 hours.
Module 2: Fluids, Electrolytes, & Acid-Base Balance

cards.q: Standard formula used to calculate hourly maintenance fluid requirements in an adult patient?
cards.a: The 4-2-1 rule.

cards.q: Hourly maintenance fluid rate for a 70-kilogram adult calculated by the standard formula?
cards.a: 110 milliliters per hour.

cards.q: Most accurate clinical method for monitoring real-time volume status in a critically ill surgical patient?
cards.a: Measurement of hourly urine output via an indwelling Foley catheter.

cards.q: Target minimum hourly urine output for an adult patient receiving standard fluid maintenance or resuscitation?
cards.a: 0.5 milliliters per kilogram per hour.

cards.q: Target minimum hourly urine output for a pediatric patient or an adult experiencing severe rhadbomyolysis?
cards.a: 1.0 milliliter per kilogram per hour.

cards.q: Preferred initial intravenous crystalloid solution for volume resuscitation in a trauma patient with hemorrhagic shock?
cards.a: Lactated Ringer's solution.

cards.q: Primary risk associated with rapid, large-volume resuscitation using 0.9% normal saline?
cards.a: Hyperchloremic metabolic acidosis.

cards.q: Earliest clinical sign of progressive hypernatremia in a postoperative ward patient?
cards.a: Altered mental status ranging from lethargy to confusion.

cards.q: Maximum safe rate of serum sodium correction in a patient with severe chronic hyponatremia?
cards.a: No faster than 10 to 12 milliequivalents per liter over 24 hours.

cards.q: Central nervous system catastrophe caused by the overly rapid correction of chronic severe hyponatremia?
cards.a: Central pontine myelinolysis.

cards.q: Life-threatening complication caused by the overly rapid correction of chronic severe hypernatremia?
cards.a: Cerebral edema and brain herniation.

cards.q: Earliest electrocardiogram manifestation seen in a patient with progressive hyperkalemia?
cards.a: Peaked T waves.

cards.q: Progression of electrocardiogram changes in worsening hyperkalemia after peaked T waves appear?
cards.a: PR interval prolongation, QRS widening, loss of P waves, and a sine wave pattern.

cards.q: First-line medication administered to a hyperkalemic patient demonstrating acute electrocardiogram changes?
cards.a: Intravenous calcium gluconate to stabilize the cardiac myocyte membrane.

cards.q: Rapid-acting medical therapies used to transiently shift extracellular potassium into the cells?
cards.a: Intravenous insulin administered concurrently with dextrose, and nebulized albuterol.

cards.q: Most common electrolyte abnormality responsible for a persistent postoperative adynamic ileus?
cards.a: Hypokalemia.

cards.q: Co-existing electrolyte deficiency that makes refractory hypokalemia impossible to correct with potassium supplementation alone?
cards.a: Hypomagnesemia.

cards.q: Primary physiological reason hypomagnesemia prevents successful correction of a potassium deficit?
cards.a: Low magnesium causes uninhibited potassium wasting through the renal outer medullary potassium channels.

cards.q: Classic electrocardiogram finding diagnostic of severe hypokalemia?
cards.a: Flattened T waves, ST-segment depression, and prominent U waves.

cards.q: Acid-base disturbance classically caused by prolonged nasogastric tube suctioning or severe persistent vomiting?
cards.a: Hypokalemic, hypochloremic metabolic alkalosis with paradoxical aciduria.

cards.q: Primary renal mechanism driving paradoxical aciduria in severe hypochloremic metabolic alkalosis?
cards.a:
Volume depletion forces aldosterone to retain sodium at the direct expense of excreting hydrogen ions into urine.
Module 3: Surgical Nutrition & Metabolism

cards.q: Timeline after which a completely fasting postoperative patient must receive nutritional support?
cards.a: 7 to 10 days of inadequate oral intake.

cards.q: Preferred route of nutritional support in a surgical patient with a functional gastrointestinal tract?
cards.a: Enteral nutrition.

cards.q: Primary physiological advantage of choosing enteral nutrition over total parenteral nutrition?
cards.a: Preserves mucosal barrier integrity and prevents bacterial translocation from the gut lumen.

cards.q: Principal route of administration for nutritional formulas with an osmolarity exceeding 900 milliosmoles per liter?
cards.a: Central venous access.

cards.q: Most common metabolic complication associated with the initiation of total parenteral nutrition?
cards.a: Hyperglycemia.

cards.q: Primary trace mineral deficiency associated with long-term parenteral nutrition lacking adequate supplementation?
cards.a: Zinc deficiency.

cards.q: Classic clinical presentation of a patient suffering from zinc deficiency during chronic parenteral nutrition?
cards.a: Perioral acrodermatitis, poor wound healing, alopecia, and altered taste.

cards.q: Pathophysiology behind the development of refeeding syndrome in a severely malnourished surgical patient?
cards.a: Carbohydrate loading induces an insulin surge that drives phosphate, potassium, and magnesium into the intracellular space.

cards.q: Most critical electrolyte abnormality to monitor and correct in refeeding syndrome to prevent cardiac failure?
cards.a: Hypophosphatemia.

cards.q: Preferred energy substrate for the specialized enterocytes of the small bowel mucosa?
cards.a: Glutamine.

cards.q: Preferred energy substrate for the specialized colonocytes of the large bowel mucosa?
cards.a:
Short-chain fatty acids like butyrate.
Module 4: Perioperative Complications & Ward Emergencies

cards.q: Most common cause of a postoperative fever occurring within the first 24 to 48 hours?
cards.a: Atelectasis.

cards.q: Most common cause of a postoperative fever manifesting between postoperative days 3 and 5?
cards.a: Urinary tract infection.

cards.q: Most common cause of a postoperative fever manifesting between postoperative days 5 and 7?
cards.a: Deep vein thrombosis or pulmonary embolism.

cards.q: Most common cause of a postoperative fever developing after postoperative day 7?
cards.a: Surgical site infection or deep intra-abdominal abscess.

cards.q: Immediate initial diagnostic step for a patient suspected of developing a postoperative pulmonary embolism?
cards.a: Computed tomography pulmonary angiography.

cards.q: First-line medical management for an unstable ward patient with a confirmed acute pulmonary embolism?
cards.a: Intravenous systemic anticoagulation with unfractionated heparin.

cards.q: Define the clinical condition known as postoperative deep wound dehiscence?
cards.a: Disruption of the fascial layer of the operative wound without evisceration.

cards.q: Define the clinical emergency known as postoperative wound evisceration?
cards.a: Disruption of all layers of the abdominal wall resulting in the protrusion of visceral organs.

cards.q: Immediate bedside management for a patient who suffers an acute abdominal wound evisceration on the ward?
cards.a: Cover the exposed viscera with sterile towels soaked in warm normal saline and arrange immediate return to the OR.

cards.q: Most common etiology of a postoperative wound infection occurring within 24 hours of skin closure?
cards.a: Infection caused by either Streptococcus pyogenes or Clostridium species.

cards.q: Distinctive physical exam finding associated with a clostridial wound infection?
cards.a: Crepitus within the surrounding subcutaneous tissues and thin, dishwater-like foul discharge.

cards.q: Diagnostic criteria used to differentiate a postoperative adynamic ileus from a mechanical small bowel obstruction?
cards.a: Radiographs showing diffuse gas throughout both the small and large bowel, including the rectum.

cards.q: Radiographic hallmark diagnostic of a mechanical small bowel obstruction?
cards.a: Dilated loops of small bowel with multiple air-fluid levels and a complete absence of gas in the colon.

cards.q: Initial management strategy for a patient diagnosed with a non-complicated postoperative adynamic ileus?
cards.a: Nothing-by-mouth status, intravenous fluid maintenance, electrolyte correction, and avoidance of opioid medications.

cards.q: Diagnostic step required for a postoperative patient who presents with sudden, unexplained oliguria?
cards.a: Immediate placement or flushing of a Foley catheter to rule out mechanical obstruction.

cards.q: Primary physiological driver of postoperative urinary retention?
cards.a: Detrusor muscle dysfunction caused by the parasympatholytic effects of anesthesia and perioperative opioids.

cards.q: Diagnostic criteria for a patient suspected of having abdominal compartment syndrome?
cards.a: Sustained intra-abdominal pressure greater than 20 millimeters of mercury associated with new organ dysfunction.

cards.q: Standard bedside method used to indirectly measure intra-abdominal pressure?
cards.a: Measurement of the transurethral bladder pressure via a pressure transducer hooked to a Foley catheter.

cards.q: Definitive management for a patient with refractory abdominal compartment syndrome?
cards.a:
Emergent surgical decompression via a midline laparotomy leaving the abdomen open.
Module 5: Shock & Advanced Trauma Life Support (ATLS) Principles

cards.q: Primary physiological definition of shock?
cards.a: Systemic tissue hypoperfusion leading to inadequate cellular oxygen delivery and cellular hypoxia.

cards.q: Earliest measurable vital sign change indicative of Class II hemorrhagic shock?
cards.a: Tachycardia with a heart rate exceeding 100 beats per minute.

cards.q: Percentage of total intravascular blood volume loss required before clinical hypotension manifests in hemorrhagic shock?
cards.a: Loss of greater than 15% to 30% of total blood volume, corresponding to Class III shock.

cards.q: Formula used to calculate the shock index as a screening tool for occult hemorrhage?
cards.a: Heart rate divided by systolic blood pressure.

cards.q: Clinical significance of a shock index value greater than 0.9?
cards.a: Strongly indicates significant occult systemic hypovolemia requiring urgent blood product resuscitation.

cards.q: Definition of the lethal triad of trauma?
cards.a: Hypothermia, metabolic acidosis, and coagulopathy.

cards.q: Ratio of blood products administered in a standard damage control resuscitation protocol for massive hemorrhage?
cards.a: A balanced 1:1:1 ratio of packed red blood cells, fresh frozen plasma, and platelets.

cards.q: Target physiological endpoints when utilizing a strategy of permissive hypotension in a trauma patient?
cards.a: A systolic blood pressure of 80 to 90 millimeters of mercury until surgical hemostasis is achieved.

cards.q: Absolute contraindication to the use of a permissive hypotension resuscitation strategy in a trauma patient?
cards.a: Presence of a concomitant severe traumatic brain injury.

cards.q: First step in the primary survey of a trauma patient according to Advanced Trauma Life Support protocols?
cards.a: Airway maintenance with strict restriction of cervical spine motion.

cards.q: Absolute clinical indication for securing a definitive surgical airway via cricothyroidotomy?
cards.a: Inability to intubate the trachea due to severe facial fractures, upper airway hemorrhage, or edema.

cards.q: Clinical triad diagnostic of a tension pneumothorax?
cards.a: Respiratory distress, unilateral absent breath sounds, and hemodynamic instability with tracheal deviation.

cards.q: Immediate management for a patient diagnosed with a tension pneumothorax before obtaining any imaging?
cards.a: Needle decompression via the fifth intercostal space just anterior to the midaxillary line.

cards.q: Diagnostic clinical signs that constitute Beck's triad for cardiac tamponade?
cards.a: Hypotension, muffled heart sounds, and jugular venous distention.

cards.q: Distinctive arterial pulse change seen in a patient with cardiac tamponade?
cards.a: Pulsus paradoxus, defined as a drop in systolic blood pressure greater than 10 millimeters of mercury during inspiration.

cards.q: Define the specific structural injury known as a flail chest?
cards.a: Two or more ribs fractured in two or more places, causing a segment of the chest wall to move paradoxically.

cards.q: Primary physiological cause of hypoxia in a patient with a flail chest injury?
cards.a: Underlying pulmonary contusion rather than the mechanical restriction of the paradoxical chest wall movement.

cards.q: Diagnostic parameter that defines a massive hemothorax upon chest tube insertion?
cards.a: Immediate evacuation of 1500 milliliters or more of blood, or ongoing output of 200 milliliters per hour for 2 to 4 consecutive hours.

cards.q: Next immediate therapeutic step for a patient who meets the criteria for a massive hemothorax?
cards.a: Urgent operative thoracotomy to achieve surgical hemostasis.

cards.q: Anatomical landmarks defining the borders of the "cardiac box" in trauma evaluations?
cards.a: Area bounded by the clavicles superiorly, costal margins inferiorly, and the midclavicular lines bilaterally.

cards.q: Next diagnostic step for a hemodynamically stable blunt abdominal trauma patient with an equivocal physical exam?
cards.a: Focused Assessment with Sonography for Trauma or a computed tomography scan of the abdomen.

cards.q: Name the four anatomical views imaged during a standard Focused Assessment with Sonography for Trauma exam?
cards.a: Perihepatic view, perisplenic view, pelvic view, and pericardial view.

cards.q: Next immediate step for a hemodynamically unstable blunt abdominal trauma patient with a positive FAST examination?
cards.a: Emergent exploratory laparotomy.

cards.q: Next immediate step for a hemodynamically unstable pelvic fracture patient with ongoing retroperitoneal hemorrhage?
cards.a:
Mechanical stabilization of the pelvic ring via an external pelvic binder placed at the level of the greater trochanters.
Module 6: Surgical Infections, Antibiotic Prophylaxis, & Wound Healing

cards.q: Timeline requirement for the administration of a systemic prophylactic preoperative antibiotic?
cards.a: Within 60 minutes prior to the making of the surgical skin incision.

cards.q: Preferred first-line antibiotic choice for standard clean general surgical procedures?
cards.a: Cefazolin.

cards.q: Recommended alternative prophylactic antibiotic for clean operations in a patient with a severe anaphylactic penicillin allergy?
cards.a: Clindamycin or vancomycin.

cards.q: Standard timing requirement for the redosing of a prophylactic antibiotic during a prolonged operation?
cards.a: Redose after two half-lives of the specific drug have elapsed, or after a blood loss exceeding 1500 milliliters.

cards.q: Definition of a clean surgical wound category?
cards.a: An uninfected operative wound in which no inflammation is encountered and the respiratory, alimentary, or genitourinary tracts are not entered.

cards.q: Definition of a clean-contaminated surgical wound category?
cards.a: An operative wound in which the respiratory, alimentary, or genitourinary tracts are entered under controlled conditions without unusual contamination.

cards.q: Definition of a contaminated surgical wound category?
cards.a: Open, fresh, accidental wounds or operations with major breaks in sterile technique or gross gastrointestinal spillage.

cards.q: Definition of a dirty surgical wound category?
cards.a: Old traumatic wounds with retained devitalized tissue or wounds that involve existing clinical infection or perforated viscera.

cards.q: Standard wound closure strategy recommended for an operation classified as a dirty surgical wound?
cards.a: Leave the skin and subcutaneous tissues open for healing by secondary intention or delayed primary closure.

cards.q: Primary mechanism of wound healing classified as healing by primary intention?
cards.a: Edges of the clean wound are mechanically approximated using sutures, staples, or adhesive tape immediately.

cards.q: Primary mechanism of wound healing classified as healing by secondary intention?
cards.a: Wound edges are left separate, allowing the wound cavity to fill via granulation tissue formation, contraction, and epithelialization.

cards.q: Principal cell type responsible for coordinating the initial inflammatory phase of normal wound healing?
cards.a: Platelets initially, followed closely by tissue macrophages.

cards.q: Primary cell type responsible for extracellular matrix deposition during the proliferative phase of wound healing?
cards.a: Fibroblasts.

cards.q: Type of collagen initially deposited in high amounts during the proliferative phase of wound healing?
cards.a: Type III collagen.

cards.q: Type of collagen that replaces temporary collagen during the remodeling phase of normal wound healing?
cards.a: Type I collagen.

cards.q: Timeline peak for the maximum deposition of collagen within a healing surgical wound?
cards.a: Between 2 and 3 weeks post-injury.

cards.q: Ultimate maximum tensile strength achieved by a fully remodeled scar compared to normal uninjured skin?
cards.a: Approximately 80% of original uninjured skin tensile strength.

cards.q: Most common localized complication that halts normal wound healing progress?
cards.a:
Tissue ischemia or high local bacterial bioburden exceeding 100,000 organisms per gram of tissue.
Module 7: Anesthesia & Hemostasis Principles

cards.q: Pathophysiology driving the development of malignant hyperthermia during general anesthesia?
cards.a: Uncontrolled release of calcium from the sarcoplasmic reticulum via mutated ryanodine receptors.

cards.q: Earliest and most sensitive clinical indicator of an impending malignant hyperthermia crisis?
cards.a: A sudden, unexplained rise in end-tidal carbon dioxide levels refractory to increased ventilation.

cards.q: Definitive pharmacological antidote for a patient experiencing malignant hyperthermia?
cards.a: Intravenous dantrolene.

cards.q: Mechanism of action of the muscle relaxant succinylcholine?
cards.a: Depolarizing neuromuscular blocker that binds to nicotinic acetylcholine receptors causing persistent depolarization.

cards.q: Major metabolic electrolyte risk associated with the administration of succinylcholine to a severe burn or crush injury patient?
cards.a: Life-threatening hyperkalemia due to widespread upregulation of extrajunctional acetylcholine receptors.

cards.q: Mechanism of action of local anesthetics like lidocaine?
cards.a: Reversibly block voltage-gated sodium channels along the neuronal axon membrane to prevent depolarization.

cards.q: Rationale for combining epinephrine with a local anesthetic solution for tissue infiltration?
cards.a: Induces localized vasoconstriction to prolong the anesthetic duration, decrease systemic absorption, and improve local hemostasis.

cards.q: Absolute anatomical contraindications to using a local anesthetic solution mixed with epinephrine?
cards.a: Infiltration into terminal vascular beds including the fingers, toes, nose, ears, and penis.

cards.q: Maximum safe dose of plain lidocaine without epinephrine for local infiltration in an adult?
cards.a: 4.5 milligrams per kilogram.

cards.q: Maximum safe dose of lidocaine mixed with epinephrine for local infiltration in an adult?
cards.a: 7 milligrams per kilogram.

cards.q: Earliest central nervous system signs indicative of systemic local anesthetic toxicity?
cards.a: Perioral numbness, metallic taste, tinnitus, and tongue paresthesias.

cards.q: Definitive rescue therapy for a patient suffering from severe cardiovascular collapse due to local anesthetic systemic toxicity?
cards.a: Intravenous infusion of a 20% lipid emulsion solution.

cards.q: Primary mechanism of action of topical hemostatic agents like oxidized regenerated cellulose?
cards.a: Provides a physical matrix that activates the intrinsic pathway of the coagulation cascade upon contact with blood.

cards.q: Mechanism of action of topical bovine thrombin used intraoperatively for hemostasis?
cards.a: Directly cleaves fibrinogen into fibrin to bypass all upstream clotting factor deficiencies.

cards.q: Most common cause of post-transfusion hemolytic reaction in the operating room?
cards.a: Clerical error leading to ABO incompatibility.

cards.q: Earliest clinical sign of an acute hemolytic transfusion reaction in an anesthetized patient?
cards.a: Unexplained hypotension and dark-colored urine indicating hemoglobinuria.

cards.q: Initial diagnostic test to confirm an acute hemolytic transfusion reaction?
cards.a: Direct Antiglobulin Test, also known as the Coombs test, performed on a post-transfusion blood sample.

cards.q: Immediate management step when a transfusion reaction is suspected in the operating room?
cards.a: Halt the transfusion immediately, disconnect the tubing, and run intravenous normal saline through a fresh line.

cards.q: Clinical presentation of Transfusion-Related Acute Lung Injury?
cards.a: Non-cardiogenic pulmonary edema causing severe hypoxia and bilateral infiltrates within 6 hours of blood product administration.

cards.q: Pathophysiology driving Transfusion-Related Acute Lung Injury?
cards.a: Donor antileukocyte antibodies activate host neutrophils inside the pulmonary vasculature, causing endothelial damage and capillary leak.

cards.q: Clinical feature distinguishing Transfusion-Associated Circulatory Overload from TRALI?
cards.a: Elevated central venous pressure, jugular venous distention, and a positive response to diuretic therapy.

cards.q: Define the specific diagnostic parameters for Heparin-Induced Thrombocytopenia?
cards.a: A greater than 50% drop in platelet count occurring 5 to 10 days after starting heparin therapy.

cards.q: Immediate medical management for a patient diagnosed with Heparin-Induced Thrombocytopenia?
cards.a: Stop all heparin products completely and immediately initiate a non-heparin anticoagulant such as argatroban.

cards.q: Gold standard confirmatory laboratory assay for Heparin-Induced Thrombocytopenia?
cards.a: Serotonin release assay.

cards.q: Most common early clinical manifestation of a systemic air embolism during central venous catheter placement?
cards.a: Sudden, severe respiratory distress accompanied by a distinctive "mill-wheel" cardiac murmur.

cards.q: Immediate bedside positioning for a patient with a suspected central venous air embolism?
cards.a: Left lateral decubitus in the Trendelenburg position, also known as the Durant maneuver.

cards.q: Primary physiological reason for placing an air embolism patient in the left lateral Trendelenburg position?
cards.a: Traps the air bolus in the apex of the right ventricle, preventing it from obstructing the pulmonary artery outflow tract.

cards.q: Formula used by the Advanced Trauma Life Support protocol to estimate initial fluid resuscitation volume in adult burn patients?
cards.a: The Parkland formula, which dictates 2 to 4 milliliters of Lactated Ringer's per kilogram per percent of total body surface area burned.

cards.q: Timeframe requirement for the delivery of the fluid volume calculated by the Parkland formula?
cards.a: Give the first half of the total volume over the first 8 hours from the time of injury, and the remaining half over the next 16 hours.

cards.q: Depth criteria that define a second-degree partial-thickness burn?
cards.a: Blistering, painful wounds that blanch with pressure, indicating intact dermal capillary networks.

cards.q: Depth criteria that define a third-degree full-thickness burn?
cards.a: Leathery, painless, inelastic wounds that do not blanch, indicating complete destruction of the dermis and nerve endings.

cards.q: Earliest absolute clinical indication for an emergent escharotomy in a circumferential burn patient?
cards.a: Loss of distal pulses or structural restriction of chest wall expansion causing ventilatory failure.

cards.q: Most common life-threatening systemic complication specifically associated with electrical burns?
cards.a: Acute kidney injury secondary to profound rhabdomyolysis and myoglobinuria.

cards.q: Target urine output when managing a patient with severe rhabdomyolysis or electrical burn injuries?
cards.a: 1.0 to 1.5 milliliters per kilogram per hour, achieved via aggressive fluid resuscitation and urine alkalinization.

cards.q: Most reliable clinical method to distinguish a primary pneumothorax from an open sucking chest wound?
cards.a: An open wound demonstrates a visible defect in the chest wall that dynamically communicates with the pleural space.

cards.q: Immediate temporary treatment for an open pneumothorax prior to chest tube placement?
cards.a: Application of a sterile occlusive dressing taped securely on three sides only.

cards.q: Primary physiological rationale for securing an open pneumothorax dressing on three sides only?
cards.a: Creates a flutter-valve that allows air to escape during expiration but prevents ambient atmospheric air from entering during inspiration.

cards.q: Most sensitive initial diagnostic imaging modality for a patient with a suspected retroperitoneal hematoma?
cards.a: Contrast-enhanced computed tomography of the abdomen and pelvis.

cards.q: Management paradigm for a Zone 1 retroperitoneal hematoma discovered during emergency laparotomy for blunt trauma?
cards.a: Mandatory surgical exploration of the midline zone regardless of stability to rule out major vascular or pancreaticoduodenal injury.

cards.q: Define the anatomical boundaries of Zone 1 in retroperitoneal trauma?
cards.a: The central midline zone spanning from the aortic hiatus down to the sacral promontory.

cards.q: Management paradigm for a Zone 2 retroperitoneal hematoma discovered during emergency trauma laparotomy?
cards.a: Exploration is indicated only if the hematoma is actively expanding, pulsatile, or associated with a known penetrating mechanism.

cards.q: Define the anatomical boundaries of Zone 2 in retroperitoneal trauma?
cards.a: The lateral flanks, encompassing the perinephric spaces and the retroperitoneal portions of the colon.

cards.q: Classic clinical presentation of a popliteal artery injury following a posterior knee dislocation?
cards.a: Distal ischemia presenting with absent pedal pulses, cold extremity, delayed capillary refill, and motor deficits.

cards.q: Next immediate diagnostic step for a knee dislocation patient with asymmetrical or diminished pedal pulses?
cards.a: Urgent measurement of the ankle-brachial index followed by an arterial duplex ultrasound or formal angiography.

cards.q: Threshold ankle-brachial index value that necessitates mandatory formal vascular imaging in a traumatized limb?
cards.a: An ABI value less than 0.90.

cards.q: Maximum warm ischemia time a mangled extremity can tolerate before irreversible muscle necrosis begins?
cards.a: Approximately 4 to 6 hours.

cards.q: Sequence of structural repair for a mangled extremity presenting with both an unstable bone fracture and an arterial transection?
cards.a: Establish temporary vascular shunting, perform rigid orthopedic bone fixation, and finish with definitive microvascular arterial repair.

cards.q: Pathophysiology of extremity compartment syndrome following successful vascular reconstruction for acute ischemia?
cards.a: Reperfusion injury causing profound intracellular edema and swelling within non-yielding fascial boundaries.

cards.q: Most reliable early clinical symptom of an impending lower extremity compartment syndrome?
cards.a: Severe, intractable pain that is completely out of proportion to physical exam findings and exacerbated by passive stretch of the muscle.

cards.q: Intracompartmental pressure threshold that mandates an urgent surgical fasciotomy?
cards.a: A pressure within 30 millimeters of mercury of the patient's diastolic blood pressure, or a absolute value greater than 30 mmHg.

cards.q: Anatomical structures routinely released during a standard two-incision, four-compartment lower leg fasciotomy?
cards.a: The anterior, lateral, superficial posterior, and deep posterior fascial compartments.

cards.q: Clinical presentation of gas gangrene caused by Clostridium perfringens?
cards.a: Rapidly progressive local pain, bronzed skin discoloration, crepitus, and systemic shock within hours of injury or surgery.

cards.q: Immediate therapeutic intervention required for a patient with confirmed necrotizing soft tissue infection or gas gangrene?
cards.a: Emergent wide surgical debridement of all devitalized tissues combined with high-dose intravenous penicillin and clindamycin.

cards.q: Standard timing guidelines for the first post-operative surveillance colonoscopy after an R0 resection for colon adenocarcinoma?
cards.a: Exactly 1 year following the primary surgical resection.

cards.q: Most common site of distant hematogenous metastasis for colorectal cancer?
cards.a: The liver, due to portal venous drainage.

cards.q: Standard surveillance lab marker used to monitor for disease recurrence in a postoperative colon cancer patient?
cards.a: Carcinoembryonic antigen.

cards.q: Clinical presentation of a pharyngeal pouch, also known as Zenker's diverticulum?
cards.a: Dysphagia, regurgitation of undigested food, halitosis, and recurrent aspiration pneumonia in an elderly patient.

cards.q: Anatomical space through which a Zenker's diverticulum herniates?
cards.a: Killian's triangle, located between the thyropharyngeus and cricopharyngeus muscles of the inferior constrictor.

cards.q: Definitive diagnostic study to confirm the presence of a Zenker's diverticulum?
cards.a: Barium swallow study.

cards.q: Absolute contraindication to performing a diagnostic upper endoscopy in a patient with a suspected Zenker's diverticulum?
cards.a: High risk of instrumental diverticular perforation due to blind esophageal advancement of the endoscope scope.

cards.q: Classic presentation of Boorhaave syndrome?
cards.a: Severe retrosternal chest pain following a bout of forceful vomiting, associated with subcutaneous emphysema.

cards.q: Most accurate initial diagnostic imaging study to evaluate a suspected Boerhaave syndrome?
cards.a: Water-soluble contrast esophagram, such as Gastrografin, to avoid mediastinal irritation from barium spillage.

cards.q: Anatomical location where a Boerhaave syndrome esophageal perforation most commonly occurs?
cards.a: The left posterolateral aspect of the distal esophagus, roughly 2 to 3 centimeters proximal to the gastroesophageal junction.

cards.q: Immediate medical stabilization steps for a patient diagnosed with an acute esophageal perforation?
cards.a: Intravenous fluid resuscitation, strict nothing-by-mouth status, broad-spectrum intravenous antibiotics, and prompt surgical consultation.

cards.q: Anatomical landmarks that define the borders of Hesselbach's triangle?
cards.a: The rectus abdominis muscle medially, the inferior epigastric vessels laterally, and the inguinal ligament inferiorly.

cards.q: Anatomical relationship of a direct inguinal hernia relative to the inferior epigastric vessels?
cards.a: It herniates medial to the inferior epigastric vessels through a defect in the transversalis fascia.

cards.q: Anatomical relationship of an indirect inguinal hernia relative to the inferior epigastric vessels?
cards.a: It herniates lateral to the inferior epigastric vessels through the deep inguinal ring.

cards.q: Primary embryological cause responsible for the development of an indirect inguinal hernia?
cards.a: Failure of the processes vaginalis to obliterate during fetal development.

cards.q: Type of groin hernia that carries the highest risk of incarceration and strangulation?
cards.a: Femoral hernia.

cards.q: Anatomical boundaries of the femoral ring through which a femoral hernia passes?
cards.a: The inguinal ligament anteriorly, the pectineal ligament posteriorly, the lacunar ligament medially, and the femoral vein laterally.

cards.q: Define the structural components of a Littre's hernia?
cards.a: Any groin or abdominal wall hernia that contains a Meckel's diverticulum within the hernia sac.

cards.q: Define the structural components of a Richter's hernia?
cards.a: A hernia in which only a portion of the antimesenteric wall of the bowel becomes incarcerated without causing complete luminal obstruction.

cards.q: Definitive surgical management for an asymptomatic femoral hernia diagnosed in an adult?
cards.a: Prompt elective surgical repair due to an exceedingly high risk of early strangulation.

cards.q: Initial management strategy for a patient presenting with an acutely incarcerated inguinal hernia without signs of systemic toxicity?
cards.a: Attempt gentle manual reduction at the bedside under adequate analgesia and sedation.

cards.q: Absolute surgical contraindication to attempting manual reduction of an incarcerated hernia?
cards.a: Presence of systemic toxicity, leukocytosis, or skin changes over the hernia sac suggesting bowel strangulation.

cards.q: Anatomical structures that must be visualized to satisfy the "Critical View of Safety" during a laparoscopic cholecystectomy?
cards.a: The cystic plate, the cystic duct, and the cystic artery, with the lower part of the gallbladder dissected free from the liver bed.

cards.q: Diagnostic criteria that define Charcot's triad for acute cholangitis?
cards.a: Right upper quadrant abdominal pain, fever, and jaundice.

cards.q: Diagnostic criteria that define Reynolds' pentad for severe, obstructive acute cholangitis?
cards.a: Right upper quadrant abdominal pain, fever, jaundice, hypotension, and altered mental status.

cards.q: Immediate first-line intervention for a patient presenting with acute suppurative cholangitis and Reynolds' pentad?
cards.a: Intravenous fluid resuscitation, broad-spectrum antibiotics, and emergent biliary decompression via Endoscopic Retrograde Cholangiopancreatography.

cards.q: Most common composition of gallstones found in patients within Western countries?
cards.a: Cholesterol gallstones.

cards.q: Primary etiology driving the formation of black pigment gallstones within the biliary tree?
cards.a: Chronic intravascular hemolysis leading to an excess of unconjugated bilirubin in the bile.

cards.q: Primary etiology driving the formation of brown pigment gallstones within the bile ducts?
cards.a: Chronic biliary tract infection or infestation leading to bacterial production of glucuronidases.

cards.q: Initial diagnostic test of choice for a patient suspected of having acute cholecystitis?
cards.a: Right upper quadrant transabdominal ultrasound.

cards.q: Ultrasonographic hallmarks diagnostic of acute cholecystitis?
cards.a: Gallbladder wall thickening greater than 3 millimeters, pericholecystic fluid, gallstones, and a positive sonographic Murphy's sign.

cards.q: Next diagnostic step for a patient with high clinical suspicion for acute cholecystitis whose ultrasound is equivocal?
cards.a: Cholescintigraphy, commonly known as a HIDA scan.

cards.q: What constitutes a positive or diagnostic result on a HIDA scan for acute cholecystitis?
cards.a: Non-visualization of the gallbladder after 4 hours, indicating complete cystic duct obstruction.

cards.q: Preferred surgical timing for a patient presenting with uncomplicated acute calculous cholecystitis?
cards.a: Early cholecystectomy performed within 72 hours of symptom onset.

cards.q: Pathophysiology driving the development of acalculous cholecystitis in critically ill ICU patients?
cards.a: Biliary stasis and gallbladder ischemia secondary to systemic hypotension, dehydration, or prolonged total parenteral nutrition.

cards.q: Immediate management for an unstable, critically ill ICU patient diagnosed with acute acalculous cholecystitis?
cards.a: Bedside ultrasound-guided percutaneous cholecystostomy tube placement.

cards.q: Clinical syndrome known as Mirizzi syndrome?
cards.a: Extrinsic compression of the common hepatic duct caused by a large gallstone impacted in the cystic duct or gallbladder neck.

cards.q: Classic clinical and radiographic presentation of gallstone ileus?
cards.a: Small bowel obstruction, pneumobilia, and a radiopaque gallstone in the right iliac fossa on imaging.

cards.q: Anatomical site where the obstructing gallstone almost always impacts in a patient with gallstone ileus?
cards.a: The ileocecal valve, due to it being the narrowest segment of the small intestine.

cards.q: Most common baseline etiology responsible for the development of chronic pancreatitis in adults?
cards.a: Chronic alcohol abuse.

cards.q: Diagnostic triad classic for advanced, long-standing chronic pancreatitis?
cards.a: Pancreatic calcifications on imaging, steatorrhea, and secondary diabetes mellitus.

cards.q: Surgical indication for a pancreatic pseudocyst developing after an episode of acute pancreatitis?
cards.a: Persistence greater than 6 weeks, size greater than 6 centimeters, or the development of symptoms like pain, obstruction, or infection.

cards.q: Preferred internal drainage strategy for a symptomatic pancreatic pseudocyst adhering to the posterior gastric wall?
cards.a: Endoscopic or surgical cystogastrostomy.

cards.q: Standard curative surgical procedure for a resectable adenocarcinoma localized to the head of the pancreas?
cards.a: Pancreaticoduodenectomy, commonly referred to as the Whipple procedure.

cards.q: Anatomical structures removed during a standard, classic Whipple procedure?
cards.a: Head of the pancreas, duodenum, distal stomach, gallbladder, cystic duct, and common bile duct.

cards.q: Most common surgical complication encountered during the early postoperative period following a Whipple procedure?
cards.a: Delayed gastric emptying.

cards.q: Diagnostic parameter confirming a postoperative pancreatic fistula following pancreatic resection?
cards.a: Drain fluid amylase concentration greater than 3 times the upper limit of normal serum amylase on or after postoperative day 3.

cards.q: Most common type of benign breast tumor found in young women under the age of 30?
cards.a: Fibroadenoma.

cards.q: Clinical presentation distinguishing a fibroadenoma from a malignant breast mass?
cards.a: A discrete, highly mobile, firm, rubbery, painless mass that fluctuates slightly with the menstrual cycle.

cards.q: Management paradigm for a biopsy-confirmed, asymptomatic breast fibroadenoma?
cards.a: Conservative clinical observation and reassurance, as they do not carry malignant potential.

cards.q: Next diagnostic step for a woman over 30 who presents with a new, palpable, discrete breast mass?
cards.a: Diagnostic mammography combined with a targeted breast ultrasound.

cards.q: Next diagnostic step for a woman under 30 who presents with a new, palpable, discrete breast mass?
cards.a: Targeted breast ultrasound alone, due to the high density of young breast tissue rendering mammography insensitive.

cards.q: Definitive gold standard procedure used to histologically diagnose a suspicious breast mass?
cards.a: Core needle biopsy.

cards.q: Clinical signs characterizing inflammatory breast cancer?
cards.a: Rapidly progressive breast erythema, warmth, edema, and a pitted skin appearance known as peau d'orange.

cards.q: Pathophysiology responsible for the classic peau d'orange skin changes seen in inflammatory breast cancer?
cards.a: Tumor emboli invading and completely obstructing the dermal lymphatic vessels.

cards.q: Define the structural boundaries of a Level I axillary lymph node dissection?
cards.a: Lymph nodes located lateral to the lateral border of the pectoralis minor muscle.

cards.q: Define the structural boundaries of a Level II axillary lymph node dissection?
cards.a: Lymph nodes located directly deep to the pectoralis minor muscle.

cards.q: Define the structural boundaries of a Level III axillary lymph node dissection?
cards.a: Lymph nodes located medial to the medial border of the pectoralis minor muscle.

cards.q: Long-term physical complication resulting from surgical injury to the long thoracic nerve during axillary dissection?
cards.a: Winging of the scapula due to paralysis of the serratus anterior muscle.

cards.q: Long-term physical complication resulting from surgical injury to the thoracodorsal nerve during axillary dissection?
cards.a: Weakness in arm adduction, extension, and internal rotation due to paralysis of the latissimus dorsi muscle.

cards.q: Most common cause of primary hyperparathyroidism?
cards.a: A single benign parathyroid adenoma.

cards.q: Classic laboratory profile diagnostic of primary hyperparathyroidism?
cards.a: Elevated serum calcium, low serum phosphorus, and an inappropriately elevated or high-normal parathyroid hormone level.

cards.q: Classic clinical triad diagnostic of congenital pyloric stenosis in an infant?
cards.a: Non-bilious projectile vomiting, a palpable olive-shaped right upper quadrant mass, and visible gastric peristalsis.

cards.q: Distinctive metabolic and electrolyte derangement caused by persistent vomiting in hypertrophic pyloric stenosis?
cards.a: Hypokalemic, hypochloremic metabolic alkalosis.

cards.q: Immediate initial management step for an infant diagnosed with hypertrophic pyloric stenosis?
cards.a: Aggressive intravenous fluid resuscitation and electrolyte correction before any surgical intervention.

cards.q: Definitive surgical procedure for hypertrophic pyloric stenosis once the infant is metabolically stable?
cards.a: A Ramstedt pyloromyotomy.

cards.q: Classic clinical presentation of intussusception in a pediatric patient?
cards.a: Sudden onset of intermittent, severe abdominal pain, drawing up of the legs, and "currant-jelly" stools.

cards.q: Diagnostic and therapeutic modality of choice for stable pediatric patients with suspected intussusception?
cards.a: Air or contrast pneumatic reduction under fluoroscopic or ultrasound guidance.

cards.q: Absolute contraindication to attempting a pneumatic reduction in a child with intussusception?
cards.a: Presence of peritonitis, clinical shock, or free air on abdominal radiographs indicating bowel perforation.

cards.q: Pathophysiology driving the development of Meckel's diverticulum?
cards.a: Incomplete obliteration of the omphalomesenteric or vitelline duct during early embryonic development.

cards.q: Rule of thumb used to remember the epidemiological features of Meckel's diverticulum?
cards.a: The Rule of 2s: occurs in 2% of the population, located 2 feet from the ileocecal valve, and is 2 inches long.

cards.q: Primary tissue types found heterotopically within a Meckel's diverticulum that cause painless lower gastrointestinal bleeding?
cards.a: Ectopic gastric mucosa or pancreatic tissue.

cards.q: Definitive nuclear medicine imaging study used to diagnose Meckel's diverticulum in a pediatric patient?
cards.a: Technetium-99m pertechnetate scintigraphy, commonly called a Meckel's scan.

cards.q: Clinical feature distinguishing an omphalocele from gastroschisis?
cards.a: An omphalocele involves herniation through the umbilical ring covered by a peritoneal sac, whereas gastroschisis is a bare herniation lateral to the umbilicus.

cards.q: Congenital condition characteristically associated with an omphalocele but rarely with gastroschisis?
cards.a: Beckwith-Wiedemann syndrome or chromosomal trisomies.

cards.q: Classic clinical presentation of an infant born with Hirschsprung's disease?
cards.a: Failure to pass meconium within the first 48 hours of life, progressive abdominal distention, and bilious vomiting.

cards.q: Pathophysiology responsible for the development of Hirschsprung's disease?
cards.a: Failure of neural crest cells to migrate, resulting in a congenital absence of intramural ganglion cells in the distal bowel wall.

cards.q: Gold standard diagnostic test required to definitively confirm Hirschsprung's disease?
cards.a: Suction rectal biopsy demonstrating an absence of ganglion cells and hypertrophied nerve fibers.

cards.q: Classic clinical triad diagnostic of a ruptured abdominal aortic aneurysm?
cards.a: Sudden onset of severe abdominal or back pain, hypotension, and a pulsatile abdominal mass.

cards.q: Diagnostic imaging modality of choice for a hemodynamically stable patient with a suspected abdominal aortic aneurysm?
cards.a: Contrast-enhanced computed tomography angiography of the abdomen and pelvis.

cards.q: Screening tool of choice used to monitor asymptomatic patients with a known abdominal aortic aneurysm?
cards.a: Abdominal duplex ultrasound.

cards.q: Absolute diameter threshold at which an asymptomatic abdominal aortic aneurysm in an adult mandates elective surgical repair?
cards.a: A diameter greater than or equal to 5.5 centimeters in men, or 5.0 centimeters in women.

cards.q: Annual growth rate threshold that serves as an indication for elective repair of an abdominal aortic aneurysm?
cards.a: An expansion rate greater than 0.5 centimeters within a 6-month period or 1.0 centimeter within 1 year.

cards.q: Classic clinical presentation of an acute aortic dissection?
cards.a: Sudden onset of severe, sharp, "tearing" chest pain that radiates directly to the back between the scapulae.

cards.q: Standard classification system used to categorize aortic dissections based on anatomical location?
cards.a: The Stanford classification system.

cards.q: Define a Stanford Type A aortic dissection?
cards.a: Any dissection that involves the ascending aorta, regardless of where the intimal tear originates.

cards.q: Define a Stanford Type B aortic dissection?
cards.a: A dissection confined entirely to the descending aorta, originating distal to the left subclavian artery.

cards.q: Management paradigm for a patient diagnosed with an uncomplicated Stanford Type B aortic dissection?
cards.a: Medical management consisting of strict heart rate and blood pressure control using intravenous beta-blockers.

cards.q: Target physiological endpoints when managing a patient with an acute aortic dissection medically?
cards.a: Maintain a heart rate below 60 beats per minute and a systolic blood pressure between 100 and 120 millimeters of mercury.

cards.q: Definitive management strategy for any patient diagnosed with a Stanford Type A aortic dissection?
cards.a: Emergent surgical replacement of the ascending aorta to prevent intrapericardial rupture or coronary artery occlusion.

cards.q: The "6 Ps" that clinically define acute arterial occlusion of an extremity?
cards.a: Pain, pallor, pulselessness, paresthesia, paralysis, and poikilothermia.

cards.q: Most common source of an arterial embolus causing acute lower extremity ischemia?
cards.a: The left atrium of the heart, secondary to atrial fibrillation.

cards.q: Next immediate therapeutic step for a patient diagnosed with acute arterial occlusion of an extremity?
cards.a: Intravenous bolus of unfractionated heparin followed by a continuous heparin infusion to prevent thrombus propagation.

cards.q: Definitive surgical management for a viable limb experiencing an acute embolic arterial occlusion?
cards.a: Emergent operative embolectomy using a Fogarty balloon catheter.

cards.q: Define the classic clinical symptom known as intermittent claudication?
cards.a: Reproducible lower extremity muscle pain or cramping brought on by exertion and completely relieved by short periods of rest.

cards.q: Initial conservative medical management for a patient presenting with stable intermittent claudication?
cards.a: Structured exercise program, smoking cessation, antiplatelet therapy with aspirin, and a high-intensity statin.

cards.q: Pharmacological agent added to improve walking distance in patients with refractory intermittent claudication?
cards.a: Cilostazol, a phosphodiesterase inhibitor with antiplatelet and vasodilatory properties.

cards.q: Absolute clinical indications that progress chronic limb-threatening ischemia to mandatory surgical revascularization?
cards.a: Ischemic rest pain, non-healing ischemic ulcerations, or localized gangrene.

cards.q: Diagnostic criteria that define Leriche syndrome?
cards.a: A triad of bilateral buttock claudication, erectile dysfunction, and diminished or absent femoral pulses.

cards.q: Anatomical site of vascular occlusion responsible for causing Leriche syndrome?
cards.a: Atherosclerotic occlusion at the level of the aortic bifurcation or bilateral common iliac arteries.

cards.q: Classic clinical triad diagnostic of acute mesenteric ischemia?
cards.a: Severe, unremitting abdominal pain that is completely out of proportion to physical exam findings, vomiting, and a history of atrial fibrillation.

cards.q: Gold standard imaging modality used to definitively diagnose acute mesenteric ischemia?
cards.a: Computed tomography angiography of the abdomen.

cards.q: Classic presentation of chronic mesenteric ischemia?
cards.a: Postprandial abdominal pain, fear of eating, and significant progressive weight loss in a patient with diffuse atherosclerosis.

cards.q: Most common underlying cause of a spontaneous subarachnoid hemorrhage?
cards.a: Rupture of an intracranial secular or berry aneurysm within the Circle of Willis.

cards.q: Most common anatomical location for a berry aneurysm to develop within the cerebral circulation?
cards.a: The junction of the anterior communicating artery with the anterior cerebral artery.

cards.q: Classic clinical presentation of a patient experiencing an acute subarachnoid hemorrhage?
cards.a: Sudden onset of an excruciatingly severe headache, often described by the patient as the "worst headache of my life."

cards.q: Immediate initial diagnostic imaging study of choice for a patient suspected of having a subarachnoid hemorrhage?
cards.a: Non-contrast computed tomography scan of the head.

cards.q: Next diagnostic step for a patient with high clinical suspicion for subarachnoid hemorrhage whose head CT is negative?
cards.a: Lumbar puncture to evaluate for the presence of gross blood or xanthochromia.

cards.q: Medication administered to prevent delayed ischemic neurological deficits from vasospasm following a subarachnoid hemorrhage?
cards.a: Nimodipine, a calcium channel blocker, initiated within 96 hours of hemorrhage onset.

cards.q: Classic presentation of an epidural hematoma following head trauma?
cards.a: Loss of consciousness followed by a transient lucid interval, subsequent rapid neurological deterioration, and an ipsilateral blown pupil.

cards.q: Most common vascular structure injured that results in the formation of an epidural hematoma?
cards.a: The middle meningeal artery, typically secondary to a fracture of the temporal bone at the pterion.

cards.q: Distinctive radiographic appearance of an epidural hematoma on a non-contrast head CT scan?
cards.a: A hyperdense, biconvex or lens-shaped fluid collection that does not cross the cranial suture lines.

cards.q: Pathophysiology driving the development of an epidural hematoma?
cards.a: Traumatic laceration of the middle meningeal artery resulting in rapid arterial bleeding that dissects the dura away from the inner table of the skull.

cards.q: Distinctive radiographic appearance of a subdural hematoma on a non-contrast head CT scan?
cards.a: A crescent-shaped or concave hyperdense fluid collection that readily crosses cranial suture lines.

cards.q: Most common vascular structure injured that results in the formation of a subdural hematoma?
cards.a: Shearing of the superficial bridging cortical veins as they cross the subdural space to empty into the dural sinuses.

cards.q: Classic clinical presentation of a subdural hematoma compared to an epidural hematoma?
cards.a: Insidious onset of progressive headache, cognitive decline, or focal neurological deficits over days to weeks, particularly in elderly or alcoholic patients.

cards.q: Classic clinical presentation of a posterior hip dislocation?
cards.a: The affected lower extremity is held in a position of adduction, internal rotation, and flexion.

cards.q: Most common nerve injury associated with a posterior hip dislocation?
cards.a: Injury or compression of the sciatic nerve.

cards.q: Classic clinical presentation of an anterior shoulder dislocation?
cards.a: The affected arm is held in slight abduction and external rotation, with a loss of the normal rounded contour of the deltoid.

cards.q: Most common nerve injury associated with an anterior shoulder dislocation?
cards.a: Injury to the axillary nerve, resulting in a loss of sensation over the lateral shoulder and deltoid weakness.

cards.q: Nerve most commonly injured in a midshaft humerus fracture?
cards.a: The radial nerve, resulting in wrist drop and sensory loss over the posterior forearm and first dorsal web space.

cards.q: Nerve most commonly injured in a supracondylar fracture of the humerus in a pediatric patient?
cards.a: The anterior interosseous branch of the median nerve, resulting in an inability to make an "OK" sign.

cards.q: Clinical syndrome that constitutes an absolute surgical emergency following a severe lumbar spinal disc herniation?
cards.a: Cauda equina syndrome.

cards.q: Clinical presentation diagnostic of cauda equina syndrome?
cards.a: Saddle anesthesia, new-onset urinary retention or fecal incontinence, bilateral sciatica, and progressive lower extremity motor weakness.

cards.q: Immediate initial diagnostic test of choice for a patient suspected of having cauda equina syndrome?
cards.a: Emergent magnetic resonance imaging of the lumbar spine.

cards.q: Most common underlying cause of a spontaneous pneumothorax in a young, healthy adult?
cards.a: Rupture of subpleural apical blebs or bullae, typically seen in tall, thin, young males.

cards.q: Definitive management for a first-time, small, asymptomatic spontaneous pneumothorax measuring less than 2 centimeters?
cards.a: Conservative observation with supplemental oxygen therapy to accelerate pleural air reabsorption.

cards.q: Definitive management for a large, symptomatic spontaneous pneumothorax or a recurrent episode?
cards.a: Placement of a pigtail catheter or a standard chest tube connected to a water-seal system.

cards.q: Clinical presentation of a patient with a diaphragmatic rupture following severe blunt chest or abdominal trauma?
cards.a: Respiratory distress, decreased breath sounds on the left side, and bowel sounds heard over the left hemithorax.

cards.q: Diagnostic radiographic hallmark of a traumatic diaphragmatic rupture on a standard chest X-ray?
cards.a: Visualization of the stomach or loops of bowel inside the thoracic cavity, frequently accompanied by a shifted mediastinum.

cards.q: Surgical indication for a thoracic empyema secondary to an unresolved parapneumonic effusion?
cards.a: Presence of gross pus in the pleural cavity, a positive Gram stain or culture, or fluid pH below 7.2.

cards.q: Preferred surgical technique for managing a multi-loculated thoracic empyema that fails standard chest tube drainage?
cards.a: Video-Assisted Thoracoscopic Surgery for lung decortication and loculation disruption.

cards.q: Classic clinical presentation of testicular torsion?
cards.a: Sudden onset of severe, unilateral testicular pain, a high-riding testis with a transverse lie, and an absent cremasteric reflex.

cards.q: Maximum time window from symptom onset to achieve testicular detorsion to avoid irreversible ischemic necrosis?
cards.a: Within 6 hours of pain onset, which yields a salvage rate greater than 90%.

cards.q: Imaging modality used to support the diagnosis of testicular torsion when clinical presentation is equivocal?
cards.a: Color duplex Doppler ultrasound of the scrotum, demonstrating decreased or absent arterial blood flow to the affected testis.

cards.q: Definitive surgical management required for a patient with confirmed testicular torsion?
cards.a: Urgent surgical exploration with bilateral testicular detorsion and orchiopexy to prevent recurrent contralateral torsion.

cards.q: Classic presentation of a patient with acute epididymitis?
cards.a: Gradual onset of unilateral scrotal pain, swelling, and fever, associated with a preserved cremasteric reflex.

cards.q: Name the physical exam sign where scrotal elevation relieves pain in epididymitis but worsens or fails to change pain in testicular torsion?
cards.a: Prehn's sign.

cards.q: Most common causative pathogens responsible for acute epididymitis in men under the age of 35?
cards.a: Chlamydia trachomatis and Neisseria gonorrhoeae.

cards.q: Most common causative pathogens responsible for acute epididymitis in men over the age of 35?
cards.a: Enteric Gram-negative rods, primarily Escherichia coli and Pseudomonas species.

cards.q: Classic clinical presentation of a patient with a ureteral calculus?
cards.a: Sudden onset of severe, colicky flank pain that radiates down toward the groin or labia/scrotum, accompanied by macroscopic hematuria.

cards.q: Non-contrast diagnostic imaging study of choice for a patient suspected of having an acute ureteral stone?
cards.a: Low-dose non-contrast computed tomography of the abdomen and pelvis.

cards.q: Absolute indications for urgent surgical decompression of the collecting system in a patient with a ureteral stone?
cards.a: Presence of a urinary tract infection with fever, intractable pain, unremitting vomiting, or a stone obstructing a solitary kidney.

cards.q: First-line surgical interventions used to decompress an obstructed and infected renal collecting system?
cards.a: Retrograde placement of a ureteral double-J stent or percutaneous nephrostomy tube insertion.

cards.q: Most common histological type of bladder cancer found in Western nations?
cards.a: Urothelial carcinoma, formerly known as transitional cell carcinoma.

cards.q: Single most important, avoidable environmental risk factor for the development of urothelial bladder cancer?
cards.a: Cigarette smoking, which increases the risk of development three- to fold.

cards.q: Classic clinical presentation of a patient with an underlying bladder malignancy?
cards.a: Painless, gross hematuria throughout the entire stream of urination in an older adult.

cards.q: Definitive diagnostic step required to confirm bladder cancer and evaluate muscle invasion?
cards.a: Cystoscopy followed by Transurethral Resection of Bladder Tumor.

cards.q: Define the primary diagnostic triad for renal cell carcinoma?
cards.a: Flank pain, hematuria, and a palpable abdominal mass, though this complete triad is found in fewer than 10% of cases.

cards.q: Most common histological subtype of renal cell carcinoma?
cards.a: Clear cell renal cell carcinoma, originating from the proximal convoluted tubule cells.

cards.q: Paraneoplastic syndrome characteristically associated with renal cell carcinoma due to ectopic hormone production?
cards.a: Erythrocytosis due to inappropriate erythropoietin secretion, or hypercalcemia due to parathyroid hormone-related peptide production.

cards.q: Preferred definitive surgical intervention for a localized renal cell carcinoma tumor measuring less than 4 centimeters?
cards.a: Partial nephrectomy to maximize long-term nephron preservation.

cards.q: Classic clinical presentation of benign prostatic hyperplasia?
cards.a: Lower urinary tract symptoms including urinary frequency, urgency, nocturia, weak urinary stream, and incomplete emptying.

cards.q: Anatomical zone of the prostate gland that undergoes hyperplasia in benign prostatic hyperplasia?
cards.a: The transition zone, which directly surrounds the proximal urethra.

cards.q: Anatomical zone of the prostate gland where adenocarcinoma of the prostate most commonly originates?
cards.a: The peripheral zone, which is readily accessible via a digital rectal examination.

cards.q: First-line medical therapy used to achieve rapid symptom relief in a patient with benign prostatic hyperplasia?
cards.a: Alpha-1 adrenergic receptor antagonists, such as tamsulosin, which relax the smooth muscle of the prostatic urethra and bladder neck.

cards.q: Mechanism of action of 5-alpha reductase inhibitors like finasteride used in the management of benign prostatic hyperplasia?
cards.a: Blocks the conversion of testosterone to dihydrotestosterone to gradually reduce the physical volume of the prostate over 6 months.

cards.q: Gold standard surgical intervention for a patient with benign prostatic hyperplasia refractory to medical management?
cards.a: Transurethral Resection of the Prostate.

cards.q: Most common early postoperative complication associated with a transurethral resection of the prostate?
cards.a: Retrograde ejaculation.

cards.q: Classic presentation of a patient with a suspected urethral injury following pelvic trauma?
cards.a: Blood at the urethral meatus, a high-riding prostate on digital rectal exam, and an inability to void.

cards.q: Mandatory diagnostic imaging step required prior to attempting any blind urethral catheterization in a patient with suspected urethral trauma?
cards.a: Retrograde urethrogram.

cards.q: Pathophysiology of a priapism classified as low-flow ischemic priapism?
cards.a: Impaired venous outflow from the corpora cavernosa leading to blood stasis, hypoxia, and painful rigid engorgement.

cards.q: First-line medical intervention for the aspiration and irrigation of a low-flow ischemic priapism?
cards.a: Intracavernosal injection of a diluted alpha-adrenergic agonist, such as phenylephrine.

cards.q: Classic clinical presentation of acute appendicitis?
cards.a: Periumbilical pain that migrates to the right lower quadrant, accompanied by anorexia, nausea, and low-grade fever.

cards.q: Anatomical landmark located two-thirds of the distance from the umbilicus to the anterior superior iliac spine?
cards.a: McBurney's point.

cards.q: Name the physical sign where pain is elicited in the right lower quadrant during deep palpation of the left lower quadrant?
cards.a: Rovsing's sign.

cards.q: Physical exam maneuver where passive extension of the right hip elicits pain, indicating a retrocecal appendix?
cards.a: Psoas sign.

cards.q: Physical exam maneuver where passive internal rotation of the flexed right hip elicits pain, indicating a pelvic appendix?
cards.a: Obturator sign.

cards.q: Preferred diagnostic imaging modality for a pregnant patient or pediatric patient with suspected acute appendicitis?
cards.a: Transabdominal graded-compression ultrasound.

cards.q: Definitive diagnostic imaging modality of choice for an adult male or non-pregnant female with suspected appendicitis?
cards.a: Computed tomography scan of the abdomen and pelvis with intravenous contrast.

cards.q: Standard surgical management for acute, uncomplicated appendicitis?
cards.a: Urgent laparoscopic or open appendectomy.

cards.q: Initial management strategy for a stable patient presenting with a perforated appendix and a well-circumscribed abscess?
cards.a: Intravenous antibiotics, percutaneous image-guided drainage, and a planned interval appendectomy 6 to 8 weeks later.

cards.q: Most common benign neoplasm found within the appendix?
cards.a: Neuroendocrine tumor, historically referred to as a carcinoid tumor.

cards.q: Surgical management for an appendiceal neuroendocrine tumor measuring less than 2 centimeters localized to the tip?
cards.a: Simple appendectomy is completely curative.

cards.q: Surgical management for an appendiceal neuroendocrine tumor that measures greater than 2 centimeters or involves the appendiceal base?
cards.a: Right hemicolectomy.

cards.q: Classic clinical presentation of acute colonic diverticulitis?
cards.a: Constant left lower quadrant abdominal pain, fever, and leukocytosis in an older adult.

cards.q: Preferred diagnostic imaging modality to confirm a diagnosis of acute diverticulitis?
cards.a: Computed tomography scan of the abdomen and pelvis with intravenous contrast.

cards.q: Diagnostic procedure that is absolutely contraindicated during an episode of acute diverticulitis due to a high perforation risk?
cards.a: Colonoscopy or flexible sigmoidoscopy.

cards.q: Standard classification system used to stage the severity of complicated acute diverticulitis?
cards.a: The Hinchey classification system.

cards.q: Definition of Hinchey Stage I diverticulitis?
cards.a: Acute diverticulitis associated with a localized pericolic or mesenteric abscess.

cards.q: Definition of Hinchey Stage II diverticulitis?
cards.a: Acute diverticulitis associated with a walled-off pelvic, intra-abdominal, or retroperitoneal abscess.

cards.q: Definition of Hinchey Stage III diverticulitis?
cards.a: Acute diverticulitis complicated by generalized purulent peritonitis from abscess rupture.

cards.q: Definition of Hinchey Stage IV diverticulitis?
cards.a: Acute diverticulitis complicated by generalized feculent peritonitis from free fecal perforation of the colon.

cards.q: Definitive surgical management for a patient presenting with Hinchey Stage III or IV acute diverticulitis?
cards.a: Emergent Hartmann's procedure, which involves resection of the diseased sigmoid colon, a temporary end colostomy, and a rectal stump closure.

cards.q: Most common type of internal abdominal wall hernia that develops through a previous surgical incision site?
cards.a: Incisional hernia.

cards.q: Single most important modifiable risk factor for the development of a postoperative incisional hernia?
cards.a: Surgical site infection at the primary laparotomy wound.

cards.q: Structural defect that defines a Richter's hernia?
cards.a: Incarceration of only a portion of the antimesenteric border of the bowel wall within a hernia defect.

cards.q: Clinical feature that makes a Richter's hernia notoriously difficult to diagnose early?
cards.a: It can progress to localized bowel necrosis and perforation without ever causing clinical signs of intestinal obstruction.

cards.q: Structural components that define a Maydl's hernia?
cards.a: A hernia containing two adjacent loops of small bowel within the sac, where the intervening loop inside the abdomen undergoes strangulation.

cards.q: Structural components that define a Pantaloon hernia?
cards.a: Simultaneous direct and indirect inguinal hernias occurring on the same side, straddling the inferior epigastric vessels.

cards.q: Pathophysiology driving hyperacute organ transplant rejection?
cards.a: Pre-existing, recipient-formed antibodies against donor human leukocyte antigens or ABO blood group antigens.

cards.q: Timeline for the manifestation of hyperacute organ transplant rejection?
cards.a: Occurs intraoperatively within minutes to hours of graft reperfusion.

cards.q: Gross physical changes visible on the operating table during an episode of hyperacute transplant rejection?
cards.a: The graft rapidly turns cyanotic, mottled, and flaccid due to widespread intravascular thrombosis and cortical necrosis.

cards.q: Management strategy for hyperacute organ transplant rejection discovered intraoperatively?
cards.a: Immediate surgical removal of the rejected graft, as there is no effective medical therapy.

cards.q: Pathophysiology driving acute cellular transplant rejection?
cards.a: Recipient T-lymphocyte-mediated immune response directed against donor human leukocyte antigens.

cards.q: Timeline for the standard manifestation of acute cellular organ transplant rejection?
cards.a: Typically occurs between 1 week and several months post-transplantation.

cards.q: First-line medical therapy used to reverse an episode of acute cellular transplant rejection?
cards.a: Intravenous pulse-dose corticosteroids, such as methylprednisolone.

cards.q: Pathophysiology driving chronic transplant rejection?
cards.a: A combined humoral and cellular immune response causing progressive, irreversible intimal fibrocellular proliferation and vascular occlusion.

cards.q: Timeline for the manifestation of chronic transplant rejection?
cards.a: Occurs gradually over months to years following the transplantation.

cards.q: Clinical presentation of a mechanical small bowel obstruction?
cards.a: Colicky abdominal pain, early bilious vomiting, progressive abdominal distention, and obstipation.

cards.q: Most common underlying cause of a mechanical small bowel obstruction in a patient with a history of prior abdominal surgery?
cards.a: Postoperative intra-abdominal adhesions.

cards.q: Most common underlying cause of a mechanical small bowel obstruction in a patient with no history of prior abdominal surgery?
cards.a: Incarcerated abdominal wall or groin hernia.

cards.q: Classic radiographic findings on an upright abdominal X-ray diagnostic of a small bowel obstruction?
cards.a: Dilated loops of small bowel greater than 3 centimeters, multiple air-fluid levels, and a lack of gas in the colon.

cards.q: Initial conservative management strategy for a stable patient with a partial small bowel obstruction?
cards.a: Strict nothing-by-mouth status, intravenous fluid resuscitation, and nasogastric tube decompression.

cards.q: Diagnostic or therapeutic substance used to predict the success of conservative management in adhesive small bowel obstructions?
cards.a: Water-soluble contrast, such as Gastrografin, administered orally or via a nasogastric tube.

cards.q: Positive prognostic sign indicating resolving small bowel obstruction after water-soluble contrast administration?
cards.a: Clearance of contrast into the colon on an abdominal radiograph taken within 24 hours.

cards.q: Absolute indications for immediate operative laparotomy in a patient with a small bowel obstruction?
cards.a: Signs of strangulation, including continuous localized pain, peritonitis, fever, leukocytosis, or free air on imaging.

cards.q: Clinical presentation of a colonic volvulus?
cards.a: Massive abdominal distention, baseline constipation, obstipation, and severe abdominal cramping in an elderly or institutionalized patient.

cards.q: Most common anatomical location for a colonic volvulus to occur?
cards.a: The sigmoid colon.

cards.q: Classic radiographic hallmark of a sigmoid volvulus seen on an abdominal plain film?
cards.a: A massively dilated loop of colon demonstrating a "coffee bean" or "bent inner tube" appearance pointing toward the right upper quadrant.

cards.q: Initial management strategy for a hemodynamically stable patient diagnosed with an uncomplicated sigmoid volvulus?
cards.a: Rigid or flexible sigmoidoscopy for untwisting and decompression, followed by placement of a rectal tube.

cards.q: Definitive management strategy for a sigmoid volvulus that presents with systemic toxicity, peritonitis, or failed endoscopic reduction?
cards.a: Emergent surgical resection without primary anastomosis, typically a Hartmann's procedure.

cards.q: Classic radiographic appearance of a cecal volvulus on an abdominal plain film?
cards.a: A comma-shaped or "teardrop" gas-filled loop of colon pointing toward the left upper quadrant.

cards.q: Definitive management strategy required for a cecal volvulus?
cards.a: Operative right hemicolectomy, as endoscopic decompression is rarely successful and carries a high risk of perforation.

cards.q: Classic clinical presentation of an acute upper gastrointestinal bleed from a Mallory-Weiss tear?
cards.a: Painless hematemesis following multiple episodes of forceful retching or vomiting, often after alcohol consumption.

cards.q: Anatomical location and structural nature of a Mallory-Weiss tear?
cards.a: A longitudinal mucosal and submucosal laceration located at the gastroesophageal junction.

cards.q: Management paradigm for the vast majority of active Mallory-Weiss tear hemorrhages?
cards.a: Conservative supportive care and endoscopic intervention, as over 80% stop bleeding spontaneously.

cards.q: Pathophysiology of Boerhaave syndrome compared to a Mallory-Weiss tear?
cards.a: Full-thickness transmural rupture of the esophageal wall caused by a sudden rise in intraluminal pressure during violent vomiting.

cards.q: Most common clinical presentation of a gastric cancer tumor localized to the pylorus or antrum?
cards.a: Early satiety, progressive nausea, and persistent weight loss secondary to gastric outlet obstruction.

cards.q: Classic physical exam sign of metastatic gastric adenocarcinoma manifesting as a palpable left supraclavicular lymph node?
cards.a: Virchow's node.

cards.q: Classic physical exam sign of metastatic gastric adenocarcinoma manifesting as a palpable periumbilical nodule?
cards.a: Sister Mary Joseph nodule.

cards.q: Classic physical exam sign of metastatic gastric adenocarcinoma manifesting as a palpable mass in the rectouterine or rectovesical pouch?
cards.a: Blumer's shelf.

cards.q: Diagnostic modality of choice to establish a tissue diagnosis for suspected gastric carcinoma?
cards.a: Esophagogastroduodenoscopy with multiple punch biopsies of the ulcer edge.

cards.q: Preferred surgical resection strategy for a resectable adenocarcinoma localized to the distal stomach?
cards.a: Subtotal gastrectomy with a minimum of 4-centimeter healthy margins and an adequate D2 lymphadenectomy.

cards.q: Preferred surgical resection strategy for a resectable adenocarcinoma localized to the proximal stomach or cardia?
cards.a: Total gastrectomy with a Roux-en-Y esophagojejunostomy reconstruction.

cards.q: Most common physiological complication resulting from a total gastrectomy due to the loss of intrinsic factor secretion?
cards.a: Pernicious anemia secondary to vitamin B12 malabsorption, requiring lifelong intramuscular supplementation.

cards.q: Pathophysiology driving the early dumping syndrome following a partial or total gastrectomy?
cards.a: Rapid delivery of hyperosmolar chyme into the small intestine, causing a massive fluid shift from the intravascular space into the lumen.

cards.q: Clinical presentation of early dumping syndrome?
cards.a: Abdominal cramps, diarrhea, nausea, palpitations, and diaphoresis occurring 15 to 30 minutes after eating a carbohydrate-heavy meal.

cards.q: Pathophysiology driving late dumping syndrome following a gastrectomy?
cards.a: Rapid glucose absorption in the small bowel triggers a massive, inappropriate insulin surge that causes reactive hypoglycemia.

cards.q: Primary dietary management strategy used to control symptoms of post-gastrectomy dumping syndrome?
cards.a: Eating small, frequent, high-protein, low-carbohydrate meals and avoiding liquids during solid food consumption.

cards.q: Definitive diagnostic criteria for a patient suspected of having a perforated peptic ulcer?
cards.a: Sudden onset of severe, generalized abdominal pain associated with free air under the diaphragm on an upright chest X-ray.

cards.q: Immediate initial management for a patient presenting with an acutely perforated peptic ulcer?
cards.a: Aggressive fluid resuscitation, intravenous proton pump inhibitors, broad-spectrum antibiotics, and urgent surgical consultation.

cards.q: Definitive surgical management for an acute perforation of a duodenal ulcer in a hemodynamically stable patient?
cards.a: Primary closure of the perforation reinforced with a vascularized pedicle of omentum, known as a Graham patch repair.

cards.q: Most common source of massive arterial hemorrhage from a posterior duodenal ulcer?
