cards.a: Erosion of the ulcer into the gastroduodenal artery running directly behind the first part of the duodenum.

cards.q: Single most common indication for surgical intervention in a patient suffering from chronic peptic ulcer disease?
cards.a: Refractory bleeding that cannot be controlled via repeated endoscopic therapeutic modalities.

cards.q: Criteria used to determine eligibility for bariatric surgical intervention in an adult patient?
cards.a: Body Mass Index greater than or equal to 40, or greater than or equal to 35 with significant weight-related comorbidities.

cards.q: Most common restrictive bariatric surgical procedure performed worldwide?
cards.a: Laparoscopic sleeve gastrectomy, which involves resecting the greater curvature of the stomach to leave a narrow gastric conduit.

cards.q: Most common restrictive and malabsorptive combination bariatric procedure performed for long-term weight loss?
cards.a: Roux-en-Y gastric bypass.

cards.q: Most serious, life-threatening early postoperative complication following a Roux-en-Y gastric bypass?
cards.a: Anastomotic leak at the gastrojejunostomy, presenting with unexplained tachycardia, tachypnea, and fever.

cards.q: Next immediate diagnostic or therapeutic step for a postoperative gastric bypass patient with high clinical suspicion for an anastomotic leak?
cards.a: Urgent return to the operating room for surgical exploration and repair, regardless of negative imaging results.

cards.q: Long-term nutritional deficiency characteristically seen after a Roux-en-Y gastric bypass due to bypassing the duodenum?
cards.a: Iron, calcium, and vitamin B12 deficiencies.

cards.q: Most common benign solid tumor of the spleen?
cards.a: Hemangioma.

cards.q: Single most common indication for an elective splenectomy in an adult?
cards.a: Immune Thrombocytopenic Purpura refractory to first-line corticosteroid and medical therapies.

cards.q: Principal hematological changes observed on a peripheral blood smear following a total splenectomy?
cards.a: Presence of Howell-Jolly bodies, Heinz bodies, target cells, and transient thrombocytosis.

cards.q: Physiological explanation for the presence of Howell-Jolly bodies on a post-splenectomy blood smear?
cards.a: Absence of functional splenic macrophages that normally pit nuclear remnants from circulating erythrocytes.

cards.q: Definitive timeline requirement for the administration of encapsulated organism vaccines prior to an elective splenectomy?
cards.a: At least 14 days prior to the planned surgical procedure to maximize the protective antibody response.

cards.q: Standard vaccine regimen required for any patient undergoing an elective or emergent total splenectomy?
cards.a: Immunizations against Streptococcus pneumoniae, Neisseria meningitidis, and Haemophilus influenzae type b.

cards.q: Recommended timeline for administering the encapsulated organism vaccine series following an unplanned, emergent trauma splenectomy?
cards.a: Exactly 14 days postoperatively, to avoid the immediate post-injury immunosuppressive window.

cards.q: Most lethal infectious complication associated with the post-splenectomy state?
cards.a: Overwhelming Post-Splenectomy Infection, characteristically presenting as rapidly progressive septic shock with high mortality.

cards.q: Standard prophylactic management strategy recommended for post-splenectomy patients who develop a sudden, new-onset fever at home?
cards.a: Immediate empirical self-administration of a broad-spectrum oral antibiotic like amoxicillin-clavulanate and urgent presentation to an emergency department.

cards.q: Diagnostic criteria that define a sliding hiatal hernia, also known as a Type I hiatal hernia?
cards.a: Upward displacement of both the gastroesophageal junction and the gastric cardia through the diaphragmatic hiatus into the posterior mediastinum.

cards.q: Diagnostic criteria that define a paraesophageal hiatal hernia, also known as a Type II hiatal hernia?
cards.a: The gastroesophageal junction remains in its normal anatomical position, but the gastric fundus herniates through the hiatus alongside the esophagus.

cards.q: Primary clinical complication that necessitates mandatory surgical repair of an asymptomatic paraesophageal hernia?
cards.a: High risk of acute gastric volvulus, incarceration, strangulation, or intrathoracic perforation.

cards.q: Standard surgical management for a symptomatic sliding hiatal hernia refractory to maximal medical management?
cards.a: Laparoscopic Cruroplasty combined with a 360-degree fundoplication, commonly known as a Nissen fundoplication.

cards.q: Primary physiological function of the Nissen fundoplication procedure?
cards.a: Restores the high-pressure zone of the lower esophageal sphincter to prevent pathologic gastroesophageal reflux.

cards.q: Most common technical complication encountered by patients in the early postoperative period following a Nissen fundoplication?
cards.a: Transient dysphagia, usually resolving within 4 to 6 weeks as tissue edema subsides.

cards.q: Define the anatomical boundaries of the hepatocystic triangle, which forms the baseline for cholecystectomy dissection?
cards.a: Bounded by the cystic duct inferiorly, the common hepatic duct medially, and the inferior border of the liver superiorly.

cards.q: Structural difference between the hepatocystic triangle and the Triangle of Calot?
cards.a: The Triangle of Calot is bounded superiorly by the cystic artery, whereas the hepatocystic triangle is bounded superiorly by the liver surface.

cards.q: Most common physiological cause of a localized mechanical small bowel obstruction in an elderly female with a history of chronic gallstones?
cards.a: Cholecystenteric fistula allowing a large gallstone to enter the intestinal lumen and impact at the ileocecal valve.

cards.q: What specific radiographic finding on an abdominal CT scan confirms the presence of a cholecystenteric fistula?
cards.a: Pneumobilia, defined as the presence of free gas or air within the biliary tree.

cards.q: Definition of an enterocutaneous fistula?
cards.a: An abnormal, pathological communication developing between the lumen of the gastrointestinal tract and the skin.

cards.q: Primary initial management paradigm for a patient with a newly diagnosed high-output enterocutaneous fistula?
cards.a: Stabilization of fluid and electrolyte balances, aggressive nutritional support via TPN, protect the skin, and bowel rest.

cards.q: Minimum duration of conservative medical management required before attempting surgical closure of a persistent enterocutaneous fistula?
cards.a: At least 3 to 6 months to allow intense intra-abdominal dense adhesions to mature and soften.

cards.q: Primary underlying risk factor that prevents spontaneous closure of an enterocutaneous fistula, remembered by the acronym FRIEND?
cards.a: Foreign body, Radiation, Inflammation/Infection, Epithelialization of the tract, Neoplasm, or Distal bowel obstruction.

cards.q: Most common site of a perforation caused by an obstructing colon cancer located in the sigmoid colon?
cards.a: The cecum, due to Laplace’s law stating that wall tension is highest where the luminal diameter is largest.

cards.q: Diameter threshold above which an acutely distended cecum carries an imminent risk of ischemic perforation?
cards.a: A diameter greater than 10 to 12 centimeters.

cards.q: Classic clinical presentation of a patient with toxic megacolon complicating severe ulcerative colitis?
cards.a: Worsening bloody diarrhea, acute abdominal distention, high fever, tachycardia, and signs of localized or systemic peritonitis.

cards.q: Diagnostic criteria required to confirm a diagnosis of toxic megacolon on imaging?
cards.a: Radiographic evidence of colonic distention greater than 6 centimeters associated with systemic signs of toxicity.

cards.q: Management strategy for a patient with toxic megacolon who fails to respond to 24 to 48 hours of aggressive medical therapy?
cards.a: Emergent total abdominal colectomy with an end ileostomy.

cards.q: Standard operative procedure performed for an elective, curative-intent resection of an upper-to-middle rectal adenocarcinoma?
cards.a: Anterior resection or low anterior resection with a total mesorectal excision.

cards.q: Definitive surgical procedure required for a distal rectal cancer located within 2 centimeters of the anal verge that invades the sphincter complex?
cards.a: Abdominoperineal resection, requiring permanent removal of the rectum and anus, leaving a permanent end colostomy.

cards.q: Crucial anatomical structure that must be protected during the mobilization of the left colon and splenic flexure?
cards.a: The left ureter, which crosses anterior to the common iliac artery bifurcation.

cards.q: Classic presentation of an internal hemorrhoid compared to an external hemorrhoid?
cards.a: Painless bright red bleeding per rectum noticed during or after defecation, whereas external hemorrhoids are typically painful when thrombosed.

cards.q: Anatomical landmark that separates internal hemorrhoids from external hemorrhoids?
cards.a: The dentate line.

cards.q: Treatment paradigm for Grade I or II internal hemorrhoids that fail lifestyle adjustments?
cards.a: In-office rubber band ligation to induce localized ischemia and tissue sloughing.

cards.q: Definition of an anal fissure?
cards.a: A painful linear tear or ulceration in the squamous epithelium of the anal canal distal to the dentate line.

cards.q: Most common anatomical location for a primary benign anal fissure to develop?
cards.a: The posterior midline of the anal canal.

cards.q: Pathological condition that should be suspected if an anal fissure is found in a lateral position?
cards.a: Crohn's disease, tuberculosis, HIV, or an underlying malignancy.

cards.q: First-line medical therapy used to heal a chronic anal fissure by reducing internal anal sphincter resting pressure?
cards.a: Topical vasodilators such as 0.2% nitroglycerin ointment or 2% diltiazem gel.

cards.q: Gold standard surgical procedure for a chronic anal fissure refractory to all conservative medical modalities?
cards.a: Lateral internal sphincterotomy.

cards.q: Most common physiological complication associated with a lateral internal sphincterotomy?
cards.a: Transient or permanent flatus or minor fecal incontinence.

cards.q: Origin of an anorectal abscess based on the widely accepted cryptoglandular hypothesis?
cards.a: Infection originating within the deep anal glands that open into the anal crypts at the dentate line.

cards.q: Definitive management strategy for any acutely fluctuant anorectal abscess?
cards.a: Immediate surgical incision and drainage at the bedside or in the operating room, without waiting for imaging.

cards.q: Routine use of postoperative antibiotics following simple incision and drainage of a perianal abscess is indicated in which patients?
cards.a: Patients with concomitant immunosuppression, extensive cellulitis, systemic signs of infection, or artificial heart valves.

cards.q: Rule used to predict the tract trajectory of an anorectal fistula based on the location of its external opening?
cards.a: Goodsall's rule.

cards.q: Pathological trajectory of an anal fistula with an external opening located anterior to a transverse line drawn across the anus?
cards.a: The fistula tract generally runs in a straight, radial line directly to the nearest anterior internal crypt.

cards.q: Pathological trajectory of an anal fistula with an external opening located posterior to a transverse line drawn across the anus?
cards.a: The fistula tract generally follows a curved path to enter the internal opening at the posterior midline crypt.

cards.q: Definitive management for a superficial anorectal fistula that does not cross significant voluntary sphincter muscle?
cards.a: Primary fistulotomy, allowing the tract to heal from the base upward by secondary intention.

cards.q: Preferred management tool for a complex, high transsphincteric anal fistula to prevent fecal incontinence?
cards.a: Placement of a non-cutting, draining seton loop to control local inflammation and prevent recurrent abscess formation.

cards.q: Standard biochemical diagnostic threshold for acute pancreatitis?
cards.a: A serum amylase or lipase concentration elevated to at least 3 times the upper limit of normal.

cards.q: Most common underlying etiology of acute pancreatitis in the Western world?
cards.a: Gallstone migration obstructing the common pancreaticobiliary channel.

cards.q: Most specific early prognostic laboratory marker used to evaluate the severity of acute pancreatitis within 48 hours of admission?
cards.a: Rising blood urea nitrogen level or a high hematocrit reflecting profound intravascular volume depletion.

cards.q: Define the Ranson criteria parameters checked at the exact time of admission for acute pancreatitis?
cards.a: Age greater than 55 years, white blood cell count greater than 16,000, blood glucose greater than 200, lactate dehydrogenase greater than 350, and aspartate aminotransferase greater than 250.

cards.q: Clinical significance of a Ranson score greater than or equal to 3 in acute pancreatitis?
cards.a: Indicates severe acute pancreatitis with a significantly higher risk of developing systemic organ failure and necrosis.

cards.q: Diagnostic imaging modality of choice to evaluate for infected pancreatic necrosis when a patient worsens 72 hours after admission?
cards.a: Contrast-enhanced computed tomography scan of the abdomen.

cards.q: Diagnostic criteria that define systemic inflammatory response syndrome?
cards.a: Two or more of: temperature below 36 or above 38 degrees Celsius, heart rate above 90, respiratory rate above 20, or white blood cell count below 4,000 or above 12,000.

cards.q: Most common source of organisms causing secondary bacterial infection of sterile pancreatic necrosis?
cards.a: Translocation of Gram-negative enteric bacteria, primarily Escherichia coli and Klebsiella, from the adjacent colon.

cards.q: Immediate empirical management strategy for a patient with fine-needle aspiration or gas on CT confirming infected pancreatic necrosis?
cards.a: Intravenous broad-spectrum antibiotics with high pancreatic tissue penetration, such as meropenem.

cards.q: Preferred surgical or procedural paradigm for managing symptomatic or infected pancreatic necrosis?
cards.a: A step-up approach, starting with percutaneous or endoscopic drainage followed by minimally invasive retroperitoneal debridement if needed.

cards.q: Timing guideline for performing a cholecystectomy in a patient with mild, uncomplicated gallstone pancreatitis?
cards.a: During the same hospital admission, once acute abdominal pain resolves and pancreatic enzyme levels trend downward.

cards.q: Pathophysiology driving the development of a pancreatic pseudocyst?
cards.a: Fibrous granulation tissue encapsulating a collection of amylase-rich fluid following pancreatic ductal disruption, lacking a true epithelial lining.

cards.q: Most common vascular complication associated with chronic pancreatitis or a large adjacent pancreatic pseudocyst?
cards.a: Thrombosis of the splenic vein.

cards.q: Classic clinical presentation of isolated splenic vein thrombosis secondary to chronic pancreatitis?
cards.a: Isolated gastric varices in the fundus of the stomach with completely normal esophageal anatomy and normal liver function.

cards.q: Curative surgical treatment for symptomatic or bleeding isolated gastric varices secondary to splenic vein thrombosis?
cards.a: Total splenectomy, which decompresses the short gastric venous network.

cards.q: Most common malignancy of the small bowel?
cards.a: Neuroendocrine tumor, followed closely by adenocarcinoma.

cards.q: Most common anatomical location for a primary small bowel adenocarcinoma to develop?
cards.a: The duodenum.

cards.q: Most common anatomical location for a primary small bowel neuroendocrine tumor to develop?
cards.a: The terminal ileum.

cards.q: Primary clinical presentation of carcinoid syndrome?
cards.a: Episodic skin flushing, wheezing, diarrhea, and right-sided cardiac valvular lesions.

cards.q: Metabolic substance measured in a 24-hour urine collection to screen for carcinoid syndrome?
cards.a: 5-Hydroxyindoleacetic acid.

cards.q: Rationale for why primary intestinal neuroendocrine tumors do not cause carcinoid syndrome until they metastasize to the liver?
cards.a: Hepatic first-pass metabolism inactivates bioactive substances like serotonin before they can reach the systemic circulation.

cards.q: Pharmacological agent administered perioperatively to prevent a life-threatening carcinoid crisis during surgical manipulation of a neuroendocrine tumor?
cards.a: Intravenous octreotide, a long-acting somatostatin analog.

cards.q: Definitive surgical management for a localized, resectable gastrointestinal stromal tumor?
cards.a: Wedge resection of the organ with microscopically negative margins, without the routine need for formal lymphadenectomy.

cards.q: Standard target gene mutation found in over 85% of gastrointestinal stromal tumors that guides targeted tyrosine kinase inhibitor therapy?
cards.a: Activating mutations in the KIT proto-oncogene.

cards.q: First-line adjuvant systemic therapy administered to patients with high-risk or advanced gastrointestinal stromal tumors?
cards.a: Imatinib mesylate.

cards.q: Most common histological type of lung cancer found in both smokers and non-smokers?
cards.a: Adenocarcinoma.

cards.q: Distinctive peripheral location and clinical hallmark of a pulmonary adenocarcinoma?
cards.a: It typically arises in the lung periphery and may develop at the site of prior parenchymal scars or inflammation.

cards.q: Histological type of lung cancer most strongly associated with a central location and a history of heavy smoking?
cards.a: Squamous cell carcinoma.

cards.q: Paraneoplastic syndrome characteristically driven by ectopic hormone production from a pulmonary squamous cell carcinoma?
cards.a: Hypercalcemia due to the systemic secretion of parathyroid hormone-related peptide.

cards.q: Histological type of lung cancer characteristically associated with central cavitary lesions and hypercalcemia?
cards.a: Squamous cell carcinoma.

cards.q: Paraneoplastic syndrome characteristically driven by ectopic hormone production from a small cell lung carcinoma?
cards.a: Syndrome of inappropriate antidiuretic hormone secretion causing severe hyponatremia, or ectopic adrenocorticotropic hormone causing Cushing syndrome.

cards.q: Neuromuscular paraneoplastic syndrome associated with small cell lung cancer characterized by proximal muscle weakness that improves with repeat use?
cards.a: Lambert-Eaton myasthenic syndrome, driven by autoantibodies against presynaptic voltage-gated calcium channels.

cards.q: Define the clinical condition known as a Pancoast tumor?
cards.a: A malignant tumor, typically non-small cell lung cancer, located at the superior sulcus of the lung apex.

cards.q: Neurological signs characterizing Horner syndrome caused by local Pancoast tumor expansion?
cards.a: Ipsilateral miosis, partial ptosis, and anhidrosis due to invasion of the sympathetic chain and stellate ganglion.

cards.q: Most common benign soft tissue tumor found in adults?
cards.a: Lipoma.

cards.q: Clinical presentation distinguishing a benign lipoma from a malignant liposarcoma?
cards.a: A lipoma is typically soft, mobile, and superficial, whereas a liposarcoma is deep, fixed, rapidly growing, and larger than 5 centimeters.

cards.q: Definitive management strategy for a patient presenting with a suspicious, deep soft tissue mass larger than 5 centimeters?
cards.a: Core needle biopsy to rule out a soft tissue sarcoma prior to any attempt at surgical excision.

cards.q: Standard curative surgical resection margin required for a biopsy-confirmed localized extremity soft tissue sarcoma?
cards.a: Wide local excision achieving negative margins of at least 1 to 2 centimeters including the surrounding investing fascia.

cards.q: Most common anatomical site for the development of a gastrointestinal stromal tumor?
cards.a: The stomach, accounting for roughly 60% of cases.

cards.q: Definitive diagnostic criteria for a classic abdominal wall desmoid tumor?
cards.a: A benign, locally aggressive, non-metastasizing fibroblastic proliferation typically associated with prior laparotomy scars or Gardner syndrome.

cards.q: First-line maintenance fluid strategy for a patient in the immediate 24-hour postoperative window following minor abdominal surgery?
cards.a: 5% Dextrose in 0.45% normal saline with 20 milliequivalents of potassium chloride per liter.

cards.q: Rationale for adding dextrose to a maintenance fluid regimen for a fasting postoperative patient?
cards.a: Provides enough baseline calories to prevent starvation ketosis and minimize muscle protein catabolism.

cards.q: Minimum physiological systemic MAP required to maintain adequate cerebral perfusion pressure in a healthy adult?
cards.a: A mean arterial pressure of at least 60 to 65 millimeters of mercury.

cards.q: Clinical significance of a high systemic serum lactate level measured during trauma resuscitation?
cards.a: Serves as a sensitive surrogate marker for occult systemic tissue hypoperfusion and anaerobic metabolism.

cards.q: Define the clinical term "cullen's sign" seen on physical examination?
cards.a: Ecchymosis localized around the periumbilical region, indicating retroperitoneal hemorrhage or severe acute hemorrhagic pancreatitis.

cards.q: Define the clinical term "grey turner's sign" seen on physical examination?
cards.a: Ecchymosis localized along the abdominal flanks, indicating retroperitoneal blood tracking from trauma or necrotizing pancreatitis.

cards.q: Initial diagnostic test of choice for a stable patient presenting with a suspected retroperitoneal soft tissue mass?
cards.a: Contrast-enhanced computed tomography scan of the abdomen and pelvis.

cards.q: Most common underlying cause of an arterioenteric fistula developing after major vascular surgery?
cards.a: Direct erosion of a synthetic aortic graft into the third or fourth portion of the duodenum.

cards.q: Classic clinical warning sign of an impending catastrophic rupture of an aortoenteric fistula?
cards.a: A self-limiting "herald bleed" presenting as transient hematemesis or hematochezia that spontaneously stops before massive exsanguination.

cards.q: Definitive management strategy for a confirmed, actively bleeding aortoenteric fistula?
cards.a: Emergent surgical intervention to explant the infected prosthetic graft, repair the duodenal defect, and construct an extra-anatomical vascular bypass.

cards.q: Definitive management paradigm for a stable patient with an infected synthetic vascular graft?
cards.a: Complete surgical excision of the infected prosthetic material combined with targeted systemic antibiotic therapy and revascularization through a clean field.

cards.q: Mechanism of action of the immunosuppressive drug cyclosporine used to prevent organ transplant rejection?
cards.a: Calcineurin inhibitor that binds to cyclophilin to block T-cell transcription of interleukin-2.

cards.q: Mechanism of action of the immunosuppressive drug tacrolimus used in transplant medicine?
cards.a: Calcineurin inhibitor that binds to FK-binding protein 12 to inhibit T-lymphocyte activation and interleukin-2 production.

cards.q: Major dose-limiting systemic toxicity characteristically shared by both cyclosporine and tacrolimus?
cards.a: Nephrotoxicity driven by profound afferent arteriolar vasoconstriction.

cards.q: Distinctive cosmetic adverse effect that clinically separates cyclosporine from tacrolimus toxicity?
cards.a: Cyclosporine characteristically causes gingival hyperplasia and hypertrichosis, which are not typically seen with tacrolimus.

cards.q: Mechanism of action of the immunosuppressive drug mycophenolate mofetil?
cards.a: Reversibly inhibits inosine monophosphate dehydrogenase to block de novo purine synthesis in proliferating T and B lymphocytes.

cards.q: Most common dose-limiting systemic adverse effect associated with mycophenolate mofetil therapy?
cards.a: Gastrointestinal toxicity, characteristically presenting as severe diarrhea, cramping, and leukopenia.

cards.q: Mechanism of action of the immunosuppressive drug sirolimus, also known as rapamycin?
cards.a: Inhibits the mammalian target of rapamycin to block downstream interleukin-2 receptor signaling and cell cycle progression.

cards.q: Distinctive surgical complication characteristically associated with perioperative sirolimus administration?
cards.a: Profound impairment of wound healing and a significantly increased incidence of incisional hernias or fascial dehiscence.

cards.q: Most common long-term cutaneous malignancy that develops in solid organ transplant recipients on chronic immunosuppression?
cards.a: Squamous cell carcinoma of the skin.

cards.q: Primary physiological driver behind the extreme risk of cutaneous squamous cell carcinoma in transplant patients?
cards.a: Chronic therapeutic suppression of T-cell-mediated immune surveillance against oncogenic ultraviolet radiation damage.

cards.q: Most common type of hernia that develops within the triangle of Grynfellt?
cards.a: Superior lumbar hernia.

cards.q: Most common type of hernia that develops within the triangle of Petit?
cards.a: Inferior lumbar hernia.

cards.q: Define the structural components that form a Sciatic hernia?
cards.a: Herniation of intra-abdominal contents through the greater or lesser sciatic foramen into the gluteal region.

cards.q: Define the structural components that form an Obturator hernia?
cards.a: Herniation of pelvic contents through the obturator canal, classically seen in elderly, emaciated females.

cards.q: Classic physical exam finding diagnostic of an obturator hernia compression?
cards.a: The Howship-Romberg sign, characterized by pain radiating down the medial aspect of the thigh to the knee during hip extension, adduction, or internal rotation.

cards.q: Primary surgical approach recommended for the repair of a diagnosed obturator hernia?
cards.a: Lower midline laparotomy or preperitoneal approach to safely reduce the hernia and inspect for bowel viability.

cards.q: Most common benign vascular liver tumor that should never be biopsied due to an extreme risk of catastrophic hemorrhage?
cards.a: Hepatic hemangioma.

cards.q: Diagnostic imaging hallmark of a hepatic hemangioma on a contrast-enhanced triple-phase CT scan?
cards.a: Peripheral, nodular centripetal enhancement tracking from the outside edge toward the center over time.

cards.q: Benign liver lesion characteristically associated with long-term oral contraceptive pill use in young women?
cards.a: Hepatic adenoma.

cards.q: Primary life-threatening complication that dictates surgical resection of a hepatic adenoma larger than 5 centimeters?
cards.a: High risk of spontaneous intraperitoneal rupture causing massive hemorrhagic shock, or a small risk of malignant transformation.

cards.q: Management paradigm for a hepatic adenoma smaller than 5 centimeters discovered in a patient taking oral contraceptives?
cards.a: Discontinue the oral contraceptive pills immediately and perform serial surveillance imaging.

cards.q: Diagnostic imaging hallmark that definitively differentiates focal nodular hyperplasia from a hepatic adenoma?
cards.a: Presence of a well-circumscribed central stellate scar that hyper-enhances on delayed contrast phases.

cards.q: Management paradigm for a biopsy-confirmed, asymptomatic focal nodular hyperplasia of the liver?
cards.a: Conservative observation and reassurance, as it has zero malignant potential and a negligible risk of rupture.

cards.q: Most common primary malignant tumor originating within the liver parenchyma?
cards.a: Hepatocellular carcinoma.

cards.q: Single most important serum tumor marker used to screen for and monitor recurrence of hepatocellular carcinoma?
cards.a: Alpha-fetoprotein.

cards.q: Primary physiological driver of a sudden bradycardia or asystole immediately upon creating a laparoscopic pneumoperitoneum?
cards.a: A vagal response triggered by rapid stretch of the peritoneum during carbon dioxide insufflation.

cards.q: Immediate initial step to manage a severe, insufflation-induced vagal bradycardia during laparoscopy?
cards.a: Release the pneumoperitoneum immediately by opening the trocar valves and stop insufflation.

cards.q: Target maximum intra-abdominal pressure range utilized during standard laparoscopic surgery?
cards.a: Between 12 and 15 millimeters of mercury.

cards.q: Primary systemic physiological change caused by prolonged carbon dioxide pneumoperitoneum pressures exceeding 15 mmHg?
cards.a: Decreased venous return, reduced cardiac output, and systemic hypercapnia from transperitoneal carbon dioxide absorption.

cards.q: Clinical presentation of an intraoperative gas embolism during laparoscopic surgery?
cards.a: Sudden, profound hypotension, a rapid drop in end-tidal carbon dioxide, and a "mill-wheel" murmur over the precordium.

cards.q: Immediate bedside positioning for a patient with a confirmed laparoscopic carbon dioxide gas embolism?
cards.a: Trendelenburg and left lateral decubitus position to trap the gas bubble in the right ventricular apex.

cards.q: Pathophysiology of capacitive coupling when using monopolar electrosurgery during laparoscopy?
cards.a: Stray electrical current is transferred from an active electrode through intact insulation into adjacent organs, risking unrecognized thermal bowel injury.

cards.q: Fundamental technical difference between monopolar and bipolar electrosurgery circuits?
cards.a: Monopolar electrosurgery requires a patient return electrode grounding pad, whereas bipolar electrosurgery passes the current entirely between the two tines of the instrument tip.

cards.q: Mechanism of action of ultrasonic surgical energy devices like the Harmonic scalpel?
cards.a: Uses high-frequency mechanical vibrations to simultaneously cut and coagulate tissue proteins at lower temperatures than electrosurgery.

cards.q: Nerve injury caused by improper padding of the lateral knee against the stirrups in the lithotomy position?
cards.a: Common peroneal nerve injury, presenting postoperatively as foot drop and loss of sensation on the dorsum of the foot.

cards.q: Nerve injury caused by hyper-abducting a patient’s arm past 90 degrees on an arm board during prolonged surgery?
cards.a: Brachial plexus injury, presenting as diffuse upper extremity weakness or paresthesias.

cards.q: Nerve injury caused by direct compression of the posterior elbow against a hard operating table surface?
cards.a: Ulnar nerve injury, presenting as a claw-hand deformity and sensory loss in the fifth digit.

cards.q: Name the three distinct phases of the standard World Health Organization Surgical Safety Checklist?
cards.a: Sign In before induction of anesthesia, Time Out before skin incision, and Sign Out before the patient leaves the operating room.

cards.q: Define the essential, non-negotiable step performed by the entire surgical team during the preoperative "Time Out"?
cards.a: Verbal confirmation of the correct patient identity, the correct surgical site, and the specific procedure to be performed.

cards.q: Define a surgical "never event" as categorized by healthcare quality organizations?
cards.a: Serious, preventable adverse events that should never occur if proper safety protocols are followed, such as wrong-site surgery or retained foreign bodies.

cards.q: Standard protocol mandated when a surgical sponge count is reported as incorrect prior to fascial closure?
cards.a: Recount all sponges, thoroughly inspect the operative field visually and manually, and obtain an emergent intraoperative plain X-ray if the sponge remains missing.

cards.q: Mechanism of action of topical fibrin sealants used intraoperatively for localized hemostasis?
cards.a: Combines concentrated fibrinogen and thrombin to directly replicate the final stage of the coagulation cascade, creating a localized fibrin clot.

cards.q: Primary contraindication to using topical microfibrillar collagen hemostatic agents in a patient undergoing contaminated surgery?
cards.a: They can serve as a physical nidus for bacterial adherence, significantly increasing the risk of a deep surgical site infection.

cards.q: Name the specific parameter on a Thromboelastography assay that guides the administration of fresh frozen plasma?
cards.a: The R-time, which measures the time until initial clot formation and reflects clotting factor availability.

cards.q: Name the specific parameter on a Thromboelastography assay that guides the administration of platelets or cryoprecipitate?
cards.a: The Maximum Amplitude, which measures ultimate clot strength and reflects platelet function and fibrin mesh binding.

cards.q: Trigger parameter that defines the activation of a massive transfusion protocol in a severely injured trauma patient?
cards.a: Anticipated need for greater than 10 units of packed red blood cells within 24 hours, or more than 4 units within 1 hour.

cards.q: Primary physiological rationale for utilizing negative pressure wound therapy, also known as a wound VAC?
cards.a: Removes localized edema fluid, decreases bacterial bioburden, increases local microvascular blood flow, and mechanically stimulates granulation tissue formation.

cards.q: Absolute contraindication to the application of negative pressure wound therapy on a chronic wound?
cards.a: Presence of untreated osteomyelitis, exposed vital organs/vessels, necrotic eschar, or underlying malignant tissue within the wound bed.

cards.q: Primary therapeutic indication for hyperbaric oxygen therapy in general wound management?
cards.a: Chronic, non-healing diabetic foot ulcers with documented tissue ischemia that have failed standard wound care interventions.

cards.q: Clinical criteria that allow a surgeon to perform an emergent operation on a minor patient without parental consent?
cards.a: Presence of an imminent threat to life or limb where delaying care to locate a legal surrogate would cause certain harm.

cards.q: Legal doctrine that guides emergency surgical interventions when a patient is unconscious and no surrogate is available?
cards.a: Implied consent, which presumes a reasonable person would consent to life-saving treatment under critical circumstances.

cards.q: Definition of a split-thickness skin graft?
cards.a: A graft containing the entire epidermis and only a variable portion of the underlying dermis.

cards.q: Definition of a full-thickness skin graft?
cards.a: A graft containing the entire epidermis and the complete thickness of the dermis layer.

cards.q: Primary mechanism by which a skin graft survives during the first 48 hours before new blood vessels form?
cards.a: Plasma imbibition, where the graft passively absorbs nutrients from the underlying capillary bed.

cards.q: Define the secondary phase of skin graft survival that occurs between 48 hours and 5 days post-grafting?
cards.a: Inosculation, where donor and recipient capillaries align and physically connect to establish primitive blood flow.

cards.q: Most common cause of primary skin graft failure?
cards.a: Hematoma or seroma accumulation beneath the graft, which physically separates it from the nutrient-rich wound bed.

cards.q: Define a random pattern local tissue flap used in reconstructive surgery?
cards.a: A tissue flap that lacks a named, specific axial blood vessel and relies entirely on the random subdermal vascular plexus for perfusion.

cards.q: Define an axial pattern tissue flap used in reconstructive surgery?
cards.a: A tissue flap that is supplied by a specific, named axial arterial and venous network, allowing for a larger length-to-width configuration.

cards.q: Most sensitive clinical parameter used to monitor the postoperative viability of a newly transferred free tissue flap?
cards.a: Serial clinical checks evaluating capillary refill time, tissue temperature, color, and handheld Doppler signals.

cards.q: Clinical presentation of venous congestion in a post-operative free tissue flap?
cards.a: The flap rapidly develops a dark blue or purple discoloration, becomes swollen, and exhibits brisk, dark capillary refill.

cards.q: Immediate surgical management step required when acute arterial insufficiency is suspected in a free tissue flap?
cards.a: Urgent return to the operating room for microvascular exploration and revision of the arterial anastomosis.

cards.q: Pathophysiology of a hypertrophic scar compared to a keloid?
cards.a: A hypertrophic scar contains parallel collagen bundles confined strictly within the boundaries of the original wound, typically regressing over time.

cards.q: Pathophysiology of a keloid compared to a hypertrophic scar?
cards.a: A keloid contains disorganized, thick Type I and III collagen bundles that characteristically expand well beyond the boundaries of the original wound and rarely regress.

cards.q: First-line medical therapy used to reduce the size and symptoms of a symptomatic keloid?
cards.a: Intralesional corticosteroid injections, such as triamcinolone acetonide.

cards.q: Most common long-term malignancy arising within a chronic, non-healing ulcer or burn scar, known as a Marjolin's ulcer?
cards.a: Squamous cell carcinoma.

cards.q: Most predictive clinical validation score used to estimate a patient's perioperative 30-day mortality risk across all surgical specialties?
cards.a: The American Society of Anesthesiologists physical status classification system.

cards.q: Define the clinical status of a patient classified as ASA Physical Status III?
cards.a: A patient with severe systemic disease that limits functional activity but is not constantly life-threatening.

cards.q: Minimum functional capacity threshold, measured in metabolic equivalents, below which a patient requires further cardiac evaluation before major non-cardiac surgery?
cards.a: Four metabolic equivalents, which is the energy required to climb two flights of stairs or walk up a hill without limiting symptoms.

cards.q: Most crucial historical risk factor included in the Revised Cardiac Risk Index for predicting postoperative major adverse cardiac events?
cards.a: A history of ischemic heart disease, congestive heart failure, cerebrovascular disease, or preoperative insulin-dependent diabetes mellitus.

cards.q: Recommended management for a patient taking a maintenance aspirin regimen for a drug-eluting coronary stent placed 3 months ago who is undergoing moderate-risk non-cardiac surgery?
cards.a: Continue the aspirin throughout the perioperative period to prevent acute stent thrombosis, weighing the thrombotic risk against bleeding.

cards.q: Standard withholding window required for oral P2Y12 inhibitors like clopidogrel prior to elective major surgery?
cards.a: Discontinue the medication 5 days before the scheduled operative procedure.

cards.q: Recommended withholding window required for direct oral anticoagulants like rivaroxaban or apixaban before a high-bleeding-risk major surgery?
cards.a: Discontinue the medication 48 hours prior to the procedure in patients with normal renal function.

cards.q: Standard preoperative management strategy for a patient on long-term warfarin therapy with a mechanical mitral valve undergoing major abdominal surgery?
cards.a: Discontinue warfarin 5 days preoperatively and initiate bridging therapy with therapeutic low-molecular-weight heparin once the INR drops below 2.

cards.q: Timing guideline for holding therapeutic subcutaneous low-molecular-weight heparin prior to a surgical incision or neuraxial anesthesia?
cards.a: Hold the medication for at least 24 hours before the procedure to minimize the risk of spinal hematoma or major hemorrhage.

cards.q: Best initial diagnostic test to evaluate an asymptomatic patient with a loud systolic murmur detected during a routine preoperative physical examination?
cards.a: Transthoracic echocardiography to rule out severe aortic stenosis, which carries an extreme risk of perioperative decompensation.

cards.q: Standard target hemoglobin A1c level recommended prior to scheduling elective major surgical interventions to reduce surgical site infections?
cards.a: An HbA1c of less than 7% to 8% is generally targeted for optimal long-term wound healing and immune function.

cards.q: Preoperative management strategy for a patient with a known history of severe adrenal suppression on chronic daily prednisone therapy?
cards.a: Administration of perioperative "stress-dose" IV hydrocortisone on the morning of surgery, followed by a tapering schedule.

cards.q: Minimum duration of smoking cessation recommended preoperatively to significantly reduce the incidence of postoperative pulmonary complications?
cards.a: At least 4 to 8 weeks of complete cessation to normalize ciliary function and reduce airway hyperreactivity.

cards.q: Most common clinical indicator of severe underlying pulmonary disease that dictates obtaining a preoperative arterial blood gas?
cards.a: Severe chronic obstructive pulmonary disease or interstitial lung disease with chronic baseline hypoxia or hypercapnia.

cards.q: Recommended management for a patient's routine morning angiotensin-converting enzyme inhibitor dose on the day of major general surgery?
cards.a:
Hold the medication on the morning of surgery to prevent severe, refractory intraoperative hypotension following the induction of anesthesia.
Module 18: Anesthetic Agents, Airway Management, & Intraoperative Mechanics

cards.q: Inhaled anesthetic agent characteristically associated with a risk of diffusion hypoxia upon discontinuation if supplemental oxygen is not provided?
cards.a: Nitrous oxide, due to its low blood-gas partition coefficient causing rapid expansion into the alveoli.

cards.q: Major systemic toxicity uniquely associated with prolonged or high-dose exposure to nitrous oxide?
cards.a: Megaloblastic anemia and peripheral neuropathy due to the irreversible oxidation and inactivation of vitamin B12.

cards.q: Inhaled volatile anesthetic agent most likely to trigger a severe, immune-mediated hepatic necrosis known as "halothane hepatitis"?
cards.a: Halothane, driven by the formation of trifluoroacetylated liver protein neoantigens.

cards.q: Intravenous induction agent of choice for a patient in severe hemorrhagic shock due to its hemodynamic neutrality?
cards.a: Etomidate, which preserves systemic vascular resistance and cardiac output.

cards.q: Major endocrine adverse effect associated with even a single diagnostic or induction dose of etomidate?
cards.a: Transient adrenal insufficiency caused by the direct inhibition of the enzyme 11-beta-hydroxylase.

cards.q: Intravenous induction agent that acts as a potent bronchodilator, making it the preferred choice for patients with acute status asthmaticus?
cards.a: Ketamine, which stimulates sympathetic catecholamine release.

cards.q: Distinctive psychiatric adverse effect characteristically observed during emergence from ketamine anesthesia?
cards.a: Emergence delirium, characterized by vivid hallucinations, confusion, and vivid dreams, which can be mitigated with perioperative benzodiazepines.

cards.q: Intravenous induction agent that provides rapid awakening and antiemetic properties, but causes profound dose-dependent vasodilation and hypotension?
cards.a: Propofol.

cards.q: Depolarizing neuromuscular blocking agent characteristically associated with transient muscle fasciculations and a transient rise in serum potassium?
cards.a: Succinylcholine.

cards.q: Absolute clinical contraindication to the administration of succinylcholine due to the risk of catastrophic hyperkalemic cardiac arrest?
cards.a: Patients with major burn injuries, massive crush trauma, prolonged immobilization, or upper motor neuron lesions older than 24 to 48 hours.

cards.q: Preferred non-depolarizing neuromuscular blocking agent for a patient with end-stage renal disease and severe hepatic failure?
cards.a: Cisatracurium, because it undergoes spontaneous Hoffman elimination independent of renal or hepatic clearance mechanisms.

cards.q: Pharmacological agent utilized to rapidly reverse deep neuromuscular blockade induced by rocuronium or vecuronium via direct chelation encapsulation?
cards.a: Sugammadex.

cards.q: First-line medical therapy indicated for the treatment of a confirmed intraoperative malignant hyperthermia crisis?
cards.a: Intravenous dantrolene, which blocks calcium release from the ryanodine receptor channels of the sarcoplasmic reticulum.

cards.q: Most sensitive and earliest indicator of an evolving malignant hyperthermia crisis during volatile gas anesthesia?
cards.a: A sudden, rapid, and unexplained rise in end-tidal carbon dioxide on the monitor.

cards.q: Maximum safe dose of plain 1% lidocaine without epinephrine administered for localized infiltration anesthesia?
cards.a:
4 to 5 milligrams per kilogram of body weight.
Module 19: Post-Anesthesia Care, Postoperative Complications, & Shock States

cards.q: Most common physiological cause of early postoperative hypoxemia in the Post-Anesthesia Care Unit?
cards.a: Alveolar hypoventilation secondary to residual neuromuscular blockade or opioid-induced respiratory depression.

cards.q: Classic clinical presentation of a patient experiencing a severe hemolytic transfusion reaction intraoperatively under general anesthesia?
cards.a: Unexplained fever, sudden tachycardia, acute hypotension, hemoglobinuria, and diffuse microvascular bleeding or oozing from the surgical field.

cards.q: Most appropriate initial management strategy for a postoperative patient presenting with suspected acute urinary retention?
cards.a: Perform a bedside bladder ultrasound scan to quantify urine volume, followed by immediate straight or indwelling catheterization if volume exceeds 350 to 400 mL.

cards.q: Standard diagnostic investigation utilized to confirm an suspected acute pulmonary embolism in a stable postoperative patient?
cards.a: Computed tomography pulmonary angiography.

cards.q: Initial management strategy for a stable patient who develops atrial fibrillation with a rapid ventricular response on postoperative day 2 following major thoracic surgery?
cards.a: Intravenous rate control utilizing beta-blockers or nondihydropyridine calcium channel blockers like diltiazem.

cards.q: Primary clinical condition that dictates immediate emergent synchronized electrical cardioversion in a postoperative patient with new-onset tachydysrhythmia?
cards.a: Hemodynamic instability, characterized by hypotension, altered mental status, or signs of acute myocardial ischemia.

cards.q: Pathophysiology of neurogenic shock secondary to high spinal cord injury?
cards.a: Loss of sympathetic vasomotor tone leading to profound peripheral vasodilation and loss of cardiac accelerator nerve input, causing a classic presentation of bradycardia and hypotension.

cards.q: Hemodynamic profile that defines distributive shock compared to cardiogenic shock?
cards.a: Markedly decreased systemic vascular resistance accompanied by a normal or elevated cardiac output and decreased pulmonary capillary wedge pressure.

cards.q: Primary physiological objective of administering continuous positive airway pressure to a patient with postoperative atelectasis?
cards.a: Recruits collapsed alveoli, increases functional residual capacity, and decreases the work of breathing.

cards.q: Define the clinical term "postoperative ileus" based on normal gastrointestinal recovery timelines?
cards.a:
Delayed return of coordinated gastrointestinal motility beyond 3 to 5 days postoperatively, characterized by obstipation, abdominal distention, and nausea.
Module 20: Intensive Care Medicine, Sepsis, & Mechanical Ventilation

cards.q: Primary screening tool utilized at the bedside to rapidly identify patients outside the ICU at high risk for poor outcomes from suspected sepsis?
cards.a: The quick Sequential Organ Failure Assessment score, utilizing respiratory rate, altered mentation, and systolic blood pressure.

cards.q: Three criteria evaluated in the quick Sequential Organ Failure Assessment score?
cards.a: Respiratory rate of 22 breaths per minute or greater, altered mentation, and a systolic blood pressure of 100 millimeters of mercury or less.

cards.q: Definitive clinical definition of septic shock according to the Sepsis-3 guidelines?
cards.a: Sepsis requiring vasopressors to maintain a mean arterial pressure of 65 mmHg or greater and a serum lactate level greater than 2 mmol/L despite adequate fluid resuscitation.

cards.q: First-line vasopressor of choice recommended for the management of fluid-refractory septic shock?
cards.a: Norepinephrine, due to its potent alpha-1 adrenergic vasoconstriction combined with modest beta-1 inotropic activity.

cards.q: Diagnostic criteria that define Acute Respiratory Distress Syndrome?
cards.a: Acute onset within 1 week of a known insult, bilateral opacities on chest imaging not fully explained by fluid overload, and a PaO2/FiO2 ratio less than or equal to 300 mmHg on a PEEP of 5 cmH2O or greater.

cards.q: Primary mechanical ventilation strategy proven to decrease mortality in patients with severe Acute Respiratory Distress Syndrome?
cards.a: Low-tidal-volume ventilation targeted at 6 milliliters per kilogram of predicted body weight to minimize ventilator-induced lung injury.

cards.q: Target maximum plateau pressure range mandated during mechanical ventilation for Acute Respiratory Distress Syndrome?
cards.a: Maintain plateau pressures less than or equal to 30 centimeters of water.

cards.q: Physiological rationale behind utilizing prone positioning in patients with severe, refractory Acute Respiratory Distress Syndrome?
cards.a: Optimizes ventilation-perfusion matching by recruiting dependent dorsal alveoli and reducing alveolar shunt.

cards.q: Most effective initial intervention to correct acute respiratory acidosis in a mechanically ventilated patient with a low arterial pH and a high PaCO2?
cards.a: Increase the minute ventilation by either increasing the respiratory rate or increasing the tidal volume on the ventilator settings.

cards.q: Primary adverse effect associated with excessive positive end-expiratory pressure titration on the cardiovascular system?
Most important objective clinical factor predicting significant post-operative cardiac complications?
cards.a: Jugular venous distention (JVD) indicative of decompensated heart failure.

cards.q: Best clinical predictor of high-risk cardiac status after JVD?
cards.a: Recent myocardial infarction within the preceding 3 to 6 months.

cards.q: Goldman Cardiac Risk Index score threshold indicating unacceptably high risk for non-cardiac surgery?
cards.a: Greater than 26 points.

cards.q: Gold standard non-invasive test for assessing cardiac risk in a patient unable to exercise?
cards.a: Dobutamine stress echocardiography or dipyridamole-thallium scan.

cards.q: Length of time an elective surgical procedure should be delayed following an uncomplicated bare-metal stent deployment?
cards.a: At least 30 days.

cards.q: Length of time an elective surgical procedure should be delayed following a drug-eluting stent deployment?
cards.a: At least 6 months, preferably 12 months.

cards.q: Best single laboratory test to screen for overall nutritional status and long-term surgical risk?
cards.a: Serum albumin.

cards.q: Serum albumin level that defines severe nutritional risk and predicts poor wound healing?
cards.a: Less than 3.0 g/dL.

cards.q: Serum prealbumin half-life compared to albumin?
cards.a: 2 days (prealbumin) vs. 20 days (albumin), making prealbumin superior for acute nutritional monitoring.

cards.q: The single most effective lifestyle intervention to decrease post-operative pulmonary complications?
cards.a: Smoking cessation for at least 8 weeks prior to surgery.

cards.q: Primary non-invasive test used to quantify hepatic functional reserve before major liver resection?
cards.a: Child-Pugh Classification score or MELD score.

cards.q: Five clinical and laboratory parameters utilized in the Child-Pugh classification system?
cards.a: Total bilirubin, serum albumin, INR, ascites severity, and hepatic encephalopathy grade.

cards.q: Child-Pugh class contraindicated for elective major hepatic resections due to prohibitive mortality?
cards.a: Child-Pugh Class C.

cards.q: Most common cause of immediate intraoperative or early postoperative adrenal crisis in a chronic steroid user?
cards.a: HPA axis suppression resulting in an inability to mount a physiologic stress response.

cards.q: Minimum daily dose and duration of prednisone requiring perioperative stress-dose steroid coverage?
cards.a: Greater than or equal to 5 mg/day for more than 3 weeks within the past year.

cards.q: Standard empiric perioperative stress-dose steroid regimen for high-stress major surgeries?
cards.a: Hydrocortisone 100 mg IV preoperatively, followed by 50 mg IV every 8 hours for 24 hours.

cards.q: Target perioperative serum glucose range recommended for optimal wound healing and reduced infection rates?
cards.a: 140 to 180 mg/dL.

cards.q: Management of metformin the night before or morning of a major surgical procedure?
cards.a: Hold the medication to minimize the risk of intraoperative metformin-associated lactic acidosis.

cards.q: Management of long-acting insulin (e.g., glargine) the night before major surgery?
cards.a: Administer 60% to 80% of the normal dose.

cards.q: Management of short-acting sliding-scale insulin on the morning of surgery while NPO?
cards.a: Hold the short-acting insulin and monitor fingerstick glucose every 4 to 6 hours.

cards.q: Routine pre-operative requirement for a healthy, asymptomatic 22-year-old female undergoing an elective laparoscopic appendectomy?
cards.a: Serum or urine beta-hCG pregnancy test.

cards.q: Reversal agent of choice for a patient on chronic Warfarin therapy requiring immediate emergency surgery?
cards.a: Four-factor prothrombin complex concentrate (PCC) and intravenous Vitamin K.

cards.q: Target INR value for safe execution of most elective major surgical procedures?
cards.a: Less than or equal to 1.5.

cards.q: Timing for discontinuation of aspirin prior to elective surgical procedures carrying high bleeding risks?
cards.a: 7 to 10 days before surgery.

cards.q: Timing for discontinuation of clopidogrel prior to elective major surgery?
cards.a: 5 days before surgery.

cards.q: Timing for discontinuation of therapeutic low-molecular-weight heparin (LMWH) prior to surgery?
cards.a: 24 hours before the procedure.

cards.q: Ideal timing for the administration of a pre-operative prophylactic antibiotic to prevent surgical site infection?
cards.a: Within 60 minutes prior to the surgical incision.

cards.q: Redosing parameter for prophylactic intraoperative antibiotics during a prolonged surgical procedure?
cards.a: Every two half-lives of the drug or after a blood loss greater than 1500 mL.

cards.q: Standard first-line prophylactic antibiotic choice for clean, non-GI/non-GU general surgical procedures?
cards.a: First-generation cephalosporin such as Cefazolin.

cards.q: Preferred prophylactic antibiotic choice for elective colorectal procedures due to anaerobe coverage?
cards.a: Second-generation cephalosporin with anaerobic coverage (Cefoxitin/Cefotetan) or Cefazolin plus Metronidazole.

cards.q: Universal ASA physical status classification of a patient with a severe systemic disease that is a constant threat to life?
cards.a:
ASA Class IV.
PART 2: Anesthesia Basics & Intraoperative Management

cards.q: Principal physiologic feature defining General Anesthesia compared to deep sedation?
cards.a: Loss of protective airway reflexes and requirement for ventilatory assistance.

cards.q: Primary mechanism of action of local anesthetics like lidocaine?
cards.a: Reversible blockade of voltage-gated sodium channels along the neuronal axon.

cards.q: Sequence of nerve fiber block by local anesthetics?
cards.a: Pain (C and A-delta fibers), temperature, touch, and lastly motor function.

cards.q: Maximum safe dose of plain local lidocaine formulation?
cards.a: 4 mg/kg.

cards.q: Maximum safe dose of lidocaine formulated with epinephrine?
cards.a: 7 mg/kg.

cards.q: Primary clinical purpose of adding epinephrine to a local anesthetic solution?
cards.a: Local vasoconstriction to prolong duration of action and decrease systemic absorption/toxicity.

cards.q: Classic early systemic symptom of local anesthetic systemic toxicity (LAST)?
cards.a: Perioral numbness, metallic taste, and tinnitus.

cards.q: First-line intravenous antidote for severe local anesthetic systemic toxicity presenting with cardiac arrest?
cards.a: 20% Intravenous Lipid Emulsion therapy.

cards.q: Primary anatomical location where spinal anesthesia (intrathecal injection) is performed?
cards.a: Subarachnoid space below the level of the L2 nerve root.

cards.q: Most common physiological side effect seen immediately after induction of spinal or epidural anesthesia?
cards.a: Hypotension due to sympathetic blockade causing profound venodilatation.

cards.q: Primary cause of a postural post-dural puncture headache (PDPH) following neuroaxial anesthesia?
cards.a: Persistent leakage of cerebrospinal fluid through the dural puncture site.

cards.q: Definitive procedural treatment for a severe, refractory post-dural puncture headache?
cards.a: Epidural blood patch.

cards.q: Primary absolute contraindication to the placement of a spinal or epidural catheter?
cards.a: Patient refusal, localized infection at the puncture site, or severe uncorrected coagulopathy.

cards.q: Principal chemical compound used to induce rapid sequence intubation that is an ultra-short-acting depolarizing neuromuscular blocker?
cards.a: Succinylcholine.

cards.q: Severe electrolyte abnormality that serves as an absolute contraindication to succinylcholine administration?
cards.a: Hyperkalemia.

cards.q: Why is succinylcholine contraindicated in patients with severe burn injuries or crush trauma after 24 to 48 hours?
cards.a: Upregulation of extrajunctional acetylcholine receptors leads to catastrophic, life-threatening efflux of potassium.

cards.q: Standard pharmacological reversal agent combination for non-depolarizing neuromuscular blockers like rocuronium?
cards.a: Neostigmine (acetylcholinesterase inhibitor) combined with Glycopyrrolate or Atropine (anticholinergic).

cards.q: Novel reversal agent that encapsulates and inactivates rocuronium or vecuronium directly?
cards.a: Sugammadex.

cards.q: Inhaled anesthetic agent uniquely associated with diffusion hypoxia and expansion of closed gas-filled body spaces?
cards.a: Nitrous oxide.

cards.q: Pathophysiology of Malignant Hyperthermia?
cards.a: Uncontrolled calcium release from the sarcoplasmic reticulum via altered ryanodine receptors (RYR1).

cards.q: Two main classes of pharmaceutical triggers for Malignant Hyperthermia?
cards.a: Volatile halogenated inhalational anesthetics and the depolarizing muscle relaxant succinylcholine.

cards.q: Earliest and most sensitive clinical sign of developing Malignant Hyperthermia in the operating room?
cards.a: Abrupt, unexplained rise in end-tidal carbon dioxide ($ETCO_2$).

cards.q: Definitive immediate pharmacological treatment for Malignant Hyperthermia?
cards.a: Intravenous Dantrolene.

cards.q: Mechanism of action of Dantrolene in treating Malignant Hyperthermia?
cards.a: Binds to the ryanodine receptor to directly inhibit calcium release from the sarcoplasmic reticulum.

cards.q: Intravenous induction agent of choice for patients in severe hypovolemic or septic shock due to its hemodynamic neutrality?
cards.a: Etomidate.

cards.q: Primary unique endocrine side effect associated with an induction dose of Etomidate?
cards.a: Transient adrenal suppression via inhibition of the 11-beta-hydroxylase enzyme.

cards.q: Intravenous induction agent that acts as a potent bronchodilator and preserves sympathetic drive, making it ideal for asthmatics or shock states?
cards.a: Ketamine.

cards.q: Adverse CNS effect classically associated with emerging from Ketamine anesthesia?
cards.a: Emergence delirium and vivid hallucinations.

cards.q: Intravenous anesthetic agent contraindicated in patients with a severe documented egg or soy allergy?
cards.a: Propofol.

cards.q: Primary hemodynamic effect observed immediately following a bolus injection of Propofol?
cards.a: Significant systemic vasodilation and myocardial depression leading to hypotension.

cards.q: Airway classification system used to predict the technical difficulty of endotracheal intubation based on visible structures?
cards.a: Mallampati Classification.

cards.q: Structures fully visible in a Class I Mallampati airway?
cards.a:
Soft palate, fauces, uvula, and both anterior and posterior tonsillar pillars.
PART 3: Post-Operative Management & Fluids/Electrolytes

cards.q: Standard maintenance fluid calculator rule for calculating hourly intravenous fluid requirements in adults?
cards.a: The 4-2-1 Rule.

cards.q: Composition of 0.9% Normal Saline relative to human plasma tonicity?
cards.a: Hypertonic relative to plasma due to unphysiologically high concentrations of sodium and chloride ($154	ext{ mEq/L}$ each).

cards.q: Acid-base disturbance characteristically induced by aggressive resuscitation with 0.9% Normal Saline?
cards.a: Hyperchloremic metabolic acidosis.

cards.q: Intravenous crystalloid fluid choice that most closely mirrors human physiologic electrolyte profiles?
cards.a: Lactated Ringer's solution.

cards.q: Why must Lactated Ringer's solution be avoided in the same intravenous line used for blood transfusions?
cards.a: Calcium present in Lactated Ringer's can bind to the citrate anticoagulant in blood products, precipitating clot formation.

cards.q: Standard daily basal physiological requirement for sodium in an adult?
cards.a: 1 to 2 mEq/kg per 24 hours.

cards.q: Standard daily basal physiological requirement for potassium in an adult?
cards.a: 0.5 to 1 mEq/kg per 24 hours.

cards.q: Most reliable clinical indicator of adequate end-organ perfusion and fluid resuscitation status in a post-operative patient?
cards.a: Urine output tracking at greater than or equal to 0.5 mL/kg/hour for adults.

cards.q: Earliest sign of volume overload in a post-operative cardiac patient on maintenance intravenous fluids?
cards.a: New-onset tachypnea and crackles on pulmonary auscultation due to interstitial edema.

cards.q: Primary physiological driver of post-operative fluid retention during the first 24 to 48 hours following major surgery?
cards.a: Physiologic stress-induced release of ADH and aldosterone.

cards.q: Immediate initial intervention for a post-operative patient presenting with asymptomatic mild hyponatremia ($132	ext{ mEq/L}$)?
cards.a: Restriction of free water intake and close monitoring of serum sodium levels.

cards.q: Maximum safe rate of serum sodium correction in severe chronic hyponatremia to avoid neurologic devastation?
cards.a: Less than 8 to 12 mEq/L per 24 hours.

cards.q: Catastrophic neurological condition caused by overly rapid correction of severe hyponatremia?
cards.a: Central pontine myelinolysis (also called osmotic demyelination syndrome).

cards.q: Earliest electrocardiogram (ECG) changes pathognomonic for significant hyperkalemia?
cards.a: Symmetrical, narrow-based, peaked T waves.

cards.q: Immediate first-line medication administered to stabilize the cardiac myocyte membrane in severe hyperkalemia with ECG changes?
cards.a: Intravenous Calcium Gluconate or Calcium Chloride.

cards.q: Pharmacological agent that promotes intracellular shifting of potassium within minutes during an acute hyperkalemic crisis?
cards.a: Intravenous regular insulin administered concurrently with 50% Dextrose ($D_{50}$).

cards.q: Electrocardiogram findings classic for severe post-operative hypokalemia?
cards.a: Flattening of T waves, ST-segment depression, and prominent U waves.

cards.q: Refractory hypokalemia that cannot be successfully corrected with potassium supplementation is almost always due to what concurrent deficiency?
cards.a:
Hypomagnesemia.
PART 4: Post-Operative Complications & Fever Assessment

cards.q: The classic clinical mnemonic framework used to diagnose post-operative fever by days?
cards.a: Wind (Days 1-2), Water (Days 3-5), Walking (Days 5-7), Wound (Days 7-10), Wonder drugs (Any day).

cards.q: Most common cause of an isolated post-operative fever occurring within the first 24 to 48 hours?
cards.a: Atelectasis or early systemic inflammatory response to surgical trauma.

cards.q: Primary intervention to prevent and treat early post-operative atelectasis?
cards.a: Incentivize aggressive use of incentive spirometry, chest physiotherapy, and early ambulation.

cards.q: Most common cause of a new-onset post-operative fever on post-op days 3 to 5?
cards.a: Urinary Tract Infection (UTI), frequently secondary to indwelling Foley catheters.

cards.q: Most common cause of a new-onset post-operative fever on post-op days 5 to 7?
cards.a: Deep Vein Thrombosis (DVT) or secondary Pulmonary Embolism (PE).

cards.q: Classic timing for a superficial or deep Surgical Site Infection (SSI) to present with fever?
cards.a: Post-operative days 7 to 10.

cards.q: Definitive initial treatment for a superficial surgical site wound infection demonstrating fluctuance and erythema?
cards.a: Removal of skin staples/sutures, opening of the wound incision, and manual drainage of the purulent collection.

cards.q: High-yield exception where a severe, necrotizing wound infection presents with fever within 24 hours of surgery?
cards.a: Necrotizing infection caused by Clostridium perfringens or Group A Streptococcus.

cards.q: Definitive management strategy for an intra-abdominal abscess identified by CT scan on post-operative day 10?
cards.a: Image-guided percutaneous drainage and targeted intravenous antibiotic therapy.

cards.q: Primary objective clinical sign indicating the resolution of a post-operative paralytic ileus?
cards.a: Return of flatus, bowel movements, and a tolerated oral diet.

cards.q: Normal expected timeframe for the resolution of a physiological post-operative paralytic ileus after uncomplicated open laparotomy?
cards.a: 3 to 5 days.

cards.q: Definition of Ogilvie Syndrome in postoperative patients?
cards.a: Acute colonic pseudo-obstruction characterized by massive dilation of the cecum and right colon without mechanical blockage.

cards.q: Cecal diameter threshold on abdominal X-ray in Ogilvie Syndrome that carries an imminent risk of perforation?
cards.a: Greater than 10 to 12 cm.

cards.q: First-line pharmacological agent used to decompress the colon in a patient with refractory Ogilvie Syndrome?
cards.a: Neostigmine.

cards.q: Most common cause of post-operative mechanical small bowel obstruction within the first few weeks after abdominal surgery?
cards.a: Early fibrinous intra-abdominal adhesions.

cards.q: Initial diagnostic imaging modality of choice to differentiate between paralytic ileus and early mechanical small bowel obstruction?
cards.a: Plain abdominal X-ray series (supine and erect).

cards.q: Primary risk factor for post-operative acute cholecystitis occurring in critically ill, fasted ICU patients?
cards.a: Gallbladder stasis and ischemia leading to Acute Acalculous Cholecystitis.

cards.q: Definitive emergent treatment of choice for an unstable patient with acute acalculous cholecystitis?
cards.a: Percutaneous transhepatic cholecystostomy tube placement.

cards.q: Primary physiological diagnostic criterion for Postoperative Pancreatic Fistula (POPF) based on drain fluid analysis?
cards.a:
Drain fluid amylase concentration greater than 3 times the upper limit of normal serum amylase on or after post-op day 3.
PART 5: Wound Healing, DVT Prophylaxis & Trauma Basics

cards.q: Definition of wound dehiscence?
cards.a: Partial or complete separation of the fascial layers of a surgical wound.

cards.q: Immediate initial management step for a patient presenting with an acute fascial dehiscence and bowel evisceration?
cards.a: Cover the exposed abdominal contents with sterile, saline-moistened dressings and transfer immediately to the operating room.

cards.q: Three components of Virchow's Triad that predict venous thromboembolism risk?
cards.a: Endothelial injury, stasis of blood flow, and hypercoagulability.

cards.q: Standard gold standard non-invasive diagnostic modality for a suspected lower extremity deep vein thrombosis?
cards.a: Compression duplex venous ultrasonography.

cards.q: Diagnostic modality of choice to rule out a pulmonary embolism in a stable post-operative patient with acute dyspnea?
cards.a: Computed Tomography Pulmonary Angiography (CTPA).

cards.q: First-line treatment for an acute pulmonary embolism in a hemodynamically stable postoperative patient where anticoagulation is safe?
cards.a: Therapeutic systemic anticoagulation with unfractionated or low-molecular-weight heparin.

cards.q: Indication for the placement of an Inferior Vena Cava (IVC) filter in a patient with a documented acute proximal DVT?
cards.a: Absolute contraindication to systemic anticoagulation or failure of anticoagulation with documented recurrent emboli.

cards.q: Management of a hemodynamically unstable patient with a massive pulmonary embolism causing obstructive shock?
cards.a: Emergent surgical embolectomy or targeted catheter-directed thrombolysis.

cards.q: The absolute first step in the primary survey of a trauma patient according to Advanced Trauma Life Support (ATLS) protocol?
cards.a: Airway maintenance with strict cervical spine motion restriction.

cards.q: Immediate intervention for a trauma patient presenting with tracheal deviation, absent unilateral breath sounds, and hypotension?
cards.a: Emergent needle decompression in the second intercostal space at the midclavicular line or fifth intercostal space at the anterior axillary line.

cards.q: Definitive treatment that must follow immediate needle decompression of a tension pneumothorax?
cards.a: Tube thoracostomy (chest tube insertion).

cards.q: Definition of a massive hemothorax according to ATLS guidelines?
cards.a: Accumulation of greater than 1500 mL of blood or greater than one-third of the patient's blood volume in the pleural cavity upon initial chest tube placement.

cards.q: Volume threshold of ongoing chest tube output from a hemothorax that serves as an indication for emergent thoracotomy?
cards.a: Greater than 200 mL/hour of blood for 2 to 4 consecutive hours.

cards.q: The classic clinical triad of physical findings diagnostic of cardiac tamponade?
cards.a: Beck's Triad: Hypotension, muffled heart sounds, and jugular venous distention.

cards.q: Immediate diagnostic test used at the bedside to screen for intra-abdominal free fluid or cardiac tamponade in acute trauma?
cards.a: Focused Assessment with Sonography for Trauma (FAST) exam.

cards.q: The four distinct anatomical zones evaluated during a standard FAST exam?
cards.a: Perihepatic (RUQ/Hepatorenal space), Perisplenic (LUQ), Pelvic (Suprapubic space), and Pericardial views.

cards.q: Next immediate step in managing an hemodynamically unstable blunt trauma patient with a positive FAST exam?
cards.a: Emergent exploratory laparotomy.

cards.q: Next step in managing an hemodynamically stable trauma patient with a positive FAST exam?
cards.a: Contrast-enhanced Computed Tomography (CT) scan of the abdomen and pelvis.

cards.q: Definition of a positive diagnostic peritoneal lavage (DPL) in a blunt trauma patient?
cards.a: Aspiration of 10 mL of gross blood or laboratory analysis showing greater than 100,000 RBCs/mm³ or greater than 500 WBCs/mm³.

cards.q: Definitive management for any patient presenting with a penetrating abdominal stab wound and signs of peritonitis or hemodynamic instability?
cards.a: Emergent exploratory laparotomy.

cards.q: Classic sign of urethral injury in a male pelvic fracture patient that serves as an absolute contraindication to blind Foley catheterization?
cards.a: High-riding prostate on rectal exam, blood at the urethral meatus, or perineal ecchymosis.

cards.q: Diagnostic test required to evaluate for urethral integrity prior to catheterization if urethral injury is suspected?
cards.a: Retrograde Urethrogram (RUG).

cards.q: Primary goal of Lethal Triad management in trauma resuscitation?
cards.a: Simultaneous correction of Hypothermia, Acidosis, and Coagulopathy.

cards.q: Standard target ratio of packed red blood cells, fresh frozen plasma, and platelets in a massive transfusion protocol?
cards.a:
Balanced 1:1:1 ratio.
PART 6: Post-Operative Pain & Specialized Critical Care

cards.q: Primary adverse respiratory effect of systemic opioid analgesics used for post-operative pain control?
cards.a: Dose-dependent depression of the central respiratory drive and decreased hypercapnic ventillatory response.

cards.q: The most common gastrointestinal side effect of chronic post-operative opioid use?
cards.a: Constipation due to decreased intestinal motility and delayed colonic transit.

cards.q: Primary benefit of incorporating non-opioid adjuvants (e.g., Ketorolac, Acetaminophen) into a post-operative pain regimen?
cards.a: Opioid-sparing effect which minimizes opioid-related side effects and accelerates bowel function return.

cards.q: Contraindication to the use of Scheduled NSAIDs like Ketorolac in the early post-operative period?
cards.a: Acute kidney injury, active gastrointestinal ulceration, or operations with high risks of severe bleeding complications.

cards.q: Definition of post-operative delirium?
cards.a: An acute, fluctuating disturbance in attention, awareness, and baseline cognition occurring after surgery.

cards.q: First-line non-pharmacological management for hyperactive post-operative delirium in an elderly patient?
cards.a: Reorientation, restoration of sleep-wake cycles, minimization of tethering lines, and avoidance of physical restraints.

cards.q: Class of medications that must be avoided in elderly patients with post-operative delirium due to the risk of worsening confusion?
cards.a: Benzodiazepines (unless delirium is due to alcohol or sedative withdrawal).

cards.q: Diagnostic criteria for Abdominal Compartment Syndrome (ACS)?
cards.a: Sustained intra-abdominal pressure greater than 20 mmHg associated with new onset organ dysfunction.

cards.q: Standard gold-standard clinical method used to measure intra-abdominal pressure at the bedside?
cards.a: Transurethral bladder pressure manometry.

cards.q: Definitive management for severe, refractory Abdominal Compartment Syndrome causing renal or respiratory failure?
cards.a: Emergent surgical decompression via open laparotomy.

cards.q: Most common cause of immediate postoperative hypoxemia in the PACU while a patient is still emerging from general anesthesia?
cards.a: Hypoventilation secondary to residual neuromuscular blockade or opioid-induced respiratory depression.

cards.q: Primary clinical indicator that a postoperative patient is experiencing severe, symptomatic hypocalcemia after total thyroidectomy?
cards.a: Perioral numbness, tingling in fingertips, and positive Chvostek or Trousseau signs.

cards.q: Electrocardiogram finding pathognomonic for severe hypocalcemia?
cards.a: QT interval prolongation, which predisposes the patient to torsades de pointes.

cards.q: Fastest, most direct way to correct life-threatening hypermagnesemia presenting with loss of deep tendon reflexes?
cards.a: Intravenous Calcium Gluconate to antagonize the neuromuscular effects of magnesium.

cards.q: Most common non-iatrogenic cause of acute postoperative hypernatremia?
cards.a: Unreplaced free water losses from unmonitored diabetes insipidus, excessive sweating, or prolonged tachypnea.

cards.q: Pathophysiology of Post-Op Heparin-Induced Thrombocytopenia (HIT)?
cards.a: IgG antibodies form against the Heparin-Platelet Factor 4 (PF4) complex, leading to massive platelet activation.

cards.q: Classic timing and presentation of Heparin-Induced Thrombocytopenia (HIT) type 2?
cards.a: A 50% or greater drop in baseline platelet count occurring 5 to 10 days after starting heparin therapy.

cards.q: Paradoxical clinical complication that makes Heparin-Induced Thrombocytopenia (HIT) highly dangerous?
cards.a: Prothrombotic state causing severe venous or arterial thrombosis, rather than active clinical bleeding.

cards.q: Immediate initial step in the management of suspected Heparin-Induced Thrombocytopenia (HIT)?
cards.a:
Stop all heparin-containing products immediately and initiate an alternative non-heparin anticoagulant like Argatroban.
PART 8: Surgical Infection, Antibiotic Management & Lines

cards.q: Definition of a "Clean-Contaminated" surgical wound according to CDC classifications?
cards.a: An operative wound where the respiratory, alimentary, genital, or urinary tracts are entered under controlled conditions without unusual contamination.

cards.q: Standard timing for the removal of a prophylactic surgical line or urinary catheter to prevent hospital-acquired infection?
cards.a: Within 24 hours postoperatively, unless there is a documented structural or monitoring requirement.

cards.q: Most common bacterial pathogen isolated from surgical site infections following clean orthopedic or cardiac procedures?
cards.a: Staphylococcus aureus (including MRSA).

cards.q: Primary bacterial pathogen suspected in a postoperative wound infection following a contaminated colorectal or pelvic operation?
cards.a: Bacteroides fragilis or Escherichia coli.

cards.q: Classic clinical presentation of a central venous catheter-associated bloodstream infection (CLABSI)?
cards.a: Unexplained fever, chills, and hemodynamic instability in a patient with an indwelling central line and no other clear source of infection.

cards.q: Diagnostic criteria for a confirmed Central Line-Associated Bloodstream Infection (CLABSI)?
cards.a:
Positive blood cultures from a peripheral vein and the central line catheter tip growing the exact same organism.
PART 9: Wound Complications, Hernias & Tubes

cards.q: Primary mechanical difference between a seroma and a hematoma at a surgical incision site?
cards.a: A seroma is a collection of acellular, straw-colored lymphatic fluid, whereas a hematoma is a localized collection of liquid or clotted blood.

cards.q: Initial management for a large, symptomatic subcutaneous postoperative hematoma that compromises overlying skin perfusion?
cards.a: Sterile opening of the incision, evacuation of the blood clot, and control of any active bleeding vessels.

cards.q: Pathophysiology of a postoperative incisional hernia?
cards.a: Iatrogenic failure of the fascial closure due to technical failure, wound infection, tissue ischemia, or increased intra-abdominal pressure.

cards.q: The single most critical risk factor for the development of an incisional hernia following an open laparotomy?
cards.a: Deep postoperative surgical site wound infection.

cards.q: Primary physiological indication for utilizing a closed-suction drain (e.g., Jackson-Pratt) rather than an open drain (e.g., Penrose)?
cards.a:
Closed-suction prevents the atmospheric entry of bacteria into a deep dead space while actively evacuating accumulating fluid.
PART 10: Pulmonary, Thromboembolic & Transfusion Nuances

cards.q: Clinical presentation distinguishing Transfusion-Related Acute Lung Injury (TRALI) from Transfusion-Associated Circulatory Overload (TACO)?
