topic: Mood disorders — major depression, bipolar I & II

cards.q: Minimum duration of symptoms required to diagnose a Major Depressive Episode (MDE)?
cards.a: Two weeks.

cards.q: Number of DSM-5 symptoms required to diagnose a Major Depressive Episode?
cards.a: At least five symptoms, with at least one being depressed mood or anhedonia.

cards.q: What does the mnemonic SIGECAPS stand for in depression screening?
cards.a: Sleep, Interest (Anhedonia), Guilt, Energy, Concentration, Appetite, Psychomotor, Suicidal ideation.

cards.q: True or False: A history of a manic or hypomanic episode excludes the diagnosis of MDD?
cards.a: True.

cards.q: Maximum time window required for "with peripartum onset" specifier in mood disorders?
cards.a: Onset of symptoms during pregnancy or within 4 weeks postpartum.

cards.q: Cardinal feature differentiating atypical depression from classic MDD?
cards.a: Mood reactivity (mood brightens in response to positive events).

cards.q: Three key vegetative/associated symptoms of atypical depression?
cards.a: Hypersomnia, hyperphagia (leaden paralysis), and long-standing interpersonal rejection sensitivity.

cards.q: Defining feature of MDD with melancholic features regarding morning symptoms?
cards.a: Depression is regularly worse in the morning, accompanied by early morning awakening.

cards.q: What defines MDD with catatonia?
cards.a: Severe psychomotor disturbance involving stupor, blunting, mutism, negativity, or waxy flexibility.

cards.q: Treatment of choice for MDD with catatonia if benzodiazepines fail?
cards.a: Electroconvulsive Therapy (ECT).

cards.q: Define MDD with seasonal pattern (Seasonal Affective Disorder).
cards.a: Onset and remission of MDEs at characteristic times of the year for at least 2 consecutive years.

cards.q: Normal time frame for typical grief (bereavement) symptoms to peak?
cards.a: Within the first 2 months following the loss.

cards.q: Pathognomonic feature distinguishing Prolonged Grief Disorder from standard MDE?
cards.a: Intense longing/preoccupation with the deceased lasting at least 12 months (6 months for children).

cards.q: Primary monoamine neurotransmitters implicated in the pathophysiology of MDD?
cards.a: Serotonin ($\text{5-HT}$), Norepinephrine (NE), and Dopamine (DA).

cards.q: Neuroendocrine axis frequently found to be hyperactive in patients with MDD?
cards.a: Hypothalamic-Pituitary-Adrenal (HPA) axis, leading to elevated cortisol.

cards.q: Structural brain change most consistently demonstrated in chronic, untreated MDD?
cards.a: Decreased hippocampal volume.

cards.q: Sleep architecture change: What happens to REM latency in MDD?
cards.a: REM latency is shortened (REM sleep begins earlier in the night).

cards.q: Sleep architecture change: What happens to slow-wave (deep) sleep in MDD?
cards.a: Decreased slow-wave sleep (stages N3).

cards.q: First-line medication class of choice for uncomplicated MDD?
cards.a: Selective Serotonin Reuptake Inhibitors (SSRIs).

cards.q: Average timeline required to assess the full therapeutic efficacy of an antidepressant dose?
cards.a: 4 to 8 weeks.

cards.q: Most common early, transient side effects of SSRIs that lead to non-adherence?
cards.a: Gastrointestinal distress (nausea, diarrhea) and headaches.

cards.q: Long-term side effect of SSRIs that does not usually resolve with time?
cards.a: Sexual dysfunction (decreased libido, anorgasmia).

cards.q: Mechanism of action of Venlafaxine and Duloxetine?
cards.a: Serotonin-Norepinephrine Reuptake Inhibitors (SNRIs).

cards.q: Major medical contraindication specific to initiating Venlafaxine?
cards.a: Uncontrolled hypertension (due to dose-dependent noradrenergic effects).

cards.q: SNRI preferred for patients with comorbid depression and chronic neuropathic pain?
cards.a: Duloxetine.

cards.q: Unique mechanism of action of Mirtazapine?
cards.a: $\alpha_2$ adrenergic antagonist, increasing release of $\text{5-HT}$ and NE.

cards.q: Two primary clinical benefits/side effects utilized when choosing Mirtazapine?
cards.a: Sedation (histamine-1 blockade) and appetite stimulation/weight gain.

cards.q: Mechanism of action of Bupropion?
cards.a: Norepinephrine-Dopamine Reuptake Inhibitor (NDRI).

cards.q: Two major clinical advantages of Bupropion over SSRIs?
cards.a: Lack of sexual side effects and lack of weight gain.

cards.q: Absolute medical contraindications for prescribing Bupropion?
cards.a: Seizure disorders, anorexia nervosa, bulimia nervosa, or active alcohol/benzo withdrawal.

cards.q: Mechanism of Trazodone and its primary clinical utility in depression?
cards.a: $\text{$\text{5-HT}$}_{2}$ receptor antagonist and reuptake inhibitor; primarily used low-dose as a non-addictive hypnotic.

cards.q: Rare, medical emergency side effect associated with Trazodone?
cards.a: Priapism.

cards.q: Mechanism of action of Vortioxetine?
cards.a: SSRI combined with $\text{$\text{5-HT}$}_{1\text{A}}$ agonism and $\text{$\text{5-HT}$}_{3}$/$\text{$\text{5-HT}$}_{7}$ antagonism.

cards.q: Primary toxic mechanism of Tricyclic Antidepressants (TCAs) in overdose?
cards.a: Inhibition of fast sodium channels in the myocardium, leading to QRS widening and arrhythmias.

cards.q: Triad of classic toxicities seen in TCA overdose?
cards.a: Cardiotoxicity (arrhythmias), Convulsions (seizures), and Coma.

cards.q: Immediate medical antidote for TCA-induced cardiac arrhythmias?
cards.a: Intravenous Sodium Bicarbonate.

cards.q: Dietary restriction mandatory for patients taking Monoamine Oxidase Inhibitors (MAOIs)?
cards.a: Low-tyramine diet (avoiding aged cheeses, cured meats, red wine).

cards.q: Pathophysiology of the hypertensive crisis caused by combining MAOIs with tyramine?
cards.a: Tyramine displaces stored norepinephrine into the synaptic cleft, causing massive vasoconstriction.

cards.q: Immediate pharmacologic intervention for an MAOI-induced hypertensive crisis?
cards.a: Phentolamine ($\alpha$-adrenergic antagonist).

cards.q: Mechanism behind Serotonin Syndrome when combining MAOIs and SSRIs?
cards.a: Overactivation of central and peripheral $\text{$\text{5-HT}$}_{1\text{A}}$ and $\text{$\text{5-HT}$}_{2\text{A}}$ receptors.

cards.q: Minimum washout period required when switching from an SSRI to an MAOI?
cards.a: 2 weeks (5 weeks specifically for Fluoxetine due to long half-life).

cards.q: Classic clinical triad of Serotonin Syndrome?
cards.a: Autonomic instability, altered mental status, and neuromuscular hyperactivity.

cards.q: Pathognomonic physical exam finding that distinguishes Serotonin Syndrome from NMS?
cards.a: Hyperreflexia and clonus (spontaneous, inducible, or ocular).

cards.q: First-line medical treatment for severe Serotonin Syndrome?
cards.a: Cyproheptadine ($\text{$\text{5-HT}$}_{2\text{A}}$ antagonist) along with aggressive cooling and benzodiazepines.

cards.q: Evidence-based psychotherapy modalities proven effective as monotherapy for mild-to-moderate MDD?
cards.a: Cognitive Behavioral Therapy (CBT) and Interpersonal Therapy (IPT).

cards.q: Quickest, most effective treatment for severe, treatment-resistant MDD or psychotic depression?
cards.a: Electroconvulsive Therapy (ECT).

cards.q: Absolute medical contraindication to performing ECT?
cards.a: None (increased intracranial pressure is a relative contraindication requiring caution).

cards.q: Most common acute side effect associated with ECT courses?
cards.a: Retrograde and anterograde amnesia (usually resolves within a few months).

cards.q: Indication for Esketamine nasal spray in major depression?
cards.a: Treatment-Resistant Depression (TRD) or acute suicidal ideation, acting via NMDA receptor antagonism.

cards.q: Standard maintenance guideline duration for an antidepressant after a patient's first MDE?
cards.a: Continue effective dose for 6 to 12 months after achieving full remission.

cards.q: Indication for lifelong maintenance antidepressant therapy?
cards.a: History of 3 or more MDEs, or chronic severe episodes.

cards.q: Minimal duration required to diagnose a manic episode?
cards.a: 1 week (or any duration if hospitalization is required).

cards.q: Core requirement regarding mood change to diagnose a manic episode?
cards.a: Abnormally, persistently elevated, expansive, or irritable mood, PLUS persistently increased goal-directed activity/energy.

cards.q: Minimum number of symptoms required for a manic episode diagnosis?
cards.a: Three (four if the mood is only irritable).

cards.q: Mnemonic DIGFAST for mania symptoms stands for?
cards.a: Distractibility, Indiscretion (impulsivity), Grandiosity, Flight of ideas, Activity increase, Sleep deficit, Talkativeness (pressured speech).

cards.q: True or False: A history of a Major Depressive Episode is required to diagnose Bipolar I Disorder?
cards.a: False (only 1 lifetime manic episode is required).

cards.q: True or False: The presence of hallucinations or delusions automatically classifies an episode as manic rather than hypomanic?
cards.a: True.

cards.q: Defining social/occupational criteria separating mania from hypomania?
cards.a: Mania causes marked impairment in functioning or requires hospitalization; hypomania does not.

cards.q: What is Bipolar I with rapid cycling?
cards.a: Four or more distinct mood episodes (mania, hypomania, or depression) within a 12-month period.

cards.q: Class of medications known to precipitate or accelerate rapid cycling in Bipolar patients?
cards.a: Antidepressants (specifically TCAs and SNRIs/SSRIs).

cards.q: Peak age of onset for Bipolar I disorder?
cards.a: Late adolescence to early adulthood (18 to 25 years).

cards.q: Diagnostic criteria combination required to diagnose Bipolar II Disorder?
cards.a: At least one lifetime Hypomanic Episode AND at least one lifetime Major Depressive Episode.

cards.q: True or False: A history of a single manic episode permanently changes a Bipolar II diagnosis to Bipolar I?
cards.a: True.

cards.q: Minimal duration required to diagnose a hypomanic episode?
cards.a: 4 consecutive days.

cards.q: Define Cyclothymic Disorder criteria regarding symptom duration?
cards.a: At least 2 years (1 year in children/adolescents) of numerous periods of hypomanic and depressive symptoms that do not meet full criteria for an episode.

cards.q: Maximum time a patient with Cyclothymia can be symptom-free during the 2-year diagnostic window?
cards.a: 2 months.

cards.q: Strongest risk factor for developing Bipolar I Disorder?
cards.a: Family history (monozygotic twin concordance rates approach 40% to 70%).

cards.q: Neurotransmitter alteration typically associated with acute mania?
cards.a: Hyperactivity of dopamine and norepinephrine pathways.

cards.q: First-line mood stabilizer uniquely shown to reduce suicide risk in Bipolar Disorder?
cards.a: Lithium.

cards.q: Baseline laboratory investigations mandatory before initiating Lithium?
cards.a: Renal function (BUN/Creatinine), Thyroid Function Tests (TSH), Electrolytes, and $\beta$-hCG (pregnancy test).

cards.q: Classic congenital cardiac anomaly associated with first-trimester Lithium exposure?
cards.a: Ebstein's anomaly (displacement of tricuspid valve leaflets into the right ventricle).

cards.q: Narrow therapeutic index range for Lithium in acute mania?
cards.a: 1.0 to 1.5 mEq/L.

cards.q: Maintenance therapeutic index range for Lithium?
cards.a: 0.6 to 1.2 mEq/L.

cards.q: Common, benign neurologic side effect of therapeutic Lithium?
cards.a: Fine resting/intention tremor.

cards.q: Long-term endocrine adverse effect of Lithium therapy requiring tracking?
cards.a: Hypothyroidism (often treatable by adding Levothyroxine without stopping Lithium).

cards.q: Renal pathology caused by long-term Lithium use resulting in polyuria/polydipsia?
cards.a: Nephrogenic Diabetes Insipidus (NDI).

cards.q: Pharmacologic treatment of choice for Lithium-induced Nephrogenic Diabetes Insipidus?
cards.a: Amiloride (blocks Lithium entry into collecting duct epithelial cells).

cards.q: Medication classes that acutely elevate Lithium levels and trigger toxicity?
cards.a: Thiazide diuretics, NSAIDs, and ACE inhibitors/ARBs.

cards.q: Gastrointestinal and neurologic signs of acute Lithium toxicity?
cards.a: Nausea, vomiting, severe diarrhea, coarse tremor, ataxia, slurred speech, and seizures.

cards.q: Definitive treatment intervention for acute Lithium toxicity with levels greater than 4.0 mEq/L (or greater than 2.5 mEq/L with severe neuro toxicity)?
cards.a: Hemodialysis.

cards.q: First-line mood stabilizer preferred for Bipolar with mixed features or rapid cycling?
cards.a: Valproic Acid (Valproate).

cards.q: Baseline and maintenance laboratory tracking required for Valproate?
cards.a: Liver Function Tests (LFTs) and Complete Blood Count (CBC) for platelets.

cards.q: Two black box warning toxicities associated with Valproate?
cards.a: Hepatotoxicity and Pancreatitis.

cards.q: Teratogenic defect caused by Valproate exposure in early pregnancy?
cards.a: Neural tube defects (e.g., spina bifida via folate antagonism).

cards.q: Therapeutic plasma concentration range for Valproate in mood disorders?
cards.a: 50 to 125 mcg/mL.

cards.q: Primary clinical indication for Lamotrigine in Bipolar Disorder management?
cards.a: Maintenance therapy to prevent Bipolar Depression (ineffective for acute mania).

cards.q: Serious, life-threatening dermatologic adverse effect of Lamotrigine?
cards.a: Stevens-Johnson Syndrome (SJS) / Toxic Epidermal Necrolysis (TEN).

cards.q: Clinical titration strategy used to minimize the risk of Lamotrigine-induced SJS?
cards.a: Extremely slow, low-dose upward titration over several weeks.

cards.q: Drug-drug interaction effect of Valproate on Lamotrigine metabolism?
cards.a: Valproate doubles Lamotrigine levels; Lamotrigine dose must be halved.

cards.q: Mechanism of action making Carbamazepine useful in Bipolar mania?
cards.a: Blockade of voltage-gated sodium channels.

cards.q: Serious hematologic side effect associated with Carbamazepine requiring CBC tracking?
cards.a: Agranulocytosis/Aplastic anemia.

cards.q: Electrolyte abnormality frequently caused by Carbamazepine (especially in elderly)?
cards.a: Hyponatremia (SIADH-like effect).

cards.q: Role of Second-Generation Antipsychotics (SGAs) in managing acute manic episodes?
cards.a: First-line monotherapy or adjunct to mood stabilizers for rapid control of agitation and psychosis.

cards.q: Which SGAs are specifically FDA-approved for the treatment of acute Bipolar Depression?
cards.a: Quetiapine, Lurasidone, Cariprazine, and the Olanzapine-Fluoxetine combination.

cards.q: Primary metabolic side effects requiring long-term monitoring with Olanzapine and Clozapine?
cards.a: Weight gain, dyslipidemia, and hyperglycemia/Type 2 Diabetes.

cards.q: Initial step in treating a patient presenting with an acute MDE who has a family history of Bipolar I?
cards.a: Screen carefully for past spontaneous manic/hypomanic episodes before starting an antidepressant.

cards.q: Dangerous clinical outcome of treating a Bipolar patient with SSRI monotherapy?
cards.a: Treatment-emergent mania or hypomania switch.

cards.q: First-line treatment strategy for a pregnant patient experiencing severe, life-threatening manic or depressive episodes?
cards.a: Electroconvulsive Therapy (ECT).

cards.q: Most common psychiatric comorbidity found in individuals with Bipolar Disorder?
cards.a: Anxiety disorders (followed closely by Substance Use Disorders).

cards.q: Percentage of individuals with Bipolar Disorder who attempt suicide at least once?
cards.a: Approximately 25% to 50%.

cards.q: First-line pharmacologic strategy for a patient presenting with a manic episode with mixed features?
cards.a: Valproate or an atypical antipsychotic (avoid lithium if severe depressive features dominate).

cards.q: Difference between a "response" and "remission" in mood disorder treatment?
cards.a: Response is a 50% or greater reduction in symptoms; Remission is the near-total absence of symptoms.

cards.q: Define Disruptive Mood Dysregulation Disorder (DMDD) age window for diagnosis?
cards.a: Onset must be before age 10; cannot diagnose before age 6 or after age 18.

cards.q: Core clinical feature differentiating DMDD from Bipolar disorder in children?
cards.a: DMDD features persistent, chronic irritability between temper outbursts, rather than episodic shifts.

cards.q: Minimum symptom duration required to diagnose Persistent Depressive Disorder (Dysthymia) in adults?
cards.a: 2 years.

cards.q: Minimum symptom duration required to diagnose Persistent Depressive Disorder (Dysthymia) in children?
cards.a: 1 year.

cards.q: Maximum period a patient can be symptom-free during the course of Persistent Depressive Disorder?
cards.a: 2 months.

cards.q: Core diagnostic symptom timing requirement for Premenstrual Dysphoric Disorder (PMDD)?
cards.a: Symptoms express in the week before menses onset, improve within a few days after menses starts, and become minimal/absent post-menses.

cards.q: First-line pharmacologic treatment options for severe PMDD?
cards.a: SSRIs (administered either daily or luteal-phase-only).

cards.q: Primary defense mechanism implicated in depression according to classic psychoanalytic theory?
cards.a: Introjection (turning anger inward against the self after the loss of an object).

cards.q: Beck's Cognitive Triad of depression consists of negative views of what three things?
cards.a: The self, the world, and the future.

cards.q: Structural brain change seen in Bipolar Disorder during neuroimaging structural studies?
cards.a: Nonspecific white matter hyperintensities and ventricular enlargement.

cards.q: Most common cause of treatment failure in patients diagnosed with Bipolar Disorder?
cards.a: Medication non-adherence (often due to missing the high of hypomania/mania or side effects).

cards.q: Preferred maintenance drug for a bipolar patient with severe renal impairment?
cards.a: Valproate (avoid Lithium).

cards.q: Preferred maintenance drug for a bipolar patient with active hepatic failure?
cards.a: Lithium (avoid Valproate/Carbamazepine).

cards.q: Primary lab marker utilized to monitor for Carbamazepine auto-induction?
cards.a: Serum Carbamazepine levels (Carbamazepine induces its own metabolism over the first 4-6 weeks).

cards.q: HLA allele screening required before starting Carbamazepine in Asian patients?
cards.a: HLA-B*1502 (due to high risk of SJS/TEN).

cards.q: Pharmacologic treatment of choice for severe Bipolar depression when multiple monotherapies fail?
cards.a: Mood stabilizer (Lithium or Valproate) PLUS an atypical antipsychotic (e.g., Lurasidone or Quetiapine).

cards.q: True or False: Psychotherapy alone is sufficient as a primary treatment for acute Bipolar I mania?
cards.a: False (pharmacotherapy is mandatory; psychotherapy is an adjunct for maintenance).

cards.q: What is "double depression"?
cards.a: Major Depressive Episodes superimposed on a chronic course of Persistent Depressive Disorder.

cards.q: Major clinical feature that distinguishes Bipolar I with psychotic features from Schizoaffective Disorder?
cards.a: In Bipolar, psychotic symptoms occur only during a mood episode; in Schizoaffective, psychosis occurs for 2 or more weeks in the absence of prominent mood symptoms.

cards.q: Most common over-the-counter medication class that can precipitate depressive symptoms?
cards.a: Systemic corticosteroids (e.g., Prednisone).

cards.q: Cardiovascular medication class classically associated with treatment-emergent depression?
cards.a: $\beta$-blocker (e.g., Propranolol).

cards.q: Neurological medication used for Parkinson’s disease that can precipitate manic-like symptoms?
cards.a: Levodopa (due to increase in central dopamine).

cards.q: Endocrine disorder that mimics a manic episode and must be ruled out with a TSH test?
cards.a: Hyperthyroidism.

cards.q: Infectious disease characterized by profound fatigue, depressed mood, and atypical lymphocytosis?
cards.a: Epstein-Barr Virus (Infectious Mononucleosis).

cards.q: Pancreatic pathology classically presenting with sudden-onset depression before physical symptoms emerge?
cards.a: Pancreatic adenocarcinoma.

cards.q: Neurological pathology presenting with depression, chorea, and dementia?
cards.a: Huntington's disease.

cards.q: Substance withdrawal that presents with dysphoria, hypersomnia, hyperphagia, and vivid dreams?
cards.a: Cocaine or Amphetamine withdrawal ("crashing").

cards.q: Substance intoxication that presents with grandiosity, paranoia, tachycardia, and pupillary dilation?
cards.a: Amphetamine or Cocaine intoxication.

cards.q: Over-the-counter herbal supplement used for depression that can cause Serotonin Syndrome if combined with an SSRI?
cards.a: St. John’s Wort.

cards.q: What defines MDD with anxious distress specifier?
cards.a: Presence of at least two symptoms of anxiety (e.g., feeling keyed up, unusually restless) during a major depressive episode.

cards.q: Diagnostic minimum for Bipolar I or II "with mixed features"?
cards.a: A full mood episode accompanied by at least three symptoms of the opposite polarity.

cards.q: What defines MDD with peri-menopausal onset?
cards.a: Onset of depressive symptoms during the menopausal transition, linked to fluctuating estrogen levels.

cards.q: True or False: Irritability can substitute for depressed mood in children and adolescents to meet Criterion A for MDD?
cards.a: True.

cards.q: Minimum duration of symptoms required to diagnose Cyclothymic Disorder in pediatric patients?
cards.a: One year.

cards.q: True or False: Subclinical hypothyroidism can cause resistance to standard antidepressant therapy?
cards.a: True.

cards.q: Statistically, which demographic has the highest rate of completed suicide in the US?
cards.a: Elderly Caucasian males (age greater than 65).

cards.q: Strongest single predictive risk factor for a future completed suicide?
cards.a: A history of previous suicide attempts.

cards.q: Gender paradox of suicide: Which gender attempts more, and which completes more?
cards.a: Females attempt suicide more frequently; males complete suicide more frequently.

cards.q: Mirroring genetic risk: What is the concordance rate of Bipolar I disorder in monozygotic twins?
cards.a: Approximately 40% to 70%.

cards.q: Mirroring genetic risk: What is the concordance rate of Major Depressive Disorder in monozygotic twins?
cards.a: Approximately 40% to 50%.

cards.q: Lifetime prevalence range of Major Depressive Disorder in the general population?
cards.a: 10% to 25% for women; 5% to 12% for men.

cards.q: Antidepressant class characterized by strong antihistaminic ($\text{H}_1$) and anti-$\alpha_1$ adrenergic side effects?
cards.a: Tricyclic Antidepressants (TCAs).

cards.q: Symptom presentation of anti-$\alpha_1$ adrenergic blockade from psychotropic medications?
cards.a: Orthostatic hypotension and reflex tachycardia.

cards.q: Receptor blockade responsible for dry mouth, blurred vision, urinary retention, and constipation from TCAs?
cards.a: Muscarinic acetylcholine receptor blockade (anticholinergic effects).

cards.q: SSRI with the longest half-life, minimizing the risk of discontinuation syndrome?
cards.a: Fluoxetine.

cards.q: SSRIs with the shortest half-lives, presenting the highest risk for discontinuation syndrome?
cards.a: Paroxetine and Venlafaxine.

cards.q: Triad of features characterizing Antidepressant Discontinuation Syndrome?
cards.a: Flu-like symptoms, electrical shock sensations ("brain zaps"), and vivid dreams.

cards.q: Mechanism of action of Vilazodone?
cards.a: SSRI combined with $\text{$\text{5-HT}$}_{1\text{A}}$ receptor partial agonism.

cards.q: Second-generation antipsychotic with a specific black-box warning for severe neutropenia/agranulocytosis?
cards.a: Clozapine.

cards.q: Mandatory laboratory tracking protocol required for prescribing Clozapine?
cards.a: Absolute Neutrophil Count (ANC).

cards.q: Mechanism of action of Ramelteon, often used for sleep disturbances in mood disorders?
cards.a: Melatonin receptor (MT1 and MT2) agonist.

cards.q: Initial medical intervention for a patient with Bipolar I presenting with acute Lithium toxicity and a prolonged QTc?
cards.a: Discontinue Lithium, administer intravenous hydration, and obtain urgent serum Lithium levels.

cards.q: Preferred mood stabilizer for a patient with Bipolar I who has comorbid juvenile myoclonic epilepsy?
cards.a: Valproic Acid.

cards.q: Maintenance treatment of choice for a patient with Bipolar II whose primary impairment stems from recurrent depressive crashes?
cards.a: Lamotrigine.

cards.q: What step should be taken if a patient on Lithium develops mild, asymptomatic hypercalcemia and elevated parathyroid hormone?
cards.a: Monitor levels; Lithium can cause hyperparathyroidism.

cards.q: First-line pharmacotherapy for a patient with MDD with psychotic features?
cards.a: Combination of an antidepressant and an antipsychotic (or ECT).

cards.q: Preferred antidepressant for an elderly patient with MDD, low appetite, and insomnia?
cards.a: Mirtazapine.

cards.q: Antidepressant class absolutely contraindicated for use with any triptan medication due to Serotonin Syndrome risk?
cards.a: MAOIs (and cautiously with SSRIs/SNRIs).

cards.q: Next management step for a patient with MDD who has shown zero improvement after 4 weeks of maximum-dose SSRI therapy?
cards.a: Switch to a different class of antidepressant (e.g., SNRI or atypical).

cards.q: Next management step for a patient with MDD who has shown a partial response (30% improvement) after 6 weeks of maximum-dose SSRI therapy?
cards.a: Augment with a non-SSRI agent (e.g., Bupropion, Lithium, or a low-dose atypical antipsychotic).

cards.q: Psychotherapeutic approach focusing heavily on changing distorted core beliefs and automatic negative thoughts?
cards.a: Cognitive Behavioral Therapy (CBT).

cards.q: Psychotherapeutic approach focusing on grief, interpersonal role disputes, and role transitions?
cards.a: Interpersonal Psychotherapy (IPT).

cards.q: Key neuromuscular physical exam finding that distinguishes Serotonin Syndrome from Neuroleptic Malignant Syndrome (NMS)?
cards.a: Hyperreflexia and clonus are present in Serotonin Syndrome; "lead-pipe" rigidity is present in NMS.

cards.q: Autonomic sign distinguishing Anticholinergic Toxicity from Serotonin Syndrome?
cards.a: Anticholinergic toxicity presents with dry, flushed skin and absent bowel sounds; Serotonin Syndrome presents with diaphoresis (sweating) and hyperactive bowel sounds.

cards.q: Lab value abnormality characteristically elevated in both Neuroleptic Malignant Syndrome and severe Serotonin Syndrome due to muscle breakdown?
cards.a: Creatine Kinase (CK).

cards.q: Cardiac conduction abnormality that is an absolute contraindication to using Geodon (Ziprasidone) or Celexa (Citalopram) at high doses?
cards.a: QTc prolongation.

cards.q: Maximum recommended daily dose of Citalopram in elderly patients due to risk of QTc prolongation?
cards.a: 20 mg per day.

cards.q: SSRI that is a potent inhibitor of CYP2D6 and can dramatically increase levels of $\beta$-blocker and venlafaxine?
cards.a: Paroxetine (and Fluoxetine).

cards.q: Enzyme induced by Carbamazepine that causes it to clear itself and other anticonvulsants faster over the first month of treatment?
cards.a: CYP3A4.

cards.q: Mood stabilizer that acts as a potent CYP3A4 inhibitor, increasing levels of Carbamazepine if co-administered?
cards.a: Valproate.

cards.q: Antibiotic class (commonly used for UTIs) that can impair renal clearance and acutely increase Lithium levels?
cards.a: Tetracyclines (e.g., Doxycycline).

cards.q: Cardiac medication used for rate control that can decrease renal blood flow and elevate Lithium concentrations?
cards.a: Verapamil (and other calcium channel blockers).

cards.q: Structural brain abnormality found on MRI in patients with severe, chronic Bipolar Disorder?
cards.a: Enlargement of the lateral ventricles.

cards.q: Functional neuroimaging finding (PET/SPECT) typically seen in the prefrontal cortex of depressed patients?
cards.a: Hypometabolism and decreased blood flow.

cards.q: Neurotropic factor found to be significantly decreased in the serum and hippocampus of patients with active MDD?
cards.a: Brain-Derived Neurotrophic Factor (BDNF).

cards.q: First-line pharmacotherapy for a patient with severe Bipolar Mania who is also in her first trimester of pregnancy and refuses ECT?
cards.a: Haloperidol or a second-generation antipsychotic (e.g., Olanzapine).

cards.q: Next clinical step when a patient on Lithium develops rapid-onset confusion, coarse tremors, and nystagmus with a normal serum Lithium level?
cards.a: Check checking serum electrolytes, renal function, and re-verify the timing of the last Lithium dose relative to the blood draw.

cards.q: Ideal time to draw blood for a steady-state therapeutic Lithium level check?
cards.a: 12 hours after the last dose (trough level).

cards.q: Medical diagnosis to suspect when an older adult develops severe depression for the first time in life with asymmetric resting tremor and bradykinesia?
cards.a: Parkinson’s disease presenting with comorbid depression.

cards.q: Treatment of choice for "Pseudodementia" (Depression-induced cognitive impairment in the elderly)?
cards.a: Antidepressants (SSRIs).

cards.q: Key clinical history feature distinguishing Pseudodementia from true Alzheimer’s Dementia?
cards.a: Patients with pseudodementia typically complain loudly about their memory loss and make little effort on cognitive tests ("I don't know" answers).

cards.q: True or False: Transcranial Magnetic Stimulation (TMS) is indicated for patients with severe psychotic depression?
cards.a: False (Psychotic depression requires ECT or combination pharmacotherapy; TMS is for non-psychotic treatment-resistant depression).

cards.q: What is the immediate next step in management for a depressed patient who admits to having a specific, actionable plan to commit suicide?
cards.a: Ensure patient safety via immediate voluntary or involuntary hospitalization.

cards.q: True or False: If a patient with severe mania refuses hospitalization but poses an immediate danger to themselves or others, you must obtain a court order before placing an emergency hold?
cards.a: False (an emergency physician-initiated hold can be placed immediately; court review follows later).

cards.q: What is the legal doctrine that allows the state to intervene and involuntarily hospitalize a severely manic patient who is unable to provide for their own basic food, clothing, or shelter?
cards.a: Parens patriae (the state acting as a protector of citizens who cannot care for themselves).

cards.q: Next step in management if a patient with severe Bipolar I mania refuses life-saving medication during an acute involuntary hold?
cards.a: Administer emergency intramuscular medication (e.g., Haloperidol or Olanzapine) under emergency treatment protocols if they present an imminent threat of violence.

cards.q: What is the immediate next step in management for a patient on Lithium who develops a mild, fine resting tremor but has a therapeutic serum level?
cards.a: Reassurance, or lower the dose slightly if clinically feasible, or add a low-dose $\beta$-blocker (e.g., Propranolol).

cards.q: Next step in management for a patient taking an SSRI who develops acute, severe suicidal ideation within the first two weeks of starting the medication?
cards.a: Discontinue or lower the dose of the SSRI, monitor closely, and ensure immediate safety/hospitalization if necessary.

cards.q: What is the preferred next step when a pregnant woman with Bipolar I stable on Lithium chooses to stay on her medication after a thorough risk-benefit discussion?
cards.a: Continue Lithium, but schedule targeted fetal echocardiography at 16 to 20 weeks of gestation to screen for Ebstein's anomaly.

cards.q: Next step in management for a patient with MDD who achieves full remission on an SSRI but develops severe, treatment-limiting sexual dysfunction?
cards.a: Switch to Bupropion, or augment the SSRI with Bupropion or Sildenafil.

cards.q: Next step in management for an adolescent patient diagnosed with MDD who fails to respond to cognitive behavioral therapy alone?
cards.a: Initiate pharmacotherapy with Fluoxetine (the SSRI with the most robust evidence and FDA approval for pediatric depression).

cards.q: How frequently should a patient's steady-state Lithium level be checked during the initial stabilization phase?
cards.a: Every 1 to 2 weeks until a stable, therapeutic level is achieved.

cards.q: Once a patient is on a stable, long-term maintenance dose of Lithium, how often should renal function and TSH be checked?
cards.a: Every 6 to 12 months.

cards.q: What baseline metric must be established before prescribing any second-generation antipsychotic for Bipolar depression due to metabolic risks?
cards.a: Fasting lipid panel, fasting blood glucose/HbA1c, body mass index (BMI), and waist circumference.

cards.q: How often should a complete blood count (CBC) be monitored during the first few months of starting Carbamazepine?
cards.a: Every 2 to 4 weeks to screen for transient or severe leukopenia.

cards.q: Core symptom domains required for a DSM-5-TR diagnosis of Schizophrenia?
cards.a: Delusions, hallucinations, disorganized speech, grossly disorganized/catatonic behavior, and negative symptoms.

cards.q: Minimum number of core symptoms required for Schizophrenia diagnosis?
cards.a: At least two core symptoms.

cards.q: Which specific core symptoms must include at least one to diagnose Schizophrenia?
cards.a: Delusions, hallucinations, or disorganized speech.

cards.q: Minimum duration of active-phase symptoms required for Schizophrenia?
cards.a: One month.

cards.q: Minimum total duration of continuous signs of disturbance required for Schizophrenia?
cards.a: Six months.

cards.q: What does the 6-month Schizophrenia duration requirement include?
cards.a: Prodromal, active-phase, and residual-phase symptoms.

cards.q: Define a delusion.
cards.a: A fixed, false belief unchanged by conflicting evidence.

cards.q: Define a bizarre delusion.
cards.a: A delusion that is clearly implausible and not understandable from shared cultural experiences.

cards.q: Most common type of delusion in schizophrenia spectrum disorders?
cards.a: Persecutory delusions.

cards.q: Define a delusion of reference.
cards.a: The belief that random, innocuous environmental cues have highly personal significance.

cards.q: Define thought broadcasting.
cards.a: The delusion that one's thoughts are being transmitted aloud to others.

cards.q: Define thought insertion.
cards.a: The delusion that outside thoughts are being placed directly into one's mind.

cards.q: Define thought withdrawal.
cards.a: The delusion that an outside force is removing thoughts from one's mind.

cards.q: Define Capgras syndrome.
cards.a: The delusion that a familiar person has been replaced by an identical imposter.

cards.q: Define Cotard syndrome.
cards.a: The nihilistic delusion that one is dead, decaying, or non-existent.

cards.q: Define Fregoli syndrome.
cards.a: The delusion that different people are actually a single person in disguise.

cards.q: Most common modality of hallucinations in schizophrenia?
cards.a: Auditory hallucinations.

cards.q: Two specific types of auditory hallucinations traditionally tied to schizophrenia prognosis?
cards.a: Voices commenting on behavior and two or more voices conversing.

cards.q: What should visual, olfactory, or gustatory hallucinations immediately prompt the clinician to suspect?
cards.a: An underlying medical, organic, or substance-induced etiology.

cards.q: Define formal thought disorder.
cards.a: Disorganized thinking inferred objectively from speech patterns.

cards.q: Define derailment (loose associations).
cards.a: Speech where ideas slip off track from one topic to an unrelated oblique topic.

cards.q: Define tangentiality.
cards.a: Replying to questions in an oblique, irrelevant, or tangential manner.

cards.q: Define incoherence (word salad).
cards.a: Speech that is linguistically disorganized and totally incomprehensible.

cards.q: Define neologisms.
cards.a: Invented words created by combining parts of existing words.

cards.q: Define perseveration.
cards.a: Persistent repetition of words, phrases, or ideas despite a change in context.

cards.q: Define clang associations.
cards.a: Choosing words based on sound or rhyming rather than semantic meaning.

cards.q: Define catatonia.
cards.a: Marked psychomotor disturbance involving decreased motor activity or excessive, purposeless activity.

cards.q: Define waxy flexibility in catatonia.
cards.a: Slight, even resistance to positioning by examiner followed by maintenance of that new posture.

cards.q: Define stupor in catatonia.
cards.a: Complete lack of psychomotor activity and unresponsiveness to the environment.

cards.q: Define negativism in catatonia.
cards.a: Motiveless resistance to all instructions or maintenance of an opposite posture.

cards.q: Define echolalia.
cards.a: Pathological repeating of another person's words.

cards.q: Define echopraxia.
cards.a: Pathological mimicking of another person's movements.

cards.q: List the "5 A's" of primary negative symptoms in Schizophrenia.
cards.a: Affective flattening, alogia, avolition, anhedonia, and asociality.

cards.q: Define alogia.
cards.a: Poverty of speech and restriction in the amount or fluency of spontaneous speech.

cards.q: Define avolition.
cards.a: An inability to initiate and persist in goal-directed activities.

cards.q: Impact of negative symptoms vs. positive symptoms on long-term functional outcome?
cards.a: Negative symptoms are much stronger predictors of poor functional outcome.

cards.q: Functional requirement essential for diagnosing Schizophrenia?
cards.a: Marked impairment in one or more major areas of functioning like work, relationships, or self-care.

cards.q: Lifetime prevalence of Schizophrenia globally?
cards.a: Approximately 1%.

cards.q: Male-to-female ratio of Schizophrenia prevalence?
cards.a: Equal (1:1), though presentation details differ.

cards.q: Peak age of onset of Schizophrenia in males?
cards.a: Early to mid-20s (18-25 years).

cards.q: Peak age of onset of Schizophrenia in females?
cards.a: Late 20s to early 30s, with a smaller bimodal peak post-menopause.

cards.q: Gender correlation with Schizophrenia prognosis?
cards.a: Females generally have a better prognosis and milder course.

cards.q: Concordance rate of Schizophrenia in monozygotic twins?
cards.a: Approximately 40% to 50%.

cards.q: Concordance rate of Schizophrenia in dizygotic twins?
cards.a: Approximately 10% to 15%.

cards.q: Risk of developing Schizophrenia if one parent is diagnosed?
cards.a: Approximately 10% to 12%.

cards.q: Risk of developing Schizophrenia if both parents are diagnosed?
cards.a: Approximately 40%.

cards.q: Common neurodevelopmental birth complication linked to increased risk of Schizophrenia?
cards.a: In utero maternal infections (e.g., influenza) or obstetric complications causing fetal hypoxia.

cards.q: Environmental factor involving season of birth associated with Schizophrenia?
cards.a: Late winter and early spring births.

cards.q: Socioeconomic trend where Schizophrenia is more prevalent in lower socioeconomic classes?
cards.a: Social drift hypothesis (downward drift due to cognitive and behavioral impairment).

cards.q: Urban vs. rural environment risk for Schizophrenia?
cards.a: Urban environments double the risk of developing the disorder.

cards.q: Classic substance abuse habit that carries a clear causal link to triggering psychotic episodes?
cards.a: Heavy cannabis use during adolescence.

cards.q: Dopamine hypothesis: underlying mechanism of positive symptoms?
cards.a: Hyperactivity of dopamine neurotransmission in the mesolimbic pathway.

cards.q: Dopamine hypothesis: underlying mechanism of negative and cognitive symptoms?
cards.a: Hypoactivity of dopamine neurotransmission in the mesocortical pathway.

cards.q: Glutamate hypothesis of Schizophrenia?
cards.a: Hypofunction of NMDA receptors on GABAergic interneurons leading to downstream dopamine dysregulation.

cards.q: Serotonin hypothesis contribution to Schizophrenia?
cards.a: $\text{$\text{5-HT}$}_{2\text{A}}$ receptor activation modulates dopamine release, serving as the basis for atypical antipsychotic action.

cards.q: Structural brain imaging finding most consistently replicated in Schizophrenia?
cards.a: Enlargement of the lateral and third ventricles.

cards.q: Cortical structural brain change observed over time in Schizophrenia?
cards.a: Diffuse reduction in gray matter volume, most prominently in the temporal and frontal lobes.

cards.q: Functional neuroimaging landmark pattern seen during executive task testing in Schizophrenia?
cards.a: Hypofrontality (decreased metabolic activity and blood flow in the prefrontal cortex).

cards.q: Microscopic histopathological finding in the hippocampus of Schizophrenia patients?
cards.a: Cellular disorientation and disarray of pyramidal neurons.

cards.q: Alteration in normal adolescent brain development accelerated in Schizophrenia?
cards.a: Excessive or exaggerated synaptic pruning.

cards.q: DSM-5-TR duration criteria for Brief Psychotic Disorder?
cards.a: At least 1 day but less than 1 month, with eventual full return to premorbid functioning.

cards.q: Key specifier often associated with Brief Psychotic Disorder?
cards.a: With marked stressors (brief reactive psychosis).

cards.q: DSM-5-TR duration criteria for Schizophreniform Disorder?
cards.a: At least 1 month but less than 6 months.

cards.q: Major diagnostic distinction between Schizophreniform Disorder and Schizophrenia?
cards.a: Schizophreniform requires a duration under 6 months and does not mandate social/occupational impairment.

cards.q: Core requirement for diagnosing Schizoaffective Disorder?
cards.a: An uninterrupted period of illness during which there is a major mood episode concurrent with Schizophrenia Criterion A symptoms.

cards.q: Essential rule for differentiating Schizoaffective Disorder from Mood Disorder with Psychotic Features?
cards.a: Delusions or hallucinations must be present for 2 or more weeks in the absence of a major mood episode.

cards.q: Name the two main diagnostic subtypes of Schizoaffective Disorder.
cards.a: Bipolar type (if a manic or mixed episode occurs) and Depressive type.

cards.q: Core DSM-5-TR requirement for Delusional Disorder?
cards.a: Presence of one or more delusions for a duration of 1 month or longer without other Criterion A schizophrenia symptoms.

cards.q: Relative level of global psychosocial functioning in Delusional Disorder compared to Schizophrenia?
cards.a: Functioning is significantly less impaired; behavior is not obviously bizarre outside the delusion.

cards.q: Define Erotomanic type Delusional Disorder.
cards.a: The central theme of the delusion is that another person (usually of higher status) is in love with the individual.

cards.q: Define Grandiose type Delusional Disorder.
cards.a: The conviction of having some great, unrecognized talent, insight, or important discovery.

cards.q: Define Jealous type Delusional Disorder.
cards.a: The central theme is that the individual's spouse or lover is unfaithful.

cards.q: Define Somatic type Delusional Disorder.
cards.a: The central theme involves bodily functions or sensations (e.g., foul odor, parasite infestation).

cards.q: Define Persecutory type Delusional Disorder.
cards.a: The belief that the individual is being conspired against, cheated, spied on, followed, or harassed.

cards.q: Subcortical dementia often presenting with prominent visual hallucinations and paranoid delusions early on?
cards.a: Lewy Body Dementia.

cards.q: Common neuroendocrine emergency characterized by neuropsychiatric symptoms, visual hallucinations, and autonomic instability?
cards.a: Thyroid storm (severe hyperthyroidism).

cards.q: Autoimmune encephalitis associated with ovarian teratomas presenting with rapid-onset psychosis and catatonia?
cards.a: Anti-NMDA receptor encephalitis.

cards.q: Infectious disease screening labs required for all new-onset psychosis workups?
cards.a: RPR/VDRL (Syphilis) and HIV serology.

cards.q: Vital urine laboratory screening test for any acute first-episode psychosis evaluation?
cards.a: Urine toxicology screen (to rule out substance-induced psychosis).

cards.q: Primary mechanism of action of First-Generation (Typical) Antipsychotics?
cards.a: Strong, competitive post-synaptic antagonism of Dopamine $\text{D}_2$ receptors.

cards.q: Pathway targeted by Typical Antipsychotics to resolve positive symptoms?
cards.a: Mesolimbic pathway.

cards.q: Pathway blocked by Typical Antipsychotics that induces Extrapyramidal Symptoms (EPS)?
cards.a: Nigrostriatal pathway.

cards.q: Name two classic high-potency first-generation antipsychotics.
cards.a: Haloperidol and Fluphenazine.

cards.q: Name two classic low-potency first-generation antipsychotics.
cards.a: Chlorpromazine and Thioridazine.

cards.q: High-potency vs. low-potency first-generation antipsychotics side effect profiles?
cards.a: High-potency have more EPS; low-potency have more antihistaminic, anticholinergic, and $\alpha_1$ antiadrenergic effects.

cards.q: Specific ophthalmic complication unique to long-term Chlorpromazine use?
cards.a: Corneal and lens deposits.

cards.q: Specific ophthalmic complication unique to long-term Thioridazine use?
cards.a: Retinitis pigmentosa.

cards.q: Four main categories of Extrapyramidal Symptoms (EPS)?
cards.a: Acute dystonia, akathisia, parkinsonism, and tardive dyskinesia.

cards.q: Timeframe for development of acute dystonia?
cards.a: Hours to days after starting or increasing medication.

cards.q: Presentation of acute dystonia?
cards.a: Sustained, painful muscle contractions of the neck (torticollis), jaw (trismus), or eyes (oculogyric crisis).

cards.q: Preferred first-line pharmacological treatment for acute dystonia?
cards.a: Benztropine or Diphenhydramine (intravenous or intramuscular).

cards.q: Define akathisia.
cards.a: Subjective feeling of intense inner restlessness and objective inability to sit still.

cards.q: First-line medical treatments for akathisia?
cards.a: $\beta$-blocker (Propranolol) or low-dose Benzodiazepines.

cards.q: Symptoms of antipsychotic-induced parkinsonism?
cards.a: Bradykinesia, rigidity, masked facies, and a resting pill-rolling tremor.

cards.q: Pharmacological management for antipsychotic-induced parkinsonism?
cards.a: Benztropine or Amantadine.

cards.q: Why should Levodopa never be used to treat antipsychotic-induced parkinsonism?
cards.a: It increases dopamine levels and will severely exacerbate the underlying psychosis.

cards.q: Timeframe for development of Tardive Dyskinesia?
cards.a: Months to years of chronic antipsychotic exposure.

cards.q: Classic visual presentation of Tardive Dyskinesia?
cards.a: Involuntary, choreoathetoid movements of the tongue, face, lips (puckering), or trunk.

cards.q: Underlying pathophysiology of Tardive Dyskinesia?
cards.a: Upregulation and supersensitivity of postsynaptic $\text{D}_2$ receptors in the nigrostriatal pathway.

cards.q: Initial step in managing Tardive Dyskinesia if clinically feasible?
cards.a: Discontinue or taper the typical antipsychotic, or switch the patient to Clozapine.

cards.q: FDA-approved drug class for the targeted treatment of Tardive Dyskinesia?
cards.a: VMAT2 inhibitors (Valbenazine or Deutetrabenazine).

cards.q: Pathway blocked by antipsychotics that leads to hyperprolactinemia?
cards.a: Tuberoinfundibular pathway.

cards.q: Clinical manifestations of hyperprolactinemia in males and females?
cards.a: Gynecomastia, galactorrhea, amenorrhea, and erectile dysfunction.

cards.q: Life-threatening idiosyncratic reaction to antipsychotics marked by rigidity, hyperthermia, and autonomic instability?
cards.a: Neuroleptic Malignant Syndrome (NMS).

cards.q: Key laboratory marker highly elevated in Neuroleptic Malignant Syndrome?
cards.a: Creatine Phosphokinase (CPK).

cards.q: First management steps for Neuroleptic Malignant Syndrome?
cards.a: Immediately discontinue the offending agent, initiate aggressive cooling, and provide IV hydration.

cards.q: Two specific medications used to treat severe cases of Neuroleptic Malignant Syndrome?
cards.a: Dantrolene (skeletal muscle relaxant) and Bromocriptine (dopamine agonist).

cards.q: Primary mechanism of action of Second-Generation (Atypical) Antipsychotics?
cards.a: Combined Dopamine $\text{D}_2$ antagonism and Serotonin $\text{$\text{5-HT}$}_{2\text{A}}$ receptor antagonism.

cards.q: Main clinical advantage of second-generation over first-generation antipsychotics?
cards.a: Significantly lower incidence of extrapyramidal symptoms (EPS) and tardive dyskinesia.

cards.q: Primary long-term metabolic risk profile of second-generation antipsychotics?
cards.a: Weight gain, dyslipidemia, hyperglycemia, and new-onset Type 2 Diabetes.

cards.q: Two atypical antipsychotics carrying the highest risk for metabolic syndrome?
cards.a: Olanzapine and Clozapine.

cards.q: Two atypical antipsychotics carrying the lowest risk for metabolic syndrome?
cards.a: Ziprasidone and Aripiprazole.

cards.q: Specific cardiac risk assessment mandatory for patients taking Ziprasidone?
cards.a: Electrocardiogram (EKG) monitoring for corrected QT (QTc) interval prolongation.

cards.q: Unique mechanism of action of Aripiprazole?
cards.a: Partial $\text{D}_2$ receptor agonist, partial $\text{$\text{5-HT}$}_{1\text{A}}$ agonist, and $\text{$\text{5-HT}$}_{2\text{A}}$ antagonist.

cards.q: Specific side effect most frequently associated with Risperidone among the atypicals?
cards.a: Significant hyperprolactinemia, even at lower doses.

cards.q: Atypical antipsychotic noted for causing significant sedation and cataracts in animal studies, requiring baseline eye exams?
cards.a: Quetiapine.

cards.q: Absolute gold-standard indication for initiating Clozapine therapy?
cards.a: Treatment-resistant schizophrenia (failure of two separate adequate antipsychotic trials).

cards.q: Only antipsychotic proven to significantly reduce the risk of suicidal behavior in schizophrenia?
cards.a: Clozapine.

cards.q: Most dangerous, black-box warning hematologic side effect of Clozapine?
cards.a: Agranulocytosis (absolute neutrophil count drops below 500/microliter).

cards.q: Mandatory laboratory monitoring protocol required for prescribing Clozapine?
cards.a: Regular tracking of absolute neutrophil count (ANC) via the Clozapine REMS program.

cards.q: Severe, non-hematologic, dose-dependent neurological side effect of Clozapine?
cards.a: Seizures.

cards.q: Gastrointestinal black-box warning associated with Clozapine that can become fatal if missed?
cards.a: Severe gastrointestinal hypomotility (paralytic ileus/fecal impaction).

cards.q: Cardiovascular emergency linked to Clozapine initiation requiring monitoring of troponins and CRP?
cards.a: Myocarditis or cardiomyopathy.

cards.q: Common, bothersome nocturnal side effect reported by patients taking Clozapine?
cards.a: Sialorrhea (excessive drooling).

cards.q: Preferred medication formulation utilized to improve treatment adherence in non-compliant schizophrenia patients?
cards.a: Long-Acting Injectable (LAI) antipsychotics (depot formulations).

cards.q: Name two atypical antipsychotics available as Long-Acting Injectables (LAIs).
cards.a: Risperidone, Paliperidone, or Olanzapine.

cards.q: Dangerous medical emergency that can occur immediately post-injection with Olanzapine pamoate LAI?
cards.a: Post-injection delirium sedation syndrome.

cards.q: Define the prodromal phase of Schizophrenia.
cards.a: A period of subclinical decline characterized by social withdrawal, irritability, uncharacteristic odd beliefs, and poor hygiene prior to the first active psychotic episode.

cards.q: Single strongest overall predictor of a poor prognosis in Schizophrenia?
cards.a: Insidious onset during early childhood or adolescence.

cards.q: List three features predictive of a good prognosis in Schizophrenia.
cards.a: Acute onset, clear precipitating stressors, late age of onset, and prominent positive symptoms.

cards.q: Impact of active substance abuse on the prognosis of Schizophrenia?
cards.a: Substantially worsens the course, increases relapse rates, and lowers medication adherence.

cards.q: Leading cause of premature death in patients diagnosed with Schizophrenia?
cards.a: Suicide.

cards.q: Lifetime percentage of Schizophrenia patients who attempt suicide?
cards.a: Approximately 20% to 40%.

cards.q: Specific demographic subset of Schizophrenia patients at the highest risk for suicide?
cards.a: Young, highly intelligent males with high premorbid functioning who have insight into their functional decline.

cards.q: Primary purpose of Cognitive Behavioral Therapy for Psychosis (CBTp)?
cards.a: To reduce the distress and functional impairment caused by persistent positive symptoms, rather than eliminating them entirely.

cards.q: Family dynamic factor strongly correlated with high relapse and re-hospitalization rates in Schizophrenia?
cards.a: High Expressed Emotion (criticism, hostility, and emotional over-involvement).

cards.q: Evidence-based community treatment model utilizing a multidisciplinary team to deliver 24/7 comprehensive care directly to severe schizophrenia patients in real-world settings?
cards.a: Assertive Community Treatment (ACT).

cards.q: Recommended psychosocial intervention designed to improve real-world interpersonal interactions and independence?
cards.a: Social Skills Training (SST).

cards.q: What is the primary role of electroconvulsive therapy (ECT) within the psychotic disorders spectrum?
cards.a: Augmented treatment for severe catatonia or treatment-resistant schizophrenia with comorbid depression.

cards.q: Neurological disease presenting with chorea and early psychiatric symptoms like psychosis and depression?
cards.a: Huntington's Disease.

cards.q: Trinucleotide repeat expansion mutation responsible for Huntington's Disease?
cards.a: CAG repeats on chromosome 4.

cards.q: Metabolic disorder presenting with psychosis, abdominal pain, neuropathy, and dark purple urine?
cards.a: Acute Intermittent Porphyria.

cards.q: Deficient enzyme responsible for Acute Intermittent Porphyria?
cards.a: Porphobilinogen deaminase.

cards.q: Heavy metal poisoning presenting with psychosis, a blue-gray line on the gums, and foot drop?
cards.a: Lead poisoning.

cards.q: Vitamin deficiency classically presenting with psychosis, macrocytic anemia, and subacute combined degeneration of the spinal cord?
cards.a: Vitamin B12 (Cobalamin) deficiency.

cards.q: Central nervous system infection to suspect in a patient with psychosis, Argyll Robertson pupils, and loss of proprioception?
cards.a: Neurosyphilis (Tertiary Syphilis).

cards.q: Define Argyll Robertson pupil.
cards.a: Pupils that constrict during accommodation but do not react to light.

cards.q: Endocrine disorder presenting with psychosis, weight gain, coarse hair, and a delayed relaxation phase of deep tendon reflexes?
cards.a: Severe hypothyroidism ("myxedema madness").

cards.q: Illicit drug intoxication characterized by psychosis, extreme agitation, and rotary nystagmus?
cards.a: Phencyclidine (PCP) intoxication.

cards.q: Illicit drug intoxication characterized by paranoia, visual hallucinations, pupillary dilation, and tactile hallucinations like formication?
cards.a: Cocaine or Amphetamine intoxication.

cards.q: Define formication.
cards.a: The tactile hallucination or sensation that bugs are crawling on or under the skin.

cards.q: Over-the-counter medication class that can induce severe delirium, confusion, and visual hallucinations in elderly patients?
cards.a: Anticholinergics (e.g., Diphenhydramine).

cards.q: Prescription medication class frequently causing treatment-induced psychosis or mania in patients treated for inflammatory or autoimmune conditions?
cards.a: Corticosteroids (e.g., Prednisone).

cards.q: Life-threatening withdrawal state characterized by visual/tactile hallucinations, severe tremors, and autonomic instability 48 to 96 hours after the last drink?
cards.a: Delirium Tremens (Alcohol withdrawal delirium).

cards.q: Medical emergency characterized by hyperthermia, rigidity, and hyperreflexia/clonus when mixing psychotropic medications?
cards.a: Serotonin Syndrome.

cards.q: Main clinical differentiator between Serotonin Syndrome and Neuroleptic Malignant Syndrome (NMS)?
cards.a: Serotonin Syndrome features hyperreflexia and clonus; NMS features severe "lead-pipe" rigidity and hyporeflexia.

cards.q: Antipsychotic medication that requires a major dose reduction if the patient completely stops smoking tobacco cigarettes?
cards.a: Clozapine (or Olanzapine).

cards.q: Why does stopping smoking alter Clozapine metabolism?
cards.a: Tobacco smoke induces the CYP1A2 enzyme; stopping smoke expression rapidly increases Clozapine blood concentrations.

cards.q: Atypical antipsychotic that is the active metabolite of Risperidone?
cards.a: Paliperidone.

cards.q: Atypical antipsychotic that must always be taken with food to ensure adequate gastrointestinal absorption?
cards.a: Ziprasidone (requires at least 500 calories) or Lurasidone (requires at least 350 calories).

cards.q: Mechanism by which low-potency antipsychotics cause severe orthostatic hypotension?
cards.a: Antagonism of peripheral $\alpha_1$ adrenergic receptors.

cards.q: Baseline metabolic tracking labs required prior to initiating any Second-Generation Antipsychotic?
cards.a: Fasting lipid panel, fasting blood glucose (or HbA1c), weight/BMI, and blood pressure.

cards.q: Follow-up timeframe recommended by the ADA for checking lipids and blood glucose after starting an atypical antipsychotic?
cards.a: At 12 weeks, and then annually thereafter.

cards.q: Quantitative QTc interval threshold on an EKG where antipsychotics should typically be held or discontinued?
cards.a: A QTc interval greater than 500 milliseconds.

cards.q: Severe cardiac arrhythmia that a prolonged QTc interval predisposes a patient to develop?
cards.a: Torsades de Pointes.

cards.q: Baseline laboratory test required before starting Clozapine to rule out benign baseline patterns?
cards.a: Baseline Absolute Neutrophil Count (ANC).

cards.q: Absolute Neutrophil Count (ANC) cutoff value below which Clozapine must be immediately discontinued?
cards.a: An ANC less than 1,000/microliter (or less than 500/microliter in verified benign ethnic neutropenia).

cards.q: Define the "Deficit Syndrome" variant of Schizophrenia.
cards.a: A subtype characterized by severe, enduring, primary negative symptoms that persist even during periods of clinical stability.

cards.q: Association between the Deficit Syndrome and overall long-term prognosis?
cards.a: It carries a significantly poorer prognosis and is highly resistant to standard antipsychotic treatments.

cards.q: What is the diagnostic significance of "Post-psychotic Depression" in Schizophrenia?
cards.a: A major depressive episode that emerges during the residual phase of schizophrenia, carrying an exceptionally high risk for suicide.

cards.q: Electroencephalogram (EEG) changes typically observed in patients with chronic Schizophrenia?
cards.a: Non-specific focal abnormalities, localized slowing, and decreased $\alpha$ wave activity.

cards.q: Polysomnography (Sleep Study) architectural changes characteristically seen in Schizophrenia?
cards.a: Decreased slow-wave sleep (Stage N3) and shortened REM latency.

cards.q: Neurological soft signs commonly found on physical exam in patients with schizophrenia spectrum disorders?
cards.a: Impaired left-right confusion, poor stereognosis, agraphesthesia, and dysdiadochokinesia.

cards.q: Define stereognosis.
cards.a: The ability to perceive and recognize the form of an object in the absence of visual and auditory information, by using tactile sensations.

cards.q: Define agraphesthesia.
cards.a: The inability to recognize symbols, letters, or numbers traced on the skin.

cards.q: Eye-tracking physical exam abnormality heavily studied and linked as an endophenotype for Schizophrenia?
cards.a: Impairment in smooth-pursuit eye movements.

cards.q: Clinical strategy used when switching a patient from a high-metabolic atypical antipsychotic to a low-metabolic one?
cards.a: Cross-titration (gradually tapering the old medication while slowly uptitrating the new one over weeks).

cards.q: Why is an immediate, abrupt switch from Olanzapine to Aripiprazole dangerous?
cards.a: It can cause a rebound cholinergic crisis or an acute exacerbation of psychosis due to sudden $\text{D}_2$ receptor unbinding.

cards.q: Symptoms of a rebound cholinergic crisis following abrupt withdrawal of low-potency or highly sedating antipsychotics?
cards.a: Diaphoresis, nausea, vomiting, diarrhea, and severe insomnia.

cards.q: Antipsychotic medication that possesses the unique property of having a highly prolonged half-life, making missing occasional doses less critical?
cards.a: Cariprazine.

cards.q: Atypical antipsychotic noted for a very low affinity for $\text{D}_2$ receptors and rapid dissociation, making it ideal for treating psychosis in Parkinson's Disease?
cards.a: Pimavanserin (or low-dose Quetiapine).

cards.q: Mechanism of action of Pimavanserin?
cards.a: Inverse agonist and antagonist at Serotonin $\text{$\text{5-HT}$}_{2\text{A}}$ receptors, completely lacking dopamine $\text{D}_2$ blockade.

cards.q: Drug-drug interaction risk when combining an atypical antipsychotic with a strong CYP3A4 inhibitor like Clarithromycin or Ketoconazole?
cards.a: Substantially increased antipsychotic serum levels, markedly elevating the risk of QTc prolongation and toxicity.

cards.q: Drug-drug interaction risk when combining Clozapine with Carbamazepine?
cards.a: Synergistic bone marrow suppression, exponentially increasing the risk of life-threatening agranulocytosis.

cards.q: Serious respiratory side effect of high-dose low-potency typical antipsychotics used in elderly patients with dementia-related psychosis?
cards.a: Increased risk of aspiration pneumonia due to impaired swallowing reflexes.

cards.q: Black Box warning shared by all antipsychotics regarding their use in elderly patients with dementia-related behavioral disturbances?
cards.a: Increased risk of all-cause mortality, primarily due to cardiovascular events (stroke, heart failure) or infectious complications.

cards.q: Primary legal justification allowing a physician to place a patient on an involuntary psychiatric hold?
cards.a: The presence of a mental illness causing the patient to be an imminent danger to themselves, an imminent danger to others, or gravely disabled.

cards.q: Does an involuntary psychiatric hold automatically give the physician the right to force medications against the patient's will?
cards.a: No, an involuntary hold and the right to refuse medication are legally distinct entities requiring separate legal or administrative review.

cards.q: Landmark legal case establishing that a psychiatrist has a "duty to protect" third parties from a patient's violent threats?
cards.a: Tarasoff v. Regents of the University of California.

cards.q: Next immediate step if a patient with active command auditory hallucinations to harm a named individual demands to sign out of the hospital?
cards.a: Deny the request, initiate an involuntary hold, and notify both law enforcement and the intended victim.

cards.q: Contrast medical "competence" versus medical "capacity".
cards.a: Competence is a legal determination made exclusively by a judge; capacity is a clinical assessment made by a treating physician.

cards.q: Four foundational elements required to determine that a psychiatric patient has decision-making capacity?
cards.a: The ability to communicate a clear choice, understand the relevant medical facts, appreciate the clinical consequences, and rationally manipulate the information.

topic: Anxiety disorders — GAD, panic, PTSD, OCD

cards.q: Minimum duration of symptoms required for a DSM-5-TR diagnosis of Generalized Anxiety Disorder (GAD)?
cards.a: Six months.

cards.q: Number of associated somatic symptoms required for adults to diagnose GAD under DSM-5-TR?
cards.a: At least three symptoms.

cards.q: Number of associated somatic symptoms required for children to diagnose GAD under DSM-5-TR?
cards.a: Only one symptom.

cards.q: List the six DSM-5-TR somatic symptoms associated with GAD.
cards.a: Restlessness, fatigue, difficulty concentrating, irritability, muscle tension, and sleep disturbance.

cards.q: Pathophysiological brain region showing hyperactivation in GAD during emotional processing?
cards.a: Amygdala.

cards.q: Pathophysiological brain region showing structural and functional hypoactivation in GAD?
cards.a: Prefrontal cortex.

cards.q: First-line pharmacotherapy classes for the long-term management of GAD?
cards.a: SSRIs and SNRIs.

cards.q: Non-benzodiazepine anxiolytic that acts as a $\text{$\text{5-HT}$}_{1\text{A}}$ receptor partial agonist?
cards.a: Buspirone.

cards.q: Timeframe required for buspirone to achieve therapeutic efficacy in GAD?
cards.a: Two to four weeks.

cards.q: Primary clinical limitation of using benzodiazepines in the long-term management of GAD?
cards.a: Risk of physiological dependence, tolerance, and withdrawal.

cards.q: First-line, evidence-based psychotherapy modality for GAD?
cards.a: Cognitive Behavioral Therapy (CBT).

cards.q: $\alpha_2$-$\delta$ ligand anticonvulsant frequently used off-label as a highly effective agent for GAD?
cards.a: Pregabalin.

cards.q: Common $\beta$-blocker used primarily for the autonomic, somatic symptoms of performance anxiety rather than generalized anxiety?
cards.a: Propranolol.

cards.q: Minimum frequency and nature of panic attacks required for Panic Disorder diagnosis?
cards.a: Recurrent and unexpected panic attacks.

cards.q: Timeframe and criteria required following a panic attack to meet Panic Disorder diagnosis?
cards.a: One month or more of persistent worry about future attacks or maladaptive behavioral changes.

cards.q: Minimum number of physical or cognitive symptoms required to define a distinct panic attack?
cards.a: Four symptoms.

cards.q: List four cognitive symptoms that can count toward a DSM-5 panic attack definition.
cards.a: Fear of losing control, fear of going crazy, derealization/depersonalization, and fear of dying.

cards.q: Define agoraphobia according to the DSM-5-TR.
cards.a: Marked fear or anxiety about two or more public situations where escape might be difficult.

cards.q: Neuroanatomical structure considered the "panic center" or primary source of norepinephrine in panic attacks?
cards.a: Locus coeruleus.

cards.q: Acute, immediate pharmacological intervention for a patient experiencing a severe, disabling panic attack?
cards.a: Short-acting benzodiazepines (e.g., Alprazolam, Lorazepam).

cards.q: Gold-standard, first-line long-term maintenance pharmacotherapy for Panic Disorder?
cards.a: SSRIs (started at low doses to avoid initial activation/anxiety).

cards.q: Specific CBT technique involving deliberate exposure to feared bodily sensations to treat panic disorder?
cards.a: Interoceptive exposure.

cards.q: Medical emergency or toxic state that can perfectly mimic a panic attack and must be ruled out via TSH?
cards.a: Hyperthyroidism.

cards.q: Substance abuse/withdrawal state that can acutely precipitate panic attacks?
cards.a: Caffeine intoxication or Alcohol withdrawal.

cards.q: Acid-base disturbance characteristically seen on an ABG during an acute panic attack due to hyperventilation?
cards.a: Respiratory alkalosis.

cards.q: Minimum age required to apply standard DSM-5-TR PTSD criteria?
cards.a: Six years of age.

cards.q: Minimum symptom duration required for a diagnosis of Post-Traumatic Stress Disorder (PTSD)?
cards.a: One month.

cards.q: Diagnosis given if PTSD-like symptoms present after a trauma but resolve within one month?
cards.a: Acute Stress Disorder (ASD).

cards.q: Minimum and maximum timeframe for a diagnosis of Acute Stress Disorder?
cards.a: Three days to one month following trauma exposure.

cards.q: Four core symptom clusters required for the diagnosis of PTSD?
cards.a: Intrusion, Avoidance, Negative alterations in cognition/mood, and Alterations in arousal/reactivity.

cards.q: Neuroendocrine abnormality characteristically seen in the HPA axis of PTSD patients?
cards.a: Hypocortisolemia due to enhanced glucocorticoid receptor sensitivity.

cards.q: Structural brain changes classically observed on neuroimaging in chronic PTSD patients?
cards.a: Decreased hippocampal volume.

cards.q: Only two FDA-approved SSRIs for the treatment of PTSD?
cards.a: Sertraline and Paroxetine.

cards.q: $\alpha_1$ adrenergic antagonist used specifically to target trauma-related nightmares and sleep disruption in PTSD?
cards.a: Prazosin.

cards.q: Most prominent side effect of Prazosin that requires nighttime titration?
cards.a: Orthostatic hypotension.

cards.q: Preferred specialized trauma-focused psychotherapies for PTSD?
cards.a: Prolonged Exposure (PE) and Eye Movement Desensitization and Reprocessing (EMDR).

cards.q: Class of medications strictly avoided or contraindicated in PTSD due to high substance abuse comorbidity and lack of efficacy?
cards.a: Benzodiazepines.

cards.q: Timeframe required to diagnose an Adjustment Disorder following an identifiable stressor?
cards.a: Development within three months of the stressor, resolving within six months of stressor termination.

cards.q: Definition of an obsession in OCD?
cards.a: Recurrent, persistent, intrusive thoughts, urges, or images causing marked anxiety.

cards.q: Definition of a compulsion in OCD?
cards.a: Repetitive behaviors or mental acts performed in response to an obsession or rigid rules.

cards.q: Minimum time-consuming threshold required by DSM-5-TR for OCD symptoms?
cards.a: Symptoms take up more than one hour per day.

cards.q: Define "egodystonic" as it applies to the obsessions in OCD.
cards.a: The thoughts are inconsistent with the patient's self-concept and are perceived as unacceptable.

cards.q: Core differentiator between OCD and Obsessive-Compulsive Personality Disorder (OCPD)?
cards.a: OCD is egodystonic (distressing to self); OCPD is egosyntonic (perceived as correct/ideal by the patient).

cards.q: Primary neurobiological circuit implicated in the pathogenesis of OCD?
cards.a: Cortico-striato-thalamo-cortical (CSTC) circuit.

cards.q: First-line pharmacotherapy class for OCD?
cards.a: SSRIs.

cards.q: Dosing strategy difference for SSRIs in OCD compared to Major Depressive Disorder?
cards.a: OCD requires significantly higher doses of SSRIs.

cards.q: Gold-standard tricyclic antidepressant (TCA) used for treatment-resistant OCD?
cards.a: Clomipramine.

cards.q: Primary neurotransmitter mechanism of Clomipramine?
cards.a: Potent serotonin reuptake inhibition (most serotonin-selective TCA).

cards.q: Most effective, specialized behavioral therapy technique used for OCD?
cards.a: Exposure and Response Prevention (ERP).

cards.q: Neurodevelopmental condition characterized by sudden-onset OCD or tics following a Group A Streptococcal infection?
cards.a: PANDAS (Pediatric Autoimmune Neuropsychiatric Disorders Associated with Streptococcal Infections).

cards.q: FDA-approved second-line augmentation strategy for OCD patients not fully responding to SSRIs?
cards.a: Atypical antipsychotics (e.g., Risperidone, Aripiprazole).

cards.q: Neurosurgical or neuromodulatory intervention approved for severe, intractable, treatment-resistant OCD?
cards.a: Deep Brain Stimulation (DBS) or Anterior Cingulotomy.

cards.q: Mechanism of action of Venlafaxine at low doses (less than 150mg/day)?
cards.a: Almost exclusive serotonin reuptake inhibition (behaves like an SSRI).

cards.q: Mechanism of action of Venlafaxine at high doses (greater than 150mg/day)?
cards.a: Dual serotonin and norepinephrine reuptake inhibition (true SNRI).

cards.q: Most critical vital sign to monitor in patients taking high-dose Venlafaxine or Duloxetine?
cards.a: Blood pressure (risk of dose-dependent diastolic hypertension).

cards.q: Unique mechanism of action of Mirtazapine?
cards.a: $\alpha_2$ adrenergic antagonist, $\text{$\text{5-HT}$}_{2}$ and $\text{$\text{5-HT}$}_{3}$ receptor antagonist, and $\text{H}_1$ histamine antagonist.

cards.q: Two most prominent side effects of low-dose Mirtazapine due to its $\text{H}_1$ affinity?
cards.a: Sedation and weight gain.

cards.q: Life-threatening condition characterized by autonomic instability, altered mental status, and neuromuscular hyperactivity caused by combining SSRIs and MAOIs?
cards.a: Serotonin Syndrome.

cards.q: Required washout period when switching from an SSRI (except Fluoxetine) to an MAOI?
cards.a: Two weeks.

cards.q: Required washout period when switching from Fluoxetine to an MAOI due to its long half-life?
cards.a: Five to six weeks.

cards.q: Active metabolite of Fluoxetine that accounts for its exceptionally long half-life?
cards.a: Norfluoxetine.

cards.q: SSRI with the shortest half-life and highest risk for SSRI Discontinuation Syndrome?
cards.a: Paroxetine.

cards.q: SSRI with the highest risk of congenital cardiac defects (Ebstein's anomaly/septal defects) if used in the first trimester?
cards.a: Paroxetine.

cards.q: Distinctive EKG abnormality associated with high doses of Citalopram and Escitalopram?
cards.a: QTc prolongation.

cards.q: Maximum recommended daily dose of Citalopram in geriatric patients to avoid arrhythmias?
cards.a: Twenty milligrams.

cards.q: Benzodiazepine with an exceptionally long half-life and active metabolites, making it a poor choice for elderly patients?
cards.a: Diazepam.

cards.q: Three benzodiazepines that undergo only phase II hepatic glucuronidation, making them safe for liver failure patients?
cards.a: Lorazepam, Oxazepam, Temazepam (Mnemonic: Outside The Liver).

cards.q: Flumazenil mechanism of action?
cards.a: Competitive antagonist at the benzodiazepine receptor site on the $\text{GABA}_\text{A}$ complex.

cards.q: Primary danger of administering Flumazenil to a patient with chronic benzodiazepine dependence?
cards.a: Induction of acute, life-threatening withdrawal seizures.

cards.q: Fatal medical risk of severe benzodiazepine withdrawal?
cards.a: Status epilepticus and cardiovascular collapse.

cards.q: Diagnosis for a patient with episodic, unprovoked shortness of breath, chest pain, and fear of dying, with normal cardiac enzymes and EKG?
cards.a: Panic Disorder.

cards.q: Diagnostic consideration for an elderly patient presenting with new-onset anxiety or panic symptoms for the first time in life?
cards.a: Anxiety secondary to a general medical condition or neurocognitive disorder.

cards.q: Lab test to order when a young female presents with panic symptoms, weight loss, and lid lag?
cards.a: Thyroid Stimulating Hormone (TSH).

cards.q: Rare neuroendocrine tumor of the adrenal medulla that can perfectly mimic a panic disorder?
cards.a: Pheochromocytoma.

cards.q: Screening lab test required to rule out Pheochromocytoma?
cards.a: Plasma free metanephrines or 24-hour urinary metanephrines.

cards.q: Over-the-counter medication class that can acutely cause anxiety, tachycardia, and insomnia?
cards.a: Sympathomimetics (e.g., Pseudoephedrine).

cards.q: Cardiac valvular abnormality heavily associated with panic disorder in clinical epidemiology?
cards.a: Mitral Valve Prolapse (MVP).

cards.q: Differentiator between Social Anxiety Disorder and Agoraphobia?
cards.a: Social anxiety is driven by fear of scrutiny/humiliation; agoraphobia is driven by fear of being unable to escape.

cards.q: Diagnosis for a patient who fears and avoids eating in public or public speaking due to fear of embarrassment?
cards.a: Social Anxiety Disorder (Social Phobia).

cards.q: First-line pharmacotherapy option for the performance-only subtype of Social Anxiety Disorder?
cards.a: $\beta$-blocker (Propranolol) or short-acting benzodiazepines.

cards.q: Contraindication for using Propranolol in a patient with performance anxiety?
cards.a: Asthma or severe chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD).

cards.q: Core feature of Body Dysmorphic Disorder (BDD) that classifies it under the OCD-related disorders spectrum?
cards.a: Preoccupation with perceived flaws in physical appearance coupled with repetitive behaviors.

cards.q: Diagnosis for a patient who persistently collects items regardless of value and experiences severe distress when attempting to discard them?
cards.a: Hoarding Disorder.

cards.q: Hair-pulling disorder categorized under the DSM-5-TR Obsessive-Compulsive and Related Disorders section?
cards.a: Trichotillomania.

cards.q: Primary defense mechanism employed in OCD where a patient separates an idea/thought from its emotional component?
cards.a: Isolation of affect.

cards.q: Defense mechanism where an unacceptable impulse is converted into its exact opposite (common in OCD spectrum)?
cards.a: Reaction Formation.

cards.q: Defense mechanism where an individual tries to counteract or "make up for" an unacceptable thought or action with a ritualistic behavior?
cards.a: Undoing.

cards.q: Most common comorbidity found in individuals diagnosed with Tourette's Disorder?
cards.a: ADHD and OCD.

cards.q: Definition of "poor insight" specifier in DSM-5 anxiety/OCD disorders?
cards.a: The patient thinks the disorder beliefs are probably true.

cards.q: Definition of "absent/delusional insight" specifier in OCD?
cards.a: The patient is completely convinced that the OCD beliefs are definitely true.

cards.q: Primary reason why patients with GAD frequently present to primary care clinics instead of psychiatry?
cards.a: They present primarily with physical, somatic complaints (headaches, GI distress, muscle pain).

cards.q: Diagnostic label for a patient exhibiting severe anxiety, hyperarousal, and flashbacks two weeks after a near-fatal motor vehicle accident?
cards.a: Acute Stress Disorder.

cards.q: Diagnostic label if the same motor vehicle accident patient still has flashbacks and hyperarousal six months later?
cards.a: Post-Traumatic Stress Disorder.

cards.q: Timeline requirement for the diagnosis of Selective Mutism?
cards.a: Consistent failure to speak in specific social situations lasting at least one month (not limited to the first month of school).

cards.q: First-line behavioral therapy for Trichotillomania?
cards.a: Habit Reversal Training (HRT).

cards.q: Standard first-line medical therapy for Excoriation (skin-picking) disorder?
cards.a: SSRIs and Cognitive Behavioral Therapy.

cards.q: First-line non-pharmacological strategy for a pediatric patient with mild Separation Anxiety Disorder?
cards.a: Parent-Child Interaction Therapy (PCIT) or family-focused CBT.

cards.q: Major risk factor for the development of Panic Disorder in adulthood?
cards.a: History of childhood separation anxiety disorder or early childhood trauma.

cards.q: Substance intoxication that causes pupillary dilation, tachycardia, hypertension, and profound acute paranoia/anxiety?
cards.a: Cocaine or Amphetamine intoxication.

cards.q: Substance withdrawal state presenting with severe anxiety, tremors, diaphoresis, and elevated vitals within 48 hours of cessation?
cards.a: Alcohol or Sedative-Hypnotic withdrawal.

cards.q: Mechanism of action of Vilazodone?
cards.a: SSRI plus $\text{$\text{5-HT}$}_{1\text{A}}$ receptor partial agonist.

cards.q: Mechanism of action of Vortioxetine?
