cards.a: SSRI, $\text{$\text{5-HT}$}_{1\text{A}}$ agonist, $\text{$\text{5-HT}$}_{1\text{B}}$ partial agonist, and $\text{$\text{5-HT}$}_{3}$/$\text{$\text{5-HT}$}_{7}$/$\text{$\text{5-HT}$}_{1\text{D}}$ antagonist.

cards.q: Primary clinical advantage of Vilazodone and Vortioxetine over traditional SSRIs?
cards.a: Lower incidence of sexual dysfunction.

cards.q: Receptor antagonism responsible for the orthostatic hypotension caused by low-potency antipsychotics or TCAs?
cards.a: $\alpha_1$ adrenergic receptor antagonism.

cards.q: Receptor antagonism responsible for weight gain and sedation in psychotropic medications?
cards.a: Histamine $\text{H}_1$ receptor antagonism.

cards.q: Anticonvulsant that acts as a positive allosteric modulator of $\text{GABA}_\text{A}$ receptors, sometimes used for refractory anxiety?
cards.a: Phenobarbital or Topiramate (off-label).

cards.q: Why is Buspirone ineffective when used "as-needed" (PRN) for acute panic or anxiety spikes?
cards.a: It requires chronic daily administration to downregulate presynaptic $\text{$\text{5-HT}$}_{1\text{A}}$ autoreceptors.

cards.q: Major drug-drug interaction risk when combining SSRIs with NSAIDs?
cards.a: Increased risk of upper gastrointestinal bleeding due to impaired platelet serotonin reuptake.

cards.q: Primary Cytochrome P450 enzyme inhibited by Fluoxetine and Paroxetine?
cards.a: CYP2D6.

cards.q: Primary Cytochrome P450 enzyme inhibited by Fluvoxamine?
cards.a: CYP1A2 and CYP2C19.

cards.q: Most sedating SSRI, often dosed at bedtime, due to mild anticholinergic and antihistaminergic properties?
cards.a: Paroxetine.

cards.q: Most activating SSRI, often dosed in the morning, due to its $\text{$\text{5-HT}$}_{2\text{C}}$ antagonist properties?
cards.a: Fluoxetine.

cards.q: Non-benzodiazepine, sedating antihistamine frequently used PRN for acute mild anxiety or insomnia in substance abuse populations?
cards.a: Hydroxyzine.

cards.q: Serious neurological side effect of long-term benzodiazepine use in the geriatric population?
cards.a: Cognitive impairment, anterograde amnesia, and increased risk of falls/fractures.

cards.q: Serious paradoxical reaction to benzodiazepines most commonly observed in children and the elderly?
cards.a: Paradoxical excitement, disinhibition, and aggression.

cards.q: Antidepressant absolutely contraindicated in patients with an active or past diagnosis of Bulimia or Anorexia Nervosa due to seizure risk?
cards.a: Bupropion.

cards.q: Mechanism of action of Ramelteon, sometimes used for insomnia in anxiety patients?
cards.a: Melatonin MT1 and MT2 receptor agonist.

cards.q: Primary clinical sign of Buspirone toxicity?
cards.a: Dizziness, nausea, vomiting, and miosis.

cards.q: Why can SSRIs initially worsen anxiety or trigger panic attacks during the first week of treatment?
cards.a: Acute stimulation of $\text{$\text{5-HT}$}_{2\text{A}}$ and $\text{$\text{5-HT}$}_{2\text{C}}$ receptors in the limbic system before downregulation occurs.

cards.q: Strategy used to prevent early SSRI-induced activation anxiety in Panic Disorder patients?
cards.a: Start at half or a quarter of the standard antidepressant starting dose and titrate slowly.

cards.q: Mechanism of action of the anxiolytic drug Ashwagandha or other herbal remedies often asked about by patients?
cards.a: Weak $\text{GABA}_\text{A}$ receptor modulation and cortisol reduction (not standard first-line).

cards.q: Primary treatment for a patient with severe Benzodiazepine Discontinuation Syndrome?
cards.a: Re-institute the benzodiazepine and switch to a long-acting agent (like Clonazepam or Chlordiazepoxide) for a very gradual taper.

cards.q: Common somatic manifestation of GAD involving the musculoskeletal system?
cards.a: Chronic muscle tension, myofascial pain, and tension headaches.

cards.q: Diagnostic criteria difference for OCD specifier "with muscle tics"?
cards.a: Up to 30% of OCD patients have a comorbid tic disorder, which predicts a poorer response to standard SSRI therapy alone.

cards.q: Structural neuroimaging finding uniquely linked to severe, early-onset OCD?
cards.a: Caudate nucleus atrophy or structural asymmetry.

cards.q: First-line medical strategy for an OCD patient who fails two separate, optimized trials of different SSRIs?
cards.a: Switch to Clomipramine or augment the current SSRI with an atypical antipsychotic.

cards.q: Primary physiological reason behind the respiratory symptoms (suffocation feelings) in panic attacks according to the "false suffocation alarm" theory?
cards.a: Hypersensitivity of brainstem chemoreceptors to carbon dioxide ($CO_2$).

cards.q: Term used when a patient experiences panic symptoms that do not meet the full 4-symptom threshold?
cards.a: Limited-symptom panic attack.

cards.q: Diagnosis for an individual who develops severe anxiety and functional impairment after losing their job, lasting 4 months?
cards.a: Adjustment Disorder with Anxiety.

cards.q: Lifetime prevalence of Generalized Anxiety Disorder (GAD) in the United States population?
cards.a: Approximately 5% to 6%.

cards.q: Gender distribution ratio for Generalized Anxiety Disorder?
cards.a: Females are twice as likely to be diagnosed as males.

cards.q: Average age of onset for Generalized Anxiety Disorder?
cards.a: Late adolescence to early adulthood, though many patients report lifelong anxiety.

cards.q: Lifetime prevalence of Panic Disorder in the United States?
cards.a: Approximately 2% to 3%.

cards.q: Peak age range of onset for Panic Disorder?
cards.a: Late adolescence to the mid-30s.

cards.q: Gender distribution ratio for Panic Disorder?
cards.a: Females are twice as likely to be affected as males.

cards.q: Lifetime prevalence of Post-Traumatic Stress Disorder (PTSD) among adults in the United States?
cards.a: Approximately 7% to 8%.

cards.q: Highest prevalence rates of PTSD are found among which specific occupational or situational cohorts?
cards.a: Combat veterans, survivors of sexual assault, and first responders.

cards.q: Lifetime prevalence of Obsessive-Compulsive Disorder (OCD) in the general population?
cards.a: Approximately 2% to 3%.

cards.q: Mean age of onset for Obsessive-Compulsive Disorder?
cards.a: Around 19 to 20 years of age.

cards.q: Gender distribution of Obsessive-Compulsive Disorder in childhood versus adulthood?
cards.a: More common in boys during childhood, but equalizes between males and females in adulthood.

cards.q: Genetic heritability estimate for Obsessive-Compulsive Disorder?
cards.a: Approximately 40% to 50% in twin studies.

cards.q: DSM-5-TR specifier for Panic Disorder when panic attacks occur during sleep?
cards.a: Nocturnal panic attacks.

cards.q: Percentage of Panic Disorder patients who experience at least one nocturnal panic attack?
cards.a: Approximately 20% to 40%.

cards.q: DSM-5-TR PTSD specifier for patients presenting with prominent depersonalization or derealization?
cards.a: PTSD with dissociative symptoms.

cards.q: DSM-5-TR PTSD specifier applied when full diagnostic criteria are not met until at least 6 months after the traumatic event?
cards.a: PTSD with delayed expression.

cards.q: DSM-5-TR specifier for OCD when an individual recognizes that their OCD beliefs are definitely or probably not true?
cards.a: OCD with good or fair insight.

cards.q: DSM-5-TR specifier for OCD when an individual thinks their OCD beliefs are probably true?
cards.a: OCD with poor insight.

cards.q: DSM-5-TR specifier for OCD when an individual is completely convinced that their OCD beliefs are true?
cards.a: OCD with absent insight/delusional beliefs.

cards.q: DSM-5-TR specifier for OCD when an individual has a lifetime history of a chronic tic disorder?
cards.a: OCD with tic-related specifier.

cards.q: Expected treatment response for an OCD patient carrying the tic-related specifier?
cards.a: Poorer response to standard SSRIs alone, often requiring atypical antipsychotic augmentation.

cards.q: Neurotransmitter theory regarding GABA activity in patients with Generalized Anxiety Disorder?
cards.a: Decreased $\text{GABA}_\text{A}$ receptor binding or overall GABAergic hypoactivity.

cards.q: Neurotransmitter abnormality involving serotonin ($5\text{-HT}$) and norepinephrine ($\text{NE}$) in GAD?
cards.a: Dysregulation and imbalance of both serotonin and norepinephrine pathways.

cards.q: Brain pathway that exhibits structural abnormalities in neuroimaging studies of Panic Disorder?
cards.a: Amygdala-prefrontal cortex fear circuit.

cards.q: Infusion of which substance can reliably precipitate a panic attack in a susceptible Panic Disorder patient in a laboratory setting?
cards.a: Sodium lactate or carbon dioxide ($CO_2$) inhalation.

cards.q: Physiological explanation for why sodium lactate triggers panic attacks?
cards.a: It induces metabolic alkalosis and alters central cheoreceptor sensitivity in the brainstem.

cards.q: Neurotransmitter changes found in the cerebrospinal fluid ($\text{CSF}$) of patients with chronic, severe PTSD?
cards.a: Increased norepinephrine concentrations and decreased serotonin metabolites.

cards.q: Functional neuroimaging finding in PTSD regarding the activity of the medial prefrontal cortex?
cards.a: Hypoactivity, leading to a failure to top-down inhibit an overactive amygdala.

cards.q: Neuroanatomical structure responsible for contextualizing memories that is functionally impaired in PTSD?
cards.a: Hippocampus.

cards.q: Neurotransmitter pathway targeted by the primary, first-line pharmacological agents used to treat OCD?
cards.a: Serotonergic pathway.

cards.q: Neuroimaging finding regarding glucose metabolism in the orbitofrontal cortex of untreated OCD patients?
cards.a: Hypermetabolism or hyperactivation.

cards.q: Function of the caudate nucleus within the cortico-striato-thalamo-cortical ($\text{CSTC}$) circuit that is faulty in OCD?
cards.a: Failure to filter out or "gate" intrusive, anxiety-provoking thoughts from reaching the cerebral cortex?

cards.q: Primary mechanism of action of Buspirone at the molecular level?
cards.a: Partial agonist at presynaptic and postsynaptic $5\text{-HT}_{1\text{A}}$ serotonin receptors.

cards.q: Why does Buspirone lack abuse potential compared to benzodiazepines?
cards.a: It does not modulate the GABA receptor complex and has no dopaminergic reward pathway activity.

cards.q: Mechanism of action of Hydroxyzine when used for acute anxiety management?
cards.a: Potent histamine $\text{H}_1$ receptor antagonist with mild $5\text{-HT}_{2}$ antagonist properties.

cards.q: Molecular target of benzodiazepines on the $\text{GABA}\text{-A}$ receptor complex?
cards.a: Allosteric binding site between the $\alpha$ and $\gamma$ subunits.

cards.q: Immediate intracellular effect of benzodiazepine binding to the $\text{GABA}\text{-A}$ receptor?
cards.a: Increased frequency of chloride channel opening, leading to hyperpolarization of the neuron.

cards.q: Molecular target of barbiturates on the $\text{GABA}\text{-A}$ receptor compared to benzodiazepines?
cards.a: Allosteric binding site that increases the duration of chloride channel opening.

cards.q: Receptor affinity responsible for the prominent weight gain and sedation caused by Mirtazapine?
cards.a: High affinity antagonism at the histamine $\text{H}_1$ receptor.

cards.q: Why does Mirtazapine cause less sexual dysfunction compared to standard SSRIs?
cards.a: It blocks $5\text{-HT}_2$ and $5\text{-HT}_3$ receptors, diverting serotonin selectively to $5\text{-HT}_1$ receptors.

cards.q: Mechanism of action of Clomipramine that distinguishes it from other tricyclic antidepressants ($\text{TCAs}$)?
cards.a: Exceptionally high selectivity and potency for inhibiting the serotonin reuptake transporter ($\text{SERT}$).

cards.q: Serious cardiovascular risk associated with an overdose of Clomipramine or any other TCA?
cards.a: Sodium channel blockade leading to QRS prolongation, cardiac arrhythmias, and seizures.

cards.q: Primary antidote for a tricyclic antidepressant ($\text{TCA}$) overdose presenting with a widened QRS complex?
cards.a: Intravenous sodium bicarbonate.

cards.q: Mechanism of action of Prazosin in treating PTSD-related nightmares?
cards.a: Competitive antagonist at central $\alpha_1$ adrenergic receptors, reducing central sympathetic outflow.

cards.q: Pharmacological rationale for using atypical antipsychotics like Risperidone as augmentation in OCD?
cards.a: $5\text{-HT}_{2\text{A}}$ receptor antagonism modulates downstream dopamine and glutamate release in the $\text{CSTC}$ circuit.

cards.q: SSRI discontinuation syndrome is most acutely severe with which medication due to its lack of active metabolites?
cards.a: Paroxetine.

cards.q: List three common symptoms of SSRI discontinuation syndrome.
cards.a: Flu-like symptoms, irritability, dizziness, paresthesias described as "brain zaps," and vivid dreams.

cards.q: Life-threatening symptom complex seen in severe Serotonin Syndrome that distinguishes it from Neuroleptic Malignant Syndrome ($\text{NMS}$)?
cards.a: Neuromuscular hyperactivity manifesting as hyperreflexia and clonus.

cards.q: Pharmacological antidote used for severe, refractory cases of Serotonin Syndrome?
cards.a: Cyproheptadine.

cards.q: Mechanism of action of Cyproheptadine?
cards.a: First-generation antihistamine with potent $5\text{-HT}_1$ and $5\text{-HT}_2$ receptor antagonist properties.

cards.q: Primary cognitive distortion targeted in CBT for Generalized Anxiety Disorder?
cards.a: Catastrophizing and intolerance of uncertainty.

cards.q: Core behavioral component of CBT used to treat Agoraphobia?
cards.a: In vivo exposure to feared public places or situations.

cards.q: Ultimate goal of interoceptive exposure in the treatment of Panic Disorder?
cards.a: Habituation to physical sensations of panic to break the conditioned fear response.

cards.q: Define the "Exposure" component of Exposure and Response Prevention ($\text{ERP}$) for OCD.
cards.a: Deliberately confronting the thoughts, images, or situations that trigger obsessional anxiety.

cards.q: Define the "Response Prevention" component of Exposure and Response Prevention ($\text{ERP}$) for OCD.
cards.a: Strictly refraining from performing the compulsive ritual that serves to decrease the anxiety.

cards.q: Primary behavioral mechanism through which Prolonged Exposure ($\text{PE}$) therapy works for PTSD?
cards.a: Emotional processing and extinction of the conditioned fear response through repeated imaginal and in vivo exposure.

cards.q: Unique mechanism of Eye Movement Desensitization and Reprocessing ($\text{EMDR}$) for PTSD?
cards.a: Using bilateral stimulation (like side-to-side eye movements) while processing traumatic memories to facilitate cognitive restructuring.

cards.q: Psychological defense mechanism where an individual shifts an unacceptable impulse or feeling from its original target to a safer substitute?
cards.a: Displacement.

cards.q: Psychological defense mechanism where an individual attributes their own unacknowledged, unacceptable thoughts or feelings onto another person?
cards.a: Projection.

cards.q: Cardiac arrhythmia that can perfectly mimic the palpitations, diaphoresis, and acute anxiety of a panic attack?
cards.a: Paroxysmal Supraventricular Tachycardia ($\text{PSVT}$).

cards.q: Diagnostic test used to differentiate Paroxysmal Supraventricular Tachycardia from a primary Panic Disorder?
cards.a: Holter monitor or ambulatory electrocardiography ($\text{EKG}$).

cards.q: Neurological disorder characterized by episodic, excessive catecholamine release that mimics panic attacks, weight loss, and diaphoresis?
cards.a: Pheochromocytoma.

cards.q: Diagnostic step when a clinician suspects an underlying Pheochromocytoma causing anxiety symptoms?
cards.a: Order a 24-hour urinary fractionated metanephrines or plasma free metanephrines test.

cards.q: Endocrine disorder that frequently presents with generalized anxiety, heat intolerance, weight loss, and tachycardia?
cards.a: Hyperthyroidism.

cards.q: Lab testing strategy to rule out hyperthyroidism in a patient with new-onset generalized anxiety symptoms?
cards.a: Serum Thyroid-Stimulating Hormone ($\text{TSH}$) and Free $\text{T}_4$ levels.

cards.q: Dietary or over-the-counter substance that a clinician must screen for in every patient presenting with generalized anxiety or panic?
cards.a: Caffeine intake.

cards.q: Cardiovascular condition involving the connective tissue of a heart valve that is epidemiologically linked to Panic Disorder?
cards.a: Mitral Valve Prolapse ($\text{MVP}$).

cards.q: Classic auscultatory finding associated with Mitral Valve Prolapse?
cards.a: Midsystolic click followed by a late systolic murmur.

cards.q: Primary clinical feature that differentiates Social Anxiety Disorder from Panic Disorder?
cards.a: In Social Anxiety Disorder, panic attacks occur only in response to social scrutiny or public performance situations.

cards.q: Diagnosis for a patient who avoids public transport and open spaces because they fear help won't be available if they develop incapacitating symptoms?
cards.a: Agoraphobia.

cards.q: Primary clinical differentiator between Acute Stress Disorder ($\text{ASD}$) and Post-Traumatic Stress Disorder ($\text{PTSD}$)?
cards.a: Symptom duration; ASD is 3 days to 1 month, while PTSD is greater than 1 month.

cards.q: Diagnosis for a patient experiencing significant distress and functional impairment from a non-catastrophic life stressor within 3 months of its onset?
cards.a: Adjustment Disorder.

cards.q: Treatment of choice for Adjustment Disorder?
cards.a: Psychotherapy (supportive or cognitive-behavioral).

cards.q: Medical diagnosis when an adult presents with severe obsessions and compulsions that began immediately after an acute cerebrovascular accident?
cards.a: Anxiety disorder/Obsessive-compulsive symptoms secondary to a general medical condition.

cards.q: Pediatric syndrome characterized by the abrupt, explosive onset of OCD or tics following an infection?
cards.a: PANDAS (Pediatric Autoimmune Neuropsychiatric Disorders Associated with Streptococcal Infections).

cards.q: Underlying pathophysiology of PANDAS?
cards.a: Molecular mimicry where antistreptococcal antibodies cross-react with the basal ganglia.

cards.q: Diagnosis for a patient preoccupied with imagined defects in physical appearance, leading to repetitive mirror checking or skin picking?
cards.a: Body Dysmorphic Disorder ($\text{BDD}$).

cards.q: First-line medical and psychological therapy combination for Body Dysmorphic Disorder?
cards.a: High-dose SSRIs and Cognitive Behavioral Therapy.

cards.q: Diagnosis for a patient who intentionally pulls out their hair, resulting in noticeable hair loss, preceded by tension and followed by relief?
cards.a: Trichotillomania (Hair-Pulling Disorder).

cards.q: Microscopic examination finding of hair shafts in Trichotillomania that helps differentiate it from Alopecia Areata?
cards.a: Broken hair shafts of varying lengths with no signs of inflammation or fungal infection.

cards.q: Diagnosis for an individual who has persistent difficulty discarding possessions, regardless of value, causing severe clutter that compromises living areas?
cards.a: Hoarding Disorder.

cards.q: Most effective long-term treatment strategy for Hoarding Disorder?
cards.a: Specialized Cognitive Behavioral Therapy tailored for hoarding behaviors (pharmacotherapy has limited efficacy).

cards.q: Diagnosis for a patient who skin-picks compulsively, leading to skin lesions and functional impairment, despite repeated attempts to stop?
cards.a: Excoriation (Skin-Picking) Disorder.

cards.q: Medication class that must be completely avoided in patients with a history of trauma who are experiencing severe acute anxiety?
cards.a: Benzodiazepines, due to high addiction potential and interference with trauma processing.

cards.q: Substance intoxication presenting with pupillary constriction (miosis), respiratory depression, and bradycardia?
cards.a: Opioid intoxication.

cards.q: Substance withdrawal state presenting with pupillary dilation (mydriasis), rhinorrhea, piloerection, yawning, and severe anxiety?
cards.a: Opioid withdrawal.

cards.q: Substance intoxication presenting with nystagmus, agitation, hypertension, and unpredictable, violent behavior?
cards.a: Phencyclidine ($\text{PCP}$) intoxication.

cards.q: Substance withdrawal state that can present with severe anxiety, tremors, tactile hallucinations (formication), and life-threatening seizures?
cards.a: Alcohol or Sedative-Hypnotic withdrawal.

cards.q: Minimum duration of maintenance pharmacotherapy recommended for a patient who has achieved remission from a first episode of GAD?
cards.a: Twelve months.

cards.q: Tapering strategy required when discontinuing long-term benzodiazepine therapy to avoid severe withdrawal or rebound anxiety?
cards.a: Gradual reduction of the dose by 10% to 25% every 1 to 2 weeks over several months.

cards.q: Clinical step to take when a patient with Panic Disorder shows zero improvement after 6 weeks on a maximally tolerated dose of Sertraline?
cards.a: Switch to a different first-line medication, such as an alternative SSRI or an SNRI (e.g., Venlafaxine).

cards.q: Adjunctive medication class that can be used safely to manage severe physical tremors and tachycardia in a patient with PTSD?
cards.a: $\beta$-blocker (e.g., Propranolol).

cards.q: Prognostic factor associated with a higher likelihood of long-term recovery from OCD?
cards.a: Good premorbid functioning, late onset of symptoms, and the presence of precipitating events.

cards.q: Prognostic factor associated with a poorer long-term outcome in patients with OCD?
cards.a: Childhood onset, presence of tics, yields to compulsions completely, or severe delusional (absent) insight.

cards.q: Long-term clinical outcome for the majority of patients appropriately treated for Panic Disorder?
cards.a: Significant improvement or complete remission, though up to 30% may experience long-term, episodic relapses.

cards.q: Diagnosis for a 24-year-old student with a 7-month history of daily unremitting worry about grades, health, and finances, accompanied by severe muscle soreness and insomnia?
cards.a: Generalized Anxiety Disorder.

cards.q: Diagnosis for a 30-year-old female presenting to the ER with chest pain, sweating, paresthesias, and a conviction that she is actively dying, with normal cardiac workup?
cards.a: Panic Disorder.

cards.q: Diagnosis for a veteran who presents with intrusive nightmares of an explosion, avoids loud crowds, stays hypervigilant, and has felt emotionally numb for 6 months?
cards.a: Post-Traumatic Stress Disorder.

cards.q: Diagnosis for a 19-year-old who spends 3 hours a day washing her hands until they bleed because she fears chemical contamination?
cards.a: Obsessive-Compulsive Disorder.

cards.q: Diagnosis for a patient who develops intense anxiety, palpitations, and sweating exclusively when asked to give a speech in front of colleagues?
cards.a: Social Anxiety Disorder, performance-only subtype.

cards.q: Diagnosis for a patient who refuses to leave her apartment because she is terrified she will have a medical emergency in public with no one to help her?
cards.a: Agoraphobia.

cards.q: Diagnosis for a man who undergoes multiple unnecessary plastic surgeries because he is convinced his nose is asymmetrical, though it appears perfectly normal to others?
cards.a: Body Dysmorphic Disorder.

cards.q: Diagnosis for a 9-year-old child who completely stops talking at school but speaks completely normally and fluidly at home with his parents?
cards.a: Selective Mutism.

cards.q: Diagnosis for an 8-year-old child who experiences extreme, unremitting distress, vomiting, and refusal to sleep alone when separated from his primary caregiver?
cards.a: Separation Anxiety Disorder.

cards.q: Diagnosis for a patient who presents with severe flashbacks, insomnia, and hyperarousal exactly two weeks after surviving a house fire?
cards.a: Acute Stress Disorder.

cards.q: Diagnosis for a patient who develops severe anxiety, depressed mood, and occupational impairment two months after a difficult divorce, which resolves four months after the divorce is finalized?
cards.a: Adjustment Disorder with mixed anxiety and depressed mood.

cards.q: Most common comorbid psychiatric condition found in individuals diagnosed with Generalized Anxiety Disorder?
cards.a: Major Depressive Disorder.

cards.q: Most common comorbid conditions found in patients diagnosed with Panic Disorder?
cards.a: Agoraphobia, Major Depressive Disorder, and Substance Use Disorder.

cards.q: Patients with Panic Disorder carry a significantly elevated lifetime risk for which tragic clinical outcome?
cards.a: Suicide attempts.

cards.q: Most common comorbid condition that co-occurs with PTSD?
cards.a: Substance Use Disorder, specifically Alcohol Use Disorder.

cards.q: Two most common comorbid psychiatric disorders seen in patients with Obsessive-Compulsive Disorder?
cards.a: Anxiety disorders and Major Depressive Disorder.

cards.q: Psychiatric condition that is strongly comorbid with pediatric OCD, appearing in up to 30% of cases?
cards.a: Tic disorders or Tourette's Disorder.

cards.q: Medical condition characterized by a paroxysmal supraventricular tachycardia that must always be ruled out during a panic disorder workup?
cards.a: Wolff-Parkinson-White syndrome.

cards.q: Endocrine disorder caused by a pituitary adenoma that can manifest with neuropsychiatric symptoms mimicking severe anxiety and panic?
cards.a: Cushing's disease.

cards.q: Neurological disorder characterized by focal seizures in which brain region that can mimic panic attacks with sudden fear and autonomic symptoms?
cards.a: Temporal lobe epilepsy.

cards.q: Neurological autoantibody disorder that can present with acute, severe psychiatric symptoms, including profound anxiety, psychosis, and catatonia?
cards.a: Anti-NMDA receptor encephalitis.

cards.q: Substance abuse state that can mimic GAD and panic, characterized by pupillary dilation, tachycardia, hypertension, and extreme alertness?
cards.a: Amphetamine or Cocaine intoxication.

cards.q: Substance withdrawal state that can mimic a severe anxiety panic state, characterized by pupillary dilation, rhinorrhea, lacrimation, and piloerection?
cards.a: Opioid withdrawal.

cards.q: Mechanism of action of Buspirone that explains why it lacks sedative and muscle relaxant properties?
cards.a: It lacks any modulating activity at the GABA receptor complex.

cards.q: Why must Buspirone be taken continuously rather than as-needed (PRN)?
cards.a: It requires weeks of daily administration to downregulate presynaptic serotonin autoreceptors.

cards.q: Primary Cytochrome P450 enzyme responsible for the metabolism of Buspirone?
cards.a: CYP3A4.

cards.q: Co-administration of Buspirone with which dietary substance can significantly increase its plasma concentrations?
cards.a: Grapefruit juice.

cards.q: Primary mechanism of action of Hydroxyzine in treating acute anxiety?
cards.a: Strong inverse agonism at peripheral and central histamine $\text{H}_1$ receptors.

cards.q: Molecular subunit of the $\text{GABA}_\text{A}$ receptor to which benzodiazepines bind to exert their anxiolytic effects?
cards.a: $\alpha_2$ subunit.

cards.q: Molecular subunit of the $\text{GABA}_\text{A}$ receptor to which benzodiazepines bind to exert their sedative and amnestic effects?
cards.a: $\alpha_1$ subunit.

cards.q: Active metabolite of Diazepam and Chlordiazepoxide that contributes to their exceptionally prolonged half-lives?
cards.a: Desmethyldiazepam.

cards.q: Why are Lorazepam, Oxazepam, and Temazepam preferred in patients with hepatic failure or the elderly?
cards.a: They are metabolized solely via Phase II glucuronidation and do not accumulate.

cards.q: Mechanism of action of Flumazenil?
cards.a: Competitive antagonist at the benzodiazepine binding site on the $\text{GABA}_\text{A}$ receptor complex.

cards.q: Absolute contraindication for the use of Flumazenil in an unknown drug overdose?
cards.a: Chronic benzodiazepine dependence or co-ingestion of tricyclic antidepressants, due to high seizure risk.

cards.q: Mechanism of action of Mirtazapine that leads to an increase in both serotonin and norepinephrine release?
cards.a: Antagonism of central presynaptic $\alpha_2$ adrenergic autoreceptors and heteroreceptors.

cards.q: Why does the sedating effect of Mirtazapine decrease as the dose is increased from 15mg to 45mg?
cards.a: Higher doses increase noradrenergic neurotransmission, which counteracts the antihistaminergic sedation.

cards.q: Mechanism of action of Clomipramine?
cards.a: Strong inhibition of the serotonin transporter (SERT) and moderate inhibition of the norepinephrine transporter (NET).

cards.q: Primary side effect profile concern for Clomipramine due to its structural class?
cards.a: Severe anticholinergic, antihistaminergic, and anti-$\alpha_1$ adrenergic side effects.

cards.q: Mechanism of action of Prazosin in the treatment of PTSD?
cards.a: Central $\alpha_1$ adrenergic receptor antagonist that blunts the overactive noradrenergic response during sleep.

cards.q: Initial dosing instruction for Prazosin to mitigate its most common immediate side effect?
cards.a: Dose at bedtime to prevent orthostatic hypotension and first-dose syncope.

cards.q: Mechanism of action of Vilazodone?
cards.a: Serotonin reuptake inhibitor combined with $\text{$\text{5-HT}$}_{1\text{A}}$ receptor partial agonism.

cards.q: Mechanism of action of Vortioxetine?
cards.a: Serotonin reuptake inhibitor combined with $\text{$\text{5-HT}$}_{1\text{A}}$ agonism, $\text{$\text{5-HT}$}_{1\text{B}}$ partial agonism, and $\text{$\text{5-HT}$}_{3}$/$\text{$\text{5-HT}$}_{7}$ antagonism.

cards.q: SSRI with the longest half-life that does not require a slow taper when discontinued?
cards.a: Fluoxetine.

cards.q: SSRI with the shortest half-life and no active metabolites, carrying the highest risk for severe discontinuation syndrome?
cards.a: Paroxetine.

cards.q: Specific cardiac risk associated with high-dose Citalopram administration?
cards.a: Dose-dependent QTc prolongation.

cards.q: Maximum recommended dose of Citalopram in patients over the age of 60?
cards.a: 20 milligrams per day.

cards.q: Primary mechanism of action of atypical antipsychotics when used as augmentation in treatment-resistant OCD?
cards.a: Serotonin $\text{$\text{5-HT}$}_{2\text{A}}$ receptor antagonism combined with dopamine $\text{D}_2$ receptor modulation.

cards.q: Core behavioral therapy component of Exposure and Response Prevention (ERP) for OCD?
cards.a: Preventing the patient from performing compulsive rituals after exposure to an obsession.

cards.q: Primary behavioral technique used in Prolonged Exposure (PE) therapy for PTSD?
cards.a: Repeatedly approaching safe but trauma-related situations that the patient has been avoiding.

cards.q: Goal of Cognitive Processing Therapy (CPT) for PTSD?
cards.a: Identifying and challenging unhelpful, stuck thoughts related to the traumatic event.

cards.q: Behavioral therapy modality considered first-line for the treatment of Trichotillomania?
cards.a: Habit Reversal Training.

cards.q: Psychological defense mechanism where an individual manages anxiety by focusing purely on facts and cold logic rather than emotions?
cards.a: Intellectualization.

cards.q: Psychological defense mechanism where an individual counteracts an unacceptable thought or behavior by performing a ritualistic action?
cards.a: Undoing.

cards.q: Psychological defense mechanism where an unacceptable impulse is unconsciously transformed into its diametric opposite?
cards.a: Reaction Formation.

cards.q: Psychological defense mechanism where an individual attributes their own unacknowledged, unacceptable impulses onto someone else?
cards.a: Projection.

cards.q: Psychological defense mechanism where an individual channels unacceptable impulses into socially acceptable, productive activities?
cards.a: Sublimation.

cards.q: Minimum duration of successful pharmacotherapy treatment before attempting to taper an antidepressant in a stable GAD patient?
cards.a: Six to twelve months.

cards.q: Recommended rate of tapering for a patient discontinuing long-term benzodiazepine therapy to avoid severe withdrawal?
cards.a: Reduce the total daily dose by no more than 10% to 25% every one to two weeks.

cards.q: Prognostic factor that strongly correlates with a poor long-term outcome in Obsessive-Compulsive Disorder?
cards.a: Early childhood onset, poor initial treatment response, and absent or delusional insight.

cards.q: Percentage of patients with Panic Disorder who achieve complete long-term remission with appropriate treatment?
cards.a: Approximately 30% to 40%.

cards.q: Medical diagnosis when a patient presents with severe obsessions and compulsions that began immediately following an ischemic stroke in the basal ganglia?
cards.a: Obsessive-Compulsive Disorder secondary to a general medical condition.

cards.q: Clinical sign that differentiates severe Serotonin Syndrome from Neuroleptic Malignant Syndrome (NMS)?
cards.a: Hyperreflexia and spontaneous clonus are prominent in Serotonin Syndrome, whereas lead-pipe rigidity is prominent in NMS.

cards.q: Immediate first-line intervention for a patient presenting with acute, severe benzodiazepine withdrawal?
cards.a: Re-initiation of a long-acting benzodiazepine followed by a structured, gradual taper.

cards.q: Term used to describe panic attacks that do not meet the full diagnostic criteria of at least four somatic or cognitive symptoms?
cards.a: Limited-symptom panic attacks.

cards.q: Specifier applied when an individual meets all criteria for PTSD but also displays persistent feelings of unreality or detachment from their own body?
cards.a: PTSD with dissociative symptoms.

cards.q: Criteria required to apply the "delayed expression" specifier to a PTSD diagnosis?
cards.a: Full diagnostic criteria are not met until at least 6 months after the traumatic event.

topic: Substance use disorders — alcohol, opioids, stimulants

cards.q: Minimum number of criteria required to diagnose a Substance Use Disorder (SUD) under DSM-5-TR?
cards.a: Two criteria met within a 12-month period.

cards.q: Timeframe required to assess DSM-5-TR criteria for Substance Use Disorders?
cards.a: Within a 12-month period.

cards.q: Number of criteria required to classify a Substance Use Disorder as mild?
cards.a: Two to three criteria.

cards.q: Number of criteria required to classify a Substance Use Disorder as moderate?
cards.a: Four to five criteria.

cards.q: Number of criteria required to classify a Substance Use Disorder as severe?
cards.a: Six or more criteria.

cards.q: Definition of "Early Remission" in DSM-5-TR Substance Use Disorders?
cards.a: No criteria met (except craving) for at least 3 months but less than 12 months.

cards.q: Definition of "Sustained Remission" in DSM-5-TR Substance Use Disorders?
cards.a: No criteria met (except craving) for 12 months or longer.

cards.q: Diagnostic requirement for Alcohol Use Disorder according to DSM-5-TR?
cards.a: A problematic pattern of alcohol use leading to clinically significant impairment or distress.

cards.q: Neurological receptor system primarily potentiated by acute alcohol consumption?
cards.a: $GABA_A$ receptors.

cards.q: Neurological receptor system primarily inhibited by acute alcohol consumption?
cards.a: NMDA glutamate receptors.

cards.q: Definition of legal intoxication for driving in most United States jurisdictions?
cards.a: Blood Alcohol Concentration (BAC) of 0.08% or higher.

cards.q: Clinical signs of acute mild-to-moderate alcohol intoxication?
cards.a: Slurred speech, incoordination, unsteady gait, nystagmus, and flushed face.

cards.q: Classic ocular sign of acute alcohol intoxication or early withdrawal?
cards.a: Horizontal gaze nystagmus.

cards.q: Screening tool for alcohol use disorder utilizing the acronym CAGE?
cards.a: Cut down, Annoyed, Guilty, Eye-opener questionnaire.

cards.q: Single most sensitive lab marker for identifying chronic heavy alcohol consumption?
cards.a: Carbohydrate-Deficient Transferrin (CDT).

cards.q: Hematologic abnormality frequently seen in chronic alcoholics due to direct toxicity or dietary deficiency?
cards.a: Macrocytosis (elevated MCV).

cards.q: Expected ratio of AST to ALT in patients with alcohol-induced liver injury?
cards.a: AST to ALT ratio greater than 2:1.

cards.q: Cellular adaptation responsible for alcohol withdrawal symptoms upon cessation?
cards.a: Downregulation of $GABA_A$ receptors and upregulation of NMDA receptors.

cards.q: Typical onset time of minor alcohol withdrawal symptoms following the last drink?
cards.a: 6 to 24 hours.

cards.q: Typical onset time of alcohol withdrawal seizures?
cards.a: 12 to 48 hours.

cards.q: Character of seizures typically observed during alcohol withdrawal?
cards.a: Generalized tonic-clonic seizures.

cards.q: Typical onset time of alcoholic hallucinosis following cessation?
cards.a: 12 to 48 hours.

cards.q: Primary feature distinguishing alcoholic hallucinosis from Delirium Tremens?
cards.a: Intact sensorium and stable vital signs in alcoholic hallucinosis.

cards.q: Typical onset time of Delirium Tremens (DTs) after alcohol cessation?
cards.a: 48 to 96 hours.

cards.q: Core clinical triad characterizing Delirium Tremens?
cards.a: Delirium, autonomic instability, and severe agitation.

cards.q: Standardized clinical scale used to objectively assess and monitor alcohol withdrawal severity?
cards.a: Clinical Institute Withdrawal Assessment for Alcohol (CIWA-Ar).

cards.q: Gold-standard medication class used to manage acute alcohol withdrawal?
cards.a: Benzodiazepines.

cards.q: Preferred benzodiazepines for alcohol withdrawal in patients with severe hepatic impairment?
cards.a: Lorazepam, Oxazepam, and Temazepam.

cards.q: Rationale for using Lorazepam or Oxazepam in patients with liver failure?
cards.a: They undergo direct glucuronidation without active hepatic metabolites.

cards.q: Long-acting benzodiazepines preferred for alcohol withdrawal protocols due to self-tapering effects?
cards.a: Chlordiazepoxide and Diazepam.

cards.q: Most common cause of death in patients experiencing untreated Delirium Tremens?
cards.a: Cardiovascular collapse or hyperthermia.

cards.q: Acute neurological syndrome caused by thiamine (Vitamin B1) deficiency?
cards.a: Wernicke's encephalopathy.

cards.q: Classic clinical triad of Wernicke's encephalopathy?
cards.a: Encephalopathy (confusion), oculomotor dysfunction (nystagmus/ophthalmoplegia), and gait ataxia.

cards.q: Irreversible chronic neurocognitive disorder that can follow Wernicke's encephalopathy?
cards.a: Korsakoff's syndrome.

cards.q: Hallmark cognitive deficit and compensatory behavioral feature of Korsakoff's syndrome?
cards.a: Anterograde amnesia and confabulation.

cards.q: Specific neuroanatomical structures characteristically damaged in Wernicke-Korsakoff syndrome?
cards.a: Mammillary bodies and medial dorsal nuclei of the thalamus.

cards.q: Critical sequence rule when administering glucose and thiamine to an alcoholic patient?
cards.a: Administer thiamine before or concurrently with glucose to prevent worsening encephalopathy.

cards.q: Mechanism of action of Naltrexone in treating Alcohol Use Disorder?
cards.a: $\mu$-opioid receptor antagonist that reduces the reinforcing effects and cravings of alcohol.

cards.q: Absolute contraindication for initiating Naltrexone therapy?
cards.a: Acute hepatitis, liver failure, or current opioid use.

cards.q: Mechanism of action of Acamprosate?
cards.a: Modulates glutamate neurotransmission at NMDA receptors to restore GABA/glutamate balance.

cards.q: Primary contraindication for the use of Acamprosate?
cards.a: Severe renal impairment (Creatinine Clearance less than 30 mL/min).

cards.q: Mechanism of action of Disulfiram?
cards.a: Irreversibly inhibits aldehyde dehydrogenase, causing accumulation of acetaldehyde.

cards.q: Classic physical symptoms of a Disulfiram-alcohol reaction?
cards.a: Flushing, tachycardia, hypotension, nausea, and vomiting.

cards.q: Second-line medication for AUD that is an $GABA_B$ receptor agonist used to reduce cravings?
cards.a: Baclofen.

cards.q: Anticonvulsant medication used off-label to reduce alcohol cravings and heavy drinking days?
cards.a: Topiramate.

cards.q: Primary receptor subtype responsible for the analgesic and euphoric effects of opioids?
cards.a: $\mu$-opioid receptor.

cards.q: Triad of clinical signs strongly diagnostic of acute opioid overdose?
cards.a: Respiratory depression, miosis (pinpoint pupils), and altered mental status.

cards.q: Exception to the rule of pupil constriction in opioid overdose due to severe hypoxia or specific agent?
cards.a: Meperidine overdose (causes mydriasis).

cards.q: Immediate, life-saving antidote for acute opioid overdose with respiratory depression?
cards.a: Naloxone.

cards.q: Mechanism of action of Naloxone?
cards.a: Short-acting competitive $\mu$-opioid receptor antagonist.

cards.q: Cardinal objective signs of acute opioid withdrawal?
cards.a: Mydriasis, piloerection, rhinorrhea, lacrimation, and hyperactive bowel sounds.

cards.q: Expected timeline for peak withdrawal symptoms from short-acting opioids like heroin?
cards.a: 36 to 72 hours.

cards.q: Expected timeline for peak withdrawal symptoms from long-acting opioids like methadone?
cards.a: 72 to 96 hours.

cards.q: Standardized objective assessment scale used to quantify the severity of opioid withdrawal?
cards.a: Clinical Opiate Withdrawal Scale (COWS).

cards.q: Non-opioid $\alpha_2$ adrenergic agonist used to manage autonomic symptoms of opioid withdrawal?
cards.a: Clonidine or Lofexidine.

cards.q: Mechanism of action of Methadone in Opioid Use Disorder maintenance?
cards.a: Long-acting full $\mu$-opioid receptor agonist.

cards.q: Essential cardiac screening required for patients on high-dose Methadone therapy?
cards.a: Electrocardiogram (ECG) to monitor for QTc prolongation.

cards.q: Regulatory restriction unique to Methadone prescription for Opioid Use Disorder in the US?
cards.a: Must be dispensed through a federally regulated Opioid Treatment Program (OTP).

cards.q: Mechanism of action of Buprenorphine?
cards.a: Partial $\mu$-opioid receptor agonist and $\kappa$-opioid receptor antagonist.

cards.q: Precaution required before administering the first dose of Buprenorphine to a patient?
cards.a: The patient must be in mild-to-moderate objective opioid withdrawal to avoid precipitated withdrawal.

cards.q: Rationale for combining Buprenorphine with Naloxone in Suboxone?
cards.a: To prevent intravenous abuse, as Naloxone blocks effects if injected but has low oral bioavailability.

cards.q: Form of Naltrexone preferred for Opioid Use Disorder maintenance to ensure compliance?
cards.a: Monthly intramuscular depot injection (Vivitrol).

cards.q: Minimum duration a patient must be completely opioid-free before initiating Naltrexone?
cards.a: 7 to 10 days to avoid severe precipitated withdrawal.

cards.q: Primary mechanism of action of Cocaine at the synaptic cleft?
cards.a: Blocks the reuptake of dopamine, norepinephrine, and serotonin.

cards.q: Primary mechanism of action of Amphetamines at the synaptic cleft?
cards.a: Stimulates the release of dopamine and norepinephrine and inhibits their reuptake.

cards.q: Cardiovascular signs of acute stimulant intoxication?
cards.a: Tachycardia, hypertension, cardiac arrhythmias, and pupillary dilation (mydriasis).

cards.q: Psychological symptoms commonly seen in severe stimulant intoxication?
cards.a: Paranoia, auditory/visual hallucinations, hypervigilance, and grandiosity.

cards.q: Name of the tactile hallucination where patients feel bugs crawling under their skin?
cards.a: Formication ("cocaine bugs").

cards.q: Life-threatening complication of severe stimulant overdose characterized by muscle breakdown?
cards.a: Rhabdomyolysis.

cards.q: Drug class of choice for treating acute agitation and hypertension in cocaine intoxication?
cards.a: Benzodiazepines.

cards.q: Medication class strictly contraindicated in acute cocaine intoxication due to risk of unopposed $\alpha$-stimulation?
cards.a: Pure $\beta$-blocker (e.g., Propranolol).

cards.q: Severe physical vascular complication of chronic intranasal cocaine use?
cards.a: Nasal septal perforation.

cards.q: Unique dermatological and dental presentation associated with chronic methamphetamine use?
cards.a: Skin excoriations (from picking) and severe dental caries ("meth mouth").

cards.q: Core psychological feature characterizing the "crash" phase of stimulant withdrawal?
cards.a: Severe dysphoria, anhedonia, and vivid, unpleasant dreams.

cards.q: Sleep disturbances typically observed during acute stimulant withdrawal?
cards.a: Hypersomnia followed by insomnia.

cards.q: Changes in appetite associated with stimulant withdrawal?
cards.a: Hyperphagia (increased appetite).

cards.q: Risk profile peak during acute stimulant withdrawal that clinicians must monitor?
cards.a: Severe suicidal ideation and behavior.

cards.q: FDA-approved maintenance medication for Stimulant Use Disorder?
cards.a: There are currently no FDA-approved medications for Stimulant Use Disorder.

cards.q: Most effective evidence-based psychosocial interventions for Stimulant Use Disorder?
cards.a: Contingency management and Cognitive Behavioral Therapy (CBT).

cards.q: Psychiatric condition that must be differentiated from stimulant-induced psychosis?
cards.a: Schizophrenia or Bipolar I Disorder with psychotic features.

cards.q: Distinguishing feature of substance-induced psychosis versus primary psychotic disorders?
cards.a: Resolution of psychotic symptoms within weeks of substance cessation.

cards.q: Most common comorbid psychiatric disorder cluster associated with Substance Use Disorders?
cards.a: Antisocial Personality Disorder and Borderline Personality Disorder.

cards.q: Term used when a patient has both a diagnosed Substance Use Disorder and a comorbid mental health disorder?
cards.a: Dual Diagnosis (or Co-occurring Disorders).

cards.q: First-line treatment for a pregnant patient with severe Opioid Use Disorder?
cards.a: Opioid Agonist Therapy with Methadone or Buprenorphine monotherapy.

cards.q: Risk associated with abrupt opioid detoxification during pregnancy?
cards.a: Fetal distress, miscarriage, or preterm labor.

cards.q: Neonatal condition resulting from maternal opioid use during pregnancy?
cards.a: Neonatal Abstinence Syndrome (NAS).

cards.q: First-line medical management for a neonate with severe Neonatal Abstinence Syndrome?
cards.a: Morphine or Methadone solution.

cards.q: Classic triad of symptoms seen in Fetal Alcohol Syndrome (FAS)?
cards.a: Smooth philtrum, thin upper lip, and short palpebral fissures.

cards.q: Fatal combination product formed when alcohol and cocaine are consumed concurrently?
cards.a: Cocaethylene.

cards.q: Clinical significance of cocaethylene formation in the body?
cards.a: Longer half-life than cocaine and higher cardiotoxicity.

cards.q: Neurotransmitter storm responsible for the life-threatening hyperthermia in MDMA (Ecstasy) overdose?
cards.a: Serotonin toxicity (Serotonin Syndrome).

cards.q: Severe electrolyte abnormality frequently triggered by MDMA use due to excessive water intake and SIADH?
cards.a: Hyponatremia.

cards.q: Principal receptor target altered by chronic stimulant use leading to anhedonia during withdrawal?
cards.a: Downregulation of postsynaptic Dopamine $\text{D}_2$ receptors.

cards.q: Medication used off-label for amphetamine use disorder due to its dual action on norepinephrine and dopamine?
cards.a: Bupropion.

cards.q: Medication combination that showed efficacy for methamphetamine use disorder in recent clinical trials?
cards.a: Injectable Naltrexone plus oral Bupropion.

cards.q: Neurological pathway primarily responsible for the rewarding and addictive properties of all drugs of abuse?
cards.a: Mesolimbic dopamine pathway.

cards.q: Specific anatomical origin and termination points of the mesolimbic dopamine pathway?
cards.a: Ventral Tegmental Area (VTA) projecting to the Nucleus Accumbens.

cards.q: Patient with history of AUD presents with confusion, horizontal nystagmus, and wide-based gait. Diagnosis?
cards.a: Wernicke's Encephalopathy.

cards.q: Patient presents with severe abdominal cramps, diarrhea, dilated pupils, and gooseflesh skin. Diagnosis?
cards.a: Opioid Withdrawal.

cards.q: Patient presents with pinpoint pupils, respiratory rate of 4 breaths per minute, and bradycardia. Diagnosis?
cards.a: Opioid Intoxication (Overdose).

cards.q: Patient presents with tactile hallucinations, extreme paranoia, dilated pupils, and a blood pressure of 180/110 mmHg. Diagnosis?
cards.a: Stimulant Intoxication.

cards.q: Patient 3 days post-appendectomy develops tremors, visual hallucinations, a heart rate of 120 bpm, and disorientation. Diagnosis?
cards.a: Delirium Tremens.

cards.q: Patient presents with profound lethargy, intense craving, hyperphagia, and vivid nightmares after stopping a drug. Diagnosis?
cards.a: Stimulant Withdrawal.

cards.q: Opioid maintenance therapy drug that carries a significant risk of respiratory depression if taken with alcohol?
cards.a: Methadone.

cards.q: Screening questionnaire for alcohol use during pregnancy?
cards.a: T-ACE or TWEAK questionnaire.

cards.q: Definitive diagnostic test to confirm recent substance ingestion in an emergency setting?
cards.a: Urine Drug Screen (UDS).

cards.q: Substance whose intoxication routinely causes horizontal, vertical, and rotary nystagmus?
cards.a: Phencyclidine (PCP).

cards.q: Laboratory finding that helps differentiate alcoholic ketoacidosis from diabetic ketoacidosis?
cards.a: Normal or only mildly elevated blood glucose levels in alcoholic ketoacidosis.

cards.q: Definitive therapy for alcohol-induced cardiomyopathy?
cards.a: Complete abstinence from alcohol.

cards.q: Common cause of death in acute severe sedative-hypnotic withdrawal?
cards.a: Status epilepticus.

cards.q: Primary psychological defense mechanism used by individuals with severe Substance Use Disorders?
cards.a: Denial.

cards.q: Stage of change where a patient acknowledges a problem exists but is not yet ready to commit to action?
cards.a: Contemplation stage.

cards.q: Stage of change where a patient has no intention of changing behavior because they do not see a problem?
cards.a: Precontemplation stage.

cards.q: Stage of change where a patient actively modifies their behavior and environment to overcome the addiction?
cards.a: Action stage.

cards.q: Evidence-based counseling technique used to move patients through the stages of change?
cards.a: Motivational Interviewing.

cards.q: Core spirit or pillar of Motivational Interviewing?
cards.a: Collaboration, Acceptance, Compassion, and Evocation.

cards.q: Electrolyte replacement that must always accompany Thiamine in alcohol withdrawal management?
cards.a: Magnesium.

cards.q: Rationale for checking magnesium levels in alcohol withdrawal?
cards.a: Hypomagnesemia causes resistance to thiamine therapy and lowers the seizure threshold.

cards.q: Characteristic sleep architecture change seen in chronic alcoholics?
cards.a: Decreased REM sleep and disrupted slow-wave (deep) sleep.

cards.q: Pupillary presentation during acute benzodiazepine overdose without co-ingestions?
cards.a: Normal or slightly dilated pupils (unlike pinpoint pupils of opioids).

cards.q: Primary mechanism of death in acute cocaine-induced myocardial infarction?
cards.a: Coronary artery vasospasm and accelerated platelet aggregation.

cards.q: Long-term psychiatric syndrome characterized by persistent motivational deficits following chronic substance abuse?
cards.a: Amotivational syndrome.

cards.q: Class of antidepressant medications that should be avoided in patients actively abusing alcohol or stimulants due to hypertensive risks?
cards.a: Monoamine Oxidase Inhibitors (MAOIs).

cards.q: Over-the-counter medication that can cause false-positive results for amphetamines on standard urine drug screens?
cards.a: Pseudoephedrine (or selegiline, bupropion).

cards.q: Opioid analgesic that does not show up on standard routine urine drug screens and requires a specific assay?
cards.a: Fentanyl (or Oxycodone/Methadone).

cards.q: Main structural brain change observed in structural neuroimaging of chronic alcoholics?
cards.a: Cerebral atrophy and ventricular enlargement.

cards.q: Specific legal exception to patient confidentiality regarding Substance Use Disorder treatment records in the US?
cards.a: 42 CFR Part 2 (requires explicit written consent, stricter than standard HIPAA).

cards.q: Phenomenon where a drug user requires larger doses to achieve the same initial effect?
cards.a: Tolerance.

cards.q: Phenomenon where a drug user experiences physiological symptoms when a substance is abruptly discontinued?
cards.a: Withdrawal.

cards.q: Primary mechanism of action of synthetic cathinones ("bath salts")?
cards.a: Inhibition of monoamine reuptake and promotion of dopamine release, similar to amphetamines.

cards.q: Major clinical challenge when treating acute pain in a patient currently maintained on Suboxone?
cards.a: High $\mu$-affinity of buprenorphine blocks other opioid analgesics from binding.

cards.q: Preferred non-opioid medication class for managing acute somatic pain in patients with OUD?
cards.a: NSAIDs or Acetaminophen.

cards.q: Name of the safe, supervised facility programs designed to reduce overdose deaths and infections?
cards.a: Harm Reduction Programs (e.g., Needle Exchange Programs).

cards.q: Alcohol withdrawal symptom that can present even while the patient's blood alcohol level is actively falling but still elevated?
cards.a: Tremor (or withdrawal seizures).

cards.q: Major endocrine abnormality caused by chronic opioid use due to suppression of the HPA axis?
cards.a: Opioid-Induced Hypogonadism.

cards.q: Clinical manifestations of opioid-induced hypogonadism in male patients?
cards.a: Decreased libido, erectile dysfunction, and fatigue.

cards.q: Clinical manifestations of opioid-induced hypogonadism in female patients?
cards.a: Amenorrhea or irregular menses.

cards.q: Primary neurological track damaged in Marchiafava-Bignami disease associated with chronic alcohol use?
cards.a: Corpus callosum.

cards.q: Characteristic clinical presentation of Marchiafava-Bignami disease?
cards.a: Dementia, spasticity, dysarthria, and gait disorders.

cards.q: Diagnostic modality of choice to confirm Marchiafava-Bignami disease?
cards.a: Brain MRI showing symmetric lesions in the corpus callosum.

cards.q: Major pulmonary risk associated with intravenous drug use of stimulants or opioids?
cards.a: Septic pulmonary emboli (secondary to infective endocarditis).

cards.q: Most common cardiac valve affected by intravenous drug use?
cards.a: Tricuspid valve.

cards.q: Most common causative organism of infective endocarditis in intravenous drug users?
cards.a: Staphylococcus aureus.

cards.q: Diagnostic screening procedure that should be performed routinely for any patient presenting with injection drug use history?
cards.a: Hepatitis C and HIV serology.

cards.q: Primary psychological driver targeted during Cognitive Behavioral Therapy for substance use disorders?
cards.a: Identification and modification of maladaptive thoughts and triggers that lead to relapse.

cards.q: Medication used to treat benzodiazepine overdose that can precipitate life-threatening seizures in chronic users?
cards.a: Flumazenil.

cards.q: Active metabolite of choice when treating alcohol withdrawal in a patient with acute pancreatitis?
cards.a: Lorazepam (due to exclusive extrahepatic glucuronidation).

cards.q: Why is Diazepam often preferred over Lorazepam in a structurally normal liver during alcohol withdrawal?
cards.a: It has active metabolites ($nordiazepam$) providing a long, smooth self-tapering effect.

cards.q: Impact of chronic alcohol consumption on the minimum alveolar concentration (MAC) of volatile anesthetics?
cards.a: Increases the MAC, requiring higher doses of anesthesia due to cross-tolerance.

cards.q: Impact of acute alcohol intoxication on the minimum alveolar concentration (MAC) of volatile anesthetics?
cards.a: Decreases the MAC, requiring lower doses of anesthesia due to synergistic CNS depression.

cards.q: The specific $GABA_A$ receptor subunit configuration targeted by alcohol that mediates its anxiolytic effects?
cards.a: $\alpha_1$ and $\alpha$-5 subunits.

cards.q: Why does the combination of Buprenorphine and Naloxone ($Suboxone$) not cause precipitated withdrawal when swallowed normally?
cards.a: Naloxone undergoes extensive first-pass hepatic metabolism and has negligible oral bioavailability.

cards.q: Expected pupil size changes if a patient co-ingests toxic doses of cocaine and heroin ("speedball")?
cards.a: Variable or normal pupillary size due to competing miotic and mydriatic effects.

cards.q: Neurological receptor responsible for the development of rapid tolerance (tachyphylaxis) in chronic stimulant use?
cards.a: Downregulation and internalization of post-synaptic Dopamine $D_1$ and $D_2$ receptors.

cards.q: Pathophysiological mechanism behind "cocaine-induced chest pain" in a young patient with normal coronary arteries?
cards.a: $\alpha_1$ adrenergic receptor stimulation causing severe coronary artery vasospasm.

cards.q: Initial choice of antihypertensive agent if a patient with cocaine intoxication remains hypertensive after maximizing benzodiazepines?
cards.a: Phentolamine (a pure $\alpha$-adrenergic antagonist).

cards.q: Why are pure $\beta$-blocker like Propranolol contraindicated in cocaine-induced acute coronary syndrome?
cards.a: They leave $\alpha_1$ receptors unopposed, causing catastrophic vasoconstriction and coronary ischemia.

cards.q: Most common structural cardiac anomaly found in long-term chronic methamphetamine abusers?
cards.a: Dilated cardiomyopathy.

cards.q: Main arterial complication associated with chronic, heavy amphetamine use that can cause acute stroke in young adults?
cards.a: Necrotizing angiitis (cerebral vasculitis).

cards.q: Renal pathology directly caused by severe stimulant-induced rhabdomyolysis?
cards.a: Acute tubular necrosis due to myoglobinuria.

cards.q: Gastrointestinal complication of acute cocaine use caused by focal mesenteric ischemia?
cards.a: Bowel ischemia or intestinal perforation.

cards.q: Demographic group with the highest statistically verified rate of successful completion of suicide during substance withdrawal?
cards.a: Middle-aged males with concurrent Alcohol Use Disorder.

cards.q: Federal schedule classification of Cocaine under the US Controlled Substances Act?
cards.a: Schedule II (due to its high abuse potential but accepted medical use as a local anesthetic).

cards.q: Federal schedule classification of Heroin under the US Controlled Substances Act?
cards.a: Schedule I (high abuse potential with no currently accepted medical use).

cards.q: Federal schedule classification of Methadone under the US Controlled Substances Act?
cards.a: Schedule II.

cards.q: Federal schedule classification of Buprenorphine under the US Controlled Substances Act?
cards.a: Schedule III.

cards.q: Medical legal requirement mandated by the DATA 2000 act for physicians prescribing Buprenorphine for OUD (historically referred to as)?
cards.a: The X-Waiver (note: federally removed in recent years, but historically heavily tested).

cards.q: Primary long-term neurodevelopmental deficit seen in children exposed to chronic intrauterine cocaine?
cards.a: Deficits in executive functioning, emotional regulation, and attention span.

cards.q: Primary obstetric complication associated with acute maternal cocaine use during the third trimester?
cards.a: Placental abruption due to acute hypertensive spikes.

cards.q: Preferred screening questionnaire specifically validated for detecting risky alcohol use in geriatric populations?
cards.a: Short Michigan Alcoholism Screening Test - Geriatric Version (SMAST-G).

cards.q: Why do geriatric patients achieve a higher Blood Alcohol Concentration (BAC) than younger peers with the same amount of alcohol?
cards.a: Decrease in total body water and decline in gastric alcohol dehydrogenase activity.

cards.q: First-line non-pharmacological behavioral therapy used to manage mild Neonatal Abstinence Syndrome (NAS)?
cards.a: Rooming-in, swaddling, and low-stimulus environments.

cards.q: Substance intoxication that uniquely mimics acute stimulant intoxication but is characterized by prominent vertical nystagmus and severe violence?
cards.a: Phencyclidine (PCP) intoxication.

cards.q: Over-the-counter cough suppressant that can cause a false-positive result for PCP on a standard urine drug screen?
cards.a: Dextromethorphan.

cards.q: Common prescription antidepressant that can cause a false-positive result for amphetamines on a routine urine drug screen?
cards.a: Bupropion.

cards.q: Common fluoroquinolone antibiotic that can cause a false-positive result for opiates on a standard urine drug screen?
cards.a: Levofloxacin (or Ofloxacin).

cards.q: Why does a standard routine urine drug screen often return negative in a patient with a confirmed acute Fentanyl overdose?
cards.a: Standard screens test for morphine metabolites, whereas synthetic opioids require a specialized gas chromatography-mass spectrometry assay.

cards.q: Life-threatening cardiovascular complication of utilizing old-generation antipsychotics to treat cocaine-induced psychosis?
cards.a: Prolongation of the QTc interval leading to Torsades de Pointes.

cards.q: First-line pharmacological management for a patient presenting with an acute, unstable aortic dissection secondary to cocaine use?
cards.a: Intravenous Sodium Nitroprusside or Phentolamine combined with Benzodiazepines.

cards.q: Preferred alternative medication for acute opioid withdrawal if a patient develops severe bradycardia or hypotension from Clonidine?
cards.a: Oral Methadone or Buprenorphine induction (if appropriate) or supportive symptomatic medications like Loperamide and Acetaminophen.

cards.q: Clinical phenomenon where an alcohol withdrawal patient's tremor worsens drastically during active movement or targeted tasks?
cards.a: Intention tremor secondary to chronic alcohol-induced cerebellar degeneration.

cards.q: Specific region of the cerebellum that undergoes selective atrophy in chronic, heavy alcohol users?
cards.a: The anterior vermis of the cerebellum.

cards.q: Evidence-based behavioral management strategy that provides tangible rewards (e.g., vouchers) for verified negative drug screens?
cards.a: Contingency Management.

cards.q: Primary objective of the "Harm Reduction" model of addiction treatment?
cards.a: Minimizing the negative health and social consequences of substance use without strictly requiring immediate total abstinence.

cards.q: Standard peer-led, 12-step recovery program utilized worldwide for Alcohol Use Disorder support?
cards.a: Alcoholics Anonymous (AA).

cards.q: Core psychological concept of 12-step programs regarding control over addiction?
cards.a: Admission of powerlessness over the substance and surrender to a higher power or group structure.

cards.q: Mandatory reporting requirement for a medical student who suspects a resident or attending physician is practicing while acutely intoxicated?
cards.a: Reporting directly to the hospital’s Physician Health Program (PHP) or the state medical board to ensure patient safety.

cards.q: Genetic polymorphism linked to a significantly decreased risk of developing Alcohol Use Disorder due to severe flushing reactions?
cards.a: Homozygous $ALDH2*2$ allele mutation (inactive aldehyde dehydrogenase).

cards.q: Specific brain region responsible for the intense cue-induced cravings and relapse vulnerability seen in chronic substance users?
cards.a: The basolateral amygdala and prefrontal cortex.

cards.q: Neurotransmitters whose depletion is responsible for the profound "washed-out" lethargy and depression following a multi-day methamphetamine binge?
cards.a: Total depletion of central intracellular Dopamine and Serotonin stores.

cards.q: Structural adaptation in cardiac tissue directly responsible for sudden cardiac death in chronic cocaine users without an acute myocardial infarction?
cards.a: Focal myocardial fibrosis and contraction band necrosis.

cards.q: Patient with severe AUD presents with vomiting, a high anion gap metabolic acidosis, but a normal or low serum glucose level. Diagnosis?
cards.a: Alcoholic Ketoacidosis (AKA).

cards.q: Primary pathophysiological driver of Alcoholic Ketoacidosis?
cards.a: Glycogen depletion combined with a high NADH/NAD+ ratio that shifts metabolism toward ketone body production.

cards.q: Immediate initial medical treatment required for a patient in acute Alcoholic Ketoacidosis?
cards.a: Intravenous infusion of normal saline and dextrose (glucose) without the immediate need for insulin.

cards.q: Patient with a history of intravenous drug use presents with acute lower back pain, high fever, and focal spinal tenderness. Diagnosis?
cards.a: Spinal Epidural Abscess.

cards.q: Immediate diagnostic modality of choice for a suspected spinal epidural abscess in an injection drug user?
cards.a: Emergency MRI of the spine with gadolinium contrast.

cards.q: Chronic stimulant user presents with severe, diffuse abdominal pain out of proportion to physical exam findings following an intense binge. Diagnosis?
cards.a: Acute mesenteric ischemia secondary to cocaine-induced vasoconstriction.

cards.q: What is the core definition of a personality disorder according to the DSM-5-TR?
cards.a: An enduring pattern of inner experience and behavior that deviates markedly from cultural expectations, is pervasive and inflexible, and leads to distress or impairment.

cards.q: At what developmental stage must the features of a personality disorder typically manifest?
cards.a: They must trace back at least to adolescence or early adulthood.

cards.q: Why can a personality disorder generally not be diagnosed before the age of 18?
cards.a: Personality traits are still developing and may represent transient developmental phases.

cards.q: What is the single exception allowing a personality disorder diagnosis in individuals under 18?
cards.a: The traits must be present for at least one year, and it cannot be Antisocial Personality Disorder.

cards.q: What does it mean for a personality disorder to be "ego-syntonic"?
cards.a: The individual perceives their behavior as natural, correct, and acceptable, rather than viewing it as a problem.

cards.q: What does it mean for a condition to be "ego-dystonic"?
cards.a: The symptoms are perceived by the individual as unacceptable, alien, and inconsistent with their self-concept.

cards.q: How do defense mechanisms in personality disorders differ from those in acute Axis I disorders?
cards.a: They are chronically deployed, deeply ingrained, and serve as the individual's primary way of navigating the world.

cards.q: Which three personality disorders comprise Cluster A?
cards.a: Paranoid, Schizoid, and Schizotypal personality disorders.

cards.q: What is the overarching descriptor commonly used for Cluster A disorders?
cards.a: Odd or eccentric.

cards.q: Which four personality disorders comprise Cluster B?
cards.a: Antisocial, Borderline, Histrionic, and Narcissistic personality disorders.

cards.q: What is the overarching descriptor commonly used for Cluster B disorders?
cards.a: Dramatic, emotional, or erratic.

cards.q: Which three personality disorders comprise Cluster C?
cards.a: Avoidant, Dependent, and Obsessive-Compulsive personality disorders.

cards.q: What is the overarching descriptor commonly used for Cluster C disorders?
cards.a: Anxious or fearful.

cards.q: What diagnostic category is used when a patient meets general criteria for a personality disorder but not for a specific cluster?
cards.a: Other Specified or Unspecified Personality Disorder.

cards.q: What is the central feature of Paranoid Personality Disorder?
cards.a: A pervasive, unjustified distrust and suspiciousness of others such that their motives are interpreted as malevolent.

cards.q: How does a patient with Paranoid Personality Disorder view benign remarks or events?
cards.a: They hidden demeaning or threatening meanings into benign remarks or events.

cards.q: How do patients with Paranoid Personality Disorder typically handle perceived slights or injuries?
cards.a: They persistently bear grudges and are unforgiving of insults or injuries.

cards.q: What is the PPD patient's typical attitude regarding the fidelity of their spouse or sexual partner?
cards.a: They harbor recurrent, unjustified suspicions regarding the fidelity of their partner.

cards.q: Why do individuals with Paranoid Personality Disorder reluctantly confide in others?
cards.a: They fear the information will be used maliciously against them.

cards.q: What distinguishes Paranoid Personality Disorder from Schizophrenia?
cards.a: PPD lacks fixed, unshakeable delusions, hallucinations, and formal thought disorder.

cards.q: Which defense mechanism is most prominently utilized by individuals with Paranoid Personality Disorder?
cards.a: Projection, where they attribute their own unacknowledged hostile feelings to others.

cards.q: What is the primary psychological barrier to treating a patient with Paranoid Personality Disorder?
cards.a: Their profound mistrust makes establishing a therapeutic alliance exceptionally difficult.

cards.q: What is the core characteristic of Schizoid Personality Disorder?
cards.a: A pervasive pattern of detachment from social relationships and a restricted range of emotional expression.

cards.q: How do individuals with Schizoid Personality Disorder view close relationships, including being part of a family?
cards.a: They neither desire nor enjoy close relationships.

cards.q: What type of activities do individuals with Schizoid Personality Disorder almost always choose?
cards.a: Solitary activities.

cards.q: How do individuals with Schizoid Personality Disorder typically respond to praise or criticism?
cards.a: They appear indifferent to both praise and criticism from others.

cards.q: What is the typical sexual history or interest level of a person with Schizoid Personality Disorder?
cards.a: They have little, if any, interest in having sexual experiences with another person.

cards.q: How is the affect of a patient with Schizoid Personality Disorder usually described?
cards.a: Emotional coldness, detachment, or flattened affectivity.

cards.q: What distinguishes Schizoid Personality Disorder from Avoidant Personality Disorder?
cards.a: Schizoid individuals prefer isolation, whereas Avoidant individuals desire relationships but fear rejection.

cards.q: What distinguishes Schizoid Personality Disorder from Schizotypal Personality Disorder?
cards.a: Schizoid lacks the cognitive, perceptual distortions, and eccentricities seen in Schizotypal.

cards.q: What is the definitive presentation of Schizotypal Personality Disorder?
cards.a: A pattern of acute discomfort in close relationships, cognitive or perceptual distortions, and eccentricities of behavior.

cards.q: What are "ideas of reference" as frequently seen in Schizotypal Personality Disorder?
cards.a: Incorrect interpretations that innocuous, casual external events have highly personally significant meanings.

cards.q: What kind of odd beliefs or magical thinking influence the behavior of an STPD patient?
cards.a: Beliefs inconsistent with subcultural norms, such as clairvoyance, telepathy, or a "sixth sense."

cards.q: What type of unusual perceptual experiences might a Schizotypal patient report?
cards.a: Bodily illusions or sensing the presence of a person or force that is not actually there.

cards.q: How is the speech of a Schizotypal patient typically characterized?
cards.a: Odd, vague, circumstantial, metaphorical, overelaborate, or stereotyped speech.

cards.q: What type of anxiety do Schizotypal individuals experience in social situations that does not diminish with familiarity?
cards.a: Severe social anxiety that tends to be associated with paranoid fears rather than negative judgments about self.

cards.q: Schizotypal Personality Disorder is genetically linked to which major psychiatric axis I disorder?
cards.a: Schizophrenia.

cards.q: What medication class can be used in low doses to treat transient psychotic episodes or severe anxiety in STPD patients?
cards.a: Low-dose atypical antipsychotics.

cards.q: What is the essential feature of Antisocial Personality Disorder?
cards.a: A pervasive pattern of disregard for, and violation of, the rights of others occurring since age 15.

cards.q: What childhood diagnosis is a strict prerequisite for diagnosing Antisocial Personality Disorder?
cards.a: Conduct Disorder, with onset before age 15.

cards.q: What is the minimum age at which Antisocial Personality Disorder can be officially diagnosed?
cards.a: 18 years old.

cards.q: How do individuals with Antisocial Personality Disorder typically behave regarding social norms and laws?
cards.a: They repeatedly perform acts that are grounds for arrest due to a failure to conform to lawful behaviors.

cards.q: What is the characteristic trait of ASPD involving a complete lack of remorse?
cards.a: They are indifferent to, or rationalize, having hurt, mistreated, or stolen from another person.

cards.q: How does impulsivity manifest behaviorally in individuals with Antisocial Personality Disorder?
cards.a: A failure to plan ahead, frequent job changes, and sudden, unprovoked relocations.

cards.q: What physical behavior is frequently exhibited by individuals with Antisocial Personality Disorder?
cards.a: Irritability and aggressiveness, as indicated by repeated physical fights or assaults.

cards.q: What is the primary secondary gain sought by patients with Antisocial Personality Disorder when interacting with healthcare systems?
cards.a: Obtaining substances, avoiding legal prosecution, or securing disability benefits.

cards.q: What happens to the severity of criminal or antisocial behaviors as an ASPD patient reaches middle age?
cards.a: The overt, aggressive antisocial behaviors often decrease or remit as they grow older.

cards.q: What is the core definition of Borderline Personality Disorder?
cards.a: A pervasive pattern of instability in interpersonal relationships, self-image, affects, and marked impulsivity.

cards.q: What frantic efforts do individuals with Borderline Personality Disorder make?
cards.a: Frantic efforts to avoid real or imagined abandonment.

cards.q: What is the characteristic pattern of interpersonal relationships in BPD?
cards.a: Unstable and intense relationships alternating between extremes of idealization and devaluation.

cards.q: What defense mechanism is classically defined by alternating between total idealization and total devaluation?
cards.a: Splitting.

cards.q: What is the nature of identity disturbance in Borderline Personality Disorder?
cards.a: A markedly and persistently unstable self-image or sense of self.

cards.q: In what areas must a BPD patient show potentially self-damaging impulsivity?
cards.a: Spending, sex, substance abuse, reckless driving, or binge eating.

cards.q: What recurrent behaviors are highly characteristic of crisis presentations in BPD patients?
cards.a: Recurrent suicidal behavior, gestures, threats, or self-mutilating acts like cutting.

cards.q: What chronic internal feeling is frequently voiced by individuals with Borderline Personality Disorder?
cards.a: A chronic feeling of emptiness.

cards.q: What happens to a BPD patient's cognitive state during periods of extreme, acute stress?
cards.a: They may experience transient, stress-related paranoid ideation or severe dissociative symptoms.

cards.q: What is the gold-standard, evidence-based psychotherapy modality developed specifically for BPD?
cards.a: Dialectical Behavior Therapy (DBT).

cards.q: What are the four core skill modules taught to patients in Dialectical Behavior Therapy?
cards.a: Mindfulness, distress tolerance, emotion regulation, and interpersonal effectiveness.

cards.q: Why should long-term benzodiazapine prescriptions be strictly avoided in BPD patients?
cards.a: They can cause behavioral disinhibition and carry a high risk for lethal overdose during impulsive gestures.

cards.q: What is the primary characteristic of Histrionic Personality Disorder?
cards.a: A pervasive pattern of excessive emotionality and attention-seeking behavior.

cards.q: How do individuals with Histrionic Personality Disorder feel when they are not the center of attention?
cards.a: Uncomfortable, unappreciated, or completely unfulfilled.

cards.q: What is the nature of the interpersonal interactions initiated by individuals with Histrionic Personality Disorder?
cards.a: Interactions are frequently characterized by inappropriate sexually seductive or provocative behavior.

cards.q: How is the expression of emotion described in a patient with Histrionic Personality Disorder?
cards.a: Rapidly shifting and shallow.

cards.q: What physical means do Histrionic individuals consistently use to draw attention to themselves?
cards.a: They consistently use their physical appearance to attract attention.

cards.q: How is the speech style of a patient with Histrionic Personality Disorder best described?
cards.a: Excessively impressionistic and strikingly lacking in detail.

cards.q: What is the nature of the emotional expression of someone with Histrionic Personality Disorder?
cards.a: Highly dramatic, theatrical, and exaggerated.

cards.q: How suggestible are individuals with Histrionic Personality Disorder?
cards.a: They are highly suggestible and easily influenced by others or by current fads.

cards.q: How do Histrionic individuals typically misjudge the depth of their relationships?
cards.a: They consider relationships to be much more intimate than they actually are.

cards.q: What is the essential feature of Narcissistic Personality Disorder?
cards.a: A pervasive pattern of grandiosity, a constant need for admiration, and a profound lack of empathy.

cards.q: With what types of fantasies are individuals with Narcissistic Personality Disorder preoccupied?
cards.a: Fantasies of unlimited success, power, brilliance, beauty, or ideal love.

cards.q: Who do individuals with Narcissistic Personality Disorder believe they should associate with?
cards.a: Other special, unique, or high-status people and institutions.

cards.q: What baseline entitlement do individuals with Narcissistic Personality Disorder possess?
cards.a: Unreasonable expectations of especially favorable treatment or automatic compliance with their expectations.

cards.q: How do individuals with Narcissistic Personality Disorder utilize other people in relationships?
cards.a: They are interpersonally exploitative, taking advantage of others to achieve their own ends.

cards.q: What core human capacity is notably absent or deficient in Narcissistic Personality Disorder?
cards.a: Empathy, leading to an unwillingness to recognize or identify with the feelings and needs of others.

cards.q: What emotion do individuals with NPD frequently experience toward others, or believe others experience toward them?
cards.a: Intense envy.

cards.q: What underlying psychological vulnerability exists beneath the grandiose exterior of an NPD patient?
cards.a: Fragile self-esteem that renders them highly vulnerable to "narcissistic injury" from criticism.
