cards.a: Forensic medical evaluation using a sexual assault evidence collection kit, along with emergency contraception and prophylactic antibiotics.

cards.q: Psychiatric condition where physical restraints are strictly contraindicated due to the risk of worsening hyperthermia and rhabdomyolysis?
cards.a: Excited delirium syndrome.

cards.q: Legal standard used to determine if a defendant was insane at the time of a crime based on the inability to know right from wrong?
cards.a: The M'Naghten Rule.

cards.q: Legal exception allowing emergency treatment without explicit informed consent?
cards.a: Emergency privilege (when delaying treatment to obtain consent would result in imminent serious harm or death).

cards.q: Key autonomic vital sign abnormality that differentiates Serotonin Syndrome/NMS from a pure severe panic attack?
cards.a: High-grade hyperthermia (panic attacks do not cause true hyperthermia).

cards.q: Neuromuscular finding that differentiates Malignant Hyperthermia (from volatile anesthetics) from NMS?
cards.a: Malignant hyperthermia causes immediate, generalized rigidity following anesthesia induction, whereas NMS develops over hours to days following antipsychotic use.

cards.q: Specific physical exam maneuver used to elicit latent clonus in suspected mild Serotonin Syndrome?
cards.a: Rapidly dorsiflexing the patient's foot to assess for sustained ankle clonus.

cards.q: Pupillary difference between anticholinergic toxicity and Serotonin Syndrome?
cards.a: Both cause mydriasis, but anticholinergic toxicity presents with completely dry skin, whereas Serotonin Syndrome presents with profuse diaphoresis.

cards.q: Key laboratory finding that differentiates Factitious Disorder from Malingering?
cards.a: There are no specific lab findings, as the differentiation relies entirely on identifying the presence or absence of an external, secondary gain.

cards.q: Over-the-counter cough suppressant that can precipitate Serotonin Syndrome when combined with an SSRI?
cards.a: Dextromethorphan.

cards.q: Antibiotic with intrinsic MAOI activity that can precipitate Serotonin Syndrome when given to a patient on an antidepressant?
cards.a: Linezolid.

cards.q: Opioid analgesic contraindicated in patients taking MAOIs due to severe risk of Serotonin Syndrome?
cards.a: Meperidine.

cards.q: Herbal supplement commonly used for depression that can precipitate Serotonin Syndrome?
cards.a: St. John's Wort.

cards.q: Severe metabolic side effect of second-generation antipsychotics (like olanzapine) that can present as an acute diabetic emergency?
cards.a: Diabetic Ketoacidosis (DKA) or Hyperosmolar Hyperglycemic State (HHS).

cards.q: Electrocardiogram monitoring requirement for a patient receiving intravenous haloperidol for acute delirium?
cards.a: Continuous telemetry monitoring to watch for QTc prolongation.

cards.q: Definitive management for a patient on clozapine who presents with an Absolute Neutrophil Count (ANC) of $850/\mu\text{L}$?
cards.a: Immediate and permanent cessation of clozapine and daily ANC monitoring.

cards.q: Benign ethnic neutropenia (BEN) adjustments for clozapine require a lower baseline ANC threshold of what value?
cards.a: $1,500/\mu\text{L}$ to initiate, and must be discontinued if it drops below $500/\mu\text{L}$.

cards.q: Toxic byproduct of metabolized sodium nitroprusside sometimes used in hypertensive emergencies that presents with psychosis and metabolic acidosis?
cards.a: Cyanide toxicity.

cards.q: Antipsychotic medication most notorious for causing severe, acute obstructive sialadenitis (salivary gland swelling) or sialorrhea as an emergency presentation?
cards.a: Clozapine.

cards.q: Landmark Supreme Court case establishing that involuntary civil commitment requires the state to prove the individual is both mentally ill and actively dangerous?
cards.a: O'Connor v. Donaldson.

cards.q: Landmark case establishing that a patient committed involuntarily still retains the right to refuse antipsychotic medications in non-emergency situations?
cards.a: Rogers v. Okin.

cards.q: Court case that established the standard that a criminal defendant must understand the charges against them and be able to assist their attorney?
cards.a: Dusky v. United States (Competency to stand trial).

cards.q: Specific legal standard that shifted the Tarasoff ruling from a "duty to warn" to a broader "duty to protect"?
cards.a: Tarasoff II (allowing options like clinical hospitalization or warning law enforcement instead of just the victim).

cards.q: Under what specific clinical condition can a physician override a patient's right to refuse medication without a court order?
cards.a: An acute emergency where the patient poses an immediate, physical danger to themselves or others in the unit.

cards.q: Legal designation for a court-appointed individual who manages the financial and personal affairs of an individual deemed legally incompetent?
cards.a: Conservator or Guardian.

cards.q: Does a patient's family member have the legal right to view a psychiatric note regarding an emergency admission without the patient's consent?
cards.a: No, psychiatric notes are protected under HIPAA laws unless an emergency exception applies.

cards.q: Legal term used when a physician holds a patient in the hospital against their will without documenting formal involuntary commitment papers?
cards.a: False imprisonment.

cards.q: First and most essential verbal strategy when managing an escalating, uncooperative patient?
cards.a: Verbal de-escalation using a calm tone, validating distress, and establishing clear boundaries.

cards.q: Maximum time limit allowed for a single adult physical restraint order before a physician must re-evaluate the patient face-to-face?
cards.a: Four hours.

cards.q: Maximum time limit allowed for a physical restraint order for a child or adolescent (ages 9–17)?
cards.a: Two hours.

cards.q: Immediate physical hazard that must be monitored continuously while a patient is in four-point leather restraints?
cards.a: Airway patency and peripheral vascular perfusion.

cards.q: Serious metabolic consequence of prolonged, forceful physical struggle against restraints in an agitated patient?
cards.a: Metabolic acidosis and worsening rhabdomyolysis.

cards.q: Drug of choice for acute behavioral control in an agitated patient with known prolonged QTc interval?
cards.a: Lorazepam (as it does not significantly alter the QTc interval).

cards.q: Why are intramuscular atypicals like olanzapine or ziprasidone preferred over haloperidol in patients with mild-to-moderate QTc baseline elevations?
cards.a: They carry a statistically lower immediate risk of inducing Torsades de Pointes.

cards.q: Diagnostic criteria minimum number of symptoms required to diagnose catatonia under DSM-5-TR?
cards.a: Three or more out of twelve characteristic symptoms.

cards.q: Definition of "catalepsy" in catatonia?
cards.a: Passive induction of a posture held against gravity.

cards.q: Definition of "mitmachen" in catatonia?
cards.a: The patient moves their body in response to slight pressure despite being told to resist.

cards.q: Definition of "gegenhalten" (negativism) in catatonia?
cards.a: The patient resists all passive movements with a force proportional to that applied by the examiner.

cards.q: Immediate physiological indication for emergent Electroconvulsive Therapy (ECT)?
cards.a: Malignant catatonia with autonomic instability or severe, life-threatening food refusal.

cards.q: Absolute medical contraindication to performing Electroconvulsive Therapy (ECT)?
cards.a: There are no absolute medical contraindications to ECT, only conditions of increased risk (e.g., increased intracranial pressure).

cards.q: Most common immediate cognitive side effect observed post-ECT?
cards.a: Transient anterograde and retrograde amnesia.

cards.q: First-line medication used to safely manage emergent agitation in a pregnant patient?
cards.a: High-potency typical antipsychotics (e.g., haloperidol).

cards.q: Primary emergency concern when a postpartum mother presents with severe command auditory hallucinations to harm her infant?
cards.a: Postpartum psychosis, requiring immediate involuntary hospitalization to protect the infant.

cards.q: Street drug known as "Spice" or "K2" that presents as an unpredictable psychiatric emergency with severe psychosis and tachyarrhythmias?
cards.a: Synthetic cannabinoids.

cards.q: Recreational drug inhalation ("whippets") that can present with acute panic, paranoia, and subacute combined degeneration of the spinal cord?
cards.a: Nitrous oxide (causing vitamin $B_{12}$ inactivation).

cards.q: Drug toxicity presenting with a combination of vertical nystagmus, high pain tolerance, and extreme, unpredictable violence?
cards.a: Phencyclidine (PCP) intoxication.

cards.q: Life-threatening withdrawal syndrome characterized by severe autonomic hyperactivity, formication (feeling bugs crawling), and tactile hallucinations?
cards.a: Severe alcohol withdrawal / Delirium Tremens.

cards.q: Antidote for severe cardiotoxicity and widened QRS secondary to diphenhydramine overdose?
cards.a: Sodium bicarbonate (due to diphenhydramine's sodium-channel blocking properties at high doses).

cards.q: Can a patient who is actively hallucinating still possess the capacity to make a specific medical decision?
cards.a: Yes, if the hallucinations do not impair or interfere with the specific logic needed for that decision.

cards.q: Most appropriate action if a patient lacks capacity and requires emergency surgery, but no surrogate decision-maker is contactable?
cards.a: Proceed with the surgery under the legal doctrine of emergency implied consent.

cards.q: Key difference between non-suicidal self-injury (NSSI) and a suicide attempt?
cards.a: NSSI is performed without any intent to die, usually to alleviate severe negative emotional states.

cards.q: Best predictor of immediate, near-term suicide risk during an emergency psychiatric evaluation?
cards.a: The presence of severe hopelessness joined with a specific, lethal plan and high intent.

cards.q: Primary clinical management strategy for a patient presenting with an explicit suicide plan involving a firearm stored at home?
cards.a: Direct counseling on lethal means restriction, requiring the removal or secure locking of the firearm by a third party.

cards.q: Mechanism of action of Selective Serotonin Reuptake Inhibitors (SSRIs)?
cards.a: Inhibition of the presynaptic serotonin transporter (SERT) pump, increasing synaptic serotonin levels.

cards.q: First-line medication class for Generalized Anxiety Disorder (GAD), Panic Disorder, and Social Anxiety Disorder?
cards.a: Selective Serotonin Reuptake Inhibitors (SSRIs).

cards.q: SSRI with the longest half-life and no need for tapering when discontinued?
cards.a: Fluoxetine.

cards.q: SSRI most commonly associated with QTc prolongation at higher doses?
cards.a: Citalopram.

cards.q: SSRI with the highest risk for GI side effects and standardly approved for OCD?
cards.a: Fluvoxamine.

cards.q: SSRI with the shortest half-life and highest risk for discontinuation syndrome?
cards.a: Paroxetine.

cards.q: Mechanism of action of Serotonin-Norepinephrine Reuptake Inhibitors (SNRIs)?
cards.a: Inhibition of both serotonin (SERT) and norepinephrine (NET) presynaptic transporters.

cards.q: Primary vital sign abnormality to monitor in patients taking high-dose Venlafaxine?
cards.a: Elevated blood pressure (hypertension).

cards.q: FDA-approved SNRI preferred for the dual treatment of depression and chronic musculoskeletal/neuropathic pain?
cards.a: Duloxetine.

cards.q: Active metabolite of venlafaxine requiring minimal hepatic metabolism?
cards.a: Desvenlafaxine.

cards.q: Main mechanism of action of Bupropion?
cards.a: Norepinephrine-dopamine reuptake inhibitor (NDRI).

cards.q: Major clinical contraindication for the use of Bupropion?
cards.a: Seizure disorders and history of bulimia or anorexia nervosa.

cards.q: Preferred antidepressant for a patient concerned with sexual dysfunction or weight gain?
cards.a: Bupropion.

cards.q: Mechanism of action of Mirtazapine?
cards.a: $\alpha_2$ adrenergic receptor antagonist that increases release of serotonin and norepinephrine.

cards.q: Two primary dose-dependent side effects of Mirtazapine at lower doses?
cards.a: Sedation and increased appetite leading to weight gain.

cards.q: Mechanism of action of Trazodone?
cards.a: Serotonin antagonist and reuptake inhibitor (SARI).

cards.q: Rare but emergency medical adverse effect associated with Trazodone use?
cards.a: Priapism.

cards.q: Mechanism of action of Vilazodone?
cards.a: SSRI combined with $\text{$\text{5-HT}$}_{1\text{A}}$ receptor partial agonism.

cards.q: Mechanism of action of Vortioxetine?
cards.a: Serotonin modulator and stimulator (SMS) via SERT inhibition and multiple $\text{5-HT}$ receptor variations.

cards.q: Mechanism of action of Tricyclic Antidepressants (TCAs)?
cards.a: Inhibition of SERT and NET, along with blockade of histamine, acetylcholine, and $\alpha_1$ receptors.

cards.q: Primary cause of lethality in a Tricyclic Antidepressant (TCA) overdose?
cards.a: Cardiac arrhythmias due to blockade of fast sodium channels.

cards.q: Immediate EKG finding that indicates a severe TCA overdose?
cards.a: Widened QRS complex greater than 100 milliseconds.

cards.q: Antidote used to treat cardiac toxicity and QRS widening in TCA overdose?
cards.a: Sodium bicarbonate.

cards.q: Mechanism of action of Monoamine Oxidase Inhibitors (MAOIs)?
cards.a: Irreversible inhibition of monoamine oxidase enzymes (MAO-A and MAO-B), preventing breakdown of monoamines.

cards.q: Life-threatening complication that occurs when a patient on an MAOI consumes tyramine-rich foods?
cards.a: Hypertensive crisis.

cards.q: Minimum washout period required when switching from most SSRIs to an MAOI?
cards.a: Two weeks.

cards.q: Specific washout period required when switching from Fluoxetine to an MAOI?
cards.a: Five weeks.

cards.q: Triad of clinical signs that define Serotonin Syndrome?
cards.a: Autonomic instability, altered mental status, and neuromuscular hyperactivity.

cards.q: Specific physical exam finding that distinguishes Serotonin Syndrome from Neuroleptic Malignant Syndrome?
cards.a: Hyperreflexia and clonus.

cards.q: First-line medication used for the pharmacological management of severe Serotonin Syndrome?
cards.a: Cyproheptadine.

cards.q: Primary therapeutic mechanism of First-Generation Antipsychotics (FGAs)?
cards.a: Strong, high-affinity antagonism of post-synaptic Dopamine $\text{D}_2$ receptors.

cards.q: Dopaminergic pathway targeted to reduce positive symptoms of schizophrenia?
cards.a: Mesolimbic pathway.

cards.q: Dopaminergic pathway responsible for extrapyramidal symptoms (EPS) during antipsychotic therapy?
cards.a: Nigrostriatal pathway.

cards.q: Dopaminergic pathway responsible for hyperprolactinemia during $\text{D}_2$ receptor blockade?
cards.a: Tuberoinfundibular pathway.

cards.q: High-potency First-Generation Antipsychotic most notorious for causing extrapyramidal symptoms?
cards.a: Haloperidol.

cards.q: Low-potency FGA associated with corneal deposits and pigmentary retinopathy?
cards.a: Chlorpromazine.

cards.q: Low-potency FGA known for causing retinal pigmentation and significant QTc prolongation?
cards.a: Thioridazine.

cards.q: Definition and timeline of Acute Dystonia?
cards.a: Sudden, painful muscle spasms of the neck, face, or tongue occurring within hours to days of starting antipsychotics.

cards.q: First-line treatment for an acute dystonic reaction?
cards.a: Intramuscular Benztropine or Diphenhydramine.

cards.q: Definition and clinical presentation of Akathisia?
cards.a: Subjective feeling of inner restlessness and the physical compulsion to move, typically occurring within days to weeks.

cards.q: First-line pharmacological options for the treatment of Akathisia?
cards.a: Propranolol or Benzodiazepines.

cards.q: Presentation and timeline of Antipsychotic-Induced Parkinsonism?
cards.a: Bradykinesia, rigidity, and a resting tremor occurring within weeks to months of treatment initiation.

cards.q: Preferred management for drug-induced parkinsonism if the antipsychotic cannot be lowered?
cards.a: Benztropine or Amantadine.

cards.q: Definition and timeline of Tardive Dyskinesia?
cards.a: Involuntary, choreoathetotic movements of the mouth, tongue, and face following months to years of antipsychotic use.

cards.q: Mechanism of action of medications approved to treat Tardive Dyskinesia (e.g., Valbenazine, Deutetrabenazine)?
cards.a: Vesicular monoamine transporter 2 (VMAT2) inhibitors.

cards.q: Tetrad of symptoms defining Neuroleptic Malignant Syndrome (NMS)?
cards.a: Severe "lead-pipe" muscle rigidity, hyperthermia, autonomic instability, and altered mental status.

cards.q: Laboratory marker characteristically elevated in Neuroleptic Malignant Syndrome?
cards.a: Creatine kinase (CK).

cards.q: Two primary pharmacological agents used to treat severe Neuroleptic Malignant Syndrome?
cards.a: Dantrolene and Bromocriptine.

cards.q: Primary therapeutic mechanism of Second-Generation Antipsychotics (SGAs)?
cards.a: Dual antagonism of Serotonin $\text{$\text{5-HT}$}_{2\text{A}}$ and Dopamine $\text{D}_2$ receptors.

cards.q: Gold-standard antipsychotic reserved for treatment-resistant schizophrenia?
cards.a: Clozapine.

cards.q: Black box warning and mandatory laboratory monitoring parameter required for Clozapine?
cards.a: Severe neutropenia/agranulocytosis requiring absolute neutrophil count (ANC) tracking.

cards.q: Threshold absolute neutrophil count (ANC) below which Clozapine must be immediately discontinued?
cards.a: Less than 1,000 per microliter.

cards.q: Two Second-Generation Antipsychotics with the highest risk for causing metabolic syndrome?
cards.a: Olanzapine and Clozapine.

cards.q: Two Second-Generation Antipsychotics with the lowest risk for metabolic syndrome and weight gain?
cards.a: Aripiprazole and Ziprasidone.

cards.q: Second-Generation Antipsychotic requiring administration with food to ensure adequate absorption?
cards.a: Ziprasidone (or Lurasidone).

cards.q: Specific mechanism of action that differentiates Aripiprazole from most other SGAs?
cards.a: Partial $\text{D}_2$ receptor agonism.

cards.q: Second-Generation Antipsychotic with the highest propensity to elevate prolactin levels?
cards.a: Risperidone.

cards.q: Antipsychotic preferred for managing psychosis in patients with Parkinson's disease due to low $\text{D}_2$ affinity?
cards.a: Quetiapine.

cards.q: First-line maintenance medication for Bipolar I disorder with proven anti-suicidal properties?
cards.a: Lithium.

cards.q: Maintenance laboratory monitoring parameters required for a patient on Lithium?
cards.a: Thyroid function tests (TSH), renal function tests (BUN/Creatinine), and serum Lithium levels.

cards.q: Target therapeutic serum concentration range for Lithium maintenance therapy?
cards.a: 0.6 to 1.2 mEq/L.

cards.q: Common ECG change seen with therapeutic Lithium use?
cards.a: T-wave flattening or inversion.

cards.q: Renal side effect of Lithium characterized by polyuria and polydipsia?
cards.a: Nephrogenic Diabetes Insipidus.

cards.q: Medication class that can dangerously increase serum Lithium levels by decreasing renal clearance?
cards.a: Thiazide diuretics (or NSAIDs/ACE inhibitors).

cards.q: Congenital cardiac anomaly associated with Lithium use during the first trimester of pregnancy?
cards.a: Ebstein's anomaly.

cards.q: Mechanism of action of Valproic Acid (Valproate)?
cards.a: Blocks voltage-gated sodium channels and increases GABA concentrations in the brain.

cards.q: Two major organ systems at risk for acute toxicity from Valproic Acid?
cards.a: Hepatic (hepatotoxicity) and Pancreatic (acute pancreatitis).

cards.q: Congenital malformation associated with maternal Valproic Acid use during pregnancy?
cards.a: Neural tube defects (e.g., spina bifida).

cards.q: Mechanism of action of Carbamazepine?
cards.a: Blocks voltage-gated sodium channels, inhibiting repetitive neuronal firing.

cards.q: Serious hematologic adverse effect associated with Carbamazepine use?
cards.a: Agranulocytosis and aplastic anemia.

cards.q: Genetic allele strongly associated with Stevens-Johnson Syndrome in Asian patients taking Carbamazepine?
Unique pharmacokinetic property of Carbamazepine regarding its own metabolism?
cards.a: Autoinduction of its own metabolism via the CYP3A4 enzyme system.

cards.q: Mood stabilizer primarily used for bipolar depression maintenance that requires slow titration?
cards.a: Lamotrigine.

cards.q: Life-threatening dermatologic adverse effect associated with rapid titration of Lamotrigine?
cards.a: Stevens-Johnson Syndrome (SJS) / Toxic Epidermal Necrolysis (TEN).

cards.q: Interaction effect when Valproate and Lamotrigine are co-administered?
cards.a: Valproate doubles Lamotrigine levels, drastically increasing SJS risk.

cards.q: Mechanism of action of Benzodiazepines?
cards.a: Positive allosteric modulators that increase the frequency of $\text{GABA}_\text{A}$ channel opening.

cards.q: Three Benzodiazepines that bypass phase I hepatic oxidation and undergo only phase II glucuronidation?
cards.a: Oxazepam, Temazepam, and Lorazepam (mnemonic: OTL / Outside The Liver).

cards.q: Benzodiazepine preferred for the management of acute alcohol withdrawal in a patient with severe liver cirrhosis?
cards.a: Lorazepam (or Oxazepam).

cards.q: Specific competitive antagonist used to reverse benzodiazepine-induced respiratory depression?
cards.a: Flumazenil.

cards.q: Major clinical danger of administering Flumazenil to a patient with chronic benzodiazepine dependence?
cards.a: Precipitation of acute withdrawal seizures.

cards.q: Mechanism of action of Buspirone?
cards.a: Partial agonist at the Serotonin $\text{$\text{5-HT}$}_{1\text{A}}$ receptor.

cards.q: Clinical timeline limitation of Buspirone for the treatment of generalized anxiety disorder?
cards.a: It takes 2 to 4 weeks to become clinically effective and cannot be used prn (as needed).

cards.q: Mechanism of action of "Z-drugs" (Zolpidem, Zaleplon, Eszopiclone)?
cards.a: Selective agonists at the $\alpha_1$ subunit of the $\text{GABA}_\text{A}$ receptor complex.

cards.q: Main clinical advantage of Z-drugs over standard Benzodiazepines for insomnia?
cards.a: Minimal disruption of normal sleep architecture and lower risk of dependence.

cards.q: Mechanism of action of Ramelteon?
cards.a: Melatonin receptor (MT1 and MT2) agonist.

cards.q: Mechanism of action of Suvorexant?
cards.a: Orexin receptor antagonist that turns off wakefulness signals.

cards.q: First-line medication for opioid overdose causing respiratory depression?
cards.a: Naloxone.

cards.q: Long-acting opioid agonist used for maintenance therapy in opioid use disorder?
cards.a: Methadone.

cards.q: EKG abnormality that requires strict monitoring in patients on high-dose Methadone maintenance?
cards.a: QTc prolongation.

cards.q: Mechanism of action of Buprenorphine?
cards.a: Partial $\mu$-opioid receptor agonist with a high binding affinity.

cards.q: Purpose of adding Naloxone to Buprenorphine in sublingual combination formulations (Suboxone)?
cards.a: To prevent intravenous abuse; naloxone has poor bioavailability unless injected.

cards.q: Competitive opioid antagonist used to prevent relapse in both alcohol and opioid use disorders?
cards.a: Naltrexone.

cards.q: Baseline laboratory test required before initiating Naltrexone therapy?
cards.a: Liver function tests (due to risk of hepatotoxicity).

cards.q: Mechanism of action of Disulfiram?
cards.a: Irreversible inhibition of aldehyde dehydrogenase, causing accumulation of acetaldehyde upon alcohol ingestion.

cards.q: Mechanism of action of Acamprosate?
cards.a: Modulates NMDA glutamate receptors and $\text{GABA}_\text{A}$ receptors to restore neurochemical balance.

cards.q: Contraindication for the use of Acamprosate in patients with alcohol use disorder?
cards.a: Severe renal impairment (Creatinine Clearance $\1$ mL/min).

cards.q: First-line pharmacological treatments for smoking cessation?
cards.a: Varenicline and Bupropion.

cards.q: Mechanism of action of Varenicline?
cards.a: $\alpha$-4-$\beta_2$ nicotinic acetylcholine receptor partial agonist.

cards.q: First-line pharmacological class for Attention-Deficit/Hyperactivity Disorder (ADHD) in pediatric and adult populations?
cards.a: Stimulants (Methylphenidate and Amphetamines).

cards.q: Mechanism of action of Methylphenidate?
cards.a: Blocks the reuptake of dopamine and norepinephrine via transporter inhibition.

cards.q: Mechanism of action of Amphetamines?
cards.a: Stimulates the presynaptic release of dopamine and norepinephrine into the synaptic cleft.

cards.q: Non-stimulant medication approved for ADHD that acts as a selective norepinephrine reuptake inhibitor (NRI)?
cards.a: Atomoxetine.

cards.q: Mechanism of action of Guanfacine and Clonidine when used for ADHD?
cards.a: $\alpha_2$ adrenergic receptor agonists that strengthen prefrontal cortical networks.

cards.q: Mechanism of action of Donepezil, Rivastigmine, and Galantamine?
cards.a: Acetylcholinesterase inhibitors used to increase synaptic acetylcholine in Alzheimer's dementia.

cards.q: Mechanism of action of Memantine?
cards.a: Uncompetitive NMDA glutamate receptor antagonist that protects against excitotoxicity.

cards.q: Pharmacological agent used to treat neuroleptic-induced sialorrhea (drooling) from Clozapine?
cards.a: Sublingual Atropine drops (or oral Terazosin).

cards.q: Antidepressant most likely to cause a dose-dependent increase in diastolic blood pressure?
cards.a: Venlafaxine.

cards.q: Antipsychotic medication that must be taken with a meal of at least 350 calories to ensure bioavailability?
cards.a: Lurasidone.

cards.q: Antidote used to treat acute anticholinergic toxicity (e.g., severe atropine or antihistamine overdose)?
cards.a: Physostigmine.

cards.q: Preferred pharmacological treatment for Moderate to Severe Alcohol Withdrawal Syndrome in a hospital setting?
cards.a: Diazepam or Chlordiazepoxide (long-acting benzodiazepines).

cards.q: Antidepressant that acts as a potent $\text{H}_1$ histamine antagonist, causing substantial sedation and weight gain?
cards.a: Mirtazapine.

cards.q: Class of medications that can precipitate Serotonin Syndrome if combined with Linezolid?
cards.a: SSRIs or SNRIs (due to Linezolid's weak MAOI activity).

cards.q: Antipsychotic drug least likely to cause hyperprolactinemia due to its $\text{D}_2$ partial agonism?
cards.a: Aripiprazole.

cards.q: Medication class used as first-line adjunctive therapy for the autonomic symptoms of performance-based social anxiety?
cards.a: $\beta$-blocker (e.g., Propranolol).

cards.q: Serious hematologic monitoring parameter required during the first 6 months of Clozapine therapy?
cards.a: Weekly Absolute Neutrophil Count (ANC).

cards.q: Mood stabilizer that undergoes zero hepatic metabolism and is excreted 100% unchanged by the kidneys?
cards.a: Lithium.

cards.q: First-line treatment for Restless Legs Syndrome (RLS) if iron stores are normal?
cards.a: Dopamine agonists (Pramipexole or Ropinirole) or $\alpha_2$-$\delta$ ligands (Gabapentin).

cards.q: Antidepressant approved for the treatment of Bulimia Nervosa?
cards.a: Fluoxetine.

cards.q: Medication class that can cause severe lithium toxicity by reducing renal perfusion?
cards.a: Nonsteroidal Anti-inflammatory Drugs (NSAIDs).

cards.q: Medication used to counteract antipsychotic-induced hyperprolactinemia if the primary drug cannot be stopped?
cards.a: Aripiprazole (added at low doses for its partial $\text{D}_2$ agonism).

cards.q: Primary receptor blockade responsible for orthostatic hypotension caused by low-potency antipsychotics?
cards.a: $\alpha_1$ adrenergic receptors.

cards.q: Primary receptor blockade responsible for the blurry vision, dry mouth, and urinary retention seen with TCAs?
cards.a: Muscarinic acetylcholine receptors.

cards.q: Active metabolite of Risperidone that has a lower risk of hepatic drug-drug interactions?
cards.a: Paliperidone.

cards.q: Only Second-Generation Antipsychotic that carries an FDA indication for monotherapy in bipolar depression?
cards.a: Quetiapine.

cards.q: Neurotransmitter system modulated by Acamprosate to reduce alcohol cravings?
cards.a: Glutamatergic (NMDA receptor modulation).

cards.q: Contraindication for using Naltrexone in a patient with alcohol use disorder?
cards.a: Acute hepatitis, liver failure, or concurrent opioid use.

cards.q: Antidepressant that is a potent CYP2D6 inhibitor and can reduce the efficacy of Tamoxifen?
cards.a: Paroxetine (or Fluoxetine).

cards.q: First-line medication class for the treatment of Obsessive-Compulsive Disorder (OCD)?
cards.a: High-dose SSRIs.

cards.q: Preferred long-term medication for a patient with comorbid Major Depressive Disorder and Migraines?
cards.a: Tricyclic Antidepressants (e.g., Amitriptyline).

cards.q: Class of medications most effective for treating panic attacks acutely?
cards.a: Benzodiazepines.

cards.q: Antidepressant with a dual mechanism that makes it highly effective for treating smoking cessation?
cards.a: Bupropion.

cards.q: Serious neurological risk of correcting chronic hyponatremia too rapidly with saline solutions?
cards.a: Central Pontine Myelinolysis (Osmotic Demyelination Syndrome).

cards.q: Life-threatening condition caused by combining Lithium with Haloperidol in high doses?
cards.a: Irreversible neurotoxicity and encephalopathy.

cards.q: Antipsychotic medication that requires a baseline eye exam every 6 months according to historical guidelines?
cards.a: Quetiapine (due to early animal study concerns for cataracts, though rarely done now).

cards.q: Antipsychotic choice for an agitated patient who refuses oral medications and requires rapid tranquilization?
cards.a: Intramuscular Haloperidol or Olanzapine.

cards.q: Medication class that should never be given concurrently with intramuscular Olanzapine due to risk of fatal cardiorespiratory depression?
cards.a: Intramuscular Benzodiazepines.

cards.q: Substance of abuse that acts as a non-competitive NMDA receptor antagonist and can cause nystagmus and agitation?
cards.a: Phencyclidine (PCP).

cards.q: Antidote used for the treatment of Benzodiazepine withdrawal seizures?
cards.a: Intravenous Phenobarbital or a long-acting Benzodiazepine taper.

cards.q: Mechanism of action of Topiramate when used off-label for alcohol use disorder?
cards.a: Potentiates $\text{GABA}_\text{A}$ receptors and inhibits AMPA/kainate glutamate receptors.

cards.q: Common benign side effect of Lamotrigine that does not warrant discontinuation?
cards.a: Benign maculopapular rash (requires close monitoring to differentiate from SJS).

cards.q: Antipsychotic that has the most prominent risk of causing significant QTc prolongation without being a low-potency FGA?
cards.a: Ziprasidone.

cards.q: Enzyme system responsible for the metabolism of most psychiatric drugs, including SSRIs and antipsychotics?
cards.a: Cytochrome P450 system.

cards.q: Medication class that can cause severe hypertensive crisis if combined with foods containing tyramine?
cards.a: Monoamine Oxidase Inhibitors (MAOIs).

cards.q: Primary symptom of Benzodiazepine toxicity when combined with alcohol?
cards.a: Respiratory depression.

cards.q: Mechanism of action of Hydroxyzine when used for acute anxiety?
cards.a: Histamine $\text{H}_1$ receptor antagonist.

cards.q: Non-habit-forming medication used for the long-term management of Generalized Anxiety Disorder?
cards.a: Buspirone.

cards.q: Preferred treatment for severe, treatment-resistant Major Depressive Disorder with psychotic features when rapid response is needed?
cards.a: Electroconvulsive Therapy (ECT).

cards.q: Mechanism by which Lithium causes hypothyroidism?
cards.a: Inhibits thyroid hormone synthesis and release.

cards.q: Target serum concentration of Lithium during an acute manic episode?
cards.a: 1.0 to 1.5 mEq/L.

cards.q: Mechanism of action of Atomoxetine?
cards.a: Selective Norepinephrine Reuptake Inhibitor.

cards.q: First-line medication class for Narcolepsy management?
cards.a: Modafinil or Armodafinil.

cards.q: Mechanism of action of Modafinil?
cards.a: Weak dopamine reuptake inhibitor that increases wakefulness.

cards.q: Medication used to treat the depressive phase of Bipolar Disorder that is also an anticonvulsant?
cards.a: Lamotrigine.

cards.q: Most common side effect of Acetylcholinesterase inhibitors used in Alzheimer's disease?
cards.a: Gastrointestinal upset (nausea, vomiting, diarrhea).

cards.q: Medication used for the treatment of severe, intractable hiccups?
cards.a: Chlorpromazine.

cards.q: Preferred antidepressant for elderly patients due to its clean side effect profile and low drug interactions?
cards.a: Sertraline (or Escitalopram).

cards.q: Antidepressant class generally considered first-line for major depressive disorder during pregnancy and breastfeeding?
cards.a: Selective Serotonin Reuptake Inhibitors (SSRIs), excluding paroxetine.

cards.q: Specific neonatal complication associated with SSRI use late in the third trimester?
cards.a: Persistent Pulmonary Hypertension of the Newborn (PPHN) or neonatal adaptation syndrome.

cards.q: Neonatal physical exam finding characteristic of Neonatal Adaptation Syndrome following in utero SSRI exposure?
cards.a: Irritability, tachypnea, tremors, and weak cry resolving within days.

cards.q: Gold-standard mood stabilizer preferred for acute mania in pregnancy if lithium or valproate must be avoided?
cards.a: Haloperidol (or Second-Generation Antipsychotics like Olanzapine).

cards.q: Floppy infant syndrome and neonatal respiratory depression are associated with maternal use of which class near delivery?
cards.a: Benzodiazepines.

cards.q: Mechanism of action of Esketamine (nasal spray) used for treatment-resistant depression?
cards.a: Non-competitive NMDA glutamate receptor antagonist.

cards.q: Mandatory post-administration monitoring protocol required for patients receiving Esketamine?
cards.a: Observation for at least two hours for sedation, dissociation, and blood pressure spikes.

cards.q: First FDA-approved oral medication specifically for Postpartum Depression (PPD) acting as a $\text{GABA}_\text{A}$ receptor positive allosteric modulator?
cards.a: Zuranolone (or intravenous Brexanolone).

cards.q: Primary clinical indication for prescribing a Long-Acting Injectable (LAI) antipsychotic?
cards.a: History of poor medication adherence in patients with severe chronic psychotic disorders.

cards.q: First-generation antipsychotic available as a decanoate formulation for long-acting injection?
cards.a: Haloperidol Decanoate (or Fluphenazine Decanoate).

cards.q: Second-generation long-acting injectable antipsychotic requiring a 3-hour post-injection observation window due to delirium-sedation syndrome risk?
cards.a: Olanzapine Pamoate.

cards.q: Long-acting injectable antipsychotic that does not require an oral medication overlap period when initiated?
cards.a: Invega Sustenna (Paliperidone Palmitate).

cards.q: Common over-the-counter herbal supplement that induces CYP3A4 and can drastically lower concentrations of oral contraceptives and cyclosporine?
cards.a: St. John's Wort.

cards.q: Lifestyle factor that induces CYP1A2, thereby lowering serum levels of Clozapine and Olanzapine?
cards.a: Cigarette smoking (specifically polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons).

cards.q: Clinical consequence of a patient abruptly quitting smoking while maintaining their baseline Clozapine dose?
cards.a: Toxic rise in Clozapine levels, increasing seizure and agranulocytosis risks.

cards.q: Mechanism by which Fluoxetine or Paroxetine co-administration renders Codeine ineffective for pain control?
cards.a: Inhibition of CYP2D6, preventing the conversion of Codeine to its active form, Morphine.

cards.q: Dietary substance that inhibits intestinal CYP3A4, leading to toxic levels of certain benzodiazepines and buspirone?
cards.a: Grapefruit juice.

cards.q: DEA Controlled Substance schedule classification for Benzodiazepines and Z-drugs?
cards.a: Schedule IV.

cards.q: DEA Controlled Substance schedule classification for Methylphenidate and Amphetamine stimulants?
cards.a: Schedule II.

cards.q: Primary clinical toxicity concern when combining a Benzodiazepine with a prescribed Opioid medication?
cards.a: Fatal respiratory depression via synergistic CNS depression.

cards.q: Black box warning applied to all antidepressants regarding their use in children, adolescents, and young adults?
cards.a: Increased risk of suicidal ideation and behavior.

cards.q: Serum Lithium concentration above which hemodialysis is strongly indicated regardless of clinical symptoms?
cards.a: Greater than 4.0 mEq/L (or greater than 2.5 mEq/L with severe neurological symptoms).

cards.q: Initial fluid management strategy for treating acute, mild-to-moderate Lithium toxicity?
cards.a: Aggressive intravenous hydration with 0.9% Normal Saline to promote renal clearance.

cards.q: Cardiac dysrhythmia risk associated with high-dose intravenous Haloperidol administration?
cards.a: Torsades de Pointes via QTc prolongation.

cards.q: Pharmacological management for an intentional overdose of $\beta$-blocker used off-label for performance anxiety?
cards.a: Intravenous Glucagon.

cards.q: Baseline screening test mandated before initiating any stimulant medication for ADHD to rule out structural anomalies?
cards.a: Thorough cardiac history and physical exam (EKG only if cardiac risk factors are present).

cards.q: Adjunctive medication used to treat the significant weight gain associated with Olanzapine therapy?
cards.a: Metformin (or Topiramate).

cards.q: Mechanism behind Second-Generation Antipsychotic induced metabolic syndrome?
cards.a: Antagonism of Histamine $\text{H}_1$ and Serotonin $\text{$\text{5-HT}$}_{2\text{C}}$ receptors stimulating appetite.

cards.q: Antipsychotic medication least likely to cause QTc prolongation or metabolic syndrome, making it ideal for cardiac patients?
cards.a: Lurasidone (or Aripiprazole).

cards.q: Landmark clinical trial that established the efficacy and metabolic side effect profiles of Second-Generation Antipsychotics?
cards.a: The CATIE trial (Clinical Antipsychotic Trials of Intervention Effectiveness).

cards.q: Only antidepressant with a definitive indication for treating nocturnal enuresis (bedwetting) in children?
cards.a: Imipramine (a TCA).

cards.q: Minimum symptom duration required to diagnose Prolonged Grief Disorder in adults according to the DSM-5-TR?
cards.a: Twelve months following the loss of a loved one.

cards.q: Minimum symptom duration required to diagnose Prolonged Grief Disorder in children and adolescents according to the DSM-5-TR?
cards.a: Six months following the loss of a loved one.

cards.q: New condition added to the DSM-5-TR section "Conditions That May Be a Focus of Clinical Attention" to track self-harm behaviors?
cards.a: Suicidal Behavior and Nonsuicidal Self-Injury.

cards.q: Outdated diagnostic terminology replaced by "Intellectual Disability" in the DSM-5-TR?
cards.a: Intellectual Developmental Disorder (or Mental Retardation in historical texts).

cards.q: Specific Obsessive-Compulsive Related Disorder that received a new diagnostic specifier ("Olfactory Reference Disorder") in the DSM-5-TR?
cards.a: Other Specified Obsessive-Compulsive and Related Disorder.

cards.q: Major change to the Clozapine monitoring protocol implemented by the FDA?
cards.a: Elimination of the requirement to submit absolute neutrophil count (ANC) results directly to a central REMS registry prior to dispensing.

cards.q: Mechanism of action of Lumateperone used for schizophrenia and bipolar depression?
cards.a: Potent $\text{$\text{5-HT}$}_{2\text{A}}$ receptor antagonism combined with post-synaptic low $\text{D}_2$ receptor antagonism and partial presynaptic $\text{D}_2$ agonism.

cards.q: Non-antipsychotic combination medication approved for treating agitation associated with Alzheimer’s disease dementia?
cards.a: Dextromethorphan-quinidine (or the newer NMDA/Sigma-1 formulation AXS-05).

cards.q: Mechanism of action of Topiramate when used for alcohol use disorder or weight mitigation?
cards.a: Potentiates $\text{GABA}_\text{A}$ receptors, inhibits AMPA/kainate glutamate receptors, and inhibits carbonic anhydrase.

cards.q: Common cognitive side effect reported by patients taking Topiramate?
cards.a: Psychomotor slowing, word-finding difficulties, and memory impairment (often called "Dopamax").

cards.q: Non-selective $\beta$-blocker used off-label to treat the physiological tremors of Lithium toxicity or performance anxiety?
cards.a: Propranolol.

cards.q: Anticonvulsant metabolized into phenobarbital that is used off-label to treat severe essential tremors?
cards.a: Primidone.

cards.q: Mechanism by which Cyproheptadine reverses Serotonin Syndrome?
cards.a: Non-selective serotonin receptor antagonist (primarily targeting $\text{$\text{5-HT}$}_{1\text{A}}$ and $\text{$\text{5-HT}$}_{2\text{A}}$ receptors).

cards.q: Primary toxic metabolite of Acetaminophen that builds up during an intentional overdose and causes hepatotoxicity?
cards.a: N-acetyl-p-benzoquinone imine (NAPQI).

cards.q: Specific antidote administered to replenish glutathione stores in an acute Acetaminophen overdose?
cards.a: N-acetylcysteine (NAC).

cards.q: Severe developmental delay and craniofacial abnormality caused by in utero exposure to Phenytoin?
cards.a: Fetal Hydantoin Syndrome.

cards.q: Stimulus and response for the Moro reflex?
cards.a: Sudden head drop causes arm abduction/extension followed by adduction/flexion.

cards.q: Normal disappearance age for the Moro reflex?
cards.a: 4 months.

cards.q: Stimulus and response for the Rooting reflex?
cards.a: Stroking the cheek causes the infant to turn the head toward the stimulus.

cards.q: Normal disappearance age for the Rooting reflex?
cards.a: 4 months.

cards.q: Normal disappearance age for the Palmar Grasp reflex?
cards.a: 4 months.

cards.q: Normal disappearance age for the Plantar Grasp reflex?
cards.a: 9 to 12 months.

cards.q: Stimulus and response for the Asymmetric Tonic Neck Reflex (ATNR/Fencing)?
cards.a: Turning the head causes ipsilateral extremity extension and contralateral extremity flexion.

cards.q: Normal disappearance age for the Asymmetric Tonic Neck Reflex (ATNR)?
cards.a: 4 to 6 months.

cards.q: Normal disappearance age for the Galant reflex (lateral trunk incurvation)?
cards.a: 4 to 6 months.

cards.q: Description and appearance age of the Parachute reflex?
cards.a: Protective extension of arms when tilted forward; appears at 7 to 9 months and persists for life.

cards.q: Normal disappearance age for the Babinski reflex in healthy infants?
cards.a: 12 to 24 months.

cards.q: Average weight of a term newborn?
Expected weight change in the first 3 to 4 days of life?

cards.q: Age by which a normal infant regains birth weight?

cards.q: Age by which birth weight triples?
cards.a: 12 months (1 year).

cards.q: Age by which birth weight quadruples?
