cards.q: Global developmental delay (GDD) definition?
cards.a: Significant delay in 2 or more developmental domains in children under 5 years old.

cards.q: Most common inherited cause of intellectual disability?
cards.a: Fragile X Syndrome.

cards.q: Most common genetic (non-inherited) cause of intellectual disability?
cards.a: Down Syndrome (Trisomy 21).

cards.q: Universal screening age for Autism Spectrum Disorder (ASD) via M-CHAT?
cards.a: 18 months and 24 months.

cards.q: Average daily sleep duration required for a neonate?
cards.a: 16 to 18 hours.

cards.q: Age at which an infant typically consolidates sleep through the night?
cards.a: 6 months.

cards.q: Physiological readiness age window for toilet training?
cards.a: 18 to 24 months.

cards.q: Psychological milestone required before starting toilet training?
cards.a: Ability to communicate the need to eliminate and desire to please parents.

cards.q: Average age window when girls achieve day bladder control?
cards.a: 2.5 to 3 years.

cards.q: Average age window when boys achieve day bladder control?
cards.a: 3 to 3.5 years.

cards.q: Age after which bedwetting is formally classified as nocturnal enuresis?
cards.a: 5 years.

cards.q: Formula for estimating lower limit of systolic blood pressure (5th percentile) for ages 1 to 10?
cards.a: 70 + (2 × age in years) mmHg.

cards.q: Minimum systolic blood pressure defining hypotension in a term neonate (0 to 28 days)?
cards.a: Less than 60 mmHg.

cards.q: Minimum systolic blood pressure defining hypotension in an infant (1 to 12 months)?
cards.a: Less than 70 mmHg.

cards.q: Normal resting respiratory rate for a newborn?
cards.a: 40 to 60 breaths per minute.

cards.q: Normal resting heart rate range for an awake neonate?
cards.a: 100 to 180 beats per minute.

cards.q: First physical sign of puberty in genetic females?
cards.a: Thelarche (breast budding).

cards.q: Tanner Stage of a female with a projection of the papilla only?
cards.a: Tanner Stage 1.

cards.q: Tanner Stage characterized by elevation of breast and papilla as a small mound, with enlargement of areolar diameter?
cards.a: Tanner Stage 2.

cards.q: Tanner Stage characterized by further enlargement of breast and areola without separation of their contours?
cards.a: Tanner Stage 3.

cards.q: Tanner Stage where the areola and papilla project to form a secondary mound above the level of the breast?
cards.a: Tanner Stage 4.

cards.q: Tanner Stage showing recession of the areola to the general contour of the breast, with projection of the papilla only?
cards.a: Tanner Stage 5.

cards.q: Timeline of menarche relative to the onset of thelarche?
cards.a: Approximately 2 to 2.5 years after thelarche.

cards.q: Tanner stage during which the female growth spurt typically peaks?
cards.a: Tanner Stage 3.

cards.q: First physical sign of puberty in genetic males?
cards.a: Testicular enlargement (volume greater than or equal to 4 mL).

cards.q: Tanner Stage 2 male genital characteristics?
cards.a: Enlargement of scrotum and testes; scrotal skin reddens and thins.

cards.q: Tanner Stage 3 male genital characteristics?
cards.a: Enlargement of penis (lengthwise) and further growth of testes.

cards.q: Tanner Stage 4 male genital characteristics?
cards.a: Increased size of penis (breadth/glans development) and darkening of scrotal skin.

cards.q: Tanner stage during which the male growth spurt typically peaks?
cards.a: Tanner Stage 4.

cards.q: Tanner Stage 2 pubic hair characteristics?
cards.a: Sparse growth of long, slightly pigmented, straight hair at the base of the penis or labia.

cards.q: Tanner Stage 3 pubic hair characteristics?
cards.a: Darker, coarser, and more curled hair spreading sparsely over the junction of the pubes.

cards.q: Tanner Stage 4 pubic hair characteristics?
cards.a: Hair is adult in type, but covers an area smaller than in most adults; no spread to medial thighs.

cards.q: Tanner Stage 5 pubic hair characteristics?
cards.a: Adult hair in quantity and type, distributed in an inverse triangle pattern extending to the medial thighs.

cards.q: Average age of onset for female puberty?
cards.a: 8 to 13 years of age.

cards.q: Average age of onset for male puberty?
cards.a: 9 to 14 years of age.

cards.q: Definition of precocious puberty in girls?
cards.a: Development of secondary sexual characteristics before age 8.

cards.q: Definition of precocious puberty in boys?
cards.a: Development of secondary sexual characteristics before age 9.

cards.q: Definition of delayed puberty in girls?
cards.a: No breast development by age 13.

cards.q: Definition of delayed puberty in boys?
cards.a: No testicular enlargement by age 14.

cards.q: Recommended age for universal autism screening using the M-CHAT?
cards.a: 18 and 24 months.

cards.q: Recommended ages for universal developmental screening using validated tools (e.g., ASQ)?
cards.a: 9, 18, and 30 months.

cards.q: Standardized screening tool used to assess a child's development from birth to 6 years across four domains?
cards.a: Denver Developmental Screening Test II (Denver II).

cards.q: Primary purpose of the Modified Checklist for Autism in Toddlers (M-CHAT)?
cards.a: To identify children at risk for Autism Spectrum Disorder (ASD).

cards.q: Next step after a positive or high-risk score on an M-CHAT screening?
cards.a: Referral for formal diagnostic evaluation and early intervention services.

cards.q: Piaget stage from birth to 2 years characterized by object permanence?
cards.a: Sensorimotor stage.

cards.q: Piaget stage from 2 to 7 years characterized by egocentrism and magical thinking?
cards.a: Preoperational stage.

cards.q: Piaget stage from 7 to 11 years where a child understands conservation of volume and mass?
cards.a: Concrete operational stage.

cards.q: Piaget stage from age 11 onward characterized by abstract and hypothetical thinking?
cards.a: Formal operational stage.

cards.q: Erikson psychosocial crisis for infants from birth to 1 year?
cards.a: Trust vs. Mistrust.

cards.q: Erikson psychosocial crisis for toddlers from 1 to 3 years?
cards.a: Autonomy vs. Shame and Doubt.

cards.q: Erikson psychosocial crisis for preschool children from 3 to 6 years?
cards.a: Initiative vs. Guilt.

cards.q: Erikson psychosocial crisis for school-aged children from 6 to 12 years?
cards.a: Industry vs. Inferiority.

cards.q: Erikson psychosocial crisis for adolescents from 12 to 18 years?
cards.a: Identity vs. Role Confusion.

cards.q: Definition of microcephaly based on head circumference percentiles?
cards.a: Occipitofrontal circumference (OFC) less than the 3rd percentile (or < -2 standard deviations).

cards.q: Definition of macrocephaly based on head circumference percentiles?
cards.a: Occipitofrontal circumference (OFC) greater than the 97th percentile (or > +2 standard deviations).

cards.q: Classic diagnostic criteria for Failure to Thrive (FTT)?
cards.a: Weight below the 3rd to 5th percentile, or weight crossing two major percentile lines downward.

cards.q: Most common etiology of Failure to Thrive (FTT) in the United States?
cards.a: Non-organic (psychosocial/inadequate caloric intake).

cards.q: First growth parameter affected in nutritional (organic or non-organic) Failure to Thrive?
cards.a: Weight.

cards.q: Second growth parameter affected in progressive nutritional Failure to Thrive?
cards.a: Height/Length.

cards.q: Final growth parameter affected in severe, chronic nutritional Failure to Thrive?
cards.a: Head circumference.

cards.q: Condition suspected when head circumference is normal but weight and height drop early?
cards.a: Constitutional growth delay or endocrine pathology.

cards.q: Condition suspected when head circumference drops disproportionately to weight and height?
cards.a: Congenital infection, genetic syndrome, or central nervous system insult.

cards.q: Clinical feature distinguishing Constitutional Delay of Growth from Familial Short Stature?
cards.a: Constitutional delay features a delayed bone age; Familial short stature features a normal bone age.

cards.q: Formula to calculate Mid-Parental Height (Target Height) for a boy?
cards.a: [Father's height + Mother's height + 13 cm (or 5 inches)] / 2.

cards.q: Formula to calculate Mid-Parental Height (Target Height) for a girl?
cards.a: [Father's height + Mother's height - 13 cm (or 5 inches)] / 2.

cards.q: Age at which iron-fortified single-grain infant cereal should be introduced?
cards.a: 4 to 6 months.

cards.q: Maximum age window to exclusively breastfeed an infant before introducing solids?
cards.a: 6 months.

cards.q: Why should whole cow's milk be avoided until 12 months of age?
cards.a: Risk of iron-deficiency anemia due to occult GI blood loss and low iron bioavailability.

cards.q: Why should honey be strictly avoided before 12 months of age?
cards.a: Risk of infant botulism from Clostridium botulinum spores.

cards.q: Age at which juice can be introduced to a child's diet, according to AAP guidelines?
cards.a: Not recommended before 12 months of age.

cards.q: Age at which the first visit to a pediatric dentist is recommended?
cards.a: Within 6 months of the first tooth eruption or by 12 months of age.

cards.q: Supplementation required for exclusively breastfed infants starting in the first few days of life?
cards.a: Vitamin D (400 IU daily).

cards.q: Supplementation required for exclusively breastfed term infants starting at 4 months of age?
cards.a: Oral iron supplementation (1 mg/kg/day) until iron-containing solid foods are introduced.

cards.q: Age until which an infant should ride in a rear-facing car safety seat?
cards.a: At least 2 years of age (or until reaching the highest weight/height limit allowed by the manufacturer).

cards.q: Age at which a child can typically safely transition from a booster seat to a vehicle lap-and-shoulder belt?
cards.a: When they reach 4 feet 9 inches (145 cm) in height, typically between 8 and 12 years old.

cards.q: Crucial positioning recommendation to reduce the risk of Sudden Infant Death Syndrome (SIDS)?
cards.a: Prone-to-supine sleep position ("Back to Sleep") on a firm surface.

cards.q: Fine motor milestone that correlates with an increased risk of household choking hazards?
cards.a: Pincer grasp (9 to 12 months).

cards.q: Gross motor milestone that requires immediate installation of safety gates at stairs?
cards.a: Crawling (9 months).

cards.q: Only paranasal sinuses present and radiographically visible at birth?
cards.a: Ethmoid sinuses (maxillary are present but pneumatize later).

cards.q: Age at which the frontal sinuses typically become radiographically apparent?
cards.a: 5 to 7 years of age.

cards.q: Age at which the sphenoid sinuses finish development and pneumatization?
cards.a: Puberty (begins around 3 to 5 years).

cards.q: Percentage of adult brain volume achieved by an infant by 1 year of age?
cards.a: Approximately 70%.

cards.q: Percentage of adult brain volume achieved by a child by 2 years of age?
cards.a: Approximately 80%.

cards.q: Most common cause of gonadotropin-dependent (central) precocious puberty in girls?
cards.a: Idiopathic (constitutional).

cards.q: Most common cause of gonadotropin-dependent (central) precocious puberty in boys?
cards.a: Central nervous system tumors (e.g., hypothalamic hamartoma).

cards.q: Genetic condition to suspect in a phenotypic male with delayed puberty, small/firm testes, and gynecomastia?
cards.a: Klinefelter Syndrome (47, XXY).

cards.q: Genetic condition to suspect in a phenotypic female with delayed puberty, short stature, and low-set ears?
cards.a: Turner Syndrome (45, X).

cards.q: Condition characterized by isolated breast development in girls under age 2 with no other signs of puberty?
cards.a: Benign premature thelarche.

cards.q: Diagnostic step to differentiate central precocious puberty from peripheral precocious puberty?
cards.a: GnRH stimulation test (central shows an LH response; peripheral does not).

cards.q: Most concerning developmental history finding regardless of domain or age?
cards.a: Loss of any previously acquired milestone (developmental regression).

cards.q: Developmental regression in a 15-month-old female with hand-wringing stereotypies points to?
cards.a: Rett Syndrome.

cards.q: Motor milestone indicating a child is delayed if they cannot run or walk up stairs by what age?
cards.a: 24 months (2 years).

cards.q: Language milestone indicating a child is delayed if they do not use single words by what age?
cards.a: 16 months.

cards.q: Fine motor delay indicated if a child cannot copy a circle by what age?
cards.a: 4 years (48 months).

cards.q: Asymmetric Moro reflex with lack of movement in one arm suggests?
cards.a: Brachial plexus injury (Erb-Duchenne palsy) or clavicle fracture.

cards.q: Retention of primitive reflexes past the first year of life is highly associated with?
cards.a: Cerebral Palsy.

cards.q: Nerve roots evaluated by the Moro reflex?
cards.a: C5 and C6.

cards.q: Neonatal reflex where stroking the spine causes lateral flexion of the lower trunk toward the stimulated side?
cards.a: Galant reflex.

cards.q: Absence of the Galant reflex may indicate?
cards.a: Spinal cord transection or lower motor neuron lesion.

cards.q: Expected response to the Landau reflex when an infant is held horizontally in prone position?
cards.a: The infant lifts the head and extends the neck and spine (disappears by 12 to 24 months).

cards.q: Well-child visit age where an infant should receive the first dose of MMR and Varicella vaccines alongside walking milestones?
cards.a: 12 to 15 months.

cards.q: Well-child visit age that pairs the 4th DTaP dose with running and a 10-word vocabulary?
cards.a: 18 months.

cards.q: Well-child visit age where toilet training readiness and parallel play are assessed before kindergarten vaccine discussions?
cards.a: 24 months (2 years).

cards.q: Age at which the final booster doses of DTaP, IPV, MMR, and Varicella are administered alongside skipping milestones?
cards.a: 4 to 6 years (Kindergarten entry).

cards.q: Principal psychological mechanism driving risk-taking behavior in middle adolescence (ages 14 to 17)?
cards.a: Belief of omnipotence and invulnerability ("it won't happen to me").

cards.q: Primary source of behavioral validation during early and middle adolescence?
cards.a: Peer groups.

cards.q: Most common somatic symptom of depression in school-aged children and adolescents?
cards.a: Recurrent abdominal pain or headaches.

cards.q: Tanner stage in males where axillary hair and facial hair growth typically begin?
cards.a: Tanner Stage 4.

cards.q: Normal variance characterized by transient, tender breast tissue under the areola in pubertal boys?
cards.a: Adolescent physiologic gynecomastia (typically resolves spontaneously within 1 to 2 years).

cards.q: Term for a child whose growth parameters are low but parallel to the normal growth curves, with normal bone age?
cards.a: Genetic (Familial) Short Stature.

cards.q: Most common presentation of growth chart deviation due to psychosocial deprivation?
cards.a: Sudden drop in weight percentile while height remains stable initially.

cards.q: Main endocrine disorder causing a child to stop growing in height while simultaneously gaining weight?
cards.a: Hypothyroidism.

cards.q: Immediate next step in management for a child with a downward deviation crossing two major weight percentiles?
cards.a: Detailed dietary intake history and calorie count.

cards.q: Definition of physiological jaundice peak timeline in a term infant?
cards.a: Total serum bilirubin (TSM) peaks at 3 to 5 days of life.

cards.q: Definition of physiological jaundice peak timeline in a preterm infant?
cards.a: Total serum bilirubin peaks at 5 to 7 days of life.

cards.q: Maximum normal velocity of bilirubin rise in physiological jaundice?
cards.a: Less than 5 mg/dL per 24 hours (or $\1$ mg/dL per hour).

cards.q: Definition of pathological jaundice based on onset timing?
cards.a: Any visible jaundice presenting within the first 24 hours of life.

cards.q: Definition of pathological jaundice based on direct (conjugated) bilirubin levels?
cards.a: Direct bilirubin greater than 1.0 mg/dL if TSB is $\1$ mg/dL, or $\1$ of the TSB if TSB is $\1$ mg/dL.

cards.q: Mechanism of Breast Milk Jaundice?
cards.a: High levels of $\beta$-glucuronidase in breast milk deconjugate bilirubin in the intestine, increasing enterohepatic circulation.

cards.q: Typical onset timing for Breast Milk Jaundice?
cards.a: Starts after the first week of life, peaking at 2 to 3 weeks.

cards.q: Mechanism of Breastfeeding Jaundice (Breastfeeding Failure Jaundice)?
cards.a: Inadequate milk intake leads to dehydration, slow gut motility, and increased enterohepatic bilirubin reabsorption.

cards.q: Typical onset timing for Breastfeeding Jaundice?
cards.a: Occurs within the first 3 to 5 days of life.

cards.q: Cephalocaudal progression of jaundice means what clinically?
cards.a: Dermal icterus progresses from head to toe as serum bilirubin levels rise.

cards.q: Primary enzyme deficient in Crigler-Najjar Syndrome Type I?
cards.a: Complete absence of Uridine Diphosphate Glucuronosyltransferase (UGT1A1).

cards.q: Primary enzyme deficiency in Gilbert Syndrome?
cards.a: Mildly decreased activity (around 10-30% of normal) of UGT1A1.

cards.q: Diagnostic response to phenobarbital in Crigler-Najjar Type II (Arias Syndrome)?
cards.a: Phenobarbital induces UGT1A1 activity, causing a significant decrease in serum bilirubin.

cards.q: Most common hemolytic cause of severe neonatal unconjugated hyperbilirubinemia?
cards.a: ABO incompatibility (usually Mother type O, Infant type A or B).

cards.q: Key peripheral blood smear finding in ABO incompatibility?
cards.a: Microspherocytes.

cards.q: Why does Rh incompatibility cause more severe hydrops fetalis than ABO incompatibility?
cards.a: Maternal anti-D antibodies (IgG) are highly destructive, whereas anti-A/B antibodies are often IgM or neutralized by tissue antigens.

cards.q: What does a positive Direct Antiglobulin Test (DAT/Coombs) indicate?
cards.a: Antibody-coated red blood cells are present in the newborn's circulation.

cards.q: Most common red cell enzyme deficiency causing neonatal jaundice?
cards.a: Glucose-6-Phosphate Dehydrogenase (G6PD) deficiency.

cards.q: Trigger factors for hemolysis in a G6PD-deficient neonate?
cards.a: Oxidative stress from maternal infection, naphthalene (mothballs), or certain medications.

cards.q: Classic triad of Encephalopathy due to acute bilirubin toxicity?
cards.a: Hypotonia/hypertonia (retrocollis/opisthotonos), high-pitched cry, and poor feeding.

cards.q: Chronic, irreversible brain damage from bilirubin deposition is called?
cards.a: Kernicterus.

cards.q: Specific neuroanatomical site targeted by unconjugated bilirubin toxicity?
cards.a: Basal ganglia (specifically the globus pallidus) and subthalamic nuclei.

cards.q: Long-term neurologic sequelae of Kernicterus?
cards.a: Choreoathetoid cerebral palsy, sensorineural hearing loss, and upward gaze palsy.

cards.q: Mechanism of action of phototherapy for neonatal jaundice?
cards.a: Converts unconjugated bilirubin into structural isomers (lumirubin) via photoisomerization, which are excreted in bile and urine without conjugation.

cards.q: Wavelength of light most effective for neonatal phototherapy?
cards.a: Blue-green light in the 460 to 490 nm spectrum.

cards.q: Crucial physical protection needed for a neonate under phototherapy?
cards.a: Eye shields to prevent retinal damage.

cards.q: Benign skin complication seen in infants with conjugated hyperbilirubinemia undergoing phototherapy?
cards.a: Bronze Baby Syndrome.

cards.q: Definitive immediate therapy for neonates with TSB at or near exchange levels despite intensive phototherapy?
cards.a: Double-volume exchange transfusion.

cards.q: Major immediate risk/complication of exchange transfusion?
cards.a: Hypocalcemia (due to citrate anticoagulant), thrombocytopenia, and portal vein thrombosis.

cards.q: First-line screening test to differentiate biliary atresia from neonatal hepatitis?
cards.a: Abdominal ultrasound (looking for the triangular cord sign or absent gallbladder).

cards.q: Gold standard diagnostic test for Biliary Atresia?
cards.a: Intraoperative cholangiogram.

cards.q: Definitive temporary surgical management for Biliary Atresia?
cards.a: Kasai hepatoportoenterostomy.

cards.q: Ideal timeframe for performing a Kasai procedure to ensure optimal prognosis?
cards.a: Before 45 to 60 days of life.

cards.q: Direct hyperbilirubinemia accompanied by cataracts and hepatomegaly suggests?
cards.a: Galactosemia (Galactose-1-phosphate uridyltransferase deficiency).

cards.q: Direct hyperbilirubinemia with a lack of interlobular bile ducts on liver biopsy describes?
cards.a: Alagille Syndrome (associated with JAG1 mutation).

cards.q: Cardinal facial features of Alagille Syndrome?
cards.a: Broad forehead, pointed chin, and deep-set, hypertoric eyes.

cards.q: Cardiac anomaly most highly associated with Alagille Syndrome?
cards.a: Peripheral pulmonary artery stenosis.

cards.q: Skeletal abnormality visible on X-ray in Alagille Syndrome?
cards.a: Butterfly vertebrae.

cards.q: Most common cause of conjugated hyperbilirubinemia in a preterm infant on long-term parental nutrition?
cards.a: Intravenous Lipid/PN-associated cholestasis (PNAC).

cards.q: Alternative medical term for Respiratory Distress Syndrome?
cards.a: Hyaline Membrane Disease (HMD).

cards.q: Primary biochemical composition of pulmonary surfactant?
cards.a: Dipalmitoylphosphatidylcholine (lecithin) and surfactant proteins (A, B, C, D).

cards.q: Primary cell type responsible for producing and secreting surfactant?
cards.a: Type II alveolar pneumocytes.

cards.q: Gestational age when surfactant production begins to rise significantly?
cards.a: Between 24 and 28 weeks of gestation.

cards.q: Gestational age when surfactant production reaches mature levels?
cards.a: 35 weeks of gestation.

cards.q: Pathophysiology of atelectasis in RDS?
cards.a: High alveolar surface tension leads to alveolar collapse at end-expiration.

cards.q: Consequence of progressive atelectasis on ventilation-perfusion matching?
cards.a: Intrapulmonary right-to-left shunting leading to severe hypoxemia.

cards.q: Key maternal metabolic condition that delays fetal lung maturation?
cards.a: Maternal diabetes mellitus (hyperinsulinemia inhibits surfactant synthesis).

cards.q: Physical stress factor that accelerates fetal lung maturation?
cards.a: Chronic intrauterine stress (e.g., maternal hypertension, PPROM) via endogenous corticosteroid release.

cards.q: Classical triad of physical signs of neonatal respiratory distress?
cards.a: Tachypnea, intercostal/subcostal retractions, and expiratory grunting.

cards.q: Pathophysiology behind the expiratory grunt in RDS?
cards.a: Partial closure of the glottis during expiration to maintain positive end-expiratory pressure (PEEP).

cards.q: Pathognomonic chest X-ray findings in severe RDS?
cards.a: Diffuse, uniform "ground-glass" reticulogranular appearance with air bronchograms.

cards.q: Reason for air bronchograms on an RDS chest X-ray?
cards.a: Aerated bronchioles are silhouetted against surrounding collapsed, fluid-filled alveoli.

cards.q: Classic arterial blood gas (ABG) findings in untreated RDS?
cards.a: Hypoxemia, hypercapnia, and mixed respiratory-metabolic acidosis.

cards.q: Preferred pharmacological strategy for a mother at 30 weeks gestation in active preterm labor?
cards.a: Antenatal corticosteroids (Betamethasone or Dexamethasone).

cards.q: Standard timeframe for maximum benefit of antenatal corticosteroids?
cards.a: At least 24 hours and up to 7 days before delivery.

cards.q: First-line non-invasive respiratory support for a preterm infant with mild-to-moderate RDS?
cards.a: Nasal Continuous Positive Airway Pressure (nCPAP).

cards.q: Primary physiological benefit of CPAP in RDS?
cards.a: Recruits collapsed alveoli and stabilizes Functional Residual Capacity (FRC).

cards.q: What does the "INSURE" strategy stand for in RDS management?
cards.a: Intubate, Surfactant administration, and Extubate to CPAP immediately.

cards.q: Route of administration for exogenous surfactant?
cards.a: Endotracheal instillation directly into the lungs.

cards.q: Major acute risk during the rapid administration of exogenous surfactant?
cards.a: Transient airway obstruction and bradycardia.

cards.q: Physiological change after surfactant that necessitates rapid weaning of ventilator pressures?
cards.a: A sharp, rapid increase in pulmonary compliance.

cards.q: Failure to properly wean ventilator settings after surfactant can cause?
cards.a: Pulmonary barotrauma/volutrauma leading to pneumothorax.

cards.q: Chronic lung disease condition resulting from prolonged mechanical ventilation and oxygen toxicity?
cards.a: Bronchopulmonary Dysplasia (BPD).

cards.q: Diagnostic definition of Bronchopulmonary Dysplasia (BPD)?
cards.a: Requirement for supplemental oxygen at 36 weeks postmenstrual age (for infants born $\1$ weeks).

cards.q: Diagnostic alternative for BPD if the infant was born at or after 32 weeks gestation?
cards.a: Requirement for supplemental oxygen beyond 28 days of life.

cards.q: Characteristic chest X-ray finding in chronic Bronchopulmonary Dysplasia?
cards.a: "Coarse lucencies" or a "sponge-like" cystic appearance with areas of atelectasis and hyperinflation.

cards.q: Major cardiovascular complication of severe Bronchopulmonary Dysplasia?
cards.a: Pulmonary hypertension leading to cor pulmonale.

cards.q: Prophylactic medication recommended to prevent RSV infection in infants with severe BPD?
cards.a: Palivizumab (monoclonal antibody against RSV F glycoprotein).

cards.q: Acute neurological complication associated with severe hypoxia and fluctuations in blood pressure in RDS?
cards.a: Intraventricular Hemorrhage (IVH).

cards.q: Screen tool used to detect Intraventricular Hemorrhage in preterm infants?
cards.a: Cranial ultrasound through the anterior fontanelle.

cards.q: Origin site of bleeding in neonatal Intraventricular Hemorrhage?
cards.a: The fragile subependymal germinal matrix.

cards.q: Main differential diagnosis for a term infant with respiratory distress and a "wet lung" chest X-ray?
cards.a: Transient Tachypnea of the Newborn (TTN).

cards.q: Pathophysiology of Transient Tachypnea of the Newborn (TTN)?
cards.a: Delayed clearance of fetal lung fluid by lung epithelial sodium channels ($ENaC$).

cards.q: Classic chest X-ray findings in Transient Tachypnea of the Newborn (TTN)?
cards.a: Prominent perihilar vascular markings, fluid in the interlobar fissures, and hyperinflation.

cards.q: Major risk factor for the development of Transient Tachypnea of the Newborn?
cards.a: Elective Cesarean delivery without a trial of labor.

cards.q: Definition of Early-Onset Neonatal Sepsis (EOS) by timing?
cards.a: Onset of systemic infection within the first 72 hours of life.

cards.q: Definition of Late-Onset Neonatal Sepsis (LOS) by timing?
cards.a: Onset of systemic infection after 72 hours of life up to 28 days.

cards.q: Primary mode of transmission for Early-Onset Sepsis?
cards.a: Vertical transmission from the maternal genital tract during labor or delivery.

cards.q: Primary mode of transmission for Late-Onset Sepsis?
cards.a: Horizontal transmission from the environment, caregivers, or nosocomial sources.

cards.q: Most common bacterial pathogen responsible for Early-Onset Neonatal Sepsis?
cards.a: Group B Streptococcus (Streptococcus agalactiae).

cards.q: Second most common pathogen causing EOS, particularly in preterm infants?
cards.a: Escherichia coli.

cards.q: Gram-positive rod associated with neonatal sepsis via maternal ingestion of unpasteurized dairy?
cards.a: Listeria monocytogenes.

cards.q: Most common pathogen group responsible for Late-Onset Sepsis in NICU patients with central lines?
cards.a: Coagulase-negative Staphylococci (Staphylococcus epidermidis).

cards.q: Major maternal risk factor for Early-Onset Sepsis involving amniotic fluid?
cards.a: Maternal Chorioamnionitis (intra-amniotic infection).

cards.q: Clinical diagnostic criteria for Maternal Chorioamnionitis?
cards.a: Maternal fever plus maternal/fetal tachycardia, uterine tenderness, or foul-smelling amniotic fluid.

cards.q: Time cutoff defining Prolonged Rupture of Membranes (PROM) as a sepsis risk factor?
cards.a: Rupture of membranes greater than or equal to 18 hours prior to delivery.

cards.q: Standard screening protocol timing for maternal Group B Streptococcus carriage?
cards.a: Rectovaginal swab culture performed at 36 0/7 to 37 6/7 weeks of gestation.

cards.q: Preferred agent for maternal intrapartum antibiotic prophylaxis against GBS?
cards.a: Intravenous Penicillin G (or Ampicillin).

cards.q: Alternative intrapartum antibiotic for GBS prophylaxis if the mother has a non-severe penicillin allergy?
cards.a: Cefazolin.

cards.q: Alternative intrapartum antibiotic for GBS prophylaxis if the mother has a severe penicillin allergy and resistant isolates?
cards.a: Vancomycin.

cards.q: Minimum duration of intrapartum antibiotic prophylaxis prior to delivery to be considered "adequate"?
cards.a: 4 hours or more before birth.

cards.q: Most common, yet non-specific, clinical sign of neonatal sepsis?
cards.a: Temperature instability (hypothermia or hyperthermia).

cards.q: Why is hypothermia more common than hyperthermia in sick preterm neonates?
cards.a: Immature thermoregulation and lack of brown fat stores to generate metabolic heat.

cards.q: Cardiovascular indicator of early neonatal septic shock?
cards.a: Prolonged capillary refill time ($\1$ seconds), tachycardia, and mottled skin.

cards.q: Standard, absolute diagnostic test required prior to starting empiric antibiotics for suspected sepsis?
cards.a: Blood culture.

cards.q: Minimum adequate volume of blood required for a neonatal blood culture bottles?
cards.a: 1 mL of blood.

cards.q: Why must a Lumbar Puncture be strongly considered in neonatal sepsis workups?
cards.a: Up to 30% of neonates with bacteremia have concurrent meningitis without focal meningeal signs.

cards.q: Cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) findings indicative of bacterial neonatal meningitis?
cards.a: Elevated WBC count (with polymorphonuclear predominance), elevated protein, and low glucose.

cards.q: First-line empiric antibiotic regimen for suspected Early-Onset Neonatal Sepsis?
cards.a: Ampicillin plus an Aminoglycoside (typically Gentamicin).

cards.q: Why is Ampicillin explicitly included in the early-onset empiric regimen?
cards.a: To provide specific, empirical coverage for Listeria monocytogenes.

cards.q: Empiric antibiotic regimen for suspected Late-Onset Sepsis/Nosocomial NICU infections?
cards.a: Vancomycin (for MRSA/CoNS) plus an antipseudomonal $\beta$-lactam (like Cefepime or Piperacillin-Tazobactam).

cards.q: Why is Ceftriaxone avoided in neonates requiring empiric therapy?
cards.a: It displaces bilirubin from albumin (increasing kernicterus risk) and can precipitate with calcium in biliary sludge.

cards.q: Preferred alternative third-generation cephalosporin used for neonatal bacterial meningitis?
cards.a: Cefotaxime.

cards.q: Target trough level timing for monitoring Gentamicin toxicity in a neonate?
cards.a: Measured immediately before the 3rd or 4th dose.

cards.q: Primary toxicities associated with Aminoglycoside (Gentamicin) use?
cards.a: Ototoxicity and nephrotoxicity.

cards.q: Primary toxicity associated with Vancomycin use if infused too rapidly?
cards.a: Red Man Syndrome (Histamine release).

cards.q: Complete Blood Count (CBC) finding that has a high negative predictive value for neonatal sepsis?
cards.a: A normal absolute neutrophil count (ANC) and low immature-to-total (I:T) neutrophil ratio.

cards.q: Formula to calculate the Immature-to-Total (I:T) neutrophil ratio?
cards.a: (Bands + Metamyelocytes) divided by (Segmented Neutrophils + Bands + Metamyelocytes).

cards.q: An I:T ratio greater than what value suggests acute neonatal infection?
cards.a: Greater than or equal to 0.2.

cards.q: Acute hematologic sign of severe sepsis due to platelet consumption?
cards.a: Thrombocytopenia (platelets $\1$,000/uL).

cards.q: Systemic inflammatory biomarker commonly used to track the treatment response of neonatal sepsis?
cards.a: C-Reactive Protein (CRP).

cards.q: Why is a single normal CRP at onset insufficient to rule out neonatal sepsis?
cards.a: CRP synthesis lags and can take 12 to 24 hours from the onset of infection to elevate significantly.

cards.q: Serious gastrointestinal complication of prematurity linked to severe systemic sepsis?
cards.a: Necrotizing Enterocolitis (NEC).

cards.q: Pathognomonic radiographic sign seen on abdominal X-ray in Necrotizing Enterocolitis?
cards.a: Pneumatosis intestinalis (gas within the bowel wall).

cards.q: Metabolic complication of sepsis caused by increased peripheral glucose consumption and poor reserves?
cards.a: Hypoglycemia.

cards.q: Target serum glucose level for immediate intervention in a symptomatic neonate?
cards.a: Less than 40 to 45 mg/dL.

cards.q: Standard management for a completely asymptomatic well-appearing infant born to a mother with inadequately treated GBS prophylaxis?
cards.a: Routine clinical observation in the hospital for at least 48 hours without diagnostic tests.

cards.q: Neonatal condition characterized by a generalized petechial rash ("blueberry muffin spots") and hepatosplenomegaly?
cards.a: Congenital TORCH infection.

cards.q: Classic triad of congenital Toxoplasmosis?
cards.a: Chorioretinitis, hydrocephalus, and intracranial calcifications.

cards.q: Pattern of intracranial calcifications in congenital Toxoplasmosis?
cards.a: Diffuse throughout the brain parenchyma.

cards.q: Pattern of intracranial calcifications in congenital Cytomegalovirus (CMV)?
cards.a: Periventricular calcifications.

cards.q: Classic long-term neurological sequela of congenital CMV infection?
cards.a: Sensorineural hearing loss.

cards.q: Classic triad of congenital Rubella Syndrome?
cards.a: Cataracts, sensorineural deafness, and congenital heart disease (Patent Ductus Arteriosus).

cards.q: Primary physical finding in early congenital Syphilis involving the nose?
cards.a: Snuffles (copious, highly infectious mucoid or bloody nasal discharge).

cards.q: Definitive diagnostic test for neonatal Herpes Simplex Virus (HSV) central nervous system infection?
cards.a: CSF HSV Polymerase Chain Reaction (PCR).

cards.q: Standard antiviral therapy for documented or highly suspected neonatal HSV infection?
cards.a: High-dose intravenous Acyclovir ($60 \text{ mg/kg/day}$ divided every 8 hours).

cards.q: What is the primary hazard of rapid, aggressive correction of profound chronic hyponatremia during exchange transfusion?
cards.a: Central pontine myelinolysis (Osmotic Demyelination Syndrome).

cards.q: Why does an infant with a large cephalohematoma have an increased risk of severe hyperbilirubinemia?
cards.a: Extravascular RBC destruction and breakdown of trapped hemoglobin increases the systemic bilirubin load.

cards.q: Which congenital cardiac lesion is classically associated with an increased incidence of neonatal hyperbilirubinemia due to polycythemia?
cards.a: Infants of diabetic mothers or transposition of the great arteries.

cards.q: What is the rule of thumb for when to initiate phototherapy based on a healthy term infant's age in hours?
cards.a: Use the AAP (American Academy of Pediatrics) nomogram, tracking risk zones based on hour-specific bilirubin levels.

cards.q: What is the effect of maternal epidural anesthesia on neonatal jaundice?
cards.a: It can sometimes cause poor initial feeding, exacerbating breastfeeding jaundice.

cards.q: What underlying structural liver anomaly must be ruled out in an infant presenting with clay-colored (acholic) stools?
cards.a: Biliary atresia.

cards.q: What nutritional deficiency must be proactively managed in infants with chronic cholestatic jaundice?
cards.a: Deficiencies in fat-soluble vitamins (Vitamins A, D, E, K) due to poor bile acid-mediated micelle formation.

cards.q: What is the significance of a "double bubble" sign on abdominal X-ray in a neonate with conjugated hyperbilirubinemia?
cards.a: Suggests Duodenal Atresia, classically associated with Down Syndrome, which also carries an increased risk of neonatal transient myeloproliferative disorder and cholestasis.

cards.q: Why does hypothyroidism cause prolonged unconjugated hyperbilirubinemia?
cards.a: Hepatic glucuronide conjugation is delayed because thyroid hormone is required for UGT enzyme maturation.

cards.q: What is the inheritance pattern of Crigler-Najjar Syndrome Type I?
cards.a: Autosomal recessive.

cards.q: What is the inheritance pattern of Gilbert Syndrome?
cards.a: Autosomal recessive (most commonly a promoter mutation variant).

cards.q: What is the target pre-ductal oxygen saturation range for a preterm infant at 5 minutes of life?
cards.a: 80% to 85% (per Neonatal Resuscitation Program/NRP guidelines).

cards.q: Where should a pulse oximeter probe be placed on a neonate to measure pre-ductal oxygen saturation?
cards.a: On the right wrist or palmar surface of the right hand.

cards.q: What causes the difference between pre-ductal and post-ductal oxygen saturations in severe respiratory distress?
cards.a: Persistent Pulmonary Hypertension of the Newborn (PPHN) causing a right-to-left shunt across the patent ductus arteriosus (PDA).

cards.q: What is the definitive echocardiographic finding that confirms Persistent Pulmonary Hypertension of the Newborn (PPHN)?
cards.a: Right-to-left shunting through the PDA or foramen ovale, and flattened interventricular septum from high right ventricular pressures.

cards.q: What is the first-line inhaled vasodilator therapy used for PPHN?
cards.a: Inhaled Nitric Oxide (iNO).

cards.q: What is the primary mechanism of action of Inhaled Nitric Oxide?
cards.a: Selectively relaxes pulmonary vascular smooth muscle without causing systemic hypotension.

cards.q: What respiratory condition is characterized by a "patchy, asymmetric infiltrates with rope-like density" and hyperinflation on chest X-ray?
cards.a: Meconium Aspiration Syndrome (MAS).

cards.q: What is the major mechanical complication of Meconium Aspiration Syndrome in the airway?
cards.a: A "ball-valve" effect leading to air trapping, subpleural emphysema, and high risk of pneumothorax.

cards.q: What is the current standard management for a non-vigorous infant born through meconium-stained amniotic fluid?
cards.a: Direct routine resuscitation at the warmer under NRP guidelines (routine endotracheal suctioning is no longer recommended).

cards.q: What defines Apnea of Prematurity?
cards.a: Cessation of breathing for more than 20 seconds, or any pause accompanied by bradycardia or cyanosis in an infant $\1$ weeks.

cards.q: What is the first-line pharmacological treatment for Apnea of Prematurity?
cards.a: Caffeine citrate.

cards.q: What is the mechanism of action of Caffeine Citrate in treating Apnea of Prematurity?
cards.a: Stimulates the central respiratory center in the medulla and increases medullary sensitivity to $CO_2$.

cards.q: At what postmenstrual age does Apnea of Prematurity typically resolve spontaneously?
cards.a: Usually by 36 to 37 weeks postmenstrual age.

cards.q: What underlying vascular complication of extreme prematurity is exacerbated by high, fluctuating oxygen saturations?
cards.a: Retinopathy of Prematurity (ROP).

cards.q: What is the pathophysiology of Retinopathy of Prematurity?
cards.a: Hyperoxia causes initial vessel vasoconstriction and cessation of growth, followed by hypoxia-driven abnormal neovascularization.

cards.q: What is the screening timeline for Retinopathy of Prematurity?
cards.a: Infants born $\le 30$ weeks gestation or weighing $<1500\text{ g}$ should be screened at 4 weeks chronologic age or 31 weeks postmenstrual age (whichever is later).

cards.q: What cardiac lesion classically remains open due to chronic hypoxia and respiratory distress in preterm infants?
cards.a: Patent Ductus Arteriosus (PDA).

cards.q: What is the classic physical exam finding of a hemodynamically significant PDA?
cards.a: A continuous, machine-like murmur heard best at the left upper sternal border, accompanied by bounding peripheral pulses.

cards.q: What is the standard first-line medical therapy to induce closure of a symptomatic PDA in a preterm infant?
cards.a: Cyclooxygenase (COX) inhibitors such as Indomethacin or Ibuprofen.

cards.q: What is a major absolute contraindication to administering Indomethacin for PDA closure?
cards.a: Active necrotizing enterocolitis (NEC), significant renal impairment, or active bleeding.

cards.q: What clinical tool is now widely recommended to determine the need for antibiotics in early-onset sepsis instead of empirical treatment based on risk factors alone?
cards.a: The Kaiser Permanente Neonatal Sepsis Risk Calculator.

cards.q: What are the three main clinical categories evaluated by the Neonatal Sepsis Risk Calculator?
cards.a: Maternal risk factors, the infant's clinical status (well-appearing, equivocal, or critically ill), and hour-specific risk.

cards.q: What is the significance of a high direct or band count on a neonatal differential without a change in total WBC?
cards.a: Left shift, indicating early bone marrow release of immature neutrophils in response to acute infection.

cards.q: Why can severe neonatal sepsis cause a normal or even low total white blood cell count?
cards.a: Depletion of the bone marrow's limited neutrophil storage pool in the face of overwhelming infection.

cards.q: What is the significance of a high serum lactate level in a neonate with suspected sepsis?
cards.a: Indicates tissue hypoperfusion and anaerobic metabolism, pointing toward septic shock.

cards.q: What fluid volume bolus is recommended for a neonate in septic shock?
cards.a: $10\text{ to }20 \text{ mL/kg}$ of isotonic crystalloid (Normal Saline) administered slowly over 10-20 minutes.

cards.q: Why should fluid boluses be delivered carefully in preterm neonates compared to older children?
cards.a: Rapid volume expansion can cause sudden shifts in cranial blood pressure, increasing the risk of Intraventricular Hemorrhage (IVH).

cards.q: What is the first-choice inotrope/vasopressor for neonatal fluid-refractory septic shock with low systemic vascular resistance?
cards.a: Dopamine or Epinephrine.

cards.q: What viral infection should be suspected in a neonate with sepsis-like symptoms, negative bacterial cultures, and markedly elevated transaminases (AST/ALT)?
cards.a: Neonatal Herpes Simplex Virus (HSV) or Enterovirus.

cards.q: What is the most common presentation of late-onset GBS infection?
cards.a: Meningitis (often presenting with irritability, fever, and focal neurological signs after week 1).

cards.q: Does maternal intrapartum antibiotic prophylaxis effectively prevent Late-Onset GBS disease?
cards.a: No, it only significantly reduces the incidence of Early-Onset GBS disease.

cards.q: What metabolic disturbance can mimic the lethargy and poor feeding of neonatal sepsis in a small-for-gestational-age (SGA) infant?
cards.a: Neonatal polycythemia (hematocrit $>65\\%$) leading to hyperviscosity syndrome.

cards.q: What is the definitive treatment for symptomatic neonatal polycythemia hyperviscosity syndrome?
cards.a: Partial exchange transfusion with normal saline.

cards.q: What classic electrolyte abnormality is seen in neonatal sepsis due to temporary adrenal insufficiency or tissue damage?
cards.a: Hyponatremia or hyperkalemia.

cards.q: What complication of neonatal central venous access lines increases the risk of fungal late-onset sepsis?
cards.a: Biofilm formation, most commonly by Candida albicans or Candida parapsilosis.

cards.q: What is the preferred empiric treatment for documented systemic neonatal candidiasis?
cards.a: Amphotericin B deoxycholate.

cards.q: Why is Amphotericin B exceptionally well-tolerated in neonates compared to adults?
cards.a: Neonates have lower baseline nephrotoxicity and structural differences in renal tubules that minimize damage.

cards.q: What does an elevated cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) protein level without an elevated WBC count suggest in a neonate with neurological symptoms?
cards.a: Normal variant (neonates naturally have higher baseline CSF protein, up to $150\text{ mg/dL}$ in preterms).

cards.q: What is the next diagnostic step if a neonate has persistently positive blood cultures 48 hours after starting appropriate antibiotics?
cards.a: Repeat the culture, check a lumbar puncture (if not done), and perform an echocardiogram or renal ultrasound to rule out an infectious focus (e.g., endocarditis or abscess).

cards.q: What is the primary criteria to discontinue empiric antibiotics in an asymptomatic infant evaluated for early-onset sepsis?
cards.a: Negative blood cultures at 36 to 48 hours of incubation.

cards.a: Central pontine myelinolysis (Osmotic Demyelination Syndrome).

cards.a: Use the AAP (American Academy of Pediatrics) nomogram, tracking risk zones based on hour-specific bilirubin levels.

cards.a: Biliary atresia.

cards.a: Deficiencies in fat-soluble vitamins (Vitamins A, D, E, K) due to poor bile acid-mediated micelle formation.

cards.a: 80% to 85% (per Neonatal Resuscitation Program/NRP guidelines).

cards.q: Where should a pulse oximeter probe be placed on a neonate to measure pre-ductal oxygen saturation?
cards.a: On the right wrist or palmar surface of the right hand.

cards.a: Right-to-left shunting through the PDA or foramen ovale, and flattened interventricular septum from high right ventricular pressures.

cards.q: What is the first-line inhaled vasodilator therapy used for PPHN?
cards.a: Inhaled Nitric Oxide (iNO).

cards.q: What is the primary mechanism of action of Inhaled Nitric Oxide?
cards.a: Selectively relaxes pulmonary vascular smooth muscle without causing systemic hypotension.

cards.q: What respiratory condition is characterized by a "patchy, asymmetric infiltrates with rope-like density" and hyperinflation on chest X-ray?
cards.a: Meconium Aspiration Syndrome (MAS).

cards.q: What is the major mechanical complication of Meconium Aspiration Syndrome in the airway?
cards.a: A "ball-valve" effect leading to air trapping, subpleural emphysema, and high risk of pneumothorax.

cards.q: What is the current standard management for a non-vigorous infant born through meconium-stained amniotic fluid?
cards.a: Direct routine resuscitation at the warmer under NRP guidelines (routine endotracheal suctioning is no longer recommended).

cards.q: What defines Apnea of Prematurity?
cards.a: Cessation of breathing for more than 20 seconds, or any pause accompanied by bradycardia or cyanosis in an infant $\1$ weeks.

cards.q: What is the first-line pharmacological treatment for Apnea of Prematurity?
cards.a: Caffeine citrate.

cards.q: What is the mechanism of action of Caffeine Citrate in treating Apnea of Prematurity?
cards.a: Stimulates the central respiratory center in the medulla and increases medullary sensitivity to $CO_2$.

cards.q: At what postmenstrual age does Apnea of Prematurity typically resolve spontaneously?
cards.a: Usually by 36 to 37 weeks postmenstrual age.

cards.q: What underlying vascular complication of extreme prematurity is exacerbated by high, fluctuating oxygen saturations?
cards.a: Retinopathy of Prematurity (ROP).

cards.q: What is the pathophysiology of Retinopathy of Prematurity?
cards.a: Hyperoxia causes initial vessel vasoconstriction and cessation of growth, followed by hypoxia-driven abnormal neovascularization.

cards.q: What is the screening timeline for Retinopathy of Prematurity?
cards.a: Infants born $\le 30$ weeks gestation or weighing $<1500\text{ g}$ should be screened at 4 weeks chronologic age or 31 weeks postmenstrual age (whichever is later).

cards.q: What cardiac lesion classically remains open due to chronic hypoxia and respiratory distress in preterm infants?
cards.a: Patent Ductus Arteriosus (PDA).

cards.q: What is the classic physical exam finding of a hemodynamically significant PDA?
cards.a: A continuous, machine-like murmur heard best at the left upper sternal border, accompanied by bounding peripheral pulses.

cards.q: What is the standard first-line medical therapy to induce closure of a symptomatic PDA in a preterm infant?
cards.a: Cyclooxygenase (COX) inhibitors such as Indomethacin or Ibuprofen.

cards.q: What is a major absolute contraindication to administering Indomethacin for PDA closure?
cards.a: Active necrotizing enterocolitis (NEC), significant renal impairment, or active bleeding.

cards.q: What clinical tool is now widely recommended to determine the need for antibiotics in early-onset sepsis instead of empirical treatment based on risk factors alone?
cards.a: The Kaiser Permanente Neonatal Sepsis Risk Calculator.

cards.q: What are the three main clinical categories evaluated by the Neonatal Sepsis Risk Calculator?
cards.a: Maternal risk factors, the infant's clinical status (well-appearing, equivocal, or critically ill), and hour-specific risk.

cards.q: What is the significance of a high direct or band count on a neonatal differential without a change in total WBC?
cards.a: Left shift, indicating early bone marrow release of immature neutrophils in response to acute infection.

cards.q: Why can severe neonatal sepsis cause a normal or even low total white blood cell count?
cards.a: Depletion of the bone marrow's limited neutrophil storage pool in the face of overwhelming infection.

cards.q: What is the significance of a high serum lactate level in a neonate with suspected sepsis?
cards.a: Indicates tissue hypoperfusion and anaerobic metabolism, pointing toward septic shock.

cards.q: What fluid volume bolus is recommended for a neonate in septic shock?
cards.a: $10\text{ to }20 \text{ mL/kg}$ of isotonic crystalloid (Normal Saline) administered slowly over 10-20 minutes.

cards.q: Why should fluid boluses be delivered carefully in preterm neonates compared to older children?
cards.a: Rapid volume expansion can cause sudden shifts in cranial blood pressure, increasing the risk of Intraventricular Hemorrhage (IVH).

cards.q: What is the first-choice inotrope/vasopressor for neonatal fluid-refractive septic shock with low systemic vascular resistance?
cards.a: Dopamine or Epinephrine.

cards.q: What viral infection should be suspected in a neonate with sepsis-like symptoms, negative bacterial cultures, and markedly elevated transaminases (AST/ALT)?
cards.a: Neonatal Herpes Simplex Virus (HSV) or Enterovirus.

cards.q: What is the most common presentation of late-onset GBS infection?
cards.a: Meningitis (often presenting with irritability, fever, and focal neurological signs after week 1).

cards.q: Does maternal intrapartum antibiotic prophylaxis effectively prevent Late-Onset GBS disease?
cards.a: No, it only significantly reduces the incidence of Early-Onset GBS disease.

cards.q: What metabolic disturbance can mimic the lethargy and poor feeding of neonatal sepsis in a small-for-gestational-age (SGA) infant?
cards.a: Neonatal polycythemia (hematocrit $>65\\%$) leading to hyperviscosity syndrome.

cards.q: What is the definitive treatment for symptomatic neonatal polycythemia hyperviscosity syndrome?
cards.a: Partial exchange transfusion with normal saline.

cards.q: What classic electrolyte abnormality is seen in neonatal sepsis due to temporary adrenal insufficiency or tissue damage?
cards.a: Hyponatremia or hyperkalemia.

cards.q: What complication of neonatal central venous access lines increases the risk of fungal late-onset sepsis?
cards.a: Biofilm formation, most commonly by Candida albicans or Candida parapsilosis.

cards.q: What is the preferred empiric treatment for documented systemic neonatal candidiasis?
cards.a: Amphotericin B deoxycholate.

cards.q: Why is Amphotericin B exceptionally well-tolerated in neonates compared to adults?
cards.a: Neonates have lower baseline nephrotoxicity and structural differences in renal tubules that minimize damage.

cards.q: What does an elevated cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) protein level without an elevated WBC count suggest in a neonate with neurological symptoms?
cards.a: Normal variant (neonates naturally have higher baseline CSF protein, up to $150\text{ mg/dL}$ in preterms).

cards.q: What is the next diagnostic step if a neonate has persistently positive blood cultures 48 hours after starting appropriate antibiotics?
cards.a: Repeat the culture, check a lumbar puncture (if not done), and perform an echocardiogram or renal ultrasound to rule out an infectious focus (e.g., endocarditis or abscess).

cards.q: What is the primary criteria to discontinue empiric antibiotics in an asymptomatic infant evaluated for early-onset sepsis?
cards.a: Negative blood cultures at 36 to 48 hours of incubation.

cards.q: Why does a neonate with Congenital Hypothyroidism display prolonged unconjugated hyperbilirubinemia?
cards.a: Hepatic glucuronide conjugation is delayed because thyroid hormone is required for the structural maturation of hepatic UGT1A1.

cards.q: What rare, life-threatening metabolic cause of conjugated hyperbilirubinemia presents with vomiting, hypoglycemia, and cataracts after introduction of milk?
cards.a: Galactosemia (Galactose-1-phosphate uridyltransferase deficiency).

cards.q: Why are infants with Galactosemia at a vastly increased risk for Early-Onset Neonatal Sepsis?
cards.a: High systemic galactose concentrations inhibit leukocyte bactericidal activity, predisposing them specifically to Escherichia coli sepsis.

cards.q: What feature on a liver biopsy distinguishes Dubin-Johnson Syndrome from Rotor Syndrome in a neonate with direct hyperbilirubinemia?
cards.a: A dark-brown/black pigmented liver due to epinephrine metabolite accumulation is present in Dubin-Johnson but completely absent in Rotor Syndrome.

cards.q: What genetic mutation confirms Alagille Syndrome in a neonate presenting with cholestasis, butterfly vertebrae, and a harsh systolic murmur?
cards.a: Mutation in the JAG1 or NOTCH2 gene resulting in paucity of interlobular bile ducts.

cards.q: What is the primary diagnostic utility of a Technetium-99m hepatobiliary iminodiacetic acid (HIDA) scan in a 3-week-old with direct hyperbilirubinemia?
cards.a: Failure of the radiotracer to excrete into the duodenum after 24 hours strongly supports a diagnosis of Biliary Atresia over neonatal hepatitis.

cards.q: What medical therapy can be used to stimulate bile flow in infants experiencing Total Parenteral Nutrition (TPN)-induced cholestasis?
cards.a: Ursodeoxycholic acid (Ursodiol).

cards.q: Why does a Coombs-negative hemolytic anemia with Heinz bodies and bite cells on a peripheral smear point to G6PD deficiency during a jaundice workup?
cards.a: Heinz bodies represent denatured hemoglobin from oxidative stress, which are subsequently "bitten" out by splenic macrophages.

cards.q: What is the critical total serum bilirubin threshold level above which a term infant is at immediate risk for acute bilirubin encephalopathy?
cards.a: Typically greater than or equal to 25 to 30 mg/dL, depending on the infant’s hourly age and risk factors.

cards.q: What specific ocular manifestation is seen in neonates with severe Type 1 Tyrosinemia causing conjugated hyperbilirubinemia?
cards.a: Corneal ulcers or crystalline corneal plaques (due to tyrosine crystal deposition).

cards.q: What structural component of the alveolus collapses first when there is a genetic deficiency of Surfactant Protein B (SP-B)?
cards.a: The terminal alveolar air-spaces, causing fatal, refractory respiratory failure at birth despite exogenous surfactant treatment.

cards.q: What rare congenital structural anomaly mimics severe RDS but presents with a scaphoid abdomen and bowel sounds heard in the chest?
cards.a: Congenital Diaphragmatic Hernia (CDH).

cards.q: What is the immediate, non-negotiable delivery room management for an infant born with a known Congenital Diaphragmatic Hernia?
cards.a: Immediate endotracheal intubation and mechanical ventilation (avoid bag-valve-mask ventilation to prevent gastric distension and lung compression).

cards.q: What respiratory syndrome presents identically to RDS on day one but occurs in a term infant born via scheduled Cesarean delivery?
cards.a: Transient Tachypnea of the Newborn (TTN).

cards.q: What specific fluid-clearance mechanism fails in Transient Tachypnea of the Newborn (TTN)?
cards.a: Delayed activation of epithelial sodium channels ($ENaC$) which normally reabsorb fetal lung fluid during labor.

cards.q: What chest X-ray finding definitively differentiates Meconium Aspiration Syndrome (MAS) from classic RDS?
cards.a: MAS shows asymmetric, patchy infiltrates with lung hyperinflation and flattened diaphragms, whereas RDS shows symmetric, diffuse ground-glass opacities with low lung volumes.

cards.q: What is the primary pulmonary vascular consequence of severe, chronic tissue hypoxia in an infant with Meconium Aspiration Syndrome?
cards.a: Persistent Pulmonary Hypertension of the Newborn (PPHN) due to reactive pulmonary vasoconstriction.

cards.q: What diagnostic test confirms a right-to-left shunt in a neonate suspected of having PPHN?
cards.a: Simultaneous pre-ductal (right hand) and post-ductal (either foot) arterial blood gas or pulse oximetry showing a $PaO_2$ gradient $>10-15\text{ mmHg}$ or an $SpO_2$ difference $>5-10\\%$.

cards.q: What chronic structural remodeling occurs in the pulmonary vasculature during prolonged, unresolved PPHN?
cards.a: Hypertrophy and hyperplasia of the smooth muscle layer of pulmonary arterioles.

cards.q: Why does maternal use of Selective Serotonin Reuptake Inhibitors (SSRIs) late in pregnancy increase the risk of neonatal PPHN?
cards.a: Accumulation of serotonin in the fetal lung can act as a direct pulmonary vasoconstrictor and alter vascular remodeling.

cards.q: What is the primary mechanism of action of Sildenafil when used as an adjunctive treatment for neonatal pulmonary hypertension?
cards.a: Inhibits phosphodiesterase-5 (PDE-5), preventing the breakdown of cyclic GMP ($cGMP$) to promote pulmonary smooth muscle relaxation.

cards.q: What mechanical ventilator strategy is optimized to minimize barotrauma in an infant with severe, non-compliant RDS failing conventional ventilation?
cards.a: High-Frequency Oscillatory Ventilation (HFOV) or High-Frequency Jet Ventilation (HFJV).

cards.q: What is the primary mechanism of gas exchange during High-Frequency Oscillatory Ventilation (HFOV)?
cards.a: Continuous alveolar recruitment via a constant mean airway pressure, paired with rapid, sub-anatomical dead-space tidal volume oscillations.

cards.q: Why do neonates have an impaired ability to localize infections, making them highly susceptible to rapid systemic bacteremia?
cards.a: They possess deficient chemotaxis of neutrophils and low levels of circulating complement proteins (C3 and C4).

cards.q: What specific bacterial virulence factor allows neonatal Escherichia coli strains to selectively cross the blood-brain barrier to cause meningitis?
cards.a: The K1 capsular polysaccharide antigen.

cards.q: Why is the absolute neutrophil count (ANC) often completely unreliable in the first 4 hours of life when screening for Early-Onset Sepsis?
cards.a: Normal physiological delivery-stress causes a transient, dramatic surge in the ANC immediately after birth.

cards.q: What does a persistently low or dropping platelet count in a neonate being treated for sepsis indicate?
cards.a: Ongoing consumptive coagulopathy (Disseminated Intravascular Coagulation/DIC) or persistent endotoxemia.

cards.q: What is the definitive, standard criteria for a positive cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) culture to rule out sample contamination in neonatal meningitis?
cards.a: Growth of a single pathogenic organism within 24 to 48 hours of incubation.

cards.q: Why is a lumbar puncture mandatory in any neonate with a positive blood culture, even if they look clinically stable?
cards.a: Up to 15-30% of neonates with bacteremia have concurrent meningitis, and treating meningitis requires significantly higher doses and a longer duration of antibiotics.

cards.q: What is the standard duration of antibiotic therapy for uncomplicated neonatal bacteremia versus confirmed GBS meningitis?
cards.a: 7 to 10 days for uncomplicated bacteremia; 14 to 21 days for bacterial meningitis.

cards.q: Why must Aminoglycoside (Gentamicin) serum levels be carefully tracked via peak and trough monitoring in neonates?
cards.a: High troughs increase the risk of nephrotoxicity (acute tubular necrosis), while inadequate peaks result in treatment failure due to insufficient bactericidal activity.

cards.q: What is the first-line empiric antibiotic choice for a neonate presenting with late-onset sepsis who has an indwelling central venous catheter?
cards.a: Vancomycin (to cover Coagulase-Negative Staphylococci and MRSA) combined with an antipseudomonal aminoglycoside or cephalosporin.

cards.q: What severe systemic complication arises if a neonate with underlying septic shock develops profound, bilateral adrenal hemorrhage?
cards.a: Waterhouse-Friderichsen Syndrome, leading to acute adrenal crisis and refractory hypotension.

cards.q: What stress-dose hormone therapy is indicated for a neonate with septic shock that remains completely refractory to both volume resuscitation and high-dose vasopressors?
cards.a: Intravenous Hydrocortisone (to treat relative adrenal insufficiency).

cards.q: What specific clinical criteria from the Neonatal Sepsis Risk Calculator automatically mandates immediate empiric antibiotic therapy, regardless of maternal risk history?
cards.a: A clinical status classification of "Clinically Ill" (defined as persistent respiratory distress, hypotonia, lethargy, or poor perfusion).

cards.q: What classic, benign skin condition can be mistaken for a septic vesicular rash but is characterized by eosinophils on a Wright-stained pustule smear?
cards.a: Erythema Toxicum Neonatorum.

cards.q: What dermatological finding in a neonate with sepsis suggests systemic Pseudomonas aeruginosa infection?
cards.a: Ecthyma gangrenosum (pustules that rapidly progress to necrotic, ulcerated lesions with central black eschars).

cards.q: What classic intracranial ultrasound finding is seen in a neonate who survived severe, late-onset bacterial meningitis?
cards.a: Encephalomalacia, porencephaly, or ventricular septation (leading to obstructive hydrocephalus).

cards.q: What is the most common long-term neurodevelopmental disability seen in infants who survive neonatal sepsis combined with severe RDS?
cards.a: Cerebral palsy, often accompanied by varying degrees of cognitive impairment or sensorineural hearing loss.

cards.q: Why does profound metabolic acidosis ($pH < 7.1$) in a septic neonate drastically impair cardiac contractility?
cards.a: Severe acidemia alters intracellular calcium availability and blunts myocardial responsiveness to endogenous and exogenous catecholamines.

topic: Common pediatric infections — otitis, RSV, meningitis

cards.q: Most common bacterial pathogen isolated in Acute Otitis Media (AOM)?
cards.a: Streptococcus pneumoniae.

cards.q: Two most common non-typeable bacterial pathogens in AOM after S. pneumoniae?
cards.a: Non-typeable Haemophilus influenzae and Moraxella catarrhalis.

cards.q: Bacterial pathogen most likely to cause bilateral AOM concurrent with purulent conjunctivitis?
cards.a: Non-typeable Haemophilus influenzae (Otitis-Conjunctivitis Syndrome).

cards.q: Primary viral pathogens predisposed to causing secondary AOM?
cards.a: Respiratory Syncytial Virus (RSV) and Influenza virus.

cards.q: Gold standard physical exam finding required to diagnose AOM?
cards.a: Bulging of the tympanic membrane with impaired mobility on pneumatic otoscopy.

cards.q: Color change of the tympanic membrane most indicative of acute infection in AOM?
cards.a: Distinct erythema or pale yellow/cloudy discoloration behind the membrane.

cards.q: Meaning of a flat, non-mobile tympanogram (Type B) on tympanometry?
cards.a: Presence of fluid in the middle ear space (effusion).

cards.q: Defining clinical feature that differentiates Otitis Media with Effusion (OME) from AOM?
cards.a: OME has middle ear effusion without signs of acute inflammation or systemic illness.

cards.q: Standard first-line antibiotic choice for pediatric AOM without penicillin allergy?
cards.a: High-dose Amoxicillin (80 to 90 mg/kg/day).

cards.q: Rationale for using high-dose Amoxicillin in treating pediatric AOM?
cards.a: To overcome penicillin-binding protein resistance in Streptococcus pneumoniae.

cards.q: Preferred initial antibiotic for AOM if the child has concurrent purulent conjunctivitis?
cards.a: Amoxicillin-Clavulanate (Augmentin) to cover $\beta$-lactamase producing H. influenzae.

cards.q: Preferred initial antibiotic for AOM if the patient received amoxicillin in the past 30 days?
cards.a: Amoxicillin-Clavulanate.

cards.q: Alternative oral antibiotic choice for AOM in a patient with a non-anaphylactic penicillin allergy?
cards.a: Cefdinir, Cefuroxime, or Cefpodoxime (second or third-generation cephalosporins).

cards.q: Alternative antibiotic therapy for AOM in a patient with an anaphylactic penicillin allergy?
cards.a: Azithromycin or Clindamycin.

cards.q: First-line parenteral treatment for AOM in a child unable to tolerate oral medications?
cards.a: Intramuscular Ceftriaxone (1 to 3 daily doses).

cards.q: Strict criteria for "watchful waiting" (observation without antibiotics) in pediatric AOM?
cards.a: Age 6 to 23 months with unilateral, mild symptoms, or age over 2 years with mild symptoms.

cards.q: Minimum age below which all patients with certain or suspected AOM must receive immediate antibiotics?
cards.a: Six months of age.

cards.q: Recommended duration of antibiotic therapy for AOM in children under two years of age?
cards.a: 10 days.

cards.q: Recommended duration of antibiotic therapy for AOM in children aged six years or older with mild symptoms?
cards.a: 5 to 7 days.

cards.q: Most common intracranial complication of poorly treated Acute Otitis Media?
cards.a: Meningitis.

cards.q: Most common extracranial, bony complication of Acute Otitis Media?
cards.a: Acute Mastoiditis.

cards.q: Classic physical exam finding in a child presenting with Acute Mastoiditis?
cards.a: Displacement of the pinna downward and outward with postauricular erythema and tenderness.

cards.q: Initial diagnostic imaging modality of choice for suspected mastoiditis or intracranial extension?
cards.a: CT scan of the temporal bones with contrast.

cards.q: Defining feature of Chronic Otitis Media with Effusion?
cards.a: Middle ear effusion persisting for 3 months or longer.

cards.q: Standard management for asymptomatic Otitis Media with Effusion noted after an episode of AOM?
cards.a: Clinical observation and reassurance, as most cases resolve spontaneously within 3 months.

cards.q: Absolute indication for tympanostomy tube insertion in chronic OME?
cards.a: Effusion persisting for 3 or more months with documented structural damage or bilateral hearing loss.

cards.q: Clinical criteria for tympanostomy tube placement due to recurrent AOM?
cards.a: 3 or more distinct episodes in 6 months, or 4 or more episodes in 12 months with at least one in the preceding 6 months.

cards.q: First-line treatment for uncomplicated otorrhea in a child with functional tympanostomy tubes?
cards.a: Topical antibiotic eardrops (e.g., Fluoroquinolones) rather than systemic oral antibiotics.

cards.q: Pathophysiologic mechanism underlying Otitis Media with Effusion in children with cleft palate?
cards.a: Tensor veli palatini muscle dysfunction leading to chronic Eustachian tube obstruction.

cards.q: Classic otoscopic finding associated with Bullous Myringitis?
cards.a: Fluid-filled blisters or vesicles visible on the surface of the tympanic membrane.

cards.q: Most common clinical manifestation of primary Respiratory Syncytial Virus (RSV) infection in infants under one year old?
cards.a: Bronchiolitis.

cards.q: Peak age range for severe RSV bronchiolitis manifestations in infants?
cards.a: 2 to 6 months of age.

cards.q: Primary pathophysiologic mechanism of airway obstruction in RSV bronchiolitis?
cards.a: Necrosis of airway epithelium, inflammatory mucus plugging, and submucosal edema in the bronchioles.

cards.q: Classic initial upper respiratory symptoms of RSV infection before lower tract involvement?
cards.a: Clear rhinorrhea, sneezing, and a low-grade fever.

cards.q: Standard auscultatory findings on lung examination during the peak of RSV bronchiolitis?
cards.a: Diffuse, high-pitched expiratory wheezing and scattered fine crackles throughout both lung fields.

cards.q: Visual physical exam signs indicative of severe respiratory distress in an infant with RSV?
cards.a: Intercostal, subcostal, and suprasternal retractions, along with nasal flaring and expiratory grunting.

cards.q: Life-threatening respiratory symptom that can be the presenting sign of RSV in premature infants?
cards.a: Apnea.

cards.q: Standard method of confirming RSV diagnosis in a hospitalized patient?
cards.a: Polymerase Chain Reaction (PCR) assay or rapid antigen detection from a nasopharyngeal aspirate.

cards.q: Typical chest radiograph findings in an infant with classic RSV bronchiolitis?
cards.a: Bilateral hyperinflation, flattened diaphragms, peribronchial cuffing, and patchy areas of atelectasis.

cards.q: Role of routine chest radiography in the evaluation of mild, uncomplicated pediatric bronchiolitis?
cards.a: Not routinely recommended, as it often leads to inappropriate antibiotic use for atelectasis misidentified as pneumonia.

cards.q: Cornerstone of management for an infant admitted with typical RSV bronchiolitis?
cards.a: Supportive care, including frequent nasopharyngeal suctioning, supplemental oxygen, and hydration.

cards.q: Primary indication for hospital admission in an infant with RSV bronchiolitis?
cards.a: Persistent hypoxemia (oxygen saturation below 90 to 92%), respiratory distress, or inadequate oral hydration.

cards.q: Role of systemic or inhaled corticosteroids in the routine management of RSV bronchiolitis?
cards.a: Not recommended, as clinical trials show no benefit in reducing hospitalization or improving clinical scores.

cards.q: Role of bronchodilators (e.g., Albuterol) in the routine treatment of a first episode of bronchiolitis?
cards.a: Not recommended routinely due to lack of impact on disease course or hospital stay duration.

cards.q: Only definitive clinical scenario where a trial of nebulized epinephrine might be evaluated in bronchiolitis?
cards.a: As a rescue trial in a hospital setting, discontinued immediately if no objective clinical improvement is documented.

cards.q: Preferred method of hydration for a tachypneic infant with bronchiolitis and a respiratory rate over 60 to 70 breaths per minute?
cards.a: Intravenous fluids or nasogastric tube feeding to minimize the high risk of aspiration.

cards.q: Target oxygen saturation parameter for discontinuing supplemental oxygen in a recovering bronchiolitis patient?
cards.a: Stable oxygen saturation at or above 90% on room air during periods of awake activity and sleep.

cards.q: Monoclonal antibody used for immunoprophylaxis against RSV in high-risk infants?
cards.a: Palivizumab.

cards.q: Absolute candidate group for Palivizumab prophylaxis during their first RSV season?
cards.a: Infants born before 29 weeks of gestation.

cards.q: Chronic medical condition qualifying an infant under 12 months for Palivizumab prophylaxis?
cards.a: Chronic Lung Disease of prematurity requiring medical intervention within six months of the RSV season.

cards.q: Maximum number of monthly doses of Palivizumab recommended during a single RSV season?
cards.a: Five monthly doses.

cards.q: Preventive immunization option for pregnant individuals to protect newborns from severe RSV?
cards.a: RSV prefusion F protein vaccine (Abrysvo) administered between 32 and 36 weeks of gestation.

cards.q: Long-acting monoclonal antibody recommended for all infants under 8 months entering their first RSV season?
cards.a: Nirsevimab.

cards.q: Most common long-term pulmonary sequela observed in children who had severe RSV bronchiolitis in infancy?
cards.a: Recurrent wheezing episodes and an increased risk of childhood asthma.

cards.q: Primary mode of transmission for Respiratory Syncytial Virus in healthcare settings?
cards.a: Large-particle droplets and fomites via direct contact with contaminated surfaces or hands.

cards.q: Essential infection control precautions required for a patient hospitalized with RSV?
cards.a: Contact and Droplet precautions.

cards.q: Acid-base disturbance typically seen on a blood gas in an infant with impending respiratory failure from RSV?
cards.a: Respiratory acidosis due to profound alveolar hypoventilation and carbon dioxide retention.

cards.q: Definition of a positive response to a trial of hypertonic saline nebulization in bronchiolitis?
cards.a: Reduced length of hospital stay in infants, though its routine emergency department use remains controversial.

cards.q: Specific antiviral agent reserved exclusively for severe, life-threatening RSV in highly immunocompromised patients?
cards.a: Ribavirin (administered via aerosol).

cards.q: Typical incubation period for Respiratory Syncytial Virus after exposure?
cards.a: 4 to 6 days.

cards.q: Most common bacterial pathogen causing meningitis in neonates (0 to 28 days old)?
cards.a: Group B Streptococcus (Streptococcus agalactiae).

cards.q: Second and third most common bacterial pathogens causing neonatal meningitis?
cards.a: Escherichia coli (and other Gram-negative bacilli) and Listeria monocytogenes.

cards.q: Most common bacterial pathogen causing meningitis in infants and children over 1 month of age?
cards.a: Streptococcus pneumoniae.

cards.q: Bacterial pathogen responsible for meningitis outbreaks in college dorms or military barracks, characterized by a rapid purpuric rash?
cards.a: Neisseria meningitidis.

cards.q: Classic triad of symptoms seen in older children and adults with bacterial meningitis?
cards.a: Fever, headache, and nuchal rigidity (stiff neck).

cards.q: Definition of Kernig sign?
cards.a: Resistance or pain upon extension of the patient's knee when the hip is flexed at a 90-degree angle.

cards.q: Definition of Brudzinski sign?
cards.a: Involuntary flexion of the patient's hips and knees when the neck is passively flexed forward.

cards.q: Why are Kernig and Brudzinski signs frequently absent in infants under 12 months with meningitis?
cards.a: Due to the immature development of neuromuscular reflexes and lack of meningeal stretch response at that age.

cards.q: Most reliable clinical signs of meningitis in a young infant under 3 months?
cards.a: Hypothermia or fever, paradoxically increased irritability when held, lethargy, poor feeding, and a bulging fontanelle.

cards.q: Definitive diagnostic procedure required to confirm or rule out suspected pediatric meningitis?
cards.a: Lumbar puncture for cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) analysis.

cards.q: Absolute clinical contraindications to performing an immediate lumbar puncture in a suspected meningitis patient?
cards.a: Signs of increased intracranial pressure (papilledema, unequal pupils), focal neurologic deficits, or cardiopulmonary instability.

cards.q: Immediate course of action if a lumbar puncture must be delayed due to clinical instability or focal deficits?
cards.a: Obtain blood cultures and immediately administer empiric intravenous antibiotics.

cards.q: Typical CSF opening pressure finding in acute bacterial meningitis?
cards.a: Elevated (usually greater than 200 mm $\text{H}_2\text{O}$).

cards.q: Typical CSF white blood cell count and differential in bacterial meningitis?
cards.a: Markedly elevated WBC count (often $\1$/microL) with a strong predominance of polymorphonuclear neutrophils (PMNs).

cards.q: Typical CSF glucose concentration relative to serum glucose in bacterial meningitis?
cards.a: Significantly decreased, with a CSF-to-serum glucose ratio of less than 0.4.

cards.q: Typical CSF protein concentration finding in bacterial meningitis?
cards.a: Markedly elevated (often $\1$ mg/dL) due to increased blood-brain barrier permeability.

cards.q: Typical CSF findings in Viral (Aseptic) Meningitis?
cards.a: Normal glucose, normal to mildly elevated protein, and mildly elevated WBCs with lymphocytic predominance.

cards.q: Most common viral etiology responsible for aseptic meningitis in pediatric patients?
cards.a: Enteroviruses (such as Coxsackievirus and Echovirus).

cards.q: Diagnostic utility of adding a CSF Gram stain during workup?
cards.a: Rapidly identifies the bacterial morphology and guides tailored antibiotic choice ahead of culture results.

cards.q: Standard empiric antibiotic regimen for a neonate (under 28 days) with suspected bacterial meningitis?
cards.a: Ampicillin plus Cefotaxime (or Ampicillin plus an Aminoglycoside like Gentamicin).

cards.q: Why is Ceftriaxone strictly avoided in neonates requiring empiric treatment for meningitis?
cards.a: It displaces bilirubin from albumin, increasing the risk of kernicterus, and can precipitate with IV calcium.

cards.q: Standard empiric antibiotic regimen for a child over 1 month of age with suspected bacterial meningitis?
cards.a: Vancomycin plus a third-generation cephalosporin (Ceftriaxone or Cefotaxime).

cards.q: Purpose of adding Vancomycin to the empiric meningitis regimen for children over 1 month?
cards.a: To provide coverage for highly penicillin-resistant strains of Streptococcus pneumoniae.

cards.q: Purpose of adding Ampicillin specifically to the neonatal empiric meningitis regimen?
cards.a: To provide mandatory coverage for Listeria monocytogenes.

cards.q: Specific adjunctive medication shown to reduce the risk of sensorineural hearing loss in children with H. influenzae type b meningitis?
cards.a: Dexamethasone.

cards.q: Optimal timing for administering the first dose of adjunctive Dexamethasone in pediatric bacterial meningitis?
cards.a: Prior to or concurrently with the first dose of intravenous antibiotics.

cards.q: Most common long-term sensorineural complication resulting from childhood bacterial meningitis?
cards.a: Sensorineural hearing loss (due to labyrinthitis ossificans).

cards.q: Electrolyte abnormality frequently caused by inappropriate antidiuretic hormone secretion (SIADH) during bacterial meningitis?
cards.a: Hyponatremia.

cards.q: Immediate management step required for close household contacts of a patient diagnosed with Neisseria meningitidis?
cards.a: Chemoprophylaxis with Rifampin, Ciprofloxacin, or Ceftriaxone.

cards.q: Indication for cranial imaging (CT or MRI) during the course of treating bacterial meningitis?
cards.a: Persistent fever after 72 hours of appropriate therapy, new focal neurologic deficits, or enlarging head circumference.

cards.q: First step in the PALS pediatric assessment triangle?
cards.a: Appearance (evaluating muscle tone, interactiveness, and consolability).

cards.q: Second step in the PALS pediatric assessment triangle?
cards.a: Work of Breathing (evaluating retractions, stridor, wheezing, or nasal flaring).

cards.q: Third step in the PALS pediatric assessment triangle?
cards.a: Circulation to Skin (evaluating pallor, mottling, or cyanosis).

cards.q: Definition of a normal capillary refill time in a well-perfused pediatric patient?
cards.a: Two seconds or less.
