cards.q: Definition of bradycardia requiring chest compressions in an infant or child with compromised perfusion despite oxygenation?
cards.a: Heart rate less than 60 beats per minute.

cards.q: Standard compression-to-ventilation ratio for two-rescuer pediatric CPR?
cards.a: 15 compressions to 2 ventilations.

cards.q: Standard compression-to-ventilation ratio for single-rescuer pediatric CPR?
cards.a: 30 compressions to 2 ventilations.

cards.q: Preferred location for checking a pulse in an unresponsive infant under one year of age?
cards.a: Brachial artery.

cards.q: Preferred location for checking a pulse in an unresponsive child over one year of age?
cards.a: Carotid or femoral artery.

cards.q: Recommended depth of chest compressions during CPR for an infant?
cards.a: At least one-third the anterior-posterior diameter of the chest, or approximately 1.5 inches (4 cm).

cards.q: Recommended depth of chest compressions during CPR for a child?
cards.a: At least one-third the anterior-posterior diameter of the chest, or approximately 2 inches (5 cm).

cards.q: Correct energy dose for the first shock during pediatric defibrillation for a shockable rhythm?
cards.a: 2 Joules per kilogram ($2\text{ J/kg}$).

cards.q: Correct energy dose for the second and subsequent shocks during pediatric defibrillation?
cards.a: 4 Joules per kilogram ($4\text{ J/kg}$).

cards.q: Maximum recommended single energy dose for pediatric defibrillation?
cards.a: 10 Joules per kilogram ($10\text{ J/kg}$) or the standard adult dose.

cards.q: First-line medication and dose administered for pediatric cardiac arrest or symptomatic bradycardia?
cards.a: Epinephrine at a dose of 0.01 mg/kg ($0.1\text{ mL/kg}$ of the 0.1 mg/mL concentration) intravenously or intraosseously.

cards.q: Preferred fluid type and initial volume bolus size recommended for a pediatric patient in hypovolemic or septic shock?
cards.a: 20 mL/kg of an isotonic crystalloid fluid (e.g., Normal Saline or Lactated Ringer's).

cards.q: Primary alternative vascular access method if intravenous access cannot be rapidly established in an unstable child?
cards.a: Intraosseous (IO) access.

cards.q: Classic dermatologic description of the rash seen in meningococcemia according to the Zitelli Atlas?
cards.a: Non-blanching, petechial or purpuric lesions that can rapidly coalesce into purpura fulminans.

cards.q: Distinction between a blanching rash and a non-blanching rash on physical exam?
cards.a: A non-blanching rash (petechiae/purpura) does not fade or turn white when pressure is applied, indicating extravasated blood.

cards.q: Classic otoscopic appearance of Tympanosclerosis in the Zitelli Atlas?
cards.a: Chalky white plaques or patches embedded within the tympanic membrane, representing organized collagen and calcium deposits.

cards.q: Significance of finding isolated tympanosclerosis patches on an asymptomatic child's ear exam?
cards.a: Benign finding usually indicating a history of recurrent otitis media or prior tympanostomy tube placement.

cards.q: Physical sign on a child's face indicating chronic mouth breathing secondary to adenoid hypertrophy?
cards.a: "Adenoid facies," characterized by an elongated face, open mouth, prominent upper incisors, and a pinched nose.

cards.q: Visual appearance of the tympanic membrane in a patient with a Cholesteatoma?
cards.a: A pearly white, keratinous mass typically located in the posterosuperior quadrant of the tympanic membrane or pars flaccida.

cards.q: Primary clinical danger associated with an untreated middle ear Cholesteatoma?
cards.a: Progressive bone destruction of the ossicles and mastoid, leading to permanent hearing loss or intracranial entry.

cards.q: Classic chest X-ray sign seen in children with croup (laryngotracheobronchitis) as a differential for respiratory distress?
cards.a: The "Steeple Sign," representing subglottic narrowing of the airway.

cards.q: Defining physical exam feature that distinguishes a simple febrile seizure from a complex febrile seizure?
cards.a: Simple febrile seizures are generalized, last less than 15 minutes, and do not recur within 24 hours.

cards.q: Defining physical exam feature of a complex febrile seizure?
cards.a: Focal onset, duration greater than 15 minutes, or multiple occurrences within a single 24-hour period.

cards.q: Age range in which febrile seizures typically occur?
cards.a: 6 months to 5 years of age.

cards.q: Primary management strategy for a child presenting with a brief, self-limiting, simple febrile seizure?
cards.a: Standard antipyretics for comfort and thorough reassurance of the parents, without routine neuroimaging or antiepileptic drugs.

cards.q: Pathogen responsible for Ramsay Hunt Syndrome affecting the ear and facial nerves?
cards.a: Varicella-Zoster Virus (VZV) reactivation.

cards.q: Ear finding that distinguishes a traumatic tympanic membrane perforation from an infectious perforation?
cards.a: Traumatic perforations show ragged, linear edges with minimal inflammation, whereas infectious perforations show a hyperemic, inflamed membrane with purulent discharge.

cards.q: Why is high-dose Amoxicillin ineffective against Mycoplasma pneumoniae lower respiratory infections?
cards.a: Mycoplasma species lack a peptidoglycan cell wall, making them inherently resistant to all $\beta$-lactam antibiotics.

cards.q: Preferred class of antibiotics for treating atypical pneumonia caused by Mycoplasma pneumoniae?
cards.a: Macrolides (e.g., Azithromycin).

cards.q: Diagnostic criteria for recurrent respiratory papillomatosis of the larynx, an uncommon differential for chronic stridor?
cards.a: Visualization of raspberry-like, exophytic growths on the vocal cords via laryngoscopy, caused by HPV types 6 or 11.

cards.q: Most accurate clinical indicator of proper endotracheal tube placement in a pediatric resuscitation setting?
cards.a: Presence of persistent waveform capnography showing bilateral chest expansion and equal breath sounds.

cards.q: Why is the respiratory rate faster in neonates and infants compared to older children?
cards.a: Infants have high metabolic demands and low pulmonary compliance, making them dependent on respiratory rate rather than tidal volume to alter minute ventilation.

cards.q: Primary mechanism of hypoxemia in a child with severe RSV bronchiolitis?
cards.a: Ventilation-perfusion (V/Q) mismatch caused by widespread mucous plugging and atelectasis.

cards.q: CSF parameter that remains most useful for diagnosing bacterial meningitis if antibiotics were given shortly before the lumbar puncture?
cards.a: Multiplex PCR testing or CSF cultures (though cultures are less sensitive post-antibiotics, PCR often remains positive).

cards.q: Characteristic feature of a "traumatic tap" during a lumbar puncture compared to true bacterial meningitis?
cards.a: Clearance of red blood cells from the first to the last tube collected, and a normal CSF glucose ratio.

cards.q: Preferred treatment for a child with symptomatic, culture-confirmed H. influenzae type b meningitis?
cards.a: Intravenous Ceftriaxone or Cefotaxime for 7 to 10 days.

cards.q: Recommended duration of antibiotic treatment for uncomplicated Streptococcus pneumoniae meningitis?
cards.a: 10 to 14 days.

cards.q: Recommended duration of antibiotic treatment for uncomplicated Neisseria meningitidis meningitis?
cards.a: 5 to 7 days.

cards.q: Standard duration of antibiotic treatment for Gram-negative bacillary meningitis in neonates?
cards.a: Minimum of 21 days, or 14 days beyond the first negative CSF culture.

cards.q: Most likely diagnosis for an infant presenting with high fever for 3 days that drops abruptly, followed by the appearance of a maculopapular rash?
cards.a: Roseola Infantum (Exanthem Subitum), caused by Human Herpesvirus 6 (HHV-6).

cards.q: Serious complication of Neisseria meningitidis infection involving acute adrenal gland failure?
cards.a: Waterhouse-Friderichsen Syndrome (hemorrhagic adrenal infarction).

cards.q: Expected appearance of a normal tympanic membrane on pneumatic otoscopy?
cards.a: Translucent, pearly gray membrane that moves briskly inward with positive pressure and outward with negative pressure.

cards.q: Recommended approach for managing a localized serous fluid level behind a non-inflamed tympanic membrane 2 weeks after an AOM episode?
cards.a: Watchful waiting, as post-AOM effusion takes up to 4 to 12 weeks to clear completely in many children.

cards.q: Cardinal sign of Gradenigo Syndrome, a rare complication of otitis media?
cards.a: Triad of otorrhea, deep facial pain in the distribution of the trigeminal nerve, and abducens nerve (CN VI) palsy.

cards.q: Initial empirical treatment for an infant with suspected bacterial meningitis who has an absolute contraindication to cephalosporins?
cards.a: Intravenous Meropenem plus Vancomycin.

cards.q: Anatomical difference in the pediatric Eustachian tube that predisposes young children to recurrent AOM?
cards.a: The tube is shorter, wider, and oriented more horizontally than in adults, facilitating the reflux of nasopharyngeal pathogens into the middle ear.

cards.q: Diagnostic criteria for Chronic Suppurative Otitis Media (CSOM)?
cards.a: Persistent purulent otorrhea through a perforated tympanic membrane lasting longer than 6 to 12 weeks.

cards.q: Primary bacterial pathogens isolated in Chronic Suppurative Otitis Media?
cards.a: Pseudomonas aeruginosa and Staphylococcus aureus.

cards.q: Recommended initial treatment for uncomplicated Chronic Suppurative Otitis Media?
cards.a: Topical fluoroquinolone drops combined with regular aural toilet (suctioning/cleaning).

cards.q: Distinctive clinical presentation of Otitis Media with ANCA-associated vasculitis or granulomatosis with polyangiitis?
cards.a: Intractable otitis media unresponsive to standard antibiotics, accompanied by progressive sensorineural hearing loss and facial nerve palsy.

cards.q: Pathophysiology of Bezold abscess as a complication of acute mastoiditis?
cards.a: Perforation of the mastoid cortex allowing pus to track into the sheath of the sternocleidomastoid muscle.

cards.q: Most common cranial nerve palsy associated with acute mastoiditis or severe AOM?
cards.a: Facial nerve (Cranial Nerve VII) palsy due to inflammation within the Fallopian canal.

cards.q: Definitive management for an AOM patient presenting with acute facial nerve palsy?
cards.a: Urgent myringotomy with or without tympanostomy tube insertion, along with intravenous antibiotics.

cards.q: Condition characterized by bluish discoloration behind an intact tympanic membrane without acute infection signs?
cards.a: Hemotympanum, typically secondary to temporal bone fracture or head trauma.

cards.q: Visual presentation of a retraction pocket on otoscopy according to the Zitelli Atlas?
cards.a: The tympanic membrane is sucked inward, collapsing onto the ossicles, most frequently in the posterosuperior quadrant.

cards.q: Primary environmental risk factors that significantly increase a child's susceptibility to recurrent AOM?
cards.a: Exposure to secondhand tobacco smoke, daycare attendance, lack of breastfeeding, and pacifier use after six months of age.

cards.q: Most common cardiac condition predisposing an infant to high-risk, severe RSV bronchiolitis?
cards.a: Hemodynamically significant congenital heart disease, particularly acyanotic lesions with pulmonary hypertension.

cards.q: Rare, severe complication of RSV in infants involving sudden, profound neurological changes?
cards.a: RSV-associated encephalopathy, presenting with seizures or altered mental status.

cards.q: Primary reason routine chest physiotherapy (percussion and postural drainage) is avoided in RSV bronchiolitis?
cards.a: It has been shown to increase distress and chest wall pain without improving clinical outcomes or shortening hospital stays.

cards.q: Expected laboratory finding on a complete blood count (CBC) during a typical RSV infection?
cards.a: Normal white blood cell count or mild leukocytosis with a lymphocytic predominance, matching standard viral patterns.

cards.q: Most common bacterial pathogen isolated when secondary bacterial pneumonia complicates RSV bronchiolitis?
cards.a: Streptococcus pneumoniae or Staphylococcus aureus.

cards.q: Pathogen causing "Swelling of the epiglottis" which must be differentiated from severe RSV or croup in an unimmunized child?
cards.a: Haemophilus influenzae type b (causing acute Epiglottitis).

cards.q: Classic lateral neck X-ray finding in a child with acute epiglottitis?
cards.a: The "Thumbprint Sign," representing a swollen, enlarged epiglottis.

cards.q: Initial step in the management of a child with suspected epiglottitis?
cards.a: Maintain the child in a position of comfort and urgently transfer to the operating room for controlled intubation.

cards.q: Diagnostic differentiation between RSV bronchiolitis and Chlamydia trachomatis pneumonia in an 8-week-old infant?
cards.a: Chlamydia presents with a staccato cough, eosinophilia, and absence of fever, often with a history of neonatal conjunctivitis.

cards.q: Rationale for avoiding routine use of humidified mist tents (cool mist therapy) in RSV bronchiolitis management?
cards.a: Clinical studies have shown no objective improvement in respiratory scores or oxygenation parameters.

cards.q: Most common cause of recurrent bacterial meningitis in children with a history of head trauma?
cards.a: Anatomical CSF leak or dural defect, most frequently tracking Streptococcus pneumoniae.

cards.q: Rare condition involving a congenital dermal sinus tract extending into the spinal cord that predisposes to recurrent meningitis?
cards.a: Spina Bifida Occulta or spinal dysraphism.

cards.q: CSF profile characteristic of Tuberculous Meningitis?
cards.a: Markedly elevated protein, significantly low glucose, and moderate pleocytosis with a distinct lymphocytic predominance.

cards.q: Anatomical predilection of Tuberculous Meningitis exudates inside the brain?
cards.a: Thick exudates concentrate around the base of the brain (basilar meningitis), frequently causing cranial nerve palsies.

cards.q: Diagnosis for a child with fever, headache, altered mental status, and focal neurological signs with temporal lobe localized lesions on MRI?
cards.a: Herpes Simplex Virus (HSV) Encephalitis.

cards.q: Preferred first-line empirical antiviral treatment for suspected neonatal HSV meningitis or encephalitis?
cards.a: High-dose intravenous Acyclovir ($20\text{ mg/kg}$ every 8 hours).

cards.q: Most common vector-borne viral etiology of pediatric meningoencephalitis in the United States?
cards.a: West Nile Virus (or other Arboviruses like La Crosse Encephalitis).

cards.q: Pathophysiologic mechanism driving cerebral edema during acute bacterial meningitis?
cards.a: Combination of cytotoxic edema (cell swelling), vasogenic edema (leaky blood-brain barrier), and interstitial edema (obstructed CSF outflow).

cards.q: Long-term ophthalmic complication that can occur secondary to untreated elevated intracranial pressure in bacterial meningitis?
cards.a: Optic atrophy or cortical blindness.

cards.q: Definition of "Waterhouse-Friderichsen Syndrome" associated with meningococcemia?
cards.a: Severe hemorrhagic necrosis of the adrenal glands leading to acute adrenal insufficiency and profound refractory shock.

cards.q: Defining difference between "compensated shock" and "hypotensive (decompensated) shock" in a pediatric patient?
cards.a: Compensated shock maintains a normal systolic blood pressure via tachycardia and vasoconstriction, whereas hypotensive shock shows a blood pressure below the 5th percentile for age.

cards.q: Formula used to calculate the lower limit of acceptable systolic blood pressure (5th percentile) for a child aged 1 to 10 years?
cards.a: $70\text{ mmHg} + (2 \times \text{age in years})$.

cards.q: Formula used to calculate the lower limit of acceptable systolic blood pressure for a term neonate (0 to 28 days)?
cards.a: Less than $60\text{ mmHg}$.

cards.q: Preferred initial intraosseous (IO) access insertion site in a pediatric resuscitation setting?
cards.a: Proximal tibia, approximately 1 to 2 cm distal to the tibial tuberosity on the flat medial surface.

cards.q: Primary sign of successful fluid resuscitation in a child presenting with hypovolemic shock?
cards.a: Decrease in heart rate, improvement in mental status, normal capillary refill time, and an increase in urine output to greater than $1\text{ mL/kg/hour}$.

cards.q: First-line medication and intervention strategy for a pediatric patient with documented Torsades de Pointes?
cards.a: Intravenous Magnesium Sulfate ($25\text{ to }50\text{ mg/kg}$).

cards.q: Target dose of Amiodarone for refractory Pulseless Ventricular Fibrillation or Ventricular Tachycardia in PALS?
cards.a: $5\text{ mg/kg}$ intravenous or intraosseous bolus (may repeat up to 3 times).

cards.q: Most common non-traumatic cause of cardiac arrest in the pediatric population?
cards.a: Progressive respiratory failure or asphyxia leading to bradycardia and asystole (hypoxic-ischemic arrest).

cards.q: Primary physiologic hazard associated with hyperventilating a pediatric patient during CPR?
cards.a: Increased intrathoracic pressure, which decreases venous return to the heart, dropping cardiac output and cerebral perfusion.

cards.q: Action taken in PALS if a pediatric patient displays organized electrical activity on the monitor but lacks a palpable pulse?
cards.a: Diagnose Pulseless Electrical Activity (PEA) and immediately resume chest compressions while administering Epinephrine every 3 to 5 minutes.

cards.q: Diagnosis for a 4-year-old child with an painful, swollen, erythematous earlobe following an insect bite, with an intact, normal tympanic membrane?
cards.a: Cellulitis of the external ear (perichondritis if sparing the lobule).

cards.q: Key physical exam feature distinguishing perichondritis from generalized pinna cellulitis?
cards.a: Perichondritis strictly spares the earlobe, as the lobe lacks underlying cartilage.

cards.q: Rationale behind performing an urgent ophthalmologic exam (fundoscopy) in a stable child with chronic papilledema post-meningitis?
cards.a: To evaluate for chronic increased intracranial pressure and rule out early optic nerve atrophy.

cards.q: Most likely diagnosis for a child who presents with sudden onset of unilateral wheezing and decreased breath sounds, without viral prodrome or fever?
cards.a: Foreign body aspiration.

cards.q: Why are systemic aminoglycosides (e.g., Gentamicin monotherapy) inappropriate for treating localized bacterial meningitis?
cards.a: Aminoglycosides have poor penetration through the blood-brain barrier into the cerebrospinal fluid, even when meninges are inflamed.

cards.q: Preferred diagnostic test to screen for localized hearing loss in an infant under 6 months of age post-meningitis?
cards.a: Auditory Brainstem Response (ABR) testing.

cards.q: Recommended screening test for hearing loss in a child older than 6 months of age who is developmentally appropriate?
cards.a: Visual Reinforcement Audiometry (VRA) or conditioned play audiometry.

cards.q: Diagnosis for an infant presenting with typical signs of meningitis who also exhibits a direct Coombs-positive hemolytic anemia and hepatosplenomegaly?
cards.a: Congenital Syphilis complicating neonatal presentation.

cards.q: Primary reason why the influenza vaccine is highly recommended as a preventative strategy against AOM in young children?
cards.a: Preventing the primary viral upper respiratory tract infection significantly reduces secondary bacterial Eustachian tube dysfunction and subsequent AOM.

cards.q: Expected CSF profile in a patient with Guillain-Barré Syndrome, a common neurological differential for weakness post-viral illness?
cards.a: Albuminocytologic dissociation (markedly elevated protein concentration with a completely normal white blood cell count).

cards.q: Pathogen responsible for Malignant Otitis Externa, a severe differential for ear pain in immunocompromised or diabetic pediatric patients?
cards.a: Pseudomonas aeruginosa.

cards.q: Distinctive physical exam finding in Malignant Otitis Externa according to the Zitelli Atlas?
cards.a: Granulation tissue visible on the floor of the external auditory canal at the osteocartilaginous junction.

cards.q: Preferred initial antibiotic treatment for a child diagnosed with Malignant Otitis Externa?
cards.a: Intravenous antipseudomonal antibiotics (e.g., Cefepime or Piperacillin-Tazobactam).

cards.q: Diagnostic criteria for Acute Otitis Media failure, prompting a switch to second-line antibiotics?
cards.a: Lack of clinical improvement (persistent fever, ear pain, or worsening bulging) after 48 to 72 hours of initial antibiotic therapy.

cards.q: Standard second-line oral antibiotic choice for AOM after failure of initial high-dose Amoxicillin?
cards.a: High-dose Amoxicillin-Clavulanate (Augmentin formatted at a 14:1 ratio to minimize diarrhea).

cards.q: Definition of a "dry perforation" of the tympanic membrane?
cards.a: A persistent hole in the tympanic membrane without current signs of active middle ear infection or otorrhea.

cards.q: Standard management strategy for an isolated, asymptomatic, small traumatic tympanic membrane perforation?
cards.a: Watchful waiting, as the majority of small traumatic perforations heal spontaneously within 4 to 6 weeks.

cards.q: Primary surgical procedure performed concurrently with tympanostomy tube placement if a child has chronic adenoiditis or nasal obstruction?
cards.a: Adenoidectomy.

cards.q: Specific cranial nerve examined to evaluate for suspected Gradenigo Syndrome?
cards.a: Abducens Nerve (Cranial Nerve VI), assessed by checking for lateral rectus palsy and diplopia on lateral gaze.

cards.q: Most accurate method to clinically distinguish severe Otitis Externa (Swimmer's Ear) from Acute Otitis Media on physical exam?
cards.a: Extreme pain elicited by manipulating the tragus or pulling the pinna upward, which is absent in isolated AOM.

cards.q: Primary physiological reason infants are obligate nasal breathers, making RSV-induced nasal congestion life-threatening?
cards.a: The infant tongue is large relative to the oral cavity, and the epiglottis sits higher in the pharynx, making oral breathing highly inefficient.

cards.q: Consequence of severe intercostal and subcostal retractions on an infant's work of breathing over time?
cards.a: Progressive respiratory muscle fatigue leading to respiratory failure and cardiac arrest.

cards.q: Underlying reason why an infant with severe RSV bronchiolitis might present with a normal $PaCO_2$ on an initial blood gas but still be in danger?
cards.a: A normal $PaCO_2$ in a severely tachypneic, tiring infant indicates impending respiratory failure, as they can no longer sustain the work required to hyperventilate.

cards.q: Most common non-infectious condition that mimics the recurrent wheezing patterns seen after an initial RSV infection?
cards.a: Gastroesophageal Reflux Disease (GERD) causing microaspiration.

cards.q: Specific laboratory test used to differentiate between a viral flare of bronchiolitis and a secondary bacterial infection in a toxic-appearing infant?
cards.a: Serum Procalcitonin or C-Reactive Protein (CRP) levels, which elevate significantly in bacterial infections compared to viral infections.

cards.q: Recommended isolation protocol variant required if an RSV patient is also co-infected with Adenovirus?
cards.a: Addition of strict Droplet and Eye protection precautions, as Adenovirus is highly contagious via conjunctival secretions.

cards.q: Why is the use of dynamic chest physiotherapy strictly discouraged in the PALS guidelines for acute bronchiolitis?
cards.a: It does not improve oxygenation or clear peripheral airway secretions, and it increases the risk of rib fractures and bronchial spasms.

cards.q: Long-term pulmonary function abnormality characteristically found on spirometry years after a severe RSV infection?
cards.a: Obstructive lung pattern with reduced $FEV_1/FVC$ ratio and air trapping.

cards.q: Indication for introducing Non-Invasive Positive Pressure Ventilation (NIPPV/CPAP) in an infant with worsening RSV bronchiolitis?
cards.a: Persistent hypoxemia despite high-flow supplemental oxygen, severe retractions, or a rising $PaCO_2$ with increased work of breathing.

cards.q: Only specific patient population where aerosolized Ribavirin should actively be considered for RSV lower respiratory tract disease?
cards.a: Severe, life-threatening RSV infection in highly immunocompromised hosts, such as recent bone marrow transplant recipients.

cards.q: Most common source of transmission for early-onset neonatal Group B Streptococcus meningitis?
cards.a: Vertical transmission from the maternal genital tract during labor and delivery.

cards.q: Most common source of transmission for late-onset neonatal Group B Streptococcus meningitis (occurring 7 to 90 days postpartum)?
cards.a: Horizontal transmission from healthcare workers, community contacts, or maternal skin.

cards.q: Specific Gram stain morphology characteristic of Streptococcus pneumoniae isolated from CSF?
cards.a: Gram-positive, lancet-shaped diplococci.

cards.q: Specific Gram stain morphology characteristic of Neisseria meningitidis isolated from CSF?
cards.a: Gram-negative, kidney bean-shaped diplococci.

cards.q: Specific Gram stain morphology characteristic of Haemophilus influenzae isolated from CSF?
cards.a: Gram-negative coccobacilli.

cards.q: Specific Gram stain morphology characteristic of Listeria monocytogenes isolated from CSF?
cards.a: Gram-positive rods or coccobacilli exhibiting characteristic tumbling motility in fluid cultures.

cards.q: Primary rationale for performing an urgent head ultrasound in a neonate with confirmed bacterial meningitis?
cards.a: To screen for early intraventricular hemorrhage, ventriculitis, or widening of the extra-axial spaces before fontanelle closure.

cards.q: Classic neuroimaging finding on a contrast-enhanced brain MRI during active bacterial meningitis?
cards.a: Diffuse leptomeningeal enhancement tracking along the cerebral sulci and basilar cisterns.

cards.q: Definitive management step for a child who develops a localized brain abscess as a complication of Citrobacter koseri neonatal meningitis?
cards.a: Prolonged intravenous antibiotic therapy (6 to 8 weeks) combined with neurosurgical aspiration or drainage.

cards.q: Expected CSF profile changes in a patient with a partially treated bacterial meningitis (antibiotics given 2 hours before lumbar puncture)?
cards.a: Neutrophilic pleocytosis and low glucose persist, but CSF Gram stain and culture sensitivity decrease significantly.

cards.q: Minimum acceptable systolic blood pressure (lower limit) for a child aged 1 month to 1 year?
cards.a: Less than $70\text{ mmHg}$.

cards.q: Target heart rate range for an infant under 1 year old experiencing symptomatic sinus tachycardia during a stress response?
cards.a: Typically less than $220\text{ beats per minute}$ (SVT is suspected if greater than $220\text{ bpm}$).

cards.q: Target heart rate range for a child over 1 year old experiencing symptomatic sinus tachycardia?
cards.a: Typically less than $180\text{ beats per minute}$ (SVT is suspected if greater than $180\text{ bpm}$).

cards.q: Definitive PALS intervention for a pediatric patient with Supraventricular Tachycardia (SVT) who is hemodynamically unstable?
cards.a: Immediate synchronized cardioversion at an initial dose of $0.5\text{ to }1\text{ J/kg}$.

cards.q: First-line pharmacological treatment for a hemodynamically stable pediatric patient with confirmed SVT?
cards.a: Adenosine administered as a rapid intravenous push ($0.1\text{ mg/kg}$, maximum first dose $6\text{ mg}$).

cards.q: Primary hazard of utilizing a standard uncuffed endotracheal tube in a pediatric patient requiring high airway pressures?
cards.a: Large air leaks around the larynx, resulting in hypoventilation and inaccurate tidal volume monitoring.

cards.q: Recommended method to calculate the appropriate internal diameter size for a cuffed endotracheal tube in a child aged 2 to 10 years?
cards.a: $(\text{Age in years} / 4) + 3.5$.

cards.q: Recommended method to calculate the appropriate internal diameter size for an uncuffed endotracheal tube in a child aged 2 to 10 years?
cards.a: $(\text{Age in years} / 4) + 4$.

cards.q: Preferred initial vasoactive medication infusion for a pediatric patient in warm (hyperdynamic) septic shock?
cards.a: Norepinephrine infusion (to correct profound systemic vasodilation).

cards.q: Preferred initial vasoactive medication infusion for a pediatric patient in cold (hypodynamic) septic shock with low cardiac output?
cards.a: Epinephrine infusion (to leverage potent inotropic and chronotropic effects).

cards.q: Visual presentation of Koplik spots according to the Zitelli Atlas, which must be differentiated from oral lesions of enteroviral meningitis?
cards.a: Small, bluish-white spots on an erythematous background located on the buccal mucosa opposite the lower molars (pathognomonic for Measles).

cards.q: Condition characterized by a high fever, severe inspiratory stridor, and a preference to sit leaning forward with the neck extended (tripod position)?
cards.a: Acute Epiglottitis.

cards.q: Visual description of "shagreen patches" and "ash-leaf spots" on a child's skin according to the Zitelli Atlas, pointing to a disease that causes infantile spasms mimicking meningitis?
cards.a: Tuberous Sclerosis.

cards.q: Most common cause of structural conductive hearing loss identified in children with a history of recurrent, severe AOM episodes?
cards.a: Ossicular chain discontinuity or fixation secondary to chronic inflammation.

cards.q: Expected physical exam finding when performing the Rinne test on a child with significant conductive hearing loss from chronic OME?
cards.a: Bone conduction is heard longer than or equal to air conduction (Negative Rinne test).

cards.q: Expected physical exam finding when performing the Weber test on a child with unilateral conductive hearing loss in the right ear?
cards.a: The sound lateralizes specifically to the right ear.

cards.q: Expected physical exam finding when performing the Weber test on a child with unilateral sensorineural hearing loss in the right ear?
cards.a: The sound lateralizes specifically to the left ear (the unaffected ear).

cards.q: Diagnostic criteria for a toxic-appearing child with fever, a barking cough, and thick, purulent tracheal secretions unresponsive to nebulized epinephrine?
cards.a: Bacterial Tracheitis (most commonly caused by Staphylococcus aureus).

cards.q: Primary treatment approach for a child diagnosed with confirmed Bacterial Tracheitis?
cards.a: Urgent airway stabilization under anesthesia combined with intravenous broad-spectrum antibiotics.

cards.q: Condition characterized by a bulging, erythematous tympanic membrane with a distinct dark purple or black hue behind it in a newborn?
cards.a: Neonatal vascular anomaly or vascular tumor of the middle ear (e.g., glomus tympanicum), which must be differentiated from acute infectious otitis.

cards.q: Minimum age for the first dose of the Hepatitis B vaccine?
cards.a: Birth (ideally within 24 hours of delivery).

cards.q: Minimum age required to administer the Rotavirus vaccine?
cards.a: 6 weeks.

cards.q: Maximum age for the first dose of the Rotavirus vaccine?
cards.a: 14 weeks and 6 days.

cards.q: Maximum age for the final dose of the Rotavirus vaccine?
cards.a: 8 months and 0 days.

cards.q: Routine ages for the 5-dose DTaP vaccine series?
cards.a: 2 months, 4 months, 6 months, 15–18 months, and 4–6 years.

cards.q: Age at which the Tdap booster is routinely recommended?
cards.a: 11–12 years.

cards.q: Routine ages for the 4-dose Haemophilus influenzae type b (Hib) series?
cards.a: 2 months, 4 months, 6 months, and 12–15 months.

cards.q: Routine ages for the 4-dose Pneumococcal Conjugate (PCV15/PCV20) series?
cards.a: 2 months, 4 months, 6 months, and 12–15 months.

cards.q: Routine ages for the 4-dose Inactivated Poliovirus (IPV) series?
cards.a: 2 months, 4 months, 6–18 months, and 4–6 years.

cards.q: Minimum age to initiate the annual Influenza vaccine?
cards.a: 6 months.

cards.q: Requirement for children aged 6 months to 8 years receiving the Influenza vaccine for the first time?
cards.a: Two doses separated by at least 4 weeks.

cards.q: Routine ages for the 2-dose Measles, Mumps, and Rubella (MMR) series?
cards.a: 12–15 months and 4–6 years.

cards.q: Minimum interval between the first and second doses of the MMR vaccine?
cards.a: 4 weeks.

cards.q: Routine ages for the 2-dose Varicella series?
cards.a: 12–15 months and 4–6 years.

cards.q: Routine ages for the 2-dose Hepatitis A series?
cards.a: 12–23 months, with the two doses separated by at least 6 months.

cards.q: Routine age to initiate the 2-dose Human Papillomavirus (HPV) series?
cards.a: 11–12 years (can start as early as age 9).

cards.q: Dosing schedule for HPV vaccine if initiated at or after age 15?
cards.a: 3 doses at 0, 1–2, and 6 months.

cards.q: Routine ages for the 2-dose Meningococcal ACWY (MenACWY) series?
cards.a: 11–12 years and a booster at age 16.

cards.q: Route of administration for MMR, Varicella, and MMRV vaccines?
cards.a: Subcutaneous (SQ).

cards.q: Route of administration for DTaP, Hib, HepA, HepB, PCV, and MenACWY?
cards.a: Intramuscular (IM).

cards.q: Route of administration for Rotavirus vaccines?
cards.a: Oral (PO).

cards.q: Preferred IM injection site for infants and toddlers ($\1$ years old)?
cards.a: Anterolateral aspect of the thigh (Vastus lateralis muscle).

cards.q: Preferred IM injection site for older children and adolescents (≥3 years old)?
cards.a: Deltoid muscle.

cards.q: Only absolute contraindication to all vaccines?
cards.a: Severe allergic reaction (e.g., anaphylaxis) after a previous dose or to a vaccine component.

cards.q: General rule for vaccinating a child with a mild acute illness (e.g., low-grade fever, mild otitis media, cold)?
cards.a: Vaccinate as scheduled; mild illness is not a contraindication.

cards.q: General contraindication for all live-attenuated vaccines (MMR, Varicella, Rotavirus, LAIV)?
cards.a: Severe immunodeficiency (e.g., advanced HIV, chemotherapy, high-dose systemic steroids).

cards.q: Absolute contraindication specific to the Rotavirus vaccine?
cards.a: History of intussusception or severe combined immunodeficiency (SCID).

cards.q: Specific contraindication to the DTaP vaccine regarding the central nervous system?
cards.a: Encephalopathy within 7 days of a previous pertussis-containing vaccine dose.

cards.q: Precaution for DTaP concerning neurological stability?
cards.a: Progressive or unstable neurological disorders (e.g., uncontrolled epilepsy) until the condition stabilizes.

cards.q: Length of time to delay live vaccines after receiving intravenous immunoglobulin (IVIG) or packed red blood cells?
cards.a: 3 to 11 months, depending on the specific blood product and dose.

cards.q: Maximum daily dose and duration of systemic prednisone that allows for immediate administration of live vaccines?
cards.a: Less than 2 mg/kg/day (or $\1$ mg/day total) for less than 14 days.

cards.q: Precaution for the Live Attenuated Influenza Vaccine (LAIV) regarding underlying chronic conditions?
cards.a: Asthma or reactive airway disease in children aged 2–4 years.

cards.q: Is a family history of seizures a contraindication to the MMRV vaccine?
cards.a: No, but it is a precaution due to a slightly higher risk of febrile seizures compared to separate MMR and Varicella injections.

cards.q: Management of a newborn whose mother is HBsAg-positive?
cards.a: Administer HepB vaccine and Hepatitis B Immune Globulin (HBIG) within 12 hours of birth.

cards.q: Post-vaccination serologic testing protocol for an infant born to an HBsAg-positive mother?
cards.a: Test for HBsAg and anti-HBs at age 9–12 months (or 1–2 months after the final HepB dose).

cards.q: Management of a newborn weighing $\1$g whose mother is HBsAg-negative?
cards.a: Delay the first HepB vaccine dose until 1 month of age or at hospital discharge.

cards.q: Management of a newborn weighing $\1$g whose mother is HBsAg-positive?
cards.a: Give HepB vaccine and HBIG within 12 hours of birth, but do not count the birth dose toward the 3-dose series.

cards.q: Target population for the Pneumococcal Polysaccharide vaccine (PPSV23)?
cards.a: Children aged 2–18 years with underlying chronic medical conditions (e.g., asplenia, sickle cell, HIV, chronic heart/lung disease) after completing the PCV series.

cards.q: Indication for Meningococcal Serogroup B (MenB) vaccination?
cards.a: Adolescents aged 16–23 years (preferred 16–18) and high-risk patients aged ≥10 years (e.g., anatomic/functional asplenia, complement deficiency).

cards.q: Indication for early MMR vaccination at 6–11 months of age?
cards.a: International travel outside the United States.

cards.q: Does an early MMR dose given at 6–11 months count toward the 2-dose routine pediatric series?
cards.a: No, the child still requires 2 routine doses at ≥12 months of age.

cards.q: Routine recommendation for Tdap vaccination during pregnancy?
cards.a: 1 dose during every pregnancy, ideally between 27 and 36 weeks gestation, regardless of prior vaccination history.

cards.q: Frequency of well-child visits recommended by the AAP during the first year of life?
cards.a: At 3–5 days, and 1, 2, 4, 6, and 9 months of age.

cards.q: Frequency of well-child visits recommended by the AAP during the second year of life?
cards.a: At 12, 15, 18, and 24 months of age.

cards.q: Universal age recommendations for autism spectrum disorder (ASD) screening?
cards.a: 18 months and 24 months.

cards.q: Age at which universal developmental screening using a validated tool is recommended?
cards.a: 9, 18, and 30 months.

cards.q: Universal age for maternal depression screening during well-child visits?
cards.a: 1, 2, 4, and 6 months.

cards.q: Universal age for initial visual acuity screening using standard charts?
cards.a: 4 years (can attempt at 3 years if cooperative).

cards.q: Age at which formal, objective audiometry hearing screening begins?
cards.a: 4 years.

cards.q: Universal screening age for dyslipidemia using a fasting or non-fasting lipid panel?
cards.a: Once between 9 and 11 years, and once between 17 and 21 years.

cards.q: Indication for targeted lead screening in pediatric patients?
cards.a: Medicaid enrollment, living in high-prevalence zip codes, or housing built before 1978.

cards.q: Routine ages for universal hemoglobin/hematocrit screening for anemia?
cards.a: 12 months of age.

cards.q: Age at which blood pressure measurement should begin routinely at every well-child visit?
cards.a: 3 years.

cards.q: Initial screening method for scoliosis in adolescents?
cards.a: Adams Forward Bend Test.

cards.q: Recommended daily Vitamin D supplementation for exclusively breastfed infants?
cards.a: 400 IU daily starting within the first few days of life.

cards.q: When should Vitamin D supplementation stop for formula-fed infants?
cards.a: When they consume at least 1 liter (approx. 32 oz) per day of Vitamin D-fortified formula or whole milk.

cards.q: Age at which iron supplementation should begin for exclusively breastfed, term infants?
cards.a: 4 months of age (at 1 mg/kg/day of elemental iron) until iron-containing foods are introduced.

cards.q: Iron supplementation rule for preterm infants?
cards.a: 2 mg/kg/day of elemental iron starting at 2 weeks of age until 12 months of age.

cards.q: Age at which solid foods should be introduced into an infant's diet?
cards.a: Around 6 months of age, when developmentally ready.

cards.q: Recommended age to introduce allergenic foods (e.g., peanut products) to prevent allergies?
cards.a: Around 4–6 months of age, after other solids are tolerated, especially in infants with severe eczema or egg allergy.

cards.q: Maximum recommended intake of whole cow's milk per day for toddlers aged 1–5 years?
cards.a: 16 to 24 ounces (approx. 500–700 mL) per day to prevent iron-deficiency anemia.

cards.q: Age at which low-fat (1% or skim) milk can be introduced instead of whole milk?
cards.a: 2 years of age (can consider at 12 months if overweight or family history of obesity/cardiovascular disease).

cards.q: Age before which raw honey is completely contraindicated?
cards.a: 12 months (due to the risk of infant botulism from Clostridium botulinum spores).

cards.q: Most sensitive indicator of a child's nutritional status or acute illness?
cards.a: Weight changes (monitored via standardized growth charts).

cards.q: Definition of failure to thrive (FTT) based on growth chart percentiles?
cards.a: Weight below the 3rd to 5th percentile, or a drop across two major percentile lines.

cards.q: Recommended safe sleep position to prevent Sudden Infant Death Syndrome (SIDS)?
cards.a: Supine (flat on the back) for every sleep period.

cards.q: Essential components of a safe infant sleep environment?
cards.a: Firm, flat sleep surface, in a crib/bassinette, with no loose blankets, pillows, bumper pads, or soft toys.

cards.q: Recommended duration for infants to remain in a rear-facing car safety seat?
cards.a: Until they reach the highest weight or height limit allowed by their car seat manufacturer.

cards.q: Criteria for switching a child from a belt-positioning booster seat to a standard vehicle lap-and-shoulder belt?
cards.a: Height of 4 feet 9 inches (143 cm) and typically between 8 and 12 years of age.

cards.q: Age before which children should always sit in the back seat of a vehicle equipped with passenger airbags?
cards.a: 13 years.

cards.q: Primary mechanism of cardiac arrest in pediatric patients according to PALS?
cards.a: Asphyxial/respiratory failure or progressive shock (rarely primary cardiac events).

cards.q: Definition of pediatric tachycardia requiring immediate evaluation based on age groups?
cards.a: Infant heart rate $\1$/min or child heart rate $\1$/min with narrow QRS complexes.

cards.q: First-line intervention for a pediatric patient with symptomatic bradycardia and compromised cardiopulmonary status despite oxygenation/ventilation?
cards.a: Cardiopulmonary resuscitation (CPR) if the heart rate remains $\1$/min.

cards.q: Classic skin finding in Zitelli's Atlas for a child with congenital dermal melanocytosis (Mongolian spots)?
cards.a: Flat, blue-grey patches with indefinite borders, most commonly located over the sacrum or buttocks.

cards.q: Physical exam finding that distinguishes erythema toxicum neonatorum from neonatal herpes?
cards.a: Erythema toxicum presents with eosinophils on a Wright-stained smear; herpes presents with multinucleated giant cells on a Tzanck smear.

cards.q: Anticipatory guidance topic regarding water safety for toddlers?
cards.a: Continuous, touch-supervision by an adult whenever the child is in or near water (including bathtubs and swimming pools).

cards.q: Water temperature threshold recommended for home water heaters to prevent scald burns?
cards.a: Below 120°F (49°C).

cards.q: Universal age recommendation for the first dental visit?
cards.a: By 12 months of age, or within 6 months of the eruption of the first tooth.

cards.q: Minimum interval between doses 1 and 2 of the HepB series in a catch-up schedule?
cards.a: 4 weeks.

cards.q: Minimum age to receive the Tdap vaccine if a child missed the childhood DTaP series?
cards.a: 7 years.

cards.q: Number of doses required for the HPV vaccine series if the first dose is given at age 16?
cards.a: 3 doses.

cards.q: Complication of Haemophilus influenzae type b that Hib vaccination effectively prevents?
cards.a: Epiglottitis, meningitis, and septic arthritis.

cards.q: Primary reason for administering the Rubella vaccine component to children?
cards.a: To prevent Congenital Rubella Syndrome (CRS) in the offspring of pregnant women exposed to infected children.

cards.q: Major neurological complication associated with Measles infection that the MMR vaccine prevents?
cards.a: Subacute Sclerosing Panencephalitis (SSPE).

cards.q: Serious complication of Mumps infection prevented by vaccination in post-pubertal males?
cards.a: Orchitis (which can cause testicular atrophy and, rarely, infertility).

cards.q: Pneumococcal serotype coverage type utilized in PCV15/PCV20?
cards.a: Capsular polysaccharide conjugated to a nontoxic diphtheria toxin protein carrier (T-cell dependent response).

cards.q: Pneumococcal vaccine type that induces a T-cell independent response?
cards.a: PPSV23 (unconjugated polysaccharide vaccine).

cards.q: Why is PPSV23 ineffective in children under 2 years of age?
cards.a: Immature splenic function and inability to mount an immune response to T-cell independent polysaccharide antigens.

cards.q: Diagnostic significance of a white pupillary reflex (leukocoria) on a red reflex exam?
cards.a: Urgent referral to an ophthalmologist for suspected retinoblastoma or congenital cataracts.

cards.q: Physical signs of developmental dysplasia of the hip (DDH) during newborn screening?
cards.a: Positive Barlow (dislocation) or Ortolani (reduction) maneuvers, or asymmetric thigh skin folds.

cards.q: Standard imaging modality used to screen for DDH in infants under 4 months of age?
cards.a: Hip ultrasonography.

cards.q: Standard imaging modality used to screen for DDH in infants 4 months and older?
cards.a: AP and frog-leg lateral radiographs of the pelvis.

cards.q: Screening recommendation for cryptorchidism (undescended testes)?
cards.a: Palpate at every well-child visit; refer to a specialist if undescended by 6 months of age.

cards.q: Anticipatory guidance regarding screen time limits for children under 18 months of age?
cards.a: Avoid screen time entirely, except for video chatting.

cards.q: Recommended limit for recreational screen time for children aged 2 to 5 years?
cards.a: No more than 1 hour per day of high-quality programming.

cards.q: Best preventive counseling regarding secondhand smoke exposure in infants?
cards.a: Strict elimination of smoking in the home and car to prevent lower respiratory tract infections and SIDS.

cards.q: Initial management strategy for a toddler presenting with physiological bowed legs (genu varum) under 2 years of age?
cards.a: Reassurance and observation, as it typically resolves spontaneously by age 2.

cards.q: Diagnostic criteria on a growth chart that suggests constitutional delay of growth?
cards.a: Growth velocity is normal, but height and weight trail parallel to and below the 3rd percentile, with a delayed bone age.

cards.q: Expected age by which an infant should double their birth weight?
cards.a: 4 to 5 months of age.

cards.q: Expected age by which an infant should triple their birth weight?
cards.a: 12 months of age.

cards.q: Expected age by which an infant should quadruple their birth weight?
cards.a: 24 months of age.

cards.q: Average increase in head circumference during the first year of life?
cards.a: Approximately 12 centimeters.

cards.q: Manifestation of congenital hypothyroidism on a newborn preventative screening panel if left untreated?
cards.a: Intellectual disability, macroglossia, umbilical hernia, hypotonia, and prolonged jaundice.

cards.q: Manifestation of phenylketonuria (PKU) on a newborn preventative screening panel if left untreated?
cards.a: Intellectual disability, musty/mousy body odor, microcephaly, and hypopigmentation.

cards.q: Immediate screening step required for an infant with a suspected critical congenital heart defect (CCHD)?
cards.a: Pulse oximetry screening in the right hand and either foot after 24 hours of life.

cards.q: Positive screening result for Critical Congenital Heart Disease (CCHD) via pulse oximetry?
cards.a: Any $\text{SpO}_2 < 90\\%$, $\text{SpO}_2 < 95\\%$ in both extremities on 3 measures separated by 1 hour, or a $>3\\%$ difference between hand and foot.

cards.q: Clinical significance of a dynamic, musical, vibratory systolic murmur at the lower left sternal border in an asymptomatic 4-year-old child?
cards.a: Still's murmur, which is benign/innocent and requires reassurance.

cards.q: First physical indicator of female puberty (thelarche) on a preventative exam?
cards.a: Breast budding under the areola, typically occurring between 8 and 13 years of age.

cards.q: First physical indicator of male puberty (gonadarche) on a preventative exam?
cards.a: Testicular enlargement ($\ge 4 \text{ mL}$ volume or $\ge 2.5 \text{ cm}$ length), typically occurring between 9 and 14 years of age.

cards.q: Primary preventative screening done for adolescents regarding mental health?
cards.a: Annual screening for depression using the PHQ-2 or PHQ-A questionnaires starting at age 12.

cards.q: Age at which universal screening for human immunodeficiency virus (HIV) is recommended at least once?
cards.a: Between 15 and 18 years of age.

cards.q: Preventative strategy for dental caries in communities without fluoridated tap water?
cards.a: Oral fluoride supplementation starting at 6 months of age.

cards.q: What finding on a pediatric skin exam should trigger an evaluation for Neurofibromatosis Type 1 (NF1)?
cards.a: Six or more café-au-lait macules greater than 5 mm in diameter in prepubertal children.

cards.q: True or false: The MMR vaccine causes autism due to the thimerosal preservative.
cards.a: False; multiple large-scale studies have disproven any link, and MMR has never contained thimerosal.

cards.q: Expected, benign local physical exam findings within 48 hours of a DTaP injection?
cards.a: Erythema, mild swelling, and localized tenderness at the injection site.

cards.q: Definition of a hypotonic-hyporesponsive episode (HHE) following vaccination?
cards.a: Sudden onset of pallor, hypotonia, and unresponsiveness within 48 hours of vaccination (most commonly DTaP).

cards.q: Is a history of a hypotonic-hyporesponsive episode (HHE) an absolute contraindication to future DTaP doses?
cards.a: No, it is a precaution; the benefits of pertussis coverage usually outweigh the risks.

cards.q: What rare, self-limiting neurological condition is historically monitored after the Influenza vaccine?
cards.a: Guillain-Barré Syndrome (GBS) within 6 weeks of administration.

cards.q: Can a child with a known, non-anaphylactic egg allergy receive the routine Influenza vaccine?
cards.a: Yes, any age-appropriate Influenza vaccine (inactivated or live) can be given safely without special precautions.

cards.q: Can a child living with a pregnant mother safely receive live vaccines like MMR and Varicella?
cards.a: Yes, transmission of the vaccine viruses to contacts is extremely rare.

cards.q: Under what specific circumstance should a child avoid a vaccine due to a household contact?
cards.a: Avoid Live Attenuated Influenza Vaccine (LAIV) if a household contact is severely immunocompromised and in a protected environment (e.g., bone marrow transplant unit).

cards.q: Most common benign side effect noted 7 to 12 days after receiving the MMR vaccine?
cards.a: Transient low-grade fever and a mild, non-contagious maculopapular rash.

cards.q: Management of a child who develops a small, non-painful subcutaneous nodule at a DTaP injection site?
cards.a: Reassurance; it is a common granulomatous reaction to the aluminum adjuvant and resolves spontaneously.

cards.q: Post-exposure prophylaxis for an unvaccinated 10-month-old infant exposed to Measles within 72 hours?
cards.a: Administer the MMR vaccine.

cards.q: Post-exposure prophylaxis for an immunocompromised child exposed to Measles within 6 days?
cards.a: Administer Intravenous Immunoglobulin (IVIG).

cards.q: Post-exposure prophylaxis for an unimmunized 8-month-old infant exposed to Varicella within 96 hours?
cards.a: Administer Varicella Zoster Immune Globulin (VarZIG).

cards.q: Post-exposure prophylaxis for an unimmunized 15-month-old child exposed to Varicella within 3 to 5 days?
cards.a: Administer the Varicella vaccine.

cards.q: Management of a clean, minor wound in a child with an unknown or $\1$ dose DTaP history?
cards.a: Give the DTaP/Tdap vaccine only; no Tetanus Immune Globulin (TIG) is required.

cards.q: Management of a deep, contaminated wound in a child with an unknown or $\1$ dose DTaP history?
cards.a: Give both the DTaP/Tdap vaccine and Tetanus Immune Globulin (TIG).

cards.q: Management of a clean, minor wound in a child with $\ge 3$ documented DTaP doses, with the last dose 7 years ago?
cards.a: Reassurance and wound care; no vaccine or TIG is needed because the last dose was $<10$ years ago.

cards.q: Management of a contaminated wound in a child with $\ge 3$ documented DTaP doses, with the last dose 7 years ago?
cards.a: Give a DTaP/Tdap booster because the last dose was $>5$ years ago for a high-risk wound.

cards.q: What additional vaccine is recommended for pediatric travelers visiting areas of sub-Saharan Africa known as the "Meningitis Belt"?
cards.a: Meningococcal ACWY (MenACWY) vaccine booster or early dose.

cards.q: Minimum age to receive the Yellow Fever vaccine for pediatric international travelers?
cards.a: 9 months (due to the risk of vaccine-associated encephalitis in younger infants).

cards.q: Physical exam finding on the Hirschberg (corneal light reflex) test that indicates strabismus?
cards.a: Asymmetrical placement of the light reflex point on the pupil or iris.

cards.q: Gold-standard management for a child diagnosed with amblyopia due to strabismus?
cards.a: Patching the unaffected (stronger) eye or using atropine drops to blur the stronger eye, forcing use of the weaker eye.

cards.q: Objective screening method used for newborn hearing screening in the nursery?
cards.a: Otoacoustic Emissions (OAE) or Automated Auditory Brainstem Response (AABR).

cards.q: Interpretation of an infant who "fails" the initial newborn hearing screening?
cards.a: Repeat screening before 1 month of age; if still failed, comprehensive audiologic evaluation by 3 months.

cards.q: Primary dental advice given to parents to prevent Early Childhood Caries (baby bottle tooth decay)?
cards.a: Never put an infant to sleep with a bottle containing milk, juice, or sweetened liquids.

cards.q: When should toothpaste containing fluoride be introduced into a child’s oral care routine?
cards.a: At the eruption of the first tooth, using a tiny "smear" (size of a grain of rice).

cards.q: Amount of fluoride toothpaste recommended for children aged 3 to 6 years?
cards.a: A pea-sized amount.

cards.q: Confirmation step required if a capillary finger-stick lead screening level returns elevated ($\ge 3.5\ \mu\text{g/dL}$)?
cards.a: Obtain a confirmatory venous blood lead level.

cards.q: First-line intervention for a venous blood lead level between $3.5\ \mu\text{g/dL}$ and $44\ \mu\text{g/dL}$?
cards.a: Environmental investigation to identify and remove the lead source, and nutritional optimization (iron, calcium).

cards.q: Threshold venous lead level at which oral chelation therapy (e.g., Succimer) is indicated?
cards.a: $\ge 45\ \mu\text{g/dL}$.

cards.q: Emergency management for a child presenting with a venous lead level $\ge 70\ \mu\text{g/dL}$ or acute lead encephalopathy?
cards.a: Hospitalization and dual inpatient chelation therapy with Dimercaprol (BAL) and Calcium Disodium EDTA.

cards.q: Most common cause of a false-positive result on a routine newborn screening card?
cards.a: Sample collection occurred before 24 hours of life (especially true for PKU and congenital hypothyroidism metabolic markers).

cards.q: Diagnostic follow-up required for a newborn whose screening panel indicates elevated Immunoreactive Trypsinogen (IRT)?
cards.a: Sweat chloride testing to evaluate for Cystic Fibrosis.

cards.q: Red flag developmental timeline: Child not walking independently by what age?
cards.a: 18 months.

cards.q: Red flag developmental timeline: Child not babbling or using gestures by what age?
cards.a: 12 months.

cards.q: Red flag developmental timeline: Child without single words by what age?
cards.a: 16 months.

cards.q: Red flag developmental timeline: Child without 2-word meaningful phrases by what age?
cards.a: 24 months.

cards.q: The ultimate developmental rule regarding any loss of language or social skills at any age?
cards.a: Immediate referral for formal developmental, audiologic, and neurological evaluation.

cards.q: Expected physical growth pattern of a child with Familial Short Stature?
cards.a: Growth curve runs parallel to but below the 3rd percentile, with a normal growth velocity and a normal bone age equal to chronological age.

cards.q: Correct compression-to-ventilation ratio for two-rescuer pediatric CPR?
Correct compression-to-ventilation ratio for single-rescuer pediatric CPR?
Target depth for chest compressions during infant CPR?
cards.a: Approximately 1.5 inches (4 cm), or one-third the anterior-posterior diameter of the chest.

cards.q: Target depth for chest compressions during child CPR?
cards.a: Approximately 2 inches (5 cm), or one-third the anterior-posterior diameter of the chest.

cards.q: Preferred method for opening the airway in a pediatric trauma patient with a suspected neck injury?
cards.a: Jaw-thrust maneuver without head extension.

cards.q: Definition of hypotension in a child aged 1 to 10 years based on systolic blood pressure?
cards.a: $\text{Systolic BP} < 70\ \text{mmHg} + (2 \times \text{age in years})$.

cards.q: First line fluid resuscitation volume bolus size for a pediatric patient in hypovolemic shock?
cards.a: $20\ \text{mL/kg}$ of an isotonic crystalloid (e.g., Normal Saline or Lactated Ringer's).

cards.q: Pathognomonic oral cavity finding during the prodromal phase of Measles (Rubeola)?
cards.a: Koplik spots (small blue-white spots on an erythematous background on the buccal mucosa opposite the molars).

cards.q: Description of the classic rash of Varicella (Chickenpox)?
cards.a: Pruritic, maculopapular rash that rapidly evolves into vesicles on an erythematous base ("dewdrops on a rose petal"), appearing in various stages of healing.

cards.q: Skin manifestation of Erythema Infectiosum (Fifth Disease) caused by Parvovirus B19?
cards.a: Bright red rash on the cheeks ("slapped cheek" appearance) followed by a lacy, reticular rash on the trunk and extremities.

cards.q: Clinical presentation of Roseola Infantum (Exanthem Subitum) caused by HHV-6?
cards.a: High fever ($>40^\circ\text{C}$ or $104^\circ\text{F}$) for 3–5 days that abruptly drops, followed immediately by the appearance of a maculopapular, non-pruritic rash.

cards.q: Physical exam sign of Hand-Foot-and-Mouth Disease caused by Coxsackievirus A16?
cards.a: Painful oral ulcers (herpangina) accompanied by maculopapular or vesicular lesions on the palms of the hands and soles of the feet.

cards.q: Definition of a malformation?
cards.a: An intrinsic morphogenetic defect in tissue development from the onset of conception.

cards.q: Definition of a deformation?
cards.a: An extrinsic mechanical force that alters the shape of normally formed tissue.

cards.q: Definition of a disruption?
cards.a: A destructive breakdown of an organ or tissue that was previously developing normally.

cards.q: Definition of a dysplasia?
cards.a: Abnormal cellular organization or architectural arrangement within a specific tissue type.

cards.q: Example of a classic mechanical deformation?
cards.a: Clubfoot (talipes equinovarus) caused by severe oligohydramnios or uterine crowding.

cards.q: Example of a classic tissue disruption?
cards.a: Amniotic band syndrome causing digital or limb amputations.

cards.q: Definition of a congenital "sequence"?
cards.a: A single primary structural defect that leads to a cascade of secondary downstream anomalies.

cards.q: Primary defect in Pierre Robin sequence?
cards.a: Micrognathia (mandibular hypoplasia).

cards.q: Downstream triad seen in Pierre Robin sequence?
cards.a: Micrognathia, glossoptosis, and a U-shaped cleft palate.

cards.q: Primary defect in Potter sequence?
cards.a: Renal agenesis or severe obstructive uropathy causing profound oligohydramnios.

cards.q: Classic physical features of Potter sequence?
cards.a: Flattened facies, low-set ears, compressed lungs (pulmonary hypoplasia), and limb deformities.

cards.q: Definition of a congenital "syndrome"?
cards.a: A recognized, recurring pattern of multiple anomalies with a single, specific underlying etiology.

cards.q: Definition of an "association" in genetics?
cards.a: A non-random statistical clustering of anomalies that occur together more often than by chance alone, without a known single cause.

cards.q: What does the acronym VACTERL stand for?
cards.a: Vertebral, Anal atresia, Cardiac, Tracheoesophageal fistula, Renal, and Limb anomalies.

cards.q: Most common type of single minor anomaly found in normal newborns?
cards.a: Preauricular tags or pits.

cards.q: Clinical significance of finding three or more minor congenital anomalies in a newborn?
cards.a: High statistical probability of an underlying, undiagnosed major structural anomaly.

cards.q: Major cause of death in the first year of life in developed countries?
cards.a: Congenital malformations.

cards.q: Percentage of congenital anomalies with a completely unknown etiology?
cards.a: Approximately 50% to 60%.

cards.q: Gestational period of highest susceptibility to major structural teratogens?
cards.a: Weeks 3 through 8 of embryonic development (organogenesis).

cards.q: Effect of a severe teratogenic insult during the first 2 weeks of gestation?
cards.a: An "all-or-none" effect, resulting in either embryonic death or completely normal recovery.

cards.q: Definition of a phenocopy?
cards.a: An environmentally induced phenotype that matches an identical phenotype caused by a genetic mutation.

cards.q: Developmental origin of the palatine tonsillar crypts?
cards.a: Second pharyngeal pouch.

cards.q: Developmental origin of the inferior parathyroid glands and thymus?
cards.a: Third pharyngeal pouch.

cards.q: Developmental origin of the superior parathyroid glands?
cards.a: Fourth pharyngeal pouch.

cards.q: Mechanism behind a persistent thyroglossal duct cyst?
cards.a: Failure of the thyroglossal duct to atrophy during thyroid migration from the foramen caecum.

cards.q: Most common chromosomal cause of moderate intellectual disability?
cards.a: Trisomy 21 (Down syndrome).

cards.q: Most common genetic cause of universal/global developmental delay in males?
cards.a: Fragile X syndrome.

cards.q: Recurrence risk of Down syndrome if caused by a Robertsonian translocation in a maternal carrier?
cards.a: Approximately 10% to 15%.

cards.q: Recurrence risk of Down syndrome if caused by a Robertsonian translocation in a paternal carrier?
cards.a: Approximately 1% to 2%.

cards.q: Most common cardiac defect associated with Trisomy 21?
cards.a: Endocardial cushion defect (Atrioventricular septal defect).

cards.q: Gastrointestinal anomalies classically associated with Down syndrome?
cards.a: Duodenal atresia and Hirschsprung disease.

cards.q: Leukemia type with increased risk in Down syndrome patients under 3 years old?
cards.a: Acute Megakaryoblastic Leukemia (AMKL).

cards.q: Triad of clinical features pathognomonic for Trisomy 18 (Edwards syndrome)?
cards.a: Micrognathia, clenched fists with overlapping fingers, and rocker-bottom feet.

cards.q: Most common structural cardiac defect in Trisomy 18?
cards.a: Ventricular septal defect (VSD).

cards.q: Classic midline defects associated with Trisomy 13 (Patau syndrome)?
cards.a: Holoprosencephaly, cleft lip/palate, and omphalocele.

cards.q: Pathognomonic limb/skin findings in Trisomy 13?
cards.a: Postaxial polydactyly and cutis aplasia of the scalp.

cards.q: Karyotype of Turner syndrome?
Cardinal cardiovascular anomaly in Turner syndrome?
cards.a: Coarctation of the aorta (bicuspid aortic valve is also common).

cards.q: Lymphatic anomaly responsible for webbed neck and puffy feet in Turner syndrome?
cards.a: Congenital lymphedema due to lymphatic dysgenesis (cystic hygroma).

cards.q: Karyotype of Klinefelter syndrome?
cards.a: 47,XXY.

cards.q: Clinical presentation of Klinefelter syndrome in adolescence?
cards.a: Tall stature, gynecomastia, small firm testes, and hypergonadotropic hypogonadism.

cards.q: Genetic mechanism behind Prader-Willi syndrome?
cards.a: Paternal deletion or maternal uniparental disomy of chromosome 15q11-q13.

cards.q: Phenotypic presentation of Prader-Willi syndrome in infancy?
cards.a: Severe hypotonia, poor feeding, and failure to thrive.

cards.q: Phenotypic switch in Prader-Willi syndrome during early childhood?
cards.a: Hyperphagia leading to early-onset morbid obesity and type 2 diabetes.

cards.q: Genetic mechanism behind Angelman syndrome?
cards.a: Maternal deletion or paternal uniparental disomy of chromosome 15q11-q13 (loss of UBE3A expression).

cards.q: Classic clinical triad of Angelman syndrome?
cards.a: Inappropriate laughter ("happy puppet"), severe ataxia, and absent speech.

cards.q: Chromosomal microdeletion in DiGeorge syndrome?
cards.a: 22q11.2 microdeletion.

cards.q: Developmental mechanism altered in DiGeorge syndrome?
cards.a: Aberrant development of the 3rd and 4th pharyngeal pouches.

cards.q: Clinical presentation of CATCH-22 in DiGeorge syndrome?
cards.a: Cardiac defects, Abnormal facies, Thymic hypoplasia, Cleft palate, and Hypocalcemia.

cards.q: Immediate life-threatening metabolic complication in DiGeorge syndrome newborns?
cards.a: Hypocalcemic tetany or seizures due to parathyroid aplasia.

cards.q: Classic facial triad of Fetal Alcohol Syndrome (FAS)?
cards.a: Short palpebral fissures, smooth philtrum, and a thin upper lip vermilion.

cards.q: Central nervous system manifestation of Fetal Alcohol Syndrome?
cards.a: Microcephaly with structural brain anomalies and neurobehavioral impairment.

cards.q: Cardiac anomaly specifically associated with maternal lithium use?
cards.a: Ebstein anomaly (atrialization of the right ventricle).

cards.q: Pathognomonic skeletal anomaly of Fetal Warfarin Syndrome?
cards.a: Chondrodysplasia punctata (stippled epiphyses) and nasal hypoplasia.

cards.q: Classic structural defects caused by Fetal Hydantoin (Phenytoin) Syndrome?
cards.a: Craniofacial clefts, hypoplastic nails, and hypoplastic distal phalanges.

cards.q: Phenotypic presentation of Fetal Retinoic Acid (Isotretinoin) Embryopathy?
cards.a: Severe microtia/otia, hydrocephalus, and conotruncal cardiac malformations.

cards.q: Primary congenital defect associated with maternal Valproic Acid use?
cards.a: Neural tube defects (specifically lumbosacral spina bifida).

cards.q: Mechanism by which Valproic Acid induces neural tube defects?
cards.a: Interference with folate metabolism and antagonism of folate transport.

cards.q: Structural anomalies associated with uncontrolled pregestational maternal diabetes?
cards.a: Caudal regression syndrome (sacral agenesis) and transposition of the great arteries.

cards.q: Pathognomonic transient cardiac pathology in infants of diabetic mothers?
cards.a: Asymmetric septal hypertrophy causing subaortic left ventricular outflow tract obstruction.

cards.q: Classic congenital anomalies associated with Thalidomide exposure?
cards.a: Phocomelia and amelia (severe limb reduction defects).

cards.q: Classic triad of Congenital Rubella Syndrome?
cards.a: Sensorineural cataracts, sensorineural deafness, and patent ductus arteriosus (PDA).

cards.q: Classic skin finding in neonatal Congenital Rubella Syndrome?
cards.a: "Blueberry muffin" spots representing extramedullary hematopoiesis.

cards.q: Intracranial finding pathognomonic for Congenital Cytomegalovirus (CMV)?
cards.a: Periventricular intracranial calcifications.

cards.q: Intracranial finding pathognomonic for Congenital Toxoplasmosis?
cards.a: Diffuse, scattered parenchymal intracranial calcifications.

cards.q: Classic triad of Congenital Toxoplasmosis?
cards.a: Chorioretinitis, hydrocephalus, and diffuse intracranial calcifications.

cards.q: Pathognomonic early skeletal sign of Congenital Syphilis?
cards.a: Wimberger sign (destructive osteopathy of the proximal medial tibia).

cards.q: Late-stage stigmata triad of Congenital Syphilis?
cards.a: Hutchinson triad: interstitial keratitis, sensorineural deafness, and notched Hutchinson teeth.

cards.q: Primary adverse structural outcome of prenatal Maternal Hyperthermia?
cards.a: Neural tube defects due to disruption of anterior neuropore closure.

cards.q: Neonatal withdrawal syndrome caused by maternal SSRI use in late pregnancy?
cards.a: Poor neonatal adaptation syndrome (hyperirritability, tachypnea, weak cry).

cards.q: Major neonatal vascular risk associated with maternal Cocaine use?
cards.a: Jejunoileal atresia or limb reduction defects due to fetal vascular disruption.

cards.q: Congenital defect linked to maternal smoking during pregnancy?
cards.a: Isolated cleft lip and palate.

cards.q: Drug of choice to prevent neural tube defects in standard pregnancies?
cards.a: Folic acid 0.4 mg daily starting pre-conception.

cards.q: Folic acid dosage recommended for mothers with a history of a prior child with a neural tube defect?
cards.a: 4.0 mg daily starting pre-conception.

cards.q: Definitive diagnostic test for fetal chromosomal anomalies after an abnormal maternal serum screen?
cards.a: Amniocentesis or Chorionic Villus Sampling (CVS) with karyotype/microarray.

cards.q: Most common congenital cardiac defect overall?
cards.a: Ventricular Septal Defect (VSD).

cards.q: Pathophysiology of an Omphalocele?
cards.a: Failure of the midgut loops to return to the abdominal cavity through the umbilical ring at week 10.

cards.q: Anatomical presentation of Gastroschisis?
cards.a: Herniation of bowel lateral to the umbilicus (usually right side) without a covering peritoneal membrane.

cards.q: Maternal serum marker elevated in both Gastroschisis and Omphalocele?
cards.a: $\alpha$-Fetoprotein (AFP).

cards.q: Syndrome strongly associated with Omphalocele, macroglossia, and hemihyperplasia?
cards.a: Beckwith-Wiedemann syndrome.

cards.q: Malignancy risk associated with Beckwith-Wiedemann syndrome?
cards.a: Wilms tumor and hepatoblastoma.

cards.q: Diagnostic imaging step for a newborn with excessive salivation and choking during initial feeding?
cards.a: Insertion of a radiopaque nasogastric tube followed by a chest/abdominal X-ray.

cards.q: Most common type of Tracheoesophageal Fistula (TEF)?
cards.a: Type C: Esophageal atresia with a distal tracheoesophageal fistula.

cards.q: Classic X-ray finding in Type C Tracheoesophageal Fistula?
cards.a: Coiled NG tube in the upper esophageal pouch with air present in the stomach.

cards.q: Diagnostic finding on an abdominal X-ray for Duodenal Atresia?
cards.a: The "double bubble" sign (air-filled stomach and proximal duodenum).

cards.q: Congenital anomaly presenting with a painless, midline neck mass that moves upward with tongue protrusion?
cards.a: Thyroglossal duct cyst.

cards.q: Congenital anomaly presenting with a lateral neck mass anterior to the sternocleidomastoid muscle that does not move with swallowing?
cards.a: Branchial cleft cyst.

cards.q: Embryological failure causing Hirschsprung disease?
cards.a: Failure of craniocaudal migration of neural crest cells to the distal colon.

cards.q: Definitive gold-standard diagnostic test for Hirschsprung disease?
cards.a: Suction rectal biopsy demonstrating an absence of ganglion cells in Meissner and Auerbach plexuses.

cards.q: Embryological failure causing Meckel diverticulum?
cards.a: Incomplete obliteration of the omphalomesenteric (vitelline) duct.

cards.q: Two tissue types most commonly found ectopically in Meckel diverticulum?
cards.a: Gastric mucosa and pancreatic tissue.

cards.q: Rule of 2s for Meckel diverticulum?
cards.a: 2% of population, 2 feet from ileocecal valve, 2 inches long, 2 types of ectopic tissue, presents by age 2.

cards.q: Most common congenital anomaly of the urinary tract?
cards.a: Ureteropelvic junction (UPJ) obstruction.

cards.q: Most common cause of severe bilateral hydronephrosis and bladder distension in newborn males?
cards.a: Posterior urethral valves (PUV).

cards.q: Diagnostic modality of choice to confirm Posterior Urethral Valves?
cards.a: Voiding cystourethrogram (VCUG).

cards.q: Embryological defect in an Exstrophy of the Bladder?
cards.a: Failure of the infraumbilical mesenchymal migration leading to a breakdown of the cloacal membrane.

cards.q: Embryological failure causing Anencephaly?
cards.a: Failure of the anterior (rostral) neuropore to close during week 4 of gestation.

cards.q: Embryological failure causing Spina Bifida Occluta?
cards.a: Failure of the embryonic vertebral arches to fuse completely midline without herniation of meninges or cord.

cards.q: Structural presentation of a Meningocele?
cards.a: Herniation of the meninges through a vertebral defect without spinal cord involvement.

cards.q: Structural presentation of a Myelomeningocele?
cards.a: Herniation of both the meninges and the spinal cord/neural elements through a vertebral defect.

cards.q: Central nervous system malformation universally associated with Myelomeningocele?
cards.a: Chiari II malformation (downward displacement of the cerebellar vermis and medulla).

cards.q: Classic cranial signs of hydrocephalus on physical examination of a newborn?
cards.a: Bulging anterior fontanelle, widened sutures, and the "setting-sun" eye sign.

cards.q: Definition of Craniosynostosis?
cards.a: Premature fusion of one or more cranial sutures.

cards.q: Most common type of single suture craniosynostosis?
cards.a: Sagittal suture synostosis (causing scaphocephaly/dolichocephaly).

cards.q: Diagnostic sign of Developmental Dysplasia of the Hip (DDH) that reduces a dislocated hip?
cards.a: Ortolani maneuver (abduction of the flexed hip with anterior pressure).

cards.q: First-line imaging modality to screen for structural anomalies in a fetus during routine prenatal care?
cards.a: Screening fetal anatomy ultrasound performed between 18 and 22 weeks of gestation.

cards.q: Serum markers included in the maternal quadruple screen for aneuploidy?
cards.a: $\alpha$-fetoprotein (AFP), human chorionic gonadotropin (hCG), estriol (uE3), and inhibin A.

cards.q: Quadruple screen pattern classic for Trisomy 21?
cards.a: Decreased AFP, increased hCG, decreased uE3, and increased inhibin A.

cards.q: Quadruple screen pattern classic for Trisomy 18?
cards.a: Decreased AFP, decreased hCG, decreased uE3, and normal to decreased inhibin A.

cards.q: Next diagnostic step when a routine newborn pulse oximetry screen is positive for suspected congenital heart disease?
cards.a: Urgent transthoracic echocardiogram.

cards.q: Criteria for a positive newborn pulse oximetry screen for critical congenital heart disease?
cards.a: Oxygen saturation less than 90%, or less than 95% in both hand and foot on three measures, or a greater than 3% difference between hand and foot.

cards.q: Immediate medical management to maintain ductal patency in a newborn with a transposition of the great arteries?
cards.a: Intravenous Prostaglandin E1 (alprostadil) infusion.

cards.q: Absolute contraindication to the administration of Prostaglandin E1 in a cyanotic newborn?
cards.a: Total anomalous pulmonary venous return (TAPVR) with severe pulmonary venous obstruction.

cards.q: Primary life-threatening side effect of Prostaglandin E1 infusion requiring close monitoring?
cards.a: Apnea, often necessitating prophylactic endotracheal intubation.

cards.q: Definitive management strategy for a symptomatic congenital diaphragmatic hernia in the first 24 hours of life?
cards.a: Immediate endotracheal intubation and mechanical ventilation, avoiding bag-mask ventilation entirely.

cards.q: Why is bag-mask ventilation strictly contraindicated in congenital diaphragmatic hernia?
cards.a: It introduces air into the herniated gastrointestinal tract, causing further compression of the hypoplastic lungs.

cards.q: Preferred initial surgical timing for an uncomplicated isolated cleft lip repair?
cards.a: Around 10 to 12 weeks of life (adhering to the "rule of 10s": 10 weeks, 10 pounds, 10g hemoglobin).

cards.q: Preferred initial surgical timing for an uncomplicated isolated cleft palate repair?
cards.a: Between 9 and 18 months of age to optimize speech development while minimizing maxillary growth restriction.

cards.q: Immediate management step for an infant born with an exposed, ruptured omphalocele or gastroschisis?
cards.a: Cover the exposed bowel with sterile, warm, saline-soaked gauze and wrap it in a plastic bowel bag to prevent heat and fluid loss.

cards.q: First-line imaging study to evaluate a suspected developmental dysplasia of the hip (DDH) in an infant under 4 months of age?
cards.a: Hip ultrasonography, because the femoral head ossification center has not yet formed.

cards.q: First-line imaging study to evaluate suspected developmental dysplasia of the hip (DDH) in an infant over 4 to 6 months of age?
cards.a: Plain pelvic radiography (X-ray).

cards.q: Standard non-surgical treatment for a reducible developmental dysplasia of the hip diagnosed within the first 6 months of life?
cards.a: Dynamic splinting using a Pavlik harness.

cards.q: First-line diagnostic imaging test for a newborn who fails to pass meconium within the first 48 hours of life?
cards.a: Contrast enema to differentiate between Hirschsprung disease and meconium ileus.

cards.q: Classic contrast enema finding pathognomonic for Hirschsprung disease?
cards.a: A narrow distal rectosigmoid transition zone with a dilated proximal colon.

cards.q: Classic contrast enema finding pathognomonic for meconium ileus in cystic fibrosis?
cards.a: A microcolon containing multiple filling defects representing inspissated meconium plugs.

cards.q: Initial therapeutic intervention for a stable infant presenting with suspected malrotation and midgut volvulus?
cards.a: Emergent surgical laparotomy and a Ladd procedure.

cards.q: First-line imaging modality for suspected biliary atresia in a persistently jaundiced 3-week-old infant?
cards.a: Abdominal ultrasonography to assess for the presence of a gallbladder and the "triangular cord" sign.

cards.q: Definitive diagnostic test for confirming biliary atresia when ultrasound and hepatobiliary scintigraphy (HIDA) are inconclusive?
cards.a: Intraoperative cholangiogram.

cards.q: Surgical procedure that must be performed early to optimize survival in patients with biliary atresia?
cards.a: Kasai portoenterostomy, ideally performed before 60 days of age.

cards.q: Primary monitoring protocol required for an infant born with Beckwith-Wiedemann syndrome due to tumor risks?
cards.a: Abdominal ultrasound every 3 months until age 8 and serum $\alpha$-fetoprotein (AFP) every 3 months until age 4.

cards.q: Management step for an asymptomatic newborn found to have a single umbilical artery on umbilical cord inspection?
cards.a: Routine clinical monitoring, as isolated cases without other anomalies do not require further renal or cardiac imaging.

cards.q: Initial empirical management for an infant born with ambiguous genitalia while awaiting definitive genetic results?
cards.a: Strict avoidance of sex assignment, immediate checking of serum electrolytes to rule out congenital adrenal hyperplasia, and a karyotype.

cards.q: Life-threatening electrolyte imbalance to anticipate in a newborn with 21-hydroxylase deficiency congenital adrenal hyperplasia?
cards.a: Hyperkalemia and hyponatremia due to a severe salt-wasting crisis.
