cards.a: QRS is negative in BOTH lead I and aVF. Axis is between −90° and ±180°. Seen in ventricular rhythms or severe conduction disease.

cards.q: Name common causes of left axis deviation.
cards.a: Left anterior fascicular block (LAFB), inferior MI, LVH, WPW, ostium primum ASD, mechanical shift (obesity, pregnancy, ascites).

cards.q: Name common causes of right axis deviation.
cards.a: Right ventricular hypertrophy, PE, COPD/cor pulmonale, lateral MI, left posterior fascicular block (LPFB), ASD (secundum), normal in children.

cards.q: Define normal sinus rhythm.
cards.a: Upright P wave in II preceding every QRS, constant PR interval (0.12–0.20 s), rate 60–100 bpm, regular rhythm.

cards.q: Define sinus bradycardia.
cards.a: Normal sinus rhythm with a rate < 60 bpm. Causes: athletic conditioning, increased vagal tone, hypothyroidism, medications (beta-blockers).

cards.q: Define sinus tachycardia.
cards.a: Normal sinus rhythm with a rate > 100 bpm. Causes: exercise, pain, fever, anxiety, hypovolemia, hyperthyroidism, anemia.

cards.q: What is sinus arrhythmia?
cards.a: Normal variant where heart rate varies with respiration — increases during inspiration, decreases during expiration. Common in young, healthy individuals.

cards.q: What is a premature atrial contraction (PAC)?
cards.a: An early beat originating from an ectopic atrial focus. The P wave morphology differs from sinus P waves, followed by a normal (narrow) QRS. Usually benign.

cards.q: What is the ECG appearance of atrial flutter?
cards.a: Sawtooth flutter waves (F waves), best seen in leads II, III, aVF, and V1. Atrial rate is typically ~300 bpm with a ventricular response in ratios (2:1, 3:1, 4:1).

cards.q: What is the typical ventricular rate in untreated atrial flutter with 2:1 block?
cards.a: Atrial rate ~300 bpm ÷ 2 = ~150 bpm. Always consider atrial flutter when the ventricular rate is ~150 bpm.

cards.q: What are the hallmark ECG features of atrial fibrillation?
cards.a: Irregularly irregular rhythm, absence of organized P waves (replaced by fibrillatory baseline), and variable R-R intervals.

cards.q: What is multifocal atrial tachycardia (MAT)?
cards.a: An irregular rhythm with rate >100 bpm and ≥ 3 different P wave morphologies with varying PR and R-R intervals. Associated with severe COPD and lung disease.

cards.q: What is the definition of supraventricular tachycardia (SVT)?
cards.a: Any tachycardia originating above the ventricles. In common usage, refers to paroxysmal SVT (AVNRT or AVRT) with rate typically 150–250 bpm and narrow QRS.

cards.q: What is the most common type of SVT?
cards.a: AV nodal re-entrant tachycardia (AVNRT), accounting for ~60% of paroxysmal SVTs. Caused by a re-entry circuit within the AV node with dual pathways.

cards.q: How does AVRT differ from AVNRT?
cards.a: AVRT uses an accessory pathway (bypass tract) outside the AV node as one limb of the re-entry circuit (e.g., bundle of Kent in WPW), whereas AVNRT uses dual pathways within the AV node.

cards.q: What is Wolff-Parkinson-White (WPW) syndrome?
cards.a: A pre-excitation syndrome due to an accessory pathway (bundle of Kent). ECG triad: short PR interval (< 0.12 s), delta wave (slurred QRS upstroke), wide QRS.

cards.q: Why is giving AV nodal blockers (e.g., adenosine, verapamil) dangerous in WPW with atrial fibrillation?
cards.a: Blocking the AV node forces all conduction through the accessory pathway, which can conduct very rapidly and may precipitate ventricular fibrillation.

cards.q: What is a junctional escape rhythm?
cards.a: A rhythm arising from the AV junction when the SA node fails. Rate: 40–60 bpm. Narrow QRS; P waves may be absent, retrograde (inverted in II), or buried in QRS.

cards.q: What is an accelerated junctional rhythm?
cards.a: Junctional rhythm with rate 60–100 bpm, faster than the intrinsic junctional rate. Often seen with digoxin toxicity, post-cardiac surgery, or inferior MI.

cards.q: What are premature ventricular contractions (PVCs)?
cards.a: Early beats from a ventricular ectopic focus. Wide, bizarre QRS (≥ 0.12 s) without a preceding P wave, followed by a compensatory pause.

cards.q: What is the difference between unifocal and multifocal PVCs?
cards.a: Unifocal: all PVCs have the same morphology (single ectopic focus). Multifocal: PVCs have varying morphologies (multiple foci), indicating more serious underlying disease.

cards.q: What is ventricular tachycardia (VT)?
cards.a: ≥ 3 consecutive ventricular beats at a rate > 100 bpm. Wide QRS (≥ 0.12 s), regular rhythm. Sustained VT lasts > 30 seconds or causes hemodynamic instability.

cards.q: How do you differentiate monomorphic VT from polymorphic VT?
cards.a: Monomorphic: uniform QRS morphology — often from a stable re-entry circuit (scar). Polymorphic: changing QRS morphology — more unstable, may indicate ischemia or long QT.

cards.q: What is Torsades de Pointes?
cards.a: A form of polymorphic VT occurring in the setting of a prolonged QT interval. QRS complexes twist around the isoelectric line. Treatment: IV magnesium and correct QT prolongation.

cards.q: What is ventricular fibrillation (VF)?
cards.a: Chaotic, disorganized ventricular electrical activity with no identifiable QRS complexes. Produces no cardiac output — requires immediate defibrillation.

cards.q: What is the Brugada ECG pattern?
cards.a: ST elevation with a coved or saddle-back morphology in V1–V3 with an RBBB-like pattern. Associated with sudden cardiac death due to VF, especially in young Asian males.

cards.q: What defines first-degree AV block?
cards.a: PR interval > 0.20 s (> 5 small boxes), constant for every beat. All P waves are followed by QRS complexes. Usually benign.

cards.q: What defines second-degree AV block, Mobitz Type I (Wenckebach)?
cards.a: Progressive PR prolongation until a P wave is not conducted (dropped QRS), then the cycle resets. Block is at the AV node; usually benign.

cards.q: What defines second-degree AV block, Mobitz Type II?
cards.a: Constant PR interval with intermittent non-conducted P waves (sudden dropped QRS without prior PR prolongation). Block is infra-nodal (His-Purkinje); high risk of progression to complete heart block.

cards.q: What is third-degree (complete) AV block?
cards.a: Complete dissociation between atrial and ventricular activity. P waves and QRS complexes are independent. Ventricular rate depends on escape pacemaker: junctional (40–60) or ventricular (20–40).

cards.q: What are the ECG criteria for right bundle branch block (RBBB)?
cards.a: QRS ≥ 0.12 s, RSR' ('M-shaped') in V1–V2, and wide, slurred S wave in I and V6. Mnemonic: 'MaRRoW' — M in V1 (R), W in V6.

cards.q: What are the ECG criteria for left bundle branch block (LBBB)?
cards.a: QRS ≥ 0.12 s, broad, notched R wave in I, aVL, V5–V6, and deep S wave (or QS) in V1–V2. Mnemonic: 'WiLLiaM' — W in V1, M in V6.

cards.q: Why does LBBB make ST/T wave interpretation unreliable?
cards.a: LBBB causes secondary repolarization abnormalities — ST segments and T waves deviate opposite to the major QRS deflection ('appropriate discordance'), masking ischemic changes.

cards.q: What are the Sgarbossa criteria?
cards.a: Criteria to diagnose acute MI in the presence of LBBB: (1) ST elevation ≥ 1 mm concordant with QRS, (2) ST depression ≥ 1 mm in V1–V3, (3) ST elevation ≥ 5 mm discordant with QRS (least specific).

cards.q: What is left anterior fascicular block (LAFB)?
cards.a: Left axis deviation (−45° to −90°), small Q in I/aVL, small R in II/III/aVF, QRS < 0.12 s. The most common fascicular block.

cards.q: What is left posterior fascicular block (LPFB)?
cards.a: Right axis deviation (> +90°), small R in I/aVL, small Q in II/III/aVF, QRS < 0.12 s. Must exclude other causes of RAD (RVH, PE, etc.).

cards.q: What is a bifascicular block?
cards.a: RBBB + LAFB (most common) or RBBB + LPFB. Indicates disease in two of three fascicles. Risk of progression to complete heart block.

cards.q: What is a trifascicular block?
cards.a: Bifascicular block + first-degree AV block (prolonged PR), suggesting disease in all three fascicles. However, true trifascicular block = complete heart block.

cards.q: What are the ECG voltage criteria for left ventricular hypertrophy (LVH)?
cards.a: Sokolow-Lyon: S in V1 + R in V5 or V6 ≥ 35 mm. Cornell: R in aVL + S in V3 > 28 mm (men) or > 20 mm (women).

cards.q: What is the LVH 'strain' pattern?
cards.a: ST depression and T wave inversion in lateral leads (I, aVL, V5–V6) — asymmetric T inversion with a gradual downslope and rapid return. Indicates pressure overload.

cards.q: What are the ECG criteria for right ventricular hypertrophy (RVH)?
cards.a: Right axis deviation, tall R wave in V1 (R > S), deep S in V5–V6, right atrial enlargement, and possible RV strain pattern (ST depression/T inversion in V1–V3).

cards.q: What ECG findings suggest right atrial enlargement (P pulmonale)?
cards.a: Tall, peaked P waves (> 2.5 mm) in lead II. Associated with COPD, pulmonary hypertension, and right-sided heart disease.

cards.q: What ECG findings suggest left atrial enlargement (P mitrale)?
cards.a: Wide, notched (bifid) P wave in lead II (> 0.12 s) and/or deep negative terminal deflection of P wave in V1 (> 1 mm deep, > 1 small box wide).

cards.q: What ECG change indicates subendocardial ischemia?
cards.a: ST segment depression (horizontal or downsloping ≥ 1 mm) in the affected leads. Also seen in demand ischemia, digoxin effect, and LVH strain.

cards.q: What ECG change indicates transmural (full-thickness) ischemia or injury?
cards.a: ST segment elevation ≥ 1 mm in limb leads or ≥ 2 mm in precordial leads in ≥ 2 contiguous leads.

cards.q: What do pathological Q waves indicate?
cards.a: Myocardial necrosis/prior infarction. Defined as Q waves > 0.04 s wide and/or > 1/3 the height of the R wave in that lead.

cards.q: What is the typical ECG evolution of an acute STEMI?
cards.a: Hyperacute T waves → ST elevation → Q wave development → T wave inversion → ST normalization. Q waves usually persist; T waves may normalize over weeks–months.

cards.q: What are hyperacute T waves?
cards.a: Tall, broad, peaked, symmetric T waves — the earliest sign of acute MI, appearing within minutes of coronary occlusion, before ST elevation.

cards.q: What are reciprocal changes in the context of STEMI?
cards.a: ST depression in leads opposite the infarcting territory. E.g., inferior STEMI (II, III, aVF) shows reciprocal ST depression in I and aVL. Supports the diagnosis of acute MI.

cards.q: Which coronary artery supplies the anterior wall and what leads show anterior STEMI?
cards.a: Left anterior descending (LAD) artery. ST elevation in V1–V4 (may extend to V5–V6 in extensive anterior MI).

cards.q: Which coronary artery supplies the inferior wall and what leads show inferior STEMI?
cards.a: Usually the right coronary artery (RCA) (~85%) or left circumflex (LCx). ST elevation in II, III, aVF.

cards.q: Which coronary artery supplies the lateral wall?
cards.a: Left circumflex artery (LCx) or diagonal branches of LAD. Changes in I, aVL, V5–V6.

cards.q: How is a posterior MI diagnosed on a standard 12-lead ECG?
cards.a: ST depression and tall R waves in V1–V3 (mirror image of posterior ST elevation). Confirmed by ST elevation in posterior leads V7–V9.

cards.q: How is right ventricular MI diagnosed?
cards.a: Suspect in inferior STEMI. Obtain right-sided leads — ST elevation ≥ 1 mm in V4R is the most sensitive indicator of RV infarction.

cards.q: What is the difference between STEMI and NSTEMI?
cards.a: STEMI: complete coronary occlusion → ST elevation → emergent reperfusion. NSTEMI: partial occlusion → ST depression/T wave inversion + elevated troponins → medical management ± intervention.

cards.q: What is Wellens' syndrome?
cards.a: A pattern of deep, symmetric T wave inversions (Type A, biphasic in V2–V3) or deeply inverted T waves (Type B) in V2–V3, indicating a critical LAD stenosis. High risk for anterior MI.

cards.q: What is de Winter's ECG pattern?
cards.a: Upsloping ST depression at the J-point in V1–V6 with tall, symmetric T waves — an LAD occlusion equivalent that does not show classic ST elevation. Treat as a STEMI equivalent.

cards.q: What ECG changes are seen in hyperkalemia (progressive)?
cards.a: Mild (5.5–6.5): peaked, narrow T waves. Moderate (6.5–8.0): prolonged PR, flattened P waves, widened QRS. Severe (> 8.0): sine wave pattern → VF/asystole.

cards.q: What ECG changes are seen in hypokalemia?
cards.a: Flattened T waves, ST depression, prominent U waves, prolonged QU interval. Severe hypokalemia can cause atrial/ventricular arrhythmias and T-U wave fusion.

cards.q: What ECG changes are seen in hypercalcemia?
cards.a: Shortened QT interval (due to shortened ST segment). Severe hypercalcemia may cause Osborn waves and arrhythmias.

cards.q: What ECG changes are seen in hypocalcemia?
cards.a: Prolonged QT interval (due to prolonged ST segment). Risk of torsades de pointes.

cards.q: What ECG changes suggest hypomagnesemia?
cards.a: Similar to hypokalemia: prolonged QT, flattened T waves, prominent U waves. Predisposes to torsades de pointes and refractory hypokalemia.

cards.q: What is the classic ECG appearance of digoxin effect (therapeutic)?
cards.a: 'Salvador Dalí mustache' — downsloping ST depression ('reverse tick' or 'scooped' ST), T wave flattening/inversion, shortened QT, and possible prominent U waves.

cards.q: What arrhythmias suggest digoxin toxicity?
cards.a: Atrial tachycardia with AV block (PAT with block) is classic. Also: accelerated junctional rhythm, bidirectional VT, frequent PVCs, any bradyarrhythmia.

cards.q: How do beta-blockers affect the ECG?
cards.a: Sinus bradycardia, prolonged PR interval, and possible AV conduction delay. They slow SA and AV nodal conduction.

cards.q: How do calcium channel blockers (non-dihydropyridine) affect the ECG?
cards.a: Verapamil and diltiazem slow AV conduction → bradycardia, prolonged PR interval. May unmask or worsen AV block.

cards.q: What ECG effects do Class IA antiarrhythmics (e.g., quinidine, procainamide) have?
cards.a: Prolonged QRS and QT intervals. QRS widening from Na-channel blockade; QT prolongation from K-channel blockade. Risk of torsades de pointes.

cards.q: What ECG effects do Class IC antiarrhythmics (e.g., flecainide, propafenone) have?
cards.a: Marked QRS widening with minimal effect on QT. Potent Na-channel blockers. Contraindicated in structural heart disease (increased mortality — CAST trial).

cards.q: What ECG effects does amiodarone (Class III) have?
cards.a: Prolonged QT interval, sinus bradycardia, and diffuse T wave changes. Despite QT prolongation, torsades risk is relatively low compared to other Class III agents.

cards.q: What are the ECG findings in acute pericarditis?
cards.a: Stage 1: Diffuse concave-up ST elevation + PR depression (except aVR: ST depression + PR elevation). Stage 2: ST normalization. Stage 3: Diffuse T inversion. Stage 4: Normalization.

cards.q: How do you differentiate pericarditis ST elevation from STEMI?
cards.a: Pericarditis: diffuse ST elevation, concave-up, PR depression, no reciprocal changes, no Q waves. STEMI: regional ST elevation, convex-up, reciprocal changes present.

cards.q: What is the classic ECG finding in pulmonary embolism?
cards.a: S1Q3T3 (deep S in I, Q wave in III, inverted T in III). Also: sinus tachycardia (most common), right axis deviation, RBBB pattern, T wave inversions in V1–V4.

cards.q: What is the most common ECG finding in PE?
cards.a: Sinus tachycardia. The S1Q3T3 pattern is classic but present in only ~20% of PE cases.

cards.q: What is early repolarization (benign) on ECG?
cards.a: J-point elevation with concave-up ST elevation, often with a notch or slur at the J-point, most prominent in V2–V5. Typically in young, healthy individuals.

cards.q: What ECG findings define Long QT syndrome?
cards.a: QTc > 0.47 s (men) or > 0.48 s (women) with risk of torsades de pointes. Causes: congenital (channelopathies) or acquired (drugs, electrolytes).

cards.q: Name 5 common drugs that prolong the QT interval.
cards.a: Sotalol, amiodarone, quinidine, haloperidol, erythromycin/azithromycin. Also: methadone, ondansetron, certain fluoroquinolones, TCAs.

cards.q: What is a pacemaker spike on ECG?
cards.a: A sharp vertical deflection (spike) immediately before the paced chamber's complex. Atrial pacing → spike before P wave. Ventricular pacing → spike before wide QRS.

cards.q: What does a VVI pacemaker do?
cards.a: Paces the Ventricle, senses the Ventricle, and is Inhibited by sensed ventricular activity. Single-chamber ventricular demand pacing.

cards.q: What does a DDD pacemaker do?
cards.a: Paces both atria and ventricles (Dual), senses both chambers (Dual), and can be triggered or inhibited (Dual response). Maintains AV synchrony.

cards.q: How does a paced ventricular beat appear on ECG?
cards.a: Pacemaker spike followed by a wide QRS complex (≥ 0.12 s) with morphology similar to LBBB (if RV apex pacing) because the RV is activated first.

cards.q: What is failure to capture in a pacemaker?
cards.a: Pacemaker spikes present but NOT followed by a P wave or QRS complex. The electrical stimulus is not depolarizing myocardium — may indicate lead dislodgement or elevated threshold.

cards.q: What is failure to sense (undersensing)?
cards.a: Pacemaker fires despite intrinsic cardiac activity — pacing spikes appear at inappropriate times. The device fails to detect native beats.

cards.q: What is electrical alternans and what does it suggest?
cards.a: Alternating amplitude of QRS complexes beat to beat. Classic for large pericardial effusion/cardiac tamponade (heart swinging in fluid).

cards.q: What is the normal QRS axis in neonates?
cards.a: +90° to +180° (right axis deviation), reflecting RV dominance in utero. The axis shifts leftward over the first months of life.

cards.q: Name 3 key differences in a pediatric ECG compared to an adult.
cards.a: (1) Right axis deviation and RV dominance (normal in neonates), (2) T wave inversions in V1–V3 (normal juvenile pattern up to age ~16), (3) Higher heart rates (newborn: 110–160 bpm).

cards.q: At what age does the ECG typically transition from RV dominant to LV dominant pattern?
cards.a: By approximately 6 months of age, the R/S ratio in V1 begins to decrease and the adult LV-dominant pattern establishes by 3–8 years.

cards.q: What is the J-point on the ECG?
cards.a: The junction between the end of the QRS complex and the beginning of the ST segment. Its position relative to the baseline is used to assess ST elevation or depression.

cards.q: What are Osborn waves (J waves)?
cards.a: Positive deflections at the J-point, creating a 'camel hump' appearance. Classically associated with hypothermia. Also seen in hypercalcemia and some normal variants.

cards.q: What is R wave progression and what does poor R wave progression indicate?
cards.a: Normally, R waves increase in amplitude from V1 to V5 (the transition zone is at V3–V4). Poor R wave progression: R wave remains small through V3–V4; causes include prior anterior MI, LVH, LBBB, and COPD.

cards.q: What is the significance of T wave inversions in V1–V4 in an adult?
cards.a: In adults, T wave inversions in V1–V4 are abnormal and may indicate RV strain (PE), anterior ischemia, Wellens' syndrome, HCM, or arrhythmogenic RV cardiomyopathy (ARVC).

cards.q: How is QRS duration measured and what does a widened QRS signify?
cards.a: Measured from onset of Q (or R) to end of S wave. QRS ≥ 0.12 s = wide, suggesting bundle branch block, ventricular pacing, ventricular ectopy, or pre-excitation (WPW).

cards.q: What is the differential diagnosis for a regular, narrow-complex tachycardia?
cards.a: Sinus tachycardia, AVNRT, AVRT (orthodromic), atrial flutter (with fixed block), atrial tachycardia. Rate and P wave morphology/location help distinguish.

cards.q: What is the differential diagnosis for a regular, wide-complex tachycardia?
cards.a: Ventricular tachycardia (most common), SVT with aberrant conduction (BBB), SVT with pre-excitation (antidromic AVRT), paced rhythm. If uncertain, treat as VT.

cards.q: What is the Brugada criteria for differentiating VT from SVT with aberrancy?
cards.a: If any step is 'yes' → VT: (1) No RS complex in any precordial lead? (2) RS interval > 100 ms? (3) AV dissociation? (4) Morphology criteria for VT in V1–V2 and V6?

cards.q: What ECG finding confirms AV dissociation?
cards.a: P waves marching through at a different rate than QRS complexes, with capture beats and/or fusion beats. Strongly supports a diagnosis of VT.

cards.q: What is a capture beat?
cards.a: During VT, a normal narrow QRS that occurs when a sinus impulse 'captures' the ventricles through the normal conduction system. Proves AV dissociation → confirms VT.

cards.q: What is a fusion beat?
cards.a: A QRS complex of intermediate morphology between a sinus beat and a ventricular beat, occurring when supraventricular and ventricular impulses activate the ventricles simultaneously. Supports VT.

cards.q: What initial intervention is used to diagnose and potentially terminate SVT?
cards.a: Vagal maneuvers (carotid sinus massage, Valsalva, cold water face immersion) followed by adenosine (6 mg IV push, then 12 mg). These transiently block AV conduction.

cards.q: How does adenosine help differentiate tachyarrhythmias?
cards.a: Adenosine blocks AV conduction transiently: it terminates AVNRT/AVRT, slows the ventricular rate to unmask atrial flutter/tachycardia, and has no effect on VT.

cards.q: What is Ashman phenomenon?
cards.a: An aberrantly conducted beat (wide QRS, usually RBBB morphology) that follows a long-short R-R cycle in atrial fibrillation. The long cycle prolongs the refractory period, causing aberrant conduction of the subsequent short cycle.

cards.q: What ECG pattern is seen in Takotsubo (stress) cardiomyopathy?
cards.a: ST elevation (often anterior leads), T wave inversions, and QT prolongation, mimicking acute anterior MI. Coronaries are normal. Triggered by emotional/physical stress.

cards.q: What is the ECG pattern in hyperkalemia-induced sinoventricular rhythm?
cards.a: Severe hyperkalemia eliminates P waves while QRS remains (widened). The rhythm appears as regularized wide-complex rhythm without P waves — the SA node still fires but the signal bypasses the atria.

cards.q: What is the significance of ST elevation in aVR?
cards.a: ST elevation in aVR with diffuse ST depression suggests left main or severe multi-vessel coronary disease, or diffuse subendocardial ischemia. Also seen in some poisonings (e.g., TCA overdose).

cards.q: How does tricyclic antidepressant (TCA) overdose appear on ECG?
cards.a: Sinus tachycardia, prolonged QRS (> 100 ms), prolonged QT, right axis deviation of the terminal 40 ms of QRS, R wave > 3 mm in aVR. A QRS > 100 ms predicts seizures; > 160 ms predicts arrhythmias.

cards.q: What is epsilon wave and what condition is it associated with?
cards.a: A small positive deflection between the end of QRS and onset of T wave in V1–V2. Pathognomonic for arrhythmogenic right ventricular cardiomyopathy (ARVC).

cards.q: What is the normal R/S ratio progression across precordial leads?
cards.a: R wave amplitude increases and S wave decreases from V1 to V6. The transition zone (R = S) is normally at V3–V4.

cards.q: What is the clinical significance of a new LBBB in a patient with chest pain?
cards.a: A new LBBB in the setting of ischemic symptoms is treated as a STEMI equivalent and warrants emergent reperfusion therapy per ACC/AHA guidelines.

cards.q: What is low voltage on ECG and what are its causes?
cards.a: QRS amplitude < 5 mm in all limb leads or < 10 mm in all precordial leads. Causes: pericardial effusion, obesity, COPD/emphysema, hypothyroidism, infiltrative cardiomyopathy (amyloid).

cards.q: How do you identify an electrode/lead misplacement on ECG?
cards.a: Suspect if: inverted P and QRS in lead I (right-left arm reversal), globally inverted complexes, or unexpected R wave regression. Right arm–left arm swap produces an inverted lead I.

cards.q: In a PA (posteroanterior) chest X-ray, where does the X-ray beam enter and exit the patient?
cards.a: The beam enters through the posterior chest wall and exits through the anterior chest wall onto the film/detector. This minimises cardiac magnification because the heart sits anteriorly, closer to the detector.

cards.q: In an AP (anteroposterior) chest X-ray, why does the heart appear magnified?
cards.a: The beam enters anteriorly and the heart — an anterior structure — is farther from the detector (behind the patient). Objects farther from the detector are magnified more, making the cardiac silhouette appear falsely enlarged.

cards.q: What is the standard distance between the X-ray tube and the film in a PA chest X-ray?
cards.a: 6 feet (1.8 m / 180 cm). This long source-to-image distance reduces magnification and geometric distortion.

cards.q: How do you assess whether a CXR is adequately exposed (penetration)?
cards.a: On a well-penetrated film you should just be able to see the thoracic vertebral bodies through the cardiac shadow. Over-penetrated films appear too dark; under-penetrated films appear too white.

cards.q: How do you assess rotation on a PA chest X-ray?
cards.a: The medial ends of both clavicles should be equidistant from the spinous process of the vertebra at that level. Unequal distances indicate rotation.

cards.q: What does the mnemonic ABCDEFGHI stand for in a systematic CXR review?
cards.a:
A – Airway/AP or PA
B – Bones & soft tissues
C – Cardiac silhouette
D – Diaphragm
E – Effusions / Edges (costophrenic angles)
F – Fields (lung fields)
G – Gastric bubble
H – Hilum
I – Instruments/devices

cards.q: What is the 'RIPE' mnemonic used for in CXR interpretation?
cards.a:
R – Rotation
I – Inspiration
P – Penetration (exposure)
E – Exposure (or Equipment position)
It is used to assess technical adequacy before interpreting findings.

cards.q: How do you assess adequate inspiration on a PA chest X-ray?
cards.a: Count the posterior ribs visible above the diaphragm. Adequate inspiration shows 5–7 anterior ribs or 9–10 posterior ribs above the right hemidiaphragm.

cards.q: What is the main advantage of a lateral CXR?
cards.a: It helps localise lesions to a specific lobe, visualise structures hidden by the heart and diaphragm on the PA view, and assess the retrosternal and retrocardiac spaces.

cards.q: On a lateral CXR, which hemidiaphragm is typically higher and how do you tell them apart?
cards.a: The right hemidiaphragm is usually higher. The left hemidiaphragm is identified by the gastric air bubble beneath it and loses its silhouette where it contacts the heart.

cards.q: Where is the carina located on a normal PA CXR and what is its significance?
cards.a: The carina (bifurcation of the trachea) is at approximately T4–T5 level (or the level of the aortic arch). A widened carinal angle (>100°) may suggest left atrial enlargement or subcarinal lymphadenopathy.

cards.q: What structures form the right heart border on a PA CXR?
cards.a: From top to bottom: SVC (upper portion) and right atrium (lower convex portion).

cards.q: What structures form the left heart border on a PA CXR?
cards.a: From top to bottom: aortic knob (knuckle), pulmonary trunk (main pulmonary artery), left atrial appendage, and left ventricle.

cards.q: What is the hilum of the lung and what does it contain?
cards.a: The hilum is the root of the lung containing the pulmonary arteries, pulmonary veins, main bronchi, lymph nodes, and bronchial vessels. The left hilum is normally slightly higher than the right.

cards.q: What are the normal costophrenic angles and what does blunting indicate?
cards.a: Normal costophrenic angles are sharp and acute. Blunting suggests a pleural effusion (≥200–300 mL of fluid on an upright PA film).

cards.q: Where are the lung fissures located and which lobes do they separate?
cards.a:
Right lung: Oblique (major) fissure separates upper/middle from lower lobe; Horizontal (minor) fissure separates upper from middle lobe.
Left lung: Only an oblique fissure separating upper from lower lobe.

cards.q: What is the normal tracheal position on a PA CXR?
cards.a: The trachea should be midline or slightly deviated to the right at the level of the aortic arch. Significant deviation suggests a mass, collapse, or tension pneumothorax.

cards.q: What is the aortic knob (knuckle) on a PA CXR?
cards.a: It is the prominence of the aortic arch seen on the left mediastinal border. It becomes prominent and unfolded in elderly patients and hypertension.

cards.q: Which structures form the anterior, middle, and posterior mediastinum?
cards.a:
Anterior: thymus, fat, lymph nodes, internal mammary vessels.
Middle: heart, great vessels, trachea, main bronchi, lymph nodes.
Posterior: descending aorta, oesophagus, thoracic vertebrae, sympathetic chain.

cards.q: Where is the right hemidiaphragm normally located relative to the left?
cards.a: The right hemidiaphragm is normally 1–3 cm higher than the left, due to the underlying liver.

cards.q: What is the cardiothoracic ratio (CTR) and what is considered normal?
cards.a: CTR = maximum transverse cardiac diameter ÷ maximum internal thoracic diameter. Normal is ≤0.5 (50%) on a PA film. A CTR >0.5 suggests cardiomegaly.

cards.q: Why is the CTR unreliable on an AP chest X-ray?
cards.a: The AP projection magnifies the heart because it is farther from the detector. This can falsely increase the CTR, making the heart appear enlarged when it may be normal.

cards.q: How does left atrial (LA) enlargement appear on a PA CXR?
cards.a: Signs include: double density sign (right heart border), splaying of the carina (subcarinal angle >100°), straightening/convexity of the left heart border (prominent LA appendage), and elevation of the left main bronchus.

cards.q: How does left ventricular (LV) enlargement appear on a CXR?
cards.a: The cardiac apex is displaced downward and to the left, extending below the diaphragm. The heart appears boot-shaped in some contexts, and the CTR is increased.

cards.q: How does right ventricular (RV) enlargement appear on CXR?
cards.a: The heart enlarges anteriorly (best seen on lateral CXR as filling of the retrosternal space). On PA, the left heart border may be elevated (upturned apex) and the heart appears globular.

cards.q: How does right atrial (RA) enlargement appear on a PA CXR?
cards.a: The right heart border extends further to the right than normal (>1/3 of the right hemithorax from midline).

cards.q: What is the classic CXR appearance of a pericardial effusion?
cards.a: A globular (flask-shaped / water-bottle) heart silhouette with sharp cardiac margins and clear lung fields. Rapid accumulation may show little change in overall size but still cause tamponade.

cards.q: What congenital heart defect produces a 'boot-shaped' heart (coeur en sabot) on CXR?
cards.a: Tetralogy of Fallot. The upturned apex is due to right ventricular hypertrophy, and the concave pulmonary artery segment causes the boot shape. Lung fields are oligaemic (decreased pulmonary vascularity).

cards.q: What congenital heart defect produces an 'egg-on-a-string' appearance on CXR?
cards.a: Transposition of the Great Arteries (TGA). The narrow superior mediastinum (the 'string') results from the anteroposterior relationship of the great arteries, and the egg is the enlarged globular heart.

cards.q: What CXR findings suggest congestive heart failure (CHF)?
cards.a: Mnemonic ABCDE: Alveolar oedema (bat-wing/butterfly pattern), B lines (Kerley B lines), Cardiomegaly, Diversion of upper lobe pulmonary vessels (cephalization), Effusions (pleural). Also peribronchial cuffing.

cards.q: What is consolidation on a CXR and what causes it?
cards.a: Consolidation is opacification of the airspaces with preservation of lung volume. The alveoli are filled with fluid, pus, blood, or cells instead of air. Common causes include pneumonia, haemorrhage, and pulmonary oedema.

cards.q: What is an air bronchogram and what does it indicate?
cards.a: An air bronchogram is air-filled bronchi visible within surrounding opacified (consolidated) lung parenchyma. It indicates the opacification is in the lung parenchyma (not pleural) and that the airway is patent.

cards.q: What is ground-glass opacity (GGO) on CXR/CT?
cards.a: GGO is a hazy increase in lung density through which bronchial and vascular markings are still visible. It suggests partial filling of airspaces. Causes include viral pneumonia, early ARDS, pulmonary haemorrhage, and hypersensitivity pneumonitis.

cards.q: What are the types of atelectasis?
cards.a:
Resorptive (obstructive): airway obstruction (mucus plug, tumour).
Compressive: space-occupying lesion compresses lung (effusion, pneumothorax).
Cicatrisation (contraction): fibrosis/scarring.
Adhesive: surfactant deficiency (e.g., ARDS, RDS).
Relaxation/passive: loss of contact between visceral and parietal pleura.

cards.q: What CXR signs suggest atelectasis (lung collapse)?
cards.a: Direct signs: displacement of fissures, increased opacity. Indirect signs: tracheal/mediastinal shift toward the collapse, ipsilateral hemidiaphragm elevation, compensatory hyperinflation of adjacent lobes, hilar displacement.

cards.q: What are Kerley B lines and what do they signify?
cards.a: Kerley B lines are short (1–2 cm), thin horizontal lines perpendicular to the pleural surface at the lung bases. They represent thickened interlobular septa, most commonly seen in pulmonary oedema/CHF, lymphangitic carcinomatosis.

cards.q: What is honeycombing on CXR/CT and what does it indicate?
cards.a: Honeycombing is a pattern of clustered thick-walled cystic airspaces (3–10 mm) typically at the lung periphery and bases. It represents end-stage pulmonary fibrosis (e.g., usual interstitial pneumonia / IPF) and is irreversible.

cards.q: What is the 'tree-in-bud' pattern on CT?
cards.a: Tree-in-bud describes centrilobular branching nodular opacities resembling a budding tree. It indicates impaction of bronchioles with mucus, pus, or fluid — seen in infectious bronchiolitis, endobronchial TB, and aspiration.

cards.q: What is a cavitary lung lesion and what are its common causes?
cards.a: A cavity is a gas-filled space within a pulmonary opacity, mass, or nodule. Common causes (mnemonic CAVITY): Cancer (squamous cell), Autoimmune (Wegener's/GPA), Vascular (pulmonary infarct), Infection (TB, abscess, fungal), Trauma, Youth (congenital).

cards.q: What is the silhouette sign and how is it used?
cards.a: When two structures of similar density are in contact, their interface (border) is lost. For example, right middle lobe consolidation silhouettes the right heart border; lingular disease silhouettes the left heart border. This helps localise disease.

cards.q: What is the difference between a reticular and a nodular lung pattern on CXR?
cards.a:
Reticular: network of lines/interstitial thickening (fibrosis, lymphangitic spread).
Nodular: discrete round opacities (metastases, miliary TB, sarcoidosis).
Reticulonodular: combination of both.

cards.q: What does 'air-space opacification' versus 'interstitial pattern' mean on CXR?
cards.a:
Air-space (alveolar): fluffy, confluent opacities with air bronchograms — represents alveolar filling (pneumonia, oedema, haemorrhage).
Interstitial: reticular, nodular, or reticulonodular patterns — represents disease of the lung scaffolding (fibrosis, lymphangitic carcinomatosis).

cards.q: How does a pleural effusion appear on an upright PA CXR?
cards.a: A homogeneous opacity at the lung base with a concave upward meniscus that is higher laterally than medially. Small effusions first blunt the costophrenic angle.

cards.q: How much fluid is needed to produce costophrenic angle blunting on an upright PA CXR?
cards.a: Approximately 200–300 mL. A lateral decubitus film can detect as little as 50–100 mL.

cards.q: What is a subpulmonic effusion and how is it identified?
cards.a: Fluid collects between the lung base and the diaphragm without spilling into the costophrenic angle. It mimics an elevated hemidiaphragm. Clue: the apparent dome of the diaphragm is laterally peaked. A lateral decubitus film confirms it.

cards.q: What is the difference between a simple and a tension pneumothorax on CXR?
cards.a:
Simple: visible visceral pleural line with absent lung markings peripherally; no mediastinal shift.
Tension: same plus mediastinal shift away from the affected side, ipsilateral diaphragm depression, and contralateral lung compression. Tension pneumothorax is a clinical diagnosis treated before CXR.

cards.q: What CXR finding is pathognomonic for pneumothorax?
cards.a: A visible visceral pleural edge (thin white line) with no lung markings peripheral to it. On a supine film, the 'deep sulcus sign' (abnormally deep, lucent costophrenic angle) may be the only clue.

cards.q: What is the deep sulcus sign?
cards.a: An abnormally deep and lucent costophrenic angle seen on a supine CXR. It indicates a pneumothorax — free air rises to the most anterior and inferior part of the thorax in the supine position.

cards.q: What is pleural thickening and what are its causes?
cards.a: Diffuse or focal thickening of the pleura seen as blunting or soft tissue density along the chest wall. Causes include prior infection (TB, empyema), asbestos exposure (pleural plaques), haemothorax, and mesothelioma.

cards.q: How do you differentiate a pleural effusion from consolidation on CXR?
cards.a:
Effusion: meniscus sign, no air bronchograms, shifts with position change (decubitus film).
Consolidation: air bronchograms present, no meniscus, does not shift with position, may have silhouette sign with adjacent structures.

cards.q: What is a widened mediastinum and what are its causes?
cards.a: Mediastinal width >8 cm on PA CXR (measured at the level of the aortic knob). Causes: aortic dissection/rupture, lymphadenopathy, mediastinal mass, tortuous aorta, and mediastinal haematoma (trauma).

cards.q: What is the '4 T's' mnemonic for anterior mediastinal masses?
cards.a:
Thymoma (and thymic cysts/carcinoma)
Teratoma (and other germ cell tumours)
Terrible lymphoma (Hodgkin's & non-Hodgkin's)
Thyroid (retrosternal goitre)

cards.q: What are common causes of a middle mediastinal mass?
cards.a: Lymphadenopathy (sarcoidosis, lymphoma, metastases), bronchogenic cyst, vascular abnormalities (aortic aneurysm, anomalous vessels), and oesophageal lesions.

cards.q: What are common causes of a posterior mediastinal mass?
cards.a: Neurogenic tumours (schwannoma, neurofibroma, neuroblastoma), descending aortic aneurysm, vertebral body lesions, paravertebral abscess, lateral thoracic meningocele, and extramedullary haematopoiesis.

cards.q: What is pneumomediastinum and how does it appear on CXR?
cards.a: Free air within the mediastinum. CXR shows lucent streaks outlining mediastinal structures, especially along the left heart border or around the aorta. It may dissect into the neck (subcutaneous emphysema). Causes include oesophageal rupture (Boerhaave), alveolar rupture, and airway trauma.

cards.q: What CXR finding is classically associated with sarcoidosis?
cards.a: Bilateral hilar lymphadenopathy (BHL), often symmetric ('lambda sign' or 'Garland triad'). Stage classification: I = BHL alone; II = BHL + pulmonary infiltrates; III = infiltrates without BHL; IV = pulmonary fibrosis.

cards.q: What is the 1-2-3 sign (Garland triad) on CXR?
cards.a: Seen in sarcoidosis: enlargement of (1) right paratracheal, (2) right hilar, and (3) left hilar lymph nodes, producing a characteristic triad of opacities.

cards.q: How does bilateral hilar lymphadenopathy (BHL) differ from prominent pulmonary arteries on CXR?
cards.a:
BHL: lobulated, dense hilar shadows that are NOT pulsatile on fluoroscopy and do not taper smoothly.
Prominent pulmonary arteries: smooth, vascular-density shadows that taper normally, pulsatile on fluoroscopy, seen in pulmonary hypertension.

cards.q: What conditions cause tracheal deviation toward the affected side?
cards.a: Conditions that cause volume loss on that side: lobar collapse/atelectasis, pneumonectomy, fibrosis. The trachea is 'pulled' toward the pathology.

cards.q: What conditions cause tracheal deviation away from the affected side?
cards.a: Conditions that cause increased volume or pressure: tension pneumothorax, large pleural effusion, large mass. The trachea is 'pushed' away.

cards.q: What is the most common site for an aspirated foreign body to lodge and why?
cards.a: The right main bronchus, because it is wider, shorter, and more vertical than the left main bronchus. In children, it may lodge in either side due to equal bronchial angles.

cards.q: What CXR findings suggest a radiolucent (non-opaque) foreign body aspiration?
cards.a: Direct visualisation is impossible. Indirect signs include: unilateral hyperinflation (air trapping), mediastinal shift away from the affected side on expiration, and recurrent pneumonia in the same location.

cards.q: What is the ideal position of an endotracheal tube (ETT) tip on CXR?
cards.a: The ETT tip should be 3–5 cm above the carina (approximately at the T2–T4 level) with the head in neutral position. If too low, it commonly enters the right main bronchus.

cards.q: How do you systematically assess bones on a CXR?
cards.a: Examine ribs (count, symmetry, fractures), clavicles, scapulae, thoracic spine (vertebral body height, alignment), and humeral heads. Look for lytic/blastic lesions, fractures, and dislocations.

cards.q: How do lytic bone lesions appear on X-ray and what are common causes?
cards.a: Lytic lesions appear as areas of decreased bone density (dark holes). Common causes: metastases (renal, thyroid, lung, breast), multiple myeloma, infection (osteomyelitis).

cards.q: How do blastic (sclerotic) bone lesions appear on X-ray and what are common causes?
cards.a: Blastic lesions appear as areas of increased bone density (white/bright). Common causes: prostate metastases, breast metastases (can be lytic or blastic), Paget's disease, lymphoma. Mnemonic for blastic mets: Pb LEMON — Prostate, breast, Lymphoma, mEdulloblastoma, Meningioma, Osteosarcoma, Neuroblastoma.

cards.q: What rib findings on CXR suggest non-accidental injury (child abuse)?
cards.a: Posterior rib fractures of different ages (varying stages of healing), fractures at the costochondral junctions ('bucket-handle' or 'corner' fractures), and multiple bilateral fractures.

cards.q: What is a vertebral compression fracture and how does it appear on CXR?
cards.a: Loss of vertebral body height, appearing as a wedge-shaped or flattened vertebral body. Most common in osteoporosis (especially postmenopausal women) and metastatic disease. Look for >20% height loss compared to adjacent vertebra.

cards.q: Where should the tip of a central venous catheter (CVC) ideally lie on CXR?
cards.a: The tip should lie at the junction of the SVC and right atrium (approximately at the level of the carina or just below). Tip in the right atrium risks arrhythmias; too high risks inaccurate CVP readings.

cards.q: Where should the tip of a nasogastric (NG) tube lie on CXR?
cards.a: The NG tube should follow the oesophagus midline, cross the diaphragm, and the tip should be visible below the left hemidiaphragm in the stomach (at least 10 cm beyond the gastro-oesophageal junction). Ensure it does not coil in the oesophagus or enter a bronchus.

cards.q: What is the danger of a malpositioned NG tube and how is it detected on CXR?
cards.a: If the tube enters the tracheobronchial tree, feeding or medication administration can cause aspiration pneumonia, pneumothorax, or death. CXR shows the tube deviating toward a bronchus rather than following the oesophagus midline.

cards.q: What are the expected positions of pacemaker leads on CXR?
cards.a:
Single-chamber (ventricular): one lead in the RV apex.
Dual-chamber: one lead in the RA appendage (curved anteriorly) and one in the RV apex.
Biventricular (CRT): additional lead in the coronary sinus (posterolateral LV wall via the CS).

cards.q: Where should the tip of a chest drain (intercostal drain) be positioned on CXR?
cards.a:
For pneumothorax: apex of the thorax (anterosuperior).
For pleural effusion/haemothorax: posterior basal region.
The drain should be within the pleural space and the side-holes (radiopaque line interruption) should all be inside the thorax.

cards.q: What are CXR signs of a malpositioned ETT?
cards.a:
Too low (right main bronchus intubation): tip beyond the carina → left lung collapse/atelectasis, right-sided hyperinflation.
Too high: tip in the pharynx → inadequate ventilation.
Oesophageal: gastric distension, bilateral poor aeration.

cards.q: Where should the tip of a PICC (peripherally inserted central catheter) lie on CXR?
cards.a: Same as a CVC: at the cavoatrial junction (SVC-RA junction), near the level of the carina. It is inserted via an antecubital vein and courses through the axillary and subclavian veins into the SVC.

cards.q: What is the CXR appearance of lobar pneumonia?
cards.a: Homogeneous consolidation confined to a single lobe with air bronchograms, no volume loss (or slight expansion). Silhouette sign helps identify the involved lobe. Most commonly caused by Streptococcus pneumoniae.

cards.q: What is the CXR appearance of bronchopneumonia?
cards.a: Patchy, multifocal opacities often bilateral and in the lower lobes. The pattern is non-segmental, centered on airways. Common organisms: Staphylococcus aureus, Gram-negatives, H. influenzae.

cards.q: How does primary TB appear on CXR?
cards.a: Typically in children or immunocompromised: middle/lower zone consolidation (Ghon focus) + ipsilateral hilar lymphadenopathy = Ghon complex. May see pleural effusion. Cavitation is uncommon in primary TB.

cards.q: How does reactivation (post-primary) TB appear on CXR?
cards.a: Predilection for upper lobes (apical and posterior segments). CXR shows patchy consolidation, cavitation, fibrosis, and volume loss. Tree-in-bud pattern on CT. May see calcified granulomas from prior infection.

cards.q: What is miliary TB and how does it appear on CXR?
cards.a: Haematogenous dissemination of TB producing innumerable tiny (1–3 mm) nodules uniformly distributed throughout both lungs — a 'snowstorm' pattern. Seen in immunocompromised patients.

cards.q: What is a lung abscess and how does it appear on CXR?
cards.a: A thick-walled cavity with an air-fluid level inside, usually in a dependent segment. The wall is irregular. Most common in the right lung (posterior segment of upper lobe or superior segment of lower lobe) due to aspiration.

cards.q: What are the CXR findings in ARDS (Acute Respiratory Distress Syndrome)?
cards.a: Bilateral, diffuse, non-cardiogenic pulmonary oedema — widespread opacification ('white-out') in both lungs. Unlike cardiogenic oedema: no cardiomegaly, no cephalization, no Kerley B lines, no pleural effusions (initially). Onset within 24–48 hours of inciting event.

cards.q: What are the CXR findings in COPD (emphysema predominant)?
cards.a: Hyperinflated lungs (flattened diaphragms, >10 posterior ribs visible, increased AP diameter on lateral view), increased retrosternal airspace, reduced vascular markings (oligaemia), bullae, and a narrow/vertical cardiac silhouette (tubular heart).

cards.q: What are the CXR features of pulmonary oedema?
cards.a: Cephalization (upper lobe pulmonary venous distension) → interstitial oedema (Kerley B lines, peribronchial cuffing, septal thickening) → alveolar oedema (bilateral perihilar 'bat-wing' opacities, air bronchograms) → pleural effusions (bilateral, right > left).

cards.q: What is the CXR appearance of a pneumoconiosis such as asbestosis?
cards.a: Asbestosis: bilateral lower zone reticular/reticulonodular opacities, pleural plaques (often calcified, bilateral), pleural thickening, and in advanced cases honeycombing at bases. Distinct from silicosis which affects upper zones.

cards.q: How does silicosis appear on CXR?
cards.a: Bilateral upper-zone nodules (1–10 mm), often with eggshell calcification of hilar lymph nodes. Progressive massive fibrosis (PMF) appears as large upper-lobe opacities. Background of small rounded opacities.

cards.q: What is the CXR appearance of mesothelioma?
cards.a: Unilateral pleural thickening (often lobulated or nodular), encasing the lung. Volume loss on the affected side with ipsilateral mediastinal shift (unlike effusion which pushes away). May have pleural effusion and rib destruction. History of asbestos exposure.

cards.q: How do you differentiate a solitary pulmonary nodule from a mass?
cards.a: A nodule is ≤3 cm; a mass is >3 cm. Masses are more likely malignant. Evaluation of a nodule includes: size, margins (spiculated = suspicious), calcification pattern, growth rate, and PET/CT.

cards.q: What calcification patterns in a pulmonary nodule suggest benignity?
cards.a: Central (target), diffuse/solid, laminated (concentric rings), and 'popcorn' calcification (hamartoma) are typically benign. Eccentric or stippled calcification is suspicious for malignancy.

cards.q: What is the 'Hampton hump' and what does it indicate?
cards.a: A wedge-shaped, pleura-based opacity in the lower zones representing pulmonary infarction secondary to pulmonary embolism. The apex points toward the hilum.

cards.q: What is the 'Westermark sign'?
cards.a: An area of focal oligaemia (decreased vascularity/lucency) in a lung zone distal to a pulmonary embolism due to reduced blood flow. It is a specific but insensitive CXR sign of PE.

cards.q: What is the 'sail sign' on a pediatric CXR?
cards.a: A triangular opacity projecting from the mediastinum resembling a spinnaker sail, representing a normal thymus in infants and young children. The thymus is prominent until age 2 and should not be mistaken for pathology.

cards.q: How does the thymus appear on a normal pediatric CXR and when does it involute?
cards.a: The thymus appears as a soft tissue density in the anterior superior mediastinum that can obscure the cardiac silhouette and mediastinum. It may show the wave sign (undulation along the rib margins). It involutes gradually, usually by puberty.

cards.q: What is the CXR appearance of neonatal respiratory distress syndrome (RDS)?
cards.a: Diffuse, bilateral ground-glass granular opacification ('reticulogranular' pattern) with air bronchograms and low lung volumes. Caused by surfactant deficiency in premature infants.

cards.q: What is a congenital diaphragmatic hernia (CDH) and how does it appear on CXR?
cards.a: Herniation of abdominal contents through the diaphragm (most commonly left posterolateral — Bochdalek hernia). CXR shows bowel loops in the thorax, contralateral mediastinal shift, absent/low ipsilateral hemidiaphragm, and scaphoid abdomen.

cards.q: What is the CXR appearance of transient tachypnoea of the newborn (TTN)?
cards.a: Prominent interstitial markings, fluid in the fissures, mild pleural effusions, and perihilar streakiness in a term or near-term infant. Lungs are usually well-inflated. Resolves within 24–72 hours. Caused by delayed resorption of fetal lung fluid.

cards.q: What is the '3-6-9 rule' for assessing bowel dilatation on abdominal X-ray?
cards.a: Maximal normal diameters: Small bowel ≤3 cm, Large bowel ≤6 cm, Caecum ≤9 cm. Measurements exceeding these suggest obstruction or ileus.

cards.q: How do you differentiate small bowel from large bowel on abdominal X-ray?
cards.a:
Small bowel: central location, valvulae conniventes (thin folds crossing the full width — 'stacked coins'), narrower diameter.
Large bowel: peripheral/frame-like distribution, haustra (thick folds that do NOT cross the full width), wider diameter, may contain faecal matter.

cards.q: What is the CXR/AXR finding of free intraperitoneal air (pneumoperitoneum)?
cards.a: On erect CXR: free air under the diaphragm (best seen under the right hemidiaphragm). On supine AXR: Rigler's sign (double-wall sign) — both sides of the bowel wall are visible. Also football sign, falciform ligament sign.

cards.q: What is Rigler's sign (double-wall sign)?
cards.a: On a supine abdominal X-ray, both the inner and outer walls of the bowel are visible because free intraperitoneal air outlines the serosal surface. It indicates pneumoperitoneum (often from bowel perforation).

cards.q: What are common causes of calcification seen on abdominal X-ray?
cards.a: Renal/ureteric calculi, gallstones (10% are radio-opaque), pancreatic calcification (chronic pancreatitis), aortic calcification (atherosclerosis), phleboliths (pelvic veins), appendicolith, calcified lymph nodes (TB), and calcified fibroids.

cards.q: What are the features of small bowel obstruction (SBO) on abdominal X-ray?
cards.a: Dilated small bowel loops (>3 cm) with valvulae conniventes, multiple air-fluid levels on erect film (≥3 levels), paucity of gas in the colon/rectum. Cause often adhesions, hernias, or tumour.

cards.q: What are the features of large bowel obstruction (LBO) on abdominal X-ray?
cards.a: Dilated large bowel (>6 cm) proximal to the obstruction with haustra. If the ileocaecal valve is competent, small bowel is not dilated. If incompetent, both small and large bowel dilate. Caecum >9 cm = risk of perforation. Common causes: colorectal carcinoma, volvulus, diverticular stricture.

cards.q: What are the main CT window settings used for chest imaging?
cards.a:
Lung window: W 1500, L -500 (optimises air-tissue contrast, best for parenchyma).
Mediastinal (soft tissue) window: W 350, L 40 (best for mediastinal structures, lymph nodes, vessels).
Bone window: W 1500–2000, L 300–500 (best for skeletal structures).

cards.q: How is pulmonary embolism (PE) diagnosed on CT pulmonary angiography (CTPA)?
cards.a: A filling defect (dark area) within a contrast-enhanced pulmonary artery. The clot appears as a low-attenuation area within the bright (white) contrast-opacified vessel. Can be central (saddle embolus at bifurcation) or peripheral.

cards.q: What is a saddle pulmonary embolus?
cards.a: A large thrombus that straddles the bifurcation of the main pulmonary artery (extending into both the right and left pulmonary arteries). It is a life-threatening emergency causing acute right heart failure.

cards.q: How is aortic dissection classified (Stanford) and how does it appear on CT?
cards.a:
Stanford A: involves the ascending aorta (surgical emergency).
Stanford B: involves only the descending aorta (medical management).
CT shows an intimal flap separating the true and false lumens, with differential contrast enhancement.

cards.q: What is the role of high-resolution CT (HRCT) of the chest?
cards.a: HRCT uses thin slices (1–2 mm) without IV contrast to evaluate interstitial lung disease in detail. It identifies patterns like ground-glass opacity, honeycombing, reticular thickening, traction bronchiectasis, and helps with distribution mapping (upper vs lower, central vs peripheral).

cards.q: What is the 'spine sign' on a lateral CXR?
cards.a: Normally, vertebral bodies appear progressively darker (more lucent) from upper to lower thoracic spine on the lateral view. If a lower vertebral body appears whiter/denser than one above it, it suggests lower lobe pathology (consolidation or effusion) — this is a positive spine sign.

cards.q: What is the 'Golden S sign' and what does it indicate?
cards.a: A reverse-S-shaped opacity at the right hilum caused by right upper lobe collapse secondary to a central obstructing mass (usually lung carcinoma). The superior convexity is the mass; the inferior concavity is the collapsed lobe.

cards.q: What CXR pattern is associated with Pancoast tumour?
cards.a: An apical lung mass (superior sulcus tumour) that may show rib destruction (1st and 2nd ribs) and soft tissue opacity at the lung apex. Clinically associated with Horner syndrome, brachial plexus involvement, and shoulder pain.

cards.q: What is the 'Fleischner Society' guideline used for?
cards.a: Guidelines for the management of incidentally detected pulmonary nodules on CT. Recommendations depend on nodule size, morphology (solid vs sub-solid), number, and patient risk factors. They guide follow-up CT intervals or the need for PET/biopsy.

cards.q: What is the 'luftsichel sign' on CXR?
cards.a: A crescent of hyperlucency along the left mediastinal border/aortic arch caused by hyperinflation of the superior segment of the left lower lobe, seen in left upper lobe collapse. The collapsed LUL drapes anteriorly against the chest wall.

cards.q: What is 'cephalization' of pulmonary vessels on CXR?
cards.a: Redistribution of blood flow to the upper lobe pulmonary veins, which appear enlarged and more prominent than the lower lobe vessels (normally the reverse). It is an early sign of raised pulmonary venous pressure, as seen in CHF.

cards.q: What is peribronchial cuffing on CXR?
cards.a: Thickening of bronchial walls seen as ring-like opacities when viewed end-on (donut sign) or as tram-tracking when seen longitudinally. Indicates peribronchial oedema or inflammation, commonly seen in CHF, asthma, and bronchitis.

cards.q: What is the difference between transudate and exudate on CXR appearance?
cards.a: CXR cannot reliably distinguish them. Both appear as pleural effusions. Diagnosis requires thoracentesis and Light's criteria. However, bilateral effusions are more commonly transudative (CHF), while unilateral effusions raise concern for exudative causes (infection, malignancy).

cards.q: What are CXR features that suggest malignancy in a lung mass?
cards.a: Spiculated or irregular margins, size >3 cm, eccentric/stippled calcification, cavitation with thick irregular walls, associated lymphadenopathy, rib destruction, pleural effusion, and growth on serial imaging.

cards.q: What is the 'incomplete border sign' (extrapleural sign)?
cards.a: A mass arising from the chest wall or pleura makes obtuse angles with the lung surface and has an incomplete visible border (part is hidden by the chest wall). This distinguishes extrapleural/chest wall masses from intrapulmonary masses which make acute angles.

cards.q: What is the 'continuous diaphragm sign'?
cards.a: Normally, the central portion of the diaphragm is obscured by the heart. If air in the mediastinum (pneumomediastinum) outlines the superior diaphragmatic surface, the diaphragm becomes visible across its entire width — the continuous diaphragm sign.

cards.q: What CXR finding is associated with Pneumocystis jirovecii pneumonia (PJP)?
cards.a: Bilateral, diffuse, perihilar ground-glass opacities with relative sparing of the apices and periphery (in early disease). May progress to consolidation. Pneumatoceles and pneumothorax can occur. Seen in severely immunocompromised patients (CD4 <200).

cards.q: What is the 'figure-of-8' or 'snowman sign' on CXR?
cards.a: Seen in total anomalous pulmonary venous return (TAPVR) — supracardiac type. The dilated vertical vein, innominate vein, and SVC form the upper circle ('snowman's head'), and the enlarged heart forms the lower circle.

cards.q: What is the preferred artery for ABG sampling and why?
cards.a: The radial artery at the wrist is preferred because it is superficial, easily palpable, and has dual collateral circulation (ulnar artery) via the palmar arches, minimizing ischemic risk.

cards.q: What is the Allen's test and when is it performed?
cards.a: Allen's test assesses ulnar collateral circulation before radial artery puncture. Compress both radial and ulnar arteries → patient clenches/opens fist → release ulnar artery → palm should re-pink within 5-10 seconds. A negative (abnormal) test means poor collateral flow.

cards.q: What angle should the needle be held at for radial artery puncture?
cards.a: 30-45 degrees to the skin, bevel up, directed against the flow of blood (toward the heart). The wrist should be dorsiflexed ~30° over a rolled towel.

cards.q: Name the six core components reported on an ABG.
cards.a: pH (acid-base status), PaCO₂ (respiratory component), PaO₂ (oxygenation), HCO₃⁻ (metabolic component), SaO₂ (oxygen saturation), and Base Excess (BE).

cards.q: Which ABG values are directly measured and which are calculated?
cards.a: Directly measured: pH, PaCO₂, PaO₂. Calculated: HCO₃⁻ (from Henderson-Hasselbalch), Base Excess, SaO₂ (often co-oximetry measured).

cards.q: What is the normal range for arterial blood pH?
cards.a: 7.35 – 7.45. Below 7.35 = acidemia; above 7.45 = alkalemia.

cards.q: What is the normal range for PaCO₂?
cards.a: 35 – 45 mmHg. PaCO₂ reflects the respiratory component of acid-base balance; it is regulated by alveolar ventilation.

cards.q: What is the normal range for PaO₂?
cards.a: 80 – 100 mmHg (on room air at sea level). Values < 60 mmHg indicate hypoxemia and correspond to SaO₂ ~90% on the oxyhemoglobin dissociation curve.

cards.q: What is the normal range for HCO₃⁻?
cards.a: 22 – 26 mEq/L. HCO₃⁻ represents the metabolic (renal) component of acid-base balance.

cards.q: What is the normal range for Base Excess (BE)?
cards.a: −2 to +2 mEq/L. A negative BE indicates a base deficit (metabolic acidosis); a positive BE indicates base excess (metabolic alkalosis).

cards.q: What is SaO₂ and its normal value?
cards.a: SaO₂ = arterial oxygen saturation, the percentage of hemoglobin binding sites occupied by O₂. Normal: 95 – 100%.

cards.q: Write the alveolar gas equation for PAO₂.
cards.a:
$PAO_2 = FiO_2 \\times (P_{atm} - P_{H_2O}) - \\frac{PaCO_2}{R}$
On room air at sea level: $PAO_2 = 0.21 \\times (760 - 47) - \\frac{PaCO_2}{0.8}$
≈ 150 − 1.25 × PaCO₂

cards.q: What is the A-a gradient and how is it calculated?
cards.a: A-a gradient = PAO₂ − PaO₂. It measures the difference between alveolar and arterial oxygen. Normal ≈ 5–15 mmHg in young adults. Age-adjusted: (Age/4) + 4.

cards.q: What does an elevated A-a gradient indicate?
cards.a: An elevated A-a gradient indicates impaired gas exchange due to: V/Q mismatch (most common), shunt (intracardiac or intrapulmonary), or diffusion impairment (e.g., pulmonary fibrosis).

cards.q: In which causes of hypoxemia is the A-a gradient NORMAL?
cards.a: Hypoventilation (e.g., opiate overdose, obesity hypoventilation) and low FiO₂ (high altitude). Both reduce PAO₂ but gas exchange itself is intact.

cards.q: What is the P/F ratio and how is it used?
cards.a: P/F ratio = PaO₂ / FiO₂. Normal > 400. < 300 = ALI/mild ARDS; < 200 = moderate-to-severe ARDS; < 100 = severe ARDS (Berlin criteria).

cards.q: Write the oxygen content equation (CaO₂).
cards.a:
$CaO_2 = (1.34 \\times Hb \\times SaO_2) + (0.003 \\times PaO_2)$
The first term is O₂ bound to hemoglobin (major contributor); the second is dissolved O₂ (minor).

cards.q: What is the normal CaO₂ value?
cards.a: Approximately 16 – 22 mL O₂/dL (assuming Hb 15 g/dL, SaO₂ 100%). CaO₂ = (1.34 × 15 × 1.0) + (0.003 × 100) ≈ 20.4 mL/dL.

cards.q: Describe the oxyhemoglobin dissociation curve.
cards.a: A sigmoid-shaped curve plotting SaO₂ (y-axis) vs. PaO₂ (x-axis). The steep portion (PaO₂ 20–60) allows efficient O₂ loading/unloading; the flat upper portion (PaO₂ > 70) ensures high saturation despite PaO₂ changes.

cards.q: What factors cause a RIGHT shift of the oxyhemoglobin dissociation curve?
cards.a: Right shift = ↓ Hb-O₂ affinity → easier O₂ unloading to tissues. Causes: ↑ Temperature, ↑ PaCO₂, ↑ 2,3-DPG, ↓ pH (acidosis). Mnemonic: 'CADET, face Right' — CO₂, Acid, DPG, Exercise, Temperature.

cards.q: What factors cause a LEFT shift of the oxyhemoglobin dissociation curve?
cards.a: Left shift = ↑ Hb-O₂ affinity → O₂ binds tightly, less unloading. Causes: ↓ Temperature, ↓ PaCO₂, ↓ 2,3-DPG, ↑ pH (alkalosis), CO poisoning, fetal hemoglobin (HbF), methemoglobin.

cards.q: What is the P50 and its normal value?
cards.a: P50 = PaO₂ at which Hb is 50% saturated. Normal ≈ 26.6 mmHg. ↑ P50 = right shift; ↓ P50 = left shift.

cards.q: Write the Henderson-Hasselbalch equation.
cards.a:
$pH = 6.1 + \\log \\frac{[HCO_3^-]}{0.03 \\times PaCO_2}$
This relates pH to the ratio of metabolic (HCO₃⁻) and respiratory (PaCO₂) components. Normal ratio ≈ 20:1.

cards.q: Name the four major buffer systems in the body.
cards.a:
1. Bicarbonate-carbonic acid (major ECF buffer)
2. Phosphate buffer (important in renal tubules and ICF)
3. Protein buffers (hemoglobin, albumin)
4. Bone (calcium carbonate, chronic buffering)

cards.q: How does the respiratory system compensate for metabolic acid-base disorders?
cards.a:
Metabolic acidosis → ↓ pH stimulates central/peripheral chemoreceptors → hyperventilation → ↓ PaCO₂ (blows off CO₂).
Metabolic alkalosis → ↑ pH → hypoventilation → ↑ PaCO₂ (retains CO₂). Respiratory compensation begins within minutes.

cards.q: How do the kidneys compensate for respiratory acid-base disorders?
cards.a:
Respiratory acidosis → kidneys ↑ HCO₃⁻ reabsorption & ↑ H⁺ secretion → ↑ serum HCO₃⁻.
Respiratory alkalosis → kidneys ↓ HCO₃⁻ reabsorption → ↓ serum HCO₃⁻. Renal compensation takes 3-5 days to be fully effective.

cards.q: What defines a primary metabolic acidosis on ABG?
cards.a: ↓ pH (< 7.35) with ↓ HCO₃⁻ (< 22 mEq/L) as the primary disturbance. PaCO₂ will be low (compensatory hyperventilation).

cards.q: What defines a primary metabolic alkalosis on ABG?
cards.a: ↑ pH (> 7.45) with ↑ HCO₃⁻ (> 26 mEq/L) as the primary disturbance. PaCO₂ will be elevated (compensatory hypoventilation).

cards.q: What defines a primary respiratory acidosis on ABG?
cards.a: ↓ pH (< 7.35) with ↑ PaCO₂ (> 45 mmHg) as the primary disturbance. HCO₃⁻ will be elevated (renal compensation).

cards.q: What defines a primary respiratory alkalosis on ABG?
cards.a: ↑ pH (> 7.45) with ↓ PaCO₂ (< 35 mmHg) as the primary disturbance. HCO₃⁻ will be low (renal compensation).

cards.q: State Winter's formula and its use.
cards.a:
$Expected\;PaCO_2 = 1.5 \\times [HCO_3^-] + 8 \\pm 2$
Used in metabolic acidosis to assess if respiratory compensation is appropriate. If actual PaCO₂ differs, a mixed disorder exists.

cards.q: If actual PaCO₂ is HIGHER than predicted by Winter's formula, what does this indicate?
cards.a: A concurrent respiratory acidosis (inadequate hyperventilation). The patient has a mixed metabolic acidosis + respiratory acidosis.

cards.q: If actual PaCO₂ is LOWER than predicted by Winter's formula, what does this indicate?
cards.a: A concurrent respiratory alkalosis (excessive hyperventilation). The patient has a mixed metabolic acidosis + respiratory alkalosis.

cards.q: What is the expected PaCO₂ in metabolic alkalosis?
cards.a:
$Expected\;PaCO_2 = 0.7 \\times [HCO_3^-] + 21 \\pm 2$
Alternatively: PaCO₂ ≈ 40 + 0.7 × (HCO₃⁻ − 24). Respiratory compensation rarely raises PaCO₂ above 55 mmHg.

cards.q: What is the expected HCO₃⁻ change in ACUTE respiratory acidosis?
cards.a: HCO₃⁻ rises 1 mEq/L for every 10 mmHg rise in PaCO₂. This is from tissue buffering (not renal compensation).

cards.q: What is the expected HCO₃⁻ change in CHRONIC respiratory acidosis?
cards.a: HCO₃⁻ rises 3.5 mEq/L for every 10 mmHg rise in PaCO₂. Renal compensation takes 3-5 days to become maximal.

cards.q: What is the expected HCO₃⁻ change in ACUTE respiratory alkalosis?
cards.a: HCO₃⁻ falls 2 mEq/L for every 10 mmHg fall in PaCO₂.

cards.q: What is the expected HCO₃⁻ change in CHRONIC respiratory alkalosis?
cards.a: HCO₃⁻ falls 5 mEq/L for every 10 mmHg fall in PaCO₂.

cards.q: Can compensation ever fully normalize the pH?
cards.a: No — physiologic compensation is never complete (pH moves toward normal but does not reach 7.40). Exception: chronic respiratory alkalosis, where pH may normalize.

cards.q: How do you calculate the serum anion gap (AG)?
cards.a:
$AG = Na^+ - (Cl^- + HCO_3^-)$
Normal AG = 12 ± 4 mEq/L (or 8-12 without K⁺). The AG represents unmeasured anions (albumin, phosphate, sulfate, organic anions).

cards.q: Why must the AG be corrected for albumin?
cards.a: Albumin is the major unmeasured anion. For every 1 g/dL ↓ albumin below 4, the AG drops ~2.5 mEq/L. Corrected AG = AG + 2.5 × (4.0 − measured albumin). Hypoalbuminemia can mask a high AG acidosis.

cards.q: List the causes of high anion gap metabolic acidosis using the GOLDMARK mnemonic.
cards.a:
G – Glycols (ethylene glycol, propylene glycol)
O – Oxoproline (acetaminophen metabolite, 5-oxoproline)
L – L-Lactic acidosis
D – D-Lactic acidosis
M – Methanol
A – Aspirin (salicylates)
R – Renal failure (uremia)
K – Ketoacidosis (DKA, alcoholic, starvation)

cards.q: List causes of high AG metabolic acidosis using the MUDPILES mnemonic.
cards.a:
M – Methanol
U – Uremia
D – DKA
P – Propylene glycol / Paraldehyde
I – Isoniazid / Iron
L – Lactic acidosis
E – Ethylene glycol
S – Salicylates

cards.q: What are the causes of normal AG (hyperchloremic) metabolic acidosis?
cards.a:
GI HCO₃⁻ loss: diarrhea, ileostomy, fistulas
Renal: RTA types 1, 2, 4; early renal failure; carbonic anhydrase inhibitors (acetazolamide)
Other: normal saline infusion (dilutional), ureteral diversion, TPN

cards.q: How do you use urine anion gap to distinguish causes of normal AG metabolic acidosis?
cards.a:
Urine AG = Urine Na⁺ + K⁺ − Cl⁻.
Negative UAG (↑ NH₄⁺ excretion) → GI loss (diarrhea) — kidneys are appropriately compensating.
Positive UAG → Renal cause (RTA) — kidneys are failing to excrete NH₄⁺.

cards.q: What is the delta-delta (Δ-Δ) ratio and how is it interpreted?
cards.a:
$\\Delta\\text{-}\\Delta = \\frac{\\Delta AG}{\\Delta HCO_3^-} = \\frac{AG - 12}{24 - HCO_3^-}$
< 1: concurrent non-AG metabolic acidosis
1-2: pure AG metabolic acidosis
> 2: concurrent metabolic alkalosis (HCO₃⁻ is higher than expected)

cards.q: A delta-delta ratio < 1 suggests what additional disorder?
cards.a: A concurrent normal anion gap (hyperchloremic) metabolic acidosis. The HCO₃⁻ has fallen more than expected from the AG elevation alone.

cards.q: A delta-delta ratio > 2 suggests what additional disorder?
cards.a: A concurrent metabolic alkalosis. The HCO₃⁻ has not fallen as much as expected (another process is raising it, e.g., vomiting or volume contraction).

cards.q: What are the two categories of metabolic alkalosis based on treatment?
cards.a:
Saline-responsive (urine Cl⁻ < 20 mEq/L): due to volume contraction — responds to NS infusion.
Saline-resistant (urine Cl⁻ > 20 mEq/L): due to mineralocorticoid excess — does not respond to NS.

cards.q: List causes of saline-responsive metabolic alkalosis.
cards.a: Vomiting / NG suction (loss of HCl), diuretics (loop, thiazide — after the effect), post-hypercapnia, villous adenoma, congenital chloride diarrhea.

cards.q: List causes of saline-resistant metabolic alkalosis.
cards.a: Primary hyperaldosteronism (Conn syndrome), Cushing syndrome, renovascular disease, Liddle syndrome, Bartter/Gitelman syndrome, exogenous mineralocorticoids, severe K⁺ depletion.

cards.q: Why is urine chloride used rather than urine sodium to classify metabolic alkalosis?
cards.a: In vomiting-induced alkalosis, filtered HCO₃⁻ exceeds reabsorptive capacity → HCO₃⁻ is excreted with Na⁺ as an obligate cation (bicarbonaturia). This makes urine Na⁺ misleadingly high. Urine Cl⁻ remains low, accurately reflecting volume depletion.

cards.q: What are the causes of acute respiratory acidosis?
cards.a: Airway obstruction (foreign body, asthma, laryngospasm), CNS depression (opioids, sedatives, stroke), neuromuscular (Guillain-Barré, myasthenia crisis), chest wall (flail chest, pneumothorax), acute pulmonary edema.

cards.q: What are the causes of chronic respiratory acidosis?
cards.a: COPD (most common), obesity hypoventilation syndrome (OHS/Pickwickian), kyphoscoliosis, chronic neuromuscular disease (ALS, muscular dystrophy), interstitial lung disease (late).

cards.q: How do you differentiate acute from chronic respiratory acidosis on ABG?
cards.a:
Look at the degree of HCO₃⁻ compensation:
Acute: HCO₃⁻ ↑ 1 per 10 PaCO₂ ↑ (minimal change, pH significantly low).
Chronic: HCO₃⁻ ↑ 3.5 per 10 PaCO₂ ↑ (significant compensation, near-normal pH).

cards.q: List common causes of respiratory alkalosis.
cards.a: Anxiety/pain/hyperventilation syndrome, hypoxemia (any cause), PE, pneumonia, early salicylate toxicity, pregnancy (progesterone), high altitude, sepsis (early), hepatic failure, CNS disease (stroke, meningitis).

cards.q: Why does pregnancy cause respiratory alkalosis?
cards.a: Progesterone directly stimulates the medullary respiratory center → chronic hyperventilation → ↓ PaCO₂ (typically 28-32 mmHg). This is a normal physiologic change; HCO₃⁻ drops to ~18-21 by renal compensation.

cards.q: Why does salicylate toxicity cause both respiratory alkalosis AND metabolic acidosis?
cards.a: Salicylates directly stimulate the medullary respiratory center → respiratory alkalosis (early). They also uncouple oxidative phosphorylation and inhibit Krebs cycle → lactic acidosis + ketoacidosis → high AG metabolic acidosis (late).

cards.q: What are the steps to systematically interpret an ABG?
cards.a:
1. Assess oxygenation (PaO₂, A-a gradient)
2. Determine acidemia or alkalemia (pH)
3. Identify the primary disorder (PaCO₂ vs HCO₃⁻)
4. Assess compensation (apply appropriate formula)
5. Calculate anion gap (if metabolic acidosis)
6. Calculate delta-delta (if elevated AG)
7. Integrate with clinical context

cards.q: How do you identify a mixed acid-base disorder?
cards.a: Clues: pH is normal with abnormal PaCO₂/HCO₃⁻, compensation does not match expected values, AG is elevated but HCO₃⁻ is normal, or delta-delta ratio is abnormal (< 1 or > 2).

cards.q: Give an example of a triple acid-base disorder.
cards.a:
Alcoholic patient with vomiting and sepsis:
1. High AG metabolic acidosis (lactic acidosis + ketoacidosis)
2. Metabolic alkalosis (vomiting → HCl loss)
3. Respiratory alkalosis (sepsis → hyperventilation)
Detected via AG elevation + delta-delta > 2 + PaCO₂ lower than Winter's prediction.

cards.q: What is the osmolar gap and how is it calculated?
cards.a:
$Osmolar\;gap = Measured\;osmolality - Calculated\;osmolality$
$Calc\;osm = 2[Na^+] + \\frac{glucose}{18} + \\frac{BUN}{2.8}$
Normal osmolar gap: < 10 mOsm/kg.

cards.q: What does an elevated osmolar gap with a high AG metabolic acidosis suggest?
cards.a: Ingestion of toxic alcohols: methanol (formic acid), ethylene glycol (oxalic acid / glycolic acid), or isopropyl alcohol (though isopropyl causes elevated OG without AG acidosis — metabolized to acetone, not acid).

cards.q: How does methanol poisoning present on labs?
cards.a: High AG metabolic acidosis + elevated osmolar gap (early, before metabolism) + visual disturbances (optic nerve damage from formate). Treatment: fomepizole (or ethanol) + hemodialysis.

cards.q: How does ethylene glycol poisoning present on labs?
cards.a: High AG metabolic acidosis + elevated osmolar gap + calcium oxalate crystals in urine + acute kidney injury. Treatment: fomepizole + hemodialysis.

cards.q: Why does the osmolar gap decrease as the anion gap increases in toxic alcohol ingestion?
cards.a: The parent alcohol (osmotically active but non-ionized) is metabolized into organic acid anions. As the alcohol is consumed, osmolar gap falls; as acid anions accumulate, AG rises. Early: ↑ OG, normal AG. Late: normal OG, ↑ AG.

cards.q: What are the differences between VBG and ABG values?
cards.a:
Venous pH ≈ 0.03-0.05 lower than arterial.
Venous PaCO₂ ≈ 3-8 mmHg higher.
Venous HCO₃⁻ ≈ 1-2 mEq/L higher.
PvO₂ is NOT useful for assessing oxygenation (typically 35-45 mmHg).

cards.q: When is a VBG an acceptable substitute for an ABG?
cards.a: VBG can reliably assess acid-base status (pH, HCO₃⁻, lactate) and trend PaCO₂. It is NOT adequate for oxygenation assessment (PaO₂). Use ABG when precise PaO₂/A-a gradient is needed or in severe shock.

cards.q: Describe the ABG findings in diabetic ketoacidosis (DKA).
cards.a: High AG metabolic acidosis (ketoacids: β-hydroxybutyrate, acetoacetate). pH low, HCO₃⁻ low, AG elevated. Respiratory compensation: Kussmaul breathing → ↓ PaCO₂. Check delta-delta for concurrent metabolic alkalosis (e.g., from vomiting).

cards.q: What is Kussmaul breathing?
cards.a: Deep, labored, rapid breathing seen in severe metabolic acidosis (classically DKA). It represents maximal respiratory compensation attempting to lower PaCO₂ and raise pH.

cards.q: What ABG pattern is seen in acute COPD exacerbation?
cards.a: Acute-on-chronic respiratory acidosis: ↑ PaCO₂ (above chronic baseline), ↓ pH, ↑ HCO₃⁻ (already elevated from chronic compensation). PaO₂ is low. The pH drop is more than expected for pure chronic respiratory acidosis.

cards.q: Why is excessive O₂ supplementation dangerous in COPD?
cards.a: COPD patients with chronic CO₂ retention rely partly on hypoxic drive for ventilation. Excessive O₂ can also worsen V/Q mismatch (Haldane effect, loss of hypoxic vasoconstriction) → further ↑ PaCO₂ → CO₂ narcosis and respiratory failure.

cards.q: What ABG pattern is seen in early sepsis?
cards.a: Respiratory alkalosis (↓ PaCO₂, ↑ pH) — due to hyperventilation from fever, cytokine-mediated stimulation of respiratory center, and early lactic acidosis-driven tachypnea.

cards.q: What ABG pattern is seen in late/severe sepsis?
cards.a: High AG metabolic acidosis (lactic acidosis from tissue hypoperfusion) ± respiratory acidosis (respiratory muscle fatigue). pH is markedly low; this is an ominous sign.

cards.q: What are the types of Renal Tubular Acidosis (RTA)?
cards.a:
Type 1 (Distal): Cannot secrete H⁺ → urine pH > 5.5, hypokalemia
Type 2 (Proximal): Cannot reabsorb HCO₃⁻ → urine pH variable, hypokalemia
Type 4 (Hypoaldosteronism): ↓ Aldosterone → hyperkalemia, urine pH < 5.5
All cause normal AG metabolic acidosis.

cards.q: How do you differentiate Type 1 from Type 2 RTA?
cards.a:
Type 1: Urine pH always > 5.5, severe acidosis (HCO₃⁻ can be very low), nephrocalcinosis/stones common.
Type 2: Urine pH > 5.5 only when HCO₃⁻ above threshold (then < 5.5 once HCO₃⁻ stabilizes below threshold), milder acidosis, associated with Fanconi syndrome.

cards.q: What is the serum K⁺ pattern in each type of RTA?
cards.a:
Type 1 (Distal): Hypokalemia (↑ K⁺ secretion distally)
Type 2 (Proximal): Hypokalemia (HCO₃⁻ wasting causes Na⁺ delivery distally → K⁺ loss)
Type 4: Hyperkalemia (↓ aldosterone → ↓ K⁺ and H⁺ secretion)

cards.q: What are the two types of lactic acidosis?
cards.a:
Type A: Tissue hypoxia/hypoperfusion (shock, cardiac arrest, severe hypoxemia, mesenteric ischemia, CO poisoning).
Type B: No tissue hypoxia — caused by metabolic derangements (metformin, liver failure, malignancy, thiamine deficiency, mitochondrial disease).

cards.q: What is D-lactic acidosis?
cards.a: Caused by bacterial fermentation of carbohydrates in the colon, typically in patients with short bowel syndrome or after jejunoileal bypass. Presents with high AG metabolic acidosis, encephalopathy. Standard lactate assays do not detect D-lactate (they measure L-lactate).

cards.q: Describe the ABG in salicylate poisoning.
cards.a:
Mixed disorder:
1. Respiratory alkalosis (direct CNS stimulation → hyperventilation)
2. High AG metabolic acidosis (uncoupled oxidative phosphorylation, ketoacids, lactic acid)
Often the pH is alkalemic early and becomes acidemic late — a sign of clinical deterioration.

cards.q: What is the expected PaO₂ for a given age?
cards.a: Approximate formula: $Expected\;PaO_2 ≈ 104 - (0.4 \\times age)$ mmHg. Example: 60-year-old → expected PaO₂ ≈ 104 − 24 = 80 mmHg.

cards.q: Define hypoxemia vs. hypoxia.
cards.a:
Hypoxemia = low PaO₂ in arterial blood (< 80 mmHg).
Hypoxia = inadequate O₂ delivery to tissues. Hypoxia can occur with normal PaO₂ (e.g., anemia, CO poisoning, cyanide).

cards.q: List the five mechanisms of hypoxemia.
cards.a:
1. Low FiO₂ (high altitude)
2. Hypoventilation (↑ PaCO₂)
3. V/Q mismatch (most common; COPD, asthma, PE)
4. Right-to-left shunt (does NOT correct with 100% O₂)
