cards.a: Pre-hepatic (↑ unconjugated): hemolysis, ineffective erythropoiesis, Gilbert's, Crigler-Najjar. Hepatic (↑ both): hepatitis, cirrhosis, drug-induced, Wilson's, hemochromatosis. Post-hepatic (↑ conjugated): choledocholithiasis, pancreatic head cancer, cholangiocarcinoma, PSC, stricture.

cards.q: How does the pattern of liver function tests help localize jaundice?
cards.a: Hepatocellular: markedly ↑ AST/ALT with mild ↑ ALP/GGT. Cholestatic: markedly ↑ ALP/GGT with mild ↑ AST/ALT. Pre-hepatic: ↑ indirect bilirubin, normal LFTs. Direct vs. indirect bilirubin ratio is key.

cards.q: Describe the anemia workup algorithm using MCV.
cards.a: Microcytic (MCV <80): iron deficiency, thalassemia, anemia of chronic disease, sideroblastic, lead poisoning. Normocytic (MCV 80–100): acute blood loss, ACD, hemolysis, bone marrow failure, renal disease. Macrocytic (MCV >100): B12/folate deficiency (megaloblastic), liver disease, hypothyroidism, myelodysplasia, alcohol, drugs (methotrexate).

cards.q: How do you differentiate iron deficiency anemia from thalassemia trait?
cards.a: IDA: ↓ ferritin, ↓ iron, ↑ TIBC, ↑ RDW, low MCV. Thalassemia trait: normal/↑ ferritin, normal iron studies, normal RDW, very low MCV disproportionate to anemia, ↑ RBC count, target cells. Mentzer index (MCV/RBC): <13 = thalassemia, >13 = IDA.

cards.q: How do you differentiate prerenal, intrinsic, and postrenal AKI?
cards.a: Prerenal: BUN/Cr >20, FENa <1%, UOsm >500, concentrated urine, responds to fluids. Intrinsic (ATN): BUN/Cr ~15, FENa >2%, muddy brown casts, UOsm <350. Postrenal: bilateral hydronephrosis on US, urinary obstruction, BUN/Cr variable.

cards.q: What is the formula for fractional excretion of sodium (FENa)?
cards.a: $\\text{FENa} = \\frac{U_{Na} \\times P_{Cr}}{P_{Na} \\times U_{Cr}} \\times 100$. <1% = prerenal. >2% = intrinsic renal (ATN). Note: FENa is unreliable with diuretic use — use FEUrea instead (<35% = prerenal).

cards.q: What is the PICO framework in EBM?
cards.a: P = Patient/Population, I = Intervention, C = Comparison, O = Outcome. Used to formulate a focused, answerable clinical question for evidence-based practice.

cards.q: What is the difference between absolute risk and relative risk?
cards.a: Absolute risk: the actual probability of an event (e.g., 2%). Relative risk: ratio of risk in exposed vs. unexposed ($\\text{RR} = \\frac{\\text{Risk}_{exposed}}{\\text{Risk}_{unexposed}}$). RR >1 = increased risk, RR <1 = protective, RR = 1 = no association.

cards.q: What is critical appraisal of a study?
cards.a: Systematic evaluation of study validity (internal: study design, bias, confounding), results (magnitude, precision, statistical significance), and applicability (generalizability to your patient). Core skill of evidence-based medicine.

cards.q: What are the Wilson-Jungner criteria for screening?
cards.a: 10 criteria including: disease is an important health problem, accepted treatment exists, facilities available, recognizable latent stage, suitable test available, test acceptable to population, natural history understood, agreed policy on whom to treat, cost-effective, screening is a continuing process.

cards.q: What are the USPSTF recommendation grades?
cards.a: A: High certainty of substantial net benefit — recommend. B: High certainty of moderate or moderate certainty of substantial benefit — recommend. C: Moderate certainty of small net benefit — selectively offer. D: Moderate/high certainty of no benefit or harms outweigh — discourage. I: Insufficient evidence.

cards.q: What is overdiagnosis in screening?
cards.a: Detection of a disease that would never have caused symptoms or death during the patient's lifetime. Leads to unnecessary treatment, anxiety, and costs. Common with prostate (PSA), thyroid, and breast cancer screening.

cards.q: What is an ROC curve?
cards.a: Receiver Operating Characteristic curve: plots sensitivity (true positive rate) vs. 1−specificity (false positive rate) at various test cutoff values. Area under the curve (AUC) measures overall discriminative ability; AUC = 1.0 is perfect, 0.5 is no better than chance.

cards.q: How does changing the cutoff value of a diagnostic test affect sensitivity and specificity?
cards.a: Lowering the cutoff (calling more results positive) increases sensitivity but decreases specificity. Raising the cutoff increases specificity but decreases sensitivity. There is always a trade-off.

cards.q: What is a gold standard in diagnostic testing?
cards.a: The reference test or method considered to have the highest accuracy for definitively diagnosing a condition. All new tests are compared against it. Example: biopsy for cancer, angiography for CAD, culture for infections.

cards.q: What mnemonic helps recall causes of microcytic anemia?
cards.a: TICS: Thalassemia, Iron deficiency, Chronic disease (anemia of), Sideroblastic anemia. Also: TAIL — Thalassemia, Anemia of chronic disease, Iron deficiency, Lead poisoning.

cards.q: What mnemonic helps recall causes of pancreatitis?
cards.a: I GET SMASHED: Idiopathic, Gallstones, Ethanol, Trauma, Steroids, Mumps/malignancy, Autoimmune, Scorpion sting, Hypertriglyceridemia/Hypercalcemia/Hypothermia, ERCP, Drugs (valproate, azathioprine, didanosine).

cards.q: What mnemonic helps recall secondary causes of hypertension?
cards.a: RENAL: Renal artery stenosis, Endocrine (Conn's, Cushing's, pheochromocytoma, thyroid), Narrowing of aorta (coarctation), Aldosteronism (primary), Lifestyle/drugs (NSAIDs, OCPs, cocaine, licorice).

cards.q: What is the Sgarbossa criteria used for?
cards.a: Diagnoses acute MI in the presence of LBBB or ventricular paced rhythm. Concordant ST elevation ≥1 mm (5 pts), concordant ST depression ≥1 mm in V1–V3 (3 pts), discordant ST elevation ≥5 mm (2 pts). ≥3 points = likely MI.

cards.q: What is Chvostek's sign and what does it indicate?
cards.a: Tapping over the facial nerve (anterior to ear) causes ipsilateral facial muscle twitching. Indicates hypocalcemia (↑ neuromuscular excitability). Present in ~10% of normals.

cards.q: What is the difference between Type I and Type II statistical errors?
cards.a: Type I (α error): rejecting a true null hypothesis (false positive — concluding an effect exists when it doesn't). Type II (β error): failing to reject a false null hypothesis (false negative — missing a real effect). Power = 1 − β.

cards.q: What is statistical power?
cards.a: The probability of correctly rejecting a false null hypothesis (detecting a true effect). Power = 1 − β. Conventionally set at 0.80. Increased by: larger sample size, larger effect size, higher α level.

cards.q: What is a confidence interval (CI)?
cards.a: A range of values within which the true population parameter is expected to lie with a specified probability (usually 95%). If the 95% CI for a difference includes 0, or for a ratio includes 1, the result is not statistically significant.

cards.q: What is a p-value?
cards.a: The probability of obtaining results at least as extreme as observed, assuming the null hypothesis is true. p < 0.05 = statistically significant by convention. A small p-value does NOT tell you the magnitude or clinical significance of the effect.

cards.q: What is the difference between intention-to-treat (ITT) and per-protocol analysis?
cards.a: ITT: analyzes all subjects in their originally assigned groups, regardless of compliance or crossover. Preserves randomization, reduces bias, preferred for RCTs. Per-protocol: analyzes only those who completed the protocol. May overestimate treatment effect.

cards.q: What is the Fagan nomogram used for?
cards.a: A graphical tool for applying Bayes' theorem. A line drawn from pre-test probability through the likelihood ratio intersects the post-test probability axis, allowing quick estimation without calculation.

cards.q: What is the CHADS₂ score?
cards.a: Older stroke risk tool for AF. CHF (1), HTN (1), Age ≥75 (1), Diabetes (1), Stroke/TIA (2). Max 6. ≥2 → anticoagulation recommended. Largely replaced by CHA₂DS₂-VASc for finer risk stratification.

cards.q: What are the Light's criteria pitfalls?
cards.a: Light's criteria misclassify ~25% of transudates as exudates, especially in patients on diuretics (concentrates protein/LDH). If clinically suspected transudate meets exudative criteria, check serum-effusion albumin gradient: >1.2 g/dL suggests transudate.

cards.q: What are the components of the Revised Cardiac Risk Index (RCRI/Lee Index)?
cards.a: Predicts perioperative cardiac risk. 6 factors (1 pt each): high-risk surgery (intraperitoneal, intrathoracic, suprainguinal vascular), CAD, CHF, cerebrovascular disease, DM on insulin, creatinine >2. 0 pts = ~3.9% risk; ≥3 = ~11%+ risk.

cards.q: What is the Centor score treatment algorithm?
cards.a: Score 0–1: no testing, no antibiotics. Score 2–3: rapid antigen detection test (RADT); treat if positive. Score 4+: empiric antibiotics or RADT then treat. Goal: reduce unnecessary antibiotic use for viral pharyngitis.

cards.q: What defines a thunderclap headache and what must be ruled out?
cards.a: Severe headache reaching maximum intensity within seconds to 1 minute. Must rule out subarachnoid hemorrhage (CT head → LP if CT negative). Other causes: cerebral venous thrombosis, RCVS, pituitary apoplexy, carotid/vertebral dissection.

cards.q: What is the approach to an elevated reticulocyte count in anemia?
cards.a: ↑ Reticulocyte count indicates adequate marrow response → consider blood loss or hemolysis. Evaluate hemolysis workup: ↑ LDH, ↑ indirect bilirubin, ↓ haptoglobin, peripheral smear (spherocytes, schistocytes), Coombs test (autoimmune vs. non-immune).

cards.q: Name the classic triad of hemolytic uremic syndrome (HUS).
cards.a: Microangiopathic hemolytic anemia (schistocytes), thrombocytopenia, acute renal failure. Typically in children after E. coli O157:H7 (Shiga toxin-producing) bloody diarrhea.

cards.q: What distinguishes prerenal azotemia from ATN on urinalysis?
cards.a: Prerenal: bland sediment, hyaline casts, concentrated urine, high specific gravity. ATN: muddy brown granular casts, renal tubular epithelial cells, dilute urine, low specific gravity.

cards.q: What is a Likelihood Ratio (LR) of 1 and what does it mean?
cards.a: LR = 1 means the test result is equally likely in diseased and non-diseased individuals. The test provides no diagnostic information and does not change post-test probability.

cards.q: How are pre-test and post-test probabilities related via the Fagan nomogram?
cards.a: Draw a straight line from pre-test probability (left axis) through the likelihood ratio (center axis). Where it intersects the right axis = post-test probability. LR+ shifts probability up; LR− shifts it down.

cards.q: What is verification (work-up) bias?
cards.a: Occurs when the decision to perform the gold standard test is influenced by the result of the index test. Patients with positive index tests are more likely to undergo the gold standard, inflating sensitivity.

cards.q: What is the difference between inter-rater and intra-rater reliability?
cards.a: Inter-rater: agreement between different observers measuring the same thing. Intra-rater: consistency of the same observer on repeated measurements. Both measured by Cohen's kappa (κ).

cards.q: Interpret Cohen's kappa values.
cards.a: κ <0 = worse than chance; 0.0–0.20 = slight; 0.21–0.40 = fair; 0.41–0.60 = moderate; 0.61–0.80 = substantial; 0.81–1.00 = almost perfect agreement.

cards.q: What is the difference between a screening test and a diagnostic test?
cards.a: Screening: applied to asymptomatic populations; must be highly sensitive (minimize false negatives). Diagnostic: applied to symptomatic patients; must be highly specific (minimize false positives). Positive screening tests require confirmatory diagnostic tests.

cards.q: What is number needed to screen (NNS)?
cards.a: The number of people who need to be screened to prevent one death or adverse outcome. Analogous to NNT. Higher NNS = less efficient screening program.

cards.q: What is the 'threshold approach' to clinical decision-making?
cards.a: Two thresholds divide probability space: test threshold (below = no test needed, disease unlikely) and treatment threshold (above = treat without testing, disease very likely). Between them = further testing is warranted.

cards.q: What is the difference between internal and external validity?
cards.a: Internal validity: the degree to which results are free from bias within the study. External validity (generalizability): the degree to which results can be applied to other populations or settings.

cards.q: What clinical features help differentiate transudative from exudative effusions before thoracentesis?
cards.a: Transudate: bilateral, no fever, associated with CHF/cirrhosis/nephrotic. Exudate: unilateral, pleuritic pain, fever, associated with infection/malignancy. However, thoracentesis with Light's criteria is needed for definitive classification.

cards.q: What is the mnemonic for causes of an elevated anion gap metabolic acidosis?
cards.a: MUDPILES: Methanol, Uremia, Diabetic ketoacidosis, Propylene glycol/Paraldehyde, Iron/Isoniazid, Lactic acidosis, Ethylene glycol, Salicylates.

cards.q: What is the mnemonic for causes of a normal anion gap (hyperchloremic) metabolic acidosis?
cards.a: HARDUP: Hyperalimentation, Acetazolamide/Addison's, Renal tubular acidosis, Diarrhea, Uretero-enterostomy, Pancreatic fistula/drainage. Also: USED CARP.

cards.q: What is the anion gap formula and normal value?
cards.a: $\\text{AG} = Na^+ - (Cl^- + HCO_3^-)$. Normal ≈ 12 ± 4 mEq/L. Must correct for albumin: for every 1 g/dL ↓ albumin below 4, AG ↓ by ~2.5. An uncorrected AG may mask a true anion gap acidosis.

cards.q: How do you apply the delta-delta (Δ/Δ) ratio?
cards.a: $\\Delta\\text{AG}/\\Delta\\text{HCO}_3 = \\frac{\\text{AG} - 12}{24 - \\text{HCO}_3}$. Ratio <1: concurrent non-AG metabolic acidosis. Ratio 1–2: pure AG metabolic acidosis. Ratio >2: concurrent metabolic alkalosis.

cards.q: What is publication bias?
cards.a: Studies with positive or significant results are more likely to be published than those with negative results. Detected by asymmetry in a funnel plot. Can distort meta-analysis conclusions.

cards.q: What is a forest plot?
cards.a: A graphical display of results from a meta-analysis. Each study shown as a point estimate (square, size proportional to weight) with CI (horizontal line). The diamond at bottom represents the pooled estimate. If the CI crosses the line of no effect (1 for OR/RR, 0 for mean difference), the result is not significant.

cards.q: What is heterogeneity in meta-analysis and how is it measured?
cards.a: Variation in study results beyond chance. Measured by I² statistic: 0% = no heterogeneity; 25% = low; 50% = moderate; 75% = high. Also by Cochran's Q test. High heterogeneity may warrant subgroup analysis or random-effects model.

cards.q: What is the difference between a fixed-effects and random-effects model in meta-analysis?
cards.a: Fixed-effects: assumes all studies estimate the same true effect; differences are due to sampling error. Random-effects: assumes true effect varies between studies; accounts for both within- and between-study variability. Random-effects gives wider CIs.

cards.q: What is the CAGE questionnaire?
cards.a: Screens for alcohol use disorder. C = felt need to Cut down? A = Annoyed by criticism of drinking? G = felt Guilty about drinking? E = needed an Eye-opener? ≥2 positive = clinically significant.

cards.q: What is the PHQ-9?
cards.a: Patient Health Questionnaire-9: screens and monitors depression severity. 9 items from DSM criteria scored 0–3 each (max 27). 5–9 mild, 10–14 moderate, 15–19 moderately severe, 20–27 severe depression.

cards.q: What is Occam's razor vs. Hickam's dictum in clinical reasoning?
cards.a: Occam's razor: prefer the single simplest diagnosis that explains all findings (parsimony). Hickam's dictum: a patient can have as many diseases as they please — multiple diagnoses may coexist, especially in elderly or complex patients.

cards.q: What is the Sutton's law in diagnosis?
cards.a: Go where the money is — pursue the most likely diagnosis first based on probability. Named after bank robber Willie Sutton. Emphasizes efficiency in the diagnostic workup.

cards.q: What is the Aunt Minnie phenomenon?
cards.a: A diagnosis made by instantaneous pattern recognition from a characteristic visual appearance, requiring no further analysis. Common in radiology and dermatology. E.g., butterfly rash → lupus.

cards.q: What are the Sepsis-3 screening tools in sequence?
cards.a: 1. qSOFA (bedside, outside ICU): ≥2 → suspect sepsis. 2. SOFA score (full assessment): ≥2-point increase → sepsis confirmed. 3. If vasopressors needed for MAP ≥65 AND lactate >2 despite fluids → septic shock.

cards.q: What is the sensitivity and specificity trade-off called?
cards.a: The threshold effect. Every continuous-value test has a cutoff point; changing it moves along the ROC curve. Choosing a lower cutoff favors sensitivity (ruling out); a higher cutoff favors specificity (ruling in).

cards.q: What is the SPIN and SNOUT mnemonic?
cards.a: SpPIn: a highly Specific test, when Positive, rules In disease. SnNOut: a highly Snsensitive test, when Negative, rules Out disease. These are most useful when sensitivity or specificity is very high (>95%).

cards.q: How is the test-treatment threshold model used?
cards.a: If disease probability is below the test threshold, no testing is needed (too unlikely). If above the treatment threshold, treat empirically (too likely to waste time testing). Between thresholds, testing provides maximum decision value.

cards.q: What is the difference between efficacy and effectiveness?
cards.a: Efficacy: does the intervention work under ideal/controlled conditions (RCT)? Effectiveness: does it work in real-world/clinical practice? Effectiveness is usually lower due to adherence, heterogeneity, and uncontrolled variables.
